Madrid, Spain, Aug. 2?—Indalecio Prieto, the strong man behind the Madrid Spanish government, today complained bitterly that France and Great Britain by withholding aid were making Spain the "Ethiopia of Europe." At the same time he asserted that should the government emerge victorious in the civil war, large sections of the country "would have to be collectivized" although adding Spain was "not ready or developed enough economically for pure communism." At the present time, he said, the Madrid government would not seek a loan from foreign governments as "the country which borrows abroad gives its lender an opportunity to dominate it politically." Prieto is head of the dominant socialist party in parliament. Speaking quietly, but with an obvious overtone of bitterness, the unofficial "man behind the scenes" in Madrid assailed the political elites of

LONDON, Aug. 27. ()—Great Britain and France today sent a joint appeal to all European powers which have not placed embargoes on arms shipments to Spain to do so immediately. France was planning to form a committee of all interested powers to coordinate the embargo measures and deal with any further neutrality proposals. Portugal, Germany, Russia and Italy have already joined in the move.

NEW YORK, Aug. 28 ——The proposed round-trip flight of Richard Merrill, veteran transport pilot, and Harry Richman, night club entertainer, to London was postponed today until Sunday. Weather conditions prevented the take off, they announced.

NEW YORK, Aug. 28.—(#)—Dick Merrill and Harry Richman made a final check of their monoplane “Lady Peace” today and planned to take off from Floyd Bennett field this afternoon on an attempted round-trip flight to London. The fliers said they expected to lunch in London Saturday, begin their return flight shortly afterward, and arrive in New York for late breakfast Sunday. Merrill, a veteran air line pilot, pronounced the 1,000 horsepower (Vultee) plane fit and ready for the hop after a test flight 710 miles up the New England coast and return yesterday. “Everything is swell,” said Richman, night club entertainer and amateur pilot who will handle radio contacts on the trip. Arrangements for the flight which Richman is financing at an estimated cost of $50,000 were completed several weeks ago. Merrill is taking a sort of “Busman’s Holiday”—he is on vacation from his airline post, but he is

Rome.—(U.P)—Italy has applied an embargo against shipment of arms to Spain, it was announced officially Friday. A communique announcing the embargo, eagerly sought by France and Great Britain as likely to lessen tension, said: "The following measures have been taken among the necessary government administrations: exportation is forbidden, both direct and indirect and in transit with Spain, Spanish possessions or the Spanish zone in Morocco as the destination, of all arms, munitions and other war materials as well as aircraft, assembled or in parts, also naval craft. The prohibition is applied to all contracts in course of execution."

1936-04-20.text: The gravity of the European crisis over Ethiopia was emphasized at Geneva today when Britain informed the League she might consider separate action against Italy and also is ready to consider new economic and financial sanctions. Italy demanded possession of Ethiopia as the price of an armistice, and Ethiopia appealed for new penalties against Italy. The Italian forces in Ethiopia were threatening Addis Ababa from both north and south and the population was evacuating the capital in panic. Berlin, meanwhile, made an impressive display of military strength in a parade in honor of Adolf Hitler’s birthday.

By The Associated Press The diplomatic feud between Great Britain and Italy broke out on the floor of the League of Nations Council today shortly after Italy had made known that its price for peace in Ethiopia was virtually the whole of the East African nation. Anthony Eden, Great Britain’s foreign secretary, attacked Italy’s alleged use of poison gas saying it cannot be passed over in silence. Baron Pompeo Aloisi of Italy answered: “I would remind the representative of Great Britain that the Italians who have been victims of atrocities also have mothers and children.” The French delegate pleaded for the continuance of conciliation efforts “until they are crowned with success.” The Russian delegate said the League was weakened by “the lack of certitude that all members will act together against any aggressor.” Ethiopia’s representative reiterated his country’s stand that peace negotiatio

Inverness, Scotland, April 20—The Loch Ness monster has officially opened the summer tourist season. Three Glasgow University students reported seeing the monster, which after years of residence is almost a community pet, “snorting and swimming through the water at tremendous speed.” It was about 35 feet long, they said, “with a snakelike head and an undulating body with three humps.”

Geneva, April 20—The council of the League of Nations after receiving a warning from Britain that she might have to take independent action against Italy if the League fails to end the Ethiopian war, decided tonight to address a supreme appeal to Italy. The appeal would urge Rome to make peace, hinting that Italy’s support is necessary to Europe in view of the danger to peace from Germany.

(Copyright, 1936, by International News Service) London, April 20 (INS)—Abys-sinia is conquered! The Italians have their hands on Haile Selassie’s throat, and whether he surrenders or chooses death by charging an Italian machine gun, his military cause is lost. This is the inevitable conclusion from today's reports that the Abyssinians are not defending the escarpment lying midway between Dessye and Addis Ababa. Just three months ago I took the same route from Dessye to Addis Ababa along which Marshal Pietro Badoglio’s motorized column is rushing now with the avowed object of capturing Addis Ababa by tomorrow to celebrate the anniversary of the founding of Rome. Even during the dry season the difficulty of surmounting the gigantic precipice called Tamba Burr was formidable. It rises a mile and a half high, and is the finest natural fortification in all Abyssinia. A narrow road, barely wi

WINDSOR, England, April 19 (—King Edward told 1000 Boy Scouts today that Great Britain “will always take a leading part in the affairs of the world.” Speaking to the scouts at Windsor Castle, the king emphasized the international character of the scout movement, adding, “In these days that is a thing of very great importance.”

ADDIS ABABA, Apr. 20 (UP)-- The government rushed stores of gun cotton out along the road to Dessye today, planning to blow up bridges over cascades and to block mountain roads in the path of the Italian advance. Natives, dazed and panic stricken, began to evacuate the city, believing the arrival of Italian troops was imminent. The road from Dessye was crowded with motor trucks from the front and tattered fugitives from the Ethiopian army. Foreigners Seek Shelter Foreigners of many nationalities besieged the bomb proof British legation for shelter. Americans prepared to take refuge there if necessary by order of American Minister Cornelius Van H. Engert. Blata Tekala, mayor of the city, tried to rally to him a mob of 5,000 nondescript warriors, some armed only with swords or spears. Women sought to take their places with the men. "All able men must make a last stand for liberty," said a

Rome, April 20, (U.P)—Italian armies pressed forward in half a dozen columns in Ethiopia today to crush the last resistance of Emperor Haile Selassie’s warriors and end the war. Three columns moved from the north toward Addis Ababa and the vital Addis Ababa-Djibouti railway. As many more moved northward through southeastern Ethiopia toward the Harar-Jijiga area, last defended portion of the country, and the railway farther east, As they advanced an enthusiastic Italian populace prepared to make holiday tomorrow, on the occasion of Rome’s 2,689th birthday, and celebrate the victories in East Africa and—diplomatically—at the League of Nations capital at Geneva. Premier Benito Mussolini showed every sign of determination to make

1936-02-23.text: LONDON, May 23.—(4)—The resignation of Colonial Secretary J. H. Thomas in Britain’s budget leakage scandal—the third desertion from Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin’s original cabinet—raised a probability today of a major shake-up in the ministry. Political sources predicted a cabinet turnover which would carry back into office Sir Samuel Hoare, former foreign secretary who was the first of this ministry to withdraw under fire. In addition to fill Thomas’ place at the colonial office Baldwin faced a possibility of having to find a successor for Viscount Monsell, first lord of the admiralty, who was reported anxious to retire. Sir Samuel Hoare, original scapegoat of the Italo-Ethiopian crisis now being hailed as a ‘far-seeing prophet’ for his peace plan to give Italy only a part of Ethiopia, might return to the cabinet as secretary for the dominions, informed sources said. Malcolm McDonald,

' Washington, Feb. 22 (4P)--Senator Borah of Idaho charged tonight that a campaign of “insidious propaganda” had been conducted from abroad against America’s neutrality policy in the Italo-Ethiopian war. He intimated directly that Great Britain was involved. In his first formal speech since openly avowing himself a Republican presidential candidate, Borah confined himself almost entirely to international issues. His Washington’s birthday radio address, urging a tenacious “aloofness from the political affairs and controversies of the old world” as advised by the first president, was made the basis for meetings of “Borah for President” clubs in various parts of the country. Discusses Britain The Idahoan did not name Great Britain in his propaganda charge. Nevertheless, after launching his accusation that foreign influence had been directed against this country’s course in the Italo-Ethiopi

LONDON (UP)—Countess Von Haughwitz-Reventlow, the former Barbara Hutton, Woolworth heiress, gave birth to a boy today. The child, born at 7:30 a.m., weighed seven and one-half pounds. The countess, granddaughter of the late Frank W. Woolworth, founder of the five-and-ten cent stores, is reputed to have a fortune of $40,000,000. Her father and mother, Mr. and Mrs. Franklin L. Hutton, are here with her. It has been reported that elaborate precautions will be taken to guard the new million-dollar baby against kidnapping. The birth of the countess’ baby was accompanied by considerable anxiety on the part of her family and physicians. In the last month, she had been suffering from an anemic condition and was given blood transfusions to strengthen her for her confinement. She spent most of the time in bed or reclining in a chair. It was believed, however, that she came through the ordeal in go

Rome, Feb. 22. (P) - The report ran through diplomatic circles tonight that Great Britain seeks to block the rumored efforts to establish an alliance of Italy with Germany, Austria, Hungary and Poland. No diplomat was willing to assert this report as a fact, but several pointed to the departure for Vienna of Sir Eric Drummond, British ambassador to Rome, as giving substance to the suggestion of a British maneuver. Sir Eric let it be known he was going to Vienna for dental work. It was said he would stay in the Austrian capital a week. The same diplomats who saw more behind this trip said they remembered that when Sir Eric was secretary to the League of Nations he was instrumental in getting financial aid for Austria. His word would mean much with that country’s officials, they suggested. Another report which ran the gamut of speculation was that Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia was ask

(International News Service) LONDON, Feb. 24—Countess Barbara Von Haugwitz-Reventlow, wealthy American heiress, gave birth to her first child today, a 7-pound boy. Both mother and child were reported doing well. The child was born at 7:30 A. M., coming into the world as a heir to a large portion of the Woolworth Five and Ten Cent store fortune through his mother, the former Barbara Hutton, and heir to one of Denmark’s oldest and most noble names. His father is Count Court Von Haugwitz-Reventlow. Secrecy Prevails Secrecy unusual even for a royal (Continued On Page Two)

ROME, Feb. 22.—-(#)—Great Britain, diplomatic sources said today, is making an effort to prevent any formation of an Italo-German-Polish-Austrian bloc in the current intensive diplomatic negotiations. Sir Eric Drummond, British ambassador to Italy, will leave here tonight for Vienna, and diplomatic sources said his trip would involve this British move. Ostensibly, his trip was arranged to see his dentist, but diplomats pointed out that Sir Eric would spend a week in Vienna where he has great personal influence. This is because during his tenure as secretary to the League of Nations, the Geneva body extended considerable financial help to Austria. Diplomats expressed belief that with Drummond leaving Rome at this time, when his presence here is so much required, owing to Italo-British relations, his visit to Vienna must be of unusual importance. (Copyright, 1936, by United Press) Rome, Feb. 22. (UP) — Premier Benito Mussolini has decided to release some 500,000 soldiers from his army of more than 1,000,000, according to information received today from usually most reliable sources. The men would be sent home by degrees, on definite furloughs and subject to recall within 24 hours if necessary. Only men now in Italy would be affected. The report was denied officially. At the same time, it was again announced that the supreme army council would meet Monday. The meeting was called February 8. An official spokesman said that the usual furloughing of farmer soldiers continued as necessity arose and soon would be intensified for spring sowing. He refused to estimate the number of men who would be involved. It was said that the proposed reduction in army strength was due first to confidence that the European political situation was much

FRANKFORT - ON - THE - MAIN, Germany, May 23 (4)—Germany’s great Zeppelin Hindenburg, delivering 52 passengers safely on its second voyage from the United States, beat today its own record for a commercial crossing of the Atlantic Ocean. The giant airship landed at its base at 4:12 a.m. for a flying time of 48 hours, 10 minutes from Lakehurst, N.J. Its previous record set on the first flight from America was 49 hours 3 minutes. Capt. Ernst Lehmann stepped smilingly from the gondola and expressed satisfaction that the second round trip proved conclusively regular airship service could be established over the North Atlantic for passengers, freight and mails. The Hindenburg after leaving Lakehurst Wednesday night, cruising over New York and striking out swiftly across the Atlantic, sped over England and the Netherlands last night and arrived over the airdrome here at 3:10 a.m. while it was

1936-02-24.text: London, Feb. 24—Ethiopian sources today declared that their soldiers had cut through Italian lines between Ma-kale and Aduwa, killing hundreds of Italian troops in a sudden thrust to the northward. This report was not verified by Italian sources which, instead, said that the army under the command of Marshal Pietro Badoglio, was continuing its move towards its immediate objective of Amba Alaji. With the Italians known to be within 15 miles of that objective, Italian newspapers were ready to print extras concerning its capture, as soon as the Italian government announced it.

London — (PF) — The House of Commons cheered Anthony Eden, foreign secretary, today when he assured its members that Great Britain's attitude toward the Italo-Ethiopian war was based solely on its duties as a member of the League of Nations. The British policy, said the young statesman, “has been inspired by no selfish or ulterior motives but solely by the consideration of the duties incumbent upon the government as a member of the League of Nations and a wholehearted supporter of the doctrine of collective security.

LONDON, Feb. 24 (UP)—Capt. Anthony Eden, making his maiden speech to Parliament as foreign secretary, issued a new appeal to Italy and Ethiopia in the House of Commons today to make peace. He suggested that the League of Nations committee of five, charged with studying peace efforts, make another attempt to mediate the war. Eden’s speech was temperate. In reply to a Laborite demand that Britain take the lead in imposing oil sanctions against Italy, he indicated that Britain's course would be moderate and that she would act only in concert with all other League powers.

(Copyright, by United Press) LONDON, b. 24, — Countess von Haugwitz-Reventlow, the former Barbara Mutton, heiress to the Wookworth millions, gave birth today to a healthy 7½ pound boy. Her residence was guarded closely against intrusion, but the joyful face of her father, Franklyn I. Hutton, showed plainly that both mother and child were in excellent condition. Hutton emerged from the house beaming and dashed to his hotel where he cabled friends and relatives, saying the baby is “beautiful” and both it and Barbara are doing well. The countess, granddaughter of the late Frank W. Woolworth, founder of the five-and-dime stores, was reputed a few years ago to be worth $40,000,000. However, it was rumored she had spent about one-third of that on benefactions and gifts to friends. She settled a million dollars with the late Prince, her first husband, who was killed in action.

London, Feb. 24.—The tightening Italo-Ethiopian war situation came before the House of Commons today for a decisive debate, designed to disclose Great Britain's attitude toward extension of sanctions against Italy. The Commons proceedings called for Anthony Eden to make his first speech before the House as Foreign Secretary, under opposition criticism that the League of Nations' war penalties were being insufficiently applied. With opposition Liberals also watching for any signs of a weakening of the government’s policy, informed political sources said Eden would reaffirm Britain's stand in full support of the League's sanctions campaign. Members of Parliament also demanded information from Eden on the Maffey report, a secret document suddenly published in Rome last week to show that British interests in Ethiopia were restricted

ADDIS ABABA, Feb. 24 (#)--The Ethiopian government announced today that its troops had killed 412 Italians, destroyed 15 bomb depots, and captured 30 tanks in an engagement in the region of Aksum. The Ethiopian forces were commanded by Ras Imru, a cousin of Emperor Haile Selassie and governor of Gojjam province, where a rebellion recently was suppressed. The fight was Ras Imru’s first engagement with the Italians. A government communique said an unspecified number of trucks and artillery pieces also were captured from the Italians.

Rome—(INS)—Premier Benito Mussolini and Chancellor Adolf Hitler have reached a definite decision to follow a joint line of action if the Franco-Soviet mutual assistance pact is ratified by the French chamber of deputies, according to reports in authoritative circles tonight. The chamber now is debating the pact in Paris and is expected to ratify it.

Rome, Feb. 23.—Fascists waited impatiently tonight for the news of the capture of historic Amba Alaji in a renewed drive by the northern army in Ethiopia. Officials confidently insisted that the push could not halt short of this objective, the farthest point reached by the Italian expedition of 1898-96 which was virtually wiped out. Preparations were being pushed for strenuous new aerial attacks in Africa.

1936-09-29.text: By The Associated Press Five nations were joined today in the break-up bloc and the march toward currency adjustment led off by France under the protection of a “monetary equilibrium” agreement with the United States and Great Britain. While the socialist government of Premier Leon Blum won a majority in its first parliamentary test of the French devaluation program, Switzerland, the Netherlands, Latvia, and Greece were listed as embarking on new currency stabilization programs. Meanwhile from Moscow came denials of the Russian state bank that sales of British pounds were intended as an effort to force down the British currency rate. The sales were “ordinary banking transactions,” the bank declared. The series of financial developments sent the price of bar gold up 75 cents an ounce on the London exchange where operations were limited and business suspended in French and Swiss francs and

PARIS, (4P)--Adjustment of the French franc with the British pound and United States dollar was approved today by a weary chamber of deputies after a 25-hour session, The vote on the government-sponsored proposal was 350 to 22. The devaluation measure, which reduces the gold content of the franc by between one-quarter and one-third, was sent immediately to the senate, Ban Exports, Imports Exportation and importation of gold was prohibited in a decree published after the session in the official journal. The order became effective immediately, Cooperation of the United States and Great Britain in establishing a “monetary equilibrium” agreement was cited by Premier Leon Blum in a final appeal to the tired deputies, He asserted the devaluation bill was one item in the French soc

LONDON, Sept. 29 (4) — Great Britain today clamped down martial law on Palestine to end the terrorism which Arabs have waged in the Holy Land for months against Jewish immigration. Military rule actually will be put in force by a proclamation to be issued by the Palestine high commissioner. The step was announced officially in the London Gazette,

(Copyright 1936, by the Associated Press) Paris, Sept. 29—Approved by the chamber of deputies in a 25-hour session, Premier Leon Blum’s plan to devalue the franc and align it with the British pound and the American dollar hit its first senate snag late today. Radical socialist senators, in caucus, rejected the government’s devaluation text. Then the radical majority party in the upper house instructed the finance committee to draw up a new text minus the clause which gives the premier a free hand to fight price rises. The radical socialists explained they were not opposed to devaluation, but objected to the plan to give the government dictatorial powers to fight a rising cost of living, without a parliamentary check.

780 reach Chamber of Deputies approved today adjustment of the French franc with the British pound and the United States dollar as the world's financial capitals prepared for the end of another episode in turbulent post-war finance. A flexible, but controlled ratio between the dollar and the pound, rather than an iron-clad figure was believed in Washington to be the probable aim of the tri-power agreement. The Italian cabinet met in Rome with Premier Mussolini to draft an announcement on the lira which, well-informed sources believed, might divulge a two-fold purpose: To protect the lira’s internal value and to lower it for international markets. In New York, meanwhile, early Stock Exchange transactions followed an indecisive trend and, in London, the American dollar improved to $4.93 1-4 after opening at $4.94. The close for the pound sterling in New York Monday was $4.894 3-4. The Fren

Vienna, Sept. 29, (P)—Prince Alfonso Carlos of Bourbon, Carlist pretender to the — non-existent throne of Spain, died last night, the Reuters (British) News Agency reported today, of injuries received when he was struck by a motor car. The 85-year old Duke De San Jaime, head of the traditionalist branch of the Spanish royal family, was considered by thousands of Spaniards as rightful king of Spain. He succeeded to the leadership of his family and political adherents in 1931 on the death of his nephew Jaime, Duke De Madrid.

Compete for $50,000 Prizes in African Derby Event, PORTSMOUTH, Eng.—U.P.— Nine planes hopped off by moonlight early today in the first England to South Africa air derby. Some of Great Britain’s best known flyers were in the competition for $50,000 prizes offered by I. W. Schlesinger, a South African. They were expected to complete the 6,500 mile race in 36 hours.

New York, Sept. 28 (4)———The former Mrs. Ernest Aldrich Simpson all but tearfully described today as “absurd and horrible” reports that Simpson might begin divorce proceedings against his second wife, a frequent companion of King Edward of England. Sitting in her small uptown apartment, she added that her successor as Simpson's wife, Mrs. Wallis “Wally” Simpson, was one of her closest friends and added that any rift between the couple would bring her the greatest pain.

1936-04-29.text: Cairo, Egypt—(#)—King Fuad I of Egypt, 68-year-old friend of the British, died today after a long illness. Crown Prince Farouk, 16 years old and now attending school in England, will come to the throne under a regency. Until his 18th birthday the regency will be composed of three men, named by the King before he died. Premier Ali Pasha Maher, in making the official announcement of his sovereign’s passing, said death came at 1 p.m., local time, (6 a.m. Eastern Standard Time). The news came as a shock to the population of Cairo, following earlier reports that the monarch had rallied after a better night. Fuad, who celebrated his 68th birthday anniversary March 26, had been in indifferent health many months. He had never fully recovered from his serious illness of 1934 when numerous foreign specialists were summoned to the summer palace at Montazah. The troubled political situation in Cairo

_ Hopedale, Mass., April 29 ().— Eben S. Draper, former state senator, announced from his home today receipt of word from Mrs. Draper, his wife, reported missing since April 19, that she was ‘perfectly well in London, England. Mrs. Draper disappeared from a New York sanitarium on April 19. Since then she was sought aboard the Cunard-White Star liner Georgic, where it was feared she might have committed suicide by jumping overboard. Draper said a cablegram arrived from Mrs. Draper after the Georgic docked in London today.

Cairo, Egypt, April 29.—(p)— Egyptians mourned today the loss of King Fuad, whose death left a confusion of national and Mediterranean issues to descend upon the shoulders of a 16-year-old boy and his advisers. The young new king, Farouk, planned to leave London tomorrow for a rail and steamer return to Alexandria. Before his arrival elections will be held—on May 2—to choose a parliament before which a Regency of three statesmen must take oath of office. The chamber was dissolved recently. Premier Ali Pasha Maher held, unopened, an envelope in which the late king had written the names of three persons to serve as Regents in the event of his death. King Fuad, 68-year-old, died yesterday of a heart ailment complicated by a throat infection. He had reigned as Khedive from 1917 until 1922 when he was crowned King upon conclusion of the British protectorate in Egypt.

Boulogne, France, Apr. 29. (CP)—Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh left France for England today after townsfolk at a seaside resort near here refused the flier’s plea for privacy. They sailed for Folkestone later in the afternoon after only six days in France, most of the time driving their car in small villages where they were not recognized—but today they were. Townsfolk besieged them in their hotel demanding autographs. The couple boarded a regular passenger ship for England, unlike their crossing to France, when they sailed on a private yacht.

LONDON.-Europe received its worst scare since Hitler's Rhineland coup today when dispatches flashed to London told of a sudden troop concentration on either side of the Austrian-Hungary frontier. Reassuring statements from Austria and Berlin served only to create fears in London where the report persisted. Berlin and Vienna both confirmed troop maneuvers insisting they were routine.

BOSTON, April 29—(UP)—Mrs. Hazel Archibald Draper, who rushed from Katonah, N.Y., on April 18 and was feared dead, is alive and “perfectly well” in London, her husband was advised by cablegram today. New York City police announced late Monday that indications were that Mrs. Draper had leaped overboard from the Georgia. But her husband, Hopedale Draper, the manufacturer, son of a former Massachusetts governor, and one-time a U.S. senatorial candidate, refused to believe that his wife was dead.

LONDON, April 28 (®) — A parliamentary committee made financial provision today for a possible new queen of Great Britain and also for a possible son and heir of King Edward in a new royal “payroll,” necessitated by the death of King George. The civil list of annuities granted to the royal family totals £433,100 (about $2,165,500) under recommendations made to the House of Commons by a select committee. This is less by £36,900 annually than during George’s reign, but through economies King Edward personally suggested the actual annual saving to the exchequer will be £155,900 (about $779,500) so long as he remains unmarried. Under the committee's proposal £40,000 a year would be set aside to provide for the contingency of the king’s marriage. This sum, however, would not be drawn as long as Edward remains a bachelor. Other figures, which will be taken up by parliament May 4, included: for

Landon, April 28. (INS)— Acceding to the request of King Edward VIII that parliament take under consideration the possibility that he may marry, the select parliamentary committee fixed 40,000 pounds (about $200,000) as the price the nation is prepared to pay for a future Queen. At the same time the committee stipulated this money must not be drawn as long as King Edward remains unmarried. The committee further recommended an annuity of 70,000 pounds — sterling (about $350,000) be provided for the King’s consort in the event she should survive him. The marriage grant recommendations contained a mass of figures representing the committee’s report, in which it was suggested that King Edward receive in the civil list 410,000 pounds sterling ($2,030,000) annually as compared to the 470,000 pounds ($2,450,000) fixed for his father, the late King George V, at the beginning of the latter’s reig

1936-07-05.text: GENEVA, July 4.—(4)—The League of Nations, turning its back on the Italo-Ethiopian conflict, decided tonight developments in the Free City of Danzig were so potent that a special committee should watch them. The council asked Great Britain, France, and Portugal to follow the situation in Danzig where a Nazi movement to withdraw from league supervision was announced. This announcement was made by Dr. Arthur Karl Grieser, the Nazi president of the Danzig senate, who said he demanded a revision of the free city’s status on behalf of the whole German people.

London, July 4.--(/?)—King Edward VIII may don the crown of England next May with a second cousin kneeling at his side. Two young European princesses, both talented and beautiful and relatives of Edward, have been mentioned directly in the British press as favorites to wed the monarch. Insurance odds against the king's marriage before his coronation recently dropped to 5 to 1 from 10 to 1. Whether insurance companies pay will depend, perhaps, on King Edward's fancy concerning: Princess Frederic - Louise-Thyra-Victoria - Margerita - Sophia - Olga-Cecelia - Isabella-Christa, a granddaughter of former Kaiser Wilhelm, only daughter of the House of Brunswick and Lunebourg, and second cousin of the king himself: Princess Alexandrine Louise, the third daughter of Prince Harold, of Denmark, niece of King Christian, and great granddaughter of King Christian IX and Queen Louise of Denmark, who als

MELBOURNE, Australia, July 5—(Sunday)—(AP)—C. James Melrose, noted Australian flier, died today when his plane crashed. Details were not immediately available. Melrose was a prize winner in the London-Melbourne air derby in 1934, and a veteran flier. In November 1935 while flying over the Bay of Bengal he was the last person to sight another noted Australian aviator, Sir Charles Kingsford-Smith, who, with his co-pilot, Tom Pethybridge, disappeared in the vicinity of Malacca Strait while on a flight from England to Australia.

By United Press With oratory, fireworks and play, Americans today observed the 160th anniversary of the United States’ Declaration of Independence from England. President Roosevelt led the speech-making with an address at Monticello, the home of Thomas Jefferson, author of the Declaration of Independence, near Charlottesville, Va. He called upon the Nation to “re-light that sacred fire of freedom” which Jefferson and the other American revolutionists kindled. Gov. Alf M. Landon of Kansas, the Republican nominee for President, enjoyed a few last hours of rest in Estes Park, Colo., planned to attend a rodeo at Greeley, Colo., in the afternoon and then leave from Topeka. With the holiday coming on a Saturday and providing a long weekend, travel was the heaviest for any holiday in years. By auto, train, bus and airplane, city folks by the millions converged on ocean, lake, mountain and count

GENEVA, July 6 (P)— The League of Nations committee of 52—the assembly's sanctions general staff—voted to lift economic penalties against Italy today. It ended an unsuccessful economic siege of Premier Benito Mussolini's government and completed the league's abandonment of Ethiopia. Italy now is able to resume her exports of wines, fruit, olive oil, textiles and other products to league members, thus checking the heavy drain on Rome's gold reserves. She may also obtain loans and credits from league members to assist in the exploitation of Ethiopia and to help cover heavy war expenditures. The unsuccessful experiment appeared to make it certain that never again will the league apply economic sanctions unless the nations near the zone of conflict are willing to apply military penalties as well. In such event the league might be asked to vote economic measures to supplement whatever militar

(Copyright, 1956, United Press PARIS, July 6 (P)—France, recovering from a weekend of violence in which scores, including 30 policemen, were seriously injured, feared a nationwide farm strike today. Severe fighting between left and right groups on the Champs Elysees was quelled only after many were arrested and Minister of the Interior Roger Salengro issued a public warning that "agitation is spreading to the countryside." The center of current strike activity shifted to southern France where a printers' walkout deprived inhabitants of Biarritz and Bayonne of newspapers. All building trades workers walked out at Limoges.

FREE CITY OF DANZIG, July 4.—(#)— Unverified reports that German troops had started on a march to occupy Danzig sped through the free city tonight. The city was gripped with feverish excitement as the result of the speech by Dr. Arthur Karl Grieser, president of the Danzig senate, before the League of Nations council in which he declared Danzig wished to break away from league supervision.

Winnipeg, July 7—(P)—Rain fell today on the Saskatchewan plains, breaking a torrid spell. The downpour extended as far as Moose Jaw, 45 miles west of Regina, the Saskatchewan capital. It was the first precipitation in 10 days and farmers throughout the prairie provinces hoped it would break a heat wave that sucked moisture from the soil and robbed growing grains of nourishment. No other points except the Regina plains reported rainfall.

1936-06-20.text: Marion, Me., June 19. (#)—Twelve carefree children, celebrating the last day of school, drowned in Lake Gardner today when a sudden gust of wind capsized the outboard motorboat in which they were riding. Four of their companions and Calvin London, 70, were saved. All came from nearby Lubec. The drowned children, whose ages ranged from 9 to 16 years were: Daniel McCurdy, Evelyn and Aaron Mahar, Ramah Knowles, Frank Keynolds, Roland Eaton, Doris Small, Glen Morey, Christine Sleight, Merle Lewis, Jr., Jerome Kinney and Verne Dinsmore. The four saved were: James Mahar, brother of Evelyn and Aaron Mahar, Miriam Kelley, Leah Wilcox and Barbara Tyler. The Wilcox and Kelley girls kept themselves afloat by thrashing about furiously until rescuers arrived. The Tyler girl swam 100 yards to shore. The children were members of a picnic party from the West Lubec section. Beverley McCarthy, 12, whose m

London, June 20 (#)— British leaders battled tonight over the question of sanctions as Prime Minister Baldwin took the stump in Scotland to defend his government's action in advancing their removal from Italy. The government chief declared that military strength was needed for collective security and said: “Let advocates of collective security who are unwilling to provide a single volunteer for our forces or a single shell for aircraft think of that. “If war should come by collective security every nation will be in it up to the neck. “I believe the horrors of another modern war in Europe might lead to a revolt of the people against all leaders. You might find Europe in a state of completely barbarous anarchy from end to end, “Let us not underrate the risks of sanctions and collective security.” Pleading for support of the government's rearmament program, Baldwin said: “If risks have to

LONDON, June 19. (U.P)—The Exchange Telegraph reported from Hong Kong today that fighting between troops of the central Nanking government and those of the southern Kwangsi Province had started at three points on the frontiers of Hunan Province, The fighting was reported at Kiyang, Henchow and Liling,

Paris, June 19. (AP)—The new French Socialist government swung into line today in the parade headed by Great Britain to remove sanctions from conquering Italy. An official communique disclosed the cabinet had agreed to “accept” the lifting of sanctions. It said: “The government, faithful to the principle of collective action, will associate itself with any decision adopted by the League of Nations. “Informed of the present situation of the sanctions question, it felt consideration of facts led it to accept their lifting.”

A debate in the House of Commons was set for Tuesday, on a motion to protest the lifting of sanctions.

LONDON, JUNE 20. (AP).—America retained the international polo cup against England's challenge today, winning the second and deciding match, 8 to 6. The cup defenders won the first match, 10 to 9, played ten days ago. Today's victory was America’s tenth straight match triumph and fourth consecutive successful defense of the cup since 1921, when the United States lifted it from England.

PARIS (#) — France has formulated her own plan for reorganization of the League of Nations and will present it at Geneva June 26, sources close to the foreign office said today. The French plan will follow the general lines of the British proposal recently rejected by Premier Leon Blum’s government, informed sources declared. (The British suggestion envisaged regional security pacts for Western, Central and Eastern Europe. France objected to the suggestion because Germany was included in the western alliance but was excluded from the east.) The French, it was reported, would substitute a different line-up of nations than that in the British proposal, imposing the regional pacts on the present collective security structure. Under the plan, signatories to the regional alliances would be required to take immediate military action in the event of aggression within their own district while ot

League of Nations sanctions against Italy collapsed with Great Britain's foreign minister sounding their death knell to the jeers of his political opponents. The economic restrictions were imposed seven months ago by fifty-two league members because of Italy's war against Ethiopia. Mussolini was undaunted. His fascist legions pressed forward to Addis Ababa. Now, with the conquest of Ethiopia an accomplished fact, Britain led the league members in an about-face admission of defeat. France has agreed. Several smaller countries already have abandoned sanctions. All that remains is their formal cancellation at Geneva late this month. It fell to Anthony Eden, Britain’s foreign minister, to announce the failure of the policy for which he had fought so vigorously. “We have to admit the purpose for which sanctions were imposed has not been realized,” he admitted to the House of Commons. 1936-03-08.text: LONDON, March 9. ()—Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden warned Germany that any attack on France and Belgium in violation of the Locarno treaty would force Britain to come to the assistance of those nations. He told the House of Commons that he was thankful that there was no reason to “suppose that the present German action poses a threat of hostilities.”

LONDON, March 7. )—British Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden summoned the French and Italian ambassadors and the Belgian charge d'affaires to a conference today after Germany's action in violating the Locarno pact. The meeting was summoned suddenly after Adolf Hitler's bombshell, in announcing military occupation of the Rhineland in violation of the Locarno and Versailles treaties, startled the foreign office into a swift pace of conferences. London, March 7.—/P—Neutral diplomatic circles, after a careful study of Adolf Hitler's memorandum, believed the situation created by the German remilitarization of the Rhineland is far from desperate if France remains calm and does not demand forceful action. This is no time, diplomats agreed, for snap decisions. Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin and Foreign Sec. Anthony Eden discussed the situation at the prime minister's country residence after Eden had talked over Hitler's bold move with the French and Italian ambassadors and the Belgian charge d’affaires. Adopting to get an example by avoiding snap judgments which might turn the situation toward war, the cabinet put off its meeting until Monday in order to weigh carefully all factors and developments and to study Hitler's proposal. To Proceed Coolly: The government, authoritative sources said, will proceed “coolly, calmly and carefully

WASHINGTON, Mar. 7.—All Europe was seen here today as placed on the threshold of a new war by Hitler’s defiant action in sending the German army into the Rhineland. Whether Europe will plunge over the brink depends on whether Great Britain can restrain France.

Under the Locarno treaty, signed by Britain, France, Italy, Belgium and Germany, the signatories are bound to come to the defense of any member attacked by another signatory. As the spokesman made his announcement, the heads of the French army, navy and air force, chiefs-of-staff and cabinet members were in anxious conference on the military aspects caused by Hitler's dispatch of troops into the Rhineland. “The government called France’s political and military allies into conversation, discussing with the representatives of Britain, Italy, Belgium, Poland, Russia, Roumania, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia means of joint resist

GENEVA, (P)—France’s decision to appeal to the League of Nations against Germany's re-occupation of the demilitarized Rhineland, Saturday raised the question whether the French government will propose sanctions against the Reich just as Great Britain asked for sanctions against Italy for making war in Ethiopia. A year ago, France appealed to the league against Germany on the ground that by re-introducing compulsory military training and by creating an airforce, Germany repudiated the military clauses of the treaty of Versailles. Soon after, Germany was condemned by the league council for unilaterally violating her international engagements. As further pressure against Germany, the league created a special committee to study the possibility of imposing measures against nations which endanger international peace by denunciation of treaties. (AP)—Adolf Hitler, thundering to his brown shirt Nazi Reichstag that the Locarno pact was dead, sent triumphant German troops goose stepping into the demilitarized Rhineland today and pronounced the fight for Germany's freedom finished. In swift, world stunning thrusts, the Reichsfuehrer offered Europe a new western demilitarized frontier on a co-operative basis, declared he was ready to sign a new non-aggression treaty and air pact with his western neighbors and expressed willingness—if these things transpire—to return to the League of Nations, Then he dissolved his standing, shouting Reichstag and called a plebiscite for March 29 to prove to the world that the German people are behind him. In these general elections Hitler and his followers expect to get a majority even greater than his previous 90 per cent. Exhorting the Reichst

Berlin, March 7.—(U.P.)—Germany sent troops into the demilitarized Rhineland zone today and thereby tore to shreds the last repressive clauses of the hated Versailles treaty. The ban on militarization of the broad strip along the Rhine was denounced by Fuehrer Adolf Hitler as had been the treaty clauses limiting the German navy and army and denying Germany

1936-06-02.text: LONDON, JUNE 2. (AP). The budget tribunal announced today it found J. H. Thomas, resigned colonial secretary, had disclosed the secrets of the British budget previous to publication in the House of Commons. The tribunal report stated there was an unauthorized disclosure of the budget information by Thomas and that use was made of unis information by two men for the purpose of private gain. The two men named were Alfred Bates, advertising agency executive, and Sir Alfred Butt, a member of parliament and horse racing enthusiast. The tribunal headed by Justice Porter cleared all civil employees and printers and all cabinet ministers except Thomas of having disclosed any knowledge of the budget secrets. The tribunal cleared the former colonial secretary's son, Leslie M. Thomas, of all blame, expressing the unanimous opinion he neither knew nor suspected Bates had improper information on the

New York, June 1.—(AP)—Great Britain's new liner, the Queen Mary, completed her maiden trans-Atlantic voyage today, failing by a fraction of an hour to beat the record speed of the French liner Normandie on her first trip to New York. As the huge liner, surpassed in size only by the Normandie, steamed into the bay she was given an enthusiastic welcome by scores of gaily decorated tugs, excursion boats and private craft as well as by thousands of persons along the battery seawall. Averaging 29.133 knots on the crossing, her total time from Cherbourg breakwater to Ambrose lightship was four days, 12 hours and 24 minutes. This was 42 minutes over the Normandie’s record.

New York, June 1.---(4’)-—An attorney for Harry Bannister who charged his former wife, Ann Harding, screen actress, with abducting their 7-year-old daughter Jane, indicated tonight an abduction warrant sworn out by Bannister will be served on Miss Harding when she reaches England. While the actress, her daughter and a manager were speeding toward England, Bannister's attorney, Stanley J. Harte, communicated with English legal representatives. The blonde actress, who eluded her former husband's attempts to serve a legal writ detaining her in Canada, said she was going abroad to make a motion picture.

LONDON: (U.P)—A tiny group of men struggled upward Tuesday in arctic cold, through howling winds and driving snow in a race to reach the top of the world--Mt. Everest, the majestic peak that dominates the Himalayas on the Tibet-Indian frontier. It was a race against time and death, against the demons who, the natives believe, are waiting on the summit to destroy any man who dares to violate this last sanctuary of nature. It was a race in which every painful step was a struggle, in which frostbite, a plunge down a precipice, pneumonia, snow blindness menaced the party at every moment. Months Preparing Dispatches from India reported in fragmentary form the final assault for this year of the sixth British Everest expedition, led by the veteran Hugh Ruttledge—who because of his age, must step aside at the last moment to let two younger men try to climb the final slopes. For months the expedi

HOLLYWOOD. (UP) — An out-of-court settlement of the controversy which has raged over who shall have Freddie Bartholomew, 12-year-old English actor, and his $1,250 weekly check, appeared imminent today as his parents agreed to abide by results of an attorney's conference. Under terms of the proposed agreement, the youthful actor will live with his parents, Cecil Llewellyn and Lillian Mae Bartholomew, while his screen career will be managed by his aunt, Miss Myiligent Mary Bartholomew. The parents will become residents of the screen colony, bringing their other two children, Eileen, 16, and Hilda, 14, here from England.

NEW YORK, June 2—(UP)—An army of stewards, seamen, and mechanics began making the giant S. S. Queen Mary ready today for a possible record making maiden voyage to England. Sir Percy Bates, chairman of the Cunard-White Star line, the $8,000 ten liner’s owner, indirectly confirmed reports that her 780,000 horsepower engines will be opened up on the eastern passage in a challenge to the transatlantic record of the French ship Normandie. “I believe that she can easily beat the Normandie’s time with favorable weather,” he said, “and she may do it on the passage home.” The Queen Mary will sail at 10:30 a. m. Friday, Cunard officials expected her to carry even more than the 1849 passengers she landed at New York yesterday at the end of her first Atlantic voyage.

MAMARONECK, N. Y., June 1 (P)—Search for 15-year-old William Webster Theile, wealthy student last seen at his home here a month ago, spread through New England tonight. A spokesman for William Theile, the boy’s father and president of the Atlantic Investing Corporation, said a boy answering young Theile’s description was reported seen variously at Kennebunkport, Me., four days ago and in Westerly, R. I., Saturday.

| PRINCE RUPERT, B. C. (?. A week of isolation faced northern British Columbia residents, cut off from the outside world by the district’s worst flood in 30 years. Still rising after a sudden rampage Sunday, the Skeena and Bulkley rivers disrupted transportation and communication facilities and forced residents to abandon their homes. No loss of life was reported. While a blistering heat wave gripped the crippled district, work trains rolled out of here and Smithers, 125 miles east, with hundreds of workmen in an effort to carry temporary relief into the stricken area. From McBride, B. C., 60 miles west of the British Columbia-Alberta boundary, to within 20 miles of this coastal city, the muddy, debris-littered water covered lowlands. Telegraph and telephone lines were down, rail and highway bridges washed out. Wireless to Victoria and Vancouver was the only means of communication with t

1936-06-08.text: WASHINGTON, June 8 (UP) — Great Britain defaulted today on its semi-annual war debt installment to the United States. In doing so it advised this government that inability to pay was due to reasons 'no less valid now' than when it first suspended all payments in 1934. Formal notice that Britain did not intend to pay the $668,474,071 installment falling due on June 15 was contained in a note transmitted to Secretary Hull by Sir Ronald Lindsay, the British ambassador. Eleven other nations are generally expected to follow a similar course. Finland, which owes one of the smallest amounts, is the only country which has not defaulted on its war obligations to the United States. Of the sum due from Britain, $85,670,765 represents the regular June 15 installment of principal and interest and the remainder the amount previously due and unpaid. In suspending all payments on June 4, 1934, the Briti

Faris, Peyrannet de Torres, French aviator, said today that Colonel and Mrs. Charles Lindbergh, and their son, Jon, probably would return to the United States in August, after their stay in England. Torres and the Lindberghs have been mutual friends for a long time. The Lindberghs went to England late in December, for an indefinite stay, believed to have been caused by the continual annoyance which they have received from people who were making threats against their son, and from cranks and persistent newspaper reporters. It was never definitely stated whether the stay of the Lindberghs in England was to be permanent or temporary. It is believed that the final settlement of the Hauptmann case has been a factor in bringing the decision to return to America.

Canton, China, June 8—(UP)— Shore leave of American and British navy seamen was curtailed today as Cantonese troops continued northward, professing determination to fight the Japanese. Crews were ordered to stand by as a precaution against possible disorder. The Japanese consul said no orders had been received as to activity of Japanese warships in the vicinity.

LONDON, June 6. (U.P)—Emperor Haile Selassie may go to Rome to negotiate directly with Premier Benito Mussolini if the League of Nations refuses to fulfill its obligation to oppose firmly Italy's conquest of Ethiopia, well-informed French quarters said today. A little before Haile Selassie fled from Ethiopia, it is known now, Mussolini was ready to offer him retention of his throne and rule over a portion of the Amharic provinces of Ethiopia. Since he arrived in London, the Emperor has said that by coming here he had made himself more accessible for negotiations. If confronted with the choice of passing his life as an exile or again ruling even a part of his country, it was believed that the Emperor might elect to rule, even if under humiliating conditions.

WASHINGTON -— The British government advised the State Department in a formal note today that it would be unable to pay a June 15 war debt installment of $468,474,071. The note just sent by Sir Ronald Lindsay, British ambassador, in reply to a notice from Secretary of State Cordell Hull reminding London that the installment was due. The answer to Hull's note, which showed Britain to be in arrears more than three years, was expected. The $468,474,071 due the United States on June 15 includes $96,000,000 due on the principal of $4,023,500,000, plus $438,199,451 interest, $45,603,828 in default under the Hoover moratorium of 1932 and $45,670,765 due June 25.

London, June 7 (4?)—Increasing evidence of a desire by Great Britain's leading statesmen to draw the United States into the League of Nations’ fold was seen today by impartial observers. Diplomatic observers here say the renewed drive evident in recent months is not alone due to the League's manifest failure to halt the Italo-Ethiopian conflict, but to serious alarm engendered by the forthcoming United States-sponsored conference of American nations in Buenos Aires just as the Latin-American ardor for the League is cooling fast.

Washington, June 8—Great Britain today notified the United States government of its intention to default outright on its $85,670,765.05 June 15 debt installment. The British note asserted that the situation remained “unchanged” insofar as the question of making a payment to this government was concerned. Britain's action marked the beginning of the debt-defaulting parade of the European nations for this year. It also increased the amount on which Britain is in arrears to this government to $663,474,071.88.

BOSTON, June 8 (UP). — A drought that has parched farm and forest land in large sections of New England entered its 22nd day today with a prospect of showers in parts of southern New England. The Weather Bureau indicated showers might occur in Rhode Island and Connecticut and on the Massachusetts coast today but that the weather would clear again by tomorrow. No rain was indicated for New Hampshire, Vermont and Maine.

1936-06-30.text: LONDON (?) — Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin's government was attacked as “a danger to our country and the peace and security of the world” Monday night but it won a vote of confidence in House of Commons debate. After the Premier and his war minister, Alfred Duff Cooper, were subjected to a bitter tongue-lashing by labor leaders, a technical labor motion for adjournment of the debate based on Duff Cooper's speech recently in Paris, was rejected 284 to 138 in the balloting, which in effect was a vote of confidence.

London, June 2. (AP)--The crumbling structure of naval limitation received two staggering blows today. Japan officially refused to adhere to the 1936 London treaty signed by Great Britain, the United States and France, and it was learned the British would shortly invoke the escalator clause of the 1930 treaty to take excess destroyers. Formal notification to Washington and Tokyo that Britain wants to invoke the escalator clause will be sent within a few days, diplomatic quarters said. The United States will benefit by Britain's use of the escalator, which will free all signatories to the same extent. The United States also has built over treaty limits but her destroyers are older. Submarine restrictions of the treaty may be upset by a subsequent invocation of the clause by Japan.

Associated Press Foreign Staff. GENEVA, June 29.—(4)—Italy, seeking to calm fears of Great Britain and France, promised the League of Nations Monday night she would not create a huge Ethiopian army. This pledge was contained in a note delivered on the eve of a session of the League Assembly before which Emperor Haile Selassie will make a personal plea for “justice.” The Italian note blamed Ethiopians for the war and sketched plans for the development of the country, promising to keep the League in touch. Haile Selassie wrote officials: “It is our intention personally to take part in one or several meetings of the Assembly at the head of the Ethiopian delegation.” The Negus, stripped of his empire by Italy, remained in seclusion in a hotel working on his appeal. LONDON — Rumors Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin may resign soon flooded official British circles. Despite a fresh vote of confidence from the House of Commons, Baldwin was reported pondering his possible resignation at his country home. His return to London was said to have been postponed until next week.

GENEVA, June 29. (#)—Speedy funeral services—with a minimum of oratory—were planned for Italian sanctions in League of Nations circles Monday. British and French diplomats, leading the “death of sanctions” campaign, conferred on the general situation and reached conclusions described as “extremely satisfactory.” Proposals to debate the Locarno question, thrust into the tangled European problem when goose-stepping German troops marched into the Rhineland last March, were definitely shelved for the present. Although the Nazi denunciation of the mutual security pact was listed on the League’s agenda, diplomats agreed debate was impossible until Chancellor Hitler of Germany replies to the British questionnaire asking details of his suggestions for a new peace framework. The assembly convenes Tuesday. One conclusion appeared certain: cancellation of the economic and financial penalties voted

| LONDON, June 29 (4)--Parliament opened a critical week of debates on government policies today with the government leader, Prime Minister Baldwin, in seclusion at his country home. He stayed at Chequers, although the opposition was describing his government as “afraid of its own shadow” and criticizing Baldwin and his ministers for their stand on international affairs. Ramsay MacDonald, former Prime Minister and Lord President of the Council, assumed Baldwin's place at a Cabinet session while Sir John Simon, home secretary, prepared to lead the government's forces in parliamentary debate. The week's commons schedule was described by some political sources as “critical.” First was a series of questions from the opposition on personal opinions expressed in Paris by Alfred Duff Cooper, war secretary. (By the Associated Press) London, June 30—Frederick H. Field, army deserter convicted of the murder of Miss Beatrice V. Sutton, was hanged today at Wandsworth prison. Field after his arrest, was reported to have told police "I had never seen the woman before in my life. I just murdered her because I wanted to murder someone." During his trial, he denied the confession, but testified he was guilty of the killing "to accomplish what I did not have the courage to do—commit suicide." Mrs. Violet Van Der Elst, feminine opponent of the death penalty, drove up to the main prison gate in her limousine before the execution but refrained from staging a demonstration.

1936-10-10.text: VIN VIN, VC, LV, ("ar )-— Three Fascist nations of Europe, accused by Russia of sending illegal aid to Spanish insurgents, were reported considering today a formal protest against the charges to the Moscow government. Italy, Germany and Portugal pondered the prospective action, informed sources said, as their representatives relaxed after a noisy, tense session of the inter- committee attempting to isolate the Spanish civil war. During the meeting, Dino Grandi, Premier Mussolini’s delegate and ambassador to London, called the Soviet representative a liar, “energetically refuted and repudiated every single point of the allegations against Italy,” and turned the Russian accusations upside down to declare Moscow was assisting the Madrid government. Akyab, Burma, Oct. 8.—(AP)— Jean Batten, aviatrix seeking a new air record between England and New Zealand, arrived here today from Allahabad, India. Allahabad, India, Oct. 8.—(AP)— Jean Batten, feminine flyer attempting to set a solo flight record from England to New Zealand, took off today for Akyab, Burma.

London, Oct. 9.—(4?)—Soviet Russia, which threw a bombshell into European diplomacy by threatening to withdraw from the Spanish nonintervention agreement, was understood tonight to have decided to continue cooperating for the present. This stand, reported by a high diplomatic authority, came after a day of stormy charges and counter-charges and the dramatic walkout of the Portuguese delegate from the neutrality committee session. Portugal, with Germany and Italy, had been accused by Russia of aiding Spanish fascists in their struggle against the Madrid leftist regime. British Threat A sensation was created in conference circles when Great Britain’s chancellor of the exchequer, Neville Chamberlain, acting premier during the absence of Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin, was quoted as having said Britain would bolt the neutrality pact if Russia could prove her charges. Action on Russia’s angry protest against alleged fascist aid to the Spanish rebels was delayed—in such manner as to take as much fire from it as possible. That Russia’s delegate consented to the sidetracking, by which the powers arranged an exchange of diplomatic notes on charges and counter-charges, was believed due in part to the failure of France to support its ally. France Inactive France did not want to antagonize Italy, and antagonize Germany and wreck any hopes that may be left for a new Locarno treaty. JERUSALEM, Oct. 9 ()—Fifteen Arabs were killed today by British troops in the Nablus-Tulkarem area during an intensive search for Palestine’s “Public Enemy No. 1,” the Syrian leader Fawzi Bey Kawkazi. Fawzi was not found. Two British tanks inflicted casualties on an Arab band yesterday before they were stopped by the rebels. Other tanks came to their rescue during the night.

Rome, Oct. 19 (Saturday) — High Italian sources said today the Italian ambassador to London had accused Britons as well as Russians of aiding the Spanish government against the Spanish Fascists, although Great Britain and Russia both are parties to the agreement for non-intervention in Spain. The ambassador, Dino Grandi, was said to have made the accusation at yesterday's closed session of the international neutrality committee in London, when he denied Russia's charge that Italy—along with Germany and Portugal—had violated the pact by aiding Spanish Fascists. Grandi, it was said in these circles, named eight British pilots who were alleged to be working for the Madrid government. The names of the aviators were not given here. Russia charged that Italy, Portugal and Germany were supplying arms to Spanish Fascists in violation of the pact, causing the breach. The three accused nations denied it. London—(INS)— With the imminent danger of a general European clash between the forces of fascism and communism brought sharply home by events at Friday’s meeting of the non-intervention committee, the British government Friday announced plans for a sweeping investigation of Spain's charges that Italian troops participated in the execution of a number of Spanish citizens in the Balearic Islands. The examination will be made, it was said, with a view to determining the authenticity of the charges. They were based upon an affidavit by a Spaniard who said he escaped from the islands after the Italian troops had been landed. British spokesmen emphasized that in placing these and other allegations before the non-intervention committee the government is not taking responsibility for their authenticity. 1936-12-18.text: Engzesfeld, Austria, Dec. 17.—The duke of Windsor, suffering again from severe headaches, received 6,000 letters today from feminine admirers applauding his “romantic gesture” in giving up the British throne for Wallis Warfield Simpson. Eight hundred of the writers also asked the British prince for jobs, most of them expressing a preference for secretarial work. Reliable sources disclosed the duke suffered last night from another attack of severe head pains, which some said might be connected with his ear affliction. Attendants at the castle of Baron Eugene de Rothschild, where the former ruler is a guest, emphasized however the duke “is not really ill.” They said he intends to continue his golf games and may go on a hunting trip.

ENZESFELD, AUSTRIA, DEC. 18. (AP).—The Duke of Windsor terminated his voluntary seclusion today to pose for a battery of photographers on the grounds of Eugene D. Rothschild's Austrian castle. Hatless and in a serious mood, the former British ruler walked alone to the courtyard where 17 cameramen awaited him. He appeared tired, "Gentlemen, how do you want me?" he greeted the photographers. "Shall I sit or stand?" A flood of replies and subsequent questions followed his remarks as the business of making pictures of the abdicated monarch began. Three minutes later, the photographers, clutching their plates, began a 500-yard sprint to automobiles and motorcycles to carry them the 23 miles to Vienna. London, Dec, 18—(4)—Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden told the House of Commons today: “We have sold a small consignment of gas masks to the Spanish government at their request.” (His statement was interpreted by Reuters news agency as meaning the gas masks were sold by the British government.)
