PARIS, Aug. 5.—(AP)—Encouraged by an affirmative reply from Great Britain adhering in principle to the French stand, France’s Socialist government decided today to communicate its appeal for non-intervention in Spain to other European powers immediately to thwart any incident which might provoke a “general conflagration.” Sources close to the French foreign office said that while it awaited a reply from Premier Mussolini, the government of Premier Léon Blum hoped to receive soon “a certain number of adhesions to the non-intervention proposition with a view to arriving at a general neutrality accord.” The foreign office heard reports that the German freighter Sevilla had been endangered during a Spanish government bombardment of Larache, a Moroccan community, arousing fears in some other capitals that an incident might develop before a general neutrality accord was reached. Tangier dispat

—— ——— | GIBRALTAR, Aug. 5, @—Two British seaplanes flying from Algiers were fired upon by Spanish government warships, authorities announced. The planes, en route to England, drew Spanish fire as they were crossing the straits. Spanish nationalists apparently mistook them for rebel ships, officials said. Neither of the planes was hit. One sailor was injured and a veteran.

Washington, Aug. 4 (#)—A program of preliminary flood control work in New England and the Middle Atlantic States was whipped into shape by Federal officials today for submission to President Roosevelt "within 24 hours." Under Presidential orders to select from the $320,000,000 omnibus flood control act projects which could readily be developed to the "contract state," a committee headed by Major General Edward M. Markham, chief of army engineers, and Dr. Abel Wolman, of the National Resources Board, completed its task at a three-hour conference. Wolman told reporters "some kind of projects" would be undertaken in New England, New York, Pennsylvania, Ohio, West Virginia and Maryland where devastating floods occurred last spring, adding work probably would start in some cases by August 15. "These may be surveys or other types of preliminary work," he explained. At his regular press confere

LONDON, Aug. 4—(AP)—Britain’s foreign office tonight “fully shared” the French fear of a general European war should other powers throw their might to either rebellious Fascists or the popular front government in Spain. In some British diplomatic quarters it was said Premier Mussolini might seek concessions from England, France, Belgium and Germany in the proposed five-power Locarno conference in October in return for his word that Italy would not lend aid in the Spanish crisis. (The new Locarno talks were made necessary by Germany’s remilitarization of the Rhineland when Hitler marched troops into the territory March 7 in violation of the pact signed in 1925. (It was agreed by the signatories that a new agreement should be drawn to re-establish a new basis for European security. Great Britain, France and Belgium initiated the move, and Germany and Italy agreed, with limitations, to join

| BERLIN, Aug. 5— (AP) —Jesse Owens streaked over the 200-meter course in 20.7 seconds, creating a new world record for the distance around one turn, in annexing his third title of the 11th Olympiad today as husky Ken Carpenter, of Compton, Calif., won the discus throw championship. Owens’ time bettered his own previous record of 21 seconds flat set last month in the final American Olympic tryouts at Randall's Island, N. Y., and shaved four-tenths of a second off the new Olympic record of 21.1 he set in yesterday's trials. Duplicates Finn's Feat Today's victor, coupled with his earlier triumphs in the broad jump and the 100-meter sprint, made him the first Olympic “triple champion” since Paavo Nurmi, the “Phantom Finn” of Paris in 1924. The 200-meter final produced a one-two finish by American Negroes just as did the 100-meter final. Then, it was big Ralph Metcalfe, of Chicago, who trail

BY RALPH HEINZEN | (Copyright 1936 by United Press). PARIS — International complications of potential danger to European peace multiplied today as the Spanish revolt neared its climax. There were increasingly frequent references to Agadir—the port on the Moroccan coast to which Germany sent a “token” gunboat in 1911 as a warning to France against encroachment—an incident that might have advanced the date of the World War three years. Leaving aside the ambitions and fears of statesmen on the fascist and anti-fascist side as Spanish fascists and anti-fascists fight for power, the danger of the situation may be shown by the following summary of today’s developments: 1—Paris the newspaper Echo De Paris charged the German pocket battleship Deutschland, accompanied by a destroyer, prevented a loyalist warship bombardment of rebel forts by steaming into Ceuta Harbor, Morocco, as the loyal ships

| PORT SAID, Egypt, (P)—Ras Imru, Ethiopian commander in the northwest, was authoritatively reported Wednesday advancing on the cities of Dessye and Addis Ababa with 40,000 warriors. The Ethiopian columns were said to be advancing from the west in the general direction of the capital and the principal city on the northern end of the mountain road leading to Addis Ababa. Many Italian outposts were reported to have been destroyed during the Ethiopian advance.

1936-12-03.text: London, Dec. 2 (4)—An editorial in the London Times hinted today a possible breakup of the British realm with Duke and Duchess of York as King and Queen of Scotland. Some readers interpreted the article, which did not mention King Edward's friendship with Mrs. Wallis Simpson, as the strongest veiled reference to the “Simpson affair” which had yet appeared in England. It was learned that the friendship of the King and Mrs. Simpson had been placed on the “permanent agenda” of the British Cabinet. London, Dec. 2 (4)—England’s stock market dropped sluggishly today, reflecting, brokers said, growing concern that King Edward's romance with Mrs. Wallis Simpson might result in the resignation of the Cabinet or even the abdication of the King. A wholly unconfirmed rumor had it that the Cabinet had decided to resign on Saturday unless the monarch accedes to the demand he give up his friendship wit

| LONDON, Dec. 3.—(AP).—King Edward of England won in a first show of strength today in his all-critical fight with Britain’s government to keep his throne and his American friend, Wallis Warfield Simpson. | Defiant, yet with his empire’s fate close at heart, England’s sovereign insisted stubbornly on his right to a private life. : Gray and shaken, Baldwin, his first minister, stood before the house of commons in emotional anti-climax to insist he had nothing to say to the British people. | Then, dramatically, the Laborite Colonel, Right Honorable Josiah Clement Wedgwood, told the British Press Association in apparent confirmation of the authoritative impression that the king was winning at least the first phase of his empire-stunning battle: “The king is beloved. The thing we have got to avoid more than anything else is abdication. Any change will tear this country in two. If a general

London, Dec. 2.—King Edward’s friendship for Mrs. Wallis Simpson, reliable sources said today, has resulted in a complete compromise proposal, whereby he could marry her without causing the resignation of the cabinet or his forced abdication. The proposal was understood to be under consideration between the cabinet and the king. It would provide that his majesty would be permitted to marry Mrs. Simpson, provided she becomes only the duchess of Cornwall and not the queen of Great Britain. One of the greatest constitutional crises in England’s history thus could be averted. The government had threatened to force through Parliament a bill making it impossible for the king to marry a commoner, and the king had threatened, in turn, to refuse to sign the bill. The cabinet worked over time to prevent disaster. Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin went to the palace and conferred with the king today,

LONDON, Dec 3 (UP)— The British public, shocked by the sudden realization that the King may abdicate if his government does not permit him to marry Mrs. Wallis Simpson, began to rally his support today. The result may be that the government will be forced to back down and at least find a compromise by which Edward may still remain King and marry Mrs. Simpson as his consort, but not

LONDON, Dec. 2—(#)—The world’s greatest empire reached a government crisis tonight because of British King Edward's friendship for an American-born divorcee—chic Wallis Warfield Simpson. For an hour today Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin was closeted with the Monarch in what was reported to have been a showdown on the king’s friendship with Mrs. Simpson and reports that he hoped to marry her. Stern and silent, the prime minister strode into the palace for a straight-from-the-shoulder talk on the crisis which has grown to such proportions that some quarters asserted Baldwin told Edward he and the cabinet would resign unless his Majesty cooled his relationship with the former Baltimore belle. He emerged at the end of the hour, went directly to the House of Commons and later to 10 Downing Street to confer with Sir John Simon, British home secretary. As the government crisis heightened in inte

CAPETOWN, South Africa, Dec. 3. —(/P)— Captain James A. Mollison and his French co-pilot, Edouard Corniglion-Molinier, were found safe today after they had vanished within 100 miles of here. The two fliers, lost overnight almost at the end of a long distance flight from England to the Cape, were reported in good health.

LONDON, Dec. 3.--(4)--Authoritative sources reported today King Edward is negotiating the sale of his Canadian “EP” ranch to Lincoln Ellsworth, American explorer. Ellsworth visited the king, who has been retrenching rigidly since his accession to the throne, yesterday at Buckingham Palace. It was understood they discussed terms for sale of the ranch, located at High River, Alta.

LONDON, Dec. 3—(#)—King Edward, of England and Stanley Baldwin, Prime Minister, stood their grounds today in opposition over the Monarch's affections for Wallis Warfield Simpson. The King, with his heir-presumptive brother, and his American divorcee friend at his side, refused to give up the throne or the friendship. Baldwin, in an unprecedented House of Commons setting, had said “no statement” on the constitutional crisis. He told Clement Attlee, opposition leader, who reputedly sided with Baldwin in a demand to Edward to relinquish the American, “the situation is of such a nature as to make it inexpedient that I be questioned at this stage.” The King won in the first show of strength. Laborite leader, Josiah Clement Wedgwood told the British Press Association “the King is beloved. The thing we have to avoid is abdication. Any change will tear the country in two. If a general election c

1936-12-09.text: CROYDON, ENG, DEC. 9. (AP)...Fourteen persons, among them Juan De La Cierva, the autogyro inventor, met sudden, flaming death today in the crash of a “K.L.M.” (Dutch) airliner, just four minutes off the runway at Croydon airdrome. Trapped by twisted steel and flames, De La Cierva died with the former Swedish Secretary of State, Admiral Arvid Lindman, and twelve others, including two of the crew. No Americans were aboard. The plane, heading into a heavy fog which cut visibility to little more than twenty yards, ripped the roofs off two houses, swerved across a street, sheared off a large tree and finally imbedded itself in an unoccupied house. The engine, ripped from its mountings, smashed through the front wall. No pedestrians on the street were injured. The Dutch plane, fog-bound two hours with four other planes headed for cross-channel airports, finally took off and safely cleared the

LONDON, Dec. 9—Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin disclosed to the distressed and anxious House of Commons today that king and government still were hesitating over the answer to the present dilemma—if Edward will marry Mrs. Wallis Simpson and lose his throne. The first minister, after a night spent in conference with his sovereign, gave hope, however, that the crisis might reach its momentous climax tomorrow and told the crowded and wearied benches and galleries, “I regret I am not in a position to add anything today, but I hope to make a statement tomorrow.” The members, increasingly concerned over the economic and political results of the suspense, pressed him vainly for more. King Edward, outwardly steadfast in his composure, remained at rural Fort Belvedere. Mrs. Simpson, conferring at length at a French villa with her solicitors, announced through a spokesman she had “signed no documen

London, Dec. 8—(AP)—Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin called the British Cabinet into a sudden unexpected session tonight to discuss late developments in the constitutional crisis. Government whips instructed all members of the House of Commons to cancel engagements outside London in preparation for the Prime Minister's expected pronouncement tomorrow on King Edward's decision to renounce either the British throne or Mrs. Wallis Simpson.

London, Dec. 8— (Copyright)—The tragic romance of King Edward VIII, with his throne at stake, moved swiftly toward a climax today. The king’s final decision appeared imminent. Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin, accompanied by Walter T. Monckton, personal legal advisor of the king, motored from No. 10 Downing Street to Fort Belvedere, perhaps to hear his majesty’s decision. They were followed in a royal car by Sir Eric Mieville, private secretary to the Duke of York, who will succeed to the throne if the king abdicates. Meanwhile, a royal mystery plane was speeding across France, presumably toward Cannes, on the Riviera, where Mrs. Wallis Simpson is in seclusion. The plane halted at Paris, then at Lyons and continued south toward the Riviera. It was reported in Paris that there were three occupants of the plane, including Sydney Baron, a member of the legal firm which represented Mrs. Simpso

LONDON, Dec. 9 (U.P) — Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin, with the country and the world waiting to hear confirmation or repudiation of a belief that King Edward VIII has decided to abdicate, told the House of Commons today he could not make an announcement before tomorrow. Baldwin expressed regret that he was not in a position to add anything to what he has already said. It had been taken for granted until just before Commons met that a statement would be forthcoming. Hope For Change— The situation has changed so often and with such rapidity during the crisis that hope was aroused in some circles that if the king already has made up his mind, as believed, further efforts would be made by the cabinet and royal family to change it. Clement R. Attlee, labor leader, asked Baldwin whether he was in a position to add anything to Monday's statement. Baldwin replied simply: "I regret that I am not

| London, Dec. 9 (Wednesday) (#P)—Edward’s choice of love or empire remained unanswered to an anxious realm early today as those who might know his decision kept tight-lipped silence. Cabinet ministers were to assemble in formal session this morning, prior to an afternoon meeting of the House of Commons, to hear from Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin a report of his long audience with Edward and two of the king’s brothers at dinner in ice-sheathed Fort Belvedere last night. If Baldwin, the man who says Edward cannot as king wed the American-born Wallis Simpson, carried away from the country retreat a final answer to his urging that the monarch renounce his love, he guarded carefully that answer—until formal announcement could be made to cabinet and commons. Some authoritative observers said they were convinced Baldwin may end the entire uproar with a simple announcement to commons that ‘the

| LONDON, Dec. 9 (UP)—Fourteen persons were killed and three others on board badly injured today when a Dutch K. L. M. airliner crashed as it took off from Croydon airdrome for Amsterdam. The three survivors, including the hostess, were removed to a hospital and small hope was held for the survival of two of them. The hostess, a Miss Bongerstam, of Holland, suffered only nerve shock. No Americans were on board. Admiral Salomon Landman, former prime minister of Sweden, and Juan de la Cierva, Spanish inventor of the autogyro, were among those killed in the crash which occurred in a fog less than a mile from Croydon. Commander Hautzmayer, an Austrian, was piloting the airliner. The visibility was limited to a few feet and when the plane failed to gain altitude as it left the airport it scraped off the roof of a house, hit a telephone pole and crashed into the side of a residence, bursting i

LONDON, Dec. 9 — (UP) — Juan De La Cierva, inventor of the autogiro, Admiral Salomon Lindman, former prime minister of Sweden and 12 others were killed today when a KLM Dutch airliner crashed in a dense fog a mile from Croydon airport. Six passengers were taken to the Purley hospital gravely injured. Four of them died. Only survivors of the 17 persons on board were Walter Schuback, a German passenger, the plane's radio operator, Jon Van Bemmel, and the stewardess, a Miss Bongerstam. She suffered only shock. The passengers had left on the regular liner for Amsterdam at 8 a.m. which turned back on account of the fog. They were transferred to another liner which took off two hours later to make connections in Amsterdam with airplanes bound for Germany and Scandinavia. The pilot was Commander Hautzmayer, an Austrian, a flyer of wide experience. As the great liner rose from the airport the fo

1936-06-17.text: London, June 17—The British cabinet placed the final seal of authority on the government's recession from sanctions today. Commons will hear the announcement of the new Italo-Ethiopian policy tomorrow. Parliamentary circles expected that the British support for the withdrawal of sanctions from Italy would be linked with a demand for guarantees that Premier Mussolini would not discriminate against the erstwhile sanctionist countries when trade channels are reopened. Coincidentally Sir Samuel Hoare, first lord of the admiralty, assured Commons today the government would not discontinue Malta. He scouted reports that the Mediterranean naval base would be discontinued because of its proximity to Italy and said the Admiralty intends to maintain the fortified island as its principal naval base in the Mediterranean as headquarters for the Mediterranean fleet. "We have no intention whatsoever of

United Press Staff Correspondent. London, June 17.—(UP)—The British cabinet decided today not only to support the lifting of league sanctions against Italy but to assume the lead in advocating their abolition from the covenant when the league council and assembly convene in extraordinary sessions at Geneva late this month. The cabinet met under the presidency of Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin at 10 Downing St. to lead 51 league members in a retreat from the sanctionist front. Today's decisions, resulting in new foreign policies designed to restore Italy to the council tables of Europe, reportedly confirmed a secret provisional verdict reached a week ago. The week-old decisions, now ratified formally, were reached a few hours before Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, uttered his famous assertion that it was madness to believe that continued sanctions could rescue Ethiopian

JERUSALEM, June 17.—(4)—Terrorists fired on a children's home in the American colony on the plain of Sharon today, but the inhabitants escaped unhurt. A rain of bullets smashed the windows of the home. Near Jaffa, an Arab was killed and several others wounded after they had ambushed a British police car. (The Palcor agency reported last night that tension was high in Palestine in anticipation of today’s anniversary of the execution of Arabs convicted of murder in connection with the anti-Jewish riots of 1929. (In the last eight weeks, since Arabs started a campaign against Jewish immigration, 30 Jews and 54 Arabs have been slain, the agency stated. (The plain of Sharon, mentioned as the site of the children's home fired upon today, is on the coast of Palestine, extending about 40 miles in length. It was famous in ancient times for its roses).

| DARJEELING, India, June 16. | (P)—The British mountain-climbing expedition abandoned its attempt today to reach the summit of Mount Everest. Members of the party headed by Hugh Ruttledge returned to their base camp after being held below the summit for weeks by raging storms and monsoonal winds. Preparations are underway already for another attempt next year, it was reported.

LONDON June 16—(%—Laborite foes cracked down on Britain's minister of war from two sides today, the eve of an anticipated formal decision to lift sanctions from Italy. A peer and a member of commons used sharp language to protect Secretary Alfred Dum Cooper's statement yesterday that “it is the duty of those in authority to frighten the people of this country out of their wits.” Lord Ponsonby, the labor peer, told a peace rally Duff Cooper should be confined as “a deliberate, dangerous and disgraceful scare-monger.” Later, Emanuel Shinwell, the laborite who ousted Ramsay MacDonald from his Sshaham harbor seat at the last general election, asked commons.

London, June 17. (P)—Lloyds’ brokers pitted 10 to 1 odds with worried souvenir manufacturers today against the chance that King Edward will bring a bride to his coronation next May. The brokers were doing a land-office business insuring pottery and knickknack makers who are beginning to turn out thousands of coronation souvenirs. The manufacturers want the insurance against either a change in the souvenir designs or postponement of the event. If King Edward married, for example, the mugs, plaques and other trinkets would require two portraits instead of one.

- NASSAU, ae — Reports from Inagua Island in the Eastern Bahamas told of the finding of the bodies of three white men beside a small vessel wrecked on a reef. A meager description of the craft indicated it might be the Girl-Pat, an English boat which was reported stolen from Grimsby, England, six weeks ago by a party of men who came to these Islands in it to look for buried gold.

PARIS, June If (?),--A collection of Napoleonic emeralds, whose purchase price was $1,200,000, was reported to be the property today of Countess Barbara Hutten Haugwitz-Reventlow, Woolworth five and ten heiress. The newspaper Paris-Midi said the countess, who now lives in London, bought the jewels yesterday from Ganna Walska, Polish opera singer and former wife of Harold F. McCormick, Chicago millionaire.

1936-06-11.text: WASHINGTON, June 11. (UP)— The government of Finland, only war debtor not in default, today assured the state department it would pay the $164,315.50 installment on its obligation due June 15. Previously Great Britain and Italy had informed this country they would not meet their payments. Negative replies also are expected from other debtors.

VICTORIA, B. C., June 11 UP— Forest fires in the wake of receding floods threatened the mining town of Anyox in northern British Columbia today and sent clouds of smoke aloft in a dozen scattered sectors along the Alaska coast. Wireless messages to the provincial police here said ships were standing by to evacuate the town's population of approximately 200 persons. Telephone and telegraph poles went down in the flames, disrupting communications. The Hidden Creek Mining company’s property was destroyed and other mine buildings and a school house were burned on the outskirts of the town.

LONDON, June 11.—Ethiopian forces are assembling in three areas to oppose the Italian conquest, Blatten Getta Herouy, Ethiopian foreign minister, said today. Ten thousand men under the acting Ethiopian government are in the Gore area in the mountainous west, he asserted, 15,000 more are in the south under Ras Desta Demtu, Emperor Haile Selassie’s son-in-law. Bitwoded Waldar Tsadik, Herouy said, is acting head of the government as regent in the emperor's absence.

CANTON, China (UT) — British naval authorities ordered the gunboats Cicala and 'Farantula to abandon their “normal routine patrol duties Thursday and stand by at Canton. + Both ships have been on West patrol duty. They are specially constructed, of 625 tons each, with complements of from 54 to 65 men, according to their assignment. Sources close to Cantonese leaders said Thursday that it was most unlikely Canton would be represented at the meeting of the central executive committee of the Kuomintang party summoned for July 10 at Nanking. The committee, to which the central Chinese government is directly responsible, is to seek means of composing internal differences. Reliable sources reported that a great anti-Japanese demonstration was planned here Friday.

LONDON, June 11, (GP). British 'Sanctionists' expressed serious alarm today over the declaration of Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, that the war penalties against Italy should be lifted. Chamberlain told the 1900 Club last night the proposal to continue sanctions against the Fascist nation for her invasion of Ethiopia is "the very mid-summer of madness."

LONDON, (U.H.—British authorities anticipate renewed Japanese military intervention in China this summer, it was learned Thursday. Japanese leaders are said to be convinced that whatever they do, Great Britain would refrain from forcible measures to protect China's independence. Therefore, authorities here believe, Japan will resume its forward action soon and the anticipated action in northern China may be accompanied by intervention further south. Fearing the possibility of civil war, the consul at Changsha has given provisional warning to British subjects to evacuate southern Hunan province, through which Cantonese troops are advancing, the Daily Mail Shanghai correspondent (Continued on Page Three)

Madrid, June 11—Antonio Romano, 62, president of the Malaga provincial parliament and the province's leading socialist, was assassinated today in the city of Malaga. Street fighting immediately broke out between partisans of the socialist and syndicalist factions, although both are members of the leftist coalition which governs Spain today. Meanwhile the government reported it had smashed a rightist movement in seven provinces. A group of unidentified men opened fire on President Romano as he appeared on the street. At the same time, a band of alleged syndicalists attacked the local socialist club and wounded one man with pistol fire. Business in Malaga was paralyzed by a general strike.

Paris, June 10. (P)—A general strike of hotel, cafe and restaurant employees in the Paris region was voted tonight as a possible cleavage in the government's leftist majority over the 40-hour week bill was seen. The new strikers joined the ranks of hundreds of thousands of others who are demanding more money and shorter hours, and all of whom are awaiting parliamentary decision on the labor bills of Premier Leon Blum before returning to work.

1936-06-04.text: WOODS HOLE, Mass.—Twenty-six passengers were rescued by coast guardsmen from the stranded and leaking British steamer Fort Amherst in fog-bound Vineyard Harbor early today. They were landed here soon after 7 a.m. EST. The 5200 ton, 350-foot Furness-Red Cross line steamer, with a jagged hole below the waterline forward and her crew of 72 men still aboard, floated herself and headed for Vineyard Haven. The ship had cleared Halifax, N.S., Tuesday and was due in New York at noon today. At 2 a.m. EST the Fort Amherst was nosing through a “pea-soup” fog when she crashed upon the rocks of East Chop on Martha's Vineyard island. Her master immediately radioed coast guards for assistance and the patrol boat Argo sped to the scene from Newport, R.I. In a calm sea, the Argo pulled alongside and the 26 passengers were transferred quickly over a gangway.

LONDON, June 6—(P)—The British people made little Haile Selassie forget momentarily today the ashes of Addis Ababa. The exiled Ethiopian ruler, arriving here today, couldn’t keep back the tears in the midst of the popular reception given him. "I have come to England confident I will be able to obtain justice," he said. Just a month after abandoning his distant African capital to fire and pillage before the steady march of the Roman legions, the Negus arrived in England. Bobbles fought waves of cheering spectators to keep them within barriers. Traveling as a private citizen, the little emperor spared British officialdom embarrassment. The Lion of Judah arrived at the same time that labor circles continued to predict that Premier Baldwin shortly would effect a deal with Premier Mussolini in the tense Anglo-Italian situation.

London, England, June 4—(?)—In a bitter denunciation of Italy's war methods, Haile Selassie said today he abandoned Ethiopia to prevent the complete annihilation of his people. His statement was made at a press legation. London in exile yesterday, was serious and sad as he faced his questioners. The negus said that when he fled from Ethiopia the fields and the streets of villages were covered with bodies of aged persons, women and children “massacred behind the lines by the pitiless airplanes of the enemy.” “I come in person to appeal to the sentiment of justice of all peoples. The covenant of the League of Nations cannot in silence and indifference.

LONDON (2)—Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia has decided to go to Geneva for the assembly of the League of Nations on the Italian-Ethiopian problem, it was learned Thursday. Unless there is a change of plan, it was said, he will go personally to (Continued on Page Twelve)

PARIS (UP) — Great Britain and France agreed today to support postponement of sessions of the League of Nations Council and Assembly until the end of June, diplomatic sources reported. The delay would allow representatives of the two nations to attempt to formulate proposals for settlement of Italy's annexation of Ethiopia, these sources asserted. (The League Council adjourned May 12 until June 16, the date its members set for further discussion of the Italo-Ethiopian question. {A request from Argentina recently asked an assembly session before the end of June for consideration of the same problem.) Diplomatic circles predicted existing sanctions against the Fascist nation would be lifted. Some quarters suggested both France and Great Britain would abstain from voting when, and if, sanctions were lifted. They would explain their action, it was reported, by saying they intend to discuss w

Strikes inspired by left wing demands for better wages and working conditions spread in several European countries today. The most serious situation was in France, where the government headed by the Socialist Leon Blum was about to take power. More than 400,000 workers were out and there was a threat of a paralyzing general strike. Similar conditions prevailed in Spain, where hundreds of thousands were on strike. The port of Antwerp, Belgium, was tied up by a strike of 5,000 dock workers. As in France, a Socialist coalition government was about to be formed in Belgium. A 20-hour general strike, attributed to Communists, was declared in Salonica, Greece.

Shanghai, June 2. (P)—Japanese authorities announced late tonight that the South China government at Canton had declared war against the National Chinese government demanding the latter order a National war against Japan. The Japanese, who earlier said they understood the Canton government had declared war against Japan, received further advices from Canton saying that instead of declaring war on Japan, the Cantonese government had issued a manifesto. This manifesto denounced Japanese aggression in North China and demanded an immediate declaration of war against Japan on the part of the national government at Nanking. In this latter announcement, the Japanese reiterated that Canton had declared war against Nanking. The Japanese said a proclamation announcing the establishment of an independent government at Canton was imminent. The South China provinces concerned are Kwangtung and Kwang-

(By Edward Kennedy) (Copyright, 1936, the Associated Press). Paris, June 4—The third republic called its first socialist premier—the cultured, well-dressed Leon Blum—to take power today over a France chaotic with industrial strikes. President Albert Lebrun encharged the socialist leader with the task of forming the 101st cabinet during the 65 years of the republic's history. As Blum went to the Elysée palace, with his tentative list of ministers already made up, France was in the midst of strikes which unofficially were estimated to embrace approximately 500,000 workers. Manufacturers declared the strikes threaten to paralyze the nation’s industry. CALL IS EARLY Blum was called to power within two hours after Premier Albert Sarraut and his coalition cabinet had resigned. Blum went to the Élysée palace in a presidential automobile. He did not smile as he stepped from the car. For the occa

1936-10-20.text: LONDON, Oct. 19 — (UP) — Individual members of parliament, emboldened by a surge of gossip, are considering representations to King Edward about his friendship with Mrs. Wallis Simpson, it was learned today. The seriousness with which these men regard the association is made clear by their knowledge that the King has angrily rebuffed respectful intimations already made by the Archbishop of Canterbury, supreme head of the Church of England, and Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin. As part of their tentative plan, the members of parliament concerned are even talking about the possibility of persuading the venerable archbishop to approach the King again. Gossip spread fast through London about the divorce suit brought by Mrs. Simpson against Ernest Simpson, former officer in the king’s own household regiments — and the gossip, if discreet, was unfavorable. The more sober-minded men in politics,

WASHINGTON, Oct. 19 (#)— President Roosevelt settled himself at the White House today for a 40-hour stay, striving to clear his desk of an accumulation of business before resuming, in New England, his fast-traveling campaign for re-election. Driving through bright early morning sunshine to the White House from a special train that brought him from his Hyde Park, N. Y., home last night, the chief executive settled to work almost at once. The streets through which his automobile moved were crowded with government employees, also bound for work. Traveling by train and motor, Mr. Roosevelt will turn northward before mid-week for a six-speech campaign drive in three New England states, taking up not far from where he ended last week a 5,000-mile mid-western tour. Except to see a few cabinet officers, including Secretary of State Cordell Hull, in his study in the executive mansion, he had no e

London, Oct. 20.—(AP)—Worried lest Russia bolt the “hands-off-Spain” agreement and harried by a Laborite demand for immediate convocation of parliament to debate Spanish neutrality, Great Britain today pressed Germany, Italy and Portugal to reply to charges they have meddled in Spain. Informed sources said merely that the government was “concerned at the delay” on the part of the authoritarian states, but it was learned that Lord Plymouth, chairman of the non-intervention committee, had taken occasion to confer with representatives of the three countries. So far, no date had been set for the next meeting of the committee, despite growing Soviet-Russian irritation. However, it was believed Lord Plymouth would (Continued on Page Four.)

By Associated Press. LONDON, Oct. 19.—Bette Davis, American film player, was restrained today from appearing in motion pictures or other performances in England for any company except Warner Brothers of Hollywood. The injunction was granted by Justice Sir George Branson in King's Bench Division upon application of the American film company.

CRAPINGTON, England, Oct. 20. Big aviator Amy Mollison, famous British flier, crashed and was slightly injured near here today en route from Paris to London. She landed in a field where houses were being built. Her plane caught in a rut and turned over on its back. Mrs. Mollison was bruised and shaken but not seriously hurt. She was taken to a doctor's house by truck and given first aid, after which she continued to Croydon field, outside London, by automobile.

LONDON, Oct. 19.—(UP)—A British court granted Warner Brothers American film producers an injunction today that restrains Bette Davis, movie star, from making a picture for a British concern. The injunction will apply for three years from the present time or for the duration of her contract with Warner Brothers, whichever is shorter. Justice Branson said that the injunction must be granted, but that it was for him to decide its length. The Warners had claimed their contract bound her until 1942.

London, Oct. 19 (4P)—Leaders of the Labor party tonight asked Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin to call parliament for an immediate session on the Spanish situation. The Laborites, in so doing, sided with the Russian representatives who were plainly irked by what they called the "tortoise-like" pace of the neutrality committee. (In Moscow, informed sources said Russia was determined to bolt the neutrality pact and would do so in a day or two. The Russians were angered over the committee’s delay in acting on Soviet suggestions for a Portuguese blockade to prevent foreign aid to the Spanish insurgents.) Clement R. Attlee, Laborite leader in the House of Commons, wrote Baldwin that "although allegations have not been proved definitely, there is strong ground for belief that the policy of non-intervention (in Spain) has been deliberately violated." "In view of the increasing gravity of the situ

London. Oct. 19—(4)— While thousands of huge newspaper posters throughout England and Scotland tempted potential readers last night with the exciting news that “the king may marry before summer,” King Edward retired to his Sandringham estate. A court circular said he was accompanied only by Maj. Ulick Alexander, keeper of the privy purse, and Commander Charles Lambe. Whether he would be joined by his American friend, Mrs. Ernest Simpson—whose husband announced last week she would soon seek a divorce—was a secret not known to the British monarch’s subjects. Mrs. Simpson accompanied Edward on a Mediterranean vacation this summer and was with him at Balmoral castle in Scotland after their return. One of the two “bobble” who night and day patrol the street in front of Mrs. Simpson's new residence on Cumberland terrace, overlooking Regents Park, declined to give any information on her whereab

1936-11-21.text: BARCELONA, Spain, Nov. 21.—(U.P)—Four loyalist seaplanes took off today to find and sink the nationalist cruiser Canarias, opening a blockade of Catalonia. France and Great Britain are acting in perfect concord, it was learned, and hope that an admittedly dangerous situation may be liquidated successfully. But there were reports of the most alarming character from many sources. France was understood to be considering a warning from Gen. Francisco Franco, nationalist dictator, that he would soon demand some $250,000,000 in gold bullion which the Madrid government has sent to France. Newspaper reports included the following: Ramon Franco, trans-Atlantic aviator and brother of the nationalist dictator, has reached an agreement with the Italian government for Italian aid in blockading Barcelona. Italy will “lend” the nationalists 15 submarines and speed up deliveries of war munitions to the

London, Nov. 20, (#).—Britain, ever-jealous of her right to sail the seas unhindered, answered tonight with the terse word “piracy” a Spanish insurgent threat to destroy the port of Barcelona if arms shipments to the Madrid Government continue. Informed sources, told of the threat of Foreign Minister Anthony Eden, turned to the international law on piracy for an answer and declared British warships will fire on Spanish insurgent gunboats, as “pirates” if the Fascist men-of-war interfere with English merchant vessels. This bristling assurance was given on the heels of Eden's declaration to Parliament that the insurgent, General Francisco Franco would wreck the port of Barcelona ‘if arms and supply shipments to his foes continued. Since the British Government has not recognized either side in the Spanish civil war as a belligerent, informed sources said, under international law any molesta
DUBLIN, Irish Free State, Nov. 21 (4)— General James A. Farley kissed the Blarney stone at Blarney castle today. Later he left for Killarney lakes for an overnight stay.

London— (U.P) —Great Britain's attitude toward the blockade threat of Spanish rebels appeared to be stiffening today in the face of unconfirmed reports that the insurgents would not recognize a neutral zone in Barcelona harbor. If reports broadcast by nationalist radio stations that there will be no such zone prove correct, it is expected Britain will play a

Mighty Britain, Fascist Italy and Communist Russia Friday night tossed out new warnings that Spain’s civil war endangered the peace of Europe. Quick to protect her power on the seas, Britain let it be known that her men-of-war would treat Fascist insurgent ships as “pirates” if they touched British merchantmen. The warning came after Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden read to Parliament a note from Fascist General Francisco Franco that he would destroy the port of Barcelona if necessary to keep armaments from the Madrid Socialists. Italy was prepared to combat any attempt to establish a communistic regime in Spain—and would be assisted by Germany and Japan. “Italy does not intend,” the authoritative Italian writer, Virginio Gayda, declared, “that there shall be planted in the Mediterranean on Spanish territory a new center of red revolution and a new base of Communist military and political

VIRGINIA WATER, England, Nov. 21, (U.P)—King Edward was at his country home at Fort Belvedere today for the week-end, and included in his party of guests was Mrs. Wallis Simpson. The flag of the King’s Duchy of Cornwall flew from the flagpole of the house and special guards patrolled the grounds to keep off the curious. It was believed that the King and Mrs. Simpson spent part of the brilliant autumn morning tending to the flower garden.

BIARRITZ (UP)—The San Sebastian insurgent radio announced Saturday that “no neutral zone for foreign ships will be established at the port of Barcelona.” The broadcast, at 2:25 p.m. was taken as an indication that General Francisco Franco intends to defy British and French demands that a safety zone be established prior to the bombardment of the city, in conformity with international law.

Liverpool, Nov. 21 (UP) — General O'Duffy, Irish fascist leader, and 40 volunteers on their way to join the Spanish insurgent forces, arrived here today. They planned to sail for Lisbon, Portugal, later in the day. Headed by O'Duffy, young Irishmen quietly prepared to go to the Catalan front in northeastern Spain, reliable reports said. In front of them was the first group of ten which left Liverpool for Lisbon, Portugal, Nov. 14. Behind they left 1,000 comrades ready to follow when they receive the order.

1936-03-30.text: Adolf Hitler's election victory Sunday, while confidently expected by everyone, appeared to pose new problems for Europe's statesmen. The British cabinet decided that German military officers should be invited to confer with the general staffs of Great Britain, France, and Belgium if Hitler sees fit to accept the Locarno treaty powers’ proposals for a Rhineland settlement. French officials indicated that France wanted to ask Hitler for direct answers to various questions before any further negotiations could be undertaken. Mainly, it was indicated, France wants to know what guarantees it could have that Germany would not violate a new treaty. The Nazis in Germany, jubilant over receiving 99 percent of the votes cast in the national election, intimated that Hitler would “astound the world” by new proposals to France, Belgium, Great Britain, and Italy, the signatories of the Locarno pact.

LONDON, March 30.—Cabinet leaders today approved a plan for early British-French-Belgian staff conferences on joint land, sea and air defense against an unprovoked attack on any nation of the three, it was learned authoritatively. The conferences will begin soon—probably April 6—even if the German reply to peace proposals of the Locarno powers

LONDON, March 30 LP—Count Haugwitz-Reventlow registered the birth of his son today, disclosing the newborn heir to part of the Woolworth millions is named Lance. The baby, just a bit more than a month old, had his daily airing in his perambulator in a private park while his mother, Countess Barbara Hutton Haugwitz-Reventlow, went outdoors for the first time since the baby's birth and her own serious illness.

London, England, March 30.—(U. P.)—Great Britain gave indications today of planning to withdraw much of her fleet, which has been concentrated in the Mediterranean because of the Italian-Ethiopian crisis. Such a withdrawal, if it is made, will do much to placate Italy and enlist her co-operation in dealing with the Rhineland crisis. The news from Gibraltar was that the 33,900-ton battleship Rodney, the largest in the world, had sailed for England today; that the destroyers Valentine, Vidette and Westcott would leave tomorrow, and the depot ship Titania and submarine Snapper on Wednesday. The admiralty explained that the withdrawals were “normal routine” to give the crews Easter leave, but it was learned reliably that further units of the home fleet were due to return shortly.

LONDON, (AP)--Strange garb- ew figures out of the past, setting forth from Charing Cross in the heart of London in a quaint old coach-and-four, drew gasps of astonishment here today. Giant two-decker buses and sleek motorcars stood aside and traffic virtually stopped as the Bay party, clad in flowing greatcoats and grey tophats, swept along with a silver-noted hunting horn to warn the unwary. It was the Pickwickians en route to Rochester in the Original Pickwick coach described by Charles Dickens—celebrating the centenary of Dickens' immortal “Pickwick Papers.” The creaky coach left from the spot where the old Golden Cross Hotel, the starting place of the Pickwickians in Dickens’ novel, stood many years ago. Thence, it rolled through the smoke-grimed streets of London out through the countryside, now bright with the colors of spring, to its destination on famous Gad's Hill, in Rochester,

London, March 30.—(AP)—Prime Minister Baldwin assured the House of Commons today that the British Staff would not be allowed to involve the government in any commitments in the forthcoming consultations with the French and Belgian army commands concerning mutual defense against possible German aggression. The prime minister's statement was made shortly after he and his cabinet had discussed a date upon which the consultations might be started. A wave of suspicion and distrust moved through parliamentary quarters. Baldwin said the cabinet would review everything to which the general staffs agreed and stated: “Assurance on that question was given the House during a recent debate and I confirm it now.”

Addis Ababa, March 25 ()— Squadrons of Italian planes virtually destroyed Harar, Ethiopia's second largest city, with incendiary bombs today, said reports reaching officials here. Victims were believed to be few, as the entire population of the ancient Moslem city fled in terror. A group of 75 Fascist bombers roared over the city from one side and 35 came in from the opposite direction after dawn, but only scouted as the population evacuated. Then 15 to 20 bombing planes arrived two hours later and dropped bombs, leaving the city in flames. The fate of four hospitals in Harar was unknown. The European quarter, until recently headquarters for more than a score of foreign correspondents, was reported badly damaged. A French Hospital, a Catholic mission and several Coptic churches were destroyed, said the sparse details. The town of Jijiga also was reported heavily bombed.

1936-08-30.text: Jerusalem, Aug. 29 (CINS)—Two British soldiers were killed and three wounded today in an Arab ambush as violence continued in the holy land's religious conflict. The ambush occurred at Esdraelon between Nablus and Nazareth,

BASRA, Iraq—(P--A transport plane of the Imperial Airways carrying eight passengers and a crew of four was forced down in the Persian Gulf, Saturday, British warships and planes of the Royal Air Force searched for it. Five hours after the plane, a flying boat, left here, the radio station received a terse message: "Forced to land. Position unknown." The plane was en route to Bahrein Island. Officials were inclined to believe that the pilot may have missed the landing field there and alighted to the south of the island. Warships and airplanes reconnoitered over the Persian Gulf while camel patrols searched the shores along the northeastern Arabian coast. Five of the plane’s passengers were British army officers.

ESTES PARK, Colo. (®) — Said the lady in riding togs to the cowboy at the livery stable: "Have you a nice gentle horse?" "Yes ma’am, and what kind of a saddle would you like? English or Western?" "Ah—er--what’s the difference?" "The western saddle has a horn on it." "A horn? Well, if the traffic is so bad around these mountains that I need a horn on my saddle, I won't go riding!" The cowboy at the stable swears it’s a true story.

GEORGETOWN, British Guiana (Canadian Press)— Eleven exhausted fugitives from the French penal colony at Cayenne landed Saturday at the mouth of the Essequibo River, 120 miles from here. Police gave them shelter, food and clothing at a police station. Following their recovery, they will be allowed forty-eight hours to leave the colony.

LONDON, Aug. 29. — (INS) — Whole families have been massacred by Spanish leftists at Ajucena with maniacal barbarity, according to a report by a correspondent of the Lisbon newspaper O Seculo who has just returned from a tour of Spanish towns, the London Daily Mail stated today in a Lisbon dispatch. “A local priest was buried with his head above the ground,” the paper quoted the correspondent as reporting. “He was still living after three hours, whereupon reds drenched his head with petrol and set it afire. Killing in Streets. “At the approach of rebels, communists commenced killing people in the streets and forbade anyone to appear at windows. “A girl of 16, wild with fear for her father, looked out of a window, unaware he had already been killed. “An infuriated horde invaded the girl’s house, dragged her into the street, tore off her clothes and was about to mutilate her when the white

Rebel bombs tore two women to bits in the Northern Spanish city of Irun today while the United States government, stunned by the bombing of an American destroyer, dispatched stiff protests to Madrid and to the Fascist insurgents alike. In a vicious attack on long-defended Irun, rebel planes blasted great holes in the streets as the city was being evacuated en masse. Before the attack had begun, more than 4,000 inhabitants had fled into France. On direct orders from President Roosevelt, now in the Middle West, the state government demanded the fighting Spaniards keep their hands off United States ships. Naval officers at Washington indicated any United States men of war similarly attacked would reply with renewed fire. The protests came after an unidentified airplane off the west coast of Spain had rained bombs about the destroyer Kane, which replied with nine volleys from its anti-aircra

(The fascist rebel general stated in Burgos that planes again had bombed the port Cuatro Vientos at Madrid and the airdrome at Villalba, destroying three government planes.) Another rebel plane flew first over the city at a tremendous height, then poised and dived. It flattened out of its power dive when but a few hundred feet up and loosed its cargo of projectiles. Strollers on Madrid's streets fled in confusion for underground shelter as the bombs exploded in the garden of the war ministry. | Moscow—(fi—The Soviet government today officially demanded that Norway expel Leon Trotzky, the exiled Russian Bolshevist leader. A government note handed to the Norwegian foreign minister by the Soviet representative in Oslo read: “The Soviet government expects the Norwegian government will not delay measures to deprive Trotzky of further refuge in Norwegian territory.” There was no indication, however, that the Soviet government had demanded the exile’s return to Russia. The note made plain that Norway's refusal would prejudice good relations between the two governments and would be considered a violation of international law.

1936-06-05.text: PARIS, June 4.—(P)— France and Great Britain are willing, diplomatic sources said tonight, to lift sanctions from Italy, if Premier Mussolini agrees to maintain the present status of the Mediterranean and of central Europe. They reached an agreement, said diplomatic sources, through their ambassadors after a talk May 15 between Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden and France's incoming premier, Leon Blum. Lifting of sanctions would permit Italy to borrow money to finance the development of Ethiopia. Officials here confirmed that France and Britain have agreed to postpone sessions of the League of Nations council until June 29. Hitler Pact Seen. Diplomatic sources said they understood Blum is willing to negotiate with Reichsfuehrer Hitler if the British insist upon conversations. Hitler, it was said, has sounded Paris and London on the prospect of early negotiations. Blum, France’s new premier,

London—(#)—The News-Chronicle, without stating its authority, said today an informal agreement had been reached between the United States and British governments to take common action in the event the French franc goes off the gold standard. An authoritative source in Whitehall scouted the report, but pointed out, however, that the operation of the exchange control fund was so secret that not even parliament is advised concerning what is done.

- Bethlehem, Pa. June 4 (%).—A Lehigh University senior and athlete, envisioning failure on the eve of graduation, shot and killed one of his teachers today, then committed suicide. Two bullets in the chest, one near his heart, killed Charles Wesley Phy, 27, an instructor in the English department. Wesley L. Clow, 23, of Pine Castle, Fla., the student, shot himself in the head. Clow, rated just below a passing grade, demanded a re-examination of the young instructor. Harry Snavely, of Lancaster, Pa., another student and the only other person in the recitation room, said the instructor told Clow he needed written approval from the dean. “Well,” uttered Clow. Phy, apparently sighting a pistol, shouted, “Oh, don't,” Snavely related. Several shots rang out. Phy, wounded, ran from the room, collapsed in a downstairs corridor. He died in a hospital. Clow stepped outside the room and shot himse

NEW YORK, June 5.—()—The British liner Queen Mary sailed today on her first return trip eastward across the Atlantic, carrying 1855 passengers. Both the commander, Sir Edgar T. Britten and Sir Percy Bates, chairman of the board of the Cunard White Star Line, said the new queen of the seas would not attempt to establish any speed record for the west to east crossing.

GREENOCK, Scotland, (UP).— Ann Harding, movie star, arrived with her daughter in the liner Duchess of Atholl today with one handbag as her sole luggage. “I am not a fugitive from justice,” she said, discussing efforts of her husband to prevent her sailing for Great Britain with their daughter. Expressing astonishment that Harry Bannister, the husband, tried to cause her detention by getting an abduction warrant for her in Canada, Miss Harding said: Legal Custody of Child. “I have come to fulfill a motion picture contract which I signed more than a year ago. I have full legal custody of my child. “I intended originally to sail in the Empress of Australia. But when I learned my husband was flying to that vessel I changed my plans at the last minute and transferred to the Duchess of Atholl. I did not have time to get my luggage taken aboard. All I had for the voyage was one handbag.” Miss H

Nanking, June 5.—(/P)—An appeal to the United States, Japan, Great Britain, and other powers to help China by non-interference was broadcast tonight by Hsu Mo, political vice-minister of foreign affairs. He referred to the pledges given by these nations in the Washington treaty to permit China a full and unembarrassed opportunity to develop her national destiny without foreign interference.

| PARIS, Sept. 9 (UP)—As labor strikes spread in protest against the French government's refusal to support the left wing government in Spain, the French labor federation called on France, England and other governments today to reconsider their neutrality and non-intervention policies. Leon Jouhaux, president of the general labor federation, issued a communique announcing that the federation reaffirms its loyalty to the popular front government of Premier Leon Blum but asks France to demand a meeting of the League of Nations to proclaim the international right of nations to aid the established Spanish government.

GENEVA, June 5 (UP) — The League of Nations assembly was convoked today to meet June 30 to consider the Italian-Ethiopian problem, and perhaps to write its own fate in its decisions. Anthony Eden, British foreign secretary, will call a meeting of the league council, of which he is president, probably June 27. The assembly meeting was called at the demand of Argentina. That republic has decided never to recognize Italy's conquest of Ethiopia, it was understood, even though every other nation in the world does.

1936-06-06.text: London, England, June 8.—(P)—Prime Minister Baldwin today brought Sir Samuel Hoare, former foreign secretary, who resigned in disfavor over the Italo-Ethiopian war, back into the British cabinet. Sir Samuel was appointed first lord of the admiralty, succeeding Lord Monsell, who resigned. The official announcement of this appointment and resignation will be made tonight. Sir Samuel’s return to the cabinet, although long predicted, may raise a new public outcry, observers said, since he was forced out of the cabinet last December because of his agreement with Pierre Laval, then France’s foreign minister, on a plan for compromise with Italy in its campaign against Ethiopia.

LONDON, June 5—(#)—Great Britain called back into its cabinet fold tonight Sir Samuel Hoare, scapegoat of the much-maligned plan to end the Ethiopian war by giving Benito Mussolini only part of Ethiopia. Since then, Il Duce has taken it all. Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin openly defied critics and made the well-groomed Sir Samuel first lord of the admiralty. He succeeded Viscount Monsell, who for some time has desired to retire. The new minister first will face the task of liquidating British-Italian fleet difficulties in the Mediterranean. His appointment, some thought, might even be followed by a reduction of the number of war ships in that sea. Sir Samuel came back to the cabinet even as Emperor Haile Selassie, the African king without a country, received Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden and thanked him for Great Britain’s efforts to stem Italian aggression. Sir Samuel resigned from the

PARIS—(U.P.)—Premier Leon Blum, fighting an epidemic of strikes and the emergence of extremists of Right and Left Wing factions into open activity, promised today that he would keep Parliament in session until measures for a 40-hour working week, paid vacations and collective labor contracts were enacted. Blum made his promise in a radio speech just after he took formal office as head of the country’s first Socialist government. News that 254 new strikes had been declared in the last 24 hours greeted him as he appealed to the country for unity. Ready for any development, Blum called his cabinet into session and made sure that police and storm guards were ready for action—against the striking men who put him and his Left Wing government in action, if necessary. Even as Blum talked, Paris department store workers joined the strike. They locked the doors, keeping girl clerks inside and push

PARIS, June 6 — (AP) — Students and police fought in the Latin quarter in an outburst of violence tonight after socialist Premier Leon Blum had temporarily withdrawn from the chamber of deputies under a personal attack. A rightist deputy had assailed Blum as a Jew. The students demonstrated with shouts of “France for the French!” Sergeants-at-arms suppressed the outburst, which approached physical violence, in the chamber of deputies. Gendarmes broke up the student demonstration, making a dozen arrests. Striking employees of the afternoon newspaper, Paris Soir, beat up carriers who attempted to run through a picket line. Blum, returning to the chamber, declared flatly there would be “no devaluation of the franc!” Leftists, supporting the new socialist head of government, and the rightist opposition cheered, jeered, banged their desk tops and shouted, wrecking all order in the legislature

PARIS, June 6 (UP)---While strikers rioted in the streets, the left wing government of Premier Leon Blum today announced a program of labor and economic reforms designed to bring France out of the crisis caused by the walkout of a million workers and loss of great sums of gold. Blum's announcement of policies to be enacted into law next week, as the answer to labor demands, expressed in the countrywide strikes, precipitated a stormy scene in the chamber of deputies. And from the streets of Paris, rioting workers invaded a Paris newspaper office, smashing forms and upsetting type. Blum called for bills providing for the following points: a 40-hour week, collective bargaining, paid vacations, public works, nationalization of the munitions industry, revision of the unpopular economies decree of the Laval government and reform of the Bank of France.

By A. &. SLTUNLS. (Associated Press Foreign Staff.) Rome, June 6.—Premier Mussolini hurled a warning, cast in steel and men, at Italy’s critics today. The Fascist dictator called 40,000 soldiers in the army’s best motorized squadrons to parade the empire tomorrow as his gauge against possible criticism at future League of Nations session on the Ethiopian question. Their triumphal review will center at Rome where Viceroy Pietro Badoglio, victorious commander of the Ethiopian campaign, now in Italy, is to receive the accolade of hero from the nation’s highest leaders.

Paris, June 10 (AP)—France’s socialist premier, Leon Blum, went before parliament today with a new deal program intended to satisfy labor’s demands, revive business, and relieve the farmer. Peace for all Europe through collective security was announced as his foreign policy in the ministerial declaration to parliament. Simultaneously Blum took action to break a nation-wide strike of nearly one million workers, to revise the government's financial structure, and to co-ordinate France’s national defense. Blum warned parliament he would ward off any ‘attack on democratic institutions’—meaning an attempted dictatorship—with force in proportion to the threat or the resistance.

Paris, June 5. ()—France’s new leftist government appeared nearing success tonight in its rapid efforts to meet the demands of nearly 600,000 workers and to end strikes that paralyzed the nation’s industrial sector. An agreement with trade unions is expected tonight, Roger Salengro, minister of the interior, announced. He conferred with leaders of the General Confederation of Labor earlier. Leon Blum, Socialist premier who took over the government last night, asked for the formation of special parliamentary committees to facilitate the passage of bills meeting labor's demands. They would provide: 1—A 40-hour week. 2—Paid vacations in private industry. 3—Collective labor contracts. The government instructed police to arrest merchants trying to make big profits because of the scarcity of goods. Walkouts Spread Strikes spread rapidly in the northern textile industry with 80,000 estimated id

1936-05-09.text: London, May 8 ()—Great Britain has put up to Adolf Hitler the next move in negotiations for peace in Europe. A questionnaire submitted to Berlin by the British government and made public today has as a major point the stand that Germany should include Soviet Russia, Latvia and Estonia in her proposed non-aggression pacts. These pacts would substitute for the Locarno treaty, denounced by the Reich. A barrage of questions was laid down for Germany to clarify before Britain considers that negotiations for treaties can open, a government white paper disclosed.

Jerusalem, May 9. (.)—Haile Selassie, fugitive emperor of Ethiopia, asked today in his first public statement in exile, that justice be done his country. The emperor intends to go to London in three or four days, one of the imperial party said. Empress Mennen, who arrived here yesterday with the Negus, their children and closest followers, will remain in the Holy Land while the emperor proceeds to Europe.

Mansfield, O., day 9. Charles Wilson, 23, faced a sentence of life in the Ohio penitentiary today after a jury of 11 men and one woman convicted him of the slaying of his sweetheart, Jean Moorhead, 17. The jurors, told by Common Pleas Judge C. H. Huston "The defense has admitted the shooting and you cannot arrive at an acquittal verdict," brought in the verdict recommending mercy after four hours deliberation. Claimed Accident Miss Moorhead was shot and killed on the night of April 4 as she sat in an automobile in front of her home with Haskell Smith, 23. Wilson, who had known the girl for three years, testified the shooting was accidental. He had asked her to enter his automobile he said, and she refused to do so. Seven ballots were taken by the jurors. Two asked that Wilson be sentenced to the electric chair on the first ballot, one on the second. Two held out for conviction for second
