LONDON. Oct. 27. (*)—After wallowing helplessly for 24 hours in a wild storm on the Irish Sea, the 7,430-ton liner American Shipper hove to in Dublin bay Tuesday, victor over a destructive 100-mile gale sweeping the British Isles. The ship had lost her rudder. An unidentified vessel was reported driven aground by the raging winds which disrupted North Atlantic shipping off the Irish coast and spread destruction through Scotland and Ireland.

LONDON, Oct. 26 UP—Communism—described by the Nazi envoy as “the most terrible of all diseases”—drew a double-barrelled attack from two fascist European states Monday night. Almost before his train stopped at Victoria station, Joachim von Ribbentrop, “personal ambassador” for Reichs-chancellor Adolf Hitler, lashed out with an stinging assault against the Soviets, coupled with a renewed plea for Anglo-German friendship. Only Real Dangers ‘Der Führer is convinced the only real danger for Europe and the British Empire as well is the spreading of communism,” he told a top-hatted welcoming delegation. The second blow came from Portugal, allied with Germany and Italy in Russian accusations of alleged aid to Spanish insurgents, which charged Soviet agitators with being responsible for the situation in Spain provoking the fascist rebellion. Russia, the Portuguese declared in a note to the intern

NEW YORK, Oct. 27.—(AP)—Wintry winds slipping over Eastern and New England States sent the mercury tumbling to new depths today, bringing an abrupt end to the balmy temperatures of Indian summer. Blasts of near gale force with accompanying snow flurries and cold rain brought discomfort to upper Atlantic Seaboard residents who witnessed temperature drops of 20 to 32 degrees within 10 hours. Mt. Washington in New Hampshire, where an 80-mile-an-hour wind blew, recorded the lowest temperature in the East—two degrees above zero. New York's reading of 31 at midnight set a new low record for October 27 and approached the all-time low October mark of 24 degrees.

IPSWICH, England, Oct. 26 GP ~Discussion among members of the royal entourage as to whether King Edward would marry his American companion, Mrs. Ernest (Wallis) Simpson, gained impetus Monday night with the virtual certainty she would be granted a speedy divorce Tuesday. Mrs. Simpson remained at Felixstowe Monday night, and friends said she would attend court Tuesday with her counsel and one woman friend, while the king will preside over the privy council in London preparatory to the reassembling of parliament Thursday. Mrs. Simpson's undefended suit, charging infidelity, heads a list of those set to be heard Tuesday at 2:15 p.m. (9:15 a.m., EST) by Mr. Justice St. John Anthony Hawke, who customarily disposes of such cases in three minutes. Mrs. Simpson's husband, former officer of the exclusive Coldstream Guards, will leave London while the case is being heard, but will not go to Ipswic

1936-08-24.text: TOPEKA, KANS., SEPT 10, (AP). — A revised schedule of Governor Alf M. Landon’s eastern campaign trip to Maine today listed 14 rear platform talks in Indiana and New England. Speeches on the return itinerary still were under consideration. A last minute added stop as the presidential nominee heads for Portland to close the Maine state campaign Saturday night was Sterling Junction, Mass. The hour of the Republican candidate’s Portland talk was set at 8 p. m. Eastern Standard time.

NEW YORK—(P)—The giant liner Queen Mary claimed the blue ribbon for a record transatlantic crossing today after speeding from Cherbourg breakwater to Ambrose lightship in 4 days, 7 hours, 12 minutes. Despite encountering fog off New England, Cunard White Star line officials said the Queen Mary lowered the Normandie’s existing record by 4 hours, 30 minutes. Her average speed was 30.01 knots, 37 knots greater than the mark set by the French liner on her maiden voyage June 3, 1935. The lines had agreed that average speed rather than elapsed time would establish claim to the pennant of speed supremacy.

WASHINGTON, Aug. 24. (UP)—Governor Alf M. Landon and Col. Frank Knox carry the Republican campaign into New York and New England this week while President Roosevelt travels west to survey the drouth ravages. With nominations to national or state office also being made in four states, the political calendar promises more activity than in any seven-day span since the June conventions. Another series of statements for and against the New Deal started it out here today. Senator Joseph F. Guffey, chairman of the Democratic senatorial campaign committee, said votes in primaries and registration in California, Idaho, Kentucky and other states “show a vastly greater number of Democrats participating than Republicans.” He called this “proof of decisive Democratic success.” Speaking at Chautauqua, N. Y., today, Landon is expected to treat of education and religious tolerance. He will confer with s

Copyright 1936 United Press LONDON, Aug. 24.—Great Britain has narrowed to the formal three-mile limit the zone in which Spanish warships may question British ships and has threatened to use force to back its edict, it was disclosed today. The warning was made, it was announced, before the British steamship Gibel Zerjon was stopped in Gibraltar Straits yesterday by a Spanish warship, and an appeal for aid was answered by a squadron. Official notice has been given the Spanish government, it was announced, that British vessels will be protected if molested beyond the three-mile limit of Spanish waters and that the government will regard as illegal "the stopping or interfering with British ships for any purpose whatsoever." NEW YORK, Aug. 24. (AP)—The royal mail steamer, Queen Mary, pride of the British merchant fleet, steamed up New York harbor today with the fastest westward crossing of the Atlantic to her credit, but she wasn’t flying the blue pennant, symbol of Atlantic speed supremacy.

Latest Spanish war developments: BERLIN— Germany informs France she has placed an embargo on shipment of arms to Spain. LONDON— Britain warns Spain its ships must be respected outside 3-mile limit and threatens to use force if necessary. Latest search of British ship considered closed incident after apology. HENDAYE— Count Romanones and Santiago De Alba, powerful Spanish political figures, confer on French soil about possible conciliation. MADRID— Government may disarm restive workers, militia in capital or force them to fight at front. Government, combating rebels on dozen active fronts, expresses confidence of victory. No sign of rebel “big push” on Madrid yet. NAVALPERIAL— Moorish advance column repulsed by loyalists 60 miles from capital. VALLADOLID— Rebels claim 20 planes bombed Madrid airports (this denied in Madrid).

Twenty-four hours after Socialist Madrid had promised Great Britain to refrain from interfering with British shipping on the high seas, Gibraltar heard officially that loyal Spanish warships had prevented a little British freight and passenger steamer, the Gibel Zerjon, from entering the harbor at Melilla, Spanish Morocco. 1936-08-20.text: LONDON, Aug. 20—(4)—The Reuter (British) News Agency today reported from Madrid that the Ponta Vedea radio station announced Paulino Uzcudun, the Spanish prize fighter, had been killed with a number of others by a government firing squad. (Previous reports of the death of Uzcudun had gone unconfirmed. There was no confirmation, immediately, of today’s report from any source).

LONDON — Great Britain has received assurances, it was said today, that Premier Benito Mussolini shares its eagerness to prevent the spread of the Spanish civil war into a war that would engulf all Europe. The assurances were given by Count Galeazzo Ciano, foreign minister, and included a statement that Italy had not attempted any arrangement with Spanish insurgents regarding the future status of Morocco or the Balearics. The assurances were the outcome of a series of events moving Europe again toward war. Italian war maneuvers start next Tuesday. British secret naval maneuvers will start off Malta, opposite Italy, three days later, with Sir Samuel Hoare, first lord of the Admiralty, personally attending. France will conduct maneuvers — on the Spanish and Italian frontier areas — September seventh and one day later Russia has its gigantic maneuvers, with a British military mission, first

New York—(#)—A close friend of Dick Merrill disclosed Thursday that the veteran airmail pilot and Harry Richman, the singer, will try a round trip non-stop flight to Newfoundland Saturday or Sunday before they attempt their proposed round trip to London. They will make a complete check on the two-way radio installation on Richman’s big monoplane. The date of departure for London depends on the weather reports—but it must be soon, as Merrill is making it during his two weeks vacation. Five days of it are gone. Merrill's boss, Eddie Rickenbacker, expressed confidence in his No. 1 pilot. “I’m sure he'll make the trans-Atlantic flight without trouble. His chances? About the same as walking across Fifth—at least 99 per cent.”

HAGERSTOWN, Md., Aug. 20.—Frank Knox, Republican vice-presidential nominee left here today to carry his party's campaign into New England, after advocating a national government of simplicity, economy and certainty. Knox and Alf M. Landon, GOP presidential candidate, within the next week will inaugurate the Republican campaign in the East, Landon with three addresses starting Saturday night at West Middlesex, Pa, and Knox at Hampton Beach, N. H. A week from tonight, Knox last night spoke to the annual convention of the United Retail Merchants Association, composed of business men from West Virginia, Pennsylvania, Maryland and Virginia.

London, Aug. 19 (#)—The government of Great Britain tonight clamped an airtight embargo on the export of both civil and military planes to either of the Spanish belligerents, and a suggestion was broached that the United States act as truce maker. The government stressed the critical importance of non-intervention of any type in the Spanish civil war. The action was described in authoritative quarters as demonstrating Britain’s earnestness by going a step beyond the limitations laid down in the original agreement to French neutrality proposals. It was pointed out Britain previously had agreed to prohibit export of planes to Spain only if the other powers pledged themselves to do likewise.

Spanish government troops today established a new line of defense about 100 miles southwest of Madrid, claiming that rebels had been put to flight. Meanwhile France and Great Britain, informed Paris sources said, may undertake mediation in an attempt to prevent the reported Spanish government search of a German merchant ship from having repercussions. The German government, in an ultimatum to Madrid, announced that its warships would prevent the repetition of the reported incident with "all of its means."

LONDON, Aug. 20. — The British government, trying to bolster by its own example the lagging European negotiations for neutrality in the Spanish civil war, issued through the air ministry today a warning threatening cancellation or suspension of the flying license of any aviator who aids either side. The warning concerned any pilot convicted of violating the ban on the export of aircraft to Spain, such as false customs declarations as to the point of destination. "All pilots," the notice said, "are warned that a serious view will be taken of any attempt to deliver aircraft directly or indirectly to Spain, Spanish possession or Spanish Morocco." The British government took a serious view of the possibility that the negotiations for a general non-intervention pact might fail. Italy, Germany, and at least one other country have all agreed, but reservations have been made by France and Italy

BY UG ASKOUIAICR ICKS, Spanish Situation at a Glance. Italian officials see possibility of neutrality accord, although press condemns alleged indirect intervention by France in Spain; Mussolini’s preparation for any eventuality called complete, Britain embargoes arms and plane shipments to Spain; U. S. mediation suggested. German government reported ready to support a Spanish fascist regime if it can maintain order and protect foreigners; rebels predict Italian and German recognition if Madrid falls. Spanish government said to be seeking allies by disclosing Italian backing of revolters. Loyalists claim victory at Avila, saying 500 insurgents killed or captured and six big guns seized. Three rebel planes and one warship bomb San Sebastián, northern city, killing three. Autonomous Catalonian government moves for virtual secession from Madrid after confiscating all private property on Russ

1936-10-07.text: LONDON, Oct. 7. Informed sources said today Great Britain, concerned over a possible competitive race to fortify Pacific insular naval bases, has approached the United States and Japan concerning renewal of article 19 of the Washington naval treaty, which expires this year. This article deals with the status quo in the Pacific. Oral discussions, the British sources stated, now are going on in both Washington and Tokyo. Answers from the two countries have not been disclosed, but were said to be, as yet, incomplete. Great Britain, it was stated, does not favor new rearmament expenditures in the Pacific, but prefers an extension of the non-fortification clause in some form. Under the terms of article 19 of the Washington naval treaty of 1922, the United States, Great Britain and Japan agreed to maintain the status quo of the Pacific in regard to fortifications and naval bases in the followi

TAIHOKU, Formosa, Oct. 7 — (AP)—Three officers of the British submarine mothership Micway were held today for examination by police under charges of photographing Japanese fortifications. The photographs were made from the ship now anchored here, police alleged.

By The Associated Press London, Eng. — A Reuters (British) news agency dispatch from Stockholm said Kurt Bjorkvall, trans-Atlantic flyer, was believed sighted today 40 miles south of Christiansund, the most southerly point of Norway.

By United Press LONDON, Oct. 7.—The Soviet government gave warning today that unless other powers refrain from giving aid to the faction in the Spanish civil war, Russia will feel free to proceed as she sees fit.

LONDON, Oct. 7.—Great Britain proposed to the United States and Japan today that article 19 of the Washington naval treaty of 1921 banning fortifications in certain parts of their Pacific possessions, be renewed. The agreement will expire at the end of this year. Great Britain at the same time proposed that the signatories agree not to establish air bases in the unfortified zone. This new suggestion results from the development of air forces and their importance since the negotiation of the original treaty. London already has inquired, it was understood, the attitude of Washington and Tokyo toward the proposal. It was understood that they have replied tentatively, although the negotiations still are in an embryonic stage. It was indicated in authoritative diplomatic circles that a failure to renew article 19 would create the danger of an expensive naval race among the great sea powers an

BATON ROUGE, La., Oct. 7.—()—The state administration and share our wealth organization in Louisiana, composed of followers of Senator Huey P. Long, were declared today to have split definitely with the Rev. Gerald L. K. Smith. Paul English, who said he had been appointed state share our wealth organizer by Gov. Richard W. Leche, asserted the administration and the Louisiana share our wealth clubs refused to recognize Smith as a share our wealth leader, spokesman or representative. English, like Smith, traveled over the United States while Senator Long was alive, organizing share our wealth clubs. English said Smith had “cut himself off” from the share our wealth movement by “allying himself” with the Townsend pension plan, and that the share our wealth societies in Louisiana would ignore him and continue to operate with the help of the state administration.

WASHINGTON, Oct. 7.—(P)—Great Britain has communicated with this government relative to possible continuation of a ban on new fortifications in the Pacific Ocean, state department officials revealed today. Officials said the British communication was under consideration by the department, but that no answer had yet been sent. They declined to reveal whether it was a formal note or merely a "feeler" to sound out this government’s sentiment. The ban in question, provided by article 19 of the Washington naval treaty which expires on Dec. 31, provides that Great Britain, the United States, and Japan will maintain the "status quo" of fortifications in the Pacific at the time the treaty was signed in 1922.

MOSCOW, Oct. 7 (®) — Karl Radek, commentator for the government newspaper Izvestia, was arrested today on charges of being implicated in the counter-revolutionary plot against the Soviet for which 16 Russians were shot last August. Radek, one of the best-known Russian editorial writers, was one of five men under investigation in an alleged plot to overthrow the government and kill Dictator Joseph Stalin. His name was announced by Prosecutor Andrey Vishinsky at the trial of the 16 confessed plotters Aug. 21. Later, Radek disappeared and his whereabouts were unknown until his arrest was announced today. The other four whose records were declared under scrutiny include M. P. Tomsky, former chief of trade unions and present head of the state publishing house; Nikolai Bukharin, editor of Izvestia; Alexi Rykov, former commissar of posts and telegraphs; and Gregory Pyatakoff, assistant commissa

1936-08-21.text: (BY THE ASSOCIATED PRESS) Stern orders to keep Spain’s civil war in bounds were flashed today to the warship bridges of two great powers—Great Britain and Germany. England, adopting a similar policy to that of the Reich, served notice on Madrid that British warships will fire warning shots, “then aim,” if they are fired upon by Spanish vessels. Only yesterday, Germany, enraged by the reported search of a German merchant ship by a Loyalist Spanish warship, ordered its men-of-war to answer “force with force.” That drew tighter the gathering international lines between Fascism and Socialist-Communist liberalism. Britain, however, made it clear her action, announced today, was independent of the Reich. Hours of anxiety, spurred by reports of a revolt in Portugal, gave way to relief when the rumors fell short of confirmation. The United States, determined as ever to remain “scrupulously” aloo

Copyright 1936 by United Press | London— (U.P) —Great Britain sternly warned Spanish loyalists and rebels Friday that it will protect its ships from any illegal interference and will fire on any airplanes that persist in flying over Gibraltar. If Spanish airplanes fly over Gibraltar, British guns will fire three warning shots. Then, if the airplane has not made off, they will fire at the planes. The order, by a government that it is understood would regard a victory for loyalists as a lesser threat to peace than a Spanish Fascist state, was regarded as dramatic evidence of the grave alarm Britons feel. Fear Explosion The stoppage of a German steamship by loyalist warships, and a consequent warning by Germany that it would meet force with force to protect its ships in Spanish waters, brought to the urgent point fear there may be an international explosion. So great was the alarm that it w

LONDON, Aug. 21—(4)—Unconfirmed reports reaching London early today said a revolution had broken out in Portugal and that it was believed President Oscar Carmona had been killed. No messages had been received here from Lisbon, the Portuguese capital, in nine hours. It had been impossible to telephone Portugal for the past ten days. Only outgoing calls had been accepted from all points in the country. It was learned the Lisbon radio station had been silent throughout the night, Ordinarily the Lisbon Radio Club has broadcast frequent bulletins at night regarding the Spanish civil war. President Carmona, first elected Nov. 29, 1926, ruled Portugal as dictator since a new constitution was adopted March 19, 1933. He was reelected president for a seven-year term Feb. 17, 1935, by an estimated majority of 1,000,000 votes. The Portuguese government, while adhering last week in principle to Franc

| HOLLYWOOD, Aug. 21 WUP— | Ruby Loraine, English film comedienne and wife of novelist Rupert Grayson, was taken to a private hospital today for medical treatment of injuries suffered when she was beaten in her home by an armed prowler. | The actress was attacked in the kitchen of her Beverly Hills home shortly before midnight and during a struggle attempted to shoot her. Miss Loraine grasped the man’s arm just before he pulled the trigger, and the bullet hit the kitchen ceiling. The prowler fled when neighbors who heard the actress scream came rushing towards the house. The only clue he left behind was a white handkerchief-mask which Miss Loraine tore from his face during her battle with him.

Paris, Aug. 21—The French minister to Lisbon today protested to the Portuguese government the arrest of a Paris newspaper correspondent as unconfirmed reports reached here that a revolution had broken out against President Oscar Carmona. (A Lisbon dispatch to London said the country was quiet). The correspondent, Jacques Berthet of the Paris Le Temps, was charged with sending a tendentious telegram which the newspaper said it had not received. After the minister intervened in an attempt to obtain the release of the correspondent, officials said the "Demarche was quite natural" but the result of the protest was not learned. The telephone company reported communications were interrupted both to Spain and to Portugal, preventing any immediate check to determine whether a second revolution was stirring the Peninsula. The government radio bureau said communications were normal with Lisbon unt

Omaha (/) Arrest of two men believed to have robbed a bank at Elliott, Ia., last Tuesday of $1,164 was announced late today by Inspector Fritz Franks of the Omaha police department. Franks gave the names of the pair as Albert England and Orie England, cousins, both of Omaha, and said Albert England had confessed.

NEW YORK, Aug. 20—(4)—Dick Merrill, Airlines pilot on a busman's holiday, and Harry Richman, flying actor, worked in the heat of the airport at Newark, N. J., today, making final preparations for their proposed round-trip flight to London. The time, they have decided now is a start at 5 P. M. Monday, a flight to London in 16 hours, tea in the British capital, and a return to New York for a late breakfast Wednesday, weather permitting.

LONDON, Aug. 21--()- Britain warned chaotic Spain today it will take “stern measures” against ships or warplanes which endanger British lives and property. Authoritative quarters stated the warning which followed Germany’s “force meet force” ultimatum, applied to the activities of Spanish warships and plans of both the Spanish socialist government and its fascist rebel foes. At the same time, informed quarters denied reports the government had warned Madrid it would not tolerate a blockade or that it had urged Germany and Italy not to act precipitously. Britain has recognized no blockade, these sources said. Nor has there been any mention of “tolerance,” they added. Authoritative quarters said in the event a British ship was fired upon, it would return three warning shots ahead of the offending craft and then, “we shall air.” The Madrid government, these quarters stated, has been informe

1936-11-01.text: by the Associated Press London—Wallis Warfield Simpson went to the country tonight—probably, her friends said, as the guest of the king at his country residence, Fort Belvedere. She sought seclusion after perhaps the most exciting week of her life, during which the marriage bonds with her second husband, Ernest Simpson, were broken. Still In Dark Only a small percentage of Britain’s population was cognizant, even yet, of the monarch’s friendship with the divorcee. One well-known laborite member of parliament expressed his feeling this way: “Bully for the king! His Majesty should marry first and tell parliament later. They'll like it. “England likes a man with backbone. The king has the backbone to do what he wants.” So They Won't Talk In diplomatic circles there was discreet silence regarding Mrs. Simpson. One diplomat whispered, “I'm afraid the slightest word about her might be misconst

NEW YORK, Oct. 31 (UP).—Members of the International Seamen's Union voted tonight to call an immediate strike on their own initiative after officers of the organization opposing the proposal were noisily overruled. The action climaxed an uproarious meeting at the Cooper Union during which more than five persons were evicted from the hall. The vote, in line with proposals to support dissatisfied marine workers on the Pacific coast, threatened to complete an incipient tie-up of shipping throughout the country.

NEW YORK, Oct. 31,—President Roosevelt drove his campaign to a climax tonight by giving what he called his “answer” to those who, silent about their own plans, ask us to state our objectives. Over and over again he repeated: “We have just begun to fight.” The chief executive spoke to a gigantic Democratic rally in Madison Square Garden, welcoming the hatred of those favoring government administrations, and giving his own definition of the campaign issue as follows: “In 1932 the issue was the restoration of American democracy and the American people were in a mood to win. They did win. “In 1938 the issue is the preservation of their victory. Again, they are in a mood to win. Again they will win.” He said the New Deal's vision for the future contains more than promises, but he left for the future what steps, legislative or otherwise, would be taken to reach them. Work for Workers “Of cours

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 31—(?)— The maritime strike extended its clutch today to certain overland railroad cargo, tied up more eastern ships, spread its chill farther along the business front and caused official concern over its possible effects upon Alaska and Hawaii. The Maritime Engineers’ union ordered its license-bearing members to resign and leave the engine rooms of strike-bound coast ships. Heretofore the unions have permitted the ships to keep engineering officers. Shipowners again refused to resume peace conversations as long as the 37,000 coast maritime and (Continued on Page 12, Col. 3.)

St. Louis—(#)—Gov. Alf M. Landon pledged a restoration of “good government” bringing “full recovery and re-employment,” in a final campaign address Saturday night, contending New Deal “broken promises” were “holding us back” by destroying confidence. “It has tried to run from its record instead of on its record,” the republican nominee said of his democratic opponent’s administration, adding that it was “shocking” to see reelection “on the basis of recovery” when 11,000,000 were unemployed. Landon told his St. Louis audience in the Municipal auditorium, and the nation over the radio, that “the two biggest jobs” today were getting the 11,000,000 back to work and “stopping the pouring of our money through the great political sieve at Washington.” “The two jobs are wrapped together,” the Kansan said. “We cannot live forever off tomorrow’s income. We cannot live forever by borrowing from our

HOLLYWOOD, Calif. (4) — Although it was paged over a thunderous public address system, the spirit of Harry Houdini failed to appear at a public seance Saturday night, on the tenth anniversary of his death. “He has not come,” sobbed his widow, the silver-haired little Beatrice Houdini. “I turn out the light.” She touched the switch on a little electric light which she said has been burning steadily over the picture of the great magician ever since his death. The seance, held on the roof of a Hollywood hotel, was attended by more than 200 persons, including newspapermen, newsreel crews, and the attendants for a temporary radio station.

NEW YORK, Oct. 31 (Header by Minnesota’s Gophers, the mighty fell in droves today in the greatest succession of upsets this or possibly any other football campaign ever saw. Stopped by Northwestern's Wildcats, 6-0, in a spectacular duel fought before 47,000 in Branson, Minnesota saw its national and Big Ten championship dreams exploded along with the shattering of the longest current winning streak in the game. The Gophers had won 21 games in a row and gone undefeated in 28 games since Michigan beat them in the final game of the 1932 season. Joining the Gophers in the battering list were Yale, Army, Holy Cross and Villanova in the East, and Texas A and M in the Southwest while Fordham’s Rams and Utah State, boasting hitherto spotless records, were toppled. Fordham, conqueror of Southern Methodist and St. Mary's in its drive for possible Rose Bowl recognition, held Pitt's formidable Panth

WASHINGTON, Oct. 31.—()— Most of the nation east of the Rocky Mountains may march to the polls Tuesday in the rain, Uncle Sam's weather men indicated today. The weather outlook for election day, which politicians watch for its effect on the farm vote, struck a particularly dubious note for the New England shopkeeper and the prairie plowman. Cold and possibly wet weather, it said, threatened polling places all along the east coast from New England down to Virginia. The outlook included, also, the vast expanse of Pennsylvania, New York, Maryland and numerous eastern states with large industrial populations. Rain was expected to start "sometime Tuesday" and continue Wednesday. Heavy precipitation was indicated for Ohio valley states and Tennessee Monday, possibly ending on Tuesday with warmer weather. Comparatively cold weather with rather frequent rainfall threatened voters of the Great La

1936-10-04.text: WASHINGTON, Oct. 3 /Pi—Treasury officials estimated Saturday that the government might claim more than $1,000,000 of a legendary treasure which salvagers hope to take from a British warship sunk 150 years ago off the east shore of Manhattan island. Search for the $4,800,000 of gold and silver reputed to be in the silt choked hull of the British frigate Hussar is being pressed by Simon Lake, 70-year-old Connecticut submarine inventor. Treasury attaches said they already had made a bargain with Lake for dividing the spoils—if they ever are fished from the bottom of the East river. Although the nation has legal rights in “wrecked or abandoned property,” treasury experts said, it usually gives a large share to the discoverer. In this case, Lake's salvaging firm would keep 90 percent of the treasure, while the government would take about $480,000. A substantial income tax would be collectable

By The Associated Press Madrid— (Sunday)—Evacuation of Madrid, nearly encircled by Fascist battle lines, was reported early today to have begun following a new bombardment by insurgent planes. Wounded government militiamen and children were understood to have been the first to leave the city. They Travel East They were said to be going to Valencia, on the Mediterranean coast to the east. (In that direction alone could persons flee from the capital without encountering the Fascist forces, which were strung south, west and north of Madrid.) Officials reported the insurgents had dropped 45 bombs in the latest raid but that there were no casualties and little damage. North of Madrid, surging fascist attacks broke on the government's defenses.

Paris, Oct. 3 (4’)—The government tonight ordered 8,500 mobile guardsmen and heavy regular police detachments to mass in the Parc des Princes where communists and rightists announced simultaneous demonstrations would be held Sunday. Police ripped down placards posted by rightist followers of Col. François de la Rocque, calling upon citizens to attend his demonstration to show “the red fascists we are on guard.” The “social party” of Col. De La Rocque, former head of the disbanded rightist “Cruz de Fue,” has been ordered the subject of criminal investigation by the government of socialist Premier Leon Blum. The communists, in the face of the mobile guard orders, appealed to their partisans to “ignore all provocations.” The guardsmen's patrols were relaxed somewhat after the one-day strike of Paris hotel, restaurant and cafe employees was settled. The men agreed to return to work Sunday af

TOKYO, UP, Tokyo residents breathed easily Saturday night after a strong typhoon, which threatened to bring death and destruction on this capital, veered eastward and passed out over the Pacific Ocean. It left a death toll estimated unofficially at 70. The 280 ton tramp steamer Kashima Maru was reported to have foundered off the west central Korean coast with a loss of 60 passengers and four crewmen. By a strange coincidence the stricken vessel had the same name as that of the Nippon Yusen Kaisha liner which carried Japanese athletes returning from the Olympic games in Germany. That ship arrived safely in Tokyo. The German steamship Ursula Rickmers, reporting she was afire off Yokohama, asked for assistance. At the Kure naval base on the island of Honshu 60 workmen were understood to have been rescued from the churning sea after their tender turned over.

With Government Troops, Mora, Spain, Oct. 3. (4) — Government forces tonight fought to outflank the Fascist southern wing closing in on Madrid from Toledo. Fresh reinforcements sent up to the front from Madrid swung in a surprise maneuver out and around the town of Olias del Rey, about 3 miles south of Madrid. The line stretched over an important railway bridge and off to Mora, which is 55 miles almost due south of the capital, thence zigzagging southwest and southeast. Fascist "black birds of death"—as the government men term the insurgent warplanes—spotted troop movements and bombed the most concentrated government units. The railroad line into Madrid, another target for the Fascist airmen, escaped serious damage. Only two houses were demolished by the bombs loosed by the sky.

VERSAILLES, France (Sunday) (Fe-The left wing of the famous Chateau of Versailles, once the home of Louis XIV and now a public museum, was damaged by fire early Sunday but the blaze did not spread to the main part of the great palace.

ROME, Oct. 3—(4)—The Italian empire celebrated today the first anniversary of the beginning of the Italo-Ethiopian war. Flags and bunting flew from houses and public buildings. Band concerts were given in the parks. Newspapers published lengthy accounts of the invasion of Ethiopia which resulted in victory for the black-shirted troops and annexation of the East African kingdom to Italy.

SHANGHAI, Oct. 3. (*)—A marked slackening of the tension which gripped Shanghai following the death sentence meted out to two Chinese over the slaying of a Japanese naval officer, resulted Saturday as the majority of Japanese guards was withdrawn from the Hongkew district. Panicky Chinese, who had begun to evacuate the Hongkew district to seek refuge in the International Settlement, began to return to their homes, still nervous but reassured by posters declaring: “The situation is the result of evil-mongers. Do not believe the rumors;

1936-07-18.text: LONDON, July 18. — (#) — Scotland Yard officials torn between a desire to please their sovereign and their duty to protect him, decided today King Edward would have to be induced to change his habits. An authoritative source, reflecting public anxiety over the attempt to assassinate the king Thursday, indicated pressure would be brought to induce the king to give up his strolls on the streets, Instead of being able to mingle with his subjects, Edward probably will be forced to travel about London in an automobile as his father, the late King Edward, always did. George Andrew McMahon, who disturbed the empire with his attempt against the king on Constitution Hill, was questioned again. It was understood he stuck to his story that he never intended to shoot the king but that he threw his revolver at the mounted monarch as “a protest.” Summoned by a public call for witnesses of the incident

London, July 17—King Edward's grateful subjects visited Scotland Yard today to tell the fateful story of Constitution Hill while physicians examined a seeming, would-be assassin in a prison hospital mental ward. The "yard" said its officers were "flooded" by callers in response to an appeal for clear versions of what happened hard by Wellington Arch yesterday. Stenographers took scores of pages of depositions for sifting evidence in the case against George Andrew McMahon, bald, crippled Irishman whom his neighbors called with British restraint: "Rather a crank." King Perfectly Calm A charge of carrying a revolver with intent to "endanger life" still stood against McMahon, although he was reported authoritatively to have declared today his loaded revolver was not knocked from his hand as the king rode by, but instead that he threw it deliberately in the street near the king. He had no int

TAMPA, Fla — () — Anxious owners asked additional aid today in a search for the British motorship Nunoca, ten days overdue on a voyage from the West Indies to Tampa with 21 aboard. The 110-foot vessel left George- town, Grand Cayman, on July 4, and should have reached here four days later. Only enough provisions for the regular trip were carried, Coast guard amphibians flew along the southwestern Florida coast yesterday. The coast guard was ready to press the hunt today with planes and boats. Capt. M. I. Kirkconnell was in command with a crew of eight, and the owners said 12 passengers were aboard.

LONDON, July 18—The Duchess of Kent is expecting the birth of a second child, a usually reliable source said today. Toward the end of the summer the duchess is expected to cancel all social engagements. The Duke and Duchess of Kent have one son, Prince Edward, born Oct. 9, 1985. The duke is the youngest brother of King Edward VIII, and the duchess is the former Princess Marina of Greece. They were married Nov. 29, 1934.

BOSTON, July 18—(AP)—John D. M. Hamilton, chairman of the Republican national committee, completed his swing through New England today, expressing hope that Alfred E. Smith would give active support to the Landon-Knox ticket. “Someone asked me the other day,” Hamilton told a Massachusetts rally last night, “if Al Smith was going to join us. “I hope so. We are going to have some very reputable and respectable Democrats with us in this fight.” Hamilton showed the gathering of party workers a copy of a letter which he said was from Governor Leslie A. Miller of Wyoming, Democrat, to a man seeking a job as foreman in the civilian conservation corps, and also a copy of an application blank which Hamilton said Miller sent to the job applicant. He said the blank asked such questions as: “How long have you been a registered Democrat? What service have you given the Democratic party, did you contr

LONDON, July 13 (Saturday). — The Reuters (British) news agency said today telephone communication between Spain and the rest of the world had been cut off. The agency stated the cause was believed to be serious political reasons. An official of the British Telephone Company stated: "We have been notified no calls will be accepted in Spain tonight." MADRID, July 18 (Saturday).— Strict censorship was being applied early today on telephone calls to and from Madrid. Officials said heavy precautions against disorder were being taken throughout the country, but that tranquility prevailed. President Manuel Azaña urgently left the presidential home at 10:30 p.m. last night and took up residence at the national palace. The foregoing dispatch, received in London by telephone, was ended by the Associated Press correspondent at Madrid with the remark, "This is all I am allowed to tell you."

LONDON, July 18. — Expectation that babies will be among the targets for aviators in the next war has led the government to develop gas mask covers for baby buggies, it was reported today. Attached to the covers will be filters through which air can be pumped to the babies by their gas masked nurses during air raids.

Rebellion broke out in Spanish Morocco today and in London and Paris there were reports, quickly denied by Spanish authorities, that there was fighting in Spain itself. In Madrid the government announced that it expected to crush the revolt shortly. Strict censorship was invoked and President Manuel Azana took up residence in the national palace while the government took precautions against trouble. Madrid was quiet but tense. Reports received at Hendaye, on the French border, that fighting had broken out at Cadiz, Seville, Burgos and Huelva, but these reports also were not borne out by any official word. The first outbreak was at Melilla, Morocco, where Colonel Elittella and the entire garrison under his command hurried to Melilla to take charge of the situation. Some of the reports attributed the revolt to monarchists while others said it was purely military in character. There was no

1936-08-15.text: (By the Associated Press) | Government forces repulsed a savage rebel attack directed today against Irun on the Bay of Biscay. A grave warning was issued by the British foreign office. The five-hour assault was the heaviest and most vicious yet thrown at government strongholds in the coastal section. The fate of hostages, held by the government and threatened with death should rebels advance against either Irun or San Sebastian, was not known. Rebel troops massed on a road leading into Irun under protection of an artillery barrage. They were met with a withering government fire. Casualties were heavy on both sides. American Reported Rescued J. O. Ambler, an American held hostage in Huelva province by government forces, was reported rescued along with 37 British subjects. Execution of seven officers charged with resisting the government’s capture of key points in San Sebastian some days a

HENDAYE, French-Spanish Frontier—(P)—The United States Coast Guard Cutter Cayuga and the British Destroyer Comet trained their guns on the Spanish rebel cruiser Almirante Cervera when it threatened to fire on them as they embarked refugees, it was understood today. The Almirante Cervera retreated. The Almirante Cervera was cruising in the Gulf of Gascony. It approached the Cayuga and the Comet, its eight 6-inch guns trained on them, as the American cutter and the British destroyer were embarking neutral refugees at San Sebastian. “We will open fire on you if you help government adherents to escape among the refugees,” threatened the rebel cruiser by wireless. “Thank you,” replied the Cayuga. The Cayuga’s one 5-inch gun and its two 6-pounders, and the Comet's four 4.7’s were turned on the Almirante Cervera. The rebel ship steamed out and lay offshore while embarking of refugees continued.

LYMPNE, Eng. (AP). Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh landed at the airdrome here after a flight from Copenhagen in their private airplane. The flying Lindberghs had been in the Danish city for a demonstration, in co-operation with Dr. Alexis Carrel, of a mechanical heart developed by the colonel and Dr. Carrel.

Withering artillery on machine gun fire from Spanish government strongholds near Irun repulsed 2 savage rebel attacks today and Great Britain warned that meddling in the civil strife might bring “serious repercussions.” Casualties were heavy on both sides in the five-hour battle, the heaviest and most vicious assault launched by the rebels thus far in the four weeks old war against any hope of Biscay city. Whipped, the rebels retreated after the bloody battle from the well-entrenched government positions. Massed along a six-mile front the rebels attacked under protection of artillery, bolstering the assault were two airplanes which bombed the city, a companion community to San Sebastián. Only one civilian was reported killed. The London warning, issued by the British foreign office, announced the British intention of using “every measure open to them to prevent supply of civil aircraft”

LONDON. (?). A crowd of 90,000 packed White City Saturday and saw America’s track and field forces defeat the British Empire 11 to 3, in the sixth quadrennial meet between the two nations. Three world records fell during the afternoon, all in the relays. Chuck Hornbostel, Bob Young, Charley Williamson and John Woodruff set a new standard of 7:35.8 for two miles; Hornbostel, Gene Venzke, Archie San Romani and Glenn Cunningham were clocked in the new record time of 17:17.2 for four miles, and a British combination established a new mark of 3:10.6 for the one mile relay.

HENDAYE — United States and British warships train guns on rebel cruiser when it threatens to fire on them while evacuating refugees; rebels start smashing drive on Irun, MADRID. — Northern miners, hurling dynamite, blast way through Oviedo. LISBON. — Rebels penetrate streets of Badajoz in fierce struggle for city. PORTB, Spanish-French border — Ruthless executions reported daily in Barcelona and other parts of Catalonia. LONDON. — British government, taking neutrality stand, warns Britons they will not be protected if they aid either side in Spain.

London, Aug. 15 (P)--Red mobs control Madrid and the Spanish foreign office admitted it could not guarantee safety of foreign representatives who were preparing to quit the capital, it was said by highly reliable diplomatic quarters. One of the diplomats still in Madrid cabled his foreign office, it was stated, and advised that a final meeting would be held today to dissolve the diplomatic corps and make plans to quit the country.

LONDON, Aug. 15, 22 — The British government announced an agreement with Paris on an arms and munitions embargo today even as it warned Europe that meddling in the Spanish civil war might bring "serious repercussions." A prohibition on shipments of war materials to revolution-torn Spain awaited, however, assent from the German, Italian, Portuguese and Russian governments. Only a few hours before the proposed embargo accord was approved, a grave warning to all Europe was issued by Downing Street. Non-Intervention Essential "Maintenance of a strict, impartial attitude of non-intervention is essential if the unhappy events in Spain are to be prevented from having serious repercussions elsewhere," the government declared in a communique. Notes were signed and exchanged between Paris and London this afternoon, the foreign office announced to bar exports of arms and munitions. The foreign offi

1936-08-27.text: Copyright, 1936, Associated Press Spain’s Socialist strong man, declaring his war-torn country the “Ethiopia of Europe,” burst out today in bitter denunciation of France and Great Britain. Indalecio Prieto, who as leader of the parliamentary Socialist party is the most important man behind the Madrid government, declared Spain had been deserted by the very countries which should be its allies in a fight against the spread of European fascism. The European neutrality pact, he asserted, will hurt Socialist Spain rather than help it because, he said, Germany, Italy and Portugal will sign the pact and go on supplying arms to the Fascist rebels. MAY GIVE UP ISLANDS Germany, he said, eventually will present its bill if the rebels win, and he suggested the possibility that Gen. Francisco Franco, the insurgent commander-in-chief, might one day give the Balearic Islands to one of the Fascist powe

London, Aug. 21—(4)—Rebel airplanes bombarded Madrid Wednesday night, private uncensored information reaching London tonight asserted. Damage to Madrid was said to have been slight. In Madrid an official government communique said that a rebel airplane had been shot down by machinegun fire in a frustrated attempt to bomb Madrid.

Washington, Aug. 27. (7)—Secretary Hull today declined to reconsider the State Department's action in declining to permit William Gallacher, communist member of the British Parliament, to enter this country because of his political belief. Answering a protest by the American Civil Liberties Union, the Secretary said Gallacher was well known as a member of the executive committee of the Communist Internationale and that “his position in the international communist revolutionary movement brings him within the excluding provisions” of the immigration law.

WASHINGTON, Aug. 27—(P)—William Gallacher, communist member of the British parliament, now traveling in Canada, was refused entrance to this country today by the United States government under the immigration act prohibiting members of groups having as their objective the overthrow of organized governments. The state department said Gallacher is a member of the central committee of Communist International with headquarters in Moscow.

Indalecio Prieto, leader of the Spanish parliamentary socialist party, denounced France and Great Britain today, saying Spain had been deserted by the very countries which should be her allies in the fight against the spread of European fascism. He said the neutrality pact hurt Socialist Spain because of Germany, Italy and Portugal signing and going on supplying arms to the Fascist rebels. Fighting went on in Spain today, the loyalists announcing a victorious counter-offensive in the Bay of Biscay, moving in on the rebel city of Oviedo. The rebels claimed they are about to capture an important southern Malaga seaport. The United States warned today that she will insist on the freedom of the seas for American shipping, saying Spain has no right to bar merchant vessels unless it applies an effective blockade.

NEW YORK, Aug. 27.—(INS)— Dr. Frank H. Vizetelly, noted lexicographer, said today that the word “cockeyed” used by Gov. Alfred M. Landon, in his speech at Buffalo last night, was derived from the Gaelic and had been in the English language for more than 100 years. The G. O. P. candidate for the presidency used the word to describe the tax on undistributed corporate earnings. Dr. Vizetelly said it came originally from the Gaelic “caogshull” and “cagoshuigeach,” meaning lopsided or squint-eyed. The first known use of the word in English literature, Dr. Vizetelly added, was when Byron, in 1821, referred to a “merry cockeyed curious looking stripe.”

COPYRIGHT 1936 BY UNITED PRESS Lisbon, Aug. 27, (U.P)—Spanish rebels, still on the aggressive, opened the second day of their attack on Irun today and disclosed plans for an attack on Madrid next week. The loyalist government at Madrid, by making a war zone of the country south and southwest of the capital, admitted by implication the steady if slow advance of a formidable force northeastward from the Estremadura country. Besieged rebels continued their surprisingly stubborn defense of Oviedo. Rebels at Toledo, holding the ancient Alcazar fortress, raised a white flag on the battlements but tore it down and fired on loyalists who approached. In small fighting zones all over

The German Reichsbank president was represented as picturing German prosperity as the best guarantee of European peace and hinting that a prosperous Germany would be much less a menace to France than a Germany driven to desperation by economic hardships. 1936-09-24.text: SHANGHAI —(U.P)— British and American troops were instructed today to prepare for the defense of their national interests in the event of a serious outbreak between China and Japan over the killing of a Japanese sailor here yesterday. British troops prepared to patrol the international settlement bridge, United States Marines stood by in barracks.

DORCHESTER, N. B., Sept. 23 (UP) — The brothers Bannister, Daniel, 20, and Arthur, 19, stood back to back on the gallows trap early today and dropped through together to death. They killed Phillip Lake, 30, his wife, and their eldest child in the New Brunswick backwoods last January, and kidnapped the Lakes’ six-month-old baby so their mother would have an infant to show two lovers whom she was blackmailing.

LONDON, Sept. 23 (4)—A scathing criticism of General John J. Pershing and of the whole American World War machine is contained in the fifth volume of the memoirs of David Lloyd George, Britain's war-time premier, to be published Thursday. Lloyd George’s indictment of Pershing is based on what he termed the A. E. F. commander-in-chief's stubborn fight to keep his divisions intact instead of having them incorporated in the allied armies. “He (Pershing) was quivering with suspicion that the British and French meant to rob him of his army,” Lloyd George writes. The Welsh statesman’s caustic chronicle describes incessant disputes with Pershing, and pillories “American indecision and bustling incompetency.” However, he praises the courage of the American troops. Men Insufficiently Fed Lloyd George declares large numbers of American soldiers in the Argonne sector were insufficiently fed, and cr

LONDON. Sept. 24.—(P)—David Lloyd George, Britain’s wartime prime minister, accused Gen. John J. Pershing of having rushed “brass hats” to France when the great need of the allies was “doughboys.” The criticism of the American wartime commander was made in the fifth volume of Lloyd George's war memoirs in which, in vigorous language, he defends his own policies.

HOLLYWOOD, Calif., Sept. 24.--(4)—Fay Wray, actress, wife of John Monk Saunders, gave birth to a six and one-half pound daughter today. She is the couple’s first child. Saunders returned here recently from a film writing assignment in England.

(Copyncht, 1926, By The Associated Press) Shanghai, Sept. 24 — (Thursday) — Japanese blue jackets, armed for war, held a huge area of Shanghai's international settlement under martial law early today in a grim search for the gunmen who, a few hours before, had shot three Japanese marines, one of them fatally.

(Copyright, 1936, Associated Press) SHANGHAI, Sept. 24, (4) —Japanese officials, backed by armed marines patrolling a large area under martial law, rejected curtly today Chinese protests against invasion of the Chinese settlement and warned the entire city to “keep its head cool.” Strong forces of blue-coated Japanese in tanks and armored cars and on motorcycles drew taut lines around a large area of the international settlement in “self-defense” measures resulting from the killing of one marine and the wounding of two others. The spot where the marine died was heavily guarded by squads with fixed bayonets. Military authorities continued their investigation of the slaying but released one Chinese, held as a suspect. “We are well in control of the situation,” asserted Rear Admiral Eijiro Kondo, commander of special Japanese forces in Shanghai. “We are taking every necessary measure to pro

northern section of the international settlement where three Japanese marines were shot, one fatally. The Japanese marines, less than three hours after the shooting, occupied the entire Hongkew area and assumed full control, supplanting the international police. Similar action was taken during the siege of 1932. Japanese authorities, reinforcing their permanent landing party of 2,000 with additional marines from the flagship Idzumo, now in the Whangpoo river, sent bluejackets also into the Chinese area adjacent to that part of the international settlement where the shootings occurred. Authorities of the international settlement immediately called out a Russian company of 600 men, part of the settlement defense corps. 1936-09-06.text: Louisburg, Nova Scotia, Sept. 5. (?)—Mrs. Beryl Markham, “feeling fine,” and “with just a bump on my head” to show for her forced landing, ended her England to New York flight unexpectedly but safely today at Baleine Cove, near here. There were scratches on her nose and face; and her plane was badly damaged, but the 33-year-old English matron was unhurt. “It was nice to have landed right side up,” she commented with a nervous laugh. “This is my first visit to America, you know.” Mrs. Markham, who lifted her small monoplane, “The Messenger,” from the Abingdon airport in England at 12:50 p.m. (eastern standard time) Friday, had been in the air 23 hours and 15 minutes when she was forced down, by lack of fuel, at 12:05 p.m. (est) today. Foul weather challenged her plane most of the way, eating up her gasoline supply more rapidly than she had anticipated. “I knew my fuel was almost gone, so

LONDON, Sept. 5—(4)—Dawn tomorrow was set today as the possible time when Dick Merrill and Harry Richman, American trans-Atlantic fliers, may take off on a return flight to New York. The fliers declared they hoped to leave if their plane was ready and the weather favorable. They said they were considering transferring the ship from Croydon airport to another airdrome where a longer and smoother runway would be available. They suggested the Abingdon Airport, from which Mrs. Beryl Markham took off on a westward ocean flight yesterday.

BALEINE, N. S., Sept 5 (UP)—Mrs. Beryl Markham, London society woman, cracked up in this tiny fishing village on Cape Breton Island this afternoon. Her airplane was wrecked but she escaped with a few minor injuries to her legs and face. Her blue monoplane, which had successfully ploughed its way through almost continuous storms since she took off yesterday from Abingdon airport, near London, was forced down when its gasoline supply ran out. The plane struck in a rough field and skidded on one wing. Mrs. Markham scrambled out, bleeding from a minor wound over her right eye. Mrs. Markham is the first woman flier to complete an east to west non-stop transatlantic crossing. Time of the crash was given as 3:30 p.m. Atlantic standard time (2:30 EDT), making the elapsed time for the crossing from London to Cape Breton 24 hours 40 minutes. LONDON, Sept. 5 — Harry Richman said today if afternoon weather reports were favorable he and Dick Merrill would take off at dawn tomorrow for their return flight from London to New York. The flyers’ monoplane, Lady Peace, in which they flew from New York to a Welsh cow pasture and thence on to London, was ready for the return. Reports of gales off the American coast delayed it. The flyers planned to take their plane from Croydon airdrome to the Royal Air Force field at Abingdon this afternoon. Mrs. Beryl Markham, young society beauty and mother of a 7-year-old boy, took off there yesterday on a solo flight to New York.

Rome.—(#)—Premier Benito Mussolini Saturday literally as well as practically wore the mantle of Haile Selassie, defeated emperor of Ethiopia. The mantle, decorated with a lion’s mane, was draped over the shoulders of Il Duce by Ras Gugsa, who deserted Haile Selassie, went over to the Italian side during the war, and now is governor of Tigrai province. In the Palazzo Venezia the pop-eyed Gugsa handed over the mantle which had been given him by Haile Selassie in the years when he was still loyal to the Negus. He also gave Il Duce a shield and other colorfully decorated ornaments. Gugsa said: “Under Italy’s banner Ethiopian populations will enjoy peace and prosperity.” Il Duce thanked him.

By The Associated Press. HENDAYE, France, Sept. 5.—Fort Guadalupe, former Spanish government stronghold, and the town of Fuenterrabia fell tonight before Fascist rebels marching victoriously westward along Spain's northern coast from captured Irun. Pressing toward San Sebastian, Spain’s one-time summer capital now held by government forces, the insurgents took the fort and the little coastal town with slight resistance. Retreating government militiamen had set fire to Fuenterrabia, determined to leave their enemies only another ruined town. It was there that United States Ambassador Claude G. Bowers made his headquarters early in the revolt, before he quit Spain. Fort Guadalupe had been evacuated when the government soldiers’ position became untenable by the fall of Irun. Fuenterrabia apparently was defended only slightly. Most of the defenders, finding themselves surrounded by the enemy

—(U.P)—The rebels were in control of the northern corner of Spain along the French border Saturday, cutting off the loyalists from contact with France and threatening the whole northern coast. The capture of Irun was complete and the once prosperous city was in smouldering ruins. The last loyalist fighting man had been driven across the border, where some of them remained disconsolately sniping. Hold 170 Hostages. Leading a force to mop up Irun, the rebels began driving westward toward San Sebastian, the next objective. The first point which must be taken is Fort Guadeloupe, outside.

Working masses raised a threat today of a general strike unless the French government accedes to their demands to send aid to Spanish Socialists. Union metal workers of the Paris region called a special meeting of factory delegates for 3 p.m.—an hour before the cabinet was to convene to consider its neutrality policy of non-intervention in the Spanish civil war. Communist party headquarters acknowledged the possibility of a new strike of metal workers if no reply is received soon to party proposals for a joint Communist-Socialist delegation to ask Premier Leon Blum to end non-intervention. The action of the extreme leftists together with the metal workers recalled the wave of “folded arms” strikes started in May by the metallurgists.

1936-09-28.text: WASHINGTON, Oct. 20 (F) — President Roosevelt hurried through a series of conferences today, and with a major speech in his briefcase, turned toward New England tonight in quest of the electoral votes of Rhode Island, Massachusetts and Connecticut. He cancelled an afternoon press conference to provide time for polishing the address which aides said would climax his third campaign trip at Worcester, Mass., tomorrow night. Later he called in several reporters to say he had no plans to start out after the New England trip on a swing through Indiana, Ohio and Pennsylvania. Washington ()—Government monetary experts disclosed today that Great Britain, France and the United States will effect a close working arrangement for handling their stabilization funds under the new monetary agreement. Secretary Morgenthau acted independently of the other two nations when he moved Saturday to halt a downward sweep in the price of pound sterling, but officials said that in the future activities of the three countries will be more closely connected. ACTED SWIFTLY They explained that Morgenthau used $5,009,000 of the treasury’s $2,000,000,000 exchange stabilization fund to buy pounds without consulting the other two countries because he wanted to act swiftly to halt the drop of sterling and because exchanges in Paris and London were closed. Government experts said handling of the three nations’ funds will be coordinated by the Bank of England, the Bank of France and the Fe

HYDE PARK, N.Y., Sept. 27.—() President Roosevelt today set aside the hours of a chilly, gray Sunday for church, work on two campaign speeches and a talk with Secretary Morgenthau about the new monetary agreement among France, England and the United States. White House officials said the President for weeks has been keeping track of every move leading up to the monetary understanding and the expected devaluation of the franc and that the meeting with the Treasury secretary merely would allow him to go into greater detail on the latest developments. Morgenthau returned from a conference with President Roosevelt at Hyde Park, N. Y., during which he discussed in detail negotiations leading to the three-party monetary agreement. Mr. Roosevelt was reported pleased with its consummation. G. O. P. BERLIN, Sept. 28—The Nazi people's court today sentenced Lawrence Simpson of Seattle to three years imprisonment on charges of treasonable activities against the Reich in connection with the sailor’s communistic activities. Simpson, who confessed to the communist activities on the stand during his sensational trial this morning, will be given credit for fourteen of the fifteen months he already has spent in prison pending trial. The prosecutor told the court that the charges of espionage against Simpson were not sustained by the evidence, concentrating on the sailor’s communist connections. Simpson's attorney, Werner Amthor, had asked the court to give the American a maximum sentence of one year in prison on the treason charge and throw out the espionage charge altogether. Amthor, in defense of the sailor, stressed that he was not the initiator of any attempt to distribute communist lite

PARIS, Sept. 27—The French government today sent to parliament its program for devaluing the franc, banning the transfer of gold and readjusting salary levels. Socialist Premier Leon Blum won first approval for the program when the chamber of deputies finance committee indicated its endorsement of the ponderous text covering the devaluation measures with what officials called “few minor changes.” Sources close to the government said the cabinet hoped to obtain final approval of the text by both houses of parliament by Wednesday. The premier explained to Socialist deputies, who pledged complete support, details of the accord with Britain and the United States to refrain from currency manipulation against the franc. Asked whether the new franc would be exchangeable for gold, Blum said such would be possible “as soon as the stabilization period ended.” To Lower Tariffs Vincent Auriol, minis

PARIS (AP)—The French government introduced its franc devaluation plan into the chamber of deputies Monday, met a radical insurrection which threatened the solidarity of the cabinet, and defeated a rightist effort to send the legislation back to committee for revision. Radicals, in caucus, voted 32 to 28 to oppose a provision in the proposed law to adjust the national wage scale to compensate for the fall of the franc, while they approved 55 to 13 the rest of the legislation. But they threatened, so intense was their feeling, to withdraw their representation in the cabinet if the sliding wage scale provision were not changed. Rightist deputies vigorously attacked the devaluation laws. One of them, Louis Marin, moved that it be referred back to the finance committee for revision. The government won its first skirmish on this point, defeating the motion 365 to 248. They did not make it a v

(Copyright, 1938, By "The Associated Press"): Madrid, Sept. 28. —— The Spanish government admitted today officially the fall of Toledo, issued an urgent call for all militiamen to hasten to their barracks and suspended the rights of all public functionaries of ministries and executive departments. The capital was quiet this morning, but detailed news from Toledo was withheld from the people. The government communique said only that Toledo defenders were compelled to retreat to the outskirts of the city but were continuing to bombard the Fascists from the gates of the ancient city. The retreat, the government said, was forced by Fascist advances from Torrijos and Maqueda.

Great Britain’s first retired king, drifted before the eyes of his subjects today. London, Oct. 17 (F)—Mrs. “Wallis” Simpson, King Edward’s American friend, was reported a royal guest again tonight while Mayfair gossips wondered whether the king's esteem for her might some day end in marriage. Sources usually accurate said Mrs. Simpson, who has brought a divorce action against her ship broker husband, was spending the weekend “35 miles from London.” That is the distance from London to Fort Belvedere, the king’s country home. Meanwhile the judge and the clerk of the court were understood to have conferred privately over the setting of the docket for Ipswich, where the hearing on the Simpson divorce plea is to be held. Mr. Justice Hawke held no public session of court to set the docket but it was pointed out that was not unusual. LONDON—(P)—Great Britain, feeling now that Belgium has no intention of turning her back on her continental obligations, found the international situation more encouraging on two fronts today. Another meeting of the International non-intervention committee is expected to be called next week, permitting a new start on the European attempt to work out a solution of the ticklish question created by charges of Spanish neutrality violations. Conditions for making a new attack on the problem were considered more suitable than they have been for some days, although Soviet Russia still was standing on its demand that the committee be called quickly to act on her charges that Portugal, Italy and Germany are guilty of open aid to the Spanish Fascists.

| By The Associated Press London, Oct. 16--A date will be set tomorrow for a hearing at Ipswich on the divorce suit filed by Mrs. Ernest (Wally) Simpson, King Edward's friend, against her broker husband. British households learned of Mrs. Simpson’s divorce suit against her husband only by word of mouth, as British newspapers generally refrained from publishing accounts of the proceedings. Aloof Nine out of 10 Englishmen professed complete ignorance of the friendship between Mrs. Simpson and King Edward, and informed persons doubted that there would ever be any public criticism of the association. The only persons who might in the future feel inclined to discuss the friendship publicly, authoritative sources said, would be country parsons who on occasion can be remarkably outspoken as they are no respectors of personages. The position Mrs. Simpson has carved for herself in British society

London, Oct. 17—King Edward VIII hotly rebuffed spiritual and political leaders when they appealed recently for greater discretion in the monarch’s relations with Mrs. Wallis Simpson, it was learned in court circles today. The leaders, including the Archbishop of Canterbury and Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin, were told by King Edward to mind their own business, it was said. The reported interview took place at Buckingham Palace.

Cairo, Egypt, Oct. 17.—(P)—A train today killed 12 persons and injured many in a crowd which had gathered to welcome Mustapha Nahas Pasha, Egyptian premier, returning from signing the Anglo-Egyptian treaty in London. The tragedy occurred at Oukh station, near Benha, 29 miles north of Cairo. The premier’s train was traveling on an adjoining line from Alexandria when the express from Cairo ran into the crowd.

Aboard Roosevelt Train Enroute to New York, (AP)--A dispatch from the Worcester, Mass., Telegram quoting President Roosevelt's son James as saying his father would seek a constitutional amendment 'to make the principles of NRA the law of the land' was noted without comment today on the president’s campaign. Officials on the train said the president would not discuss the subject. Meanwhile, a check of the president's campaign speeches to date disclosed nothing to indicate he had any such intention as that attributed to him by the Worcester Telegram’s quotation of his son.

LONDON, Oct. 16—British laborites tonight joined Russia in demanding the Spanish neutrality committee act on concrete proposals aimed to halt alleged foreign aid to the Spanish Insurgents. Clement H. Attlee, leader of the labor party in the House of Commons, conferred with Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden and was reliably reported to have demanded clarification of the British government's attitude on the Spanish situation. Emphasizing that his party was still a cogent factor in British public opinion, Attlee was said to have demanded further assurance that the government would see that the European non-intervention agreement was carried out to the letter. The Russian representatives today chatted restlessly under what they termed the “negative” reply of Lord Plymouth, chairman of the neutrality group, to their recent demand that the neutrality committee be reconvened immediately. 1936-10-18.text: LONDON, Oct. 17—(AP)—Friends of Mrs. Wallis Simpson talked more than ever tonight about the possibility of a royal romance when they heard reports the American woman again was a guest of King Edward at his country estate, 35 miles from London. The king is at Fort Belvedere, where he has been accustomed to seek relaxation. Conjecture over whether King Edward might exert his personal will over the sentiment of his subjects and marry outside the pale of royalty was revived when Mr. Justice Hawke was reported to have held private conferences on the setting of a date for hearing Mrs. Simpson's divorce suit against her husband, Ernest. LONDON, Oct. 17. (U.P)—King Edward VIII has administered a stinging rebuff to both the spiritual and political leaders of England for attempting to interfere with his friendship for Mrs. Ernest Simpson, his American favorite, it was learned in court circles today. The report was that the Archbishop of Canterbury, head of the Church of England, and Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin, head of the government, had constituted themselves an unofficial committee, gone to Buckingham Palace and appealed to the monarch for greater discretion in his relations with Mrs. Simpson. The King in effect told the tall, stern archbishop and the moral, gospel-loving premier to mind their own business. His visitors were discountenanced when the King, his lips twitching nervously in an attempt to conceal his anger, delivered the royal snubbing. (By The Associated Press) UVALDE, Oct. 17.—Vice President John N. Garner declared tonight in his first speech of the campaign that the administration’s program represented “the highest type of true American conservatism,” and that “the safest thing that could happen to this country is the re-election of President Roosevelt.” In a nationwide broadcast from his home, the vice president defended the president against charges that he welcomed Communistic support, asserting that “Franklin D. Roosevelt is no more of a Communist than I am and in my own country I am generally estimated as a hard-headed business man.” Jones Congratulates Him Garner spoke from the library of his home here. Topeka, Kan., Oct. 17.—(#?)—Governor Alf M. Landon and Colonel Frank Knox mapped the close of their campaign today in a final conference which ended with the Chicago publisher predicting victory in a “real fight.” Sitting on the front porch of the executive mansion where he lunched with Landon, Knox puffed a pipe and told reporters: “We had a general discussion of the campaign situation. It is the last time we'll see each other before the election. I think our timing has been perfect and that we're coming very strong—in no state more so than in New York.” Landon was inside as his running mate talked, conferring with William R. Castle, former under-secretary of state, and J. Reuben Clark, former ambassador to Mexico. Motor to Excelsior Springs. CHICAGO, ILL. A nation-wide radio address by Senator Arthur H. Vandenberg (R. Mich.) was cut off the eastern division of the Columbia Broadcasting Company chain tonight in the midst of a speech directed against President Roosevelt. H. Leslie Atlas, vice president of Columbia, said the address was cut off stations in the East by the chain’s New York officials "because the program included phonographic recordings in violation of the company’s rules." Leslie said the address, interspersed with recordings of speeches made by President Roosevelt in 1932 and 1933, was broadcast by the major portion of the Columbia chain's member stations. Pledges The chain official said he had been assured by Hill Blackett, Public Relations Director for the Republican National Committee, sponsors of Vandenberg’s address, that recordings were not to be used in connection with the broadcast.
