London, Nov. 2—(AP)—With her back broken, rammed hard on the rocks at Pendennis Point, the 5,686-ton American freighter Bessemer City, of New York, was abandoned to pounding seas today. A life-boat from St. Ives, three miles west of Pendennis Point, rescued the last 23 members of the crew early today after ten others had been taken ashore earlier, including the ship’s mascot, a cat. The ship was reported breaking up. “She’s broken in two,” said Captain A. Herman, the last to leave the stricken vessel. “She’s lost.” “Visibility was wretched. We didn’t even get a peep at the shore lights. We were on the rocks before we knew what had happened.”

Galoshes and rubbers will be in order for voters in many parts of the United States tomorrow, if the weather bureau's predictions are correct. Wet weather is expected over much of the nation east of the Rockies, with rain from the northern New England border down to parts of the south, and inland to such states as Ohio and Kentucky. Further west snow is expected in several states.

SHANGHAI, Nov. 2— (7) — British naval officers charged tonight Japanese police pushed a fountain pen under the fingernails of a British seaman and forced ink into the wounds to make him sign a "confession" he cheated a taxi driver. He was one of three British sailors said to have been beaten by Japanese police at Keeling, Formosa, a Japanese island, Oct. 7. Vice-Admiral Sir Charles Little, commanding the British far eastern naval forces, postponed a trip to Japan because of the incident. (British authorities in London said today they had known for a week of the allegations that the seaman was tortured. They declared the incident still was under investigation.)

WASHINGTON, July 6 (P)—Returning to the capital from a weekend tour of the Old Dominion, President Roosevelt went ahead with a study of campaign plans today before turning northward for a sailor’s vacation off the New England coast. Before Farley went to the White House, three administration officials discussed the severe western drought with the President. They were Rexford G. Tugwell, Resettlement administrator; Aubrey Williams, assistant Works Progress Administrator, and J. B. Hudson, acting administrator of the AAA. After dedicating Shenandoah National Park and making a speech from Thomas Jefferson’s home last week, the President left Virginia's shores at Yorktown last night. He boarded the Potomac, the president-! (Continued on Page 14)

LONDON, Nov. 2.—(UP)—London awaited today one of the most colorful of its many gorgeous "shows"—the state opening of parliament by King Edward—and asked itself the question: "Will Mrs. Wallis Simpson be there?" The king is driving to parliament tomorrow, in the uniform of colonel in chief of one of his regiments of guards and the smothering black and red mantle, ermine collared, to read the speech from the throne. Peers in their rich robes of state, members of the commons in formal black, peeresses in their gowns and jewels, will crowd the chamber. But most people will be looking up into the distinguished strangers’ gallery to see whether Mrs. Simpson, a veritable will o' the wisp since her divorce, is watching the king.

1936-08-10.text: SEATTLE, Aug. 10—(AP)—Silence engulfed two famed Russian fliers today—forced down by adverse weather at an isolated village on the Northern British Columbia coast. The failure of Segismund Levanesky and Victor Levchenko to report or answer wireless calls after they landed at Bella Bella, B.C., at 3 p.m. last Saturday, concerned their representative here, N. A. Sokoloff. He suggested they probably had no idea wireless stations from Seattle to the Arctic Circle were trying to reach them. He said probably they went ashore from their pontoon-equipped plane to await better weather and did not hear the calls. The radiophone on their plane is the only means of prompt communication with the outside world from the little village 300 miles north of Vancouver, B.C.

LONDON, Aug. 10 “UP—Sir Henry Chilton, British ambassador, today protested to Spanish rebel authorities against the killing of Capt. Rupert Savile, British yachtman, by shells from the rebel cruiser Almirante Cervera, and the wounding of Savile’s wife. The British protest reserved the right to claim compensation for the incident.

LONDON, (UP).—Officials of the Royal Yacht Squadron, the most exclusive club in the world, investigated today the origin of a pair of women's pink silk step-ins found yesterday fluttering from the club flagstaff on the Isle of Wight. It was believed that some member hoisted the emblem on a bet.

Croydon, Eng., Aug. 10.—Tests of a night air freight line ended in disaster today when the twin-motored biplane Vellox crashed in flames into the side of a house five miles from Croydon aerodrome, killing four Imperial Airways aviators. Victims were Capt. J. Orr and Capt. Miles Fergusson, and Radio Operators Arbuckle and Dear. Cause of the crack-up was not determined.

SAINT JEAN DE LUZ, France, Aug. 9--()-—Capt. Rupert Savile, a retired British naval and air corps officer, was killed today and his wife, reported to be an American, was injured as a shell from a Spanish rebel cruiser struck their yacht in Gijon harbor. Officers of the British destroyer Comet, which brought Mrs. Savile to Saint Jean de Luz, said a 16-inch shell from the cruiser Almirante Cervera almost cut Savile in two. His wife, who stood next to him on the deck of the yacht Blue Shadow, was wounded. She was taken to a hospital at Bayonne, where officials said her condition was not critical. Hospital authorities asserted they believed she was an American but were unable to give details of her identity. Leftist boatmen from Gijon brought the Blue Shadow ashore under rebel fire... The Comet took Mrs. Savile and her husband's body to Gijon. The dead man was brought ashore here by members

London— ( —The British government today forwarded a protest to Spanish belligerents in connection with the death of a British subject, C. Rupert Saville, reported slain by insurgent gunfire on a yacht in Gijon harbor. The British foreign office said it was advised the shell which took Saville’s life and wounded his wife was fired by the Almirante Cervera, rebel cruiser. The protest was wirelessed by Ambassador Henry G. Chilton from a British destroyer for relay to the Spanish vessel. Pending instructions from London, said the message, the British government reserved the right “to obtain compensation.”

LONDON, Aug. 10.—The French government is preparing to invite the United States to adhere to the proposed European pact of non-intervention in the Spanish civil war, it was said reliably today. The proposal was said to have originated in Germany. When Dr. Konstantin Von Neurath, German foreign minister, received the British and French ambassadors on Friday and Saturday, it was understood that while conveying Germany's agreement in principle to join the pact, he also characterized United States adherence as “a necessity.” NAVAL PLANS WASHINGTON, Aug. 10.—The possibility of the recreation of the U. S. Navy's European squadron was discussed with President Roosevelt today.

1936-03-24.text: (C ight, 1936, By The Associated Press) LONDON, March 24--UP)—The League of Nations council, without waiting to hear directly from Reichsfuehrer Hitler, voted today to adjourn without taking further action on Germany’s violation of the Locarno treaty. The council members decided they would reassemble at Geneva whenever their president, Stanley M. Brice of Australia, called them to meet. In the meantime, Great Britain, France, Belgium and Italy—the co-signatories and guarantors of the Locarno pact—are to continue negotiations with Germany. An authoritative source said France was disappointed by Great Britain’s attitude toward Germany and consequently sought adjournment of the league body. Situation Complicated The council was called into session here to consider Germany’s violation of the Locarno treaty through remilitarizing the Rhineland and now awaits Reichsfuehrer Hitler’s answer to p

(Copyright, 1936, by The Associated Press) LONDON, March 23.—The "committee of 18" of the League of Nations’ council ordered a new, direct plea for peace transmitted to Italy and Ethiopia today. The committee, which comprises every member of the council except Italy, made this effort toward a quick armistice in Africa while it awaited a reply from Reichsfuehrer Hitler of Germany to proposals for ending the crisis precipitated by Germany’s remilitarization of the Rhineland. At the same time that the council made its bid for peace in Africa, it decided to send to the Italian government a new Ethiopian protest concerning the use by Italian forces of asphyxiating gas. The next meeting of the League council, which had been scheduled for this afternoon, was postponed to 4 p. m. Tuesday.

MANCHESTER, Eng., (Py) -- Alfred Molyneux, 31, of Lancashire, was sentenced to four months imprisonment today on a charge of attempting to extort £200 (about $1,000) from Countess Barbara Hutton Haugwitz Reventlow. Count Haugwitz Reventlow attended the court hearing, ready to testify, but he was not called. Molyneux admitted writing a letter to the Woolworth heiress, offering to disclose a plot to kidnap her new-born son, but declared his story of such a plot was “pure invention.”

GLASGOW, March 24 (#)—Great Britain's new super-liner, the Queen Mary, started her slow journey down the Clyde river today toward the open sea, while a great throng, estimated at 1,000,000 persons, watched and cheered from the banks. Glistening with fresh paint—the hull black, the superstructure white, the three enormous funnels red—Britain's rival in speed and size to France’s Normandie was backed out of her fitting basin shortly before noon. A bidder for the blue ribbon of fast ocean travel, the Queen Mary was calibrated, on the eve of her sailing, at 80,773 tons. Her length was set at 1,018 feet. The Normandie has a gross tonnage of 82,000, French line officials estimate, and is 1,029.2 feet long after recent alterations. The hull structure of the Queen Mary comprises 12 decks.

By The Associated Press Berlin, March 23—Sir Eric Phipps, British ambassador, was disclosed today to have made a personal appeal to the German government to accept the Locarno treaty powers’ proposals for settlement of the European crisis. Sir Eric is generally regarded as having more influence upon Chancellor Hitler than any other foreign diplomat.

Rome—Mussolini, asserting next war is inevitable, abolishes chamber of deputies and large private industries; signs accords with Austria and Hungary. London—League sends fresh peace appeal to Italy and Ethiopia; Locarno powers await Hitler’s answer to their program. Berlin—Hitler expected to turn down Locarno offer, but in such a way as to leave way clear for further negotiations, probably will submit counter proposals. ROME, March 23.—(P)—Premier Mussolini, standing under the shadow of a statue of Julius Caesar, abolished large private industries and Italy's chamber of deputies today in preparation for an expected European war.

Berlin, March 24—Joachim Von Ribbentrop, Adolf Hitler’s special envoy, left by airplane for London today. He carried the German reply, it was understood, to British, French, Italian and Belgian proposals for settlement of the Rhineland dispute. Ribbentrop took off on the 628 mile flight at 2:05 p.m. (8:05 a.m. EST) in a plane that had awaited him at Templehof airdrome.

Berlin, Mar. 24. (P)—Germany has rejected important features of the Locarno proposals of the four former allies, it was announced officially here tonight. The German answer described the London offer as “unacceptable” because it was “based on unendurable discrimination.” One feature of the program advanced by Great Britain, France, Italy and Belgium provided for the stationing temporarily of British and Italian soldiers in the Rhineland. Joachim von Ribbentrop, right hand diplomat to Reichsfuehrer Hitler, carried Germany’s reply by airplane to the Locarno treaty signatories in London today. With a small party of aides, he left Tempelhof airdrome at 2:12 p.m. with a secret note from Hitler tucked in a briefcase. Wilhelmstrasse sources repeated their statements of the last few days that the memorandum contained counter-proposals but left the door open for further negotiations on the powers

1936-10-21.text: LONDON, OCT. 21, (AP). — The British press will make its first mention of the celebrated divorce case of “Simpson, W., versus Simpson, E. A.” in tomorrow's issue of the news magazine “News Review”, it was learned today. A six-line item on page 23 will read: “Reporters were last week laying their lines at Ipswich, Suffolk, in readiness for the divorce suit between Mr. and Mrs. Ernest Aldrich Simpson, expected to come up for hearing next week before Mr. Justice Hawke.” There was absolutely no mention of King Edward's friendship for the American-born “Wallie” Simpson. (Additional news of the Simpson case appears on Page 5.)

LONDON, Oct. 22. (4)—The towering 200-pound detective who is King Edward's personal bodyguard has been assigned to watch Mrs. Ernest Simpson, the monarch's American-born friend. He is Chief Inspector David Storier of Scotland Yard. His assignment is to shield the former Baltimore debutante pending hearing of her divorce suit against her. In the fashionable Mayfair district until she is safe inside again, Storier's bulk hovers close by. Anyone venturing near her receives a sharp warning from the detective. Mrs. Simpson makes frequent excursions in a big closed automobile identical with one belonging to the monarch himself. The first evidence the vivacious American woman was enjoying royal protection while Edward was away grouse hunting at Sandingham was disclosed today.

By the Associated Press Great Britain, France, and 13 Latin-American nations moved in diplomatic concert today to save thousands of Spanish noncombatants from death in besieged Madrid. In two hemispheres, there were these humanitarian efforts as Fascist armies closed in on the Spanish capital from the south and west: 1. Great Britain ordered its navy to stand by for a "mission of mercy" to rescue hostages held by both sides in the war. Estimating there were 8,000 of these hostages in Madrid alone, the British government pressed both the Madrid government and the Fascist authorities for the exchange and evacuation of the women prisoners, in particular. 2. Carlos Saavedra Lamas, the Argentine foreign minister, conferred secretly with Premier Leon Blum of France in Paris on the possibility of rescuing endangered persons by plane, while refugees told of spreading Spanish anarchy and violent

By The Associated Press “Eastward Ho!” became the unofficial slogan of both major party nominees Wednesday. Traveling into New England, President Roosevelt said: “We will not again allow people to be regimented by selfish minorities into bankruptcies and breadlines.” He planned several more speeches, culminating in an address at Worcester, Mass., Wednesday night. The “Sunflower Special” started across the continent from Los Angeles, where Governor Landon told an audience Tuesday night that “if we are to preserve our form of government this administration must be defeated.” Sharp words broke out between Landon and Secretary Ickes, PWA chief. The latter said in a radio broadcast at Washington Tuesday night that in 1934 and 1935 Landon was a “state Socialist” seeking federal funds for state-owned telephone and gas distribution systems but that recently the Kansas governor became a “rugged i

- ENROUTE WITH PRESIDENT ROOSEVELT IN MASSACHUSETTS (AP) — President Roosevelt campaigned through Massachusetts today at the head of a wild-riding motor cavalcade after setting the key for his New England campaign by a speech at Providence, R. I. Leaving Providence, his trip into Massachusetts developed into a catch-as-catch-can motor race over a three-lane highway from Rhode Island to Fall River and New Bedford. Local politicians, eager to be up near the President's ear, raced wildly for preferred positions, squeezing out of line and on several occasions nearly forcing into the ditch motor cars bearing members of the President's own party. Police appeared to be helpless once the situation got beyond their control and made no effort to restore even a semblance of order to the parade. At one time, automobiles were racing three and four abreast at 60 miles an hour. At one point, the car be

LONDON, Oct. 20.—(UP)—A detective normally assigned to King Edward aided Mrs. Wallis Simpson today in her elaborate precautions to conceal her movements about London. Mrs. Simpson apparently spent the night in her new home in Cumberland Terrace. A little before noon she left. Her automobile drove up in front of the house. The detective was loitering outside. He spoke to the chauffeur, who drove off around the block and picked up Mrs. Simpson, who made her exit from a side entrance to the house. While his friend was here, King Edward entertained his shooting party in bleak Norfolk. The news of Mrs. Simpson’s impending divorce spread on by gossip in ever widening circles.

| IPSWICH, England, Oct. 20. a | The leading hotel in Ipswich tonight was booked full for next Saturday, the day on which Mr. Justice Hawk is expected to hear the divorce suit of Mrs. Wallis Simpson, King Ed- ward's companion, against her hus- band, Ernest.

Berlin, Oct. 21 — (>) — The German charge d'affaires in London, it was announced tonight, has handed to the chairman of the international non-intervention committee a list of alleged arms embargo violations by Soviet Russia in assistance of the Madrid government. At the same time, it was stated, a German note in reply to Soviet accusations of German neutrality violations in behalf of the Spanish insurgents denied the charges categorically as “completely without foundation.”

1936-12-14.text: From Mrs. Simpson. Enzesfeld, Austria, Copyright, Dec. 14—(U. P.)—The Duke of Windsor, nerves racked by the ordeal which he has been through since his abdication from the throne of Great Britain, issued a public appeal for privacy today, and at the same time received consoling messages from Mrs. Wallis Warfield Simpson. Lord Brownlow, who was gentleman-in-waiting when Edward was king and has been looking after the safety of Mrs. Simpson in her retreat on the French Riviera, arrived today from Cannes. Lord Brownlow motored at once to the Enzesfeld castle where the duke is staying. It was said he brought letters and verbal messages from Mrs. Simpson to the former king. Reports were current that Lord Brownlow came here to discuss a possible meeting between the duke and his sweetheart about Christmas time. Today was his 41st birthday, but by royal command there was no official observance beyond the firing of the customary royal salutes—one round for each year of the monarch's life—in Hyde Park and at the Tower of London. Flags flew from public buildings in honor of the occasion. The new king, hard at work at his official headquarters, left his queen at their home mildly ill with an attack of influenza. Condition Not Serious. The queen was reported “distinctly bet

London, Dec. 13.—(P)—The Archbishop of Canterbury tonight castigated “the social circle” in which former King Edward VIII moved, in a broadcast to Britain bidding farewell to the old king and welcome to the new King George VI. “Strange and sad it must be,” said the archbishop, “that for such a motive, however strongly it was pressed upon his heart, he (Edward) should have disappointed hopes so high and abandoned a trust so great. “Even more strange and sad it is that he should have sought his happiness in a manner inconsistent with the Christian principles of marriage, and within a social circle whose standards and ways of life are alien to all the best instincts and traditions of his people.” The head of the Church of England was one of the strongest forces backing Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin in his opposition to any union between Edward and Wallis Warfield Simpson so long as Edward

By United Press Staff Correspondent LONDON, Dec. 4.—(UP)—Guns thundered throughout Great Britain today in honor of the 41st birthday of the new king, George VI. Queen Elizabeth was suffering a mild attack of influenza which will keep her in the family home at 45 Piccadilly. But there was a quiet lunch there and flags flew throughout the kingdom in the king's honor. At his own request, there was no other celebration except for the royal salutes. A salute of 41 guns, one for each year of the king's life, roared almost in the ears of the queen and the two little princesses, Elizabeth and Margaret Rose, who are the heirs to the throne, from Hyde Park. There was a salute of 62 guns at the Tower of London, in the old city of London—a salute of 21 guns in addition to the birthday salute. There were 21-gun salutes at all army posts in the country. Receives Congratulations King George motored fro

London (P)—King George VI, in a message read in the house of lords today, said: "I have succeeded to the throne in circumstances which are without precedent and at a moment of great distress to me, but I am resolved to do my duty and I am sustained by the knowledge that I am supported by widespread goodwill and sympathy, from all of my subjects here and throughout the world. "It will be my constant endeavor, with God’s help and supported by my dear wife to uphold the honor of the realm and promote the happiness of my people."

Chester, Dec. 14.—(AP)—President Roosevelt, en route home from South America, will cross the Gulf Stream tonight, exchanging summer for winter. He will arrive in Charleston, S.C., about 7 a.m. tomorrow morning and will reach Washington tomorrow night. Mr. Roosevelt was hopeful that complete success will attend the inter-American peace effort he initiated at Buenos Aires on the mission that will have carried him nearly 14,000 miles when his ship, the cruiser Indianapolis, docks tomorrow. A check-up today showed that he spent 22 days at sea and six days in port since he left Charleston on Nov. 18. He is returning in excellent health, ready to begin work on messages and a legislative program. He returns, however, saddened by the death of Gus Gennerich, his personal bodyguard, who will be given a White House funeral Wednesday morning.

Fighting was expected in the vicinity of Sian-Fu, provincial capital (Continued on Page 2, Column 3)

Vienna, Dec. 14.—Enjoying the luxury of the palatial castle Enzesfeld after his rapid dash from London, the Duke of Windsor slept late today and then arose to make a 23-minute telephone call to Mrs. Wallis Simpson at Cannes, France—the woman for whom he renounced Britain’s throne. Afterwards he took a short stroll through the castle park and expressed hopes, it was reported, of an opportunity for a round of golf. Staying at the castle as guest of Baron Eugene de Rothschild, the ex-king was understood to be occupying a suite of six rooms on the ground floor. From the windows of his rooms, he has a magnificent view across the valley of the river Triesting. Later in the day, it was understood, he planned to visit Professor Neumann here in Vienna for an examination of the ear which has caused him some slight trouble in the past. 1936-05-26.text: Jerusalem.—(AP)—The long-smoldering Holy Land Arab anti-Jewish disorders developed today into open, armed conflict between Arabs and British soldiers and police. British forces, campaigning to restore order after forty days of violence in which at least fifty persons have been killed, fought two engagements, dispersing a mob of 200 Arabs in one clash but withdrawing before an Arab advance in the other. The Arab supreme council defied the government's demand that their general strike be ended, the Palestine agency reported, and issued a proclamation calling upon Arabs to continue their present program until Jewish immigration is stopped, along with sale of land to Jews, and an Arab national government is established. Arab workmen at the Royal Air Force airport at Ramleh struck and were replaced by the government with 100 Jews, the agency added, and twenty more Arab leaders, charged with a

ROME, May 26 (UP)— War talk was renewed today while Emperor Haile Selassie approached Gibraltar in a British warship on his way to London. Mounting anger seemed to point clearly to a new period of dangerous tension. Great Britain was spotlighted once more as pursuing policies inimical to Italy. Anger was expressed not only because Britain put a cruiser at the disposal of the Emperor called here “Signor Tafari” ---but at the prospect, which Italians regard as a certainty, that with his arrival London will become a focal point for a campaign of anti-Italian propaganda.

LONDON, May 26—(4)—Six men were reported missing and probably drowned today after the steam trawler Picador sank three minutes after colliding with the cages San Salvador in the North. This report, received by the owners of the San Salvador, added that the 14 other members of the Picador’s crew had been rescued by the San Salvador.

JERUSALEM, May 26. Trans-Jordan troops under British officers fought a long range rifle battle with Arab snipers in the Esdraelon Valley. Snipers opened fire on the Jewish settlement. The troops, working from the skirmish, advanced against the concealed riflemen. No casualties were reported. Official London reports said the serious spread of Arab riots were being met with "thoroughly reorganized and adequate forces" to prevent rebellion.

SOUTHAMPTON, ENG., May 26.—(4)— Britain's greatest shipbuilding achievement, the 80,773-ton liner Queen Mary, was pronounced ready today for the start tomorrow afternoon of her maiden voyage to New York. Set to enter the struggle for supremacy in Atlantic passenger service—especially the race for the blue ribbon on fast travel—the new super-liner awaited only the 2,650 passengers who will make the first crossing. The vessel is 1,018 feet long and 118 feet wide with 12 decks and accommodations for 3,800 persons including the crew of 1,200.

" ANGELES—Two celery field strikers shot, 40 arrested. ~ PORTSMOUTH, O. — State troops requested to guard strikers at the Wheeling Steel Corp., plant. SYRACUSE, N. Y—Call for a general strike in six plants of Remington Rand, Inc., issued. AKRON, O—Thirty Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. employees held on charges they violated an anti-rioting law in their “sit down” protest. MEMPHIS, TENN. — Officials report East Arkansas cotton fields peaceful despite claims of terrorism by members of southern tenant farmers union. NEW YORK—The industrial union of marine and shipbuilding workers of America weighed a possible strike against the United Dry Docks, Inc., one of the east’s largest shipyards. Strike of 6,000 barbers in the Wall Street section and lower Manhattan called.

LONDON, May 25.—(4)—Great Britain and Russia proceeded to a discussion of fundamental issues in their negotiations for a naval agreement today, just after Moscow announced any London limitation of the Soviet Far Eastern fleet must also bind Japan. One of the principal problems was raised, an authoritative source said, by the Soviet Union's desire to divide its naval undertakings into two spheres—the Far Eastern and the European. The British preferred to treat the Soviet fleet as one unit. The program for the conversations was settled in a preliminary exchange of views at the first meeting of the conferees last Wednesday, designed to make clear the Soviet attitude toward the London naval treaty between Britain, the United States and France. The second session was called for this afternoon at the foreign office, to get down to essentials in the movement for an Anglo-Russian accord to bring

SOUTHAMPTON, Eng., May 25. (P)—King Edward VIII, again choosing to fly, inspected the great liner Queen Mary from kitchen to bridal suite Monday. Taking to the air for the second time since he became sovereign, the king flew from Windsor to head the Royal family’s tour of inspection and then flew back again. His plane took off from Eastleigh airdrome on the return trip to Windsor at 4:05 p. m. The liner—Britain’s bid for the blue riband of the Atlantic waterways—sails on her maiden voyage to America Wednesday.

1936-05-23.text: LONDON, May 22 (#) - James H. Thomas, who rose from errand boy and engine wiper to high position with the nickname of “Dress-shirt Jim,” quit the cabinet under fire tonight exactly one month after the budget leak sensation broke over Great Britain. His resignation as colonial secretary, an official announcement said, was immediately accepted by King Edward and Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin. Dated May 20 The dated resignation was handed in May 20, the day a judicial tribunal concluded an investigation of the leakage to which it linked Thomas. It caused the greatest political scandal in England since the World War. Thomas, a pioneer in the National Railway Union, broke with the Labor party when he followed Ramsay MacDonald into the national government in 1931, Labor officials now call both him and MacDonald “traitors.” Secret News Escaped The budget inquiry centered around the escape of s

London, May 23—(4)—Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia will board the British cruiser Capetown at Haifa this afternoon en route to London, the foreign office announced today. The King of Kings submitted the proposal to visit the English capital and received approval from the government, it was learned officially. The length of his visit was not disclosed. The emperor is to travel only as far as Gibraltar on the cruiser and will make the rest of the trip by regular passenger steamer. He will bring a party of eight persons but official sources in London are not certain whether the empress will be included.

Paris, May 23.--(/P)—Leon Blum, bidding for better American and British friendship, has decided to inaugurate personally the foreign policy of France’s incoming “People’s Front” government, informed sources said today. The premier-designate, Socialist leader of the Leftist bloc that comes to power in the new Chamber of Deputies next month, intends to head the French delegation to the June 16 session of the League of Nations council. Informed sources said he would attempt to form a close Franco-British diplomatic front at the special meeting called in the Italo-Ethiopian controversy. Yvon Delbos, Radical-Socialist deputy and minister of justice in the present coalition cabinet of Premier Albert Sarraut, was considered a likely candidate for the Quai d'Orsay post in the new ministry. Former Premier Herriot’s refusal to take over the foreign ministry was accepted generally now as final. Ass

HAIFA, Palestine, May 23.—(U.P)—Emperor Haile Selassie, exiled ruler of Ethiopia, left Palestine today for England aboard the British cruiser Capetown. With the former Ethiopian monarch aboard the British warship were his sons and Ras Kassa, Ethiopian chieftain who led an Ethiopian army prior to the Italian victory.

Jerusalem, May 22,—Authorities, with tension undiminished and this holy city like an armed camp, imposed an emergency ban tonight on all motor traffic in the Southern half of Palestine. Effective at noon tomorrow, a special police permit will be required for motorists. British authorities called on additional troops to stamp out terrorism in which 28 Jews, 16 Arabs and 1 Christian have been killed since April 19 when an Arab civil disobedience strike began. The Arabs are demanding that British authorities stop Jewish immigration and sale of land to Jews. Jerusalem and Jaffa where all street traffic is now protected with armed convoys, are included in the new emergency ban.

London, May 23—(UP)— Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia will embark in the British cruiser Capetown at Haifa, probably today, for London, it was announced officially. The emperor, with a party of eight, will go as far as Gibraltar in the Capetown and then proceed to London according to his own plans, it was said. His visit to London was arranged in consultation with Gen. Sir Arthur Wauchope, British high commissioner for Palestine. He has been in contact with Wauchope since he arrived in Jerusalem, as exile. Officials said that the emperor would be allowed unrestricted liberty of movement on British soil on condition that he refrain from furtherance of hostilities. It was believed that soon after his arrival here the emperor would confer with King Edward, and probably with Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden and Foreign Office experts regarding developments to be expected at the June 16 meeti

SAN QUENTIN, Calif, May 22—(?)—Great Britain's repeated efforts to save the life of Alexander Mackay, subject of that government condemned as a kidnapper, failed today as he dropped to his death through the trap of San Quentin’s prison’s gallows. He was one of three prisoners hanged in California today, Mackay and his companion, Joseph Kristy, paid the penalty for slugging the warden of San Quentin and escaping with four prison board members as hostages. British Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden, Sir Ronald Lindsay and local British consuls petitioned in vain for clemency for Mackay. The courts declined to intervene. Governor Frank F. Merriam granted two reprieves but refused further action. Mackay, 29, and Kristy, 27, were hustled to the gallows this morning, their hands strapped to their sides. The Briton called out “so long” to his Attorney Melvin Belli, who was among the 100 witnesses.

London, May 23,—Great Britain’s gigantic rearmament program has entered the production phase with a speed and thoroughness reflecting the possibility of war against which the plan was devised and approved by the people in last November’s elections. After two months of survey work, the imperial defense committee has entered its second stage—development of productive capacity of the empire's factories to supply shells and implements of war. Five Departments. The committee under Sir Thomas W. Inskip, minister for defense coordination, has undertaken immediate allocation of contracts for machines, tools and gauges necessary to speed up supplies. Sir Thomas divided the rearmament work roughly into five departments: 1. Preparations to hasten naval building. 1936-04-27.text: New York, April 27.—(P)—The master of the British freighter St. Quentin, toward which two giant liners were speeding after aid had been requested, notified the vessels today that she could proceed without assistance. The liner Pilsudski, which raced through heavy seas to stand by the Ivanhoe after the latter’s rudder broke, notified the line’s New York office that she again was making her way. Liners Speed to Aid The St. Quentin, however, was believed to be in a more precarious position. The last wireless report from the British cargo ship last night said her steering apparatus was damaged and her radio room flooded. The Bremen and the Washington, queens of the German and American merchant marines, sped to give assistance although bad weather and high seas slowed them up. (Copyright, 1936, by United Press) LONDON, April 27—(UP)—Complete Italian conquest of Ethiopia would be in the interest of civilization, George Bernard Shaw said today. He said he did not think the Italian-Ethiopian situation would lead to war in Europe. He hoped that it would affect the constitution of the League of Nations. "Its present constitution is a greater nuisance than the United States constitution, if that is possible," he commented. Shaw was asked if Italy could hold Ethiopia permanently. "Of course she can," he replied, "though it may end in Ethiopia holding Italy. In empires, the tail sometimes grows big enough to wag the dog."

criminal appeal today dismissed an appeal by Dr. Buck Ruxton, “devil’s beef tub” killer, from the death sentence for the murder of his wife. Lord Hewart, the lord chief justice of England, announced the decision after the three judges of the court had considered a long plea by Dr. Ruxton’s attorney, Norman Birkett, who claimed the judge had misdirected the jury in the original trial. Dr. Ruxton killed his wife and a servant “on or about” Sept. 15, 1935. Their bodies were dismembered and thrown in a ravine on the Scottish border called the “Devil's Beef Tub.” Ruxton was to have been hanged April 1, but the hanging was postponed pending the appeal to the high court. LONDON April 26 — The first big scale move by the Ethiopian government to remedy its appalling weakness in military aviation, possibly late in the day, has been launched here by Dr. Azay Martin, Plenipotentiary minister to Great Britain. Dr. Martin has appealed for a private loan of $5,000,000 at two percent from 100,000 subscribers to buy a huge air fleet for Ethiopia. Even if gray-haired Dr. Martin gets his money and his planes, his country faces a seemingly hopeless task to enroll or train enough pilots and mechanics to man them. The lack of aerodromes or even practical sites for aerodromes in the rugged African empire, and the cost of upkeep, including oil, would be desperate problems for an emperor whose war funds are already reported running short. But Mr. Martin’s enthusiasm in his new campaign is not in the least dampened by this outlook. “Already several thousand pounds have bee

Three ships in distress in Atlantic waters tonight, turning liners from their courses to give aid. The British freighter St. Quenten first reported herself in trouble with her radio room rendered inoperable and her steering gear damaged. Her call was answered by the North German Lloyd liner Bremen, the German-American liner Pilsudski, and the U.S. liner Washington. Later the freighter Ivanhoe reported a broken rudder and the U.S. liner turned from the search for St. Quenten to give the Ivanhoe aid. The third distress call was received by the Radiomarine Corporation from the British cargo steamship Rushpeal. The message did not reveal the nature of her trouble and other sources had not received.

Communists had secured 10 seats, their number in the outgoing chamber, although an official count at 2:30 a.m. (8:30 p.m. EST) gave them only five. They made such a show of ballots in other districts where the issue was undecided that moderate observers forecast they would enter the new chamber having 40 places. In many of the first 400 districts, the battles were so hot that candidates failed to obtain the necessary absolute majority, and only 155 were elected. Even some opponents of the leftist people's front, of which the radical socialist party is the strongest unit, said they expected it would obtain a majority in the chamber following next Sunday's vote. Among the communists’ seats were three new ones. The right gained five new seats. Rightists and communists took places from socialists, who lost 4; independent socialists, who lost 2; radical socialists, 1, and center parties, 1. J

CAIRO, April 27. (4)—The condition of King Fuad, gravely ill with a throat and mouth infection, became worse today, the royal physicians announced. An official bulletin said the monarch passed a restless night and that his mouth infection was spreading, increasing circulatory troubles. The king has taken no food for four days.

ADDIS ABABA, April 27 — An Italian airplane circled Addis Ababa today, dropping leaflets threatening destruction of the Ethiopian capital if the advance by Marshal Badoglio's troops from Dessye were resisted. "Our mission is to occupy Addis Ababa and Ethiopia for civilization," the leaflets said. "If Addis Ababa is delivered without resistance, we will not bomb it; otherwise, we will destroy it all." The leaflets, signed by Marshal Badoglio’s chief of staff, declared that the Italians would enter Addis Ababa soon "with the help of God." They warned the populace that resistance was futile since the entire northern Ethiopia was already captured by the Italians, and asked the Ethiopian people to desert Emperor Haile Selassie and pledge allegiance to Italy. 1936-09-11.text: VIENNA, Sept. 11 UA— King Edward of Great Britain, long the world's leader in men’s fashions, has 'gone on a diet' to keep the royal waistline down to its usual slenderness, according to close associates. The king, vacationing in Austria, worked out the details of his diet himself. Since following it, the king has told friends that he has lost several pounds and that his health and efficiency have improved 50 per cent.

LIVERPOOL, Sept. 11.—(4)—Harry Richman, New York night club owner and singer, announced tonight he and Dick Merrill, his transatlantic speed pilot, planned to take off for New York at 4 a.m. tomorrow (9 p.m. Central Standard Time today).

LONDON, Sept. 11 (UP)——Fear was expressed today in responsible circles that the attack on Soviet Russian leaders by Dr. Paul Goebbels at the Nazi congress yesterday might result in a diplomatic break between Russia and Germany and the consequent cancellation of the forthcoming Locarno conference. Although Russia would not be a party to the conference, a break in relations between her and Germany would upset relations so that the meeting would become virtually impossible. France, for instance, is one of the most important prospective participants and France has an alliance with Russia for mutual protection.

IE EERE IIR EIS IONE Soon After 5 p. m. NEW YORK (UP) Harry Richman and Richard Merrill will begin their return flight to New York from England shortly after 5 p.m. on Friday. Eastern Airlines was advised by cable.

LIVERPOOL, Sept. 11—(CUP)— Richard Merrill and Harry Richman, transatlantic fliers, announced today that they would take off for New York at dawn tomorrow if weather reports continued favorable. The pair, who crossed the Atlantic to England more than a week ago, made this announcement at a luncheon given in their honor by the city’s Lord Mayor at the Guild Hall. They said they intended to begin fueling their ship, the Lady Peace, at 3 a.m. tomorrow with 800 gallons of gasoline. The ship will carry 250 pounds more than on its eastward flight.

Forest Hills, N. Y., Sept. 11 Py Donald Budge, the chief American contender, defeated Frank Parker, of Spring Lake, N. J., 6-4, 6-3, 6-3 today and gained the final round of the U.S. Singles Tennis Championship. Helen Jacobs, of Berkeley, Calif., vanquished Kay Stammers, British Southpaw, 6-4, 6-3, and advanced to the finals of the U.S. singles tennis championship in her bid for her fifth straight title.

TORONTO, Sept. 11 (/P).—Lawson Little, former American and British amateur champion, today shot a 68, four strokes under par and one better than his first round score, to hold his lead in the Canadian open golf championship at the St. Andrew’s club with a 36-holes total of 133.

(Copyright, 1936, by the Associated Press) SAINT JEAN DE LUZ, France, Sept. 11—44)—Gen. Emilio Mola's rebel artillery bombarded the outskirts of San Sebastian this afternoon, apparently as a warning to defenders to heed a demand for immediate surrender. Officers of the British destroyer 'Escort' said the shelling lasted less than half an hour and that no shells fell inside the city. Government officials at San Sebastian viewed the bombardment as a first warning following their refusal to accept the rebel ultimatum. Later, the rebels apparently turned their fire on Pasajes and the nearby fort where shells were dropped into the harbor.

1936-07-14.text: . BONNEVILLE SALT FLATS, Utah, July 14—(AP)—Capt. George Eyston, British king of the speedways, capped an unprecedented conquest of world motor car records today by shattering the established mark for the grueling 48-hour drive. His unofficial speed, made without a hitch in his huge, shark-nosed “Speed of the Winds,” was 136.354 miles per hour. The record was held formerly at 109.54 by Perrot, Dhome, Girod and Delahaye of France. He traveled a reported 6,545 miles. Both speed and distance remained unconfirmed by AAA officials pending final checking. The iron-nerved Londoner, who started his record run Sunday at 7:29 a.m. Pacific standard time, shattered a dozen or more official and unofficial records for various distances on the way to the 48-hour triumph. He set his new marks on a 10-mile circular course within sight of the dazzling white speedway on which his countryman, Sir Malcolm Ca

Hyde Park, N. Y., July 13.—President Roosevelt turned longing vacation eyes toward Maine tonight after promising a delegation of the United States Flood Control Congress he would set in motion preliminary machinery for flood works in the Ohio Valley, New York and New England, and make a personal survey of those areas next month. The president left by special train for Rockland, where tomorrow he will board the chartered schooner Sewanna 10 miles off shore for a two-weeks’ sailing cruise in Maine and Canadian waters with three of his sons—James, Franklin, Jr. and John.

Taltal, Chile, July 13.—JP—A strong, three-minute earthquake demolished two schools, a lecture hall, the British consulate and other structures here today. No lives were lost, the governor reported to the undersecretary of the navy. The postal and telegraph offices were in ruins, but employees expected to restore normal service soon. Reports from Copiapó and Chañaral also said a strong quake was felt there, with only minor damages. "An earthquake shook the town; the sea oscillated approximately one meter. “Telegraph and telephone services were interrupted, while water pipes were seriously damaged. “Stores suffered serious losses. The population is panicky. “There are no reports of damage to the copper mines in Pouterillog. “No lives were lost.”

BONNEVILLE SALT FLATS, Utah, July 14 U.P— Capt. George E. T. Eyston of England ended a record-smashing 48-hour race against time today, leaving 20 shattered world automobile speed records in the wake of his flame-colored racer, Speed of the Wind. Haggard, partly deaf from the roar of his car’s thundering motor and his face burned bronze by the brilliant sun and whipping wind of the vast salt beds, Eyston jockeyed his car into the pits shortly after 8:30 a.m. A minute earlier he bettered by 27 miles an hour the world's 48-hour speed record with an official time of 136.36 m.p.h. The 48-hour mark represented the greatest achievement of setting a new 24-hour record. Yesterday at 8:29 a.m. the Englishman roared his racer past the 24-hour mark for a new record of 149.09612 m.p.h., nine miles an hour better than the 140.52 m.p.h. pace he set over the same period last year.

LONDON, July 14 (#)—Great Britain, fearing an attack from the skies, bolstered her air raid precautions today. A supplementary civil service estimate filed in the House of Commons asked for an additional $4,250,000 with which to purchase gas masks. Of this amount, $125,000 was earmarked for the purchase and adaptation of two factories producing masks in the Manchester area. An additional $25,000 was allotted for the civilian anti-gas school.

Chicago (P)—The historically famous New England Congregational church, a survivor of the great 1871 conflagration, was wrecked by fire early Tuesday. The church housed the rock on which the Pilgrims were baptized before going from England to Holland and thence to America in 1621. The rock, which dated back to the 14th century, came originally from Scrooby, England. The cornerstone of the church, laid in 1865, was part of the original Congregational church in Plymouth, Eng. Beside it was a piece of the Plymouth rock. The stone pieces were saved, as were numerous ancient Bibles, and a hymn book which was scorched in the great Chicago fire. Among the church's past members was Dwight L. Moody, famous evangelist. The present exclusive membership numbers 300. The church was the oldest in Chicago, and one of the wealthiest. Its regular pastor, the Rev. Theodore Hume, is on a speaking tour of En

EDMONTON, Alberta, July 14 (P) - Physicians considered a skin grafting operation today to cover the exposed heart of a new-born baby boy. “We do not know what to do,” said Dr. E. W. Svaries, who delivered the baby Saturday. “It might be possible to operate, grafting an artificial chest wall over the heart.” The child, weighing eight pounds, was born to Mrs. Fred Sadonsk of Wasel, 37-year-old mother of six other children. The baby’s heart is fully exposed through an opening in the chest wall two inches wide and three inches long. The vital organ protrudes from the body, its only covering being the outer wall of the heart itself. A solution has been placed on the heart at frequent intervals to keep it moist because of fear it might deteriorate if allowed to become dry.

PARIS, July 14 (Pi)—Two Red parades swarmed through Paris today as France celebrated the anniversary of the fall of the Bastille in 1789. The marchers were celebrating not only the revolution which overthrew the monarchy but also the victory of the “People's Front” in the elections six weeks ago. Police and mobile guards, watchful lest the celebrations develop into riots with nationalists, broke up a series of petty clashes. Mobile guards were called for brief actions in Bar-le-Duc and Lille. In the capital, the People’s Front processions converged on the Bastille following a great army parade through the length of the city. The soldiers were reviewed by President Lebrun and, for the first time in history, a Socialist premier, Leon Blum. In the civilian processions, masses of Red flags, with the Communist hammer and sickle emblem in the center and tricolor patches on one corner, waved ab

1936-10-13.text: WASHINGTON, Oct. 13.—The United States government Tuesday put into effect what Secretary of the Treasury Morgenthau termed “a new kind of gold standard.” Great Britain and France took similar action as the result of a three power agreement. Officials here said the pact was designed to curb currency speculation, put a check on exchange fluctuations and establish a free movement of gold among the three governments. Other nations were invited to join the new “gold bloc,” and some government economists predicted it might spread within a few weeks to a large part of the world. ‘Stabilization Step’ The understanding provided that the stabilization funds of the three

| Washington, Oct. 13. (UP)—The United States went on a “new gold standard” today under an agreement with Great Britain and France designed to aid further stabilization of world currencies. Secretary of the Treasury Henry Morgenthau, Jr., in announcing the agreement, said it is designed to stimulate foreign trade and stabilize international exchange by routing international money speculators. The agreement will permit an exchange of gold for the conversion of paper currencies of the individual countries. The three nations will cooperate in establishment of exchange price of gold from day to day, Morgenthau said. “This agreement,” Morgenthau said, “represents a divorcement of control of exchange markets from the few individual international speculators. SHANGHAI, Oct. 13.—(UP)— Mingled amazement and perplexity today greeted reports that Japanese quasi-official financial agencies have invited British capital to share in the economic penetration of North China. Officials in the Hsin Chung Kungssu, a subsidiary of the Japanese-owned South Manchuria railway, were said to have invited "British interests," particularly the Kailan Mining administration, to co-operate in the development of the Tientsin Electricity company—a Sino-Japanese company capitalized at 8,000,000 Chinese yuan. Apparently the official Japanese reason is that Japan wants to show she has no intention of driving out non-Japanese interests from North China, as feared.

SYDNEY, Australia, Oct. 13.—Jean Batten arrived here Tuesday from Long Reach, New South Wales, on her attempt to set a new air flight record between England and New Zealand. The 26-year-old woman pilot planned to rest for a few days before attempting the hazardous trip across the Tasman Sea.

By The Associated Press ST. PAUL, Oct. 12.—An eminent English surgeon—himself afflicted with the disease—today advanced a new method for diagnosing diabetes before 1,200 delegates to the International Medical Assembly. — Dr. Robert D. Lawrence of Kings College Hospital in London suggested the blood used in examinations be taken from the ear lobe instead of from a vein in the arm. "This is like catching a sugar train before it reaches a town instead of catching the train after it returns from the town where the sugar has been unloaded," he said. He said he believed such a practice would greatly reduce the percentage of doubtful cases. In making the tests, patients are given a large dose of sugar. The blood is examined every half hour for two hours. The results are compared to the reactions of normal persons and thus the extent of the disease can be more accurately determined. Diabetes is

Paris, Oct. 13.—(AP)—The German embassy announced today an official protest had been delivered to France against a Communist “insult” to Reichsführer Adolf Hitler. The German charge d'affaires made an “oral” protest, the embassy declared, to a French foreign office official concerning alleged statements during a speech at Strasbourg by Maurice Thorez, secretary-general of the French Communist party. The French official was declared to have promised to transmit the Nazi objection to Premier Léon Blum and Foreign Minister Yvon Delbos. The German embassy asserted it expected an early response from the French government.

A tour of the battle front by Premier Francisco Largo Caballero resulted in the decision to attack the insurgents all along a 3-mile front extending from northward of Navalperal de Pinares to southward of San Martin de Valdeiglesias. Soon long columns of trucks, marching men and artillery batteries were moving westward to the front on all roads leading from Madrid. Accompanying the men were many thousands of women who, realizing that the nationalists were almost within sight of Madrid, mobilized spontaneously

1936-10-31.text: Croydon, England, Oct. 30 — Shattering all speed records for an eastward crossing of the Atlantic, Captain James A. Mollison landed here today only 13 hours and 17 minutes after hopping off from wintry Newfoundland. Roaring across the stormy Atlantic in his Bellanca monoplane, the lone pilot averaged approximately 160 miles an hour to reach his goal at 9:57 am. (3:57 a.m. C. S. T.) It was the first time a flight with London as the eastern goal had been successfully completed without a forced landing en route. Counting the six hours and 41 minutes he took to reach Harbor Grace, Newfoundland from New York, he had made the entire flight in 19 hours, 59 minutes. Badly Exhausted Only a dozen spectators were on hand to cheer the veteran flier’s brilliant success, made in the face of forbidding weather conditions. LONDON, Oct. 30.—(U.P)—Captain James A. Mollison, British flying hero, completed his third crossing of the North Atlantic by airplane at 9:53 a.m. (4:53 a.m. SST) today, 13 hours and 13 minutes after his take-off from Harbor Grace, Newfoundland. He brought his green-yellow American made Bellanca monoplane down at Croydon airdrome before 200 spectators, including reporters and photographers. He still was dressed in the evening clothes which he wore when he took off from New York Wednesday. Mollison planned to take off within 24 hours for Cape Town, South Africa. Mollison said he had a very cold trip and lost nearly an hour trying to get his bearings at one time. “Soon after I started I ran into a snow storm,” he said. “When I was 700 miles out I had to circle over the ocean for about an hour in an effort to rid the airplane of ice which was beginning to form on the wings. ROME, Oct. 31—()—Italy intends to double its naval personnel, authoritative sources said today, preparing to meet any threat from England in the Mediterranean. Naval sources also disclosed plans for development and expansion of the Italian war fleet. Doubling of the naval personnel, just increased from 50,000 to 60,000 men, would raise it to at least 100,000. The purpose of the move, it was said, was to match Britain's naval rearmament in order to maintain the ratio of Italian naval strength to the British fleet. Following Mussolini’s recent announcement to the cabinet that “several scores of warships are now under construction,” naval sources said: 1. Many light warships from submarines to cruisers are being added to the two 35,000-ton battleships Littorio and Vittorio Veneto now under construction. London—U.P)—King Edward, in his first formal address to his parliament—an address studded thickly with “I’s” instead of the traditional “we”—issued a clearly implied invitation Friday for central European nations to seek peaceful revision of World War treaties. He covered the world situation and the domestic situation, on topics ranging from the Spanish Civil War to the new Anglo-Egyptian treaty, using plain “I”, “me”, and “my”, where his royal forbears used the kingly “we,” “us” and “our”. The king did not appear in person. His speech was read in the House of Lords to the assembled lords and commons by the Earl of Onslow, chairman of committees of the House of Lords. King Edward was at Buckingham Palace when the speech was read. He is to appear in person—and in his royal robes—at the state opening of parliament next Tuesday and speak from the throne. HOLLYWOOD, CAL., OCT. 31, (AP) ..Trapped in an overturned automobile, Hugh Buckler and his son, John Buckler, both actors of British birth, were drowned at midnight in Malibu Lake, the sheriff's office was informed today. The automobile slipped from the road during the rain storm and plunged into the little lake on the shore of which many Hollywood movie stars live, the officers were told. Malibu Lake where the Bucklers had a home is in the hills about 20 miles northwest of Hollywood. Young Buckler, who appeared in several American cities, came to Hollywood for pictures several years ago. For the last year he had been engaged in playing the villain in “Tarzan Escapes.” The tragedy did not become known until morning when residents of the lake colony saw the wheels of the Buckler car above the surface of the lake.

London, Oct. 30.—Capt. James A. Mollison logged a trans-Atlantic speed record tonight and indicated he might take off Saturday in his announced attempt to better the London-Capetown record held by his wife, the former Amy Johnson. Mechanics at Croydon airport tuned the motor of his monoplane in which he landed early in the morning, after flying from Harbor Grace, Newfoundland, in 13 hours and 18 minutes. His actual flying time from New York to London, irrespective of his 24-hour lay-over in Harbor Grace, was 19 hours and 59 minutes. Before going to bed, the haggard pilot said he awaited only favorable weather before taking off for Cape Town. The present record is held by Mrs. Mollison who traversed the route in 78 hours, 26 minutes flying time earlier in the year. Rivalry between Mollison and his wife over the Cape Town-London record dates back several years and has been held by each in

LONDON, Oct. 30 (P) — Wallis Warfield Simpson and King Edward still see each other, friends said tonight, but thus far have avoided formal public appearances when together. Twice this week, since Mrs. Simpson divorced her ship's broker husband, the king and his American-born friend have been reported in each other’s company. Mrs. Simpson was included in a small party the king gave for close friends at Buckingham Palace, reliable informants said, although court circulars of royal guests did not include her name. On another occasion the king was reported visiting Mrs. Simpson in her Cumberland Terrace home. Friends who professed authentic knowledge of King Edward’s views said it was unlikely he would escort Mrs. Simpson in public as he did on his continental tour this summer. In the future, these friends said the king probably would prefer to call on her in her new home.

LONDON, Oct. 34 -- (AT) -- Haiy Graham, 61, dramatic author and songwriter, died at his London home today. Graham, the son of Sir Henry J. L. Graham and Lady Edith Graham, and a former officer in the Coldstream Guards, began his playwriting career with “State Secrets” in 1914. Among his other plays were “Sybil,” “Madame Pompadour” (with Frederick Tenadale), and adaptations of “White Horse Inn,” “Casanova,” “The Maid of the Mountains,” “Our Peg,” “Head Over Heels,” and “The Good Companions.”

1936-10-15.text: London, Oct. 14.— (#P)— Ernest Simpson said tonight his wife, Mrs. Wallis Simpson, friend of King Edward, has filed suit for divorce. The case has been set for hearing before Justice Hawke at the Ipswich Assizes, opening Oct. 27, said Simpson, a commercial broker. To Let Her Go He asserted the case would not be defended. Beyond that, he declared, he had no statement to make. Legal sources pointed out Mrs. Simpson will seek her divorce on grounds of adultery, the only method by which it can be obtained in England. The proceedings will be placed on the "undefended" list, with Simpson not contesting the charges. If the divorce is granted, the former Baltimore woman will be freed from her second unsuccessful matrimonial venture. She was divorced in 1927 from Lieutenant Earl Spencer, whom she married in 1916. Protected Under no circumstances will the name of King Edward be mentioned in court,

Moscow—(U.P)—Russia, in a note to the non-intervention committee in London, has proposed a virtual naval blockade of Portugal to prevent shipment of war supplies to Spain, it was revealed officially Wednesday night. The note, delivered on Monday to the Earl of Plymouth, chairman of the committee, proposed that the French or British or their combined fleets should take immediate control of Portuguese harbors. Russia has threatened, if the committee does not act on its demand for drastic action to enforce neutrality, to quit the committee, thus implying that Russia will feel free to aid the leftist government forces in Spain. Samuel Kagan, Soviet charge d’affaires at London, who delivered the note to Lord Plymouth, urgently asked the committee to discuss its proposals without delay.

They pressed him a second time to convoke the committee immediately to act on their demand for a virtual blockade of Portuguese ports to stop Fascist arms shipments to Spain. News of the action circulated through fashionable Mayfair without benefit of headlines due to British laws against printing details of divorce petitions. MOSCOW — Russia Wednesday night demanded blockade of Portuguese ports to prevent shipment of arms to the Spanish insurgents. An official communique calls upon the neutrality committee to urge the British or French navy, or both, to patrol Portuguese ports. The Russian demands, the communique said, were handed directly in the form of a note to Lord Plymouth, chairman of the Spanish non-intervention committee in London. The note also demanded, it was said, that the body be reconvened immediately to consider concrete proposals which Russia advanced to prevent neutrality violation. - London.—-Lloyds, the insurance people, decided last week not to bet there will be no war in England. The firm announced it will issue no more war insurance to land owners in the British Isles. For many years Lloyds has been ready to insure any land owner against war damage at a rate of 1-5 per cent. Recently, it was explained, Lloyd’s was startled by a sudden increase in requests for war insurance and decided to decline such policies entirely and probably permanently. One reason advanced was too much publicity has been given to bomb shelters recently constructed on several English estates.

LONDON, Oct. 14—Bette Davis, popular American motion picture star, was called “a rather naughty young lady who wants more money” today in the King’s Bench court in London. The characterization of the actress was made during arguments in a lawsuit relating to her contract with Warner picture producers. Sir Patrick Hastings, attorney for Warner Brothers, gave expression to the remark. The company, alleging that it had exclusive

LONDON (UP)— The refusal of Lord Plymouth, chairman of the Spanish non-intervention committee, to call a meeting to consider Soviet Russia's proposal for a naval blockade of Portugal threatened Thursday to start an open truce between fascist and leftist powers to their favorites in the Spanish civil war. Russian diplomats expressed anger over Lord Plymouth’s refusal. Moscow already has warned that it will withdraw from the agreement unless fascist powers cease their alleged aid to the rebels. Germany, in turn, has served notice that it will reserve "freedom of action" if Moscow withdraws. Russia, in a note to the committee, asked that the British and French navies blockade Portugal to see that arms were not sent into Spain. 1936-07-13.text: LONDON, July 13 (4)—Lord Cranborne, undersecretary of state for foreign affairs, told the House of Commons today he understood Heligoland was being fortified by Germany. Asked if the island was being fortified by leave of the British government, Lord Cranborne said, "No, it is not being fortified by leave of anyone." Lord Cranborne, acting in the place of Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden, made the announcement in answer to a question from Oliver Locker-Lampson, a conservative member, whether Germany's promise not to fortify Heligoland had been kept. He added that no right to inspect the island exists. (Heligoland is a fifth-of-a-square-mile rock island off the German and Danish coasts in the North Sea, a strategic defense position to protect Germany’s Kiel canal and the ports of Bremen and Hamburg. NEW YORK—(U.P)—Followers from many faiths today mourned the death of Dr. S. Parkes Cadman, a one-time English coal miner who became one of the most beloved and influential men in America. His body was brought here today from Plattsburg, where he died Sunday, a week after he was stricken with appendicitis and peritonitis. He was 71. Funeral services will be held at 11 a.m. Wednesday, in Brooklyn Central Congregational Church, which he had served as pastor for 35 years. Bishop Francis J. McConnell of the Methodist Episcopal Church — the faith in which Dr. Cadman was born and in which he maintained membership—will conduct the service at the request of the family.

BY The Associated Press Plattsburg, N. Y., July 13—Dr. S. Parkes Cadman, 71, the Brooklyn pastor whose voice became familiar to millions of Sunday afternoon radio listeners, is dead. Dr. Cadman, who walked out of the Shropshire mines in England as a youth to attain international fame as a churchman, succumbed last night to peritonitis which developed from a ruptured appendix. An emergency operation was performed Monday after he had been stricken ill while delivering a lecture the previous night. Describing his passing, Frederick L. Cadman, a son, said he ‘fell asleep as peacefully as a child.’ Others present at the end were the preacher’s daughter, Miss Marie L. Cadman, of Brooklyn, his daughter-in-law, Mrs. Frederick L. Cadman, and his personal physician, Dr. George L. Buist, of Brooklyn. Dr. Cadman’s wife, the son said, was at the family summer home at Lakeville, Conn. He said that she

Rome—(#)—The Italian government today ordered the withdrawal of 40,000 troops from the Italian colony of Libya, along the Egyptian border, in answer to Great Britain’s removal of her home fleet from the Mediterranean. These troops, ending their African service, will be assigned to duty along the frontier of France. The first unit to leave Africa will be the motorized Trento division, the first section of which embarked today for Italy. Previously this division was stationed at Alto Adige, near the frontier of Austria. The Austro-German accord of Saturday released that frontier from the previous tension.

BONNEVILLE SALT FLATS, Utah, July 13.—(#)—Captain George Eyston, Great Britain’s knight of the roaring road, smashed his twenty-four-hour world land speed record today with an unofficial average of 149.16 miles an hour. TRAVELS 3580 MILES The tall, steel-nerved Englishman, alternating at the wheel of “Speed of the Winds” with a fellow countryman, Bert Denly, sent the twelve-cylinder racer roaring over 3580 miles of glistening white salt in the day and night grind. The record far surpassed the 140.52 miles an hour which Eyston established over the same track last September. The twenty-four-hour run completed the first half of a projected forty-eight-hour grind in quest of a greater speed than the 109.54-mile-an-hour record four European drivers established several years ago. Eyston was jubilant as the record tumbled. He stopped at the pits for oil and gasoline and roared away again on the

JERUSALEM, July 13.—Seven Arabs were killed and one wounded today in a clash with British troops. The soldiers went to the rescue of a signal force repairing telephone lines in the Jenin district and surrounded the Arab band on a hilltop.

HYDE PARK, N. Y. (1) Representatives of the New England, New York and Ohio valley groups of the United States flood control federation laid a three-way emergency program before President Roosevelt and said afterward the chief executive had promised to visit some of these areas sometime in August. Representatives of a half dozen eastern and inland states came to urge President Roosevelt to set aside a large chunk of the 1936 relief act funds for emergency flood control reservoirs and other works. Spokesmen for the groups said many projects could not wait until Congress appropriated money to carry out authorization recently approved under the $320,000,000 omnibus flood control law. The president will leave Monday night by special train for Rockland, Me., to board the 56-foot schooner Sewanna. With three of his sons, James, John and Franklin, Jr., he will sail up the Maine coast and in New

TORONTO, July 13—(4)—The heat wave claimed a new victim today—this time a bulldog valued at $10,000. He was Bunjie, three-year-old international champion owned by R. P. Sparkes. Bunjie, brought to Canada from England 18 months ago, was installed in a kennel equipped with electric fans. Despite the precautions, he became ill Friday night and died early today. Veterinarians attempted to save his life by packing him in blocks of ice and administering oxygen, but were unsuccessful.

1936-07-28.text: WIMBLEDON, England. (4) England won the Davis Cup, prized trophy of the tennis world, for the fourth straight time as Fred Perry vanquished the veteran Jack Crawford, 6-2, 6-3, 6-3, for the third and clinching victory over Australia. The final score of the five match series was England 3, Australia 2. Perry’s triumph came after Adrian Quist squared the count at two all with a 6-4, 3-6, 7-5, 6-3 win over England’s dapper and usually machine-like H. W. “Bunny” Austin. England pulled away to a flying start in the series, winning both singles matches Saturday as Austin toppled Crawford and Perry conquered Quist. The Australians broke into the scoring column Monday when Quist and Crawford beat Charles Tuckey and Pat Hughes in the doubles.

MADRID. — The Spanish government, pressing new offensives against insurgent strongholds, claimed Monday night in a radio broadcast "the rebel government has been mastered by the republican government." The official assertion of success in Spain's eleven-day civil war came as American and British refugees fled from this capital by train to Alicante, where they were expected to board a British destroyer. Toledo Surrenders Premier Jose Giral Pereira’s administration declared Alcazar fortress at Toledo, south of Madrid, a rebel stronghold for several days, had surrendered to government troops, who took control of the whole city. Revolters in the Guadarrama mountains north of Madrid were forced to retreat with heavy losses before government troops and militiamen, the government declared. The capital and central Spain in general were firmly in the grasp of the government, together with virtual

LONDON, July 27—(AP)—The British government announced termination of its Mediterranean mutual assistance pledges today and then went on to win two votes of strength against its opposition in the House of Commons. Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden, making a final sweeping survey of international affairs before parliament adjourns for the summer, disclosed Britain had ended its assurances to aid Yugoslavia, Greece and Turkey if Italy should take aggressive action against any nation in the compact. The foreign secretary declared he looked for a “real spirit” of collaboration in solving European security problems, as he announced the end of the agreement which had been in effect since Italian animosity was aroused by application of sanctions for her Ethiopian war.

JERUSALEM, July 28.—(INS)— A big battle between rioting Arabs and British troops, the most serious engagement of several months’ of Arab disturbances broke out today south of Nablus and still was raging tonight. The conflict apparently started when Arabs attacked a British patrol and killed a British constable, Christopher John Wren. Authorities immediately dispatched airplanes, troops, and armored cars to pursue the attackers. Four Arabs were believed killed in an early clash, and the fighting continued tonight without sign of abating.

London, England, July 28.—(>)— For twenty years Mrs. Rosina Kemp of Calgary, Canada, had told her friends: “When I have seen my husband’s grave at Vimy Ridge I shall be prepared to die.” She fulfilled her wish Sunday, as one of the pilgrims to the unveiling of the Canadian war memorial on the bloodsoaked heights of Vimy. Then she boarded the steamer Antonia at Le Havre. Four hours later she was dead of a heart attack.

Intensified terrible punishment from the air was ordered in a new attempt to sound the knell of fascist revolt in outlying cities. From the northwest came official information that the long besieged rebel barracks at Loyola near San Sebastian had been taken by the government and that the rebel offenders had surrendered. In the Guadarrama, however, government claims of successes contrasted with rebel announcement of the capture of a defended village and the prediction of the insurgent general, Emilio Mola, that his men would reach Madrid within three days. MOSCOW, July 27, (#)—Russia henceforth is going to buy less and borrow less, sell more and save more—toward the goal of self-sufficiency. Furthermore, foreign trade Commissar Archibald Rozengoltz told the conference for foreign trade today, it won’t be necessary to send so many Soviet salesmen abroad—the buyers are flocking to Moscow. The reason for the self-sufficiency program, he asserted, is clear: “In the present period of increasing military dangers, the necessity to prepare for defense and the significance of increasing gold reserves is apparent. “Reduction of imports will be continued and intensified,” during the third and current five year plan by which Soviet Russia maps its future, Rozengoltz said. He added: “We hope to get along almost without imports.”

SAN SEBASTIAN, July 28.—Government troops today stormed and captured the barracks at Loyola in which were quartered more than a regiment of insurrectionists who had held the post stubbornly against repeated thrusts by loyalist troops. After occupying the barracks, the loyalist militia started a drive toward Navarre against Gen. Emilio Mola, northern rebel leader. After a bombardment and bayonet attack on the barracks, the insurgents, comprising infantry, artillery and Fascist units, surrendered unconditionally. The officers and non-commissioned officers marched under escort to government headquarters to await their fate. A war directive committee composed of the popular front and Basque nationalists was formed to war on Mola. The committee rigorously prohibited looting and ordered the requisitioning of clothing and shoes for the militia.

1936-03-23.text: (By the Associated Press) Ohio Valley—Kentucky and West Virginia tributaries pour fresh floodwaters into Ohio river, sending it on a renewed rampage through lower valley. Hundreds flee as crest moves towards Portsmouth, which is protected by flood wall. New England—Floods recede, leaving Hartford, Conn. and numerous other communities virtually paralyzed. Hartford establishes 9 o'clock curfew in stricken section. Pennsylvania—Rivers rise again at Pittsburgh, following blizzard, but no further damage expected. Electric power still off. Disease and fire dangers acute. National guardsmen police Pittsburgh and other Pennsylvania towns.

BERLIN, March 23.—Germany’s answer to the proposal of Great Britain, France, Belgium and Italy in the Rhineland crisis will leave the way open for negotiation of a peace consolidation program, it was announced today. LONDON, March 23. (U.P) — The League council today instructed Salvador De Madariaga of Spain and Joseph A. Avenol, the League's secretary general, to approach Italy and Ethiopia with a view of arranging a final peace settlement. The council met as the committee of 13, as it calls itself when it meets without Italy to consider the Italian-Ethiopian war. Madariaga, Spain's delegate, is chairman of the committee of five nations formed many months ago to seek a means of pacifying Italy and Ethiopia.

LONDON, Mar. 22.—(AP)—The Italo-Ethiopian war, temporarily neglected in the greater crisis caused by Adolf Hitler’s denunciation of the Locarno Treaty, will be considered tomorrow by the committee of 13 of the League of Nations. Plans call for the appointment of a sub-committee to determine peace terms. Italy accepted a League bid for peace negotiations with reservations and Ethiopia agreed to the same appeal without reservations. Premier Mussolini has not disclosed his terms but officials believe they will be heavy. Emperor Haile Selassie warned in an official communication yesterday he would not enter direct negotiations with Rome and that only a peace made through the League, “within the spirit of the covenant,” will be acceptable. The Negus further said reports of disastrous Ethiopian military reverses were preposterous. He characterized the existing financial and economic sanctions

Disease gained headway against military quarantines. Authorities feared that an established death toll of 37 would be increased by additions from an estimated 30 or 40 persons missing in areas where there still—seven days after New England rivers surged over their banks—were no communication or travel facilities. National guardsmen supplanted civil authorities under unproclaimed martial law in portions of almost every New England state. Two thousand enforced a 9 P.M. to 7 A.M. curfew in Hartford and a quarantine against typhoid fever and diphtheria in East Hartford. LONDON, March 23.— (#) The drafting committee of the international naval conference, in its final session, today made about 20 more changes in the text of the new naval treaty, most of them at the instigation of the American delegation. An American spokesman said the essential features of the treaty, which had been known even before the committee set to work, were not altered although there were no less than 14 drafts written before the completion of the text. The treaty will be signed Wednesday at St. James Palace, the delegations hoping it will go into effect Jan. 1, 1933, when the Washington naval limitation treaty expires, and remain in force for a period of six years. Although now only a tri-power treaty between the United States, Britain and France, it will be left open for adherence later by Japan and Italy.
