DETROIT, March 23.—(UP)— Lack of preparation and inadequate flood control systems in the Ohio river valley and in New England, Father Charles E. Coughlin charged in his address Sunday, were the fault of America’s financial interests bent on perpetuating their ‘rackets.’ Construction of permanent and effective control systems was not permitted, he said, because such construction would eliminate the necessity of the American people “going to their (financier’s) swill ‘pall year after year and bonding ourselves and future generations for the benefit of those who profit through disaster.” The current chaos in the flooded zones, he said, exemplified the practice of the “money changers,” who permitted destruction of wealth “lest their racket be taken out of existence.”

Milwaukee—Two Shawano merchants and their nephew, Julian Breakstone of New London, surrendered today to federal authorities who held warrants charging them with receiving property stolen from interstate freight shipments. With Breakstone were Sam and William Chaimson. Sam Chaimson is president of the Chaimson Mercantile Company of Shawano. Breakstone operates a store at New London. The trio were arraigned before U. S. Kerr of the Chicago detective bureau said was a roundup of “the best gang of receivers I have encountered in the last 10 years.” In addition to the three arrested today, Meyer Rubin of Chicago, Oscar Chaimson of Shawano, and Al Le Fevre, a clerk in the Chaimson store, have been taken into cust

1936-02-25.text: By The Associated Press. LONDON, Feb. 25.—Great Britain, anticipating failure for the four-power naval conference, has proposed an Anglo-German-American naval agreement, it was learned today from authoritative sources. Members of the United States delegation, asked to confirm this report, refused to discuss it. High naval sources described the proposal as one of the most important affecting the United States, Great Britain and Germany since the World War. The agreement would limit the sizes and types of ships and guns among the three countries concerned and would provide for an annual exchange of information on construction programs. Word of the Anglo-German-American proposal came shortly after Italy had injected the Italo-Ethiopian war question into the naval conference as a fresh barrier to the achievement of a naval limitation treaty. London, Feb. 24.-(AP)—A son was born today to Countess Barbara Hutton Haughitz-Reventlow, heiress to the Woolworth millions. The Countess was married to Count Court Haughitz-Reventlow May 14, 1935, following her divorce from Prince Alexis Mdivani. Mdivani was killed a few months later in an auto accident in Spain. The young mother’s father and stepmother, Mr. and Mrs. Franklin Hutton, came to England from the United States for the event. The British press recently has printed reports that the Count and Countess would make their home in England, fearing that their child might be kidnapped if taken to the United States; the Count, however, denied this report flatly through The Associated Press.

LONDON, Feb. 24 (4)—A British plan to induce all nations including the United States to join a world-wide system of collective security in an effort to end war was outlined to the House of Commons today by Anthony Eden, foreign secretary. LONDON, Feb. 24 (@)—Anthony Eden, foreign secretary, declared today that the future of disarmament depended in a large extent upon the military strength of Great Britain. In his first speech as chief of the British diplomatic service in the House of Commons, the young statesman declared: “The road to disarmament lies through increased power and authority of the League of Nations.” He said the league, in turn, depended to a considerable measure upon 'the arms and strength of our own country.' He stated that Great Britain had not yet decided upon the application of an oil embargo against Italy but declared that the British government stood firm in the pol

QUICK CONFERENCE Washington, Feb. 24. (P)—The house agreed quickly today to a conference with the senate on the new $500,000,000 Farm bill. DEPENDS ON BRITAIN London, Feb. 24. (P)—Anthony Eden, foreign secretary, declared today that the future disarmament depended in a large extent upon the military strength of Great Britain.

(BY the Associated Press) London, Feb. 25.—Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden’s much-heralded House of Commons speech, which side-stepped a stand on the oil sanction issue, aroused belief today that only a slender chance remained of Britain pressing for an embargo against Italy. General satisfaction greeted some sections of Eden’s maiden speech to the Commons as Foreign Secretary, especially his proposal for a world-wide system of collective security, rather than a policy of European “encirclement.” Disappointment spread in political circles, however, because Eden gave no indication of the government's final intentions concerning an oil sanction, uppermost question in the League of Nations campaign against the Italo-Ethiopian war.

Both the mother, the 23-year-old Countess Barbara Hutton Haugwitz Reventlow, and the little count were reported to be doing “very well.” Count Haugwitz-Reventlow dispelled rumors the child would be kept permanently in Europe through fear of kidnapping in America. “He will be taken to the United States very soon,” the Danish nobleman said, “probably within a month or six weeks. | LONDON, Feb. 25 (4.P) - Countess Von Haugwitz-Reventlow, American Five and Ten Cent Store heiress, has transferred part of her fortune to England, reliable sources said today. Her one day old boy, it was understood, is to be brought up in Europe, his time divided between England and Denmark. Despite reports to the contrary, it was understood that the baby born yesterday to the former Barbara Hutton is unlikely to be seen in the United States for a long time. The baby is under heavy guard at No. 2 Hyde Park Gardens, in a cozy imported French cradle, and close friends say that the countess is so afraid of kidnappers that she intends to live permanently in Europe. It is understood on good authority that the countess intends at present to keep her baby entirely on this side of the Atlantic, and it is even said that she may not take him to the United States before he is grown up. |

1936-05-16.text: Washington, May 15, (4)—The senate foreign relations committee formally approved the London naval treaty today and put it before the senate for action Monday. The pact was described variously by senators as a “step toward limitation” and as a measure so “full of holes it ought to be called the Swiss cheese treaty.” But Admiral William H. Standley and Norman H. Davis, delegates to last winter’s conference in London at which the treaty was negotiated, said it was the best that could be worked out. Chairman Pittman (D.-Nev.) of the foreign relations committee predicted it would be ratified with little opposition. The treaty provides that the signatory nations shall exchange information as to proposed new construction, and while it imposed no limitation on the number of ships that could be built, it attempted to limit the size and gun power of each type of ship. CROYDON AIRDROME, Eng., May 15—(AP)—Mrs. Amy Johnson Mollison, England’s number one airwoman, put three new records into her logbook tonight. She returned from Capetown, South Africa, setting records each way for the solo flight and a new one for the round trip. She made it back in 4 days, 16 hours, 18 minutes, trimming the record of Flight Lieutenant Tommy Rose of 6 days, 6 hours, 57 minutes. She covered the total distance of more than 14,000 miles across the Sahara and Africa's jungles and back in a flying time of 7 days, 22 hours and 43 minutes.

London, May 15.—(4)—Sylvia Sidney, Hollywood star, collapsed tonight in the midst of an excited crowd of autograph seekers who jostled her at Waterloo station. She was carried to an automobile. Anita Louise, American actress who arrived with Miss Sidney on the liner Berengaria from America, also was bothered by the movie fans and left the station in tears. o Galesburg, Ill., May 15.—(#)—S. A. Ingersoll, 78, former head of the Coulter Dise company here, died tonight after a brief illness. Ingersoll owned ranches at Martinsdale, Mont., and Pueblo, Colo.

An official communication to the League said the Red Cross could not respond to an appeal from its Ethiopian branch because the request failed to specify the purpose for which the masks would be used. The republic's withdrawal, which cannot be effective for two years, led league circles to wonder if the action was the start of a "stampede engineered by Premier Mussolini or merely an isolated incident.

Paris, May 15.—Leon Blum, expected to become France's first Socialist premier, told the American club today “in France we believe the question of debts is eliminated.” The leader of the People’s Front deplored the existence of what he termed a “misunderstanding” between the United States and France due to France's unpaid war debts, but gave no indication the question would be reopened. Instead, Blum expressed hope world recovery—based on new stabilization and disappearance of trade barriers—would eliminate bad feeling. Claims Misunderstanding “A misunderstanding exists between the two countries,” he said, “and the only means of eliminating it, I believe, is by frankness. “I believe Americans fail to understand to what extent the Dawes plan and Hoover moratorium created in our minds a logical connection between the payments of debtor Germany (to France) and our payments to creditor Americ

MOSCOW, May 10—(Saturday)—(AP)—An official Soviet news agency dispatch from Khabarovsk, Siberia, today said a Soviet border patrol had been subjected to rifle fire from the Manchoukuoan side of the frontier, breaking more than a month of quiet along the boundary. The official Tass agency stated the Russian soldiers, anxious to avoid a clash, did not return the fire. The incident, the account asserted, occurred May 13. The last Russo-Japanese border encounter reported here occurred April 9 at Sosnovaya Piat, when two Japanese soldiers were killed in a clash which the Soviets declared resulted from an invasion of Soviet territory. Since that time negotiations have been continuing between the Japanese and Soviet government for settlement of frontier troubles.

Rome, May 16.—(U. P.)—Upsetting the prediction of dissenting votes, the Italian Senate today unanimously approved royal decrees annexing Ethiopia to Italy, proclaiming King Victor Emanuel emperor and appointing Marshal Badoglio governor general and viceroy. The unanimous vote surprised observers since several non-Fascists participated in the secret ballot cast by the 337 senators. Italian senators are appointed for life and it had been anticipated that there might be some votes against the decrees, either directly or by abstention. The Chamber of Deputies has already ratified the decrees.

VIENNA, May 15. (4)—Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg issued a definite challenge to the Fascist Heimwehr led by the ousted Vice-Chancellor Ernst Von Starhemberg, by announcing tonight that Austria's bickering private armies must dissolve. Schuschnigg thus moved to ensure continuance of his one-man dictatorship, substituted for a two-man dictatorship when Prince Von Starhemberg was removed two days ago. He explained his plans in a radio speech to the nation. With Von Starhemberg in Rome, immediate reaction to the chancellor's speech was not available, but Heimwehrmen in Upper Austria, where Von Starhemberg got his start, were in a belligerent mood. “Dualism in control of Austrian affairs is a thing of the past,” the chancellor asserted. “It was replaced not because of great differences between the leaders, but because in these stern times even slight differences cannot be tolerated.”

1936-05-25.text: Jerusalem—()—An Arab girl was wounded fatally and a British constable was injured seriously today in persisting disorders arising from Arab opposition to the Jewish influx to the Holy Land. Tension mounted higher in Palestine, with continued banishment of Arab agitators spurring fresh resistance to British military forces attempting to restore order. Arab women, posted on rooftops, stoned troops and police searching houses in the village of Kafr Kanna, near Nazareth. Sporadic gunshots and bomb explosions were heard at midnight on the outskirts of Jerusalem.

Southampton, Eng., May 25 (P) — King Edward flew from Windsor today — the second time he has taken to the air since becoming sovereign — to head Britain’s royal family in a final inspection of the liner Queen Mary. The monarch was in the air 31 minutes, landed at the Eastleigh airdrome five miles away and drove to the dock to meet Queen Mary and other members of the family who came from London by train.

Miami, Fla., May 25. (UP)— One of the world’s richest young men and the daughter of an unemployed Pittsburgh steel worker were honeymooning in British West Indies waters aboard their yacht today after a wedding at sea. The bridegroom is William B. Leeds, sportsman heir to a fortune made in the tinplate industry. The bride was Miss Olive Hamilton, 24, daughter of William Hamilton. Leeds was divorced in 1930 by the former Princess Xenia of Russia. Leeds announced the wedding, which climaxed a romance of the sort of which shop girls dream, in a radiogram to shore. The ceremony was performed Saturday aboard his yacht.

LONDON, (#) - The Anglo-Russian naval conversations snagged on the issue of the Soviet Far Eastern fleet. Britain opposed Soviet contentions that this fleet should be excluded from a contemplated limitation pact unless Japan also were bound by a direct Russo-Jap agreement. Failing such an accord, the Russians desired to be free to withhold advance information on Far Eastern fleet construction.

Moscow, May 24—The Soviet Union announced today it cannot consider limitation of its Far Eastern fleet as long as there is no similar agreement binding Japan. Conversations now going on in London will therefore have to do only with armaments in European waters, it was officially stated. The announcement was made in the government newspaper Izvestia over the signature of the authoritative spokesman, Karl Radek. He said the Soviet Union has been striving to conclude a separate agreement with Japan but thus far the efforts have been fruitless. Throwing the blame on the shoulders of Japan, the statement said the situation was a "direct result of the fact Tokyo broke the Washington agreement and abandoned the London conference." Since Japan has its hands free in regard to naval armaments, the statement said, and the Soviet Union cannot send reinforcements from European to Asiatic waters excep

Dublin, May 25.—(UP)—Four Americans won residual prizes of £5,337 ($26,685) each in the final day’s draw of the Irish Hospital sweepstakes today. They included “Bruin Bears,” care of B. C. Kellz, Box 263, Bruin Butler County, Pa.; “Buddies,” (22 Lodge Avenue, Poten) Pittsburgh, Pa., and (Turn to Page 7, Col. 5)

Jerusalem, May 24. — (Jewish Telegraphic Agency)—One British soldier was reported shot dead today when an Arab mob attempted a daring delivery of prisoners serving terms at hard labor in a prison near Tulkarem. (Nearly 40 persons, most of them Jews, have been killed since an Arab general strike began April 19 in protest against Jewish immigration and sale of land to Jews.) Reinforcements sent to the prison from Hadera routed the attackers, who retired to the hills maintaining their fire. The convicts recently rebelled in sympathy with the anti-Jewish general strike. Terrorists also attempted to bomb the German steamer Richard Burchard, flying the Nazi swastika, when it entered the temporary harbor at the all-Jewish city of Tel Aviv to unload, passing up the neighboring Arab port of Jaffa. Two bombs were thrown at the ship from lighters. Eight bombs were thrown in the vicinity of Tel Aviv

Miami, May 25.—(UP)—One of the world’s richest young men and the daughter of an unemployed Duquesne, Pa., steel worker were honeymooning in British West Indies waters aboard their yacht today after a wedding at sea. The bridegroom is William B. Leeds, sportsman heir to a fortune made in the tinplate industry. The bride was Miss Olive Hamilton, 24, daughter of William Hamilton. Leeds was divorced in 1930 by the former Princess Xena of Russia. His mother was the former Princess Anastasia of Greece. Leeds announced the wedding, which climaxed a romance of the sort of which shop girls dream, in a radiogram to shore. The ceremony was performed Saturday aboard his yacht, Moana, by Capt. John B. Fox, and witnessed by members of the crew. “The only story possible both very happy,” Leeds radioed. Leeds and his bride met under circumstances that made the progress of a courtship easy. 1936-05-30.text: (Copyright, 1936, by United Press) London, May 29,—The United States today indicated readiness to reopen the whole question of Great Britain's war debt to America, but the British, mindful that another payment is due June 15, declined. The American offer was revealed when the foreign office received the customary U. S. Department of State reminder that another installment on Britain's war debt is about to fall due. The routine reminder, a mere formality since Britain ceased making even “token” payments to the United States, differed from the ordinary somewhat because the American note expressed a willingness to negotiate a settlement of the debts question. The British government, however, is preparing a reply announcing its inability to resume debt payments to the United States at present. The reply, it was understood, will indicate that the moment is not suitable for a reopening of the

GIBRALTAR, May 29. (4)—Haile Selassie, emperor of a lost empire, arrived at Great Britain’s rock of Gibraltar as a private citizen today. He came here from Palestine in the British cruiser Capetown. British military authorities exchanged courtesies with him aboard and then the emperor hastened ashore to recover from seasickness. He will continue his trip to England Sunday.

ABOARD S.S. QUEEN MARY EN ROUTE TO NEW YORK, May 30—(1P)—A thick fog tonight diminished hopes that the gigantic British liner, Queen Mary, would set a new Atlantic record. The ship’s speed was sharply cut as the visibility was reduced to about 50 yards. Officers claimed that she already had set a record.

ROME, May 30 (UP).—The Italian cabinet met today, for the first time since the proclamation of the “second Roman empire,” to discuss Strained relations with England and plans for consolidating the conquest of Ethiopia. Premier Benito Mussolini was expected to seize the occasion to warn League of Nations powers in positive terms of the danger of continuing economic sanctions against Italy. It was indicated that he would deliver an ultimatum—sanctions to be withdrawn, or Italy to leave the league.

en Route to New York, May 29. (—The giant liner Queen Mary, coursing steadily westward through calm seas, ran close behind the French Normandie’s record one-day run of 748 miles tonight. The British contender for trans-Atlantic crossing honors covered 747 nautical miles in a 25-hour day run. One mile behind the French record set from noon to noon June 1-2 last year. The Queen Mary's average speed during the one-day trial was 29.76 knots, only slightly slower than the Normandie’s one-day average of 29.92 knots.

London, May 29 (4’)--Government Opposition quarters expressed belief tonight Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin is preparing to “strike a bargain” with Italy to end Anglo-Italian tension. This belief was sharpened as the cabinet discussed sanctions on the heels of an implied threat by Premier Mussolini to withdraw from the League of Nations if sanctions are not halted. There were open rumors in labor circles of the House of Commons that the government is toying with the idea of making a ‘deal with Italy.’ Since there is a fortnight of grace before the League Council meets at Geneva June 16, the cabinet delayed final decisions on sanctions until Parliament reconvenes June 9. Instructions then will be given Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden.

QUEBEC, May 29 (P)—Ann Harding, blonde screen actress whose former husband, Harry Bannister, had pursued her here to prevent her leaving for Europe with their seven-year-old daughter, sailed Friday night for England. She and the child, Jane, sailed aboard the liner Duchess of Atholl. Originally passage had been booked for them on the Impress of Australia which does not leave until Saturday. Miss Harding was overtaken in Quebec by Bannister, who flew here from Montreal scarcely two hours after she had established herself at the Chateau Frontenac. Secret plans were made when word was received that the actress’ former husband was en route, and the party boarded the liner quietly. Arrives by Train Miss Harding arrived here by train from Montreal, closely followed by Bannister who flew there today from Newark, N. J. The Duchess of Atholl, which sailed from Montreal Friday morning, was not due
BROCKENHURST, Eng., May 30 (AP)—Lord Darling, 86, poet and retired barrister, died yesterday. He retired from the bench of the High Court of Justice in 1923.

1936-03-25.text: London, England —(Copyright)—Adolf Hitler's absolute refusal to withdraw his forces from the Rhineland or to accept a judgment by the world court tightened Europe’s crisis Wednesday, throwing the delicate negotiations back to the chancellories of the Locarno powers. The councilors of the League of Nations, after days of waiting for the word from Der Fuehrer, left London, putting up to Britain's foreign secretary, Anthony Eden, and the other Locarno diplomats the task of finding a way out of the new greater impasse. With the departure of the league council, informed sources said, the first phase of the international crisis—reassertion of the sanctity of treaties, coupled with condemnation of Germany for its occupation in violation of the Locarno pact—was past. LONDON, March 25—(4)—The United States, Great Britain, and France signed a new international naval treaty today. The pact removes restrictions on the sizes of navies, but the United States and Great Britain, possessors of the world’s mightiest fleets, agreed separately to maintain their navies at the same level. This Anglo-American agreement was expressed in an exchange of letters between Norman H. Davis, head of the American delegation, and Anthony Eden, British foreign secretary. Davis hailed the treaty as the “foundation of a new structure” for world fleet limitation. His address at the signing ceremony contained an open invitation to Japan and Italy to adhere to the pact. WILSON London, March 25—(/)—A new international naval treaty was signed today by delegates of the United States, Great Britain and France while Italy’s delegates, remaining aloof, attacked British naval activities in the Mediterranean. Ambassador Dino Grandi of Italy declared: “A potential naval menace exists in the Mediterranean.” He referred to the concentration of British craft there. Japan was not represented at today’s ceremony since the Japanese walked out of the conference after its demands for equality were refused. Drop Restrictions The new treaty drops the restrictions on the size of the world’s greatest navies. The chief American delegate, Norman H. CORK, Ireland (UP)—Civil guards throughout southern Ireland sought today a ‘murder car in which four men escaped after killing Vice Admiral Henry Boyle Somerville, retired, one of Great Britain’s most distinguished naval officers, at his home at Castletownshend. There were two clues—tire marks in the road before the admiral's home and a British recruiting poster which the assassins threw on the floor in the hall of the home. The poster was believed to disclose the motive for the murder, as Somerville had been active in the campaign to obtain recruits for the British navy. Four men drove up to the admiral’s home late last night. One of them knocked at the door, an aged maid servant answered, and called the admiral. He was riddled with bullets and fell on the front doorstep. Carried to a drawing room, he died before a doctor arrived.

LONDON, Iing. (UP) — The United States and Great Britain set an example to the world today by agreeing to maintain naval equality. The agreement was disclosed while delegates of the United States, the British Empire and France signed a six-year naval treaty, which limits ships by size and gun calibre, but makes no restrictions on the number of ships a signatory may build. Japan, Germany and Italy, all important naval powers, are not parties to the treaty. Norman Davis, American delegate, and Anthony Eden, British foreign secretary, effected the equality agreement by an exchange of letters. Davis’ letter emphasized that the British-American naval equality remains the guiding policy of the United States. Eden’s acknowledgment said the principle of equality was one to which Britain also adhered. Davis in a speech at the signing ceremony pleaded eloquently for real naval limitation, and expr

LONDON, Mar. 24 (P)— Europe’s crisis was thrown into a new and more complicated muddle tonight when Adolf Hitler refused outright to take his troops out of the Rhineland and rejected the Hague Court as a tribunal. Der Fuehrer’s answer to the Locarno program, made public shortly after the council of the League of Nations adjourned, left the Rhineland dispute unsettled. Joachim Von Ribbentrop, Hitler's special ambassador, arrived in London with a personal message to the British government from the German dictator just as the council broke up. Although the Locarno demands were emphatically rejected, the Reich said that on Mar. 31 — two days after the German Reichstag election — it would “place at the disposal of the royal British government a statement of its position, together with its positive proposals.” Council To Reconvene The council will reconvene in Geneva some time after the German

(Copyright, 1936, by United Press) London, March 25 (UP)—Great Britain urged angry France today to refrain from precipitate action in the Rhineland problem until Germany made its position clear. France was the central figure for the moment, not Germany. It was understood that French anger was so strong that there was some fear of temporarily strained relations between the British and French governments over means of dealing with Fuehrer Adolf Hitler. It was believed that France would continue to insist that proposals submitted to Germany by Britain, France, Belgium and Italy were a definite take it or leave it offer and that Germany's rejection of them in a provisional or intermediate reply called for prompt action. Washington, March 25. — The new naval treaty signed today by the United States, Great Britain and France was hailed by Norman H. Davis as the foundation of a new start for world fleet limitations. His address as a signor of the ceremony in London contained an open invitation to Japan and Italy to join in the limitations.

1936-09-21.text: | NEW YORK, Sept. 21.~-(>— Diek Merrill and Harry Riehman brought down their silvery monoplane ‘Lady Peace’ at Floyd Bennett airport at 1:10 p. m. (EST) today to complete a round trip trans-Atlantic flight to London begun Sept. 2. The ship of the adventuresome night club singer and the Commercial Airlines’ pilot, which twice came to earth in forced landings during the stop and go flight to Croydon airdrome and return, bogged down in the mud as it came to rest. Floyd Bennett field was soft from overnight rains and the ‘Lady Peace’ settled heavily as Merrill pulled the machine to a stop. A truck pulled the plane out of the mud.

NEW YORK, Sept. 21 (U.P)—Harry Richman and Dick Merrill landed the monoplane, “Lady Peace,” at Floyd Bennett Field at 2:16 P. M. today, a week late on their return flight of a round-trip to England. The non-stop flight here from Harbor Grace, N. F., today ended a troublesome week during which the fliers’ relations were strained. They quarreled high above the Atlantic when Richman dumped gasoline which later forced them to land in a bog at Musgrave Harbor, N. F.

CROYDON AIRPORT, LONDON, Sept. 21—(UP)—Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia took off from here unexpectedly today for Geneva where the question of the League seating his country’s delegation is for settlement.

NEW YORK (#) — Lady Nancy Aster, Virginia-born first woman member of Britain’s parliament, described President Roosevelt and Governor Alf M. Landon as “decent fellows” Sunday — and steered clear of expressing any political preference between them. The “great thing” about Anglo-Saxon countries, she observed, was that “political enemies can still meet and be courteous to each other.”

GENEVA, ()—The League of Nations assembly, by a vote of 39 to 4 tonight adopted a report of its Credentials committee recommending that the Ethiopian delegates be seated. The report also decided against submission of the Ethiopian question to the World Court. The Ethiopians refrained from voting.

Government militiamen retreated today before a relentless charge of Moorish legionnaires on Maqueda, a vital highway junction 40 miles from Madrid. Thousands of other government soldiers, meanwhile, organized into bombing squads, surrounded the shell-leveled alcazar in Toledo for a decisive assault on the insurgents besieged in the ruins of the fortified palace. The well-drilled Moors, recruited to the insurgent ranks from Spanish Morocco, drove forward halfway from Talavera de la Reina to Maqueda behind a shield of machine gun bullets which left bodies of government troops in their war-torn path. Government bombing planes sought to scatter the advancing Fascists; but most of their shells went wide of the mark. Gen. Jose Asensio, commander of all government troops in central Spain, ordered hasty entrenchments dug for a pitched battle and a radio appeal summoned all government reserves to

GENEVA, Sept. 21 (#)—Haile Selassie won a preliminary skirmish today in his fight to save the lost kingdom of Ethiopia a seat on the League of Nations assembly. The League credentials committee notified the assembly it had approved the credentials of all delegations except Ethiopia, on which a special report would be submitted later. However, members of the committee announced that under the rules, the Ethiopians might sit on the assembly until that body decides otherwise. TOKYO, Sept. 21—(U.P)—The navy department announced today that it had ordered Japanese marines to land at Hankow in China to protect the life and property of Japanese nationals. “The navy fears,” said the announcement, “that it may be forced to resort to some defensive measures in the near future.” This action resulted from the alleged murder of a Japanese by a Chinese in Hankow, latest of a series of several such incidents, and the consequent embitterment of Japanese-Chinese relations. Two Japanese destroyers were en route to Hankow, an important industrial city on the Yangtze river. DOUBTS SINCERITY The navy department said the sincerity of the Nanking government in wanting to end anti-Japanese feeling in China was not dependable and hence the protective measures were taken. 1936-03-18.text: Copyright 1936. by The Associated Press LONDON, March 18—(7)—A prominent member of the League of Nations Council predicted tonight that the League would remove all sanctions from Italy in order to obtain a unanimous condemnation of Germany for denouncing the Locarno treaty.

LONDON (OP) — Captain Anthony Eden, British foreign secretary, urged the league council Wednesday to declare Germany a treaty violator and to notify the signatories of the Locarno treaty to that effect. Eden reaffirmed his previous declaration that Germany had violated both the Versailles and Locarno treaties. The heads of the Locarno powers just before the council met, adjourned their meeting until 10 a.m. Joseph Boncour of France said no full accord had yet been reached.

Representatives of Great Britain, France, Belgium and Italy struggled in the foreign office to find a new way to restore the shattered security framework of Western Europe. A delegation of German diplomats, assured of Great Britain's consideration of Reichsfuehrer Hitler’s new peace proposals, was flying by airplane from Berlin but was due too late for today's session of the League of Nations’ council. By the Associated Press Stormy dissent from France in the form of new demands upon Germany interrupted progress toward a solution of the Locarno crisis in western European affairs Tuesday. Hope that had arisen with the acceptance by Germany of a seat at the conference tables was dimmed by the insistence of Foreign Minister Pierre-Etienne Flandin that Germany be branded with treaty violation and withdraw her troops before new peace negotiations are undertaken. Joining him in the attack was Maxim Litvinoff, foreign commissar of Soviet Russia, who characterized the German peace proposals as a “smoke screen for aggression.” He pledged full support to council measures to punish the Reich. London, March 18—Europe's high diplomats awaited the arrival of a German delegation today to start work on a program of peace consolidation which they hoped would remove the danger of a European war in favor of a period of security and friendship. The situation precipitated by Germany’s reoccupation of the Rhineland in defiance of the Versailles and Locarno treaties was still difficult and dangerous. France, Great Britain, Belgium, and Italy, comprising with Germany the signatories to the guarantee of the Locarno treaty, still were far apart in their views as they met today, seeking agreement to a program. France was angry because she believed that Britain put compromise with Germany before complete support of France and Belgium. Leaders said that the next 48 hours would be fateful for all Europe—that negotiations today and tomorrow would tell whether there was to be a new, stronger syst

LONDON—U-P)—Great Britain France and Belgium sought urgently today to compose their wide differences on the Rhineland crisis as they awaited a German delegation from Berlin. It was admitted that Germany had won a big success by its acceptance on reasonable terms of an invitation to participate in conferences of Locarno treaty signatories and the league council on the crisis. Not only France, but Belgium, it was understood, had rejected a British proposal, designed to give a friendly start to real security negotiations, for demilitarization of a buffer zone extending 30 miles on either side of the French-Belgian-German frontiers. French circles were angry at the proposal and held it to be unacceptable to the cabinet and the general staff. 1936-12-11.text: London, Dec. 11.—(AP)—The greatest empire on the earth gave up Edward VIII as king today and placed his oldest brother, Albert Frederick Arthur George, on its throne. In three swift hours, the Houses of Commons and Lords approved the abdication of the 327-day sovereign who chose marriage to a twice-divorced American instead of his ancient crown. Then, with quick precision, a royal commission gave royal assent to the act. At 1:52 p.m., (8:52 a.m. E.S.T.) Edward the Eighth ceased to reign. At that very moment the quiet Duke of York became King of England and the Dominions Beyond the Seas, Emperor of India, defender of the faith.

Cannes, France — (#) — Mrs. Wallis Simpson, for love of whom King Edward renounced his throne, said through a spokesman today she expects to obtain her final divorce decree without any complications. The American-born fiancée of the former ruler said she was not aware of any move in England to invalidate her temporary divorce decree from Ernest Aldrich Simpson, the intermediary asserted. "No Arrangements." Mrs. Simpson has "no arrangements to meet Edward," the spokesman declared, reiterating that the former Baltimore belle expected to remain in southern France for several weeks at least. He declared the "understanding at the villa (where Mrs. Simpson is in seclusion) is that Edward will have left London by tomorrow." Mrs. Simpson arose at 10:30 a.m. and had breakfast with her hosts, Mr. and Mrs. Herman Rogers, of New York, as sunlight seeped feebly through an overcast sky. Guards Maintai

Vatican City — Lying in bed, Pope Pius XI assisted at mass today in a chapel adjoining his sick room, after what was described as his most tranquil night since he was stricken with paralysis of the legs. He went to sleep Thursday night after reciting his rosary and expressing gratitude the British throne had not fallen and a divorcee would not become queen. His holiness was given a draught of digitalis shortly before dawn. This was the only medicine he took during the night, attendants said. Vatican officials said the holy father was holding his own against a paralysis which has confined him to bed for the past week.

(Copyright) London, Dec. 11 (UP) — Edward VIII ended his brief reign today by giving his royal assent to the bill legalizing his abdication. His brother, the Duke of York, 41 next Monday, became king emperor to rule as George VI, one-fourth the world’s territory and people. The tragic crisis in the life of Edward VIII was over. He was free to marry Mrs. Wallis Warfield Simpson, former Baltimore society belle, when she obtains her final divorce decree. All that remains was for Edward VIII to make, as a private citizen, his farewell to his people in a broadcast to the empire at 4 p.m. today. The House of Commons passed the bill through all its stages in a two-hour session and recessed to await the Lords’ action. It took the Lords at the other end of Westminster Palace only 11 minutes to pass the bill. At 7:50 a.m. (CST) a royal commission sitting before the throne in the Lords announced th

Dublin, Irish Free State, Dec. 11—(AP)—A bill to abolish the office of governor general and the use of the British king’s name in conducting the Irish Free State’s domestic affairs was introduced in the Dail Eireann (parliament) today. The measure was presented by President Eamon De Valera who earlier had summoned the Irish parliament to consider King Edward’s abdication. The measure also provided for the recognition of Edward’s abdication and the Duke of York’s succession; but would limit British control over any Free State activity to foreign affairs. De Valera’s action was the first specific indication of organized opposition by a dominion to ratification of the former king’s renunciation of the throne. The Free State president had already indicated his intention of substituting a “ceremonial head of the state” for the governor general, the king’s representative, when he announced rec

London, Dec. 11—(Friday)—Edward VII renounced the throne of the British empire for a woman’s love today. The Duke of York, his brother and successor, took on his shoulders the problems of a troubled world. Thus forces were set in motion which may not be fully judged in this generation. Still king and emperor, Edward awaited one last document, the law of abdication, before becoming David Windsor who would marry Wallis Warfield Simpson, American born and twice divorced. Last Dinner Together The king and the king-to-be had probably their last dinner together in Edward’s retreat at Fort Belvedere. There Edward gave what counsel he could to the brother who will succeed him when the law dethroning the one and enthroning the other is passed.

By The Associated Press, Cannes, France, Dec 10—Wallis Warfield Simpson waited tonight for her unthroned King. She held herself a prisoner in her Riviera haven, whence she came December 3, from England when the waves of controversy, surrounding King Edward’s intention to marry her, began to beat about her head. Today she knew the world learned that the monarch had given up his imperial charge in order to make her his bride. She had been in telephonic communication with London during the morning. The way cleared for their marriage, she refused through her spokesman to comment on Edward's world-shaking pronouncement. Then she retired to seclusion. French and English police surrounded her villa to see that her withdrawal into privacy is observed. A crowd gathered during the afternoon in a soaking rain, but the officers had little to do. There was no sign of the striking brunette divorcee. “

LONDON. (WP). Great Britain’s new monarch—the man who will become either King Albert I or King George VI—Thursday night faced the challenge voiced by the man who was king: “My brother Bertie,” said ex-King Edward, when he was Prince of Wales, “would make a better king than I would.” The sallow-cheeked “Bertie,” who once wryly complained in a public statement that his chief claim to fame seemed to be that he was the father of two small, golden-curled princesses in effect took over the reins of dynasty at 10 a.m.—the moment a thin ribbon of ink traced the signature “Edward R. I.” on the formal document of abdication. At that historic moment, as Edward’s pen dotted the last period of his signature as rex imperator, the erstwhile duke of York stepped out of his lifelong role of “second fiddle” and became sovereign of the greatest empire on earth—subject only to the formal approval of the Bri

1936-05-20.text: Washington, May 20.—(4)—The British embassy has called on the United States for succor against an invasion of 17-year locusts. The gardener of the embassy, noticing the locusts among his beloved shrubs and flowers, put in an urgent telephone call to the Department of Agriculture and invoked diplomatic immunity. The official entomologists advised him today that the thing to do was just sit tight; the locusts, they said, are practically harmless. They warned, however, that the better diplomats, like other residents of the eastern United States, must prepare for a long, loud and persistent serenade when the locusts begin courting next month. The cicadas complete their mating and die off early in July.

LONDON— (U.P) —British feminists are heatedly indignant today at a suggestion to lawmakers that women automobile drivers be compelled to display a large red letter W on the front and rear of their cars. A similar law already compels student drivers to carry the red letter L for 'Learner' on their cars.

Boston, May 20.—(AP)—Samuel A. Boone, vice president of the Brotherhood of Firemen and Enginemen, announced today 92 percent of the employees of four New England railroads had “expressed a desire to leave the service” unless the railroads made a satisfactory adjustment of differences with the union. Boone said the union employees of the Boston and Maine, Maine Central, Portland Terminal Company and New York, New Haven and Hartford railroads objected to the operation of Diesel-powered engines with but a single man in the cab. They claimed such operation created a hazard to employees and the public. The chairmen of the local unions, however, would have to be polled, Boone added, before a strike call could be issued. He said it would take at least 72 hours before the result of the poll of the chairmen would be known. The poll of the employees who voted a desire to leave the service was take

LONDON, MAY 20. (AP).—Colonial Secretary J. H. Thomas voluntarily went to the witness box today for the second time and denied in two minutes testimony that he knew any of three men who mentioned his name in connection with an alleged budget leakage. The minister ended the testimony before the judicial inquiry into reports that an escape of official secrets led to a rush for insurance against tax increases with an emphatic declaration that he “never heard of” a financier who was reputed to have declared he could learn budget professions from the cabinet members.

WARSAW, Poland, May 20 (UP) — Poland’s new government today exposed an alleged Nazi plot to separate Upper Silesia from Poland and join it to Germany. The cabinet ordered that 118 members of the Nazi party in Upper Silesia, known as the National Socialist German Workers movement, be tried for conspiring to execute the plot. The trial, at which sensational evidence will be introduced by the government, will open at Katowicz on June 2. The defendants were arrested several weeks ago in connection with the military activities of their leader, Paul Maniura, who hanged himself recently. An intensive investigation by government agents revealed that Maniura’s followers had plotted to separate Upper Silesia from Poland and join it to Germany.

PARIS, May 20—(AP)—Edouard Herriot, thrice premier of France, weighed today an appeal from Leon Blum, premier-designate of the incoming Leftist government, to come foreign minister and take a leading part in proposed league nations reform. Blum, leader of the socialist party, urged Herriot personally last night to accept the foreign affairs portfolio in the new cabinet, to be formed after the left-dominated chamber of deputies convenes early in June. Sources close to Herriot said he was reluctant to take the post but deferred his final answer. One reason for Herriot’s unwillingness to take charge of the quai d'Orsay was reported to be the problem of writing a reply to the United States formal notice of the June 15 payment due on the war debt. Herriot, once overthrown by the chamber of deputies for his insistence that France should pay its war debts installments to America, announced only

Starhemberg Takes Steps to Oppose Kurt Schuschnigg’s Orders. Vienna, May 20—(U. P.)—Prince Ernst R. von Starhemberg, ousted co-dictator of Austria, today called a war council of the commanders of the Heimwehr, his private army. Fresh from his Rome conference with Premier Benito Mussolini, Starhemberg arrived in Vienna by airplane and at once took steps to oppose the orders issued by Kurt Schuschnigg, who ousted him from the cabinet, that the Heimwehr be disarmed. Starhemberg intimates said that the conference of Heimwehr commanders supported their leader's determination to oppose Schuschnigg’s disarmament orders. After today’s conference, conducted secretly at Starhemberg’s heavily guarded headquarters, a call went out for a national meeting of the Heimwehr leaders to discuss further action of the militant organization.

MOSCOW, (UP).—Applied for the first time in general practice, hypnotic treatment to ease the pain of childbirth has produced phenomenal results in Leningrad and Moscow clinics. Hypnotism was tested as part of a campaign to minimize the suffering of the mothers who bring into the world more than 15,000 babies each day—5,440,000 each year, a birthrate of 32 per thousand for a population of 170,000,000. In addition to hypnotism, all modern medical methods except those involving the use of morphine preparations or scopolamine have been used to induce 45,000 painless or semi-painless childbirths since Jan. 1. The goal is 400,000 such births during 1936. Each will be carefully recorded. On the basis of experience the best methods will be extended throughout the Soviet Union. The medical methods are familiar to physicians throughout the world. Use of hypnotism, however, is an innovation except

1936-09-02.text: LONDON, Sept. 2.—-(AP)—Japan formally disclosed today intentions of having a submarine strength one-third superior to that of either the United States or Great Britain. In a note, the Japanese signified they expected to retain 15,598 tons of submarines in excess of either of the other powers, LONDON, Sept. 2.--(AP)—Japan, in a formal note, today announced it intended to retain 15,598 tons of submarines in excess of the United States and Great Britain. That will make Japanese submarine strength one-third superior to that of the other two naval powers, The Japanese move was taken in reply to Great Britain's recent invocation of the Escalator clause of the London naval treaty of 1930, under which the British announced their intention of keeping 40,000 tons of overage destroyers in excess of the 150,000 tons allowed by the treaty. LONDON, Sept. 2.—The Japanese embassy delivered a note to the foreign office today in effect announcing Japan’s intention of possessing a submarine fleet approximately 80 per cent larger than either that of the United States or Great Britain, as from the end of this year. The decision replaces the submarine parity among the three powers established by the 1930 London naval treaty. Japan notified Great Britain it was determined to keep afloat 11,059 tons of destroyers and 15,598 tons of submarines above the 1930 London treaty quotas. This tonnage, if the treaty’s provisions were carried out, would be scrapped at the end of this year. (The first London treaty will expire January 1, 1937. A second treaty, negotiated this year, places no numerical limit on total tonnage, but only on the unit tonnage of ships. It was signed by Great Britain, the United States and France, but not by Japan.) Ja

It is 5:20 a.m. I am telephoning from the central telephone building. Firing is breaking out down the street. There are occasional thuds and crashes. I am unable to see what is happening. But I can hear the sirens of the police cars screeching their air raid warnings to the sleeping people of the capital. Bells are clanging. The anti-aircraft guns are popping now as the raiders fly over the city. Raid a Failure. Despite the noise, it seems as if the raid will be a failure. BROOKLYN, N.Y., Sept. 2—(4)—Dick Merrill and Harry Richman took off from Floyd Bennett airport at 2:37 p.m. (CST) today on their projected round-trip speed flight to London. Merrill, veteran air mail and transport pilot, was at the controls as the fast low-wing monoplane "Lady Peace" made a smooth takeoff on one of the most unusual attempts in aviation history. The big (Vultee) ship was heavily loaded with about 1,000 gallons of gasoline—three tons of fuel.

ie 5: {eal Sn amma 0, New York, Sept 2—Dick Merril and Harry Richman announced today they would take off this afternoon on their round-trip flight to London. They hoped to leave Floyd Bennett Field between 3 and 4 p. m, E.D.T. Merrill, veteran transport pilot, and Richman, night club entertainer and owner of the big monoplane "Lady Peace," have postponed the flight several times because of unfavorable weather. They notified the field manager, Kenneth Behr, today that weather reports were good, and that they intended to take off. They plan to fly the North Atlantic route up the coast to Newfoundland and across to Ireland. The $95,000 Vultee monoplane is powered with a 1,000 horsepower motor whose design was said to have been an army secret during the past year. Its wings are packed with thousands of ping pong balls to give buoyancy should the plane be forced down in the ocean.

MAIL -- Rebel airships bombed the capital for the fourth time. Rounds of planes and bombs telephoned to United Press in London. New exodus of Americans arranged. Government hears Loyalists captured Huesca, strategic center near Zaragoza. AVILA--Four Rebel planes bomb and set afire the Hispano-Suiza automobile plant of Chindalajer, used by government to make airplane motors and war material. BUZATOU—Inim Loyalists execute Rebel hostages in retaliation for bombardment. Rebel attackers reinforced. Loyalists say they have force of twenty airplanes. OUTSIDE OVIEDO — Besieged Rebels make desperate sortie as Loyalist net threatens. BIRIATOU, Spanish Frontier—A smashing Rebel offensive against the Loyalists was resumed at two p.m. today after a lull during the morning due to fog. The combatants fought under a broiling rain. Insurgent infantry for the eighth time captured the fortified position o

New York, N. Y., Sept. 2—(U. P)— Dick Merrill, veteran airline pilot, and Harry Richman, night club entertainer, roared away from Floyd Bennett Field in a 1000 horsepower monoplane today on a projected round trip flight to London. The sky was overcast when they took off at 2:38 p.m. central standard time, but on the route along the New England Coast to Newfoundland and thence over the Atlantic they expect favorable conditions.

LONDON, Sept 2.--(INS)--Japan created a new naval sensation today by officially notifying Great Britain of her intention to retain 15,598 tons of excess submarines which should be scrapped before the end of the year under terms of the London Naval Treaty. Retention of this tonnage will give Japan nearly a 30 per cent supremacy over the United States and Britain in submarine strength.

1936-03-16.text: Manchester, Eng. Mar. 16 (4).— A jobless Englishman was jailed today after police said he admitted attempting to extort £200 (about $1,000) by an offer to disclose a kidnap plot against the three-weeks’-old son of Countess Barbara Haugwitz-Reventlow. Police said Alfred Molyneux, 31, of Lancashire, confessed to the plot, saying: “I admit I wrote the letter, knowing perfectly well that I know of no such plot or any persons who intended to kidnap the child. I wrote it in moments of depression as I am without money and with a wife and two children to support on 30 shillings ($7.50) a week. “I sincerely regret my action and hope I have not caused the count and countess any worry or anxiety.” Molyneux was trapped when he went to collect the money. London, March 16.—The League of Nations Council in secret session, agreed today to Reichsfuehrer Hitler's demands for equality but flatly rejected his “condition” that the council must discuss his peace proposals. Hitler had offered to send a representative to the council's deliberation on Germany's remilitarization of the Rhineland only on a basis of full equality in the conference and with the understanding that his recent offer of new peace pacts would be considered. Six nations headed by France opposed Hitler's insistence on bringing his peace proposals up simultaneously with the discussion of the Rhineland reoccupation. The other nations with France were Turkey, Spain, Russia, Poland, and Rumania. Qualified Refusal, The council then voted unanimously to accept Hitler's first condition and to reject the second. The council agreed that Germany could attend on the same basis as the other parties to the dispute, but, like France and Belgium, who convoked the council, she cannot vote. Hitler’s first condition in his conditional acceptance of the invitation was that Germany be on equal terms with the representatives of other powers, which was regarded as implying the right to vote. The council, avoiding the onus of burning its bridges, partially accepted the first condition, but denied Hitler the right to vote which would have enabled Germany to block all the council’s decisions. MANCHESTER, England Mar. 1/16 (UP)—Alfred Molyneux was held today, charged with sending a threat to Countess Von Haughwitz Reventlow, Woolworth heiress, that her newly born son was about to be kidnapped. The charge was that of false and fraudulent pretenses. He was accused of sending the former Barbara Hutton a note telling her that two men were on the way to kidnap the baby and demanding $1,000 for giving her information about the plot. He was remanded in custody for trial.

(Copyright, 1936, Associated Press) LONDON, March 16.—The fate of the present negotiations concerning the critical relations of Germany with the rest of Europe hangs on the translation of a German word. It developed today that the League of Nations council may seek from Reichsfuehrer Hitler a clarification of his reply to an invitation to attend a council session. The clarification, it was said, would be to clear up just what was meant by the word “alsbald” contained in the telegram Joseph A. C. Avenol, secretary-general of the League, received from Hitler last night. The German embassy in London, while the British cabinet was considering the situation, informed the foreign office that the correct translation of the word is “in due course” instead of “forthwith,” as the council secretariat officially translated it. 1936-12-04.text: LONDON, Dec. 4. (AP)—Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin told the House of Commons today the government will not permit King Edward to marry Wallis Warfield Simpson and keep his throne, then motored to Belvedere and made a final appeal to the monarch to put the empire before love. While the American-born commoner fled for refuge to France from the spotlight of one of the deepest crises in England’s history the prime minister once more tried to dissuade the strong-willed monarch to give her up. The premier also called a cabinet meeting for tomorrow. Baldwin arrived at Edward's rural retreat shortly after 5 p.m. and was conducted immediately to Edward's apartments. It was his third conference in less than 46 hours. The Duke of York, who many Englishmen believe may succeed his brother as king over the weekend, it was revealed, consulted with his mother, Queen Mary, and his secretary called on Ba

ABOARD THE U. S. S. CHESTER, DEC. 4. (AP).-President Roosevelt, tanned after 16 days at sea and in good spirits, sped homeward today on the cruiser Indianapolis. The Indianapolis, which he boarded yesterday afternoon at Montevideo, Uruguay, was expected to dock at Charleston, S. C., next week in time for the President to reach Washington by December 15. The President turned from his receptions in Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay to consider the weighty tasks confronting him when he returns to his desk. He must prepare then for the opening of congress, the inauguration of his second administration and the filling of numerous vacancies.

(Copyright, 1936, by the U. P.) LONDON, Dec. 4.—Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin faced historic session of parliament today and threw a clear-cut challenge to King Edward VIII to drop his plans to marry Mrs. Wallis Simpson or abdicate. There could be no mistaking the meaning of the blunt country squire who heads his majesty’s government. Baldwin informed commons that a Morganatic marriage is contrary to English law and anyone the king marries automatically becomes queen. Since the government has taken an irrevocable stand against Mrs. Simpson's becoming queen, the king would have no choice but to give up his throne and empire if he persists in marrying her.

DOUEN, FRANCE. Dec. 4. (P)—Wallace Warfield Simpson, whose friendship for King Edward of England created a government crisis, arrived here early today after crossing the English channel by night from London. The American-born divorcee drove swiftly up to the Hotel de la Poste here shortly after 4 o'clock with a chauffeur, bodyguard, and secretary. The party spent the morning at the hotel after a call from the British embassy at Paris advised the hotel manager it would not be necessary for the party to register. As the party walked out of the hotel lobby to resume the journey to Cannes, the French actress Nidia Dauty attempted to take a picture of the former Baltimore belle. The bodyguard, hotel employees said, pushed the actress aside and knocked her hat and the camera to the floor. An amateur photographer also was knocked aside by the secretary and struck back. The empire within the next 48 hours, the London News-Chronicle declared today. If the king should decide to speak over the radio, it said, "authorities will see to it he has the widest possible audience. The king's word would be treated as a command at broadcasting houses." London, Dec. 4. (Friday) ()—Great Britain’s precedent-breaking monarch, staunch in the face of demands he give up his throne or Mrs. Wallis Warfield Simpson, sped early today to a rendezvous with the woman the empire’s strongest forces said he must not marry as long as he is England's King. A swift series of conferences between Edward VIII, his prime minister, and the queen mother apparently were unsuccessful in their purpose: to break the strong-willed ruler’s determination to live his private life as he chooses. ABOARD U.S.S. CHESTER, Dec. 4.—(U.P)—President Roosevelt was off the coast of Brazil today, en route home from his visit to South America which he is confident will produce a united front against war in the western hemisphere. Mr. Roosevelt will land Dec. 14 or 15 at Charleston, S. C., and proceed from there by train directly to Washington, having abandoned his previous plan to land at Mobile, Ala., and go to Washington by way of Warm Springs, Ga. The cruiser Indianapolis, which is carrying him, and its escort, the cruiser Chester, will put in at Port Au Spain, Trinidad, for fuel, on the way home. The president was expected to go ashore, if weather permits, during the six-hour fueling stop, to return the official calls made on him by British officials on his trip south. Mr. Roosevelt left Montevideo yesterday afternoon with the same ringing farewells he received in Buenos Aires and Rio D

LONDON, Dec. 4 (®)—The girl at the counter and the man in the “pub” are behind King Edward, despite cabinet opposition to his possible marriage to Mrs. Wallis Simpson. Under-the-surface murmurings showed the royal bachelor is “trumps” with those British citizens who have to count their pennies, even if he doesn’t stand so high in the circles where formal dress for dinner is obligatory. The so-called “masses” have a deep-seated respect for the throne, some individuals indicated in their comments, but many of them want the situation worked out so the king may marry his American friend without bestowing the title of queen upon her. NEW YORK, Dec. 4 (4)—Parallel to the present impasse between King Edward VIII and his government occurred six centuries ago when Richard II clashed with parliament over his personal acts. This support has been evidenced in President Roosevelt's speech at the opening session of the inter-American peace conference at Buenos Aires; his speech before the Brazilian Congress and Supreme Court at Rio de Janeiro last week, and by the public utterances of Secretary of State Cordell Hull. 1936-04-28.text: (Copyright 1936 by United Press) CAIRO, (UP).—King Faud II, ninth sovereign of the present Egyptian dynasty, died today in the 15th year of his reign, at 68 years of age. Prince Farouk, his 16-year-old son, about to leave London for Cairo, automatically succeeded him, to reign under a regency headed by Prince Mohammed Ali, his third cousin. King Faud died after a long period of ill health. Death was due to stomatitis, (inflammation of the mouth), complicated by gangrenous tendencies. Faud lapsed into coma yesterday after summoning his daughters to his bedside, where Queen Nazli was constantly beside him. Prince Farouk was summoned to Cairo by telephone late last night. He has been living in a great home in the London environs, under close guard, to be educated by a selected staff of tutors and disciplinarians.

LONDON, April 28 UP— King Edward's wife—if he takes a wife—will cost £40,000 ($200,000) a year, a select committee on the civil list reported today. This amount, the committee prescribed, will remain undrawn from the king's civil list while he remains a bachelor. The committee also chiselled down the total grant to the king. Where King George V was allotted £470,000 ($2,559,000), King Edward is allowed £433,100 ($1,165,000) saving £56,000 ($144,500.)

NEW YORK, April 27.—Three liners resumed their course today after crashing through a southwest gale to the aid of two crippled freighters in mid-Atlantic. The freighters, the Ivahoe of Norway and the St. Quentin of Great Britain, succeeded in riding out the storm and canceled their calls for help. Both had steering gear trouble. The liners Bremen and Washington were plowing toward the St. Quentin when the British freighter wirelessed: "Weather moderating. Sustained considerable deck structure damage. After effecting repairs to steering gear will proceed this afternoon without assistance. Thank you all." The Polish liner Plisudski already had reached the Ivanhoe, but the Norwegian decided to wait for a salvage tug. A third freighter that experienced trouble in yesterday's gale, the Rushpoot, in the absence of any further word, is believed to have effected repairs.

ADDIS ABABA, April 28 U.P Foreign Missions united today under Fred Russell of Seattle to care for refugees and warriors flocking into the capital from the north at the rate of 10,000 a day. All are destitute. Many are naked, wounded or suffering from serious poison gas burns. The hungry refugees are being given food, clothing and medical treatment. Among them are women and children deserted or separated from husbands and fathers. They arrive staggering on the road, and must be kept here because they have no place to go. Warriors who arrive say that their brothers have turned against them—a reference to the raids of brigands. They say they do not fear the Italian airplanes and bullets but admit that they fear the Italian poison gas. Many of the burned are being taken into hospitals.

Rome, April 28—Italy's war leader in Ethiopia, Marshal Pietro Badoglio, reported today to his government that a motorized column moving on Addis Ababa already has covered nearly two-thirds of the distance from Dessye to the Ethiopian capital. Three separate columns, two on foot and one aboard motor trucks participated in the climatic movement of the six months long Fascist campaign of conquest. Italian dispatches reported two columns of native Eritrean Askari advanced far ahead of the main motorized column of 15,000 Italian white soldiers, protecting both flanks and clearing the countryside of roving Ethiopian bands. Direct advices from the main unit, which rumbled out of Dessye, former headquarters of Emperor Haile Selassie at dawn Sunday, said it reached a point 62 miles to the south yesterday after its advance guard encountered brief resistance. Addis Ababa, April 27 (4). A warning that the Italians would bomb and “destroy” Addis Ababa if their advance on the capital is resisted, was made today in leaflets dropped from a Fascist airplane. “Our mission is to occupy Addis Ababa and Ethiopia for civilization,” said the leaflets, which were signed by the chief of staff of Marshal Pietro Badoglio. “If Addis Ababa is delivered without resistance, we will not bomb it. Otherwise, we will destroy it all.” (Three separate Italian columns are advancing on Addis Ababa, Rome dispatches reported.) The leaflets urged Ethiopians to desert Emperor Haile Selassie and pledge allegiance to Italy. They warned that resistance was useless, asserting Italy already has captured the entire northern half of Ethiopia. “We have destroyed Haile Selassie’s armies and have occupied Dessye,” said the leaflets. “Soon Harar will be occupied. “We are your friends.

Paris, Apr. 2/ (4).-Communist gains in the Chamber of Deputies election yesterday, along with the prospect of a leftist victory in next Sunday's runoffs, caused French issues to sag heavily today on the Bourse. Financial authorities anxiously wondered whether the new chamber, with a majority possibly more radical than heretofore, might not drag the franc to devaluation. The stock market's slump was attributed to uneasiness over the outcome of the runoffs, when many Communist, Socialist and Radical Socialist candidates are expected to withdraw to give victory to the strongest candidates in their "Peoples Front." All French issues suffered under the selling wave, Rentes falling 4 points and a half and Bank of France shares dropping significantly. GENEVA. April 20. (AP)—The League of Nations admittedly was in peril tonight because of its failure to settle the Italo-Ethiopian war. Anthony Eden, foreign secretary of Great Britain, issued two warnings as a result. The first was that unless nations are prepared to take combined action against an aggressor now, they must not expect help from Britain if they get themselves into difficulties later. By aggressor, Eden meant Italy. His second warning was that unless nations fulfill their duty of collective security, Britain may lose her faith in the value of the League and turn to other methods of safeguarding her interests. This was a hint that Britain may one day abandon the League. Clash on Poison Gas A spirited clash between Eden and Baron Pompeo Aloisi of Italy over Italy’s alleged use of poison gas against Ethiopia took place today. London, Apr. 21 (UP)—Neville Chamberlain, Chancellor of the Exchequer, presenting a national defense budget calling for $3,989,485,000 to the House of Commons today announced that the already heavily burdened taxpayers would have to submit to higher income taxes. Chamberlain informed the House that the basic income tax rate would have to be raised to 23 3/4 percent. Married men with dependents would have exemptions increased. Chamberlain did not mention Britain's war debt to the United States. He ignored a Laborite’s shout, “What about war debts?” He also proposed to draw a large sum from the road building fund to swell the budget.

| London — Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, disclosed to the House of Commons today that the British government operated at a profit last year but will go into the red in the next 12 months. In his annual budget report, he stated that the government’s receipts over expenditures during the fiscal year just closed amounted to 2,941,000 pounds—$14,700,000. He said that next year, however, there would be a budget deficit of 21,291,000 pounds—$106,450,000. He said Great Britain would have to produce 707,897,000 pounds ($3,987,480,000)—including at least 20,000,000 pounds ($100,000,000) for additional defense purposes—for expenditures in the 1936-37 fiscal year. He made this estimate before the House of Commons in presenting the government's budget for the ensuing 12 months. The chancellor announced that he was setting aside 20,000,000 pounds for supplemental estimates for def

LONDON, April 21— (P) — “Uncle David” sent a note of apology today to soften the disappointment of little Princess Elizabeth, second in succession to the British throne, who had expected the wearer of the crown of Britain to attend her 10th birthday party. The note said “Uncle David” otherwise known as King Edward VIII, was prevented by state affairs from attending his niece's party.

Boston, April 20 (7) — Two red-coated National Guard cavalrymen, impersonating Paul Revere and William Dawes of colonial fame, galloped today over roads from which autos long since have driven horses, and shouted over the countryside their warning: “The British are coming!” The occasion was the 161st anniversary of the battles of Lexington and Concord, where, some say, was fired “the shot heard ‘round the world.” But the cavalrymen — Sergeants John C. Ferguson and William H. Vose — received a warmer reception than the early patriots. A British patrol nabbed Revere at Lexington, and also forced Dawes to turn back. The 1936 “Revere,” however, galloped into a holiday gathering where stars and stripes flew, a band played and crowds cheered.

London, April 21 (UP)--The Addis Ababa correspondent of the Exchange Telegraph Agency reported tonight a fast moving Ethiopian infantry column had reached the Italian airdrome northwest of Dessye and burned 19 Italian planes and the entire gasoline supply. Earlier in the day, the correspondent said he had heard unofficially that the column had cut through the line of advancing Italian troops near the new Italian general headquarters at Dessye.

The chancellor occupied 87 minutes to explain Great Britain's financial position. He said the government had operated at a profit of £2,941,000—($14,700,000) last year but that the total estimated revenues from usual sources would put the government £21,291,000 ($103,450,000) in the red during the next 12 months.
