London, Sept. 4. — (4) — Arabs from Iraq and Syria invaded Palestine and battled British troops, a Daily Herald dispatch said today, while Britain called out reserves as possible reinforcements in the Holy Land. The newspaper said uniformed Arabs equipped with machine guns crossed the border and ambushed a party of the Lincolnshire regiment between Tulkarem and Jenin. At least 25 Arabs were killed, the dispatch said, and many were wounded, but no casualties were reported among the British. The war office tonight announced troops were being held in readiness for transport to Palestine, where disorders continued unabated throughout the day. The war office’s moves were made as it was learned in London that another British soldier had been killed and two injured in a sabotaged train near Kalkilieh.

| HARRISON, N. Y., Sept. 5 (?)-— Peggy Rich, actress, was married last night in the office of Town Clerk William A. Wilding by Justice of the Peace Leo Mintzer, to Theodore Royce, 25-year-old British orchestra leader. Miss Rich gave her age as 31 and her address as Chicago. She was married under the name of Margaret Lawton Rich Maxwell. Mr. Royce gave his address as Manchester, Eng., and his occupation as impresario and business manager.

Baleine, Nova Scotia, Sept. 5—Mrs. Beryl Markham, 31-year-old London society matron, was forced to land in a rough field near this fishing village today after piloting her plane through rain and fog over the north Atlantic, the first of her sex to complete the perilous east to west flight alone. St. John’s, N. F., Sept. 5—Mrs. Beryl Markham, 31-year-old English mother, crossed the Atlantic Ocean today in her turquoise blue monoplane, the first woman ever to succeed in a solo flight over the hazardous east to west route. The plane in which Mrs. Markham is attempting a non-stop flight from Abingdon, England, to New York City, was sighted at 11 a.m., Newfoundland summer time, over Renews, approximately 25 miles north of Cape Race, southeastern tip of Newfoundland. Fifteen minutes later, the plane was sighted passing the Cape, moving at tremendous speed. The daring Englishwoman succeeded in

[COPYRIGHT 1936 BY ASSOCIATED PRESS] Irun, Spain—Government resistance in the ruined city of Irun ended today after rebel forces had driven off a desperate counter-attack by government militiamen. Rebels were complete masters of the town by early afternoon. Cleanup squads stalked among the ruins hurling hand grenades at a few individual government militiamen who refused to flee with their comrades. Fascist fighting men walked over the bodies of 10 black-shirted government militiamen on the approach of the international bridge into Hendaye. Frontier Is Closed The government men had recaptured the bridgehead earlier only to be driven off by a relentless rebel barrage. On the bridge itself were the bodies of three other government militiamen. The victorious rebels posted a guard on the frontier and closed the Spanish entrance to the bridge to prevent government defenders still in Spain from

1936-10-29.text: | Harbor Grace, Nfld. (—Storm over much of the Atlantic and a deep meteorological depression be- low Greenland were reported to- day to Captain James A. Mollison, waiting here to resume his one stop New York-to-London flight. He said he hoped to get away late this afternoon,

London, Oct. 28 (#—Fresh Italian counter-charges—detailing 20 alleged acts of Russian aid to Spanish Socialists — were debated tonight by the International Non-Intervention Committee. The new allegations, in reply to earlier accusations by the Soviets against Italy, Germany and Portugal, were tossed into the tangled situation by Dino Grandi, Fascist Ambassador to London. Grandi demanded an investigation to confirm the charges as representatives of 27 European nations which accepted the “hands off Spain” accord renewed discussions pointed toward isolation of the Spanish Civil war. Two other problems faced the delegates: Russian and Portuguese threats to walk out of the meeting. The Lisbon government's objections were based on alleged British violation of the general agreement by bringing the Russian charges before the committee without investigation.

LONDON, Oct. 29.—Mrs. Wallis Warfield Simpson, whose name twice has appeared on the court circular as a dinner guest at Buckingham palace, will be absent from the first formal dinner to be given by King Edward since the end of court mourning for George V. Only men have been invited to-morrow night to the dinner, honoring Carlos Saavedra Lamas, the Argentine foreign minister. The function will be held in the white and gold state dining room, the palace’s gold plate will be used for the first time in King Edward’s reign.

LONDON, Oct. 29.—(UP)—Britons read today the first open reference since Mrs. Wallis Simpson's divorce, her close friendship with King Edward. It was an article in the radical weekly, “The Week,” which was at once a denunciation of American newspapers for the prominence with which they played the story; a denunciation of British newspapers for suppressing the story, and a clear indication that the idea of a marriage between the king and Mrs. Simpson would be opposed bitterly by many persons. When Mrs. Simpson obtained her decree of divorce from Ernest Simpson at Ipswich, thus obtaining the right to have the decree made absolute so she could remarry if she wished at the end of six months, the British newspapers carried bare factual reports of the divorce. There was a hint that the king even knew her.

(By the Associated Press) Steadfast in the face of bitter opposition, Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden of Great Britain told the reassembled House of Commons today that England, had it not adhered to a “hands-off-Spain” policy, might have seen Europe plunged into war. At the same time he declared there was no support whatsoever for caveat Russian charges that Portugal has been a base for the shipment of fascist arms to the Spanish insurgents. The non-intervention committee, he reminded his listeners, is “still intact.” The government counter-offensive, starting at dawn south of the capital, was reported making headway. But insurgents, hauling up long-range guns which could drop projectiles completely over the capital to bombard retreating government troops in the event of an evacuation, said it would be not more than 10 days before they march into Madrid. Heavy artillery, field pieces and

London, Oct. 29 (AP)—Standing firm on Spanish non-intervention, Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden told the British House of Commons today "not a single one of the Soviet charges against the Portuguese government" has been proved. Russia, contending Portugal has been a base for Italo-German shipment of war materials to Spanish Fascist insurgents, has asked for a neutral naval blockade of Portuguese ports. The young foreign secretary faced down belligerent opposition to defend his government's stand for non-intervention with the parliament late today with the declaration, "Any other policy might have set Europe on fire." At the same time, he asserted: "Supplies sent from this country would not have had an important bearing on the result in Spain." Eden, as the bitter Spanish neutrality issue shifted from the committee room to British House of Commons halls, pointed out the "hands-off-Spain" g

Capt. James Mollison Ready To Take Off Across North Atlantic HARBOR GRACE, N. F., Oct. 29, (U.P) — Weather conditions today caused a further postponement in the departure of Capt. James Mollison, British aviator who left New York yesterday on a speed flight to London and Cape Town.

HARBOR GRACE, N. F., Oct. 28 —Capt. James Mollison, British flyer, prepared to take off at noon today for London. He still was wearing the evening clothes, covered by a flying suit, in which he left New York yesterday morning, determined to reach Croydon Airport in seventeen hours so he could keep a party engagement. Bad weather grounded his fast monoplane "Dorothy" when he landed her eight hours later to refuel and he decided to remain overnight. Mollison said he hoped to reach London after dawn tomorrow, as the Croydon airport is not equipped with a radio beam for night flying. His plane's cruising speed is 240 miles an hour. From London, he planned to fly on to South Africa, a total distance of 10,500 miles.

1936-10-22.text: United Press White House Writer PROVIDENCE, R. I. — President Roosevelt opened his campaign for the votes of industrial and Republican New England from the steps of the Rhode Island State House this morning by asserting that ‘we will not again allow people to be regimented by selfish minorities into bankruptcies and headlines.’ BAL SAVOP ESSE: “You have been told of regimentation. I am opposed to the kind of regimentation under which you labored and suffered in the days of the false prosperity and in the days of the great depression. We believe that people are even more important than machines. We believe that the material resources of America should serve the human resources of America.” Mr. Roosevelt's speech was brief. It was the first of three scheduled for the day. This afternoon he speaks on the Commons in Boston. Tonight he delivers a major radio address to the nation at 10 o'cloc

United Press Staff Correspondent LONDON, Oct. 21—(U.P)—King Edward has given Mrs. Wallis Simpson a $125,000 emerald necklace, it was learned today. There have been other gifts, but it is understood that they have not nearly reached the total of $1,000,000 ascribed to them by some reports. One gift is believed to have been a big black sedan. The king ordered two and only one was delivered to him. Mrs. Simpson has been seen many times in an identical car. Dozens of stories circulated in London today regarding the friendship between the king and (Concluded on Page & Column 6)

LONDON, Oct. 21 - Ambassador Ivan Maisky of Soviet Russia will inform the next meeting of the Non-Intervention Committee that his country no longer feels obligated to refrain from helping Spanish loyalists, it was learned reliably today. Russia, it was learned authentically, considers itself morally free from the obligation due to its conviction that Fascist powers are aiding the rebels. It will state its position officially at the first opportunity. The next meeting of the committee has not been scheduled. Russia, with Great Britain's support, insists it be held this week. It has been delayed to await answers from Germany, Italy and Portugal to charges that they are aiding the rebels. Presided over by Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin, the British cabinet met two hours today and discussed the Spanish crisis. It was reported in diplomatic quarters that a revolt against the non-intervention

Aboard Roosevelt, Train En Route To Hartford, Conn., Today. —(AP)— President Roosevelt swung his flying 32 hour campaign of southern New England into Connecticut today after telling a Massachusetts audience the New Deal had cut taxes for the ‘average American’ and the choice in this election, as in the past, lay between “democracy” and “special privilege” in taxation. Carrying memories of Bay State crowds that surpassed in numbers all others in his reelection campaign travels, the chief executive headed by special train for Hartford for early morning flood control conferences, a brief talk on the capitol steps, and another long auto tour.

LONDON, Oct. 21.-(—Officials today protected Mrs. Ernest Simpson from the curious as London was intrigued by stories of hand-painted gifts from King Edward to her. Bars against the inquisitive attentions of the public toward the former Baltimore debutante were put up in London where police around Mrs. Simpson's home told loiterers they were on crown property and in Ipswich where county officials took special steps in preparation for the hearing of Mrs. Simpson's divorce suit against her ships broker husband, Ernest. Friends of King Edward and his American favorite meanwhile declared they knew the monarch had given her “many expensive gifts.” They estimated the total value at near 20,000 pounds sterling ($100,000) and minimized one story he had given her a pearl necklace costing 40,000 pounds ($200,000). Gossipers were trying to guess also whether Edward had given her a new Canadian-made

Lendon, Oct. 21.—(AP)—The British navy was ordered to stand by today for a ‘mission of mercy’ to rescue thousands of hostages held by both sides in the Spanish civil war. In messages to both the Madrid regime and the Fascist high command, the government stressed fear of ‘wholesale massacre’ of hostages. Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden instructed the embassy at Madrid and the ambassador at Hendaye, France, to press for early replies. In a two-hour session today, the cabinet was understood to have paid slight attention to a Laborite bag for immediate convocation of parliament to consider the Spanish neutrality situation. It was believed, however, the question will be aired on the regular scheduled opening day of parliament Oct. 29. As for the hostages, informed held said about 8,000 were held in Madrid alone. Many of them were said to be women and children. The British messages, envisioning

LONDON, Oct. 21. (LRI—Powers of two continents opened a gigantic diplomatic game today as the Spanish civil war blazed to its climax. At stake were the fate of the Madrid government; the lives of many thousands of men, women and children held prisoners in Madrid or sheltered in Latin American embassies and legations; and perhaps, even, the power of Europe. Spain, in a desperate move to obtain arms, announced its intention to pay immediately more than $11,625,000 in sight drafts due to other countries. Latin American governments, in an emergency meeting of the diplomats at Buenos Aires, agreed to dispatch notes to the Madrid government in hope that more than 2000 Right Wing sympathizers, including representatives of some of Spain's richest families, might remain in the (Continued on page 4)

CHICAGO, (F), The Most Rev. Edward Hutson, D. D., 63, archbishop of the Church of England in the West Indies, died at a hospital. He was stricken Monday with pneumonia after attending the Pan-American conference of Anglican bishops here last week.

1936-07-12.text: ROME, July 11.—(U.P.)—Italy tonight officially declined to attend the Locarno conference among Great Britain, France and Belgium to be held at Brussels next week. It marked the second time in a week that the Fascist state turned her back on opportunities to resume collaboration with European powers. Premier Benito Mussolini also declined to send a delegation to the Dardanelles conference at Montreux, Switzerland, despite repeated announcements he would return to European council tables following official abolition of sanctions. In refusing to attend the Locarno conference, Italy pointed out that anti-Italian mutual assistance accords between Great Britain and several Mediterranean states are still in existence. France formally notified Britain Thursday that she would consider her obligations under those pacts ended on July 15, the date set for lifting of sanctions. However, Britain has i

LONDON, July 15. -- The Sunday Graphic said Col. Charles A. Lindbergh has invented a new type of airplane known as the flying caravan. The paper said a British firm was constructing the machine, which was understood to have seats that could be converted into bunks, and unusually large fuel tanks. The plane will be delivered to the American firm in the next two weeks, the Graphic said. It added that F.P.G. Miles, noted British constructor, co-operated with Lindbergh on the design.

BELFAST, July 11 —(@) —Northern Ireland will become one of the noisiest and gayest spots in the world tomorrow as 250,000 Orangemen celebrate the 246th anniversary of the battle of the Boyne. Hundreds of bands in 60 different demonstrations will lead parades along bunting-spanned roadways. Armored cars will follow at a modest distance in the rear. The machine-gun nozzles peeping from the armored cars are not a part of the parade, but a precaution against rioting such as marked last year's celebration when Protestant-Catholic clashes resulted in 11 deaths, hundreds of injuries and extensive property damage. Fifty thousand will march in Belfast alone as this year's celebration will be on a more lavish scale than ever before because of improved economic conditions. When King William III's army of 35,000 men sent King James II's forces scurrying southward from the river Boyne, he won his cau

Berlin, July 11.—(AP)—The German government announced tonight it recognized the independence of Austria—thereby apparently bringing to an end a situation fraught with danger to Europe. The announcement, made after agreement with the Austrian government, contained a significant proviso that Austria declares herself to be ‘a German state.’ Paul Josef Goebbels, Germany's minister of press and propaganda, described the accord to the German people in a radio broadcast. To Be Aloof In addition to establishing Germany’s recognition of Austria's independence, the accord provides that the two nations agree to refrain from interfering in each other's internal affairs. (Hitherto, Austrian leaders have contended the Nazi movement in Austria was directed from Germany, alleging that Austrian governments were menaced by German politics). Both nations agreed to cooperate toward the stabilization of the

VIENNA, July 11 (P)—An accord between Austria and Germany, re-establishing the two nations’ traditionally friendly relations, was announced by the foreign office in an official statement tonight. By the terms of the agreement, Austria acknowledges it is a German state but remains a member of the Rome pact signed by Austria, Italy and Hungary. Germany, it was stated, will not join the Rome protocol conversations but will take a friendly attitude toward the arrangement. Germany and Austria agreed not to interfere in each other’s internal affairs. The new accord, the foreign office said, acknowledges the prohibition against the Nazi party in Austria. The prohibition remains in effect. The Austrian form of government is not changed. Germany and Austria, by the terms of the accord, will pursue a common foreign policy except that Austria will observe all previous obligations under the Rome pac

VIENNA, July 11—A working agreement between Germany and Austria restoring a measure of the prewar solidarity between the two countries without impairing the sovereignty of Austria has been reached in direct negotiations, it was announced officially Saturday night. Diplomatic observers saw back of the official communique a hint that Italy would be indirectly a third party to the accord, thus creating an alliance stretching from the North Sea to the Mediterranean and balancing the alliance of Britain and France. Germanic State The text of the communique revealed that Austria recognizes herself as a Germanic state and therefore in close accord with Germany. Nevertheless, Germany recognizes Austria's full sovereignty, thereby disavowing any intention of Adolf Hitler to foment a Nazi regime there or to interfere with the restoration of the Hapsburg monarchy, if Austria wishes to have it. @ssining, N. Y., July 11. (®)— Paralyzed from the waist down and almost speechless from fear, Mrs. Mary Frances Creighton, 36, mother of two, tossed on a cot in Sing Sing’s sweltering death house tonight as prison officials made arrangements to carry her bodily to the electric chair Thursday night. Mrs. Creighton was sentenced to die with Everett Applegate for the poison egg-nog murder of Applegate’s ponderous wife, Ada, last October. Attendants disclosed that physicians had satisfied themselves, by thrusting pins into Mrs. Creighton’s legs, that she was not shamming. The pin pricks brought no reaction whatever, they said. Asked how she felt, Mrs. Creighton moaned, “very miserable.” As the hour for Mrs. Creighton’s execution neared, her only remaining hope of reprieve lay with Gov. Herbert Lehman. Some prison attendants thought a last minute physical examination might be made in efforts

SAN FRANCISCO, July 11.—UPI— Shopkeeper Hyman Gorwitz pleaded innocent today to setting big steel-jawed traps to catch the hands of little children who assertedly annoyed him. Two housewives testified Gorwitz, 56, concealed the dangerous instruments under thin layers of dirt in his back yard and baited them with shiny pieces of metal resembling dimes. "The traps were strong enough to hold a wolf," said Assistant District Attorney Terence Boyle. Municipal Judge Daniel S. O’Brien called the traps "the most vicious ever brought into this court." He raised Gorwitz's bond from $500 to $2500 and sent him off to jail pending the posting of security for release until his trial, July 15. Gorwitz was charged with assault with force to produce great bodily harm. Upon conviction the maximum penalty is 10 years in prison, a $5000 fine, or both. 1936-05-07.text: Capetown, Union of South Africa, May 7 (AP)—Mrs. Amy Johnson Molison set a new record for the flight from England today by landing her airplane here at 2:31 p. m., Greenwich Mean Time (9:31 a. m., Eastern Standard Time). Since she hopped off from Gravesend, Eng., Monday she had been on her way 3 days, 6 hours, 26 minutes, in comparison with the record of 3 days, 17 hours, 38 minutes set by Flight Lieutenant Tommy Rose in February.

VAPEIOWN, South Africa May 7 (UP) Mrs. Amy Johnson Mollison, British aviator, arrived at 4:30 P. M. today, creating a record for the flight from England to South Africa. Mrs. Mollison's time was three days, six hours and 25 minutes. The previous record, set last February by Flight Lieut. Tommy Rose was three days 17 hours and 38 minutes. Rose beat the earlier record of Mrs. Mollison, but she has now regained it.

Friedrichshafen, Germany, May 6 (#)—Germany’s giant new airship, the Hindenburg, pointed its nose tonight for the English Channel on its first North Atlantic crossing. The 813-foot dirigible rose easily and lightly from its moorings at 9:30 P. M. (3:30 P. M. EST) with 61 passengers and a crew of 56 aboard. In command was Dr. Hugo Eckener, veteran Zeppelin commander who has supervised the Hindenburg’s construction and trial flights for the last three years. A crowd of several thousand persons watched the Zeppelin, named in honor of the late German President Paul von Hindenburg, move slowly from its hangar. After the four Diesel engines, burning crude oil, had warmed up Eckener gave the command “Up ship.” To the martial strains of “Deutschland über Alles,” played by the Friedrichshafen town band the huge craft started its journey toward Holland and the United States. Anthony Eden, Britain’s young foreign minister, who told the House of Commons yesterday that ‘the league must go on,’ will be given wide latitude in determining his nation’s course. It was understood, however, that he would press for maintenance of sanctions only in the event that other leading powers agree. | ABOARD DIRIGIBLE HINDENBURG, en route to the United States—Germany’s giant new dirigible Hindenburg sped out over the Atlantic today on the first regular passenger flight from Europe to the United States. The ship passed Land's End, the southwestern tip of England, at 6:30 a.m. Greenwich mean time today (1:10 a.m. EST). Almost two hours later we were about 120 miles west southwest of Land's End and heading in the general direction of the Azores. This weekend, if all goes well, the ship will be in New York. The sea was calm. We sighted a few ships. The passengers, except the newspaper correspondents, were asleep in their staterooms. Capt. London, May 7 (4)—The gold crown of Emperor Haile Selassie lay safely hidden today in the dim vaults of a London bank. The crown and other imperial insignia of the Ethiopian negus were brought secretly to London when the Italian advance began to threaten Addis Ababa, it was disclosed. The heavy crown is brimless and is surmounted by a large cross.

PORT SAID, Egypt, May 1 (UP) — Emperor Haile Selassie, fleeing into exile with his family and 117 followers, passed the port of Haifa, Palestine, today aboard the British cruiser Enterprise without stopping. It had been expected the emperor would stop at Haifa and go from there to Jerusalem.

1936-11-05.text: London, Nov. 3 ()—King Edward pledged his government to “pacific settlement of international disputes” in centuries-old ceremonies opening the British Parliament today. “The government will continue to do all in their power to further the appeasement of Europe,” he told a brilliant assemblage of peers, officials and spectators in the House of Lords. In his first Parliamentary appearance since his accession to the throne, the King dispelled previous reports his coronation next May might be postponed and announced his intention of going to India to be crowned Emperor. Mrs. Wallis Simpson, the monarch’s American friend, was not among the throngs of ceremonially dressed spectators who crowded the galleries to capacity. Reads His Speech First affirming his declaration of Protestant faith, the King began the reading of his speech standing

LONDON. (4. Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden in parliament pledged Great Britain to rely on the League of Nations and indicated his country would not desert Russia for Germany and Italy. The foreign policy of the British government, as outlined by Eden's speech, is committed to adherence to the league as the best way of keeping peace in Europe. Eden said his government's efforts would be devoted “first to strengthening the authority of the league, to which Great Britain will devote every endeavor.” “Because there has been one failure,” Eden said apparently referring to the league's failure to prevent the Italo-Ethiopian war, “there is no reason to say that the world must turn back on an endeavor which is the only alternative to catastrophe and failure.” “Our second aim is for negotiation of European settlement, and the third is re-equipment of our nation.” Britain, he said, was amenable to

- LONDON, Nov. 5 ()—The tradition-steeped House of Lords faced today the necessity of answering one of the most extraordinary questions in its long history: Has the sufferer of an incurable ailment the right to select death to escape lingering pain? The question was contained in a “mercy death” bill introduced in Parliament yesterday to authorize medical men to kill hopeless patients who want to die. Lord Ponsonby, its sponsor, thus climaxed a year’s campaign by many medical and church leaders for euthanasia, easy death.

London, Nov. 4 ()—A “mercy death” bill to permit medical men to kill incurable patients was introduced in Parliament today. It was presented by Lord Ponsonby, climaxing a year's campaign by many medical and church leaders for euthanasia— their term for “easy death.” It would enable physicians and surgeons legally to put to death patients suffering great pain from conditions diagnosed as hopeless.

| From far-off Moscow and Shanghai, across Europe to South American capitals, foreigners today applauded the re-election of President Roosevelt with few dissenting voices. “Roosevelt, we think you're grand. Salute,” declared Lord Beaverbrook’s London Daily Express. In Paris, fiercely-wrangling Rightists and Leftists were momentarily united in expressions of satisfaction. “If France lives tragic hours again,” commented the Leftist newspaper L'Oeuvre, “she will certainly have as the head of the great American democracy the man who will be able to do most for her.” And the Rightist newspaper Le Journal hoped continuation of America’s reciprocal trade policy, under the renewed Roosevelt regime, would stimulate international commerce. Fascist circles in Rome welcomed the Democratic victory partly because he is better known than Gov. Landon and partly because Roosevelt's energetic action has b

LONDON, Nov. 5.—"Great Britain has no desire to threaten nor any intention to attack any Italian interests in the Mediterranean," Capt. Anthony Eden, foreign secretary, told the House of Commons today. Eden responded to a speech by Premier Benito Mussolini at Milan, Italy, last Sunday declaring Rome was prepared to sponsor an "armed peace," if necessary, in Europe. He accepted Il Duce’s olive branch of peace, but reminded Italy that for Britain the Mediterranean is a vital main arterial route to her possessions. "It should be possible for each country to maintain its vital interest in the Mediterranean without a conflict with each other," Eden said, "and even with mutual advantage." The youthful foreign secretary described himself as no believer in the inevitability of catastrophe, adding: "But a stronger Britain today means a greater certainty for peace." Eden described the three primar

United Press Staff Correspondent | London, Nov. 4—(UP)—The Spanish non-intervention committee tonight acquitted Soviet Russia of virtually all German charges that it had broken its compact by sending munitions to the Spanish Loyalists. On two of the eight German charges which were left in abeyance, Ambassador Ivan Maisky promised to obtain more information from Moscow to substantiate Russia’s denial of guilt. Today's session of the committee was marked by a stormy debate between Maisky and Ambassador Dino Grandi of Italy in which they cast aspersions on each other’s intelligence and political beliefs. Besides denying the German allegations, Maisky also presented to the committee a note denying re-

"se Fr LONDON (UP) - Britain will be second to none in the defense of her legitimate interests, Capt. Anthony Eden, British foreign minister, told the House of Commons Thursday. He said, however, that such defense as Britain may adopt will not be directed against the interests of any other nation.

1936-07-30.text: London —(/)— Reports received in London from rebel sources in the last 24 hours indicated today Spanish insurrectionists were gaining ground. These advices filtered in as the British government began an investigation of rumors that the Leftist government at Madrid had seized British and American banks and factories for war purposes. The Ford Motor Company was advised its Barcelona plant had been occupied by the government. From Cordoba it was announced Madrid would be surrounded today so tightly that not even diplomatic representatives would be able to evacuate. Hendaye learned that Gen. Emilio Mola, northern rebel commander, had dispersed loyal militia three kilometers from Proble Gordo in the Guadarrama. Word from Vigo said the Spanish cruiser Libertad had surrendered to rebels. General Motors officials here said they were unable to confirm reports their properties in Spain had been se

New York, July 30. (AP)—In their efforts to make a Republican basis this year for the old political saying—“As Maine goes, so goes the nation”—the Republican campaign forces have mobilized many of their leaders for speaking tours of the New England state prior to the September 14 election. As given out today at the office of Rep. Joseph W. Martin, Jr., chairman of the eastern division of the Republican national committee, the tentative list includes Col. Frank Knox, vice presidential nominee, National Chairman John D. M. Hamilton, Colonel Theodore Roosevelt, Senator Arthur Vandenberg of Michigan, Senator Daniel O. Hastings of Delaware, and Senator Arthur Capper of Kansas. Also, as seen yesterday by party leaders and close friends, efforts are being put forth to have former President Herbert Hoover make an address in Maine in the last week of the state campaign. Discussing the concentrati

| — (By the Associated Press) Tangible evidence of a long pre| dieted naval building race came Thursday with informed Tokyo | predictions Japan probably will arrange for the replacement of four capital ships next year. | Wednesday Britain announced she would lay the keel of two battleships in 1937 and United States authorities said this nation probably would follow suit. | Thursday, an Anglo-Russian ‘Naval agreement, to bring the ‘Soviet Union into line with the new London pact between Britain, France and the United States, was announced by the British foreign office, This pact limits the size of indi- — warships but not their numbers.

Londen, July 30 UF.—An Anglo-Russian commercial agreement establishing a £10,000,000 ($50,000,000) credit for Soviet orders for British exports was announced to the House of Commons today by Sir Walter Runciman, president of the Board of Trade. The agreement was entered into Tuesday between the export credits guarantee department and the Soviet trade representative. The department gave guarantees in connection with orders which the Soviet government organizations are to place in Great Britain. Russian orders are to be placed by Sept. 30, 1937, Sir Walter said the Soviet trade representative had given formal assurance that Russia intends to place orders up to the full limit of the credit. They will not, however, include munitions.

LONDON, July 30.—(4)—Lord Sempill took off today from Hanworth airport at 10:30 a.m. (3:30 a.m. C.S.T) in a second attempt to fly to Australia in 3½ days. Three companions accompanied him on the flight on which they hope to reach Melbourne. A previous attempt, begun July 10, failed when mechanical trouble forced them down in Vienna.

JERUSALEM, July 29—(Jewish Telegraphic Agency)—Fifteen Arabs were killed today in a battle with British troops near Jenin, raising the death toll to 37 in two days engagements between soldiers and desert warriors.

LONDON, July 30.—(7—An Anglo-Russian naval agreement “on 2h points” was announced in Whitehall today. No date was set for signing the treaty, but it was stated to be completely drafted. This accord provides for imitation of the tonnage of individual ships, but not of their numbers, and for an exchange of building information between signatory powers.

COLUMBUS, O.--(UP)—Another attempt to obtain a $2,000,000 appropriation for construction of a new penitentiary on the site of the present London prison farm will be made in the state welfare department’s next budget request, Mrs. Margaret Allman, director, announced today. Erection of the new prison was included in Governor Davey's $20,000,000 welfare program which was defeated last year by the legislature, she said. “There is an immediate need for a new state prison,” Mrs. Allman said, “We have the nucleus for such a building at London, along with 2000 acres of land. The Ohio penitentiary is no longer adequate to house the state's prisoners.” The penitentiary’s normal capacity is 3980 prisoners. At present it houses 3759 inmates. “The penitentiary is nearly 100 years old. It was constructed in 1813 and then reconstructed in 1834 after a fire destroyed the original building,” the directo

1936-09-17.text: Paris, (P)—Premier Leon Blum warned the world tonight that France, although divided by conflicting doctrines and parties, would in the face of necessity unite to “defend her soil.” The Socialist premier, in a speech broadcast in English, German, Italian and Spanish from stations near the countries which speak those tongues, declared: “There are in France doctrines and parties which clash, France sees that as a principle of force, not weakness. “But as France is unanimous in her wish for peace, she will be unanimous tomorrow, as in all the hours of her history, if it is a question of preserving the security of the fatherland—even more so, to defend her own soil.”

JACKSONVILLE, Fla. Sept. 1—(P)—A fierce tropical hurricane gave indications today of a change in course which might imperil Bermuda. Even if the extensive disturbance continued its reported north northwesterly movement, the British winter resort apparently would be raked with strong gales. The final weather bureau advisory last night placed the center of the storm about 350 miles south southwest of Bermuda. It gave the course as northwest, but Meteorologist Gordon E.B. Dunn said later reports indicated the movement was north northwest. Several vessels encountered winds of 50 miles an hour and one freighter reported a velocity of 70 miles.

LONDON, Sept. 15 (4)—British hopes for negotiating a new Locarno treaty Oct. 19 received a severe wrench today when both Germany and Italy sought a delay for diplomatic preparations. Germany informed Great Britain she did not consider the interim between now and the suggested date for a five-power Locarno meeting to be sufficient for diplomatic groundwork. At the same time, Ambassador Dino Grandi of Italy called at the foreign office and suggested a delay in fixing the date until further diplomatic exchanges have been made between the five powers. Belgium and France, however, notified Britain they were ready to proceed with an October meeting in London to work out some sort of new European security arrangement.

Quarter Finals announce OL National Golf Championship. Garden City, N. Y., Sept. 17—(U. P.)—Three American favorites, a British Walker cupper and four golfing unknowns, today moved into the quarter final round of the 40th national amateur championship. Two top entries, Johnny Goodman, of Omaha, and Albert F. Campbell, of Seattle, marched along with impressive triumph. Johnny Fischer, of Cincinnati, who was only three strokes over par for his five matches, was pressed to the limit before he downed Gus Mooreland, of Chicago. The other “name” player still in the tournament was Jock McLean, of Glasgow, Scotland.

LONDON, Sept. 17. U.P)—An attempt to span the Atlantic from New York to England within 17 hours will be made by the British flier, James Mollison, early in October in a plane capable of 270 miles per hour, it was learned today. Mollison, already famous for a number of long-distance flights, plans to sail for New York today aboard the liner Paris. In America he will take over a new Bellanca "Flash," low-wing monoplane, the only one of its kind in existence, now awaiting him in Delaware. Taking off from Floyd Bennett Airport early in October, Mollison plans to make the fastest flight on record across the Atlantic, then, within 24 hours, attempt a new time-mark from London to Cape Town.

LONDON, Sept. 16. (UP) — Lloyd's, insurance underwriters, today lowered the odds against a European war within six months from 50 to one, the rate set in February, 1934, to six and two-thirds to one. The action was indicative of increasing fears because of the Spanish civil war and the Russo-German verbal controversy. The latest war risk premium is payable to insure against total loss in event of a European war. The premium requires 15 pounds ($75) to cover 100 pounds ($500) in event of total loss, compared to a premium in February, 1954, of only two pounds ($10).

(Copyright, 1936, by the Associated Press) Toledo, Spain, Sept. 18.—Government plans to blow up the shell-battered alcazar and its 1,700 fascist occupants virtually are complete, a reliable authority disclosed tonight. Socialist sources said the “terrible decision” to blow up the crumbling fortress atop Toledo had been taken after 10 days of futile efforts to induce the fascist commander, Jose Moscardo, to release women and children in the building under pledges of safe conduct from both the government and the diplomatic corps. Cables Are Connected: High explosive charges, each containing more than a ton of TNT, have now been set in place. Electric cables connect with the charges along two underground mines leading beneath the alcazar, each 100 yards long. A troop train of regular army soldiers was sent from Madrid to reinforce Toledo's militia garrison. There troops will storm the sides

Carbonear, N. F., Sept. 16.—(#) Captain Eddie Rickenbacker substituted the motor ship Lincoln for an airplane today in fresh efforts to reach Harry Richman and Dick Merrill in Musgrave Harbor. Rickenbacker is leading an expedition carrying gasoline and spare parts to the American trans-Atlantic fliers. He transferred his expedition fuel and a new propeller for Richman’s plane Lady Peace to the motorship Lincoln, leaving his plane at the Harbor Grace airport. He expected to reach Musgrave Harbor by noon and expressed belief the Lady Peace could be repaired quickly to continue its flight to New York. Richman, night club entertainer, and Merrill, veteran pilot, were forced down on the isolated Newfoundland coast Monday when their plane ran short of fuel after they had battled rain, fog and sleet during the last stages of a trans-ocean flight from Southport, England. The New York Daily News

1936-12-30.text: WASHINGTON, Dec. 3 (#)-- Momentous decisions on naval construction and Far Eastern lie ahead of the United States with the termination at midnight tomorrow of the Washington and London naval limitation treaties. Coincident with the lapse of restrictions on the size of the world’s fighting fleets for the first time in 15 years, these problems will be uppermost: 1. Whether two new battleships are to be added to the American navy. 2. What the United States intends to do about fortification of its territories in the Pacific ocean. Authoritative quarters predicted President Roosevelt would lose little time after the treaties expire in ordering construction of two $50,000,000 men-of-war. Authorized by Congress. The last congress authorized him to do so if similar action were taken by any other signatory to the London limitation pact of 1930, which provided for a “building holiday” in capital s

SHANGHAI, Dec. 29 (4)—Local British authorities wanted to know today whether corpulent Atma Singh had been hanged. As Singh, a British Indian and former local police officer, plunged through the scaffold trapdoor for murder, the rope parted. He suffered a brain concussion but was expected to recover. Perplexed officials appealed to the British embassy for an answer to the question — Must Singh be hanged or has he been hanged? The embassy is looking it up.

LONDON, Dec. 30 (4) — Dame Fanny Lucy Houston, wealthiest woman in England, died today. Lady Houston came into great wealth when she inherited £5,000,000 (about $25,000,000) in 1926 after the death of her second husband, Sir Robert Houston, shipping magnate. She was known as England's “Lady Bountiful.” Most of her gifts were to hospitals and charities. Once “just on an impulse,” she gave the British government £12,000,000 — death duties on her husband's estate to which the government was not legally entitled under the law of the Isle of Jersey where he died.

TAINDON, Dec. 34.--(U P).—Dame Fanny Lucy Houston, one of Great Britain's wealthiest women and one of its most colorful, died last night. Almost to her last hour, she conducted her affairs, including her $24,000,000 fortune and her exciting magazine, “Saturday Review.” She slashed right and left at people she did not like, in ordinary life and in politics, and particularly at Ramsay MacDonald, former prime minister.

Bombay—Mahatma Gandhi was described by close associates today as ready to forsake his negative policy of non-resistance and lead India’s masses in an active campaign for independence from Great Britain. Amazement was expressed throughout India at the astute comeback from retirement the little Indian leader staged at the Faizpur nationalist congress, regarded as a certain harbinger of a new era of activity.

SHANGHAI, Dec. 30 (?)—Atma Singh, British Indian and convicted murderer who escaped death on a scaffold, achieved “immortality” today in a police hospital. The husky, bearded Atma Singh, a Sikh from British India, was to have been hanged yesterday but the rope snapped as he plunged through the trap. He suffered a brain concussion but lived. The several thousand Indian inhabitants of Shanghai regarded Atma Singh's survival as an act of Heaven. His Sikh co-religionists believed he was a man favored by the deities, therefore a minor divinity himself. Sha Kur, his young wife, was weak with joy but she glowingly expressed belief a divine hand severed the rope to save her husband. It was to avenge an insult against her that Atma Singh slew another constable of the Shanghai international settlement police force. The British consulate intimated the embassy had decided tentatively to spare the Si

New York, Dec. 29. (#)—Oscar England, 34-year-old blind musician, miscounted his steps in a Union Square subway station (B.M.T.) in which he had made his way successfully innumerable times, and was killed by an express train today. James Sumners, 34, co-member with England of a well-known trio of blind musicians who recently advanced from street minstrelry to a WPA radio program, was with England at the time of the accident, but drew back just as his companion took one step too many and plunged off the subway platform.

Paris, Dec. 29 (#)—France and Britain will make a second representation to Berlin if Chancellor Hitler evades answer to the pending request to ban "volunteer enlistments" to Fascist Spain, French Foreign Office circles said tonight. Asked what France would do if such representation proved barren, one official said: "First of all we expect Germany to accept. "But in case Hitler should refuse, there is nothing we could do but see that all volunteers necessary were sent to aid the Madrid Government to balance the German aid. "We cannot watch the constitution of a veritable German army on the other side of our Pyrenees frontier without meeting the threat." Circles close to the Foreign Office expressed fear Hitler's delay in answering the note, delivered Sunday but made known last week, may be because of an effort to make a separate "deal" with Britain—thus isolating France. These circles sai

1936-01-13.text: WASHINGTON, Jan. 13.— Evidence that some American munition makers in the United States pledged themselves to fill British orders regardless of United States needs was introduced before the Senate's Special Committee on the Investigation of the Munitions Industry. J. P. Morgan of the New York Banking House of New York, which was the agent of France and Britain in making their American munitions purchases and in marketing their bonds in the United States, protested that his banking house was not to blame for the assurance he gave that France and England could never afford to go back on their debts in the United States.

PARIS, Jan. 13.—(U.P.)—Premier Benito Mussolini has sent to Premier Laval his personal assurance that he will not quit the League and will not attack England, the United Press learned today. Vittorio Cerutti, Italian Ambassador, returning here after a week in Rome, brought official confirmation of Mussolini’s two-fold promise to Laval, which was conveyed last week to Count Charles de Chambrun, French Ambassador at Rome. Cerutti, like De Chambrun, brought Laval no new Italian peace overtures, but the pledges were believed to have cleared the atmosphere greatly a week before the important League meeting at Geneva. Observers doubted that new peace overtures would be possible at present, the occasion being unpropitious because neither side has gained a sufficiently crushing military victory.

GEORGETOWN, British Guiana, Jan. 13—(4—The jungle search for Paul Redfern, long-lost United States flier, drew a fourth expedition today to the South American hinterland. Three rescue parties already penetrating the interior in the hunt for the man who disappeared in 1927 on a flight from Atlanta to Rio De Janeiro, and for whom hope was only recently revived, were not expected to report for at least a month. Dispatches from Cristobal, Canal Zone, said the new expedition, from the Albert S. Waid post of the American Legion, sailed yesterday for Trinidad and Paramaribo, Dutch Guiana, vowing not to return until the Redfern mystery was solved. The members of this expedition were reported to be James Ryan and Arthur J. Farrel, a past commander of the post.

LONDON, Jan 13 — Dr. Marcel Junod, International Red Cross delegate, announced today he would recommend withdrawal of all Red Cross units from Ethiopia unless Italy definitely promised not to bomb them, the Exchange Telegraph Addis Ababa correspondent reported. Just returned from an investigation of the bombing of the Swedish Red Cross Hospital in the Dolo area, Dr. Junod said, according to the correspondent. “There is no doubt that the bombing was deliberate.” Dr. Junod, delegate in Ethiopia of the International Red Cross said he would make his conditional recommendation for withdrawal to Red Cross headquarters at Geneva. “Survivors of the Swedish hospital,” Dr. Junod was quoted as saying, “are living in terror of their lives at Muggeh (west of the former position near Dolo). Fearing another bombing, members of the unit spend their days in the surrounding forest, treating the wounded wh

LONDON, Jan. 13—(4)—Eight children and their mother, Mrs. Sarah Alice Tyrer, forty years old, perished today when fire destroyed their miner’s cottage at Tydesley, Lancashire. Adam Tyrer, the father, was the only survivor.

LONDON, England. (UP) — Naval limitations negotiations entered a delicate, dangerous phase today that may determine definitely whether there is going to be competition in building, adding scores of millions of dollars to tax schedules in the United States, Great Britain and Japan. Japanese delegates had a series of fresh instructions from Tokio, the result of an emergency cabinet meeting. Delegates of the other powers America, Great Britain, France and Italy, expressed hope that the instructions would deter the Japanese from withdrawing, as they threatened, unless their demand for equality of strength with America and Britain is conceded. But Japanese delegates told the United Press they believed their departure was inevitable. A Japanese spokesman indicated to United Press that if the Japanese demand for equality were rejected, Admiral Osami Nagano, chief delegate would: 1. Propose agai

LONDON, Jan. 13.—(4)—Informed naval conference observers understood today that Japanese delegates interpret their new instructions from Tokyo as authorizing them to make demands regarding the rejection of the Japanese demand for equality. A Japanese spokesman indicated an Anglo-Japanese conference some time today was expected to determine the immediate course of the Nipponese delegation. The conferees will be Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto, Matsuzo Nagai, Viscount Monsell, first lord of the British admiralty; Admiral Sir A. E. M. Chatfield and possibly Anthony Eden, the British foreign secretary.

LONDON, Jan. 13. — Informed sources affirmed tonight that the British Government is ready to go ahead with oil and other raw material sanctions against Italy if there is a collective agreement at the League of Nations Council meeting January 20. The disclosure followed upon a long meeting of cabinet ministers charged with the Empire's defense.

1936-05-02.text: Washington—(#)—After betting off one vicious assault by Ethiopian bandits, the minister to Ethiopia today told Washington the "situation is getting worse" and appealed for British assistance to protect America’s legation. Evidencing the danger threatening the tiny group of Americans still holding the legation against marauders was the serious wounding of two native women in the servants quarters. Cornelius Van H. Engert, the minister, reported with pride how a handful of Americans and native servants had driven off a bandit attack at 9 o’clock in the morning (1 a.m. Central standard time) after his wife narrowly escaped bullets of the rioters. "I can not speak too highly of comrades who grasped at once the importance of energetic action," he said. Appeal to British But six hours later, Engert appealed for British aid through the state department, hoping London could reach Sir Sidney Bart

(Copyright 1936 by United Press) LONDON—Foreigners in Addis Ababa took refuge behind the barbed wire entanglements of the British legation today, in imminent danger of an attack by warriors enraged at the Italian victory. Emperor Haile Selassie abandoned his capital with his family. Looting and shooting broke out in the city. Foreigners fled to the fortified British legation compound for the protection of its barbed wire, its five machine guns, and its little company of 250 Sikh infantrymen, pick of the British Indian army, under British officers. The legation had sufficient food to withstand a siege for three months. Commercial wireless communication with Addis Ababa was severed without warning this morning soon after the capital’s station opened for business. News of the imminent danger to foreigners was transmitted in a dispatch from Sir Sidney Barton, British minister, to the foreign

LONDON, May 2 (P)—A Reuters (British) news agency dispatch from Paris said today the French foreign office has received a telegram from Addis Ababa reporting the sacking of the imperial palace of Emperor Haile Selassie. The message to the French foreign office confirmed that the emperor joined the empress and other members of the royal family at the last moment on a special train bound for Djibouti.

London, May 1.—(/P)—Europe's workers called for peace and condemned war in May Day celebrations characterized by parading and speech-making. There was practically no violence, Reichsfuehrer Adolf Hitler in Berlin, Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin in London and War Commissar Klementi E. Voroshiloff in Moscow also voiced pleas for peace. London had one of the quietest May Days in its history. A force of 300 policemen watched thousands of workers march in Hyde Park carrying red banners. Teuts Rally In Germany, millions of Nazis rallied around May poles and praised the country's change from strikes and riots before Hitler to a 'workers’ holiday.' They enjoyed free beer and sausages at employers’ expense, In Spain, aside from the killing of an alleged fascist at Seville and the arrest of a number of fascists in Barcelona, there was tranquility. In Austria and southeast Europe elaborate police p

PARIS, (UP).—A French government official today said he had been informed that Emperor Haile Selassie will arrive at Djibouti, French Somaliland, tomorrow en route to Palestine. The official said the emperor would embark on a British ship at Djibouti for his voyage to Palestine.

ADDIS ABABA—Foreigners in the Ethiopian capital took refuge behind barbed wire entanglements guarded by 250 Sikh troops of the British embassy as looting and shooting broke out, according to an official British report received in London. Emperor Haile Selassie and his family abandoned the capital, entraining for Djibouti in French Somaliland. LONDON—Exchange telegraph correspondent with Italian armies reported that the main Italian column advancing on Addis Ababa had occupied Egersa, a village 35 miles north of the capital. A landslide was holding up the main body many miles farther back. ROME—Italian troops, fighting rain and mud, proceeded on the last stage of their march to the capital. Ethiopian chieftains along the route were submitting with resistance. LONDON—Wireless communication with Addis Ababa was severed soon after the government station in the Ethiopian capital started busin

Washington, May 2 (P)—The state department said today an offer of Great Britain, extending facilities of its stoutly-protected legation at Addis Ababa to all American nationals in event of trouble in the Ethiopian capital, has been accepted.

By H. R. ANICARERBOURER | International News Service Staff Correspondent (Copyright, 1936, by International News Service) LONDON, May 2.—Emperor Haile Selassie’s spectacular flight from Addis Ababa threw Europe into confusion today. It bitterly humiliated Britain, exalted Italy, and crushed hopes of all remaining believers in the League of Nations, but at the same time it opened the prospect of one more breathing space for peace on this continent. Escape of the emperor utterly dumbfounded all who had known him and destroyed a great structure of illusions about the heroic resistance of Ethiopia. Coming atop his declaration of yesterday that Ethiopia would fight to the last man, the emperor's apparent decision to save his own skin evoked shocked dismay among those who had advocated that this country risk war with Italy to save him. | Only Excuse Offered. 1936-05-05.text: LONDON, May 6,—(U.P)—Italy completed her conquest of Ethiopia today when a stream of triumphant Italian troops poured into Addis Ababa, relieving the menace to more than 4,000 Americans, British, French and other foreigners besieged in the legations. The Italian troops, in motor trucks, rolled down the imperial highway into the eastern quarter of the city and past the British legation compound, where the British and American residents of the capital had been holding out behind wire entanglements against ferocious attacks by the natives. News of the occupation was flashed to the foreign office here by Sir Sidney Barton, British minister, over his own wireless. Sir Sidney said the Italians began passing the legation at about 4 p.m. Addis Ababa time, 8:10 a.m. CST. From the British legation the Italian troops had two miles of rough, hilly road through thick eucalyptus groves and scattered h

Washington—(?)—The State Department was notified today that the American legation in Addis Ababa had been reoccupied by its own officials and that all of its contents were undamaged. London—-(?)—Sir Sidney Barton, British minister to Ethiopia, reported to the foreign office today that a large force of Italian troops in motor trucks entered Addis Ababa this afternoon. The arrival of the Italians, who had fought their way up from Dessye over mountain roads, had been expected for the last two days. Addis Ababa itself had been in the throes of rioting by natives who had started marauding through the streets of the capital after Emperor Haile Selassie had fled the country. Foreigners hoped that the Italians would be able to restore order at once. The arrival of the Italians, who had fought their way up from Dessye over mountain roads, had been expected for the last two days. Addis Ababa itself had been in the throes of rioting by natives who had started marauding through the streets of the capital after Emperor Haile Selassie had fled the country. Foreigners hoped that the Italians would be able to restore order at once. LONDON, May 4 (#)—The British government today asked Sir Sidney Barton, its minister to Ethiopia, to do everything possible to help the United States legation in Addis Ababa. Sir Sidney, who has 150 Sikhs, the famous British fighters from India, at his command, was expected to attempt a relief of the embattled American legation which was reported surrounded by a mob of armed Ethiopians.

Rome’s conquering legions reached their goal of Addis Ababa today and all Italy celebrated. The fascist troops entered an Ethiopian capital through which, for four days, hordes of rioting natives had spread terror. First word of the fall of Addis Ababa was given by the British minister, who reported that a large force of conquering Italian warriors entered Addis Ababa today to relieve thousands of besieged foreigners. This word was wirelessed to London by Sir Sidney Barton, the British minister, shortly after the sorely pressed American legation had been evacuated. Shortly afterward a British patrol went into action with machine guns to repel an attack on the Belgian legation by rampaging rioters. Incoming French troops from French Somaliland were blocked temporarily by destruction of part of Ethiopia’s lone railway 30 miles from Addis Ababa. The leaders of the southern Ethiopian forces,

WASHINGTON, May 20 UP—The United States has received assurances from the Italian government that lives and property of foreigners in Addis Ababa would be protected according to the rules of war as soon as Italian forces occupy the city. This was learned today shortly after word from London that a large force of Italian troops had entered Addis Ababa. Earlier, America’s fighting envoy, Cornelius Van H. Engert, and the little band which staved off attacks of Ethiopian bandits, had been evacuated safely to the British legation. Assures Safety. The Italian assurances were given to the American embassy in Rome in response to an inquiry from Secretary Hull asking it to ascertain from the Fascist government what steps it was taking to meet its responsibility to protect the lives of foreigners in the Ethiopian capital as far as possible. The inquiries were made officially by Alexander Kirk, char

DJIBOUTI, French Somaliland, May 5,—(4#)—Emperor Haile Selassie went into exile laden with rich treasures. When the Ethiopian monarch sailed aboard a British cruiser yesterday for Palestine, his possessions included the imperial family jewels and many cases of gold bullion, gold coins and silver Maria Theresa thalers. Even six automobiles were listed among the imperial belongings. The emperor was reported to have stopped at Diredawa, while coming here by railway from Addis Ababa over the week-end, and to have removed all cash from the treasury and customs house there.

WASHINGTON, May 4. (?)—Defenders of the American legation at Addis Ababa for three riotous days hung grimly to their post tonight despite State Department instructions to abandon the diplomatic mission and take shelter at the British legation. Upon receipt of an urgent message from Secretary Hull to abandon the legation in the interest of safety, the American Minister Cornelius Van H. Engert notified the State Department that he felt the mission should not be evacuated except as a last resort. Earlier, the British legation had advised, through London and the State Department, that it would be unable to send soldiers and guns from its own guard to aid in the defense of the American legation. The British offered, however, to send a military convoy to assist in the evacuation of the remaining occupants of the American legation. Secretary Hull “urged” Engert to abandon his valiant defense of

1936-05-03.text: By Associated Press Sir Sidney Barton, British minister to Ethiopia, reported to his government today that Emperor Haile Selassie had left Addis Ababa and that the capital city was the scene of widespread disorder. The emperor was declared to have taken a train for the French Somaliland port of Djibouti. British official circles in London interpreted the emperor's departure as the collapse of organized defense against the Italian invasion. Advance Is Halted The Italian northern army, meanwhile, had temporarily halted its advance on Addis Ababa as the fascist troops prepared to push forward in the wake of an advanced guard. Between the blackshirts and the gates of Addis Ababa was an undetermined number of Ethiopian defenders. Await Out Post O.K. The motorized column commanded by Marshal Pietro Badoglio camped beside the river Robi awaiting word from the Italian outposts that the route to

LONDON, May 2—The bulk of the foreign population of Addis Ababa slept in guarded compounds tonight as Ethiopia’s civil authority collapsed with the flight of Emperor Haile Selassie. The British government was informed that armed bandits in the Ethiopian capital were burning, looting and shooting. Sir Sidney Barton, the British minister, in whose protective legation compound there were sheltered and cared for 3,000 foreigners, reported to the government early this evening that the situation in Addis Ababa was satisfactory so far as the life of foreigners was concerned. It was stated officially that the British had received no report that the Emperor was abdicating. Authoritative sources said they considered he remained legally the emperor until he formally renounced the title. In actuality, however, these sources considered Ethiopia was without an emperor at present. Since Sir Sidney had

Rome, May 15 (Sunday) (4)—Italian press dispatches from Djibouti, French Somaliland, early today said Emperor Haile Selassie and his family would reach that city by special train today after fleeing from Addis Ababa. The news of the Negus’ departure threw Rome into an impromptu celebration last night. The sources for the news were the British and French governments, Italy remaining without direct information. Newspapers printed extras, crowds packed around news-stands, snatching up the papers as fast as they were delivered for sale. The joy of victory was expressed without the regimentation prepared by the government, which already had ordered the nation to prepare for a nation-wide “adunta”—a mobilization in honor of the Italian army’s arrival in Addis Ababa. The adunta, when it does come, will mark the climax of Italy’s third victorious war in 24 years. Marshal Pietro Badoglio’s forces

Paris—(#)—The lines between France's political left and right were drawn sharply today for the final election for a new chamber of deputies. Voters in the 433 districts where no candidate received a clear majority last Sunday will return to the polls tomorrow for run-off elections, to decide the contests between the unified leftists and the rightists.

MADRID. May 2—Frustration of a plot to assassinate Premier Manuel Azana was announced tonight by police who said they had arrested seven persons alleged to have been implicated. Those arrested were Emiliano Carmelo Ruano, a former member of the Spanish foreign legion, three men whose names were not given who are alleged by Ruano to have conceived the plot and engaged him to carry it out, and three police officers who, it was alleged, agreed to shield the assassins.

PARIS, May. 2-(AP)—The flow of gold from France has injected new anxieties into the French jigsaw puzzle of politics which voters will piece together tomorrow with run-off election for the chamber of deputies. Bankers said anxiety was already shown in the steady flow of gold abroad from the Bank of France, while French hoarders had ceased buying gold because they were afraid the metal might be requisitioned. The total amount of gold withdrawn from the Bank of France in the last five weeks has amounted to $247,538,000. The stock market recovered from a sharp break early in the week, but financial writers continued to warn of possible monetary dangers, including the possibility that France would be devaluated. After showing a decided trend toward the left in the inconclusive balloting of last Sunday, the voters will go to the polls tomorrow for the run-off elections which will determine de

Panama, Man — The Italian general staff is awaiting conclusion of secret negotiations with the Ethiopian government before its advancing northern army enters Addis Ababa, according to dispatches received here today. Forty thousand troops under Marshal Pietro Badoglio, the Italian commander, are reported to have been ready to enter the Ethiopian capital since last night. The negotiations were said to have resulted in a long night session of the Ethiopian cabinet with Emperor Haile Selassie. The emperor reportedly urged resistance to the invading army. Most of his cabinet members and tribal chiefs were said to have demanded surrender and the abdication of the emperor. His cabinet’s attitude reportedly caused Haile Selassie’s flight from the capital inasmuch as he no longer could count on support from his troops. French observers expect that Italo-Ethiopian peace negotiations will begin at

WARSAW, May 2. — A sneeze at the wrong moment, plus an alert traffic policeman, ruined the act for 15-year-old Josek Teleiman. Determined to drive his father's car, Josek purchased a false moustache which he thought would make him look at least 17, the age limit for driving. Everything went well until an unsuspecting traffic policeman signalled a halt and Josek sneezed right in front of him. The glue gave way and the moustache fell in his lap. Josek's father paid the fine.

1936-03-10.text: London, March 10 (#)—Earl Beatty, former admiral of the fleet, died tonight. He had been ill for several weeks. He was 65 years old. Death came to the former naval official at the London home for the aged where he had been under treatment. His son, Viscount Borondale, and a doctor and nurse were at his bedside. Beatty's condition became serious after he attended the funeral of the late King George V.

Paris, March 10.—(U.P.)—France assured Great Britain today that she does not intend to go to war against Germany. The declaration immeasurably relieved the tension which prevailed when the signatories of the Locarno treaty gathered here to discuss their answer to Germany’s re-armament of the Rhineland. France and Britain could not agree on joint action and will make no decision until after the League council meets at Geneva this week. Capt. Anthony Eden, British foreign secretary, telephoned the results of today’s conference to Premier Stanley Baldwin in London. Eden said Foreign Minister Pierre Etienne Flandin of France insisted on economic and financial sanctions against Germany but did not ask for military sanctions. Flandin was understood to have assured Eden that French policy is 100 per cent pacific and is not intended to lead to conflict.

Paris, March 10 (AP)—A reliable source reported tonight that Anthony Eden, British Foreign Secretary, had offered France strong military guarantees if she will negotiate with Germany. The exact nature of the proposal was not defined. It was stated that in the form presented it is merely an idea for which the details must be worked out.

Paris.—French officials declared today that a war with Germany to oust Hitler's troops from the Rhineland was impossible and that Great Britain's apparent sympathy with the reichsfuehrer’s peace offers blocked the French demands for ‘justice.’ They said France was ‘strong in her right,’ but that she still believes in collective security — that is, joint action by allied nations. The speech made this afternoon by Anthony Eden, the British foreign secretary, in the House of Commons, aroused exclamations of bitter disappointment in the French atmosphere of profound gloom. Officials said that France had relied upon the loyalty of her allies, the little entente of Jugoslavia, Czechoslovakia and Romania, and upon her newly-found friend, Russia. But, they said, France, even with the major portion of her “iron ring around Germany,” must hesitate to take drastic action “if Great Britain deserts u

{COPYRIGHT 1936 BY ASSOCIATED PRESS} Berlin—The Third Reich expressed gratification officially today over Great Britain’s attitude toward the German march across the Rhine and willingness to consider the new treaty proposals which accompanied the violation of the Locarno pact. The public pronouncements of Britain’s Prime Minister, Stanley Baldwin, and Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden were declared by foreign office spokesmen to be a cause for satisfaction after responsible German officials first took an opportunity to study yesterday's House of Commons debate. “We have full understanding for the fact that the British government is not alone master of its decisions and that the whole apparatus of the League of Nations must be set in motion before Britain’s final answer can be given,” a spokesman said. He proclaimed his government's determination to get a clear and precise decision on “the agonizing problems of the strength of right against might.” Premier Sarraut declared that if Reichsfuehrer Hitler was justified in violating the Locarno Treaty, “then we must turn resolutely toward military alliances and armament races and, let us admit it frankly, to war made by th

London, England, March 9.—(UP)— Dr. Hermann Gortz, German lawyer, was found guilty by a jury today of violating the Official Secrets Act by making a sketch of an army flying field. He was sentenced to four years in prison. The jury deliberated only briefly after listening to an appeal by Defense Counsel Reginald Croom-Johnson to keep "your heads cool" in deciding the case. The jury declared the German attorney to be guilty of two counts, after they had examined one of Gortz’ diaries, in which he described motorcycle expeditions to many of Great Britain’s supposedly secret air fields. Gortz previously had admitted making the sketch, but declared the drawing had been made to use in a novel he was writing. Summing up the case for the jury, the presiding judge said, "There is no doubt that the sketch is a sketch of a prohibited place and the type aimed at by the legislatures in passing the O

LONDON, March 9.—Great Britain linked a plain warning to Adolf Hitler not to make war today with an agreement to examine his security proposals following the scrapping of the Locarno treaty. Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden, in a pronouncement to the House of Commons just before entraining for Paris, said Great Britain is honor-bound to march to the assistance of France and Belgium if Germany should attack them. No Reason For War There is no reason to suppose the German action threatened war, he said, however, and he pledged that Great Britain would make the best of an admittedly serious situation by trying to rebuild Europe’s shaken peace structure. Eden’s failure to mention sanctions or any other possible punishment of Germany was considered significant in diplomatic quarters. They interpreted his speech as definitely conciliatory and as indicating that Britain is not prepared to take an

1936-07-27.text: Washington, July 27.— (#) —An increasingly alarming situation at Vigo, Spain, prompted American Consul William W. Corcoran today to advise the state department he was evacuating 23 Americans and Cubans on a British cruiser. At the same time the American cruiser Quincy was steaming toward Alicante, on the southeast coast of revolution-wracked Spain, to rescue more than 100 Americans and other foreigners reported taken there by train from Madrid. Asserting that apprehension in Vigo was increasing hourly "as the military and right elements are apparently becoming less hopeful and increasing nervous," Corcoran said that if the military authorities should fail mob rule and anarchy would follow. The cruiser proceeded immediately to the port on the southeast coast after touching briefly at Malaga. While the navy department was advised of this reserve effort the state department received a messa

American and British refugees, beleaguered in their Madrid embassies for a week, fled revolution-torn Spain today with the aid of the leftist government. On a train provided for them, the foreigners sped toward Alicante, on the southeast coast, where they were expected to board a British destroyer tonight. Their departure from Madrid, which the rebels threaten to "starve out," coincided with government announcements of fresh and successful assaults against the fascist insurrectionists, but increasingly ominous reports of trouble to the American state department. Ambassador Claude G. Bowers’ aides abandoned the American summer embassy at San Sebastian, observing there may be "terrible bloodshed" there. San Roque Bombed. From the piece-meal war front throughout Spain trickled reports of renewed assaults by loyalists on rebel-held strongholds, Gibraltar heard that government planes had bomb

| NEW YORK, July 27 (AP).— Great Britain's S. S. Queen Mary docked today after making the fastest crossing ever recorded for a steamer between Europe and New York—but her commander did not claim the blue pennant of Atlantic supremacy. - “We very well do not deserve it,” said Sir Edgar Britten, skipper of the liner. So the blue ribbon, emblem of Atlantic speed, remains with France's Normandie, which in June, 1935, averaged 29.64 knots for the crossing as compared with the Queen Mary's 29.61 knots. The reason is that the Normandie started her best run from Southampton and traveled 3,192 nautical miles. The Queen Mary was clocked from Cherbourg, 3,098 nautical miles away. The English ship made the crossing in four days, eight hours, 37 minutes; the French ship covered the longer route in four days, 11 hours, 45 minutes. Aboard the Queen Mary were 1,795 passengers. Many of them witnessed the

Aboard S.S. Exermont—Eight men, survivors of a fateful airplane dive into the Atlantic Ocean off Nantucket Lightship, and their dead companion were rushed to New York today. The large Bellanca cabin plane, piloted by Captain William Wincapaw, veteran New England flyer, crashed yesterday after it had circled the British liner, Queen Mary, just completing a record-making trip, so several Boston newspaper photographers could take pictures. Edwin T. Ramsdell, 46, Boston Post photographer, died shortly after the accident, apparently from internal injuries. Walter Jordan, of the Christian Science Monitor, and William Reiter, vice president of La Touraine Coffee Company, owner of the plane, suffered deep head gashes in their attempts to escape from the plane. Others in the party, all uninjured, were Herbert Stier, Boston Herald photographer, George Mason, of Boston, vice president of the Nation

VIMY, France, July 20-() King Edward of England, standing bareheaded before a silent throng of pilgrims, unveiled a gleaming World War monument atop Vimy Ridge today as a symbol of British-Canadian-French friendship and peace. Extreme precautions were taken to protect the king, who less than two weeks ago rode into range of the loaded pistol of a discontented Briton. Troops were lined up around the station when his train arrived, and no photographs were permitted. But as soon as he reached the monument, the king escaped his bodyguard and mingled among the pilgrims. The anxious escort almost broke into a run trying to keep up with (Continued on Page 2, Col. 7.)

Madrid July 27. —()— (By secret courier to Hendaye, France)—After a week of terror huddled in their embassies American and British refugees today were being evacuated to Alicante on the southeast coast of Spain. The government placed a special train at their disposal. It was assumed they would board a British destroyer at Alicante where the refugees were due to arrive tonight. Unconfirmed reports said two British women refugees were violently assaulted by rioters before they found sanctuary in the embassy.
