Exermont, En route to New York, July 26.—A ten-passenger seaplane, roaring a welcome to the British liner Queen Mary, crashed into the Atlantic Ocean five miles off Nantucket early tonight, fatally injuring one man. Eight others, including myself, were rescued. Edwin T. Ransdell, 40, a Boston Post photographer, died several hours after the crash on the Exermont, from which a boat crew was dispatched to our rescue. The other eight suffered bruises and severe shaking up. The plane splintered to bits. For 20 minutes we clung to the wave-washed pontoon until the boat reached us. We had gone down from Boston to meet the Queen Mary. Ransdell was taking a picture as we sailed lightly in the rear of Queen Mary’s stern. Then our plane started downward. It struck and started to sink. We climbed through the door to the pont

(By Associated Press) NEW YORK, July 27—The Queen Mary rode into New York harbor today with a new trans-Atlantic record. Britain’s superliner wrested the blue ribbon of the Atlantic from the French liner Normandie by completing the passage from Cherbourg breakwaters to Ambrose Lightship in four days, eight hours and 37 minutes. This record, given as the official time by the Queen Mary’s commander, Sir Edgar T. Britten, clipped three hours and five minutes from the record established last summer by the Normandie on her maiden voyage. The 80,000-ton ship, after anchoring at 12:15 a.m. eastern standard time, off Ambrose Light, proceeded leisurely toward quarantine. The Cunard White Star line, owner of the Queen Mary, laid no claim to the speed-by-hour record. Officials said the ship’s average speed was 29.61 knots, or .03 short of that of the Normandie. They explained the Queen Mary had tak

1936-07-08.text: LONDON, July 8—(4)—An explosion ripped through the research department of the Royal Arsenal at Woolwich late today, killing five persons, one a department official. One other employee was injured seriously. Five departments from the town, a metropolitan borough of London, aided arsenal squads in combating flames which broke out after the blast. The war department, for the time being, did not disclose the cause of the explosion at the great arsenal, which is a key factor in the empire's huge scheme of defensive rearmament. Likewise, the extent of the damage was not known.

By BURDETTE T. JOHNS. (Associated Press Foreign Staff.) London, July 8.—-(AP)—Three new estimates, filed in the House of Commons, pointed Great Britain today toward a billion dollar defense programme. The government informed Parliament it would ask additional appropriations of $100,000,000 or more to bolster army, navy, and (Continued on Page Two.)

Montreux, Switzerland—(>)—The Soviet delegation announced today that Foreign Commissar Maxim Litvinov had been instructed by Moscow to leave the present Dardanelles conference unless he received considerable concessions from the British. The conferees, assembled to study Turkey’s demands for the right to refortify the famous straits connecting the Black Sea with the Mediterranean, recently have been close to a deadlock over rival Russian and British desires. Great Britain demanded the right of unrestricted passage through the Dardanelles for her warships; Russia has contended that the eastward passage of non-Black Sea powers should be restricted. At the same time, Russia, herself a Black Sea power, has demanded the right to move her warships in either direction through the Dardanelles in unrestricted numbers.

LONDON, July 8 (®).—King Edward inspected the Royal Air Force by air today—flying in his own airplane on a tour of several airdromes, With him, in the blue and red ship, traveled the Duke of York, heir-apparent to the throne.

LONDON, JULY 8. (AP).—An explosion in the royal arsenal in Woolwich killing five persons was announced today by the war office. The cause of the explosion and the extent of the damage was not immediately disclosed. The announcement merely said: “The war office regrets to announce an explosion at the research department of the royal arsenal at Woolwich this afternoon which caused the death of five persons.”

LONDON, July 8.—(INS).—Making his fourth airplane flight since his accession to the throne, King Edward VIII, accompanied by the Duke of York, today began a day-long aerial tour of royal air force stations. The king’s plane was piloted by 32-year-old Flight-Lieutenant Edward Hedley Fielden, known among British airmen as “Mouse,” and regarded as one of the best pilots in Britain. He has acted as Edward's pilot since 1929.

Plattsburg, N. Y., July 7. (P)— With members of his family at the bedside, Dr. S. Parkes Cadman clung to a slender thread of life tonight with the same determination that carried him from Shropshire miner lad in England to internationally known churchman. Peritonitis complicated his grave illness and surgeons held in abeyance plans to remove a ruptured appendix. Dr. Cadman underwent an emergency operation last night in the Champlain Valley hospital, but attending surgeons said his “very critical” condition precluded relief beyond the insertion of two rubber drainage drains.

London, July 8—Great Britain, increasingly perturbed by the gravity of the European situation, prepared today to spend another huge sum, estimated at between 15,000,000 and 25,000,000 pounds ($75,000,000 to $125,000,000) to speed up defenses. With the empire already facing an overdraft as the result of the rearmament program, the army, navy and air force will issue supplementary estimates Thursday, asking Commons to appropriate additional money to build ships and airplanes and to whip the mechanization of land forces into first-class shape. The navy, which has had ample opportunity to test its theoretical strength or weakness during the Mediterranean crisis, may ask as much as 10,000,000 pounds extra, members of Parliament believed. The air force, already carrying out plans to triple its strength, is expected to ask almost as much. The army, attempting to reach a high standard of mechani

1936-08-25.text: PEIPING, Aug. 25.— (4) — Three British soldiers were fired upon while returning to their barracks from a motion picture, the British embassy disclosed today. The shots came from a moving automobile and one soldier was wounded in the leg. As a result of the incident the British embassy requested the Chinese government to protect lives and property in China.

By United Press GIBRALTAR, Aug. 25 — The British destroyer Cyprus arrested the Spanish government trawlers San Adrian, Lolita and Ortiz last night when they were found without lights in British waters, it was announced today. Brought to Gibraltar, the trawlers were found to be carrying war materials destined for the loyalists at Malaga. CRUISER UNDER TOW GIBRALTAR, Aug. 25.—The British admiralty tugs Energetic and Rollicker are towing to Gibraltar the distressed Italian cruiser Gorizia, it was announced today. The warship, it was reported, sent distress signals off the Straits. It was understood the Gorizia was damaged by the explosion of the oil tanks in her bows. No casualties were reported. The Gorizia, launched in 1920, is of 10,000 tons, one of the four ships of the Zara Class. It has eight 8-inch guns and 32 anti-aircraft guns, ranging from 3.9 inches to 60. Though its complement i

The civil war in Spain increased in violence Tuesday while at the same time the threat of war in Europe diminished and there was every prospect that the Spanish outbreak would be confined to Spain and Morocco. Britain, France, Germany, Italy, and Russia were close to an agreement on non-intervention and an embargo on arms exported to Spain. The fighting in Spain proper was bitter. Authentic dispatches gave no reason for assuming that either side is winning. The outcome of the war may be settled in the mountains north of Madrid. A heavy artillery duel began in the hills Tuesday presaging a possible desperate drive by the rebels before the Madrid defenders can be reinforced from the northwest by the Asturias miners and militia. The latter are closing in on Oviedo. Dispatches seemed to indicate that the fall of the city is imminent. Another fierce fight was in progress in the northeast corn

LONDON (Tuesday)—(”) — The Reuters (British) News Agency reported Tuesday all 16 defendants in the Moscow conspiracy trial had been shot following rejection of their appeal for clemency by the president of the central executive committee of the Soviet Union. The 16, including the one-time prominent Bolsheviks, Gregory Zinovieff and Leon Kameneff, were convicted and sentenced early Monday after a five-day trial. They all confessed to participation in a conspiracy to overthrow Dictator Joseph Stalin and the Soviet regime. Many of them, going beyond the prosecution charges, even admitted they "deserved" death.

Great Britain and France were reliably reported to be in communication on diplomatic proposals to check acts of brutality in the Spanish civil war. Germany's doubling of military service term intensified Europe’s Left-Rightists struggle. Reich's propaganda ministry estimated the decree meant an army of between 700,000 and 800,000 after October recruits are called to colors. French press reckoned Germany's 1937 armed strength at 3,200,000, twice as large as that of France. Moscow, at which military decree was aimed, said it demonstrated Germany’s “intensive preparations” for war. Spain's Socialist government, in a new purge of Madrid's Fascists, arrested the one-time confessor of former King Alfonso and executed four officers accused of starting an ill fire and mutiny. Both Rebels and Loyalists claimed victory in Spanish mountain fighting north of Madrid. Rebel war planes again bombed.

WARSAW, Aug. 25.—The Polish government, it was learned today in official circles, has consented to release Mrs. Frederick Atkinson of Minneapolis, Minn., arrested at Ostrów for unwittingly violating English currency regulations.

Gibraltar, Aug. 25 (UP)—The British Admiralty tugs Euergetes and Rollicex are towing to Gibraltar the distressed Italian cruiser Gorizia, it was announced today! The warship, it was reported, sent distress signals off Tangier, Morocco, and the tugs were sent all at once across the Straits. "It was understood the Gorizia was damaged by the explosion of the oil tanks in her bows. No casualties were reported. The cruiser will be repaired temporarily at Gibraltar before leaving for Italy.

OMAHA, Neb. (AP)—Police Tuesday announced that Albert England and his cousin, Orin, confessed robbers of the Elliott, Ia., branch bank would be turned over to the Wayne county, Neb., authorities. The two men had confessed to the robbing of the Cooperative Savings and Loan Association bank at Carrell, Neb., in which $1,200 had been taken.

1936-08-09.text: | Calais, France, Aug. 8.—Edward VIII of Great Britain today took his first vacation as king in an air, land and sea trip across Europe to the troubled Mediterranean, focal point of European unrest. He flew the English Channel and rode by train in a special car from Calais toward Yugoslavia. Once he enters that country his route lies by nebulous public announcement to some point on the Adriatic coast where he will board his yacht. The king traveled incognito as the Duke of Lancaster.

Madrid, Aug. 8 (4P)——Moroccan Rebel troops, hardened in north African hill campaigns, tramped northward toward beleaguered Madrid tonight, with the Fascist commander-in-chief, Francisco Franco reported at their head. That word, reaching the capital from Rebel headquarters in Burgos, to the north, hastened, rather than delayed, slashing government attacks on three fronts. The Fascists, said Leftist authorities, were losing all hopes of winning the fight. They pictured General Franco as still in Spanish Morocco attempting to land more troops on the Spanish peninsula. Already he had brought, by ship and plane, an estimated 8,000 soldiers from Africa to Spain. (In some Rebel quarters it was feared Loyalist success at Algeciras, southern seaport burned during a government bombardment yesterday, might upset defenses created to protect troop transport, especially since the Rebel gunboat Dato wa

ROME, Aug. 6. — Two Italians were killed in Spain, it was officially announced tonight, and formal protests have been lodged holding the leftist Spanish government responsible. Edoardo Marcelli, it was charged, was killed “barbarously in his own home” on August 5. The names of the other Italians were given as Dogliotti. Another Italian was wounded. First representations were made by the Italian consul in Barcelona, followed by a protest to the government from the embassy in Madrid.

Berlin, Aug. 8—#—Ensconced in a luxurious car of French manufacture, former King Alfonso of Spain entered Germany tonight, as officialdom wrestled with the question of neutrality in relation to Spain's civil war. Germany answered French queries as to Reich adherence to a general hands-off policy with acceptance in principle and with another question: “Will Russia be neutral?” As Alfonso was whirled along German highways, ostensibly for a visit to the Olympic games in Berlin, the foreign office denied any knowledge of his arrival. “Foolish” Reports, Earlier in the day the foreign office had described as

Pavis, Aug. 8—/P—France tonight banned exports of all war materials to Spain as an indication of its confidence that world powers would agree to keep out of the Spanish civil war. The cabinet’s decision that it no longer needs to reserve “liberty of action” on the shipment of war supplies followed the agreement by Portugal “in principle” to remain neutral in her neighbor's revolution. Portuguese Reply. With Portugal's reply in hand, officials indicated that all nations to whom the French appealed to join a neutrality agreement in the Spanish crisis had answered favorably, despite the reservations of some. After a lengthy meeting with Pres. Lebrun, Premier Leon Blum's cabinet also planned to launch an immediate inquiry with a view to suppressing false reports of the Spanish situation. Britain's formal acceptance of the French proposal for an international agreement to withhold arms from b

HYDE PARK, N. Y., Aug. 7 (UP) —President Roosevelt announced today he would invite Governor Alf M. Landon, Republican nominee for president, to a conference of state executives on the drought situation. The meeting to work out a cooperative state and federal program is being arranged for "somewhere" west of the Mississippi, and no date has yet been fixed. It was expected, however, that the conference would take place within a month in Iowa. Mr. Roosevelt startled his press conference by casually mentioning that the Kansas governor, in his capacity as such, would be asked to attend along with those of Iowa, Nebraska, and Oklahoma. In connection with the Landon invitation it was recalled that while president-elect, Mr. Roosevelt was invited by President Hoover to Washington to discuss foreign debt problems. A. B. Reynolds is confined to his

FAIRBANKS, Alaska, Aug. 8 UF John Hajdikovich, prospector, flew here today with word he and two companions found the Arthur F. Hines plane, missing with Pilot Hines and three passengers almost a year, on a barren mountain range 175 miles east of here. Bearing the motor plate from the plane he said was found on the mountains, Hajdikovich told of discovering the ship burned and only a few bones remaining. The numbers on the plate checked with those of the orange-winged ship in which Pilot Hines, Mr. and Mrs. John Long and Alton Nordale, all of Fairbanks, took off from Dawson August 19, 1935, to Fairbanks. Their ship vanished en route and an airplane search in which many of Alaska's famous aviators joined failed to disclose it. Hajdikovich said he found the plane at about 5000 feet elevation on the range rising from the Healy River, a tributary of the Tanana.

CONNERSVILLE, Ind., Aug. 8 —(4)—Col. Frank Knox, Republican vice presidential candidate, told “what his party has to offer” tonight by outlining a program he said would “unleash recovery” and return “millions of unemployed to honest work.” Addressing a statewide rally of Indiana Republicans, the candidate put forward the proposals and intentions after charging that the government of the United States “is the worst-managed business in the world today” under the present administration. The speech was the opening address of the Republican national campaign, Colonel Knox told his audience. To “drive out the sweat-shop and the exploiting employer” is one of the party’s resolutions, Colonel Knox said, if it is successful in the fall election. Another is to battle monopolies, while encouraging and fostering “honest business.” For a third he listed cutting taxes and shifting their weight from “t

1936-08-31.text: | ATHENS, Greece. Aug. 31— With King Edward VIII of England on deck of the royal yacht ‘Nahlin, the craft today smashed into a bridge at Chalkis on the Aegean Sea island of Euboea. The yacht, which is carrying the monarch on a holiday cruise in the Adriatic and Aegean seas, apparently was not seriously damaged. The vessel proceeded after a brief inspection had been made of her. A motorboat on the deck of the yacht was slightly damaged. The bridge had already swung open to permit the Nahlin's passage when the crash occurred. The cause is ascribed to choppy waters. The king was not perturbed. He waved to the cheering crowd after the accident.

BROOKLYN, N. Y., Aug. 31. (®)—Reports of bad weather over the Atlantic caused Dick Merrill and Harry Richman today to postpone again the takeoff of their projected round trip flight to London. Merrill said they hoped to get away tomorrow.

LONDON, Aug. 31.—Hope dwindled today for a peace consolidation agreement among European nations who are to attend, in October, a conference of Locarno treaty powers. Opinion was that Benito Mussolini of Italy, in his warlike speech of yesterday—particularly his statement that it was impossible now to check the armaments race—reduced prospects of agreement and increased European tension. It was believed Mussolini's speech, coupled with the prospective increase of strength in the German army, would strengthen Britain's determination to accelerate the pace of its rearmament. Mussolini's statement—that he could mobilize 8,000,000 Italians—was hardly likely to reassure Britain, whose position in the Mediterranean he is challenging. His reference to dubious political combinations was regarded as a direct reference to the French and Czechoslovakian mutual defense agreements with Russia, and hen

London, Aug. 31—()—A new record—this time for the fastest eastward crossing of the North Atlantic—was entered today in the log of the super-liner Queen Mary. The huge Cunard-White Star vessel steamed past Bishop’s Rock off the English coast last night three days, 23 hours and 57 minutes after she passed Ambrose Light off New York. This time shortened the previous record held by the French liner Normandie by more than three hours.

Athens, Aug. 31.—(AP)—The yacht Nahlin, on which King Edward of England is spending a holiday, was damaged today when it collided with a bridge while passing through Chalkis strait, 36 miles north of Athens. News of the Nahlin’s mishap followed reports the yacht had been forced into shelter in Karystos bay, on the south end of the Island of Euboea, by a storm. Because of the bad weather, King Edward had radioed to Athens, suggesting that an escort of destroyers be withdrawn. Accordingly, the destroyers turned back toward Athens.

began a tour of New England today aboard his special campaign train, The train will carry the Chicago and Manchester publisher into 32 states, At Lowell, Mass., the train's first stop, Knox told a platform audience the Republican campaign was one for “the preservation of the democratic principle in America,” adding it was part of a “contest of ideas” of government, Knox was applauded when he said he expected the Lowell audience probably would “get a chance to see the next president of the United States, Gov. Alf M. Landon, during the campaign. “I vow you will find him a straight thinker and a straight shooter,” Knox said, Steady Jobs G.O.P. Aim. At Lawrence, where the 6-car train halted for 10 minutes, Knox stated the primary objective of the Landon administration, if the Republican campaign is successful, would be “to get people back to work at steady jobs.” He also declared “I’m told t

Aboard Knox Campaign Train, Sept. 1.—Frank Knox, Republican vice-presidential candidate, declared today that “full wages at full time” in private industry is “our aim.” Knox's first speech on his second day's swing through New England was at Bridgeport, Conn.

London, Aug. 31—Great Britain announced a new recruiting scheme today, whereby youths may try the army for six months with the privilege of quitting if they dislike the life. If they quit, they will be subject to 14-days annual training for five years. Otherwise, they will become regular enlisted men in the standing army. Those between the ages of 17 and 25 may take advantage of the trial enlistment.

1936-08-03.text: New Bedford, Mass., Aug. 3, (U.P)—The Rev. Charles E. Coughlin was en route to his Royal Oak, Mich. parish today after a whirlwind week-end tour of New England during which he pledged his efforts to remove “a Communist from the (presidential) chair once occupied by Washington.” To the cheers of about 50,000 followers here and in East Providence, R. I., and Worcester, the radio priest described the president as “the commissar of promises” who is “surrounded by reds and the frankfurters of destruction.”

Paris— (7) —The appeal by France to other European powers to let Spain settle its insurrection without outside intervention likely will be approved by both Great Britain and Italy, it was said in official circles today. Significant in words dropped in diplomatic quarters was confidence that the plan for nonintervention would win the support of Premier Mussolini, of Italy. Earlier, it had been expected that Britain would send its approval, but Rome was understood to look on the proposition in none too kindly a spirit and with decided reservations. (Last week's incident in French Morocco, when two Italian airplanes ostensibly bearing arms to Spanish insurgents were forced down, led to an international uneasiness.)

BERLIN, Aug. 3.—(#)—The standing of the nations in Olympic men’s track and field competition: United States 4; Germany 31; Finland 30; Japan 1; Sweden 5; Holland 4; Great Britain 2; Argen- tina 1. Women’s track and field: Germany 16; Ireland 4; Austria 3; Japan 2.

In the seventeenth day of the fratricidal war in Spain, with reports indicating that assaults are progressing along the northern, central and southern fronts, an agreement was seen imminent Monday among governments of France, Britain and Italy to let the peninsular nation settle its family squabbles alone. The agreement is regarded as a tacit guarantee of peace in Europe for the moment. It was apparently a successful French appeal to Britain and Italy to agree to a non-intervention policy. Similar appeals are expected to be made to Germany and Russia. Barcelona advices said that the government claimed the capture of Lazaide in a renewed drive along the Aragon front against the rebel stronghold of Zaragoza, Loyalists gathered for a push against the rebels in the Guadarrama mountains above Madrid. The government said that it had complete control of Madrid.

(Copyright 1936 By The Associated Press) { MADRID, AUG. 3. (AP) Strengthened loyalists massed their forces today for a fresh assault on rebels in the jagged Guadarrama mountain passes, New columns of liberals were mobilized for action in the northeast where rebels hold Zaragoza and in the south at Cordoba and Seville. The fascists were reported, in advices from the northern side of the line, to be moving toward San Sebastian in an effort to regain control of the resort town. Small forces of rebels still held their position in the mountain gateways to Madrid these advices declared. Renewed bombardment by loyal fliers turned gas and electric plants at Palma Mallorca Island into “formidable bonfires.”

Madrid, Aug. 2.—(AP)—Spain’s leftist government today conscripted railroads and utility plants, bolstered its forces with troops from loyal provinces and launched a new siege to dislodge fascist rebels from the mountain passes outside Madrid. Bombardment and the firing of cities spread new terror on the sixteenth day of the violent civil war. The gas factory and surrounding buildings of Barcelona were a “formidable bonfire,” loyalist aviators said after a flight over the Mediterranean city. Loyalists hold the city but much violence and disorder have been reported there. Streets of Palma in the Balearic islands were fired by leftists. Planes which bombed rebel barracks, ammunition storehouses and utility plants there, leftists fled the southern part of the city as the fire encroached, the aviators said. BURG IN, Aug. 3, (AP)—OLE the mark fast and moving into the lead after the first 16 meters, Jesse Owens today won the Olympic 100-meter sprint championship, achieving the first of three gold medals he had set as his goal in the 1936 Olympiad. The brown Buckeye bullet, a top-heavy favorite from the start of yesterday's preliminaries in the sprint feature, for the second time in as many days equaled the Olympic and world record of 10.3 seconds in capturing the title. Ralph Metcalfe, husky Chicago negro runner, finished a yard and one-half behind Owens. Metcalfe was timed in 10.4 seconds. American negroes, running one-two for the second straight Olympiad, dominated the event from start to finish, each winning their semifinal heats and then fighting it out in the final. Metcalfe also was a close second to Eddie Tolan, Detroit negro, in the 200 final. Woeokot? Pourta Martin Osendarp of Hollan

OLYMPIC STADIUM, Berlin—(UP)—Jesse Owens, the Buckeye Bullet, won the 100-meter sprint title in the 11th Olympic games today—the first track victory of the games for the United States. Ralph Metcalfe, Marquette club, finished second. Metcalfe was runner-up in 1932 to Eddie Tolan of the United States. Martinus Osendarp of Holland was third. Frank Wykoff of Glendale, Cal, finished fourth. Erich Borchmeyer of Germany was fifth, and Hans Strandberg of Sweden was sixth and last. Ties Olympic Mark. Owens, who hopes to score an Olympic “triple,” whipped along the rain-soaked red clay track in 10.3 seconds, tying the Olympic and existing world records. The Olympic record was set by Tolan in 1932 and equalled by Owens yesterday in winning his opening qualifying heat. Owens created a world record of 10.2 in winning his quarter-final heat yesterday but it was announced today that the mark would not

1936-12-21.text: CANNES, France, Dec. 21. — Wallis Warfield Simpson cleared away the mystery surrounding her immediate future today with a plain indication she would not see the man who gave up the throne of England for her until her divorce is absolute. The statement Mrs. Simpson would stay at her haven in Cannes for “several months,” and “there is absolutely no possibility” she will see Edward of Windsor until spring, was made by Herman Rogers, her Riviera host as Mrs. Simpson held a formal press conference for the first time in her life. In the end the conference yesterday turned out to be more of a social reception than an interview. Adroitly Mrs. Simpson discussed the beauty of the Riviera, the weather and the dangers of driving over mountain roads.

Copyright, 1936, by United Press LONDON, Dec. 21.—Russian anger over reports that Spanish Nationalists set fire to a Soviet freight ship caused new fears today that the Spanish civil war might yet develop into an international conflict. At Russia's request, Great Britain has consented to use its channels of information to aid in determining the ship's fate. Pending definite evidence, Russia has decided to withhold a decision on action to be taken if its fears for the ship prove true. It was understood that if it is proved that Nationalists set fire to the ship—possibly with loss of life—Russia may ask that all governments declare the Nationalist ships pirates, to be sunk on sight. An alternative, even graver, would be that Russia might alone declare the Nationalist fleet pirates and risk a clash with warships of Italy or Germany, both of which are favorable to the Nationalists.

SELSEY, Eng., Dec. 21 (4)—Mme. Marie Schmeder, sought by French police for shooting her co-pilot during a flight over Villacoublay yesterday, was ordered held on French charges after a warrant for her arrest had been issued at Versailles. Mme. Schmeder fled from France in the same plane in which she was alleged to have shot Pierre L'Allemand, her co-pilot during a flight Sunday morning. Several hours later, after the trans-channel trip, she brought her ship down in a Sussex field, damaging the plane in the landing. Slightly dazed by a cut in the head, she told English officials her name was Chappelut, although she carried no passport. British authorities said they were notified by French police that Mme. Schmeder shot L'Allemand in the back of the head while he was making his first flight at the controls of the plane owned jointly by the two fliers. He told French police he managed to la

Cannes, France, Dec. 20 (#)— Mrs. Wallis Warfield Simpson made known today "there is no possibility" she will see the Duke of Windsor before the spring. For the first time in her life, the woman for whom Edward VIII abdicated the throne of England talked to the press at a formal conference. Clad in a trim sports costume and graciously hospitable, Mrs. Simpson received a few correspondents in the garden of Mr. and Mrs. Herman L. Rogers' villa Lou Veiet. For a half hour she smiled and chatted vivaciously with the newspaper men, enjoying several laughs over the interest of the world in her affairs. She consented to the meeting after months of refusals to entertain the press in any manner or to be interviewed. The meeting was arranged on two conditions: That no questions be put to Mrs. Simpson and that she not be quoted. An exception was made for the final remark which she blurted out teasin

SELSEY, Eng. Dec. 21 (P)—A pretty French aviatrix whom police believed to be the principal in an astonishing aerial drama at Villacoublay airdrome Sunday recovered today from shock following a crash in a Sussex field. A dispatch from Versailles said the woman of Villacoublay, Mme. Marie Schneder, was indicted today for assault in connection with an attack on the flier Pierre L’Allemand, who was shot in the back in midair. The investigating magistrate Grenier announced he would seek to extradite Mme. Schneder from England. She flew away in the plane which she and L’Allemand owned jointly after the (Continued On Page 12)

LONDON, Dec. 21 —(*)—Thousands of pieces of silver plate were offered for sale today by Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia. The emperor, who is living near Bath after leaving his kingdom with the fall of Addis Ababa to the Italians, did not attend the sale. The collection included 16,000 ounces of silver in various forms, of which many were plates marked with the royal crest and Amharic lettering. A service of meat and pudding dishes weighed 7,000 ounces. Another contained 300 knives and forks. One series of 24 plates was mounted with gold and silver coin, each plate representing a different country.

LONDON (UP) — It was reported today that Great Britain had notified Italy and France of the transformation of its legation at Addis Ababa into a consulate general. Such action would mean recognition in fact (de facto) though not in law (de jure) of Italy's conquest of Ethiopia. The foreign office refused to confirm or deny the report.

NZESFELD, Austria, Dec. 21. UP—Baron and Baroness Eugene de Rothschild, hosts to Edward, Duke of Windsor, busied themselves today with preparations for a Christmas party designed to take the former British monarch’s mind off his troubles. Hours before the Duke bestirred himself numerous messengers arrived at the castle with big packages which were hidden away as soon as they were delivered. All the packages were delivered afoot or on bicycles so that there would be no noise of trucks. But, in his enforced separation from Mrs. Wallis Simpson for whose love he left his throne, the Duke already had the consolation of two presents—songs dedicated to him in honor of the sacrifice he made for love. One is “Poor Young King,” the other “Come to Kitzbühel!”

1936-06-29.text: | WIMBLEDON, Eng., June (?P)—Donald Budge, flaming red Oakland, Calif., star, was the lone American survivor in the All-England tennis championships today as Bryan M. (Bitsy) Grant and Wilmer Allison the American champion, were eliminated in the quarter-final round. Allison and Grant met at the hands of England's cup stars, Fred Perry and H. (Bunny) Austin, Perry, for his third straight title, took down the pint-sized Grant in straight sets, 6-4, 6-3, 6-1, and toppled Allison, 6-1. Budge advanced to the semi-final at the expense of Quist, champion of Petronas, 6-4, 6-4. It was Budge's second major victory over the Americans this year. He defeated them in the North American Zone cup final at Philadelphia last month.

WIMBLEDON, Eng, — (WP) — Donald Budge, the red-topped California youngster, became America’s sole hope in the All-England tennis championship today when his two Davis Cup mates, Bryan (Bitsy) Grant of Atlanta, and Wilmer Allison of Texas, were defeated by England’s two top-ranking players in quarter-final round matches. Budge gained the semi-final round with a 6-2, 6-4, 6-4 victory over Adrian Quist, Australia. Grant and Allison bowed to Fred Perry and Wilfred (Bunny) Austin, respectively. Perry, defending champion and No. 1 in the world, toyed with the little southerner to win, 6-1, 6-3, 6-1, while Austin overwhelmed Allison.

London, June 9. (7)—Japan formally notified the British government today she would not adhere to the 1936 international naval treaty. The move was authoritatively characterized as a serious blow to British hopes of working out a universal naval treaty. It was stated that it might jeopardize some provisions of the new treaty signed by the United States, Great Britain, and France, since certain provisions become operative only if Japan joins.

MANCHESTER, England, June 28.—An angry crowd of 3,000 stoned the automobile of Sir Oswald Mosley, leader of the British Fascist Party, and smashed windows at the Fascist club at Hulme tonight. The disturbance came after a blackshirt demonstration at the town hall. The crowd tore down the Fascist’s flag and tried to overturn and set fire to their trucks. Eight were arrested.

Geneva, June 29.—Prospects for a tame, routine League of Nations assembly tomorrow vanished today when Emperor Haile Selassie indicated he would appear personally to plead his nation’s cause. Italy countered fresh attempts to make the fate of Ethiopia an international bone of contention by moving to establish the Ethiopians responsible for the East African war. "While the Italians and Ethiopians fought for a solution of their own problems, neutral statesmen, on the eve of the extraordinary assembly session, considered procedure to be adopted in the face of proposals calling for reformation and reorganization of the League. France and Great Britain agreed to sponsor Premier Paul Van Zeeland of Belgium as a candidate for election as president of the assembly. Compare Impressions The French and British delegates, after comparing impressions at a conference between British Foreign Secretary

' Geneva — (#) — Emperor Haile Selassie’s spokesmen announced today the conquered Negus would ‘personally address the League of Nations assembly in an eleventh hour appeal for “justice.” The assembly will meet at 5 p. m. (10 a. m., CST) Tuesday in Geneva’s municipal auditorium. Selassie, now known by his Italian conquerors as “Signer Tafari,” worked on the text of his appeal in the seclusion of his hotel suite today. It will be delivered in French.

PARIS, June 29 (UP).—Serious violence at Toulouse marked the protracted general strike in France today. The strikes hitherto have been comparatively peaceful. At Toulouse several were injured. The casualties occurred during a violent clash between adherents of the conservative right and left wing elements supporting the new popular front government of Premier Leon Blum. Many were arrested. Police guarded the public squares and boulevards. Twenty thousand workers went out in the Moselle Valley industrial district, making a total still on strike of about 180,000. Five thousand dock workers at Marseilles threatened to go out again, tying up shipping.

Paris, June 29 (#)--France’s general confederation of labor was stated officially today to have more than doubled its membership in the last few weeks. Its rosters now list 3,500,000 names. . . Roger Salengro, minister of the interior, announced the increased support to the labor union movement. Prior to the Socialist government’s rise to power, the confederation membership was approximately 1,250,000, composed largely of government employees and railroad workers. Many residents left hotels on the French Riviera after owners proclaimed a lockout of 450 hostelries. They were closed “indefinitely” after the employers declared they could not meet workers’ demands for more pay and shorter hours. Members of the Croix De Feu and of the People’s Front, government adherents, fought a street battle in Toulouse in which several persons were injured. Police broke up the fighting and arrested a numb

1936-06-22.text: GOSPORT, ENG., June 22—(i)—A royal air force bombing plane crashed on the deck of the S. S. Normandie today. No one was hurt. The freak accident occurred while the ship was in Cowes Roads, disembarking its passengers from New York. The plane was being flown by Lieut. G. K. Horsey. As Horsey piloted the bomber over the big French liner, it struck the stay of a mast, then fell on the deck across the bows of the ocean vessel. The pilot, shaken up, went ashore, leaving his airplane on the deck of the Normandie which steamed off for Le Havre still carrying its unexpected cargo.

A dazed and frightened young Royal Air Force pilot crawled out of the wreckage of his plane on a deck of the giant French liner S. S. Normandie today and told Captain Rene Pugnet: “I am terribly sorry about this.” The pilot, who was only shaken up, crashed when he tried to fly over a huge steaming funnel and struck the stay of a mast. Hot air robbed his wings of their lift and only a supreme effort prevented his dropping into the funnel. “The landing,” said Captain Pugnet, “was one of the most extraordinary sights I have seen. The bomber just sat down like a stone. The undercarriage ripped to bits a few inches from the forward mast.” The plane crashed into a derrick unloading an automobile, the derrick broke and the car crashed on the deck, half on and half off the ship. The pilot, Lieut. G. K. Horsey, said when he flew over the funnel he felt as if the plane were being “sucked in.” The

ROME, June 22—(AP)—Italy moved toward military and commercial accords with Great Britain and Germany today as Premier Mussolini warned he could take care of nations ‘crazy with the heat.’ Army sources reported agreement in principle with Great Britain on a four point military pact in the Mediterranean. After five days of negotiations, Italy and Germany have agreed on the terms of a commercial treaty concerning clearing house payments. The military agreement would assure British naval supremacy in the Mediterranean and hand supremacy of the air to Italy, it was understood.

LONDON, June 23.—(UP)— Great Britain has no intention at the forthcoming League of Nations meeting in Geneva “to propose or assent to recognition of Italy's annexation of Ethiopia,” Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden told the House of Commons today. Great Britain also has no intention of consulting the United States or other signatories about Italy's violation of the Briand-Kellogg peace pact, Eden told questioners. “The time for that would have been at the opening of hostilities,” he said. “We preferred to work through the league.”

LONDON (UP)-- Great Britain will not recognize Italy’s conquest of Ethiopia despite her policy of abandoning sanctions as futile, Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden revealed in the House of Commons Monday. “The government has no intention at the forthcoming meeting of the League to propose or assent to Italy’s annexation of Ethiopia,” Eden said. Eden also stated that Great Britain would also permit Emperor Haile Selassie to communicate with the armed forces in western Ethiopia through the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan but would not permit the shipment of arms or munitions at least for the present.

JERUSALEM—U.P.—British military authorities pressed airplanes, tanks and armored cars into service today to quell Arab demonstrations against Jewish immigration that resulted in three pitched battles Sunday. The fighting took the lives of two British soldiers. Several others were injured. Many Arabs were killed or wounded. Airplanes opened fire with machine guns near Nurel-Shams, North Palestine, where 60 Arabs ambushed a detachment of royal fusiliers escorting a convoy. One soldier died of his wounds and two others were injured seriously. The airplanes harassed the attackers until reinforcements of Seaforth Highlanders arrived. The Arabs divided into two groups when the Highlanders were ordered to pursue them.

London, June 22—- (®) —Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden told the House of Commons today that the British government does not recognize Italy's annexation of Ethiopia. Questioned by members of the house concerning the government’s stand on this question, Eden replied: “His Majesty’s government has no intention at the forthcoming meeting of the League of proposing or assenting to the recognition of Italy’s annexation of Ethiopia.” Eden told the house last week Great Britain would move at Geneva for the abolition of the League of Nations’ sanctions against Italy. A member asked whether Great Britain would consult the United States and other signatories of the pact of Paris “with a view to appropriate action being taken to deal with the breach by Italy of the obligations under the treaty.” Eden replied: “No, sir.”

1936-08-08.text: By the Associated Press, Great Britain and Germany took a hand Friday in the Spanish civil war with vigorous protests against the treatment of their nationals by both rebels and loyalists. The U.S. government Thursday asked Spanish authorities in Madrid to protect American property in the area of the revolt and asserted indemnification would be expected for any damage. The execution of four young nazis near Barcelona was called “murder” by a foreign office spokesman in Berlin. Protests were lodged in Barcelona with leftists by the Germans against the deaths, and another complaint was made to Madrid authorities over the “unprovoked shelling” of a German steamer by a Spanish destroyer. Both sides were warned by Great Britain that suitable steps would be taken to prevent the endangering of neutrals by either leftists or rightist fighting in the area of Gibraltar. Victorious advances by loya

LONDON, AUG. 8. (AP)—Piloted by the new official "Captain of the King’s Flight," King Edward took off today from Fort Belvedere, near London, for Calais, France, for the start of his month's holiday with a party of friends on the steam yacht Nahlin. His Majesty, incognito as the Duke of Lancaster, established a precedent as the first British king to fly abroad. He will board the Nahlin "somewhere in the Adriatic Sea." The exact route of the cruise was kept a closely guarded secret. The crew of 50 on the yacht wore spic and span new uniforms from caps to shoes. They were pledged to secrecy about the royal holiday. The king is expected to sail leisurely among the lovely little islands of the Dalmatian Archipelago off the coast of Yugoslavia, across the water from the heel of Italy's boot. Two British destroyers will accompany the royal party, which will be absent from England about a month

CHICAGO, Aug. 8.—(UP)—Former Mayor William Hale (Big Bill) Thompson, sworn antagonist of everything pro-British, barged back into Illinois’ political maelstrom as the Lemke-Townsend candidate for governor. “I'm going to announce a platform that'll curl their hair,” promised the blustery three-time mayor who once threatened to punch the King of England in the nose if he came this way.

(By the Associated Press) Britain will return fire if ships again fired on by either Loyalist or Fascist eraft. Nazis, angered by reported execution of four citizens, talk of intervention to save Spain from “red peril.” France's eight-power neutrality proposal endangered by German reaction. Fascist gunboat burned by Loyalists; Algeciras rebel fort damaged. Government claims capture of numerous small towns; revolution appears deadlocked with no major advances by either side.

PARIS, Saturday, Aug. 8—(UP)—An “eminent personage” in the entourage of Chancellor Adolf Hitler has telephoned the British foreign office warning that Germany will take action in Barcelona today, Genevieve Tabouis, usually well informed political writer for the newspaper Oeuvre, reported. It was believed that Berlin will present Madrid with a virtual ultimatum giving a time limit for punishment of those allegedly guilty of executing four German citizens at Barcelona and for making reparations, the writer asserted. Otherwise, Germany will break off relations with the popular front government of Madrid, she said. Tabouis believed that Germany is deliberately seeking to rupture Spanish-German relations.

LONDON, Aug. 7 (Great Britain warned tonight her warships will immediately return the fire of any “accidental” shelling by either rebel or Spanish government forces. As the British government issued its second warning of the day through authorities at Gibraltar, officials at Whitehall made it clear retaliatory measures will be taken on the spot against any further attacks. Carried to General Francisco Franco, insurgent leader, was a protest from Gibraltar that rebel airplanes had fired on H.M.S. Basilisk. Madrid received the British request that the leftist regime must keep its ships clear of Gibraltar to prevent endangering British life and property.

CALAIS, France. UPI. King Edward of Great Britain, flying to France on the first leg of a month’s holiday on the Adriatic, landed on the outskirts of Calais at 4:32 p.m. Saturday. The king traveled in such strict incognito as the Duke of Lancaster that the St. Inglevert airfield which had flown the British flag in anticipation of his arrival, was instructed to haul it down just before his plane came to rest. Accompanied by six members of his staff, Edward rode to Calais in a private automobile driven by the son of a French landowner who contributed the machine for the occasion. At Calais the king immediately boarded a train for Strasbourg en route to Yugoslavia.

Gibraltar, Aug. 6. (4°) — Three loyalist Spanish warships hurled shellfire today against rebel forts at Algeciras, damaging the British consulate and destroying the Argentine consulate. Mrs. E. G. Beckingsale, wife of the British consul, received minor injuries. (The British government warned that British warships will immediately return the fire of any “accidental” shelling by rebels or loyalists.) The Algeciras revolters were bombarded twice during the day. The second attack brought no return fire from the rebel fortifications, indicating their artillery may have been damaged irreparably. The Jaime I, loyalist warship, accompanied by the gunboats Libertad and Cervantes, pulled close into shore and unlimbered its heaviest guns against ships in the harbor and the Fascist fortifications. The two gunboats fired a half-dozen shots from a longer range and huge clouds of smoke and flame were

1936-07-10.text: PARIS, July 10. —-(#)— Premier Mussolini and Chancellor Hitler have formed a diplomatic partnership, informed sources asserted today, in the face of British and French efforts to return Italy to the Locarno treaty union. The dictators of Italy and Germany already have agreed on the fate of Austria, diplomats declared, and probably have reached an understanding on the Locarno problem. France attempted to gain Fascist friendship by denouncing her part of the Mediterranean mutual assistance agreement, authoritative sources indicated, while Great Britain extended an offer of diplomatic peace through her announced intention of reducing British naval strength in the vicinity of North Africa. Italian rates in prospective Locarno discussions where the principal subject is expected to be Germany’s re-occupation of the Rhineland. Italy's decision not to attend the Locarno session except under at l

London, July 9 — Britain's first lord of the admiralty announced to commons today the withdrawal of part of the greatest war fleet ever massed in the Mediterranean—but served notice the empire is hard at work building an even greater navy. Even now, Sir Samuel Hoare told the members, the navy could put to sea immediately seven battleships and battle cruisers and raise steam for three more on short notice—if embroiled in war. His words came on the heels of publication of supplementary defense estimates which brought the year’s total funds for the army, navy and royal airforce to £187,870,000 (about $940,000,000). The gravity with which Britain views the world panorama and its determination to rearm with the greatest possible speed were seen in the fact the estimates included the second supplementary provision in three months for the navy.
LONDON, July 10--(#)--King Edward wrote finis today on sanctions against Italy. He approved an order for termination of the economic blockade in a privy council meeting at Buckingham Palace.

Paris, July 9.—(#)—France officially denounced her Mediterranean mutual assistance agreement with Great Britain tonight. Officials said the government had informed Great Britain and Italy that she considered the arrangement promising her assistance in the case of an Italian attack on the British fleet ended when sanctions were lifted. France's action, it was indicated, was taken in an attempt to further satisfy Italy and win her participation in the forthcoming Locarno conference at Brussels, as well as the Dardanelles conversations now in progress at Montreux. SHOCK London, July 9.—(#)—France’s disavowal of the Mediterranean mutual assistance pact came tonight as a shock to government supporters. Official comment was lacking in Whitehall. But members of parliament wondered whether the rate of moving warships away from the sea might not be slowed down as a result of the new developments.

ROME, July 10. — (UP) — Radio stations operating at the American and British legations in Addis Ababa were outlawed today by Marshal Rodolfo Giaziani, viceroy of Ethiopia. Giaziani ruled, according to official dispatches from Addis Ababa, that communications at the disposal of the Italian government are adequate. He issued a decree forbidding the operation of private radio stations in Ethiopia. In the future it will be unlawful to transmit or receive messages on the radio sets of the United States and British legation.

PARIS, July 10.—(AP)—Ethiopians have taken complete possession of the town of Mojjo, approximately 30 miles southeast of Addis Ababa, the newspaper L’Oeuvre reported today. By their occupation, the Ethiopians have cut the railroad connection between the capital and Djibouti, French Somaliland, the paper declared. L’Oeuvre said one of two hastily armored trains which left Addis Ababa for Mojjo was derailed and the other forced to return after escaping an attack in which many Italian soldiers were killed.

PARIS, July 10.—Accused of delivering to Russia an airplane gun secretly designed by France, Air Minister Pierre Cot of the French Cabinet denied the charge in the Chamber of Deputies today and the Deputies responded with a vote of confidence in him. The accusation was made by the Rightist Party. Minister Cot is a Socialist. The vote was 403 to 162 in his favor. The Air Minister refused to discuss if the air gun was delivered. He declared the French government differentiates between indispensable secrets and necessary exchanges. The Rightists charged that the Air Minister gave Russia a model of France’s 22 millimeter airplane gun, which, mounted in an airplane, fires 800 shots a minute. Only six such guns exist.
SANTANDER, Spain. (PF) — The deaths of 20 persons in a storm which swept the northern coast of Spain yesterday were reported today. Most of those who died were lost from fishing boats at sea.

1936-02-20.text: (Copyright, 1936, By United Press) ROME, Feb. 20. (U?)—Publication of a purported secret British report on Ethiopia, recognizing Italy's paramount interest in Ethiopia and asserting that Italian control over the country might prove beneficial to British territory agitated diplomats today. In the report was a frank discussion of the possibility that Ethiopia might disappear as an independent state. In that event, the report said, the British government would have to provide for territorial control of Lake Tana, heart of the Nile navigation project, and a corridor linking it to the Sudan. In event that Italy absorbed Ethiopia, the report said, every effort must be made to ensure equal treatment for British subjects and the maintenance of the open door policy. It concluded, as quoted: “It would be necessary if possible to seize the opportunity for obtaining rectification of the confines (th

LONDON, Feb. 19. (P)—American and British naval conference delegates have agreed to limit battleships to 35,000 tons with guns of 14 inches, it was announced today. The formula for limitation will be submitted now to the French and Italian delegates, who have insisted so far that battleship tonnages and gun calibres ought to be smaller. It was learned that Great Britain has proposed that the life of the naval limitation treaty now being negotiated shall endure for 10 years, beginning next January 1, instead of six years. The British-American agreement on battleships was effected by an exchange of notes. The British handed Norman H. Davis, chief American delegate, a note yesterday proposing the limitation and specifying that signatories to the naval treaty might consult during the treaty’s life in case it might be thought desirable to modify the limits set. Provision was made for calling

LONDON, Feb. 20—(P) — The slight, fair-haired Edward VIII completed the first month of his reign today with public evidence that he has become Britain's “informal monarch.” The new King-Emperor, whose rule began the instant his father, George V, died just before midnight January 20, in keeping with the tradition that “the king never dies,” has already settled down to his tasks “with characteristic thoroughness.” Just as he toured the empire as Prince of Wales, making scores of informal trips as “Britain's ambassador of business,” so has he demonstrated that 20th-century informality, rather than stiff regard for precedent, will mark his reign.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 20. --(4)— The State Department today cabled instructions to the American consul at Trinidad, British West Indies, to investigate the statement by Alfred Harrod at Georgetown, British Guiana, that he had seen and talked to Paul Redfern, missing American aviator. The department acted on reports quoting Harrod as saying Redfern was held captive in the jungle fastness of Guiana by an Indian tribe. It asked the consul at Trinidad, the nearest place of American representation, to seek further information from Harrod, whose story was the first report that any outside actually had contacted the missing flier.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 20, UP — The State Department today ordered investigation of the possibility that Paul Redfern, American aviator lost on a flight to South America nine years ago, is a captive of savages in the jungles of North Brazil. The United States consul at Trinidad, British West Indies, was ordered to investigate the latest reports of private expeditions that the missing flier was believed to have been located near the village of Spokat or the village of Duniya, both near the Brazilian frontier. These advices, relayed by British diplomatic channels in Brazil, came to the State Department indirectly from Art Williams, who has been conducting an aerial search for Redfern. Williams was described as visiting a village where he was convinced Redfern was held, but as failing to see the missing flier.

LONDON, Feb. 20.—(4#)—Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh visited the House of Commons today, to observe British parliament procedure, for 15 minutes during the early part of the session. They were accompanied by Harold Nicolson, author.

LONDON, Feb. 20 (AP).—A report circulated today that Italy may refuse to enter the proposed new agreement on naval limitations until other nations stop their sanctions against Italy. This report added to the concern of United States delegates who oppose maneuvers tending to bring European political problems before the international naval conference.

WASHINGTON, (UP). Acting Secretary of Navy Henry L. Roosevelt insisted today that battleships of 35,000 tons were best for the United States navy, despite an appeal by France for a lower tonnage limit. The United States and Great Britain agreed at London on retention of the 35,000-ton limit and on reduction of guns to a 14-inch limit, on condition that all major naval powers agreed. France, through diplomatic channels, appealed to the state department for a lower tonnage limitation, but received no definite reply. Questioned about the agreement Roosevelt said that high naval officers were willing to limit gun caliber to 14-inches provided other principal naval powers did likewise. He insisted, however, that the 35,000-ton battleship still was the best type for the United States navy indicating that American admirals would be opposed to any reduction.

1936-10-05.text: ROME, (P) - Premier Mussolini reduced the value of the Italian lira 41 per cent today in a sweeping financial decree approved by the cabinet. The new value of the Italian monetary unit was set officially at 19 to the United States dollar and 40 to the British pound although the lira’s gold content was registered at £2.46 to the pound. Order New Taxes The cabinet also approved a capital levy on property owners who were required to subscribe to a loan to the extent of five per cent of the valuation of their property. Il Duce, in addition, ordered new taxes on stock dividends and company profits, prohibited price rises for increases in public service rates and decreed a 65 per cent reduction in customs duties for grains and cereals. (The premier's action fixed the value of the lira at approximately 5.2 cents as compared to 7.6 cents, the closing quotation on the New York Foreign Exchange ma

| London—()—Fifty marauders invaded the Jewish colony in London's east end Monday to raid shops after the police had quieted an earlier anti-Fascist demonstration. With bricks and stones, the roaming band smashed windows and plate glass fronts in a renewal of street rioting which forced cancellation of a parade planned by Sir Oswald Mosley, British Fascist leader. Disturbances developed Sunday as Mosley’s followers congregated near the town of London and anti-Fascist demonstrators in the east end threatened to charge the procession. Police persuaded Sir Oswald to call off the parade although scattered skirmishes broke out at a number of points. Police pulled down barricades erected by Communist demonstrators along the projected line of march.

LONDON, Eng, (Special) — Thousands of anti-fascist demonstrators massed in London’s east side and raised their fists in communist salute with shouts of defiance to charging police, and the cancellation of a parade by the British Union of Fascists. "Down with Mosley!" the crowd shouted in derision for Sir Oswald Mosley, leader of the fascist group. Nearly a half million people surged through the streets in the demonstration, it was estimated unofficially. Police halted the planned fascist parade, scheduled to march through the heart of the Jewish quarter, after rioting broke out at a number of points and threatened to spread with serious mob fighting. The demonstrators erected barricades at many points along the route of the abandoned parade, and many gave the communist salute as the fascists assembled near the walls of the ancient tower of London.

Spain’s desperate battle between a fascist army and a socialist communist government cast its shadow over France and Great Britain Sunday night. Mobs in Paris and London fought in the streets over the same principles which embroiled Spain in civil war — fascism versus communism. It was the danger of such clashes leading to widespread European war that led socialist Premier Leon Blum of France weeks ago to sponsor a pledge by interested powers to strict neutrality in Spain’s conflict. “Remember Spain!” was the warning cry of communist orators in the Parc des Princes, jammed by 100,000 demonstrators against fascism. “Unite to save the Nation from the Horrors of Fascism,” exhorted flaming red banners. Communists fought throughout the day with rightist followers of Col. Francois de la Rocque, who ordered a counter-demonstration against the communist gathering, held with government permission

bride A, seed, GEORGETOWN, British Guiana, Oct 4.—Pundit Mahangoo celebrated his 106th birthday Saturday by evening married the third time. Munching a combined birthday-wedding cake, he said: "I believe love rejuvenates a man." His youthful bride endorsed his opinion.

St. Quentin, France, Oct. 4.—(AP)—Gen. John J. Pershing, commander of the American Expeditionary Forces in France during the World War, attended ceremonies today commemorating the 18th anniversary of the recapture of this city by American, British and French troops. The city was occupied by Germans from August, 1914, until Oct. 4, 1918.

ROME, Oct. 5 (UP)—The Italian cabinet today approved an approximate 40 per cent devaluation of the lira, reduced import duties as a protective measure and gave favorable consideration to the general trend toward world currency stabilization. The lira stood at 19 to the dollar. An Ethiopian "victory loan" to exploit the new empire obtained by conquest was approved. Funds will be raised by taxing each estate to five per cent of its value.

(By The Associated Press) Madrid, Oct. 5—A hard driving socialist column battling for the life of the capital, the government reported today, split the insurgent arc-like grip on the city. Government troops, ministry of war communique said, pushing westward from their base at Santa Cruz del Retamar, captured the important road junction town of Macaeda and fought their way to within a few miles of Santa Olalla, on the road to the insurgent supply base at Talavera de la Reina. (The wedge movement, if correctly reported, would separate fascist forces operating out of Toledo from their comrades to the northwest, completely breaking their line of communication.) (The insurgent-controlled radio station at Cadiz reported that fascists having taken Llescas, only 22 miles south of Madrid had turned across country to Navalcarnero on the Madrid-Talavera tri road.) (This movement would cut off Santa

1936-10-08.text: LONDON, Oct. 8 -- The Swedish ocean flier, Kurt Bjorkvall, and his Bellanca monoplane were aboard the French trawler Imbrin, enroute to Valentia, Ireland, today after being picked up from the ocean eighty miles off the southwest coast of Ireland. The 31-year-old aviator, flying from New York to Stockholm, Sweden, had not been sighted after he passed Newfoundland, until the air ministry received a wireless report of his rescue. It was not known whether his plane was damaged in the landing at sea. It remained afloat until sighted by the trawler. Wednesday night, a full moon illuminated the sea and the weather was mild, enabling a lookout on the Imbrin to spot the dark outline of the plane on the horizon. The vessel swung off its course and came up alongside the plane. Cold and tired but supremely thankful, the stranded aviator was brought over the side. Reports to the air ministry did not

London, Oct. 8—Britain’s foreign secretary, Anthony Eden, suddenly broke off a Monte Carlo holiday today and turned back toward London to take charge of the foreign office in the grave atmosphere created by a Soviet ultimatum threatening Spanish intervention. Captain Eden, en route home, will confer in Paris tomorrow with Premier Leon Blum of France concerning Anglo-British action in the new crisis. Others Ready. Adding to the dangers of the situation it was reported other countries in addition to Russia are ready to raise the question of breaches of the international Spanish neutrality pact at tomorrow’s meeting of the non-intervention committee. British officials maintained the most discreet silence concerning the affair, pending tomorrow’s meeting. Apparently they had recovered from the initial shock of outspoken communication which flatly accused Italy, Germany and Portugal of giving

Copyright, 1946, By The Associated Press. LONDON.-- Paper profits to European national treasuries from currency devaluations were estimated at considerably more than $1,000,000,000. France was termed the greatest gainer, with her profits predicted at 17,000,000,000 francs, of which 10 billion were earmarked for the stabilization fund to keep the franc on a parity with the United States dollar and the British pound. The remainder went into the French treasury. Italy added between 1,000,000,000 and 2,000,000,000 lire to stock of gold and foreign currency whose pre-devaluation value was estimated at 5,000,000,000 lire. The exact amount of Italy's gold stock has not been revealed since before the beginning of the Italo-Ethiopian war. Italian officials have declared they will use realized profits for paying expenses of the East African campaign and other national necessities. They said they d

Moscow, Oct. 8.—Informed sources said today Soviet Russia hopes Great Britain and France will abandon their “indifference” to alleged violation of the Spanish neutrality pact and take an equally strong position as the Bolshevists. Last night, directly accusing Germany, Italy and Portugal of violating the pact through alleged war shipments to the Spanish Fascist insurgents, the Russians threatened to “free” themselves from neutrality obligations “if the violations are not stopped immediately.” Today, authoritative sources said the Kremlin was withholding further action, awaiting moves by (Continued on Page Three.)

By United Press Today’s development in the Spanish civil war: London—Russia precipitates diplomatic crisis by two notes charging Portugal, Italy and Germany with aiding Spanish rebels and threatening herself to aid loyalists. BURGOS — Final rebel offensive starts in full force in Madrid area; news that main body has started northward from Toledo expected. MADRID—insurgent drive accompanied by terrific airplane-artillery attack, rebels bomb Aranjuez railroad station on only road open to east coast from Madrid. HENDAYE—Reported loyalist miners fought way to center of Oviedo, killing 200 rebels. SAN SEBASTIAN—Reports by insurgents that seamen of loyalist battleship Jaime Primero killed 39 hostages aboard prison ship at Bilbao, in retaliation for sinking of loyalist destroyer.

LONDON, Oct. 7—(U.R.)—Kurt Bjorkvall, Swedish pilot, was rescued Wednesday night from the north Atlantic 80 miles southwest of Valentia, Ireland, where his Pacemaker monoplane was forced down on an attempted nonstop flight from New York to Stockholm. He had covered less than two thirds of the distance. He was reported uninjured and to have been forced down because his gasoline supply was exhausted. The French trawler Imbrim radioed the British air ministry that it picked Bjorkvall and his plane out of the ocean at 6:45 p.m. (4:45 p.m., B.S.T.), 80 miles out from Valentia off the southwest tip of Ireland. The Imbrim headed for Valentia to put Bjorkvall and the plane ashore. The rescue was made by moonlight, in a moderate sea. The crew of the Imbrim spotted the plane half submerged in water some distance away. The ship pulled up alongside and hauled the plane aboard. Bjorkvall, soaking wet

STOCKHOLM, Oct. 7 (AP)—A report that Kurt Bjorkvall, 31-year-old America-to-Sweden flier, had been sighted off the southern coast of Norway caused a brief flurry of excitement today, but investigation disclosed the plane probably was not that of the non-stop airman. The newspaper Tidningen, after an inquiry announced the plane seen 40 miles south of Christiansand, Norway, was equipped with pontoons. Bjorkvall, who left New York at 6:35 a.m. (C.S.T.), Tuesday, was flying a landplane. It was believed the plane sighted might have been one of those sent out to look for the aviator.

1936-02-07.text: ALSO Free for Fight Sleets London, March 6.--Great Britain ordered its ambassador to Rome today to protest strongly against the alleged bombing of a British Red Cross unit in Ethiopia by Italian planes. Sir Eric Drummond, the British ambassador, was instructed to urge Premier Mussolini's government to press an investigation of the attack and to order his military leaders on the war front to make certain such an incident did not occur again. Government officials asserted they had no official word of Addis Ababa reports that Major G. A. Burgoyne, attached to the British Red Cross unit near Quoram, Ethiopia, had been killed. Reports Are Denied Information from Dr. Melley of the Red Cross group, relayed through Sir Sidney Barton, British minister to Ethiopia, stated reports in Addis Ababa that three Kenya subjects of Great Britain had been killed were not true. Dr. Melley reported a bomb str

A faint possibility of a new peace move was seen today in a renewal of discussions in the Italian press of the Franco-British plan for the settlement of the Italo-Ethiopian dispute. Observers of the situation were interested in this trend for the press of Italy largely reflects government opinion and they believed therefore that this smoke of discussion might indicate a fire of interest in peace on the part of the government. For the last few months the Franco-British plan which envisioned the independence of the government of Ethiopia in exchange for territorial and trade concessions to Italy has been in the discard.

London, Feb. 7—(AP)—The Italian delegation to the international naval conference backed up the French today in an attack on the United States policy of maintaining large battleships. The Franco-Italian attack was launched before the technical committee of the conference. This body is charged with the specification of qualitative limitation—that is, naval limitation according to categories and types of vessels and guns. The French delegates demanded that the maximum size of battleships be 27,500 tons. Representatives of the United States, however, stood firm in their demand that the maximum limit remain at 35,000 tons. Contending that the needs of the United States, with great areas of the world’s surface to be covered, made it necessary that American battleships be sufficiently large for long cruising radius. Each delegation, including the British, set forth its views as to all types of

London, Mar. 6 (#).—Great Britain’s air force will ask parliament to increase its budget for 1936 by £13,015,000 (about $65,000,000) over last year because of special expenditures “in connection with the Italo-Ethiopian dispute,” it was announced officially today. Viscount Swinton, secretary for air, said an appropriation of £39,000,000 (about $195,000,000) will be sought. The proposed increase makes the 1936 budget approximately 1½ times that of 1935. Viscount Swinton also disclosed that Imperial Airways, subsidized by the government, will begin experimental flights this summer looking toward opening of a transatlantic airline.

LONDON, Feb. 7.--Greta Garbo’s doctor has forbidden her to leave for Hollywood for some weeks, the Daily Mail Stockholm correspondent reported today. The doctor has ordered her to take plenty of sleep and not to worry about business matters until late in the spring. The physician's order, the correspondent said, apparently was the result of nervous trouble the famous movie star has suffered.

Italian newspapers discussed the dead Franco-British peace proposal yesterday, leading to unofficial belief in some quarters that peace talks again have started. This, however, was denied by authoritative circles. The supreme commission for defense met for the second time this week. Before presiding over this session Premier Mussolini received army corps commanders for a conference. There were rumors that Marshal Pietro Badoglio, commander-in-chief of the armies in Africa, would be recalled to resume his post as chief of staff because of the European situation. Press dispatches said a British officer "smilingly" requested soldiers of the southern army to remove a marker which he said had been placed six feet inside the border of Kenya, British colony. The request was complied with, the dispatches added. The Ethiopian government published an affidavit by a Belgian officer denying Italian

U. S. STAND ATTACKED LONDON, Feb. 7—(P)—The Italian delegation to the international naval conference backed up the French today in an attack on the United States policy of maintaining large battleships.

Berlin, March 6.—(@)— Adolf Hitler tonight called a special session of the German Reichstag for tomorrow and invited ambassadors of the other four nations which signed the Locarno treaty to visit him before the national assembly convenes. Well-informed sources said Hitler, speaking personally before the Reichstag, will make a last appeal to the Locarno signatories to observe the spirit and the letter of the treaty guaranteeing mutual security in Western Europe. Only if this appeal fails, these informed sources declared, will Germany move to the final consequence of denouncing the five-power pact. It was further learned that the army general staff met today to consider a subject the nature of which was not disclosed. Announcement of the parliamentary session climaxed a day crammed full of diplomatic maneuvering in expectancy of Hitler’s latest gift to the nation before the annual memorial

1936-09-18.text: by The Associated Press London—J. A. Mollison, Australian flier, announced today he would take off from Floyd Bennett field, Brooklyn, October 17 on a trans-Atlantic flight to England. He said he hoped to reach London in 17 hours on a flight through the sub-stratosphere. After the New York-England flight, he asserted, he may try for two new aerial records, including a solo trip around the world.

: MUSGRAVE HARBOR, Nfld. (Canadian Press). Harry Richman and his pilot Dick Merrill hoped to resume Friday noon their interrupted London to New York flight. The fliers, prevented by shortage of fuel from reaching their New York destination, said they hoped to have the big monoplane towed to the beach where they could take off for Harbor Grace to refuel before hopping to New York. Mechanics brought here by Capt. Eddie Rickenbacker found the plane had suffered little damage when it nosed into an isolated swamp on its return flight from England Monday.
SYDNEY. (UP)—Australia has succeeded in making Mother Country England apple conscious. In a single recent month 1,000,000 cases of Australian apples were supplied to the English palate.

MADRID, Sept. 18. (47—Besieged Fascists at Toledo's Alcazar withstood an explosion of a ton of TNT today, and fired machine guns from the cellars of the ruined fortress to hold off government troops. The first of three mines under fortifications where 1,700 persons were stationed exploded today. There was no way to determine the number of casualties, Powerful Syndicalists at Madrid said the only effective way to crush Fascism was through the conscription of every able-bodied man. Both sides claim the capture of Siguenza, near here. Sporadic fighting broke out during the day in the Guadarrama Mountains rimming Madrid on the northwest. Government leaders cast about for more and more reinforcements, remembering Franco's boast that he could hurl 1,000,000 men against Madrid in two weeks if he had a mind to.

Cairo, Egypt. —(®) — Forty-five Egyptian workmen, their wives and children were drowned today in the collision of their outing steamer with a sailing boat in the flooded River Nile. The tragedy occurred just at the outskirts of Cairo. Only four of the holiday party were saved. Rescuers were hampered by the swiftness of the current, since the Nile now is at full flood stage.

| MADRID, Sept. 17. (4—Spanish Fascists flung 175,000 men at Toledo and Madrid today on three main fronts. The fiercest battle since the outbreak of the revolution was raging near Toledo, where a last minute delay gave 1,700 Fascists a final chance to evacuate besieged Alcazar before they were blown to bits from underground mines. The Fascist drive began west of Madrid. The government announced that foreign “daredevil” pilots were being recruited to start an aerial offensive with a fleet of new bombing and fighting planes. French demands for indemnities for the execution of a Frenchman in Spanish Morocco has gone unattempting to obtain the release of three American newspaper men held by the insurgents.

GENEVA, Sept. 0. Big European powers, convening in Geneva amid new war fears over Europe's "instability" have found a formula to bar vanquished Ethiopia from Monday's assembly meeting and to obtain renewed collaboration of Italy's Duce, League officials disclosed today. The officials said they expected Haile Selassie’s delegation of three, due in Geneva Sunday, to be refused seats at the assembly table on the grounds they do not represent an effective government. They added, however, that the League is not prepared to recognize the Italian conquest of Ethiopia.

(Copyright 1936 By The Associated Press) TOLEDO, SPAIN, SEPT. 17. (AP) — Execution by explosion of 1,700 men, women and children in Toledo's Alcazar was postponed at the last minute today, the mayor of the city told the Associated Press, to give the besieged fascists one more chance to surrender. The postponement also was ordered to put finishing touches to the mining of the shell-battered citadel, the mayor asserted. However, he said the Alcazar is likely to be blown up “soon.” Socialist laborer soldiers, working in cramped quarters in tunnels under the Alcazar, completed laying the charges of TNT yesterday. Each charge consists of more than a ton of the high explosive. The mines were placed on either side of the southwest tower of the ancient fortress palace under the Puerta de Carros, “carriage gate,” and under the Puerta Capuchinos, “gate of the Capucines.” Electric cables connected
