London, (®)—King Edward and a small party of friends were the guests of Mrs. Wallis Simpson at No. 16 Cumberland Terrace last evening, it was learned today while the king was at Portland inspecting units of the home fleet. While a typical November-in-London rain beat down on the deserted street and its lone bobby on guard, the American divorcee entertained the monarch and his intimates until it was time to depart for Portland, after midnight. The king went to “No. 16” after attending Armistice Day services in Albert Hall.

Rome, Nov. 13 (Friday) (/P)—Informed Italian sources today stated they saw the possibility of a diplomatic rupture between Italy and Russia on the heels of a bitter denunciation of Russia by Signor Dino Grandi, last night before the international non-intervention committee in London. These sources declared Grandi’s attack on Russia last night served only to accentuate the growing bitterness between Rome and Moscow. They pointed out that an Italian ambassador for the first time had accused the Moscow government and Josef Stalin directly, rather than Communism or Bolshevism, of intervention in the Spanish civil war.

LONDON—The privately circulated and mimeographed magazine, The Week, concludes there is little possibility of King Edward either abdicating or marrying Mrs. Wallis Simpson, a copy of the magazine revealed Thursday. High Betting Rates Explained Under the heading “The King and the Rumors,” the magazine deals at length with high rates for insurance that Edward’s coronation will take place next spring as scheduled and asserts: “The idea behind the rate is that the king will insist on marrying Mrs. Simpson and that the opposition of the bishops (England’s two archbishops) to such nonconformity and of the Conservative party generally will force him from the throne.” There has been, the magazine said, conflict in court circles between the “old guard” which resents the king’s friendship with his American friend and “the newer type of courtier” who apparently thinks Mrs. Simpson is “ace high.” “I

LONDON, Nov. 12.—(4)—The International “Hands Off Spain” Committee tonight acquitted Russia of three Italian charges she had aided the Madrid government after a bitter denunciation of Russia by Signor Dino Grandi, Italian ambassador to London. The committee decided three of the allegations by Italy against Russia had not been substantiated and adjourned to await receipt of further information from Russia regarding a fourth Italian allegation.

LONDON, Nov. 13.—Two big moments in King Edward's day today. He makes the first call between 10 a. m. and noon, the second in for nearly half an hour. The post-dinner call is not made when the king dines with Mrs. Simpson, which is several times a week, but there are odd-times calls during the day. Friends of the king, who favor strongly his friendship with Mrs. Simpson, say that he laughs heartily during the conversations at Mrs. Simpson’s witty talk, and seems to forget the strain and pressure which attaches to the official side of his life.

LONDON—(UP)—Diplomatic relations between Italy and Soviet Russia were strained toward the breaking point today following a furious denunciation of each other's activities in the Spanish Civil War. The recriminations were expressed in violent remarks made before a session of the non-intervention committee. They were the most bare-worded declarations made before an international diplomatic gathering in recent years. The Soviet envoy, Ivan Maiski, accused Premier Benito Mussolini of being a satellite of Adolf Hitler. He declared that Italy's foreign policy was now subservient to that of Germany. The Italian Ambassador, Dino Grandi, thundered a 40-minute speech. He recited a list of alleged atrocities committed by the Spanish Loyalists. Grandi referred sarcastically to the withdrawal of the Spanish Government from Madrid to Valencia last week, adding: 'Thus ends amidst fire and blood the gre

London, Nov. 13.--(™—Out of a bitter clash between Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin and Winston Churchill, assurances appeared today that Great Britain would speed up its rearmament in order to match strides with rapidly rearming Europe. Baldwin and Churchill, wartime minister of munitions and first lord of the admiralty, crossed oratorical swords in the House of Commons last night, Churchill defending and Baldwin defending the government's policy. Observers, however, noted their accord on the urgency of British rearmament and believed the duel had cleared the air of bitter inter-party strife. Churchill charged Britain never had been more imperiled "since the U-boat campaign was crushed." He told the House of Commons it should demand a parliamentary inquiry into what he described as neglect of the national defense. Baldwin retorted in a sensational speech in which he told the House he had

1936-11-26.text: London, Nov. 25. (P)—Col. Charles A. Lindbergh landed at 4 p.m. yesterday at the Royal Air Force airdrome at Sealand, near Chester, and drove away without a word, it was established tonight. That settled definitely a day and a night of near-alarm resulting from absence of any report of the colonel’s arrival following a three-hour flight from Ireland. He was presumed Lindbergh had gone to his home, “Sevenoaks,” in Kent. Even before his whereabouts were established, anxiety had been eased by the terse assurance, “the colonel is quite safe,” from a woman at the flier’s country house. “Reports that he is missing are silly,” she said over the telephone. “He is quite all right.” Then she hung up, refusing further information. Telephone exchanges at Dublin and Belfast were flooded with inquiries throughout the night. Attendants at airports around London also were deluged with queries. They coul

ABOARD U. S. S. CHESTER, At Sea, Nov. 25. (U.P)—President Roosevelt looked forward today to a big Thanksgiving dinner at sea working on his Rio De Janeiro speech aboard the U. S. S. Indianapolis steaming steadily south, Turkey dinner, with cranberry sauce and mince pie will be the menu for the President and members of his party while speeding at 25 knots under summer skies on a calm sea off the Brazilian coast. The chief executive will deliver his address at the Brazilian capital before a joint session of the Brazilian Congress, according to the present program, when he reaches port there Friday. It will be his first “good neighbor” appearance in South America, and the President is looking forward to greeting the Brazilian republic in a spirit of goodwill which he is spreading on his voyage below the equator. The President kept abreast of domestic and international developments as the cr

By The Associated Press LONDON, Nov. 24.—Great Britain, backing up her age-long right to sail the seas unhindered, tonight sent submarines to Spain with a destroyer flotilla ready to sail Thursday. The admiralty announced the depot ship Cyclops and eight submarines already were en route from Malta to the war-torn Spanish peninsula to add force to verbal warnings Britain would tolerate no interference with her shipping.

Chester, England, Nov. 25— Col. Charles A. Lindbergh was the unexpected guest tonight of officers on duty at the Royal Airforce airdrome at Sealand. The officers rushed out to question a strange pilot who made a perfect landing in dense fog on the war office property. To their amazement the famous American flier stepped from the plane. Greatest secrecy was maintained at Sealand, while the British officers entertained their distinguished visitor. News of Lindbergh’s whereabouts was not made known for nearly 24 hours after a night and day of near-alarm resulting from absence of any report of the colonel. “He’s been a welcome visitor,” said Captain Norton, “He knows all about the game.”

| London, Nov. 26. (4)- Newspaper (editorials on relations between the cabinet and King Edward, apparently aimed at the undercover dispute over Mrs. Wallis Simpson, were interpreted Thursday by the publication “The Week” as a “threat to the position of the monarchy.” The weekly said two editorials in the Times and one in the Daily Telegraph constituted “the first occasion on which the muttered, whispered Hapeate of ‘the old guard’ as to what they would do ‘in certain eventualities’ have begun to reach the printed cane.” The Times and Telegraph editorials criticized the Daily Mail, another newspaper, for its editorial which drew a contrast between the King’s energy and the cabinet’s inaction in dealing with problems facing “depressed” areas in Wales,

Fascist warplanes again bombed and machine-gunned besieged Madrid yesterday while the Spanish ambassador in London protested to the British foreign office against alleged activities of German and Italian vessels in Spanish waters. The French cabinet voted down a communist proposal to scrap the international nonintervention committee and reaffirmed its support of that body. Machine-gun bullets from planes cut into lines of Spanish militia on the northern and western edges of the city. While the defenders of Madrid pressed every available man into the battle for possession of the University City section, 55 Americans completed preparations to leave their embassy in Madrid for Valencia before dawn Thursday.

Aboard the U. S. S. Chester at Sea, Nov. 25. — (7) — President Roosevelt, now a “shellback” by virtue of his initiation into King Neptune's court, got his first view of land today since leaving Trinidad Sunday. The cruiser Indianapolis, bearing the president to Rio de Janeiro and the Inter-American peace conference at Buenos Aires, passed close to Pernambuco and other eastern Brazilian towns with its companion ship, the cruiser Chester. The United States warships met the Argentine tanker Juvenal, the first vessel they had encountered in four days, and the Juvenal loaded a welcome from South America to the North American president.

LONDON. (UP). Walter Runciman, president of the board of trade, introduced a bill in the house of commons forbidding British ships to carry war materials to Spain from foreign ports. The bill launches the proposed neutrality program of Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden. The first reading was approved without debate and the measure is scheduled to pass along stages and go to the house of lords by next Thursday.

1936-11-25.text: LONDON, Nov. 25 (UP).—An all-day flurry over the whereabouts of Col. Charles A. Lindbergh, unreported since he left Naidonnel air port near Dublin yesterday morning, was ended late today when officials at the Sealand Royal Air Force airdrome at Chester, near Liverpool, informed the United Press that he had landed there at 4 p.m. yesterday. The duty officer at the airdrome confirmed statements previously made by Lindbergh's household that he is safe and well.

DUBLIN, Nov. 25.—(Wednesday)—(AP) — Col. Charles A. Lindbergh’s long absence, on a projected flight from Ireland to England, caused official Irish fears for his safety early today. Frank Aiken, Irish minister of defense, expressed concern for the safety of the American flier, but at the same time expressing an opinion Lindbergh might have landed at an English airport. Lindbergh was en route from Ireland to his country residence in England. An earlier report he had landed at Newtownards in northern Ireland could not be confirmed. Aiken said Lindbergh took off from Dublin this afternoon. The flier told him, Aiken said, he was planning to go straight to Croydon airdrome outside London but that he had enough gasoline to take him farther if necessary. Lindbergh had been receiving weather reports, Aiken said, before he started. (A check of airdromes in the London vicinity disclosed Lindbergh h

«Copyright, 1836, by United Press) LONDON, Nov. 25.—A British depot ship, vanguard of a fleet, steamed across the Mediterranean toward Spain today and 10 more warships were ready to follow it from Malta. All shore leaves at Malta were cancelled. In Berlin, it was announced that Germany and Japan had signed an agreement expressing their mutual opposition to Communism and inviting other nations to join them in opposing it. Officially, the British fleet is going to Spain to replace ships already there and the short leave at Malta was cancelled because of a big storm raging in the area. Actually, the move was regarded here as a notification to the Spanish Nationalists that Great Britain does not intend to tolerate interference with its ships in any nationalist attack to blockade Barcelona. Officially also, the German-Japanese agreement is merely an expression of their detestation of Bolshevi

Aboard U. S. S. Chester, at Sea, Nov. 25, (#)—Still more than a thousand miles from Rio De Janeiro, two naval cruisers carrying President Roosevelt's party to Buenos Aires turned southwest off Pernambuco today as the President busied himself with the rough draft of his address before the Inter-American peace conference. King Neptune's fun-fest, the initiation of passengers who never had crossed the equator, was concluded in elaborate mock trials yesterday. The President participated and received a diploma attesting him as a “Shellback.”

Eight British submarines sailed from Malta to Spain last Tuesday as the international situation of the Spanish civil war became increasingly acute. All naval leaves at Valetta, Malta, were cancelled. Socialist militia in Madrid seized and sealed the Italian and German embassies, arresting several political refugees found in the building which formerly housed Reich diplomatic representatives. By inference, a communique issued by Indalecio Prieto, minister of air and navy, charged that German submarines torpedoed the Spanish cruiser Miguel de Cervantes in Cartagena harbor Sunday. Heightened anxiety over danger to foreigners in Madrid caused the decision to close the U. S. embassy Thursday. With a British destroyer flotilla ready to steam out of Malta Thursday to replace vessels already in Spanish ports, France joined Great Britain in declaring she would not tolerate interference with her s

BERLIN, Nov. 25. (UP)—Germany and Japan, symbols of military might in Europe and far off Asia, banded today in a fight against Communism, a fight which is regarded as a warning to Soviet Russia. It was announced that Joachim von Ribbentrop, ambassador to Great Britain, and Kintomo, Viscount Mushakoje, Japanese ambassador to Germany, signed the agreement at noon in behalf of Emperor Hirohito and Fuehrer Adolf Hitler. As announced officially the agreement is directed against the Third or Communist International, the supreme Communist body with branches all over the world, whose headquarters are in Moscow. It does not mention Russia and Russia denies that the International is connected with the Russian government. Abroad it was reported despite denials that the agreement contains secret clauses providing for diplomatic and military cooperation. As it is, the agreement as announced, with thr
| DUBLIN —(U.P)— W. T. Cosgrave, Opposition leader in the Free State Parliament, introduced a motion today proposing that the Free State recognize the Spanish nationalist government.

LONDON, Nov. 24 (UP),--Persons usually well-informed on court matters believed today the friendship between King Edward and Mrs. Wallis Simpson had reached its peak. They predicted there would soon be some plain intimation that the king and Mrs. Simpson did not intend to marry. They also predicted there might be some plain sign that the friendship itself was to be more formal. The informants said a realization that the kingdom and the empire faced a most difficult period and that the king himself was closely, inescapably bound to his duties, entered into an altered situation.

1936-07-25.text: London —(?)— Sir Henry Wellcome, 83, famous British scientist and explorer, died Saturday following an operation. Sir Henry's scientific achievements ranged from the establishment of physiological achievements to pioneering in the field of archaeological survey through the use of airplanes. He won the Royal Humane Society life saving medal in 1885 and as late as 1927 founded the Lady Stanley maternity hospital in Uganda, Cen-

‘London, July 24—(4)—His eyes feverishly bright, George Andrew McMahon, the man who dared approach King Edward with a revolver in his hand, sat through a rendition of his grievances against the government today. At the close of his preliminary hearing in the grimy Bow Street police station courtroom, he was remanded to jail for a week on the plea of his counsel that the prisoner wished to testify himself and to call witnesses. The bald McMahon protested fiercely to his lawyer at one point in the court session while his face crimsoned. Charges Persecution, He was charged specifically with producing a weapon “with intent to alarm his majesty” at the king's military parade eight days ago. Lunging forward in the prisoner’s dock, he climaxed the hearing with his demand, transmitted through counsel, Alfred Kerstein, that he be allowed to tell his own story of what he termed a three-year persec

PARIS, July 25 (#)—American British and French vessels, cooperating today in the evacuation of refugees from Spain, brought more than 3,000 foreigners, including United States citizens, from the scene of civil war. The American export liner Exeter steamed to Marseille bearing 160 American refugees and other nationals from Barcelona, while the U. S. Oklahoma arrived at Bilbao and the coast guard cutter Cayuga stood by at San Sebastian. The French liners Djénne and Chella have already taken more than 2,000 foreigners from Barcelona to Marseille. British and French warships carried approximately 1,200 persons from San Sebastian to nearby French ports.

LONDON, July 25—(#)—King Edward VIII prepared today to embark for France on the British Admiralty yacht Enchantress to honor Canada’s war dead at Vimy Ridge. Dedication Sunday of the Canadian National war memorial, in the heart of old French battlefields will mark the first time his majesty has left his country since ascending the throne. Present plans call for his return to London Sunday night either on the Enchantress or, if weather permits, in his own private plane.

CANNES, France, July 25 (U.P)——Cannes workers have been striking like most other Frenchmen in the last few weeks but they are not going to let revolutionary ideas interfere with hospitality to a visiting monarch. Out of deference to King Edward VIII of England, who is to begin a vacation here this week-end, gardeners at an establishment across the road from the King’s leased villa hauled down their red flag yesterday and called in their pickets. STORK Kiss PORTLAND, Ore., July 25 (UP)—An early morning burglar stole one thing before he was frightened away, Mrs. Charles H. Kenneth reported to police. That theft was a kiss.

Malvern, England, July 28—George Bernard Shaw, who in his ‘Back to Methuselah’ spake of extreme age, chuckled Saturday over the fact he will be 80 years old Sunday. Plans? he repeated. "A man of 86 has a past but no future. I cannot contemplate anything." And then he belled his own words. "I daresay I shall go on writing as long as I can remember how to write. Those you know, in the end, forgot how to write. He spent his mornings trying to learn how again like a child."

International copyright and all other rights reserved} PARIS may not equal London’s recent rainfall of 35,000,000 tons of water in one day, spread over 450,000 acres but for persistent, consistent and variegated rainfall, Paris has easily the world’s championship. Rain in France is like the war scare all over Europe, some days worse than others, but it rains every day. And Paris having more kinds of roofs than any other city in the world has more kinds of rain sounds. There is one dull sound on the roofs made of lead, other sounds for roofs of stone, cement, asphalt, slate, tin, gravel; flat roofs, slanting roofs, peak roofs, the mansard roofs that disguise the real height of buildings. In Chicago rain is rain, in Paris it is an orchestra. There are probably forty different rain sounds on the roof of Notre Dame Cathedral alone. However,

Berlin, July 25—(#)—Franz von Papen, Germany’s minister to Austria, was made today an ambassador extraordinary on special mission, by Chancellor Adolf Hitler. The promotion was believed in political circles to qualify him for appointment at the earliest moment to an ambassadorial post in London or Rome. Der Fuehrer granted the promotion in recognition of Von Papen’s two years of endeavor culminated by an accord between the Reich and Austria. The new ambassador, however, will continue as head of the German mission in Vienna which remains a legation, not raised to the rank of embassy.

1936-07-07.text: London, July 6 (?)—A barrage of questions in Commons and Whitehall's grave view of the Danzig situation gave evidence tonight of Britain's growing concern over Germany. Anthony Eden, the Foreign Secretary, announced abruptly to Parliament he was through asking Reichsfuhrer Adolf Hitler for an answer to the British Locarno questionnaire. The members cheered him as he declared: “I am not going to ask for an answer any more.” Questioners who wanted to know about Danzig drew little from Eden except a reference to what was said at the League of Nations Council session, but informed sources did not disguise their anxiety over the outburst at Geneva by Dr. Arthur Karl Greiser, Nazi president of the Free City’s Senate.

LONDON, July 7 (UP) — An army of salesmen scurried to Italy today and Europe hastened headlong toward a new epoch of military alliances. These were the first results of the League of Nations abandonment of Ethiopia as manifested in the decision to lift anti-Italian economic sanctions, effective July 15. Diplomatic quarters believed that when the League is reformed by the September assembly it will be transformed into a screen for new military alliances. They feared that new regional pacts, negotiated ostensibly to supplement the League covenant, would in practice replace it. Seek to Regain Markets Commercial circles were as interested as the diplomats in the League assembly's death blow at sanctions. Salesmen heading for Italy were engaged in a mad scramble for orders. The business houses of 18 European sanctionist nations launched a fight for lost markets in efforts to recoup combined l

DERBY, Eng., July 7 (--Former Prime Minister David Lloyd George says the present British government is “completely devoid” of nerve, courage, resolution and vision. The fiery Welshman told an election campaign meeting last night: “The battle for peace has been lost through feebleness and poltroonery on the part of the greatest nation in the world, through her leaders. “Who ratted?” he asked, and when a voice from the audience replied “Simon” (Sir John Simon, home secretary) retorted: “Yes, well, that’s the kind of an animal he is.” Lloyd George referred to “another great minister” and then declared abruptly: “They bolted. Who ratted? Rats, I am told, desert a sinking ship. These are the rats that scuttle the ship.” “In Europe, this government is not thought much of,” he continued. “In America, they have lost confidence in us,”

CHARLOTTESVILLE, Va. — America's traditional policy of freedom of the seas will be the danger point in the event of another general European war, P. H. W. Almy, British banker, told the University of Virginia Institute of Public Affairs today. It was freedom of the seas that drew the United States into the World War and not a desire to preserve democracy, Almy said.

TOKIO, July (P) — Seventeen leaders of Japan’s bloody coup were condemned to death today by a high military court. There is no appeal. Hence the 17, two of them captains in the Emperor’s proud army, probably will be shot within a matter of days. The court also handed down sentences of life for five conspirators and ordered prison terms from 18 months to 15 years for 44 non-commissioned officers and eight civilians.

COPENHAGEN, July 7, (®)—The approaching marriage of Mrs. Ruth Bryan Owen, United States minister to Denmark, to a tall, fair-haired captain of King Christian’s bodyguard was announced today by the captain's mother. The prospective groom is Capt. Boerge Rohde, 42 years old and bearing the title of “Kammerjunker”—honorary gentleman groom to the king. He was reported on his way to the United States, and it was said he would join Mrs. Owen there within the next few days. It was understood the wedding would be July 10 in the Long Island home of Mrs. Owen's daughter, Mrs. Robert Lehman. (Mrs. Owen's secretary, in New York, said the minister “had no comment to make” but friends of the family said the report of the engagement was correct). Mrs. Owen reached the United States last Sunday on a 60-days’ leave, during which she will take part in the election campaign on behalf of President Roosevelt

DANZIG, July 7.—U.P)—Danzig announced officially today its severance of relations with the League of Nations, which has been nominal guardian of the free city after it was separated from Germany at the end of the World War.

Tokyo, July 7 — Seventeen leaders of Japan's military rebellion last February — probably will die before a firing squad "within five days", army authorities said today. The execution is being planned for dawn, the officials declared, but announcement of the shootings will be delayed several hours. A high military court handed down the death sentences yesterday in a judgment more than 10,000 words long after an exhaustive investigation of the uprising, which brought death to three of Japan's elder statesmen. Five conspirators were given life imprisonment, and 44 non-commissioned officers and eight civilians were ordered sent to prison for from 18 months to 15 years. The court suspended sentences of 27 lesser offenders. Early indications showed widespread public approval of the court martial’s drastic action. A communique, however, issued by the army recognized "some degree of righteousnes

1936-02-13.text: (Copyright, 1936, by The Associated Press) — London, March 12 (#)—France demanded that "the whole Rhineland be absolutely evacuated" of all troops after four former World War allies, meeting in one of the gravest conferences since 1914, indicted the Nazi government as a violator of the Locarno and Versailles treaties. The unyielding French position was proclaimed in face of Adolf Hitler's refusal of a British plea that he draw all but a few of the troops. "France will not negotiate with Germany as long as the status quo ante is not restored," a French spokesman declared. He said now that Great Britain, Italy, Belgium and France found Germany guilty of treaty violation, it is up to the League Council to discuss punishments and steps to be taken. He voiced the demand even as Hitler thundered from a rostrum at Karlsruhe, in the remilitarized area: "I assure you nothing, absolutely nothing,

LONDON, Feb. 13.—At least 133 persons have been killed by icy storms that in the past three days have swept Europe and Asia Minor. The toll of death may be higher when present disrupted communications are restored to normal conditions and more detailed reports are received of the ravages of the elements. List of Fatalities The list of fatalities includes: Sixty-eight in Bulgaria. Twenty-five in Macedonia. Twelve in Anatolia and Thrace, all these 12 having resulted from freezing. Ten drowned in the Gulf of Sal- Eighteen drowned in the Adriatic Sea. The snow storm which lashed Thrace and Anatolia is the most severe in 25 years. Snowdrifts nine feet high are reported in Thrace. Report Many Missing Besides the fatalities listed in many parts of Europe and Asia Minor many persons are reported missing. Three hundred and fifty small ships have been wrecked in various waters.

LONDON, Feb. 13.—More than 160 persons were known dead today, and much higher casualty figures were indicated, in snow, rain and wind storms which affected the British Isles and all Europe. The death toll included Britain, 28; Italy and the Adriatic Sea, 26; Greece, 75; Bulgaria, 36; France, nine and Spain seven. Deaths included people frozen, killed in railway accidents and washed overboard from all ships in storms at sea. Rain froze rapidly, to cause railway accidents and injuries to pedestrians. One hundred and twenty persons were injured in Paris by slipping on rapidly freezing streets after a rain storm.

LONDON, Feb. 13.—A secret decree providing for expulsion of all Jews from Germany as rapidly as possible has been prepared by Nazi chieftains for Adolf Hitler's signature, the Daily Herald, organ of the labor party, said today. The statement was not confirmed elsewhere. The alleged decree, the Daily Herald said, provided for confiscation of property of Jews expelled. Hitler, the Daily Herald said, was hesitating whether to sign the decree because of considerable opposition, particularly from Dr. Hjalmar Schacht, minister of economics and in effect economic and banking dictator. Others who opposed signature, the newspaper said, urged that Hitler await the completion of the Olympic games.

(Associated Press) New York, Feb. 13—New strike threats from hotel employees and building service workers arose suddenly after garment workers had reached a tentative peace with dress manufacturers. The day’s developments are: first, a strike of 11,000 workers in 210 city hotels in 48 states is threatened unless the Hotel Association replies to union demands; second, leaders of the building service workers’ union said a strike in the mid-town garment district was inevitable unless building operators sign a new agreement; third, officials of the dressmakers’ union and the five manufacturers’ associations reached an agreement after an all-night conference, thus averting a strike of 105,000 workers in the vast metropolitan dressmaking industry. The hotel workers demand adjustment of wages and hours.

- KARLSRUHE, Germany, March 12 —(P)—Adolf Hitler, wildly cheered by an election meeting of 60,000 persons, proclaimed tonight that “nothing will move us to renounce” Nazi sovereignty in the Rhineland, but assured France, Czechoslovakia and Poland that armed German forces will not move against them. In a campaign speech loaded with appeals for “common sense statesmanship” he criticized sharply what he called Soviet interference with the tranquility of other nations. The Reichsführer reaffirmed his overtures for a new European peace pact characterizing his offer last week as the “most magnanimous ever made anywhere.” His denunciation of Russia was based on a double criticism of Soviet policy extending even to what he declared was an “international movement to prevent the nations from coming to the Olympics.” His plea for peace, historically founded on relationships between Poland and Germa

TOKYO, Feb. 13. (Thursday) (AP) — Japanese general headquarters at Hsinking, Manchoukuo, announced today that one Japanese officer and seven Japanese soldiers were killed in the bloodiest battle of the year-long Russo-Japanese friction on the border between Manchoukuo and Outer Mongolia. The Domei (Japanese) news agency said the general headquarters announcement stated that the Mongols apparently suffered many casualties in the conflict Wednesday, in which a Japanese-Manchoukuoan column recaptured the town of Oalhudka, southwest of Lake Bor. The Outer Mongolians were said to number at least 200 and to have been armed with two cannon and many machine guns. It was reported they retreated into Mongolian territory after several hours of heavy fighting at Olahudka, which is claimed by both Manchoukuo and Outer Mongolia. The official communique said one Japanese officer and three Japanese sold

PARIS, Feb. 13.—(—President Lebrun issued a decree today disbanding all militant royalist organizations in France. The president's drastic action followed an emergency session of the cabinet called by Premier Albert Sarraut. The governmental action came hard on the heels of royalist-socialist disturbances which began early in the day with a group of young "king's henchmen" beating up Deputy Leon Blum, socialist party leader. Socialists immediately retaliated with threats against the Sarraut government. Premier Sarraut addressed the chamber of deputies in the midst of pandemonium. The day's disturbances started with a group of the king's henchmen returning from the funeral of the royalist historian Jacques Bainville.

1936-03-03.text: Copyright, 1936, by Associated Press LONDON, March 3—Great Britain’s government announced today a vast immediate expansion of its army, navy and air forces and industrial mobilization for instant readiness in case of war. A White Paper, or government report, said the rearmament and increased national defenses were made necessary by complications of the international situation, combined with a “deplorable and undeniable worldwide expansion of armament.”

Geneva, March 5 —(U. F.)— The League of Nations committee of thirteen today adopted a resolution appealing to Italy and Ethiopia to make a "peace agreement within the framework of the League." The resolution was offered by Great Britain and France, coupled with an appeal to warring nations to begin negotiations at once with a view to ceasing hostilities. The committee, comprised of all members of the League council except Italy, then voted to reconvene on March 10. Italy and Ethiopia were thus given one week to consider the appeal for peace. If Italy rejects the League's general committee of eighteen on penalties, it is expected to proceed promptly to impose an embargo on shipments of oil to Italy. The Franco-British resolution was adopted at the session which lasted only fifteen minutes. Although an appeal was regarded as the League’s last alternative to the imposition of an oil embargo

LONDON, March 3. UP)—A government plan to organize industry for a lightning turnover from commercial to war production in event of an emergency was announced today as part of a gigantic defense program. It was disclosed that preliminary steps leading to the emergency preparation of industry already have been taken. The plan was announced in an official white paper, promised by the government to explain to the country the necessity for its great defense program, which has been estimated to call for a total of 300,000,000 pounds ($1,500,000,000). In addition to the industrial organization plan, the white paper gave the first specific rearmament program, calling for: Two new battleships during 1937. Continuation of modernization of existing battleships. Five new cruisers during 1936, with the object of bringing the total cruiser strength to 70. Rapid replacement of destroyers and submarines

| LONDON, Mar. 3—(#)—A reliable source said today that France had agreed to the United States’ demand for a maximum limit of 35,000-ton battleships, agreeing to that figure until 1940. It removes one of the greatest obstacles to the naval conference's conclusion. Observers see a treaty between the United States, Britain and France in sight. Simultaneously, Britain announced a big British ship-building and replacement program beginning in 1937. Plans were projected for the expansion of the army, navy and air forces and industrial mobilization in case of war. It was asserted that the United States, Germany, Belgium, France, Italy and Russia had already embarked on a similar program.

London, March 3 (UP)—Almost the final technical obstacle to the initialing of a naval treaty among Britain, United States and France was cleared away today when France accepted a limit of 35,000 tons and 14 inch guns for battleships. The treaty permits the building of an unlimited number of battleships until the end of 1940.

WASHINGTON, March 3—(?)— Grist from a quickening political mill today included a Democratic declaration that an upturn in industry results from New Deal policies and a Republican assertion that poverty problems are still here, as it was in 1933. In industrial New England, chairman James A. Farley, of the Democratic national committee, opened a drive for delegates pledged to President Roosevelt at the Philadelphia convention in June. Representative Mott (R), Ore., on the other hand, said in a broadcast under the auspices of the Republican congressional committee, that industrial recovery and farm solvency are “just where they were when the New Deal came into power.” He attacked governmental advisors whom he termed “a weird crowd of professors and sub-professors.” Mott assailed the new farm program as “transparently unconstitutional,” adding that “its only real purpose is to keep the farm

LONDON, March 3.—Edgar Leaverton, 33, serving a life term in the London prison farm on a murder conviction in Highland County, escaped yesterday while delivering mail in the state office building at Columbus. Leaverton, a trusty for three years, drove to Columbus daily to deliver mail and milk. Authorities believed he may have escaped in a state highway department car, stolen from near the state office building. Before leaving here, Leaverton had borrowed a watch from Ben Rudner, serving a life term for the murder of Don Mellett, Canton editor.

| Manchester, Eng., March 3 (Fi Dr. Buck Ruxton glowered today as a crown prosecutor asked whether there had been any intimacy between a witness and Mrs. Ruxton, the wife whom Ruxton is accused of murdering in the “Devil's Beef-Tub” case. Robert James Edmondson, an assistant solicitor in the Lancaster town clerk's office, was placed in the stand before a courtroom packed with spectators who had fought to gain admission to the most notorious trial of recent years. The prosecutor asked: “Was there the slightest atom of any description between you and Mrs. Ruxton?” Ruxton, alleged by the crown to have killed his wife and a nurse maid, dismembered their bodies, and thrown them into the Devil's Beef-Tub ravine, watched the witness narrowly. “No,” answered Edmondson. “Most certainly not.” Chief Constable Thompson of the town of Clitheroe and former inspector of Lancaster, where the Ruxtons liv

1936-02-14.text: LONDON—Britain wins delay in action against Germany on eve of league council session, hoping Hitler will come through with conciliatory gesture; France demands sanctions against Reich but Italy opposes them; Russia backs Paris. PARIS—Usually reliable source says German financial emissary is in capital to warn sanctions would mean financial collapse of Reich and heavy losses to French investors, new suggestions sent London delegation. BERLIN—Hitler suddenly cancels speaking tour, returns to capital for conference; German papers warn sanctions would hurt others as well as Reich.

LONDON, Feb. 14. — (#) — A heightened blizzard raged across Turkey today killing 78 persons and raising the death toll of storms in Europe and Asia Minor to approximately 275. From Istanbul, it was reported that the cold storm which has been underway there three days has frozen 48 persons to death, drowned 22, and killed 8 in accidents. The property damage in Turkey was estimated at no less than $2,000,000.

(Associated Press Leased Wire) | LONDON, Feb. 14.— Fresh French efforts to link the European political situation with the international naval conference resulted, today in a new deadlock among the delegates of the United States, Great Britain, France and Italy. Charles Corbin, the French ambassador to London, decided to go to Paris to place the situation before the French cabinet and to report back Monday or Tuesday at a meeting of the four delegations. British sources said there was still hope that the difficulty could be adjusted. At a meeting with the British this morning, the French insisted again that it was important that European political questions affecting Great Britain, Germany and France be included in the discussion and settled as part of the conference agreements. The questions include Franco-British co-operation, the security situation, the Rhineland and German rearmament

LONDON, Feb. 14, — Mystery surrounding a report that a German seaplane crashed with 30 persons in the Azores islands was believed dissipated today with news that a German plane with a crew of four arrived at Ponta Del Gada, in the Azores, without incident yesterday. The plane in question left Las Palmas, Canary islands, yesterday morning, according to dispatches, and arrived at Ponta Del Gada in the afternoon. The dispatch reporting the loss of a German plane with 30 persons was not carried by the United Press.

LONDON, Feb. 14 (#)—The Reuters (British) News Agency reported today that the German airliner Samum, on a trial flight from Las Palmas, Canary Islands, to the Azores Island had arrived there safely at 2:30 P.M. (9:30 A.M. E.S.T.) yesterday. Earlier reports from Tenerife, Canary Islands, said a German seaplane carrying 30 passengers was reported to have fallen near Ponta Delgada, in the Azores.

[COPYRIGHT 1936 BY ASSOCIATED PRESS] Tokyo—The Manchoukuoan government took a most grave view of the latest border clash with Soviet-influenced Outer Mongolia, a Domei (Japanese) news agency said today, especially since the enemy allegedly used bombing planes. The dispatch from Hsinking, capital of the Japanese-advised state of Manchoukuo, quoting a spokesman for the Manchoukuoan foreign office, said the encounter yesterday at Olahodka was the most serious thus far of the last year’s frontier incidents. Military reports from the border confirmed reports that planes attempted to bomb the Japanese-Manchoukuoan column involved, but failed to inflict casualties, the dispatch said. Accounts differed as to whether two or three planes took part in the engagement, and as to whether they were Russian or Outer Mongolian. War Minister Yoshiyuki Kawashima proclaimed Japanese concern over a vast alle

SEEPS: Hers Ee See Press} Paris (?) —The outlawing of France’s royalist brigade, The King’s Henchmen, provoked short-lived disorders and aroused apprehension today over possible consequences of the ban, virtually denied by the most militant royalists. Premier Albert Sarraut, whose decree dissolving all militant royalist organizations in France was signed by President Albert Lebrun and promulgated today, took command of the situation in his capacity as minister of the interior. Police searched the headquarters of the Action Francaise—the royalist party, the Marching Wing of which is known as The King’s Henchmen—but Sarraut indicated he was reluctant to order the arrest of the leaders, for fear of rekindling the flames of rioting which flared two years ago. The premier was confronted at the same time by socialist demands for stern action against royalist leaders because of an at- fContinue

(Copyright, 1936, United Press.) Tokyo, Feb. 14 (UP) — Japanese and Manchukuoan air forces were reported to be prepared for instant action today, and military chiefs in consultation, as the result of the latest of a series of clashes on the Mongolian frontier. The clash occurred Wednesday. Unofficial reports say seven Japanese-Manchukuoans and seven Mongolians were wounded. Though the clash was only one of many in past months on the frontiers of Mongolia and Russia, there were indications in Japanese reports that this incident may lead to strengthening of the Japanese-Manchukuoan frontier forces. On the Japanese side there are suspicions that Soviet Russia is involved in the clashes, even on the outer Mongolian frontier; on the Russian side, Japan is suspected. It was indicated that this clash was regarded more seriously than previous ones, perhaps because it may be believed that the fig

1936-01-21.text: - London—(/)—The funeral of King George V will be Tuesday, Jan. 28 in St. George’s chapel of Windsor Castle. The body will lie in state in Westminster Hall from Thursday until the time of the funeral. At the present time it is in Sandringham, the place of death. A full state procession will accompany George’s body from Westminster Hall to Paddington station, from where the body will be taken to Windsor.

| Copyright by Associated Press | Sandringham, Eng., Jan. 21, (P)— Great Britain’s Royal family mourned the death of the 70-year-old King George V at private services in Sandringham's little church today while the new monarch Edward VIII flew to London for accession ceremonies. The beloved old sovereign died as he had always wished in the quiet and peace of his Norfolk country estate last night with his family at his bedside. An official announcement said that the Queen Mother Mary was bearing up under her grief remarkably. With the vast empire and virtually the world sharing their sorrow the Princess Royal, the only daughter of King George and Queen Mary and other members of the Royal household went to St. Mary of Magdalene’s church this morning for Holy communion services. The service was conducted by the Archbishop of Canterbury, who only a few hours before had given the last blessing

(Pictures and additional information concerning the death of King George V will be found on Pages A, B, C, D and 2.) LONDON, Jan. 21.—(U.P)—His face bearing the marks of grief for his dead father, Edward Albert, Prince of Wales, formally was proclaimed King Edward VIII today by the Privy Council. The age-old ceremony was held 16 hours after King George V died. The new King is ruler of one-fourth of the world, King of Great Britain and Ireland and of the Dominions Beyond the Seas, and Emperor of India.

Washington, Jan. 20 - President Roosevelt tonight sent to the new monarch of England a message expressing deep sorrow at the death of King George V. At the same time the President sent messages of condolence to Queen Mary and to the Governors General of Australia, Dominion of Canada, Irish Free State, New Zealand and the Union of South Africa. Secretary Hull simultaneously dispatched messages of sympathy to the Prime Ministers of Great Britain and the dominions. Tomorrow Hull will pay courtesy calls in person at the British embassy, and dominion legations to express sympathy on behalf of the President, the government and the people of the United States. Cablegrams Sent In his cablegram addressed to "His Majesty the King, Sandringham Palace, Norfolk, England," President Roosevelt said: "It is with deep sorrow that I learn of the death of His Majesty. To you, your father, I send to you my

Sandringham, Eng., Jan. 20.—(AP)—Instantly upon the death of King George V, the Prince of Wales became Great Britain's first bachelor king to ascend the throne in 176 years. Wales automatically succeeded to the crown which is the sole legal symbolic link among the peoples of the British Empire. Few Remain Single Since the time of William the Conqueror there have been only two adults who remained unmarried throughout their reigns—William II, who ruled from 1087 to 1100, and Elizabeth, who was queen from 1558 to 1603. As quickly as the new reign began, ritual laid down by constitutional practice and tradition set in motion the proclaiming of the death of the old monarch and the accession of his son. News of George's death was telegraphed immediately to all members of the royal family not at Sandringham house, to ministers of the crown and to foreign courts. Bell Tolls Upon the notification

WASHINGTON, Jan. 21.—President Roosevelt led the nation today in mourning with the British empire the death of King George V of England, White House social functions were cancelled. The President dispatched messages to King Edward VIII, the new ruler of England, to Queen Mary and to governors of the British dominion. Secretary of State Cordell Hull will call on the British ambassador, Sir Ronald Linday, today, to convey regrets. The British embassy lowered its flag to half mast and entered immediate mourning, cancelling all social events. At the White House however, it was said no orders had been issued for half-masting the Stars and Stripes over government buildings.

(Copyright, 1936, by United Press) Sandringham, England, Jan. 21 (UP)—The heavy dark red curtains of the death chamber at Sandringham House, from whose windows King George V looked out so often over the gardens of his estate toward the village church where he worshipped, were drawn tightly closed today. Over the church—St. Mary Magdalene—fluttered the royal standard of his successor, Edward VIII. Complete Repose In the four-poster bed of the death chamber, his features in complete repose, the late king’s body lay where he passed almost imperceptibly into death at 11:55 o'clock last night. Edward VIII, his face drawn and tired, was up early to plunge into the business for which he has been groomed since his infancy—a business to which he could succeed only by the death of his father. LONDON (UP)—King Edward VIII came to his capital today by airplane to assume sovereignty over one-fourth of the people and territory of the world, to rule as King of Great Britain and Ireland and of the British dominions beyond the seas, and as Emperor of India. As he took off with his brother and presumptive heir the Duke of York and his private pilot, the late king, George V, his father, his features serene in painless death like deepening of sleep, lay at Sandringham house, where he died at 11:35 o’clock last night. First king of England ever to fly; King Edward announced to his people by this gesture that he is of a new order of monarch. He took off from Bircham Newton airdrome near Sandringham and landed at Hendon airdrome, on the outskirts of London, his face. 1936-01-16.text: LONDON, Jan. 16. (P)—Rudyard Kipling lost some of the ground he had gained toward recovery from the emergency operation he underwent Monday for a perforated stomach ulcer. ‘“Kipling’s condition is not quite so satisfactory this morning and still gives rise to great anxiety,” said a bulletin issued today,

LONDON, Jan. 16—(#)— The captain of the Discovery II, searching for the missing explorer, Lincoln Ellsworth, indicated in a report today that an airplane had been sighted in Little America and that a man had been seen on the Bay of Whales. The report did not identify the man or the airplane. The committee in charge of the Discovery IV's rescue expedition announced officially: "A message has been received by the Discovery committee from the master of the Discovery II reporting that the boat arrived safely at the Bay of Whales at 10 P. M. January 15. The message indicates one man was sighted from a plane and also a machine at Little America."

Three Italian bombing planes (Associated Press Staff Writer) destroyed a Red Cross unit headed by a British officer at Walida on the northern Ethiopian front, an official communique from Addis Ababa reported today. Seven women and seven old men died in the aerial assault Tuesday morning, the government said, and 35 others were injured. Major Gerald Burgeyne, the hospital director, was reported unhurt. Along the entire southern front more than 100,000 warriors rushed into fierce engagements in what was described at Rome as the “most important” battle of the Italo-Ethiopian war. France Troubled At Paris, radical socialists demanded resignations of party members holding cabinet positions, (Continued On Page 2),

LONDON, Jan. 15.—(?)—Japan walked out of the international naval conference tonight and 13 years of limitation of sea armaments ended. A naval race immediately loomed as a possibility, but all delegations said they wanted to avoid this costly competition, Japan's move, reminiscent of her withdrawal in 1933 from the League of Nations, was because the four other powers refused to grant her naval parity with the United States and Great Britain. Abandonment of the parley was followed by a rain of statements and explanations from all delegations. Britain, the United States, France and Italy voted to continue tomorrow in an attempt to work out a limitation agreement without Japan, The Washington and London naval treaties expire at the end of this year. Under the former Japan is held on the short end of a 4-5-3 capital ship tonnage ratio with the two Anglo-Saxon powers. Officials expressed hope

WASHINGTON, Jan. 16—(7)— J. P. Morgan expressed resentment today at what he said was an insinuation that “we were brought into war with English money.” Morgan told Senator Clark of the investigating committee: “You are saying we were bought into the war with English money and I don’t like the insinuation.” Investigators had contended that the United States, before entering the war, tried to keep American banks liquid and ready for war, but not to stop trade with the allies. An extract from the diary of Colonel Edward House, Woodrow Wilson’s advisor, showing that Secretary of State Lansing wanted Wilson to break with Germany early in January, 1917, was also introduced.

DESSYE, ETHIOPIA, Jan. 16, (P)—Italian airplanes have bombed and severely damaged an Ethiopian Red Cross caravan at Wuldia, North of Dessye, it was announced today. The caravan was commanded by a British former army major named Bur-Boyne. The announcement from the Emperor’s headquarters said two tents of the hospital unit were destroyed, that many instruments and bandages and other equipment were burned, and that half the town was razed. It was asserted three Italian planes bombed the town and hospital caravan for an hour between 10 and 11 A.M. yesterday. A heavy wind spread flames from the bombs through the town’s grass thatched houses, it was said. Sixteen Known Dead A British unit is leaving for the North today to the aid of the Red Cross caravan and townspeople. Wuldia is believed to be the town otherwise called Ualdia, 60 miles north of Dessye on the way to Makale, on the Italian fr

Copyright 1936 by U. P. LONDON, Jan. 16— American, British, French and Italian delegates constituted themselves a four-power naval limitation conference today. Japan’s delegation prepared to leave for home, after their withdrawal from the conference because other nations refused to concede them the right of full equality of strength with America and Britain. It was forecast that Sir John Monsell of Evesham, as chairman of the conference, would invite the Japanese today to leave observers at the conference. The Japanese, anticipating such an invitation, considered their course. Little Excitement There was little excitement today as delegates prepared for a four-power meeting. Nobody ever expected the conference to succeed, at the present time, in its task of replacing the Washington and London naval treaties which expire Dec. 31. Delegates remaining at the conference intend to invite Germ

(Copyright, 1936, By The Associated Press) London, Jan. 16—Japan disavowed frankly today any intention of precipitating a costly competition in fleet construction, despite its historic self-elimination from international naval affairs. While its withdrawal from the five-power naval conference was being communicated officially to the delegates and the other four powers drafted plans to continue their efforts to achieve fleet limitations, Japan’s chief delegate, Admiral Osami Nagano, announced: “Japan has no intention of engaging in a naval race, despite the absence of a limitation agreement and I sincerely hope no competition in building of warships will develop between Japan and the United States.” To Formally Announce Bolt Admiral Nagano announced his delegation’s bolt from the conference in an official statement last night, but the other delegates’ first formal information of the move

1936-01-24.text: (Copyright, 1936. by The Associated Press) LONDON, Jan. 24. — Sorrowing pilgrims filed today past the bier of the late King George V—a black catafalque, approached on purple-carpeted steps, in the ancient palace of Westminster. There, the new King Edward VIII and the bereaved royal family left their liege for four days of public homage before the final service and burial next Tuesday at Windsor. - As Big Ben boomed 8 a.m. the nation’s pilgrimage began. - When the famous clock strikes 10 p.m. Monday, authorities said, at least 1,000,000 of the dead sovereign’s subjects — men, women and children alike — will have joined in this last act of tribute. A queue more than a mile long swelled outside the hall by noon today — as the first of the ranks, four abreast, marched into the great hall and past the coffin. Seven women, among the first to enter, collapsed and were treated at a nearby hospit

LONDON, Jan. 33.—Britain's King Edward VIII stood in silent prayer today before the body of his father, George V, borne in state to a catafalque of state in medieval Westminster Hall. Haggard and apparently weary, he prayed with all of England as the body of King George was placed in its black and gold resting place amid simple ceremonies, at the end of a journey from Sandringham where the monarch died Monday night. Troops Stand Watch Tonight yeomen and household troops, their brilliant uniforms partly hidden by cloaks of black, stood watch over the body as it lay in its oaken casket, beneath the royal standard. Eight persons were all who stood there through the night. At each of the four corners of the catafalque was a guard, head bowed. Above the royal standard, at one end of the bier, the jeweled crown of empire glistened. At the other end, above the head, lay the floral crosses of Ed

(By The Associated Press) Rome, Jan. 24—Italy warned the sanctionist nations of the world today that Great Britain's action in arranging a Mediterranean security pact constituted a “danger for European peace.” A memorandum prepared for Geneva distribution to the sanctionist powers protested that Great Britain had acted outside the League Covenant in initiating the Mediterranean discussions. The move, Italy contended, was made in the face of Italian assurances that she had no desire to drag a “colonial conflict” into a European war.

Rome spoke out in bitter warning against Mediterranean security arrangements amongst “sanctionist” powers while her armies claimed aggressive successes on both northern and southern African fronts. Il Duce prepared for Geneva distribution to the sanctionist nations a warning that Great Britain’s action in arranging Mediterranean mutual assistance agreements with four other powers constituted a “danger for European peace,” and that it was outside the League of Nations covenant. Marshal Pietro Badoglio, Mussolini's high commander in Africa, reported “complete victory” for the Italians at the end of a three-day battle in the southern Tembien mountains. Down in the arid Ogaden, General Rudolfo Graziani, mounted in modern fashion on a truck, rode at the head of his “hell on wheels” column into Neghell, capital of Galla Borana, to climax a six-day drive in which the southern army plowed straig

By CLIFFORD L. DAY (Copyright 1936 by United Press) LONDON—King George's people began paying him their final tribute today. At 8 a.m. a column of mourners eight deep filed into Westminster Hall, split into two columns each four deep and passed the catafalque on which his body lay. The first to enter the great hall had waited outside since 6 o’clock last night. The body will lie in state from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. today, Saturday, Sunday and Monday and will be buried at Windsor Tuesday after a funeral service at Westminster Abbey, across from the hall, and a state funeral procession to Paddington railway station. There were 3,000 people in line when the hall was opened this morning. As the day advanced the line stretched ever farther westward along the Thames on whose bank the houses of parliament, of which Westminster Hall is part, are situated. King George’s royal standard flew at half mast

London, Jan. 24.—The majestic strains of Rudyard Kipling’s “Recessional” struck the only note of pomp and splendor when the ashes of the great poet were laid among Britain's immortal writers Thursday in the poet's corner of Westminster Abbey. A marble urn containing his ashes was lowered into a small purple-lined cavity between the graves of Charles Dickens and Thomas Hardy. Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin, a cousin of the poet, and a host of celebrities, including representatives of King Edward and the Duke of York, stood behind the weeping Mrs. Kipling during the service. Kipling was the third person in this century to be buried in the poet's corner. The others were Thomas Hardy and Sir Henry Irving.

ROME, Jan. 24. (UP)—Italy published a note today addressed to Britain and other sanctionist powers protesting that Britain's recent mutual accords for military aid in event of an attack in the Mediterranean are “a danger to European peace.” “Such initiatives and such accords of a military character in fields foreign to the Italian-Ethiopian conflict,” the note said, “are causing and already have caused an atmosphere of grave uneasiness and are therefore a danger to European peace.” The note said Britain's measures were based on a “hypothesis which Italy must consider not only arbitrary but completely non-existent.” It then cited Premier Benito Mussolini’s speech on the day of Italy's “test mobilization” in which he said Italy would do everything possible to keep a colonial conflict from assuming European proportions.

Associated Press Foreign Staff PARIS, Jan. 24.—Senator Albert Sarraut formed today a new cabinet for France—the 101st government of the Third Republic. Sarraut, who already has served as premier, is a veteran of the Radical-Socialist Party. The cabinet he has formed is a transition body to keep the government running until the parliamentary elections in April or May. In the list of nominees he submitted to President Lebrun, it was indicated that Sarraut intended to take over the ministry of the interior himself, together with the premiership.

1936-08-18.text: ALBUQUERQUE, N.M., Aug. 18. —(#)—Harry Richman, New York actor and singer, took off from Albuquerque airport in his $100,000 specially constructed transport plane at 5 a.m. (6 a.m. CST) today for New York, base of his contemplated round trip flight to London. With Dick Merrill, his pilot-radio operator and companion on the proposed trans-Atlantic "commutation" hop, Richman headed for Kansas City, where he planned to stop briefly. He said he hoped to arrive in New York by 4:30 o'clock this afternoon. Jubilant Over Flight. The musician was jubilant over yesterday’s flight from Los Angeles. The airplane averaged approximately 227 miles an hour en route here but has a top speed of 260 miles an hour.

Trip to New York and London in New $100,000 Airplane. Kansas City, Mo., Aug. 18.—(U. P.)—Harry Richman, radio and stage entertainer, and his pilot, Dick Merrill, took off in his $100,000 plane at 11:17 a.m., central time today, on a non-stop flight to New York. They plan a round trip hop from New York to London. Richman and Merrill landed here at 9:50 a.m., central time, after leaving Albuquerque at 5:15 and refueled. Richman dismissed the projected flight to London and back with the assertion "there is nothing to it. Just a little hop."

ALBUQUERQUE, NM, Aug. 18. — Harry Richman, stage and screen star, headed toward New York and London by plane at dawn today. Dick Merrill of Eastern Air Lines, Richman's pilot, lifted their plane from TWA airport here at 4:15 MST (6:15 EST). They planned to reach New York today. Richman, who plans to make a round trip from New York to London in twenty-four hours, declared last night that his huge plane is virtually “fool proof.” He claims that—should anything go wrong with the motor—40,000 ping-pong balls, stuffed in the wings, would keep the ship afloat. Richman and Merrill landed here last night from Los Angeles.

JERUSALEM, Aug. 18 U.P)—Two Jewish nurses reporting for night duty at the government hospital at Jaffa were shot dead, a dispatch said today. Three Jewish settlers were wounded when Arabs attacked Kiryat Anavim, the settlement near Jerusalem, yesterday and British troops were called. A young woman settler, doing sentry duty at a watch tower at the Ramath HaKovesh settlement was killed in an Arab attack last night. An Arab and an Armenian were killed and 12 Arabs, including some women, were wounded by shots fired at a train near Jaffa. An Arab was found stabbed to death at the city boundary between Jaffa and Tel Aviv.

| HOLLYWOOD, Aug. 18—Eddie Cantor said today he received a second cable from London stating that his £40,000 offer for Jesse Owens to turn professional “looks very favorable” to the famous negro athlete and his coach, Larry Snyder.

By The Associated Press Six-inch shells from the rebel cruiser Almirante Cervera silenced the guns of the government fortress of Guadelupe, defending the Irun-San Sebastian sector of Spain’s Bay of Biscay today. Coincidentally uncensored dispatches from Madrid reported government leaders, fearing the fall of the capital was imminent, were holding three airliners in readiness for flight. Guadelupe’s armament was regarded as still a menace to a rebel land attack which was being attempted over the hills from the direction of Enderlaza, in the face of government machine gun fire and assault by government bombing planes. The San Sebastian radio station reported a civilian on the roof of a maternity hospital had been killed by a shell from the rebel cruiser España. At Hendaye Beach, France, American Ambassador Claude G. Bowers set up a temporary embassy in a hotel after completing an evacuatio

(Copyright, 1936, Associated Press) MADRID, Aug. 17 (2) — Enraged by the massacre of 1,500 government hostages in Badajoz, 20,000 Loyalist troops tonight clashed with rebel forces in a bloody "battle of extermination" all along the rebel blockade of the Portugal border. The fierce hand-to-hand fighting was reported to be the most sanguinary of the 31-day old civil war. No quarter was being asked or given by either side, as the government hurled bayonetted legions against the stubbornly fighting rebel defenders of strategic border positions. (At Burgos, the rebel northern stronghold, Gen. Francisco Franco, leader of the Insurgents, was said to have decided to tighten the rebel lines around Madrid in hopes of cutting off the capital’s water supply and thirsting the defenders into surrender. North of Madrid the steady bombardment of Guardarrama continued into the night unabated. Continue Ad

GENERAL HEADQUARTERS, SPANISH NORTHERN ARMY, BURGOS, Aug. 18 (U.P) — Loyalist forces, fighting desperately to save the Red Madrid popular front government, have resorted to the use of gas on the northern front, General Emilio Mola, commander of northern Rebel armies, announced officially today. Mola said the Madrid forces used gas on Monday when they were attacking San Rafael, near Guarrarama, in the mountains north of Madrid. Protesting the alleged use of poison gas, Gen. Mola said: “We have important stocks of gas ourselves but have refused to violate international law.” The national defence junta of the rebels met to consider informing all foreign offices of the alleged use of the gas as a violation of international law.

1936-08-14.text: London, Aug. 14, (U.R)—Armed Loyalists are holding captive 37 Britons and one American at the Rio Tinto mines in Huelva, advices received here today said. The American is J. O. Ambler, from Montana. “The reds controlling the mines offered the staff safe conduct several days ago,” Preston continued, “but when they tried to use it yesterday, they were not allowed to leave.”

| WASHINGTON, Aug. 14—(2)—The State Department made efforts today to effect the rescue of an American reported to be among 38 members of the staff of a British mining company held as hostages by government forces in the Huelva Mines near the city of that name in Spain. The American was reported to be J. O. Ambler, whose address is listed here as San Antonio, Tex. William Phillips, acting Secretary of State, directed the American consul at Seville, Charles A. Bay, to communicate with the British consul there and “associate yourself in a most emphatic manner with representations looking to the safety and rescue of Mr. Ambler.”

LONDON, Aug. 18 — The British government today looked on the strife in Spain as a possible spark for setting off a general European war. It took under urgent consideration the question of banning the export of civil planes as an aftermath of the departure yesterday of six British aircraft, reported to be destined for belligerents in the peninsula Civil War. Both Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin and Foreign Minister Anthony Eden kept in closest touch with the foreign office. In official circles, increasing fears mounted that various European powers might alter their stance, and even reported supplies of guns and ammunition could prolong the conflict in Spain and might lead to a general European war through active participation of outside powers.

Athens, Aug. 13.--(UP)—The engagement of King Edward of Great Britain to one of King George's sisters, either Princess Katherine or Princess Irene, was forecast today by the Republican newspaper Patris. Patris said both princesses are arriving at Corfu this week to visit King George and that King Edward, now on a cruise in the Adriatic, is expected at Corfu later.

Rebel planes bomb San Sebastian in renewed attack. Four English, two Dutch airplanes believed en route to Spain; Britain fears neutrality won't work. France agrees to ban mass enlistment of volunteers to answer Italian charges she permits "moral support" of Loyalist government. Rebels march on Estepona Gibraltar; government warships attack Algeciras. Seville radio station says 40 Loyalist aviators captured, executed in battle at San Rafael Espinar. Government predicts quick armament renewal. The revolt, Loyalists proclaimed, must be stamped out "within a few hours." Outside northern Oviedo, the Socialist fighters hurled heavy artillery fire in an effort to recapture the munitions center from the Fascist rebels. Men and women fought side by side with antiquated rifles and ancient cannon to hold San Sebastian and Trun, the northern strip of greatest importance because of its command of the

Irun, Spain ()—Scores of persons opposed to the Madrid socialist government were seized and held as hostages in San Sebastian and Irun today in reply to a rebel threat to destroy the two government-held towns with sea and air bombardments. Some of the more radical government partisans said they would be killed in the event yesterday’s attack by five rebel airplanes was renewed. San Sebastian city officials already had served notice on the rebel cruiser.

MADRID, Aug. 12 (P) — Spain’s Socialist-Communist government tonight hurled troops against the northern seaboard and girded for a merciless purge of southern Fascist rebels in a great offensive to end the bloodshed of civil war throughout the nation. Loyalist troops battered again at the gates of Oviedo, close by besieged San Sebastian on the Bay of Biscay, and sought to turn back the Fascist march in that sector. Far to the south, troops reinforced with new militia, volunteers were flung against the African forces imported by Rebel Gen. Francisco Franco. Aerial bombardment of Fascist Granada, Cordoba and Seville impended. Bitterly, the government forces fought to stem the threat of the Fascist rebels who seek to substitute a military government for the Socialist regime of President Manuel Azana.
