Copenhagen.—(/P)—Col. Charles A. Lindbergh Tuesday demonstrated his mechanical heart to a large audience of fellow scientists. America’s noted flier, who turned to the laboratory in cooperation with Dr. Alexis Carrel to invent an artificial heart, appeared on a platform before the International Congress of Experimental Cytology to explain the apparatus.

MADRID — Jubilant at its resistance to rebel thrusts, the government asserted today that the end of the rebellion was approaching. The ministry of war, in an official broadcast to the country, laid claim to control of three fourths of the country, including the entire coast line, mines, foundries, textile and other important factories and wide communication lines. Loyalist forces had refrained from attacks in full force on Cordoba, Seville, Valladolid, Burgos, Avila and Segovia and other cities of the noble Spanish tradition, the ministry asserted, only in order to avoid destruction of precious architectural and artistic gems. Loyalist troops and militiamen in the Guadarrama mountains resumed activity all along the line in preparation for a general offensive to free the capital from threat of a rebel thrust. 1936-05-12.text: MANCHESTER, Eng., May 12 — (AP)—Dr. Buck Ruxton died on the gallows of the Strangeways jail today for the “devil's beef tubs” slaying of his wife and a nursemaid. Mrs. Violet Van Der Elst, militant campaigner against capital punishment, encountered a hostile reception from a large crowd outside the jail while the dark, sallow-skinned Parsee physician was hanged for England's most gruesome crime since the turn of the century. Mrs. Van Der Elst, determined to protest against the execution, drove up to the jail in a limousine accompanied by two loudspeaker vans. Police turned back the trucks, not permitting them to approach the jail. The crowd pressed about the limousine, which drove within 70 yards of the main gates, shouting, jeering and hooting.

(Copyright, 1936, The Associated Press) Rome, May 12.—(AP)—Sug- gestions that the League of Nations will be disrupted and that Great Britain and Italy may break diplomatically were made by Italian sources today. Senator Roberto Forges-Davanzati stated, following the Italian delegation’s withdrawal from Geneva, that the league would be shattered through the action of other league members. Reliable sources said that if British diplomats continued to "flourish the whip of sanctions," a diplomatic break would be inevitable. Forges-Davanzati, in an editorial in La Tribuna, wrote: “Since Italo-Ethiopian affairs continue to be managed by Mr. Eden (the British foreign secretary) who, as a good Conservative, is awaiting the collaboration of the future cabinet of the French popular-Masonic-Communist front, one can be certain Mr. Eden will carry out the policy he has carried on for about a year wit

ABOARD THE ZEPPELIN HINDENBURG, ENROUTE TO GERMANY, May 12.—The Hindenburg’s high tail, and encouraged by favorable weather reports, predicted today a 40-hour trip from Lakehurst to the English Channel. Dr. Hugo Eckener, president of the Zeppelin company, declared as the huge craft headed out over the sea on the return leg of its maiden North American voyage: "The last weather reports indicate we'll make favorable progress all the way across, reaching the channel in 40 hours." Officers and crew of the Hindenburg were visibly touched at the salute of whistles as the Zeppelin flew low over New York just after midnight. Captain Ernst Lehman said he was "overwhelmed" by the hospitality shown at Lakehurst, during the Zeppelin’s two-day stop, and in New York and Washington.

| Geneva, May 10.—A belief that sanctions would be continued despite Italy’s annexation of Ethiopia was general tonight on the eve of a crucial session of the League of Nations council. Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden and his British colleagues remained coldly non-committal. There seemed to be no crusading spirit manifested in contrast to last fall when the “war of aggression” began. Smaller states of Europe, however, were plainly alarmed over the possible repercussions of Premier Mussolini's seizure of a league state. They expressed loyalty to the league but are waiting for France and Britain to take the leadership in the present crisis and to save the league, to which they cling because they themselves have no mighty fleets or armies. ATHENS, (UP).—Amy Mollison, British flyer seeking a Cape Town-London flight record, landed her airplane from Cairo at 11:25 a.m. today (5:25 a.m. CST), refueled and proceeded at once toward Croydon, the London airport.

NEW YORK, (UP).—The shadowy bulk of the Zeppelin von Hindenburg, her lights blinking in a thin haze, slid over the New England states today and out to sea for the great circle course to Europe and the second leg of the first round-trip commercial flight linking the United States and Europe. From Cape Race, Nfd., to mid-ocean the great dirigible faced overcast skies and possible early fog. But winds were favorable and the Hindenburg was considered virtually certain to break the Graf Zeppelin’s record of 55 hours 22 minutes for an eastward passage of the Atlantic. 47 Passengers. There were 47 passengers and 55 members of the crew aboard when the dirigible left Lakehurst naval air station at 11:27 p. m. last night. Baron Pompeo Aloisi, Duce's representative, finding the council opposed to him, simply walked out of an opening council session with his colleagues. Refuses to Sit “Futile,” exclaimed the Italian baron, refusing to sit at the table with Wolde Mariam, whose country—Ethiopia—he said, no longer exists. Resistance by the League, said the British, means: 1. The League does not recognize Italy's claim to sovereignty over Ethiopia. 2. The League does recognize the continued existence of Emperor Haile Selassie’s Ethiopian government. Already the president had been charged with “gross incompetency in failing to carry Maine and Vermont” in the national election. The cruisers in route to the inter-American peace conference at Buenos Aires steamed steadily ahead, making 25 knots an hour in a smooth sea. Dutch and French Guiana were left behind at midnight.

- LONDON, Nov. 23 (#) — Great Britain has demanded an apology from the Japanese government for the beating and torture of three British sailors at Keelung, Formosa, Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden disclosed to the House of Commons today. Japanese police, officers of the British Asiatic squadron reported, jabbed a fountain pen under the fingernails of one sailor and squirted ink into the wounds to make him sign a “confession.” (The incident occurred Oct. 7.) (According to British naval officers the three sailors were arrested for alleged failure to pay a taxi fare and, when they protested their innocence, were beaten in the face by the police and plainclothes officers. (U.?)——British ships on the high seas will be protected against interference by either side in Spain, Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden informed the House of Commons today. "His Majesty's ships if necessary will protect British merchant ships on the high seas against interference by either party to the Spanish conflict outside the three-mile limit," Eden announced. A report in responsible British circles that a German light cruiser was in the vicinity when the Madrid government cruiser Miguel de Cervantes was crippled by an explosion on Sunday, was believed to have been the reason for intense diplomatic activity behind the scenes in London yesterday and today. It was surmised that information about the explosion was in the hands of Admiral Chatfield when he discussed the incident with five members of the cabinet yesterday.
: Dy United Press THE HAGUE, Nov. 23—It was officially announced today Holland agrees to the principle of monetary cooperation with the United States, Great Britain, and France.

LONDON — (UP) — The House of Commons, perturbed by reports that a German or Italian warship might have been responsible for an explosion which crippled the Madrid government cruiser Miguel De Cervantes off Cartagena Sunday, was assured by Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden today that British shipping would be protected against interference. Eden said neither side in the Spanish civil war would be recognized by Britain as a belligerent on the high seas and would protect British merchant vessels outside the three-mile limit with warships, if necessary. The mystery of the explosion on the Miguel Cervantes was unsolved. It was reported a German light cruiser was in the vicinity at the time. However, Pablo De Azcarate, Spanish ambassador, professing ignorance of the report, said: “The latest advices I have received from Madrid indicate the possibility that Italian submarines may have torpedoed th

Britain promised today her warships would protect her merchant vessels on the high seas from “either side” in the Spanish war, and moved simultaneously to make illegal the carrying of Spanish arms by British merchantmen from whatever port. While new bombs and shells from fascist besiegers fell in Madrid, Spanish socialist sources hinted at grave international repercussions from the alleged torpedoing “by foreign submarines” of a government cruiser. “There are nations on Spain's side which can lend it assistance in a thousand ways,” warned the newspaper El Socialista, in Madrid. Unconfirmed reports circulated in London diplomatic circles today that Germany might be considering breaking off relations with Moscow so the Nazis could assume a free hand in Spain. LONDON, Nov. 21. () —Britain jockeyed for peace in the Mediterranean tonight in the face of Spanish Fascist Gen. Francisco Franco's threat to blockade Barcelona, but kept her warships ready. Refusing to concede the Franco ultimatum was a serious blow likely to snap the taut nerves of Europe, British diplomats pressed efforts to line up other nations behind the theory the Spanish conflict should be kept within Spain at all costs. The admiralty kept close check on British warships in the Mediterranean, determined to protect merchant shipping; but the question what Britain would do if one of her ships were attacked on the seas was not answered.

1936-09-25.text: GENEVA— (UP) —Foreign Minister Anthony Eden of Great Britain today began paving the way for Germany’s return to the League of Nations. Speaking before the assembly, he suggested that the covenant be rewritten to divorce it from the Versailles treaty, so hateful to the Reich. Germany long has demanded that the league covenant be separated entirely from the peace treaties. “A Changing Thing.” The young British statesman even implied his support of revising the whole Versailles treaty, declaring. “Human life is not static, but a changing thing.” Eden offered still another olive branch to Germany, which has insisted that it must have colonies in order to obtain raw material. Great Britain, he said, would support an “impartial expert inquiry under the auspices of the league” with the idea of assuring all nations access to the supplies of nature. RACINE, Wis., Sept. 25.—UP.—William Horlick, Sr., 91, founder of the Horlick milk company, died at his home today. Horlick was the inventor of the malted milk upon which he built a fortune after coming to the United States from England. Despite his age, he had been active in the management of the firm which has plants here and in Canada until a few days ago when he became ill.

Jerusalem, Sept. 25—() —Fifty-four Arabs were killed by British soldiers and fliers during a bloody engagement near Jenin, official figures disclosed today. Machine gun bullets from the scouting planes accounted for 41 of the Arab rioters, the figures showed, while the remainder died from infantry rifle shots. The skirmish resulted in one of the British planes being shot down. The pilot was taken to a hospital but the troops suffered no fatalities.

GIBRALTAR—()—The British trawler Sycamore fired a warning shot at the Spanish government destroyer Almirante Ferrandiz. The Spanish war vessel immediately obeyed the warning and abandoned its effort to take shelter within the Gibraltar three-mile limit from insurgent gun fire. The Almirante Ferrandiz steamed off in the direction of Malaga while the Fascist artillery continued its futile fire from Carnero point.

LONDON, Sept. 25 dp—Japan advised Sir Robert Clive, British ambassador to Tokyo, yesterday that Japan does not intend to take 'hasty action in China,' it was said officially today. The Japanese ambassador to China, it was asserted, is continuing negotiations intended to diminish anti-Japanese feeling and prevent further incidents.

(Copyright, 1936, by The Associated Press) SHANGHAI, Sept. 25. (4?)—Japanese marines seized police control of the Chiest Chapei district of Shanghai today as Tokyo government officials asserted ‘We will proceed according to events and necessities.’ Blue-coated Japanese marines, brought in to patrol streets of the Hongkew section of the international settlement after an attack on three comrades Wednesday, moved into the Chinese district with pistols and rifles with fixed bayonets. Traffic was limited on two main highways and even foreigners, driving to two golf courses north of the city, were stopped and searched. GENEVA, SEPT. 25. (AP) -- The Spaniard Julio Alvarez Del Vayo told the League of Nations assembly today "the blood-stained soil of Spain already is the battlefield of world war." In what delegates construed as an attack on Germany, Italy, and Portugal for allegedly arming the Spanish insurgents, the Madrid envoy warned the assembled statesmen that future war will not be a conflict between states. Instead, he said, the battle will be between two groups of ideas, between "democracy and oppression." Considerable applause followed the conclusion of his speech. He mentioned no nation by name but grouped the states which he accused as those whose political structure coincided "with that to which the rebels desired to reduce Spain." Del Vayo spoke after Anthony Eden of Great Britain had declared his nation, ardently believing in democratic government, will "allow none to wrest it from us."

BILBAO, Spain, (By warship to Saint Jean De Luz, France) — Insurgent bombing planes rained projectiles on Bilbao today, killing more than a hundred persons and wounding many more. The bombardment caused heavy property damage and set part of the city afire.

1936-04-09.text: GENEVA, April 9—(UP)—France in a verbal communication to Great Britain has warned that she intends to seek concrete action against Germany if Adolf Hitler fortifies the Rhineland, it was reported today. It was assumed the action contemplated was to seek economic and financial penalties, to be imposed by other signatories of the Locarno treaty and the League of Nations. Pierre Etienne Flandin, French foreign minister, delivered the message to Anthony Eden, British foreign secretary yesterday, it was learned. Refers to Rejection Flandin was reported to have said that Hitler's April 1 note to Locarno powers constituted a rejection of proposals made to him, and that now the Locarno nations—France, Britain, Belgium and Italy—must consider the next step, especially if Germany erected fortifications. Flandin was reported to have emphasized that fortification would infringe article XLII of the V

France injected the Rhineland issue squarely into the Geneva deliberations on the Locarno crisis and the Italo-Ethiopian conflict today, reserving the right to take any steps the situation might justify if Germany erected fortifications along the Rhine. French ministers informed British Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden of this stand, while Salvador De Madariaga of Spain, chairman of the League of Nations conciliation committee of 13, sought definite statements from Italy and Ethiopia of their terms for negotiations of East African peace. The French pointed out that building of fortifications in the Rhineland would be another violation of the Versailles treaty, already broken by Germany’s remilitarization of that zone. Trinidad, Colo.—Governor considers spreading martial law patrol on all borders to keep destitute workers out of state.

Britain's action was taken inside a meeting of the league’s committee of 18 which resumed its efforts today to open the pathway to peace. France Warns Hitler. Geneva, April 9. — Italy has shipped 200 tons of poison gas to Ethiopia via the Suez Canal, Anthony Eden, British foreign secretary, announced today at a meeting of the League Council's committee of 12. He urged that both belligerents be asked to pledge not to use gas in the future. The committee received a jurists' report indicating that the committee is without authority to prevent Italy from using the gas. The report suggested that the signatories of the 1925 anti-gas convention might call Italy's attention to her alleged violation of it.

NEW YORK, April 8 (*)—Twelve-year-old Freddie Bartholomew, the movie actor, was cast in an episode in his own life drama today—a renewal of his parents’ fight to regain the custody of their son. The parents, Mr. and Mrs. Cecil Llewellyn Bartholomew, were due to arrive from England on the Europa, their attorney said, prepared to contest the guardianship of Freddie which was granted last October 22 by a Los Angeles court to his aunt, Miss Millicent Bartholomew. Freddie, a star of “David Copperfield” and several other movies, has lived with his aunt almost continuously since he was three. Philip A. Levey, New York lawyer, announcing he had been retained by Freddie's parents, said they planned to seek an “amicable settlement” with Miss Bartholomew, but if this failed they would go to the courts to try to void her guardianship.

| LONDON, April 9.—(Is)—An Italian Government spokesman tonight stated that in view of the army’s successes in Ethiopia, Italy is expected to be able to conclude Peace with the Ethiopian Government within a few weeks, according to an Exchange Telegraph from Rome.

1936-08-19.text: Broklyn, N. Y., Aug. 19—(P)— Two men of different ways of life— the skyways and Broadway— worked over an airplane at Floyd Bennett field today, preparing it for a round trip to London. They are Dick Merrill, the quiet veteran of 2,500,000 miles of airmail flying, and Harry Richman, theatre and night club songster. The plane is Richman’s $100,000 (Vultee) monoplane. They flew from Albuquerque, N. M., yesterday, in a non-stop jump from Kansas City in five and one-half hours — which even Merrill thought was "pretty good." "We hope to start out for London Saturday morning," said Richman. "We have to get department of commerce permission first, of course, and a decent weather report, but the ship’s all set. Just this bit of checking over to do."

New York, Aug. 19, (U.P)—Harry Richman, singer, and Dick Merrill, veteran transport pilot, announced today they will take off as soon as instruments in Richman's new $100,000 monoplane are checked, on a round trip flight to England. “Unless the weather's too bad we'll leave before Friday,” Merrill said. The two plan to stay in England only long enough to refuel. The fliers landed at Floyd Bennett Field at 7:50 p.m. (EST) last night.

While Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden began the active task of seeking to further European non-intervention in the Spanish civil war, Whitehall officials said America was best qualified for the role of mediator.
LONDON, Aug. 19--The Board of Trade announced today that all licenses for the exportation of arms, ammunition and aircraft to Spain are revoked, effective today.

It was announced the defendants had confessed complicity in a plot to undermine the influence of present Soviet leaders but would defend themselves—having refused counsel—against specific charges of plotting assassination. More than 1500 delegates, including 30 Americans and 50 Canadians are expected to attend the congress designed to coordinate efforts of the various countries sponsoring peace movements.

British authorities threatened the dog with another trip across the English Channel, the dog's fourth in three days, because he lacked proper credentials. Washington, Indiana, Sept. 22 (AP)—Mrs. Ruth Bryan Owen Rhode, former United States minister to Denmark, and daughter of the late William Jennings Bryan, suffered a broken left leg in a fall here last night. While the emperor without an empire was en route, the league assembly, fearing to create a precedent which might work against other nations, delayed an anticipated decision to eject the Ethiopians. Pending a report by the league credentials committee, the Ethiopian delegation will be allowed to participate in discussions. Another source of worry for the delegates is the question of foreign intervention in the Spanish civil war. GENEVA (®)— Haile Selassie, Monday night tasted victory, however temporary it might prove to be, over the representatives of Italy’s Premier Mussolini. Flying from London on a last-minute decision, the erstwhile “king of kings” arrived to learn that representatives of his lost Ethiopian kingdom were sitting in the league general assembly. Mussolini, whose Fascist legions wrested Selassie’s empire from him, insisted that unless Ethiopia were barred from League discussions, Italy would stay away. Italian delegates did not attend sessions.

LONDON, Sept. 22. (#)—The sisters, who killed the imbecile brother they had nursed day and night for 20 years and who were given a “mercy” sentence, were released today from the Broadmoor institution for the criminally insane. The sisters, Catherine Walsh, 40, and Mrs. Evelyn Constance Alexander, 36, were found insane by a court, July 17, 1935. The verdict spared them from a prison term or death on the gallows. According to custom in such cases, they were sentenced “to be detained during the king's pleasure.” The sisters were charged with killing Sylvester Walsh “by administering gas and tablets.” They admitted killing him, declaring they had done it to fulfill a promise to their mother and “for love of our brother.”

London, Sept. 22 (Tuesday) — Informed sources said early today Spanish Fascist troops were advancing on Madrid from four sides. Madrid dispatches added that the Fascists launched a major onslaught on their final goal from the south. These accounts said a bitter battle was fought 40 miles from the capital. They added, however, that it was not known in Madrid whether the government forces had successfully defended a vital cross-road there. (The intersection mentioned apparently is at Maqueda. A Fascist communique from Seville asserted that point had been occupied by the insurgents after they defeated government troops, who suffered heavy losses.)

WASHINGTON, Sept. 22. (WP) — Senator Copeland of New York today asked Secretary Hull to make a “friendly intimation” to the British government to take “positive action” to quell rioting in Palestine which is endangering the lives of 12,000 American Jews there.

| MADRID, Sept. 24 (AP)— | Madrid’s defenders, in a new and extreme thrust to stave off insurgent columns, announced today they had loosed the waters of Alberche dam over San Marten de Valdeiglesias, scheduled point of convergence for fascist columns 36 miles west of the capitol. The government said it believed the town had been destroyed and with it considerable amount of insurgent guns, trucks, horses, and mules. (Dispatches from Burgos, seat of the insurgent junta, said Fascist northern armies were driving through mountain passes with the intention of meeting a southern column in the vicinity of San Marten.)

(Associated Press) Berlin, Sept. 22. “Germany Tuesday discussed a widely-circulated report that Adolf Hitler may resign as Nazi chancellor and retain the simple title of “Der Fuehrer” (the leader). The same report mentioned General Hermann Wilhelm Goering as Hitler’s possible successor. Persons in authoritative circles refused to comment on the predictions, confining their expressions to an evasive “we have not heard of it.” However, the persistency with which the report has cropped up again and again and the diverse and cautious quarters from which it emanates has led some observers to believe there is an actual basis for the forecast. Before assuming power, the Reich chancellor often told his supporters: “I am merely your torch bearer; You must close in behind me and attend to the details.” In addition, Hitler's declarations at the recent Nuremberg convention of the National Socialist

1936-08-01.text: Quebec, July 31.—(AF)—Cementing anew America’s friendship for her neighbor on the north, President Roosevelt in a speech today called for ‘frank dealings’ and a ‘spirit of give and take’ in settling all problems facing the world. Standing on a platform covered with American and British flags at the foot of the monument to Wolfe and Montcalm on Dufferin Terrace, the American chief executive, speaking in English and French, responded to a big ovation and official greetings by holding up dispute-free Canadian-American relations as a fine example for other nations to follow. Heard by Host Thousands spread out on the broad terrace heard his address and those of Lord Tweedsmuir, governor-general; Premier MacKenzie King, and other ranking Canadian officials. Scarlet-coated troops, mounted and on foot, served as a guard of honor at the depot and at the terrace, where a 21-gun salute echoed over

PARIS, Aug. 1, (A.P)—France, gravely alarmed at international complications which have arisen in the Spanish revolt, failed today in an effort to effect an international neutrality agreement. Great Britain, it was understood, refused to participate in any such agreement because it might be interpreted as implying interference in an internal Spanish problem. The cabinet, many of whose members had been up almost all night at a turbulent Chamber of Deputies session, met at the Elysee Palace today with President Albert LeBrun to decide on its position in the revolt. Reason for the alarm that was intensified by the crash of airplanes of Italian bomber type on the Moroccan frontier, was made clear today in the declarations of the leading French political commentators. They reflected clearly a fear that there is a secret agreement between Spanish and Italian Fascists which might, in event of a

WATERBURY, Vt., Aug. 1—-()—President Roosevelt started his personal tour of New England flood control projects, leaving his train here to motor to the Winooski dam. This was his first stop since crossing the boundary line from Canada on a trip which will take him to Hyde Park. After a brief stop here the President planned flood control conferences with federal and state officials at Montpelier, Vt., Hanover, N. H., and Springfield, Mass. Governor Charles M. Smith of Vermont met the chief executive's train here and drove with him to the state capital. Among the large crowd which saw the President detrain were U.S. Senators Warren R. Austin and Ernest W. Gibson of Vermont, both Republicans, and Major General Edward M. Markham, chief of army engineers.

Foreign Madrid.—Spain uses artillery and planes in quelling military rebels, monarchists reported marching on Madrid. London.—Foreign Secretary Eden negotiates with France and Belgium for Locarno conference and asks report of Danzig on Free City’s disturbances. Domestic Chicago.—Corn belt greets drouth-easing showers and prospect of a 90-per-cent crop on at least half Iowa's acres. Milwaukee.—Veterans commander urges military training for CCC camps. Los Angeles.—Movie “star theft” suit values Gary Cooper at $4,000,000.

St. Helier, Jersey, England.— (AP) Airplanes and lifeboats searched the sea today for a plane carrying eight passengers and a crew of two which has been missing since last night. Five women were among the passengers. Jersey Airways officials asked French authorities to aid in the search, Royal Air Force planes joined in the hunt while vessels in the territory were asked to keep a sharp lookout.

PARIS, Aug. 1--(U2)—The French government, after proposing a neutral agreement among Britain, France and Italy in the Spanish civil war, announced tonight that it considers itself no longer bound not to furnish arms to the Spanish government because "other foreign powers are furnishing arms to the insurgents." The left-wing French government apparently is unwilling to see Italy or any other fascist or Nazi country aid in the establishment of a fascist regime in its southern neighbor. France has been perturbed by the discovery that airplanes from Italy bearing arms and ammunition have been flying to Morocco to aid the rebels, as was evidenced by the forced landing of several planes in North Africa on Thursday. The official announcement of the neutrality proposal to Britain and Italy disclosed that the French government had sent them a telegraphic invitation to join in an agreement of the

| S$. HELIER, JERSEY, England. July 31—(4)—An airplane carrying eight passengers, a pilot and a radio operator was missing tonight in stormy weather on a short hop from Guernsey to Jersey Island in the English Channel. The Jersey Airways amphibian plane took off at 7 P.M. on a flight normally requiring 20 minutes, but had not arrived here at 10 P.M. A lifeboat put out from St. Helier to make a search, despite the heavy seas.

PARIS, Aug. 1. (UP) — The French Government announced tonight it has invited Great Britain and Italy to join an agreement not to export arms to the Spanish government or the rebels. Copies of the invitation were telegraphed to London and Rome.

1936-01-30.text: | By RICHARD G. MASSOCK. (Associated Press Foreign Staff.) Paris, Jan. 30.--(AP)—Premier Albert Sarraut today threw in his lot with Great Britain declaring that nation’s “cooperation with France is the essential guarantee of the peace of Europe.” In a seven-minute ministerial declaration read to parliament, the premier admitted his main task was to assure “impartial elections,” but he promised to try to reduce unemployment, encourage trade, and protect the gold franc in the struggle toward “a happier tomorrow.” The elections to which he referred are those for parliament, com- (Continued on page Seven.)

London, Jan. 22 — Great Britain's new King Edward VIII attacked today the grave international problems surrounding his empire. He received distinguished foreign visitors, including representatives of Nazi Germany and anti-Nazi Austria. Observers said he is anxious to strengthen international relations. He engaged them in a general discussion of state affairs. Sees Visiting Diplomats After conferring with Anthony Eden, foreign secretary, the king saw Baron Konstantin Von Neu-Prin, German foreign minister; Prince Ernst Von Starhemberg, vice chancellor of Austria; Maxim Litvinoff, Soviet commissar for foreign affairs; Nicholas Titulescu, foreign minister of Rumania; Armindo Monteiro, foreign minister of Portugal; and Joaquin Urzaiz Cadaval of Spain. The king, Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin and Eden spent hours conferring with visiting diplomats here for the funeral of King George V yesterda

(Copyright by The Associated Press) London, Jan. 30.—UP—An authoritative source said today the recent political talks Anthony Eden, foreign secretary, has held with visiting dignitaries during the last few days have successfully quieted the political situation in western Europe. These talks, according to this authority, have strengthened a British belief that there is no likelihood of any thrust by Germany into the demilitarized Rhineland. Premier Alfred Sarraut of France today threw in his lot with Great Britain declaring that nation’s “cooperation with France is the essential guarantee of the peace of Europe.” It was indicated that this belief of peace, for the present at least, is the result of conversations Eden had with the foreign minister of France and the foreign minister of Germany.

LONDON, JAN. 30. (AP).—King Edward in a formal audience granted Norman H. Davis, United States ambassador at large, was understood to have emphasized his high regard for the United States and the American people today. The new monarch and the American envoy talked half an hour. The King expressed his deep appreciation for American sympathy at the death of his father, the late King George, and at the kindliness with which his accession to the throne had been regarded.

PEIPING, China, Jan. 30.—(INS)—The last American, British and other foreigners in Kweiyang, capital of Kweichow Province, were urgently warned to flee today as fierce Communist troops hammered at the walls of Lungli, fourteen miles southeast of the capital. Sweeping all resistance before them in a relentless eastward drive from Hunan Province, some 40,000 reds yesterday tramped through the ancient streets of Kweiyang after emergency breastworks had been torn down in a bitter battle. With government troops falling back on Kweiyang, where they expect to make a decisive stand, the Communists opened a smashing attack on Lungli. Thousands of loyal coolies and soldiers were put to work in Kweiyang to bolster the city walls. Kweiyang is a city of 100,000. A majority of the missionaries had fled farther into the interior when the Communist advance first became threatening late last week. Simulta

PARIS, Jan. 30. (UP)—Collaboration between France and Britain is “for Europe the essential guarantee of peace,” Premier Albert Sarraut told the chamber of deputies today in his ministerial declaration on which he asked a vote of confidence in his new cabinet. His speech was taken as proof that he intends to make such collaboration the chief object of his government's foreign policy. With reference to the Ethiopian war he said: “The government will endeavor through diplomatic action to find a solution under the auspices of the League of Nations in order to stop the cruelly bloody hostilities.” In expressing a wish for friendship with Germany Sarraut declared: “Republican France is ready to meet all pacifically inclined nations in the first row of which she sincerely hopes to find Germany. This would accomplish the wish of our war heroes whom national gratitude salutes and who see in the r

(By ‘The Associated Press: NOW, sleet and ice covered most of Texas Wednesday night, greatly hampering air and highway traffic and threatening serious damages to livestock. The severe weather, first general blizzard of the year, extended from the snow-covered Panhandle to the Gulf coast and lower Rio Grande valley, where it was feared vegetable crops would be badly injured. Ted Kincannon, pilot, was injured fatally and five passengers were shaken up when an American Airlines plane crashed into a wooded section in a forced landing in a snowstorm near Denton. Traffic Hazardous Ice-covered streets and highways in nearly all parts of the state made traffic hazardous, and more ice was promised as snow, sleet and rain continued to fall in sub-freezing weather. The Panhandle and South Plains regions were covered with two to six inches of snow. The temperature ranged between 13 and 16 degrees al

LONDON (WP)—The Daily Mail correspondent at Addis Ababa reported Thursday in a dispatch sent by special courier, that there were plain signs of potential revolt in Ethiopia. He quoted European businessmen in the capital as saying that the possibility of a revolt was a more serious threat to Emperor Haile Selassie than Italian bombs. It took 6,000 picked troops a month to suppress the recent uprising in Gojjam province, he asserted.

1936-09-12.text: LIVERPOOL, Eng., Sept. 12. — Heavy rain and strong westerly winds caused Harry Richman and Dick Merrill, American trans-Atlantic fliers, to postpone their return flight to New York today. The time for the takeoff was set tentatively for Sunday.

| BONNEVILLE SALT FLATS, Utah, Sept. 21 (4.—John Cobb, race-loving London fur broker, set a new world 24-hour motor car speed record today—and shattered half a dozen minor marks along the way. His unofficial average speed for the grueling run, aided by three relief drivers, was 150.1621 miles per hour as contrasted with the former record of his countryman, Capt. George E. T. Eyston, 149.0 m.p.h.

A call for new naval treaties, based on parity with Great Britain and the United States, was hinted today by Admiral Osami Nagano, minister of the navy. Admiral Nagano, in an exclusive interview, expressed confidence peace will continue in the Pacific with expiration of the London and Washington pacts next January. “NO REASON TO FEAR” He disclaimed Japanese intent to inaugurate a naval building race with the United States and Great Britain after termination of the treaties. “I see no reason to fear that the prospects of continued peace in the Pacific should be darkened by the termination of the treaties a few months hence,” the cabinet minister asserted. The hint of new treaties was linked with an emphatic declaration equality in naval strength must be granted to Japan.

Rome, Sept. 12 (UP)—Negotiations for a new trade agreement with Russia have been completely broken, and suspended with Great Britain and the Netherlands, Foreign Minister Galeazzo Ciano told the cabinet today. He said negotiations had been broken off with Russia because Italy can no longer permit Russia to maintain a large margin in her favor. Ciano announced that trade negotiations with Britain had been suspended because Britain “pretended that Italian exports should be used to pay off trade credits.”

By United Press: JERUSALEM, Sept. 12 — A British infantry sergeant and five Arabs were killed in a five-hour fight on the slopes of Mt. Carmel, where Elijah destroyed the prophets of Baal, a dispatch said today. As the result of the Italian consul's warning yesterday to Italians to have their passports ready in case it was necessary to leave Palestine, and a rumor that the German consul had given a similar warning to Germans, some Italians and Germans prepared today to take "vacations" in Italy and Lebanon. No general exodus was expected. "Many Germans and Italians drew crucifixes on doors and gates of their homes, hoping that the symbols would protect them against Arabs attacking Jews.

See Son, Critically Ill With Hemophilia. New York.—(AP)--Only the gravity of her son's condition, friends agreed today, could have persuaded Victoria, unhappy former queen of Spain, to come to America to see the Count of Cavadonga. Today the middle-aged Victoria, granddaughter of Britain's famous queen of that name, passed through the Straits of Gibraltar en route from Nice to New York. From her ship Victoria could see the war-torn shores of the country where her own life was often in peril. In a New York hospital, awaiting the arrival of mother, September 17, Count Cavadonga lay critically ill after the eighth blood transfusion in two weeks designed to offset the ravages of hemophilia. Accompanying Victoria are her daughter, Princess Beatrice, the latter's husband, Prince Amedeo Torlonia, son of the late Elsie Moore of New York, and their 7-months-old baby.

LIVERPOOL, Eng. Sept. 12—(INS)—Clouds and squalls as dark and blustery as those that today caused another postponement of their return flight to New York were seen by fellow airmen in the relations between Harry Richman and Dick Merrill. In spite of denials on both sides, rumors hummed rapidly through aeronautic circles that friction has developed between the night club entertainer and his pilot during the nine days’ delay since they landed in Wales. While rain poured down all night on the muddy banks of the river Mersey, Merrill announced early that because weather conditions over the Atlantic were reported good, he was going to “give it a push.” Richman, however, decided to postpone the take-off until at least tomorrow morning. After one of the co-flyers’ innumerable conferences regarding starting on the westward hop, Merrill today rushed out of the airport headquarters visibly distrac

Bonneville Salt Flats, Utah, Sept. 12 (UP)—John Cobb of England completed a triumphant 24 hour automobile speed run on Utah's salt bed speedway today, smashing the world record established early in July by Captain George E. T. Eyston of London. One of the British driver’s relief pilots flashed Cobb’s high wheeled Napier-Railton speedster across the finish line for a 24 hour average of 150.1621 miles an hour, shattering by a small margin Captain Eyston’s mark of 149.09 m. p. h. In the 24 hours since 9:25.05 a. m. CST yesterday, Cobb and his co-pilots have driven the racing machine 3,603.9 miles.

1936-04-16.text: BIRMINGHAM, Eng. April 16.--(2 —Mrs. Dorothy Waddingham, 34-year-old mother of five children, died on the gallows of the Winson Green prison today while police guarded the approaches against a demonstration in protest at “this disgrace.” Mrs. Violet Van Der Elst, energetic campaigner against capital punishment, organized the demonstration, broadcasting appeals to a crowd of 2,000 to attempt to prevent the hanging. The throng looked on quietly, however, some smiling at Mrs. Van Der Elst's exhortations, some praying for Mrs. Waddingham, while the convicted poison slayer of a patient in her Nottingham nursing home died within the prison. King Edward himself was the only one who could have saved the woman from the gallows by granting a last-minute reprieve, after Home Secretary Sir John Simon denied appeals for clemency.

LONDON, April 15.—(P)—Former Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald underwent an operation today which the nursing home he entered announced was “successfully performed.” “He is doing well,” a bulletin said. MacDonald, now Lord President of the Council, entered the nursing home yesterday for the operation which he described as “minor.” He hoped to return to his official duties within a few weeks.

LONDON, April 15.—-(UP)—General staff chieftains of the British, French and Belgian fighting forces met today to perfect a plan for mutual defense in event Germany attacks France or Belgium pending the adoption of a general plan for European peace solidification. It was understood a major feature of the plan would be to reply to any German attack with a terrific aerial bombardment by massed fleets on German industrial centers, railways, army headquarters, airdromes and seaports. High officers of the air forces, armies and navies of the three countries took part in the talks, assisted by experts assigned to them. They met as representatives of three signatories of the Locarno treaty, which bound Britain, France, Belgium, Italy and Germany to respect each others’ frontiers and to rally to the defense of any of the five nations which was attacked by another of the five. Germany's denunciati

| BIRMINGHAM, England, April 16 (UP).—Mrs. Dorothea Nancy Waddingham, 36, a trained nurse and mother of five children, was hanged at Winson Green prison today for the murder of a patient. Sir John Simon, home secretary, refused to recommend that King Edward VIII commute the sentence. Mrs. Waddingham was charged with murdering, by means of an overdose of morphine, Miss Ada Baguley, 50, a crippled patient in her nursing home at Nottingham. Ronald Joseph Sullivan, father of two of Mrs. Waddingham’s children, was tried with her but was acquitted of any complicity.

BIRMINGHAM, Eng., April 16, (#)—Mrs. Dorothy Waddingham, 84-year-old mother of five children, was hanged in the Winston Green prison today for the poison slaying of a 55-year-old crippled patient in her Nottingham nursing home. King Edward himself was the only one who could have saved the woman from the gallows by granting a last-minute reprieve, after Home Secretary Sir John Simon denied appeals for clemency. PRESS COUNTERS PROTEST WAVE A wave of protest throughout Britain over the hanging of the mother of five children, including a six-months-old baby, was countered by press statements, terming the poison death of the patient, 50-year-old Ada Louisa Baguley, a flagrant offense. Mrs. Waddingham also was accused, but not convicted, of the death of Miss Baguley’s aged mother. Newspapers insisted the crime must have been premeditated and that even the strong recommendation of mercy by the

SEE, Se Rome, April 16.—Italian soldiers have resumed their advance southward along the Sudanese frontier of Ethiopia, moving further into a zone vital to Great Britain because it is the source of the Nile. Dispatches from Italian General headquarters said today. Their immediate objective was believed to be Borni, Ethiopian frontier town commanding more caravan routes and another tributary of the Nile, the Rahad river, 28 miles down the frontier from Gallabat which they took several days ago. Next they were expected to go on another 1744 miles to Zair, to consolidate beyond question their control of every important caravan route between the whole Tana region and the Sudan. The military situation preoccupied everyone to the neglect of the diplomatic negotiations at Geneva, where the League Council is trying to persuade Italy to agree to an immediate armistice and formal peace negotiations

Associated Press Foreign Staff PARIS, April 15.—France warned Great Britain tonight not to play a “lone hand against Italy” under penalty of withdrawing French support to the British fleet in event of an attack in the Medi- terranean. The French caution to England came on the heels of an Italian warning to France that the Fascist nation refuses to allow its military campaign against Ethiopia to be “frustrated.” Support Demanded The Italian declaration, which diplomatic sources reported was made by Ambassador Vittorio Cere ruti to French Minister Pierre- Etienne Flandin, was accompanied by a demand for French support in lifting war sanctions against Italy and a Fascist offer to stand with France against Germany in the Locarno treaty negotiations. In the midst of the international complications, Premier Albert Sar- raut told provincial newspaper edi- tors France may be forced to quit the L

LONDON, April 16.—(#)—With tension and uncertainty mounting in Geneva, the British admiralty has hurried a new, “secret type of anti-submarine craft to Gibraltar to bulwark the grand fleet scattered through the Mediterranean. The publication of the Admiralty list today showed that 15 especially designed ships described as mine-sweeping trawlers had arrived at Gibraltar from England within the last week. Most of them left the Portland base on Easter Sunday. Five destroyers arrived at Gibraltar from the Eastern Mediterranean. (Mine-sweepers, designed primarily for cutting underwater mines from their moorings, are equipped with depth charges, that is, huge bombs which are exploded under water by time fuses. Depth bombs are the outstanding armament devised against submerged submarines. During the world war, the trawlers ordinarily were not fast enough to compete with the speed of submarines,

1936-10-19.text: LONDON, Oct. 19.—(#)—King Edward planned royal entertainment today for his prospective house party guests at Sandringham but whether Mrs. Ernest Simpson would be included among the visitors remained undisclosed. The British Monarch motored to his country residence yesterday for the first stay there since his father died. A court circular announced the ruler was accompanied by Maj. Ulick Alexander, keeper of the privy purse, and Commander Charles Lambe. Mrs. Simpson, the king’s American friend who last week began suit to divorce her husband on misconduct grounds, was reported invited to attend the royal house party.

LONDON, Oct. 19—(#) Bette Davis, American film player, was restrained today from appearing in motion pictures and other performances in England for any company except Warner Brothers of Hollywood. Her counsel's plea that the Warner contract was so stringent that it constituted a “restraint of trade” was rejected by the court. The order prohibited her from working in a picture for a British company.

Columbus, O., Oct. 20.—(UP)—A recommendation for police registration of all persons came before the convention of the United Lutheran Church in America today as Dr. G. H. Bechtold of Philadelphia reported on a three-month study he made in England and America. "Many Americans throw up their hands in horror at the thought of such universal registration," he declared. "But some such step is necessary for the proper control of our shifting population—those children of the depression who roam over the country as they please." Police registration is effective in curbing crime and in halting the wanderings of people without regular places of abode. "When I entered a German or English city to spend the night I had to register, and my registration went to the police authorities," said Bechtold. "At first it seemed strange but I realized that such a system was necessary because of the great number

PALERMO, Sicily, Oct. 19--(UP)—Four Italian members of the crew of the trans-Atlantic liner Vuleania were killed during a fire which broke out in third cabin quarters early today. Two waiters were suffocated while fighting the flames below decks in the third cabin section of the liner, which was enroute to New York. A third man was asphyxiated while taking a shower when fumes penetrated the bath. The fourth victim was a member of the ship's orchestra, reported drowned when he became panic-stricken and fell overboard.

MOSCOW, Oct. 19. (*)— Russia, angered over delay in application of practical measures to enforce neutrality in the Spanish civil war, is determined to withdraw from the non-intervention accord, informed sources declared Monday. Soviet denunciation of the “hands off Spain” agreement signed by twenty-seven European nations will be based on the assertion public opinion can no longer tolerate the “disgraceful situation” to which the neutrality pact has sunk, these sources asserted. The Kremlin has made up its mind on the withdrawal, it was reported, and was to announce its decision Monday or Tuesday. Statements in authoritative Russian newspapers made it plain Russia desires to break up the agreement so that nations friendly to the Madrid government will not be bound by the pact. Observers saw in the Russian diplomatic maneuver an effort to force Great Britain and France to unite against fas

MADRID, Oct. 19.—(U.P)—Loyalist militiamen, their backs to Madrid on the last defense line outside the city proper, steeled themselves today for a supreme effort to hold back the ferocious attack of a machine-like nationalist army. The climax was approaching fast. Again the left front men had weakened under a terrible combination of airplane and artillery barrage and the direct attack of the insurgent Moors and Foreign Legionnaires. Leftist militiamen were massed in semi-circular defense order in front of the last key points before the siege of Madrid itself became a fact. Before El Escorial, on the main highway northwest of the city; before San Martin de Valdeiglesias to the west; before Naval Carnero on the main highway to the southwest; before Torrejon, on the main highway to the south, the militiamen swore to acquit themselves honorably. Navalcarnero, 18 miles southwest of the capita

Madrid, Oct. 19.—The Madrid government today mobilized thousands of taxicabs to rush reinforcements to stem the advancing Spanish hordes. Three thousand taxis were placed in readiness to carry aid to any point on the civil war fronts around the capital in event of surprise enemy moves. Drivers from the mechanics brigade were assigned to the machines for duty if the government finds it necessary to duplicate the famous taxi ride of troops from Paris to the Marne which saved that capital from the Germans in the World War. New Food Supply Arrives. Huge posters plastered throughout the capital urged every Madrid citizen to volunteer his services in the militia. The government was cheered by the arrival at Alicante of the Russian steamer Neva with 2,800 tons of foodstuffs. Desperate in the face of a surging Fascist advance, the Socialist government massed strong forces at Torrejon De La Calza

MADRID. Oct. 19. (#)—Desperate in the face of a surging Fascist advance, the Socialist government massed strong forces today at Torrejón De La Calzada, 16 miles south of the capital. Gen. Jose Asensio, commander of government forces, ordered militiamen defending the Toledo-Madrid highway to take up strong positions near Parla, a small settlement north of Torrejón. (Fascist commanders declared their forces were sweeping northward under artillery and aviation protection after occupying the strategic town of Illescas, 22 miles from the capital.) On the western front, Socialist troops entrenched at Brunete in preparation for an expected insurgent drive eastward from Chepineria. Await Order To Attack North and west of the capital, other

1936-08-23.text: Latest War Developments. London—Spain takes important step to placate Europe by pledging herself not to molest British ships on the high seas, and, inferentially, ships of any other power. Berlin—German wrath rises against Russia and alarmist stories are circulated in Berlin of a Russian fleet concentration in the Baltic. Reports denied in Moscow. Madrid—Loyalist offensive in progress on eight of 11 fronts. With northern rebel army — Gen. Mola, rebel leader, determined to fight to end, organizes for north and south drive on Madrid. Bilbao—Flaming slaughter of hundreds of rebels in loyalist capture of Gijon described by eye-witness. Paris—War so far has cost 35,000 men and €5,000,000,000, incalculably damaging nation's resources. End may be many months off.

Madrid | Government promises quick settlement of Kamerun incident with Germany: neutrality pact way opened for Nazis. Britain is assured ships will not be molested on high seas by Spain; puts pressure on Madrid to return sequestered Nazi plane demanded by Berlin. Rebel forces near Toledo in “big push” on Madrid; air battle reported over Huesca and Vicen. Acceptance, foreseen pacific settlement of Kamerun, plane incidents. Defeat In Victory? Paris —(P)— The nearer either side in Spain comes to ultimate victory, the greater may be the danger of international complications, it was declared in circles closely following the situation. The losing side, it was declared in diplomatic circles, may be interested in avoiding European entanglements, and could see one way to salvation in bringing on intervention by European powers sympathetic to its political cause. The fascist-monarchists

MOSCOW, Aug. 22.--(AP)—The death penalty for all 16 confessed conspirators against the Soviet Union was demanded today by Prosecutor Andrey J. Vishinsky. “The mad dogs must be shot,” Vishinsky demanded. His dramatic demand concluded arguments of the prosecution lasting more than three hours. The prisoners blanched visibly before the onslaught of words. “A pitiful and disgraceful end awaits these people,” said Vishinsky. “I add my voice to the millions of indignant voices of the toiling masses in demanding the death penalty for all 16 defendants.”

Madrid, Aug. 22—The government, taking the initiative on eight of the 11 war fronts, claims pronounced successes in the northwest and south today. An optimistic manifesto predicted the prompt fall of Cordoba and the beginning of a smashing offensive against Oviedo, key point of the southern and northern campaigns. The fall of Fort Simancas at Gijon released 2,500 besiegers of that city to march to Oviedo on the northwest coast thirty miles away, strongly armed with a huge quantity of guns and ammunition seized at Simancas. Barcelona dispatches reported success in the Aragon country in northeastern Spain, the strong army garrison in the country. It is firmly held by the rebels but the Loyalists were advancing. Aviation and artillery in cooperation set a fire to Belchite which the rebels abandoned leaving three cannon and two machine guns behind. It was the beginning of the sixth week of t

Paris—War so far has cost 35,000 men and $5,000,000,000, incalculably damaging the nation's resources. End may be months off. MADRID, Aug. 22.—(UP)—Loyalists took the offensive on eight of 11 civil war fronts today. On two more at Madrid and San Sebastian, they were on the defensive. On the 11th, at Zaragoza, they were not within reach of the rebel stronghold. It was the beginning of the sixth week of the rebellion led by high army officers against the left wing government. A revolt which both sides thought would last a few days has grown in area, size and ferocity until Spain is a welter of men fighting in bands ranging from handfuls to tens of thousands, until one has not far to travel to see the ruins or the blazing shells of homes, churches and public buildings, until the country faces ruin. Rebel and loyalist leaders, believing now the civil war cannot reach a definite result within
GENEVA, Sept. 21 (.—Carlos Saavedra Lamas, Argentine foreign minister, was elected president of the League of Nations Assembly tonight.

HENDAYE, France (AP) - An unconfirmed report Saturday night said the captain of the German destroyer Seeadler had informed the Berlin government that Spanish loyalists at Fort Guadalupe, Irun, had attempted to shell his ship. Officers of the vessel, now at Bayonne, France, refused to confirm or deny the report.

Madrid, Aug. 22—-(7)—A fresh admonition to all Americans to evacuate Spain as soon as possible was posted tonight at the United States embassy, following receipt of a cable from Washington. Every day of additional delay means the possibility of being cut off entirely from the only method of evacuation, the note said.

1936-06-19.text: 4onaon, June 18. (4’)—Opposition members of the House of Commons shouted “Shame! Resign!” at Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden today when he announced Great Britain would lead a move for the lifting of League of Nations sanctions from Italy. From government benches there came a little loyal cheering but the roars of “Shame” created turmoil in the house. Eden, himself, assumed much of the responsibility for the government’s about face on the question of the sanctions applied in an effort to prevent Italy’s conquest of Ethiopia. The storm of shouts burst out after Eden had announced: “His majesty’s government, after a mature consideration on advice which I as foreign secretary thought it my duty to give, has come to the conclusion there is no longer any utility in continuing these measures as a means of pressure on Italy.”
| London, June 18——Prime Minister Baldwin declared in the House of Commons today that collective security has failed and called for a peace alliance of Great Britain, Germany and France.

LONDON, June 19.—Embittered sanctionists sought today to loose a storm of public protest against the government's decision to back suspension of Italian sanctions. Four labor leaders, who cabled the cabinet’s recommendation “the great betrayal” of the League of Nations, led a movement for a nationwide series of campaign meetings. * Their plan of opposition, pointing toward a parliamentary censure debate Tuesday, followed the same lines as the public storm created against the stillborn Hoare-Laval proposal to end the Italo-Ethiopian war. Sponsors of the weekend campaign took their cues from the fiery David Lloyd George, wartime prime minister who led the attack against Prime Minister Baldwin and his ministers yesterday with the ringing pronouncement: “There they sit—the cowards!” as he pointed scornfully at the ministerial benches. Already National Labor and National Liberal members were

London, June 18, — Britain’s cabinet decided today sanctions against Italy must be scrapped and approved a pronouncement of new policy dealing, it was reported, both with League of Nations reform and with Germany. The ministers, convinced continuance of the present measures against Italy must be halted, gave authority to the statement which Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden will make in Commons tomorrow. That statement from the cabinet’s slim and fashionable lead-off man was expected to follow these three main lines: 1—Sanctions: Britain is ready to scrap them if the other sanctionists at Geneva are willing. 2—The League must be supported but reformed. 3—European peace: A way to settlement must be opened and Germany holds the key to it. How and when the sanctions can be lifted is a question to be settled at Geneva. The council meets June 26; the assembly, June 30. Parliamentary circles anti

Paris, June 19.—(U. P.)—France joined Great Britain in a new policy today when the cabinet agreed to follow London's example and advocate abolition of League sanctions against Italy. The government accepted the proposal to raise sanctions, after a report on foreign affairs.

Georgetown, British Guiana, June 19.—(P)—A Guianan government steamship rammed and captured the long-elusive English trawler Girl Pat today, ending a romantic and runaway voyage in quest of pirate gold. The capture of the ship and the arrest of her crew of five climaxed a hunt in many seas for the 25-ton motor trawler, which set out from Grimsby, England, on April 2, presumably bound for her regular North Sea fishing grounds. Instead, her owners traced her down past the Salvage Islands, legendary hiding place for the stolen millions of Capt. William Kidd, to the African coast, and across the South Atlantic. Fuel Supply Gone The end came when the Girl Pat’s fuel supply was gone and all ports virtually closed to her. She anchored yesterday four miles off the Georgetown beach and her crew shouted to a police-filled launch which came alongside: “We're outside the three-mile limit. Get out, o

Georgetown, British Guiana, June 19.—(#)—The government S.S. Pomeroon forcibly captured today a vessel believed to be the runaway British trawler Girl Pat. The vessel taken had been harboring outside the 3 mile limit for several days. A conference called by Gov. Sir Geoffrey Northcote last night decided to ask London for instructions and it was understood the capture was in accordance with London's reply. Police officials reported the craft answered the description of the Girl Pat whose crew ran away with her from Grimsby, England, early in April presumably on a search for pirate treasure. The captured craft was without fuel but her crew fought off the government ship's efforts to capture her for 2 and a half hours. The crew was placed under arrest.

LONDON, June 1 (4--Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, announced in the House of Commons today that the British government had agreed "in principle" to the construction of a sister ship to the S.S. Queen Mary. The chancellor said the Cunard-White Star Line had applied for authority to enter into an agreement for the sister ship. He agreed in principle, he added, but reserved the right to further consultation before the contract was signed.

1936-01-19.text: | LONDON, Jan. 18—(4)—Rudyard Kipling, Great Britain’s poet and storyteller of empire, who died early today, may be buried in Westminster Abbey among the nation’s greatest sons. Kipling’s own wishes for his burial place, friends said, probably will be the only deciding factor. Throughout his life he shunned national honors, refusing knighthoods several times, and this attitude, it was pointed out, also may have led him to prefer burial in some quiet spot. Final arrangements will be made tomorrow. The British Museum disclosed that Kipling, shortly before his death, gave it the manuscript of “Kim,” probably the greatest as well as one of the most popular of his longer works. The body will be cremated, the family has announced. It was taken to a chapel from the hospital bed where an emergency operation Monday for a perforated stomach ulcer was performed. His American wife and their daughter

The death of King George V at Sandringham, England, drew messages of condolence and expressions of mourning from virtually every country. Governments, high officials and royalty of many nations sent messages of sympathy to Queen Mary and the British royal family. Ottawa, Can. “I am heartbroken,” said Baron Tweedsmuir, governor-general of Canada, in a message to the new king. Opening of the Toronto legislature was postponed indefinitely. Social and sports events were cancelled. Tokyo—The imperial household announced three weeks official mourning by the emperor's court. Paris—President Albert Lebrun postponed the diplomatic ball set for Jan. 22. Geneva—The League of Nations council set a special session to honor the dead king, and all other council activities were cancelled. Delegates from all countries represented sent messages of condolence to British Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden. Door

BY THE ASSOCIATED PRESS The British Empire's new king is its first bachelor ruler since George III ascended the throne in 1760. George III, however, married the next year, giving rise to speculation whether the new monarch might follow suit before his coronation in 1937. Three kings and one queen—William IV, Edward V, Edward VI, and Elizabeth—never married. Thirteen others were single on taking the oath but subsequently wed. Of the three other bachelor kings, Edward V and Edward VI, died as youths. The former, who ascended in 1483, was killed in the Tower of London with his brother Richard. The latter died when he was fifteen. King William II was killed in a hunting accident after he had ruled from 1087 to 1100. The new king is the thirty-eighth sovereign since William the Conqueror was crowned. He is a great-grandson of Queen Victoria, who also was unmarried when she succeeded her uncle

GENEVA. Officials of the League of Nations predicted Saturday night that the greatly advertised proposed oil boycott against Italy would not see the light of day at a meeting of the council beginning Monday. Great Britain, they pointed out, seems opposed to any British initiative toward imposing new sanctions. Premier Pierre Laval of France has always regarded the oil sanction with disfavor. Soviet Russia is occupied with its appeal to the League against Uruguay's action in breaking off diplomatic relations with her. Other powers, it was said, are likely to follow the lead of the big ones.

By the Associated Press. The bachelor prince of Wales, 41, is first in line of succession to the British throne. Little Prince Edward, son of the duke and duchess of Kent, who was born Oct. 9, 1935, ranks seventh. The order: The prince of Wales. The duke of York, Princess Elizabeth (first daughter of the duke of York), Princess Margaret Rose (second daughter of the duke of York). The duke of Gloucester. The duke of Kent. Prince Edward.

Washington, Jan. 18—Inspector Arthur Bishop of Scotland Yard told reporters today that America’s kidnappings, rackets, swindles and gang crimes “couldn't happen in England.” He avoided talk of the Lindbergh case, but defended the death penalty for violent crimes. “Men show they have no right to live when they do certain things,” the inspector declared. Dressed in gray morning coat and black trousers, the man from the famous “C. I. D.” met reporters in the office of Chief Postoffice Inspector Kidray P. Aldrich. Bishop was referring to the death in the “Drake Estate swindle” case in Chicago. The first question drew a quick reply. “I can tell you that,” he smiled, “but no kidnapping in England.” “Persistence” is the secret of the bird's success,” he said. “That and the cooperation of the police. But I think that persistence is the real answer. We don't leave a case until we've got the fello

Dingwall, Scotland, Jan. 18.—() Malcolm MacDonald's effort to reenter parliament brought him a black eye tonight. The son of former Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald was being cheered by his supporters at a meeting when a snowball flung by a member of a rival party hit him in the right eye, breaking his spectacles and cutting his nose. MacDonald's eye was heavily bandaged when he addressed the meeting later.

| {Or 251” ADOVUIALIERY FRE The proposal for an oil boycott against Italy is as good as dead, officials of the League of Nations asserted Saturday night. Discussing an important meeting of the league council opening Monday, they said Great Britain, France and Russia, for various reasons, do not want to lead the drive for additional sanctions and that the smaller powers likely will follow in their trail. Italy claims a great triumph on the southern front. An official communique in Rome said the troops had pushed forward 125 miles into enemy territory and killed 5,000 Ethiopians. Newspapers estimated 3,000 had been taken prisoner. These reports were vigorously denied by Ethiopian officials in Addis Ababa, who called them “absurd.” Reliable reports from Addis Ababa received in Djibouti, French Somaliland, said a serious revolt is under way in Gojjam province of Ethiopia and that armies have

1936-12-12.text: NEW YORK, Dec. 11 (#)—Britain’s new king “Bertie,” who likes to knit and can cast an iron plate in a smelting factory, steps into the world spotlight today as a perfect example of bulldog grit overcoming terrific obstacles. He had a brooding inferiority complex. He stuttered. He had wretched health. He couldn't make friends—just couldn't “warm up.” He excelled at nothing. Nobody noticed him, in a room or a crowd. Shy, he simply didn't “register.” Even now, at the glittering climax of his “success story,” he gets the job only because his brother gave it up. But down the years, doomed to understudy his brother, in his quiet, soliloquizing way he perfected his role with dogged perseverance that must command admiration. Has Beaten the Odds. Today, at the pinnacle, he has beaten the odds. If ever a man was self-made, the record shows it is Albert Frederick Arthur George, “by the grace of God”

CANNES, France, Dec. 12.—(2)— Mrs. Wallis Simpson has not heard from Prince Edward since he left England and does not know where he is or where he is going, a spokesman for the American woman said today. NOT COMING TO CANNES He repeated his former statement that Edward is not coming to Cannes and that Mrs. Simpson is remaining at the villa of Mr. and Mrs. Herman Rogers. Lord Brownlow, once gentleman-in-waiting to the British ruler, said an automobile, which Mrs. Simpson sometimes uses for country drives, had been taken from his garage for his use during part of his return trip to London. He said he intended to leave Cannes this afternoon but may stop off on the way for a short vacation. He insisted he would not see the abdicated monarch. REFER TO DECREE “There is no reason why the former king should come here,” said a spokesman for Mrs. Simpson. “There is every reason why he cannot come.

LONDON. (Saturday). CP. Edward David Windsor of England, sailed into exile after bidding dramatic farewell to the empire he renounced for a woman. Twelve hours after becoming a private citizen, the former monarch dashed by automobile to Portsmouth, where he embarked amid the greatest of secrecy. He sailed aboard the admiralty yacht Enchantress which slipped from the harbor under sealed orders. The ex-ruler’s destination was not announced but unconfirmed reports circulated in Portsmouth he was bound for the Mediterranean. Where he would disembark was a secret closely guarded by naval authorities but most of those he left behind believed it would be some port in France, the land where Wallis Simpson waits. In the evening of Friday, the day when he ceased to be Britain's king, Edward broadcast his farewell to the half billion people in the realm he once ruled—the realm now in the hands of h

Washington, Dec. 11, (P)—The British government defaulted again today on its war debt to the United States but did not say—as in the past—that it was unable to meet its annual installment. Instead, it made a reference to new debt discussions. Every year, since the king’s government first refused to pay in 1932, its default has been accompanied by an assertion of its inability to meet the demand. The December installment due the United States from Great Britain is $117,670,765. Declining to pay over that amount, a note transmitted to R. Walton Moore, acting secretary of state, through the British ambassador, Sir Ronald Lindsay, said that “his majesty’s government will be ready to reopen discussions on the matter whenever circumstances are such as to warrant the hope that a satisfactory result might be reached.” Of thirteen debtor nations, all but Finland have been in default since 1932.
