The government, adopting the new British policy of “preventive warning” to nations that might be tempted to strike, authorized Prime Minister Yvon Delbos to announce in the chamber of dep- uties Friday that any aggression against Britain would cause im- mediate mobilization of the whole of France's land, air and naval strength. The same guarantee will apply to Belgium. Big Navy Program France's declaration is to be backed up, it was learned, by the introduction in parliament of a supplementary 15,000,000,000 franc ($700,000,000) navy pro- gram, on top of the gigantic navy, army and air force expen- ditures already envisa

MADRID, Nov. 28.—-()—Artillery shells dropped near the British embassy today and sent citizens scurrying for cover as clearing skies brought a renewal of the Fascist-Socialist battle for possession of Madrid. The shells were from Fascist batteries, the government said, and the Socialist troops turned their big guns against the Casa De Campo region across the Manzanares river from the capital. The shells falling near the British embassy dropped into Fernando El Santo street which the militia and pedestrians had considered comparatively safe. Shrapnel sprayed the street to a point within a few yards of the embassy gates. Meanwhile, the Fascist insurgents launched a new offensive from Valverde, a short distance south of Madrid along the Aranjuez road, Their attack was supported by mortar crews and machine gunners but was unsuccessful, the government said. The Madrid militia in a counter-att

LONDON. (®) Great Britain prepared for possible war with the appointment of a food committee to guard her supplies and ordered the British cabinet to "alert duty" for emergency sessions over the weekend. The new food defense plans department was designated to work with the board of trade and the minister for co-ordination of defense. H. L. French, secretary to the ministry of agriculture, was named director. The food department was designed to assure a food supply in the event of a blockade of English ports during war. The "second line of defense," topped by the navy, estimated needs for a 12 month reserve supply at 3,650,000 tons of wheat, 5,000,000 tons of potatoes, 2,250,000 tons of onions, 1,250,000 tons of cheese, 625,000 tons of butter or substitutes and uncounted tons of milk. The government kept clear of official statements on the newest Spanish crisis. Evacuation of non-combatan

(Copyright, 1936, by United Press) LONDON, Nov. 26—(UP)—The British cabinet's surprise meeting yesterday was devoted to discussion of the divorce of Mrs. Wallis Simpson, American-born friend of King Edward VIII, responsible British sources said today. It was reliably understood that the urgent cabinet session was called as a result of many letters—according to one version, hundreds of letters—which the king’s proctor received challenging the granting of a decree nisi to Mrs. Simpson at the Ipswich Assizes. The letters, it was reported, urged the king’s proctor to intervene and prevent the decree from becoming absolute at the end of the prescribed six months’ period. It is the duty of the proctor to investigate if a decree is challenged, and annul it if he finds collusion~ (Concluded on Page 5, Column 3)

LONDON. (7), Capt. James A. Mollison announced he and Co-Pilot Edouard Corniglion-Moliniers would take off Sunday morning on an attempted one stop flight to Capetown, South Africa, if the weather permits. Mollison said they hoped to reach Cairo, Egypt, before nightfall for their only halt. Mollison has been planning the Capetown flight, in an effort to break the record held by his wife, Amy Johnson Mollison, since he landed in England, Oct. 30, at the end of a record shattering eastward Atlantic hop.

By The Associated Press Geneva — Great Britain and France were represented tonight as desiring to keep the Spanish civil war from League of Nations consideration lest new threats to international peace result from bitter public debate. The two nations felt the European neutrality committee should continue to deal unhampered with the civil war crisis, League circles declared. The Spanish government asked the League council yesterday to consider what it termed a menace to world peace created by Italo-German recognition of the Insurgent Fascists now besieging Madrid. The League council would meet in Geneva early in December to consider a course of action unless Franco-British pressure succeeded in allowing the European committee to handle the troublous problem alone. At best, League sources said, the council would pass a resolution declaring danger to world peace as a result of the civil co

VIRGINIA WATER, England (UP)—King Edward VII, an old sword in one hand and a hatchet in the other, slaughtered weeds right and left as he worked in the garden of Fort Belvedere Saturday with Mrs. Wallis Simpson. Both the king and Mrs. Simpson are keenly interested in gardening and plan together how to improve the grounds of the king’s estate. LONDON. (AP) — Reports may be true that the friendship between King Edward and Mrs. Wallis Simpson is to become a more formal one—but Mrs. Simpson still uses the “garden gate” entrance to Buckingham Palace, the one which members of the royal family use themselves. Mrs. Simpson drives in at the front gates of the palace. The red-coated guardsmen on duty do not salute. The car passes across the palace courtyard to the right-hand side. At the moment it arrives, policemen swing open the big oaken nail-studded double gates, set in the brick wall of the g

1936-12-27.text: LONDON, Dec. 27 (Sunday) — Germany’s ultimatum of the Spanish socialist government and the Europe-wide discussion of prospects for return of some of the Reich’s pre-war colonies Saturday gave the British government two new items for anxious study in Europe's crisis. Berlin's threat of unspecified “reprisals” against the Madrid-Valencia regime if the steamer Palos is not released immediately introduced a fresh disturbing element into an already ominous situation, London officials said. A foreign office spokesman characterized the outlook as “disquieting,” but expressed hope a satisfactory adjustment can be made. Suggestions that some of her former colonies be returned as one means of lessening the Reich's economic difficulties and thereby aligning Germany on the side of peace evoked reiteration of the official British contention that all such questions must be handled through the League o

LONDON, Dec. 26 (P) -- England's newest royal baby may be called Mary, it was reported tonight, because that is the name of the queen mother and because she was born on Christmas. The child, sixth in line of succession to the throne, and her mother, the duchess of Kent, were said to be “doing very well.”

LONDON, Dec. 26.—(7)—With Edward in self-exile and a king no more, superstitious Englishmen are recalling incidents which they now dub omens of a brief unhappy reign. First they place the mishap to the imperial crown during King George the Fifth’s funeral procession. As the gun-carriage bearing the body rattled through the sanded streets to Westminster Hall for the lying-in-state, the Maltese cross surmounting the crown worked loose and fell into the road. An officer of the escort picked it up, found it damaged and put it in his pocket. To the superstitious this was portent number one. Next came the disastrous scenes on the day of the state funeral procession, when the route was so thickly jammed with spectators that many were injured and police arrangements for a time broke down. When King Edward began to make his first public appearances, hundreds commented on the fact that he failed t

TOKYO, Dec. 27. (Sunday) (4— The Domei (Japanese) news agency reported today the town of Nishima, in the Tokyo prefecture, was destroyed in an earthquake at 8:15 a. m. today (7:15 p. m. Saturday E. S. T.) It said the casualties were not known. The earthquake, which was exceptionally severe, had its center at the bottom of the sea near Oshima, Chiba prefecture. A number of houses ashore collapsed and the shock was followed by many landslides. The official meteorological bureau described the earthquake as one of the strongest ever recorded in Japan.

BERLIN, Dec. 26,—(A”)—Germany hinted tonight that return of her colonial empire would do much to lessen the danger of European war and solve the crisis over foreign aid to Spanish civil war combatants. Chancellor Hitler's frequently voiced desire for colonies to supply raw materials, increased in fervor by the current lack of many food supplies, was discussed in Paris over (Continued on ‘Page 10, Col. 4.)

Rome, Dec. 26. — (A?) — Efforts were begun tonight to raise the 8,000-ton steamship Cesare Battisti which sank in the Massaua, Italian Eritrea, harbor after an explosion in which 26 were killed and 100 injured. Of the injured, 20 were in critical condition. The ship had to be raised, officials decided, to clear the harbor. The explosion started a fire which spread along the waterfront and destroyed several buildings, including the offices of the port authority. An official communique issued at Rome stated: “The explosion tore the vessel open amidships and the ship sank near the dock. Twenty-six persons were killed and 100 injured, of whom 20 are in a serious condition. “Identification of the victims was delayed because all documents aboard the steamer were destroyed.”

Nanking, Dec. 26. —— (P) Generalissimo Chiang Kai-Shek, restored to his place as leader of the Chinese nation, announced tonight he would recommend that the government deal leniently with Marshal Chang, penitent leader of the rebellion in northwestern China that ended yesterday with the generalissimo’s release. Marshal Chang, arriving here ‘to face the music,’ declared himself “ready to suffer whatever the government desires, whether it be death or not.” In a letter to the generalissimo the former rebel leader said, “I realize my wickedness and my sin against you and the nation.” He referred to the rebellion against the central government he launched at Siantu, Shensi province, December 12, and to his holding General Chiang a prisoner there for thirteen days. In Plane Marshal Chang was brought to the capital by airplane this afternoon from Loyang, Honan province, whither he had flown wit

KELLOGG, Idaho, Dec. 26 (UP).— A tired trapper mushed into Kellogg today to report he and three other men had found the wreckage of a long-sought Northwest Airlines transport in the snow-mantled north Idaho mountains but not the bodies of the two pilots who apparently died in the smash-up eight days ago. "I know it was the plane because I touched it," said Fred Cunningham, the trapper. "The wreckage was covered with snow and only portions of the fuselage were sticking out. Found In Snow Cunningham said he did not attempt to locate the bodies of Pilots Joe Livermore and Arthur A. Haid and did not pry into the wreck pending the arrival of postal inspectors to care for the mail involved. The trapper said the wreck lay in three to four feet of snow near the top of an unnamed ridge 15 miles south of here, not far from 6000-foot high Cemetery Ridge about which the search had centered since las

1936-10-30.text: LONDON, Oct. 30.—()—King Edward told his Parliament today the British government has “spared no pain” to check the brutality of the Spanish war and to keep it within its Iberian boundaries. In his first address to the Parliament as sovereign, the monarch declared: “I have viewed with concern and anxiety the events in Spain during the last three months.” The speech was read by the Earl of Onslow, acting as Lord Chancellor in the illness of Viscount Hailsham, on the occasion of prorogation of Parliament. The king himself was not present. He will open the new Parliament in state on next Tuesday. “I am addressing you for the first time as sovereign,” the king’s speech said. “I desire before all to express once more my deep appreciation of the sympathy which has been extended to me and my dear mother in every part of my dominions. “I have viewed with concern and anxiety the events in Spain du

—_— a EE SE SS eS Harbor Grace, Nfld., Oct. 29.— Defying adverse weather, Captain James A. Mollison headed tonight across the Atlantic with the hope of breakfasting in London. Thrice conqueror of the Atlantic, the noted British long-distance flier sought to establish a new record in spanning the storm-tossed ocean on a 2,100-mile flight. He lifted his speedy Bellanca monoplane from the ground here at 3:40 p.m. (EST) after stating he hoped to reach Croydon Airdrome, near London, in between 10 and 12 hours. 250-Mile Cruising Speed. Having taken six hours and 41 minutes yesterday to reach Harbor Grace from New York, he had 10 hours and 49 minutes in which to reach Croydon and still make good his hope to bridge the distance between New York and London in 17½ hours actual flying time. The “Dorothy,” as he has named his plane for “a very dear friend,” carried 610 gallons of gasoline for the At

(By Associated Press) London, Oct. 30—A stern British warning voiced by Sir Samuel Hoare, first lord of the Admiralty, today told the Moscow-dominated “Comintern” (Communist international organization) not to interfere with affairs in England. “It is almost always disastrous to interfere in the affairs of other countries,” Sir Samuel declared, addressing a West End meeting. “I commend that observation to agents of the Comintern. They will find the more they interfere in the domestic affairs of this country the worse it will react against their activities.” Sir Samuel’s statement, carrying with it the weight of official authority, followed the government's firm declaration in the House of Commons that non-intervention in Spain must be preserved to prevent chaos in Europe.

LONDON, Oct. 20, — (7) — Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin declared in Parliament tonight that the British government felt the Spanish non-Intervention pact had been broken by foreign sympathizers with both factions in the civil war. “The general impression the government has formed,” he said, “is that there have been some breaches, and arms sent to both sides. But they have not been anything near sufficient importance to cause us to modify our policy in regard to non-Intervention.” Defends Portugal. (Copyright, 1936, United Press) LONDON; Oct. 30 (P)—Mrs. Wallis Simpson was King Edward's guest at a dinner party at Buckingham Palace Wednesday night—the first time they had seen each other since her divorce the day before, it was learned today. It was described as a “very, very private” party and after the dinner, it was understood, the king escorted Mrs. Simpson to her home at 16 Cumberland Terrace. Gardening Is Link Gardening is the link that binds the friendship of the king and Mrs. Simpson, friends in court circles said today. As a result of the mutual liking for flowers, and for tending them, the friends reported, King Edward, in a pair of old gray flannel trousers and a turtle neck sweater, may soon be seen in the gardens of Buckingham Palace, making them simpler and less formal. Mrs. Simpson is expected to be there, the friends said, giving on the scene suggestions which she alr

British government leaders Thursday night in the House of Commons, briskly defended the in-peace agreement. Meanwhile, in Spain, according to authoritative Spanish Socialist sources in Paris, the Madrid government has concentrated a secret army equipped with tanks and war planes for a rear attack on the fascist forces besieging Madrid. In a day-long counter offensive Socialist troops regained at least three towns and claimed two more were virtually within their grasp. Spain's government announced cryptically it had “everything necessary for victory,” meaning new fascist ammunition and food, and began what it described as a successful counter attack on the press. Urgents, however, maintained Madrid would fall quickly. The government announcement came on the heels of Italian protests against Russian violation of the neutrality agreement and listing of incidents in which Russia pressed for

LONDON, Oct. 29 (#)—There was not a single copy of American newspapers dated Oct. 16, 17, and 18 for sale on the largest international newspaper stands in London tonight. Those dates immediately followed upon the announcement of Mrs. Wallis Warfield Simpson's divorce suit. It was also disclosed that four pages would be ripped from Time magazine which appears on stands here Tuesday.

Croydon, England, Oct. 30 (CINS) — Exhausted, on the point of collapse, James Mollison zoomed into Croydon airdrome today in record time for his fourth transatlantic crossing. Straining his Bellanca monoplane to its utmost speed to make his goal just before he broke under the stress, Mollison flew from Harbor Grace, Newfoundland, in 13 hours, 19 minutes. Risking his life merely to deliver a plane in Cape Town, South Africa, Mollison sped in hazardous out-of-season flying weather through snow, sleet, rain, and fog, battling an ocean blizzard and performing aerial gymnastics to get rid of ice on his wings. He kept up his wild speed to the last second, swinging over London's chief airport at more than 100 miles an hour, circling five times, and setting his plane down at 9:53 a.m. (4:53 a.m. EST). 1936-06-24.text: LONDON, June 24. — (#) — Great Britain led today the procession of nations agreed to drop sanctions against Italy. With 14 votes more than expected, Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin's government received official approval from the House of Commons to recommend suspension of the war penalties to the League of Nations. The vote, after extended debate, gave the government a 384 to 170 victory, sending a labor motion to censure to defeat. Criticized for his turn-about policy of first demanding sanctions for Italian aggression against Ethiopia and then recommending their cancellation, Prime Minister Baldwin wound up the government’s case personally. He acknowledged the League “has received a bad setback” but quickly added: “Failure in the first attempt to apply collective security in no wise means the death of the League. We must see how far we can make collective security a reality.” The attit

Missionaries were ordered to evacuate danger areas Wednesday when extensive troop movements indicated the imminent outbreak of hostilities between central government forces in southern Hunan province created an electric situation, deemed likely to jeopardize the lives of foreigners. British consular authorities instructed missionaries at Kweilin to establish a concentration center. Missionaries at Yungchow were instructed to evacuate to Kweilin. Reports from Kiyang said that Nanking troops concentrating in southern Hunan preparatory to an offensive against General Li Tsungjen’s and General Pei Tsung-Hsi’s forces now are separated from the Kwangsi armies by only a few miles. General Chen Chi-Fang, head of the autonomous Canton government, has doubled the strength of his troops on the Guangdong province borders against the expected central government invasion from Fukien.

HOYLAKE, England June 24. (P)— Henry Cotton, the favorite, led the 36-hole qualifying test in the British open golf championship here today with a total of 139. His 71 over the Wallasey course today added to his record-breaking 68 at Hoylake yesterday put him four shots ahead of Gene Sarazen, the American favorite, who shot a 72 over Wallasey today, and Percy Alliss, British Ryder cup star, who had a 74 over the same course. Two American professionals, Ted Turner, Pine Valley, and Willie Goggin, San Francisco, also assured themselves of qualifying. Turner shot a 72 over the difficult Hoylake course for a total of 146, while Goggin’s 73 at Wallasey gave him a score of 150. Errie Ball, Mobile, Ala., made a fine comeback today. He posted a 74 at Wallasey and appeared reasonably sure of qualifying with a total of 154.

HURLINGHAM CLUB, London, June 24 (P)—Using a revamped lineup, America’s polo team trounced Great Britain, 15 to 9, in the third and final game of the international series. The match was, in effect, an exhibition, for America had clinched the international trophy by winning the first two games of the series.

London, June 24. (/P)—Viscount Cranborne, undersecretary of state for foreign affairs, told an inquiring member of commons today "no plans, either for an Italian attack on Egypt or of any other description," were found in the burned wreckage of an Italian plane near Cairo last August. The questioner was Geoffrey Mander, opposition liberal. We then asked Lord Cranborne: "Is he able to say that no document of this kind was found in any Italian airplane during the summer months of last year?" Cranborne replied: "I should like notice of that question, because it is not the same question." He meant Mander should file formal notice of his inquiry with the speaker, for reply at a later sitting. Mander agreed. Today’s reply to the widely-circulated Mander’s question came after prime minister Stanley Baldwin's government, with 14 votes more than it had expected, received approval from the house o

| CONVENTION HALL, Philadelphia, (UP) - New Dealers hit the | back against the London-Knox t last night after they were roused to fighting fury at the Democratic national convention by a keynote orator whose knuckles bled from hammering the sprak- ers’ stand. Senator Alben W. Barkley, a free-swinging orator from Ken- tucky, commanded the party to charge! and not stand idle in the trenches and await the Repu- blican attack. Delegates went | wild, swept the standards off their bases and marched and counter- marched in the most turbulent demonstration seen in either convention. Governor George I. Biddle of Pennsylvania, billed as a se- cond string orator, captured the imagination of the delegates when he said he had deserted the Re- publcians several years ago because they were “the party of predatory wealth.” Ride on Donkeys Men rode donkeys into the Au- ditorium on this wild night in whic

PARIS. June 23, —(@— Premier Leon Blum’s government announced today it would attempt to hasten the negotiation of three regional mutual assistance pacts to safeguard Europe against war. One pact, based on the Locarno treaty, would apply to Western Europe. The other two would embrace the countries of the Danube Basin and the countries along the Mediterranean. Premier Blum personally read to the Senate a declaration in which was explained France's willingness to remove sanctions against Italy. Yvon Delbos, foreign minister, read the same declaration to the Chamber of Deputies.

PARIS (47) — Fear of international isolation haunted France today as she slowly emerged from internal strife. The Socialist government, encouraged by a 382 to 198 parliamentary vote of confidence, struck out vigorously to strengthen its position among European nations. Premier Leon Blum carried forward a double drive to bind France more firmly to her present allies through regional security pacts which would, in their turn, fortify the League of Nations collective peace agreement. A few fresh strikes and renewed clashes between Leftists and Nationalists complicated the domestic situation, but Roger Salengro, minister of the interior, assured the cabinet firm measures would bring an end to the internal struggles. Openly fearful France may be left out if Great Britain, Germany and Italy settle their differences, Blum advanced two proposals to bolster European relations. The first would per

1936-08-12.text: PLYMOUTH, Eng., Aug. 11 (U.?)— Mark Weston, 30, the former woman athlete, Edith Weston, who underwent a sex change operation two months ago—was married yesterday to Alberta Bray, for years his girl friend while he still was a girl. They were married secretly at the Plymouth registrar's office, Weston was one of England's greatest “women” athletes until surgeons informed him he had the option of remaining a woman or becoming a man. It was said the possibility of marriage to Miss Bray was one of the reasons that impelled him to seek complete masculinity, Two operations were performed at Charing Cross Hospital after which Weston, who had held the women's shot put and javelin titles, was given a certificate which read: “Mr. Mark Weston, who was always brought up as a female, is male and should continue life as such,”

BERLIN, Aug. 12 (4°—The University of Washington won the first heat in the Olympic eight-oared rowing competition today, defeating Great Britain in a split-second finish to set a new course record of six minutes and eight-tenths of a second. Jack Medica gave the United States its first swimming victory in winning the 400-meter freestyle championship in four minutes and 44.5 seconds, clipping one second off the former Olympic mark. Majorie Gestring of Los Angeles and her two teammates swept the springboard diving championship. The United States basketball team soundly defeated the Philippines in a second Olympic test.

BERLIN, Aug. 12—(UP)—Ger- man officials regard a decree for an increase in Russia's vast army as a new, dangerous complication in Europe's troublous affairs, it was learned today. Joachim von Ribbentrop, new German ambassador to Great Britain, is expected to cite the army increase in an effort to enlist British cooperation in Germany's opposition to the French and Czechoslovakian military treaties with Russia. If Britain agreed to support the German argument, one of the greatest single aims of German foreign policy would have been achieved. Russia’s announced increase was called another move in an effort to force Russian influence on Europe—a continent, in the official German belief, to which Russia rightly does not even belong. It was argued that Russia's move comes at a time when tension over the Spanish revolt is producing charges and counter charges that various nations are assisting

MADRID, Aug. 12—()—Spain’s northern seaboard was the focal point today for the government's drive to crush the Fascist revolution in the face of a smashing attack by the rebels to break through to the sea. Madrid looked upon prospective capture of the rebel stronghold of Oviedo, in the northwest, as the beginning of a “great turn” in its efforts to crush the rebellious forces. Immediate attacks afterward on Cordoba and Granada, in southern Spain, were scheduled. The government said rebels in Cordoba, Granada and Seville had been without electricity and water for 24 days. The rebels, attempting to install a Fascist-complexioned regime in Madrid to replace the present Communist-Socialist government in the infant republic, were not idle. Dispatches from Tangier indicated the troops of the rebel generalissimo, Francisco Franco, were under orders to begin their major drive on Madrid from the

(Copyright, 1996, By The Associated Press) DELLACH, Austria, Aug. 12— Former King Alfonso may try to fly back to war-torn Spain. He called his two sons, Jaime and Juan, into family council today to decide their course. What the three agreed to do, the exiled monarch would not say. "As long as the disturbances continue," he told the Associated Press, "I cannot discuss my plans." The one-time monarch, stripped of his regal prerogatives in the revolution of 1931, seemed perturbed when told that an airplane flown to him in Czechoslovakia by an English pilot was confiscated at Innsbruck yesterday. It was rumored that the machine, nevertheless, would be taken to Venice to fly Alfonso to Spain at the moment such a move appeared to be propitious.

Rebels reach Tolosa on road to San Sebastian. Loyalists capture Adamuz, near Cordoba, in vigorous offensive against southern Fascists. Two rebel leaders condemned to death at Barcelona. France may ask United States to join neutrality pact. Thirty-eight Americans board warship at Valencia after flight from Madrid, Madrid, Aug. 11. (P)—The government’s air force tonight launched an intense bombardment of all rebel concentration lines and reported many Fascist forces disorganized and in retreat, Rebel rear guards, the government said, were so severely damaged that in their haste to retreat they had placed their fronts in grave danger. One of the strongest air drives was against Pozoblanco, key point of the loyalist attack on Cordoba in the south. Attacks also were launched against Jaen and Granada. (Copyright, 1936, by The Associated Press) BY BARON BLARDONY MADRID, Aug. 12.—The Spanish government staked its life today on two desperate offensives on shell-shredded fronts of the nation’s civil war. On the northern seaboard and in the south government militia fought with two objectives: To prevent Fascist rebels from controlling the area bordering the Bay of Biscay, and to stop in its tracks a blood-drenched rebel drive on Madrid. Major Drive Today In the northwest Madrid’s militia smashed relentlessly toward capture of Oviedo to effect a “great turn” in the drive to suppress the Fascist rebellion. In the south, concentration point for thousands of Moroccan troops brought from North Africa by the rebel general, Francisco Franco, for the offensive against Madrid, government militia harried the insurgents in the Cordoba, Granada and Seville areas. Copenhagen, Aug. 11 (#)—Col. Charles A. Lindbergh, in his first public appearance as a scientist, and Dr. Alexis Carrel today displayed their mechanical heart to eager, excited members of the International Congress of Experimental Cytology. Scientists pushed into a small room to learn intricacies of the apparatus by which organs of the body can be kept alive indefinitely for observation and study. Dr. Carrel, who supplied technical knowledge for construction of the heart, answered questions in French. Col. Lindbergh, who developed the mechanical apparatus, explained its details in English. The exhibit will be open the remainder of the week. The program was held up because the Colonel could find no thyroid gland necessary to make the heart work. Finally, a cat was located, deprived of the thyroid, and the show went on. The scientists asked questions excitedly, and peered intently through

1936-07-01.text: GENEVA, July 1 —(UP). Anthony Eden, British foreign secretary, asked the assembly of the League of Nations today to refuse to recognize Italy's conquest of Ethiopia. At the same time he urged the dropping of sanctions against Italy because of the failure of the League machinery to halt the war in Ethiopia. Eden suggested that a reform of the covenant might be considered usefully at the September assembly. Eden's address followed one by Premier Leon Blum of France, who, admitting the League's failure in the Ethiopian affair, suggested that Europe has returned to a situation similar to that of 1914. He asked for prompt action to preserve peace and declared ominously that France would not remain passive if her soil or that of her allies is invaded. Eden informed the Assembly that Britain's special Mediterranean obligation resulting from the Italian-Ethiopian war would not be discontinued un

WIMBLEDON, England, July 1 (P).—Fred Perry, bidding for his third straight title, gained the final round of the all-England tennis championship today as he came from behind to trim California's Don Budge, 5-7, 6-4, 6-3, 6-4. For the second straight year Perry's opponent in the final, to be played Friday, will be Baron Gottfried Von Cramm, Germany's Davis Cup star. Von Cramm defeated Perry's cup mate, H. W. (Bunny) Austin, 8-6, 6-3, 2-6, 6-3, in the other semi-final match.

WIMBLEDON, Eng., (U. P.)— Frederick J. Perry of England, No. 1 in the world, and Baron Gottfried Von Cramm of Germany today gained the final round of the All-England tennis championships for the second successive year. Perry, seeking his third straight Wimbledon title, defeated Donald Budge, California youngster, 5-7, 6-4, 6-3, 6-4, while Von Cramm halted Wilfred H. (Bunny) Austin, Perry’s Davis cup partner, 8-6, 6-3, 2-6, 6-3.

Dublin, Irish Free State, June 30 (P)—The question of Anglo-Irish relations was pushed to the forefront and subjected to serious discussion in Dublin today in connection with Great Britain's “war scare” and hasty plans for complete rearmament. While President Eamon De Valera was in Geneva to discuss sanctions, other officials talked over the possibility of a settlement of long-standing problems. The matter is not dormant in London either. Emanuel Shinwell, Laborite member of the House of Commons, tomorrow will ask the Dominions minister whether negotiations for the settlement of outstanding difficulties are proceeding between the British and Free State governments and whether there is any prospect for an early settlement.

GENEVA, July 1—(UP)—Confessing the League of Nations failure in the Italo-Ethiopian crisis, Premier Leon Blum of France, in his maiden speech at Geneva, said today Europe had returned to a situation equivalent to that prevailing in 1914. Plagued by new Italian and Argentine threats to quit the League and shamed by Emperor Haile Selassie’s denunciation for its failure to prevent conquest of his empire, the assembly was amazed by the vigor of Blum’s speech. He denied that strikes in France and French failure to mobilize after Germany’s remilitarization of the Rhineland were signs of weakness. “Does anybody think our reaction would have been the same if they (the Germans) touched our soil or the soil of the others we guarantee?” Blum asked the startled world statesmen. Blum declared France wants peace. But, he said, this does not mean that she will be silent before force or recognize victor

Paris, July 1—4)—Striking opera performers danced on the stage of the closed opera Comique today with police guards for an audience. The entire company voted last night to begin an “occupation strike” shortly after the curtain fell on the last performance of the season. The professional walkout added one more worry to the harassed socialist government, whose decision to dissolve Rightist Leagues was upheld by the Chamber of Deputies after vociferous debate. The chamber approved the government decree against the four nationalist organizations by a vote of 375 to 192.

PARIS, June 30—(Ar) - France’s new Leftist People’s Front government won another vote of confidence in the Chamber of Deputies tonight after hours of bitter debate in which Rightists and Leftists exchanged threats and charges. The cabinet of Premier Leon Blum was upheld, 375 to 192, on so-called Fascist Rightist leagues. Government fears of grave disorders and Rightist threats of insur-

(Associated Press Foreign Staff) GENEVA, July 1—Premier Leon Blum of France indicated to the League of Nations assembly today that France will not recognize Italy’s annexation of Ethiopia. The socialist government head declared France would not give absolution constituting encouragement of actions contrary to the right. He warned that only through general disarmament could the spectre of war be dissipated. France, said Blum, was dedicated to the search for peace and, consequently, had not resorted to arms when Germany put troops into the Rhineland. However, he gave notice: "France preferred peace procedure, but things would be different if anyone dared to attack France on her own soil." Blum spoke softly, after the manner of a professor, and his words held the members of the assembly in attentive silence. He said the world's people wish to be relieved of the great insomnia of war. 1936-04-11.text: Plymouth, Eng., April 10.—Detectives were called tonight to investigate suspected sabotage on the submarine L-54 at the Devonport dockyard. It was the ninth reported case of suspected international damage to British vessels since last autumn. A large spanner, or wrench, was found under the casing of the submarine’s main motor, half an hour after the electrical equipment had been examined, it was learned.

PORT-OF-SPAIN, Trinidad, April 11 (AP).—Three persons drowned today when the Pan-American Airways Brazilian Clipper turned over in the harbor in an attempt to avoid a fishing boat as the plane was taking off. The dead, including two passengers and one member of the crew, were: Eric Brogh, London, Eng., passenger. E. Roman Martinez, New York City, passenger. Lopez, steward. The plane sank after it had "ground looped" on the water and was almost totally submerged. The accident occurred at 5:30 a.m. local time (4:30 a.m., E.S.T.) The Brazilian Clipper type ships, until the advent of the ton heavier Martin-built craft, the largest airliners in the world, were built to carry 35 passengers and 2,000 pounds of mail, baggage and express. The wings measure 114 feet and two inches, and the metal hull is 68 feet from nose to rudder. The planes fly at a cruising speed of 160 miles an hour. The take-

WASHINGTON, April 10. (P)—The United States and Great Britain today were engaged in a survey of Anglo-American trade, which may result in negotiations of a reciprocal trade pact with this country’s biggest customer. A highly authoritative quarter disclosed also that preliminary discussions designed to explore the feasibility and possibility of concluding an agreement, actually are under way both in Washington and London. Administration authorities emphasized, however, that no actual negotiations have started, and as yet there has been no discussion involving specific commodities, or tariff rates. Under the trade agreements act, Secretary Hull must make public announcement of intention to negotiate prior to any actual negotiations, in order to give time for submission of data on commodities by all interested parties. Conclusion of a trade pact with Great Britain would constitute a major s

GENEVA, April 11. U.P)—Two of Europe's gravest post-war problems, the reoccupation by Germany of the Rhineland and the Ethiopian problem, and of British, French, Belgian and Italian delegates as representatives of Locarno treaty nations, did nothing to bring nearer a solution of either matter. Great Britain and France remained completely divergent both on the Rhineland and Italian matters. It was arranged that Salvador De Madariaga of Spain should talk to Italian and Ethiopian delegates Tuesday on peace possibilities, and that the committee of 13 should meet next Thursday to hear Madariaga’s report. Britain threatened to demand new penalties against Italy if—as was expected—Italy refused to agree to peace on terms acceptable to the League. Great Britain was left to negotiate with Germany on the Rhineland problem and a program of peace consolidation, pending a meeting of the League Counci

ANKARA, Turkey.— (*) —The Turkish government, taking a long-expected step, asked signatories of the Lausanne treaty Friday night to amend clauses of the Straits Convention to allow her to re-fortify the Dardanelles. Foreign Minister Aras handed the note to diplomatic representatives of the signatory powers stating the Turkish government's decision.

Friedrichshafen, Germany, April 10.—(AP)—Germany's giant new airship, the Hindenburg, was stowed away safely in its hangar tonight after a return trip across the South Atlantic during which two of the dirigible’s four motors went out of commission. The flight up the French Rhone valley, under special permission from the French air ministry, was accomplished without incident and the huge ship landed at 6:30 p.m. (German time) to complete its round trip to Rio de Janeiro. Never in Danger Capt. Ernst Lehmann, the dirigible’s commander, denied the 38 passengers and crew of 40 had ever been in danger on the return flight.

MOSCOW, April 10.—(AP)—A new patrol clash on the Soviet-Manchoukuo frontier was reported tonight in Soviet dispatches after the government here charged its embassy in Tokyo was held in a "veritable blockade." An undisclosed number of trespassers, in the dispatches said, were discovered 1,000 yards inside Soviet territory by a frontier patrol of six Thursday. Refused to Halt When the Russians ordered the others to halt, the accounts continued, the trespassers opened fire and after 20 minutes of fighting retired to Manchoukue. The clash took place at a spot known as Sosnovaya Piat. The dispatches, from Kharbarovsk, did not state whether the trespassers wore uniforms, and did not mention casualties. Japanese sources here confirmed Russian claims several Japanese employees of the Soviet embassy in Tokyo had been arrested, but said they were merely being "detained" pending legal proceedings.

(Associated Press Foreign Staff) Rome, April 10 (4)—Marshal Pietro Badoglio’s blackshirts in Ethiopia drove to within 60 miles of the stronghold of Dessye tonight as Fascist statesmen attempted to puzzle out what they called ‘confused’ conciliation efforts at Geneva. In the face of fresh Italian advances, the diplomats at the capital, informed sources declared, expressed a willingness to enter peace negotiations but asserted ‘we do not know what Geneva wants.’ The success or failure of the peace attempts apparently lay with Salvador de Madariaga, Spanish delegate to the League of Nations who was entrusted with canvassing Italian and Ethiopian replies to a league appeal for peace. One well-informed source said Premier Mussolini had asked Madariaga to come to Rome after the Easter holidays to discuss conciliation plans but so far had not received an answer from the arbiter. 1936-06-16.text: LONDON—(U.P.)—Amid controversy on the merits of a shift in foreign policy, the cabinet prepared today to face the House of Commons Thursday and defend its decision to support abolition of league sanctions against Italy. The cabinet will meet formally Wednesday to ratify the recommendations of its Foreign Affairs Committee, which Monday night voted against continuing sanctions. It will discuss the defense of its new policy to be made by Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden, who has agreed to House of Commons debate on foreign affairs Thursday. The procedure was believed satisfactory to Premier Benito Mussolini, but the government, mindful of the controversy it has precipitated, was reported ready to make its anti-sanctions attitude more palatable to British league enthusiasts by withholding recognition of Italy's annexation of Ethiopia. The disturbed European situation was believed responsible

LONDON (P) — Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden intends to support—if not actually propose—lifting of sanctions against Italy, political circles believed today. Interest in the war penalties question heightened as the British cabinet was called to meet tomorrow to determine the government's official attitude for announcement in the House of Commons Thursday. Despite an increasing clamor from opposition quarters, the government seemed assured of a majority if it proposes immediate suspension of the sanctions. Two semi-official opinions in favor of this move were on record to guide the ministers’ course. The conservative, private members committee, the most influential bloc of government supporters in the Commons, debated the proposition last night without a single voice raised in support of continued sanctions. Many of the 80 members of parliament at the session lauded what they called the “c
Washington, June 16 (AP)—The White House announced today President Roosevelt would be unable to go to New London, Conn., for the Harvard-Yale boat race Friday because of the congressional situation.

AUGUSTA, Me. June 16.— (UP) — Secretary of State Lewis O. Barrows won the Republican gubernatorial nomination today by a substantial margin over Blin W. Page, Skowhegan banker endorsed by the Townsend organization, returns from yesterday’s primary showed today. With only a few scattered precincts missing, Barrows was leading by more than 19,000 votes.

Paris, June 15.—(/?)—A drive in two directions against 'enemies of the regime' was begun tonight by the new leftist French government, determined not to allow an ebbing strike movement get out of hand. Police raided officials of a newspaper allegedly owned by Leon Trotsky, exiled Soviet leader. The government charges the paper attempted to turn the strike movement into a revolution. Indictments against followers of the Bolshevik were drafted by a public prosecutor. Minister of the Interior Roger Salengro, after drafting decrees aimed at 'seditious organizations,' announced he would ask President Albert Lebrun to sign them at once. No Favorites Through this step, the government will strike both at the rightist Croix de Feu, semifascist organization of World War veterans, and extreme leftists, if necessary. Labor conditions were said to be nearing normal gains after 21 days of the walkout.

PARIS, June 16.—()—France’s socialist government countered threats of rightist civil war and communistic revolution with vigorous prosecution today. Its lessening strike worries complicated by armed rightists and “foreign influences,” the cabinet invoked two actions: 1. Stringent application of laws dissolving “armed political leagues,” directed specifically against the Croix de Feu (fiery cross). 2. Indictment and prosecution of extreme leftists on charges of attempting to turn the labor disputes into an economic revolution. “The Croix de Feu is the army of big capital,” charged Premier Leon Blum's newspaper, Le Populaire, “it is armed and preparing for civil war.” Other leftist publications accused the rightists of preparing to make desperate efforts to prevent the program of the Socialist people's front government from being carried out.

BRUSSELS, June 16.—(UP)— Troops were summoned to duty to assure maintenance of essential public services today as striking Belgian workers increased to 220,680. As soon as electrical supply workers walked out in Brussels, soldiers took their places. Meanwhile, public service employees went on strike in Liege and Herstal. Dock workers in Ghent decided to walk out tonight, following the example of harbor workers at Antwerp. Premier Paul Van Zeeland’s new government ordered drastic precautions to prevent violence by workers striking for wages and working hours concessions similar to those won in the just-ended great French walkout.

BRUSSELS (#) — Belgian troops were ordered mobilized today to protect public services as the ranks of striking workmen neared 200,000. The mayor of the fortified city of Liege, where first clashes occurred yesterday, prohibited assemblies on the streets. A panic-stricken public, faced with shutdown of stores and shops, rushed to purchase necessary provisions before all commerce was suspended. Overnight the strikers' movement was joined by more than 20,000 workmen. Their demands are, in almost all instances, for higher wages. Miners at Limburg and Charleroi were expected to walk out. New strikers among river boat crews joined dockworkers who went out several weeks ago. Shoemakers at Liege voted to join the movement.

1936-05-14.text: Aboard The Zeppelin Hindenburg, En Route To Germany, May 12. (A) —Dr. Hugo Eckener, after predicting a 40-hour flight by the Zeppelin Hindenburg from Lakehurst, N. J., to the English Channel, hit today at critics of arrangements at Lakehurst to handle the giant airliner. A small group was discussing what one called “primitive” arrangements at Lakehurst when Dr. Eckener, president of the Zeppelin company, said sharply: “Do you realize what a tremendous debt we owe the United States government for courtesies extended? Why, Lakehurst would have been closed long ago except for a promise to me to keep it open for the Hindenburg. “Do not criticize details in view of this magnanimity.” Shortly after the Hindenburg left the United States coast on the return of its maiden North American flight, Dr. Eckener said optimistically: “The last weather reports indicate we'll make favorable progress all t

London. May 14. -—— Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin today revealed for the first time that the September assembly of the League of Nations may be set to the task of refashioning the league covenant. Addressing 7,000 people packed into Albert Hall for a meeting of the conservative women’s organizations, Baldwin also expressed hope that league reforms would be undertaken with a view toward bringing the United States, Germany and Japan into the Geneva organization. Baldwin intimated that Article XVI of the league covenant, providing economic, financial and military sanctions against an aggressor, may require re-examination.

London, G, May 14.—(AP)—Harty Bradford, 28, of Lima, saved himself an extra 365 days in jail by returning voluntarily to the London farm yesterday after escaping from a labor gang. Instead of the usual two-year penalty added to a prisoner's sentence when he escapes, prison officials said Bradford would only have to serve one year. He was sentenced in 1933 to serve five years for selling mortgaged property.

LOS ANGELES, May 14 (4)-- The following things have happened to Steeplejack Charlie England this week: He fell 140 feet before catching in a maze of ropes; his pants caught fire from a blowtorch and a pulley fell on his head. “Once a woodpecker lit on my shoulder and began a tattoo in the region behind my ear,” England recalled. That, he said, was something.

Los Angeles, May 13.— 2 — Charlie England's performance atop the Hall of Justice is following the pattern of a serio-comic movie thriller. Yesterday England, a steeplejack, fell 140 feet before he saved himself by snatching a rope. His pants caught fire today. The acetylene torch which he was using set his trousers afire, England had a busy few moments putting out the flames. Shortly after, a pulley fell and hit him on the head. England said such incidents were nothing to a steeplejack. “Why, I remember once when a woodpecker lit on my shoulder and began a tattoo in the region behind my ear,” he said.

ROME, May 13. UP — Rome today expected a dramatic proclamation by Premier Benito Mussolini that Italy has resigned from the League of Nations. Il Duce’s statement, scheduled to be made before the Chamber of Deputies tomorrow, was reported by Virginio Gayda, editor of the Giornale D'Italia, regarded as Mussolini's mouthpiece. “Italy has had enough of Geneva,” the newspaper said. “The unjust verdict of the League of Nations has been accepted in terms with discipline but with little disdain. The departure of the Italian delegation from Geneva is significant of the resolute detachment of Italy from the League.” Baron Pompeo Aloisi and his Italian delegates to the League arrived from Geneva at 3:15 p.m. He refused to comment on his pre-departure yesterday, beyond saying Il Duce had ordered Italy to cease all participation in League activities.

Geneva, May 13.—A fresh effort to build up security for uneasy Europe crumbled last night when the Italian delegation to the League of Nations brusquely bolted from Geneva at the imperative command of Premier Mussolini. The fascists walked out after the council adopted a resolution which virtually was a new condemnation of Italy’s conquest of Ethiopia. Asserting it needed further time to consider the situation, the council adjourned until June 15. Sanctions meantime will continue against Italy. Pessimism Is Widespread Widespread pessimism also was based on the fact that the Italians boycotted a scheduled meeting of the remaining Locarno powers to act on Germany’s renunciation of the treaty. Mussolini was reported flirting with Adolf Hitler. Some saw the possibility of an alliance between the two dictators. A reliable source here said a secret exchange of Italo-German views took place in

Geneva. — (AP) — Whether Benito Mussolini and Italy will resign from the League of Nations and join with Adolf Hitler and Germany worried diplomats today. Well-informed Italians said the possibility that Italy would resign from the League, following the example of Germany, should not be excluded as a possibility. Such an act, political observers surmised, would mean the political alignment of Europe in two camps, and might even bring about the resuscitation of the famous "triple alliance"—the military association of Germany, Italy and the former Austro-Hungarian empire. (The power of this alliance was broken at the outset of the World War when Italy turned her back on Kaiser Wilhelm and Emperor Franz Josef to throw in her lot with France, Great Britain, and Russia— the "entente cordiale"). Hinges On Council Attitude. Diplomats said they believed Premier Mussolini would try to ascertain t

1936-02-06.text: LONDON, May 6—(AP)—Anthony Eden, foreign secretary of Great Britain, declared to the House of Commons today “the League of Nations must go on.” The cabinet minister, upon whom has devolved British relationship to the Italo-Ethiopian struggle, said the government was beginning immediately a study of the problem raised by the Italian victory in East Africa. For this purpose, he stated, the government is entering into consultations with the dominions. “It is clear that the League of Nations must go on!” said Eden. “In the modern world, it is absolutely indispensable for the organization of international affairs. “No doubt a blow has been struck at the structure of the League and the conception of collective security. We must face these facts frankly.” The foreign secretary side-stepped attempts to have him clarify what policy Great Britain would pursue at Monday's meeting of the League coun

San Francisco, Feb. 6—4— Whereabouts of Mrs. Maryon Cooper Hewitt, one of three persons accused of mayhem in the sterilization of her daughter, Ann Cooper Hewitt, puzzled authorities today. From New York police came word Mrs. Hewitt had checked out of her hotel, leaving a London forwarding address. Hotel officials, however, said the woman in question was not Mrs. Hewitt.

San Francisco, Feb. 6, (U.P.)—Police of New York and San Francisco today sought Mrs. Maryon Cooper Hewitt, mother of Ann Cooper Hewitt, sterilized heiress, who may have fled to England to escape criminal prosecution and a $500,000 civil damage action filed by her daughter. Warrants charging mayhem and based on the sterilization operation were issued against Mrs. Hewitt and two local physicians Monday. Officers here doubted Mrs. Hewitt had left the country and favored the theory that, land distraught by the sensational case, she has gone into seclusion. Her attorneys denied she had left.

By United Press | PARIS, Feb. 6. — The French and British governments reached an agreement today to invite Germany shortly to attend a conference of the principal European powers interested in peace on the Continent.

LONDON — (7).— The House of Commons turned down, yesterday, a proposal to sponsor a new international peace conference, but affirmed its confidence the government will “take all practicable steps to promote international prosperity. The suggestion for a “peace round table” came in the motion of George Lansbury, 77-year-old Laborite, and was defeated 228 to 137. An amendment which eliminated the conference proposal but kept the language of the original resolution on the “futility of war” and “grave concern of world-wide preparations for war” passed. The amendment was offered by Paul V. Evans, Conservative. Viscount Cranborne, parliamentary under-secretary for foreign affairs, said preliminary examination of the problem of an international conference already had been started, “but we cannot fix a date until circumstances favor further negotiations.” The last world economic conference, he s

PARIS, Feb. 5 (B)—A British loan to enable France, her treasury virtually empty, to finance the government until a revival of confidence makes a home loan possible, will be announced soon, it was reported reliably today. The loan of 3,000,000,000 francs (about $201,000,000) was discussed by Foreign Minister Pierre-Etienne Flandin while in London recently.

Rome, Feb. 6 (4).—Italian newspapers discussed the now dead Franco-British proposal of December and led today to unofficial reports peace talks again have started. In authoritative circles, however, it was said: “Nothing is doing in the peace line.” Diplomatic quarters said the British and French are not taking new initiative to end the four-months old warfare. Premier Mussolini presided today over the second meeting this week of the supreme commission for defense. Presumably it discussed the nation’s preparedness in the event of any eventuality—including a war at home. Earlier he conferred with army corps commanders.

Lympne, England. Feb. 8 (P).— Two British flying officers, Toramy Rose and David Mewellys, took off today on separate solo flights to Cape Town, South Africa. Mewellys left Hanworth in a midget plane in an attempt to reach Cape Town in 10 days, and a few hours later Rose started from Lympne in an effort to lower Mrs. Amy Johnson Nicholson’s England-Cape Town record of 8 days, 8 hours, 5 minutes.

1936-04-01.text: BERLIN, April 1 —(AP)— Adolf Hitler, in a memorandum to British Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden, proposed today negotiations covering a period of four months for what might be termed a new Locarno, replacing the pact broken by Germany. During these negotiations, Der Fuehrer suggested, Germany, Belgium and France should accept control of their frontiers by a commission of one representative each from Great Britain, Italy and one neutral power. Both sides, Germany, which remilitarized the Rhineland in violation of the Locarno pact; and France and Belgium, which protested this action, should refrain from casting aspersions on each other either in publications, public utterances or teachings. A plebiscite of the three peoples involved was proposed by Hitler to give solemn sanction to the work of the statesmen, once the negotiations were concluded successfully. LONDON, April 1— Germany today offered the Locarno treaty powers a four-month period of military inactivity on the Rhineland frontiers while negotiations could be started for a new political deal for Europe. The cabinet went into session at once to consider the note and, at the same time to arrange for general staff talks with France and Belgium on a plan of mutual defense. Joachim von Ribbentrop, Fuehrer Adolf Hitler's special envoy, delivered the German offer to Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden this morning. The German delegation informed the United Press officially that the note proposes a virtual truce on the German - French - Belgian frontier for a four-month interim period. The words truce or status quo are not specifically mentioned in the note, but Germany suggests that there should be no military changes on either side during that period. (4) = Adolf Hitler’s fateful reply to the four-power Locarno security proposals was brought to London tonight as mounting suspicion and opposition in British circles were attached to forthcoming military staff talks with France and Belgium. Joachim von Ribbentrop, Hitler’s special ambassador who arrived by plane from Berlin shortly after 8 p. m., was scheduled to deliver the dictator’s message tomorrow to Anthony Eden, British foreign secretary. Whether the contents would be divulged immediately was uncertain, since the British believed it necessary to transmit the contents to Paris and Brussels first. Great Britain was said authoritatively to have decided to accept the proposals as a basis of discussion. Germany offered to re-write the Locarno treaty which she scrapped when she moved her troops into the Rhineland. The German note reiterated Berlin's intention of not increasing the number of troops in the Rhineland or moving them closer to the frontier. Hitherto, Germany has proposed non-aggression pacts with her neighbors. Now for the first time she offers to place her entire armed forces at the disposal of France, Belgium, Britain and Italy on a reciprocal basis to resist aggression. PARIS, April 1.—(UP)—Douglas Fairbanks and his bride, the former Lady Ashley, arrived from Cannes today and will hurry by plane to London to the bedside of Douglas Fairbanks Jr., who is critically ill of influenza.

MANCHESTER, Eng., April 1, Dr. Buck Ruxton, who was to have been hanged today for the murder of his wife and a nurse, still lives because of a legal maneuver by his attorneys. His counsel appealed his conviction to a higher court, thereby automatically postponing his execution indefinitely. Ruxton and the servant were killed 'on or about' Sept. 15. Their bodies were dismembered and thrown into a Scottish ravine known as the 'Beef-Tub.' Ruxton’s trial, which lasted ten days, brought out evidence which shocked England with a gruesome thrill.

| Bedford, April 1 (AP)—Floyd Horton’s attorneys laid the groundwork for the defense of the 39-year-old farmer today by seeking to establish that Horton was “all broken-up” after his wife’s death. | Horton, depicted by the state as a philandering farmer that was unfaithful to his wife as well as his paramour, is on trial for the poison murder Feb. 13 of his pretty wife, Elta. State witnesses testified that he was little moved by his wife’s death. Guy Horton, brother of the man on trial for his life, said he went to his brother’s home and that his brother “took it awful.” “I never saw Floyd and Elta fight or scrap and I worked for Floyd and lived with them for a year. Floyd often joked Elta, but it was all in fun.” He said his brother told Mrs. Johnston after Mrs. Horton's death, “Anna you'd better go home, you better not stay here.”

1936-05-06.text: LONDON, May 5. ()—Europe will take a realistic view of Italy's triumph in Ethiopia, will accept the facts and face them. No continental problems will be solved by this, but they will not be made worse nor will the danger of a European war be made more serious immediately by Il Duce's victory and the “King of Kings” flight. Out of the debacle of Geneva's futile efforts to frustrate an “aggressor” nation may come a rebirth of the ‘League of Nations along more effective lines. These were the prospects in Europe, my office May 5 and 6 the State Department.

GLENEAGLES, Scotland, May 6,—The third renewal of the International Curtis cup golf competition between American and British women players, with the invading forces defending the cup, ended in a 4½ to 4½ deadlock today. The rival teams each won 3 foursomes, and three singles matches, and one foursome ended in a draw. "With the United States leading 4½ to 3½ and the final result hanging on the outcome of the singles match between Mrs. Leona Cheney and Jessie Anderson, 1935 New Zealand champion, Miss Anderson spared John Bull his third straight defeat in the series by holding out a 15-foot putt on the 18th hole to win one up.

London, May 7.—(INS)—Relatives of Dr. A. J. M. Melly, head of the British Red Cross ambulance unit in Addis Ababa, were officially informed today that he died of wounds received Saturday during the rioting at the Ethiopian Capital. The advices stated Dr. Melly died at the British legation there Tuesday night. He was wounded in the lung while attempting to aid wounded Ethiopians at the height of the rioting.

He spoke earnestly and pounded the heavy oak table before him in the great Marble floored room. Ethiopia's political and juridical destiny remains to be determined, he said. He expressed belief that some minor military operations might be necessary in eastern Ethiopia. But now, he added, he was giving his attention to Europe... “It has become a matter of common agreement,” he said, “that the League of Nations needs reorganizing. Italy is ready to help. (By the Associated Press) London—Italian troops occupy Addis Ababa, relieving legations menaced by marauding tribesmen. Rome—Mussolini declares peace is here and Ethiopia is Italy’s as Italians wildly celebrate fall of Addis Ababa. London—League powers to take “realistic” view of Italy's triumph over Ethiopia and the League; League framework may be revamped. Vatican City—Pope thanks God in prayer for end of war. Alexandria—American associate says Haile Selassie, en route to Palestine aboard British cruiser, is relatively poor man.

ALEXANDRIA, May 6. (P). — Egypt’s new sovereign, 16-year-old King Farouk, came to his native land today for the first time as monarch, arriving in Alexandria en route from London to Cairo. All British warships in the harbor were decorated with flags of honor and thousands of cheering Egyptians lined the streets as the king disembarked from the British vessel, escorted by a cruiser and destroyers, which brought him across the Mediterranean. The former crown prince, who was proclaimed king after the death last week of his father, Fuad, was pale but smiling bravely.

PARIS, May 6 — (AP)— Authoritative sources said today France would throw its full weight against outright annexation of Ethiopia as an Italian colony or raising of an army which might be used in a European conflict, France was reported likely to propose that Great Britain's treaty with the Arab kingdom of Iraq be made a model for Italian domination of Ethiopia, with the African empire retaining nominal sovereignty and League of Nations membership. Under such a plan, France would insist that it be accorded trade privileges equal to those given foreign countries under the French protectorate over Morocco and that Djibouti, French Somaliland, remain the port of entry for Ethiopia. Despite Premier Mussolini’s assertions that he would not negotiate with other nations on his course in Ethiopia, French sources expressed belief his need of money for East African development would make him yield

DJIBOUTI, French Somaliland, May 5 (W.P.)—Ethiopia’s last high chieftains were refugees on foreign soil today, the resistance to Italy over in all theaters of the war. Emperor Haile Selassie and his family were on a British cruiser steaming up the Red Sea toward Palestine. The Emperor is going to Jerusalem, capital of his traditional ancestor, King Solomon. That the war was over was made plain yesterday when by special train arrived Ras Nassibu, commander-in-chief of all the eastern armies; Gen. Wehib Pasha, brilliant Turkish strategist who organized the defenses in the East, and the Dedjazmatch Makonnen Abeba Damptu. They went to the crack British cruiser Enterprise, waiting with the Emperor, his family and chief advisors. 1936-05-11.text: London, May 10 (y)—Europe is confronted tomorrow with the choice of continuing the post-war system of collective security through conciliation at Geneva, or reverting to the pre-war doctrine that “might makes right;” to secret alliances and the “balance of power.” These alternatives are present as the League council, faced by Premier Mussolini's new empire as an accomplished fact, meets tomorrow at Geneva. Smaller nations, including the Little Entente and Scandinavian countries, have demanded that the League go on. But the position of the two major League powers, Great Britain and France, has not been defined—especially as to whether sanctions against Italy should be lifted. While the council meets, Britain will conduct a gigantic test mobilization of her land and air defenses on the island of Malta, only 60 miles from Italy's Sicily. London, England, May 11.—(>)— The home office declined today to reprieve Dr. Buck Ruxton, Indian-blooded physician convicted of the “Devil’s Beef Tub” slaying of his wife, despite a petition signed by 5,500 persons. Ruxton, who was accused of slaying both his wife and his maid, dismembering their bodies and casting them into the “Devil’s Beef Tub” ravine near Moffat, must hang at 9 a.m. (3 a.m. central standard time) tomorrow in Strangeways jail, Man-

GENEVA, May 11 (UP).—Baron Pompeo Aloisi, chief Italian delegate, today quit the League of Nations council table rather than sit with "Wolde Mariam." The council, despite Aloisi’s belt, seated the Ethiopian, who is minister to Paris. "I cannot accept the presence of delegates of the so-called Ethiopian government," Aloisi said as he strode from the room. Observers interpreted the council's invitation to Mariam and its willingness to provoke the Italian withdrawal as formal recognition that Ethiopia remains a sovereign state and a member of the League. ADDIS ABABA, May 11 (UP).—A warning to Europe that Italy has won its war in Ethiopia and is ready for anything that may happen in Europe was seen today in a decision that the first troops to be sent home shall be the crack Alpini. These men, brought here to fight in the mountains on the northern front, are to be sent direct to the Brenner p

MADRID, May 14—(AP)—Manuel Azana, abandoning active politics to assume Spain’s highest post, became the second president today of the second Spanish Republic. The former premier was elected to the presidency yesterday, 754 to 120, in a quiet session of the parliament and presidential electors in the crystal palace. He was the only candidate. Azana, who assumed the premiership after the Leftist victory in the February parliamentary elections, succeeded Niceto Alcala Zamora as president after the first executive of the Republic was deposed by parliament on a charge of malfeasance. Azana is 56 years old, a lawyer, orator, playwright and one of Spain's ablest politicians. His term runs until 1942.

PARIS, May 11 — (4) -- Leon Blum, leader of the dominant Socialist party, undertook to outline a "new deal" for France today after announcing he would accept the premiership. His projects included a vast public works program, France's Socialists remained "hostile" to devaluation of the franc, he announced, but attached more importance to relief of "unemployment and misery" than to the financial problem.

Athens, May 11, (U.P)—Striking workers of Salonica called a mass meeting in the streets of that city today in defiance of an army threat to attack them with soldiers, tanks, airplanes and warships. The strikers tried unsuccessfully to occupy police stations. A state of siege obtained in the area and troops and warships were on the way to reinforce the garrison. Ten persons were wounded in a fight between workers and police at Piraeus, the port of Athens, as disorders spread to the capital district. All workers in the Salonica area were out. Workers at Larissa, in Thessaly, decided to walk out in sympathy. Strike leaders at Salonica ordered a mass meeting in Liberty Square. Gen. Nicholas Zeppos, commanding the Salonica military district announced that if the order was obeyed he would attack the meeting with all forces at his command, specifying tanks, airplanes and warships. Strikers proc

Madrid, May 10.—--(/P)—-Premier Manuel Azaña, a candidate "under protest," became president of the world’s youngest republic by an overwhelming majority from 874 electors gathered in a perfunctory session today in the crystal palace. The 56-year-old lawyer, orator and playwright, regarded as Spain's ablest politician, was the sole candidate. He was elected by a vote of 754 to 120. The only incident to enliven the convention was an exchange of blows between two leftist members as an outgrowth of an alleged reflection upon the character of one of them. Azaña consented to run for president under protest because as president he must forsake active direction of the powerful left republican party. He succeeds Niceto Alcalá Zamora, who was removed from the presidency on a charge of malfeasance by parliament April 7, following a leftist victory in the February elections.

May 10—A 101-gun salute in every garrison and city in Italy today, booming in a new as the window-shaking salvoes literally millions of Italians in their public squares continue last night's demonstrations and cheer a revival of the empire of the Caesars. Rome crowd cheered before Royal Quirinal Palace but Emperor Victor Emanuel did not appear. Morning newspapers carried headlines in some instances eight tall reporting the proclamation by Premier Mussolini last night annexing Ethiopia and conferring upon the king the title of Emperor. Behind the effervescent demonstrations, however, there was sober thought. "What will England and France go about it?" asked many at Geneva tomorrow would be a rigid one. LONDON, Eng. (UP) — Sir Philip Ben-Greet, 79, famous Shakespearean actor, died yesterday at a nursing home. He had been ill for several weeks.

“My life work is ruined,” the Mahatma Gandhi said today in discussing, in his Ashram retreat here, the results of the recent Lucknow nationalist congress. “Not even the firmness and depression of the British government,” he said, "have harmed my work as much as the new policy outlined by Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru” (new president of the Indian national congress). He referred to a quarrel which has been brewing for a long time; a quarrel which has left Gandhi sullen and disappointed, with the feeling that he has been betrayed by his best friends. By the Associated Press LONDON, May 18—Dr. Nahum Sokolow, 75, Jewish leader who was honorary president of the World Zionist Organization and the Jewish Agency for Palestine, died last night.

LONDON, MAY 18. (AP).—Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden told the House of Commons today he was unaware of any steps which could be taken usefully to bring the United States into the League of Nations. His statement was in reply to a question by Ellis Smith, Labor Party member of the House, who asked if anything was being done to induce the United States to join the Geneva body. Smith also asked Eden if he would ask the United States to open negotiations with a view to reaching an agreement on economic cooperation.

1936-03-07.text: PARIS—.(UP)—The much publicized, long enduring romance of Douglas Fairbanks and Lady Sylvia Ashley, British noblewoman, culminated in marriage today in the town hall of the eighth Paris district. American Ambassador Jesse I. Strauss was among the guests. The ceremony was performed by district mayor Gaston Drucker. He wore the tri-colored sash of his office and read the marriage clauses from the code in rapid French which neither understood. The code specifies the husband must be faithful to the wife, that the wife owes obedience and must follow the husband everywhere. The marriage culminated a romance of years’ standing that resulted in two divorces. Lord Ashley divorced his beautiful, former actress wife in London, naming Fairbanks as co-respondent. Mary Pickford divorced Fairbanks in Los Angeles for desertion. For two days Fairbanks had argued with French officials to get the marriage

LONDON, March 7.—(UPI)—European statesmen, electrified by Adolf Hitler's history-making move, called urgent meetings to consider their course. While France cancelled some week-end army leaves and considered calling an urgent meeting of the League Council, there were indications that the British government, confronted with a crisis that forced the facing of realities, might be ready to negotiate a peace plan on the basis of Hitler's declarations. It was announced that Anthony Eden, foreign secretary, received Leopold Von Hoesch, German ambassador, at the foreign office yesterday and revived the offer of a Western European air pact for mutual defense. Hoesch at once sent the offer to Berlin. This offer was made when there was every indication that Germany might announce today its reoccupation of the Rhineland.
