LONDON—The scores of thousands of men and women who are making munitions for Europe’s next war stopped work for two minutes today in those countries where November 11 is observed as Armistice Day. In Germany, Italy and other countries where Armistice Day is observed on other days, or is not observed at all, the workers kept right on working and gained the two minutes for the armies, navies and air forces. Czechoslovakia celebrated the day by acquiring control of the majority of stock of the Skoda Arms factory, one of the greatest in the world. Previously the Schneider-Creusot Company of France had control of 51 percent. In Paris, 8,250 mobile guards were concentrated in fear of disorderly demonstrations by fascists. In Rome, 25,000 troops, the entire garrison, paraded in full dress but with full war packs also, before King Victor Emmanuel in celebration

SAN DIEGO, Calif. —(?)— Mrs. Wallis Simpson, an American friend of England’s King Edward, was described here Tuesday as a “wonderful woman” by her former husband, Commander Earl W. Spencer, USN. The naval officer, who has refused any comment about Mrs. Simpson since publicity attendant upon her acquaintance with the king, agreed to an interview Tuesday. He did not discuss her friendship with Edward VIII.

SAN DIEGO, Calif. Nov. 11. The American naval officer who was Mrs. Wallis Simpson's first husband still regards her as “a wonderful woman.” Avoiding all mention of his ex-wife's friendship with King Edward of England, Commander Parl W. Spencer paid tribute to her beauty and character in an interview at the Naval hospital here. Spencer, executive officer of the aircraft carrier Ranger, broke his leg on a hunting trip last weekend. “A wonderful woman * * most attractive * * one of the strongest characters I have ever known any woman to possess,” ran the thread of his comment. “Mrs. Simpson has gone her way and lived the life she wanted, and I have done the same. What she does is no concern of mine.”

(Ry United Press). London, Nov. 11. — The Exchange Telegraph's Lisbon correspondent reported today that civil guards in Madrid revolted in favor of the rebels, but militiamen forced them to surrender. Most of the revolters were shot, the report said.

Copyright, 1936, by United Press San Diego, Calif, Nov, 11— (UP) —Naval Commander Earl Winfield Spencer, first husband of Mrs. Wallis Simpson, sat propped up in a hospital bed today and spoke of the now famous ‘friend of King Edward VIII at England as “one of the finest women I have ever known.” He refused to comment on the friendship of the King and Mrs. Simpson because it would be “untactful as a gentleman and undiplomatic as an officer.” But, Commander Spencer willingly and perhaps somewhat eagerly told of his first wife, his impressions of her and how they “drifted apart.” It was the first comment that had come from the young Baltimore society woman's first husband since she met King Edward. All previous attempts to find him had been fruitless: Naval headquarters reported him ‘on indefinite leave’ and refused to give his whereabouts. He is in the service hospital here suffering a bro

AL PAA CE PE ARN EE TIO | MADRID, Spain, (AP) — Flames spread through 40 blocks of the northwest section of Madrid Tuesday night after a Fascist airplane and artillery bombardment of the capital. Fire from the Fascist battery between the Campamento and El Escoral road caused severe damage to the city’s defenses. The Paseo de Rosal, at the western extremity of the city above the Norte station along the Manzanares River, became a blazing inferno after heavy shells crunched a barricade at the station and the Montana barracks. On the site of the former royal stables where the government's powerful batteries were emplaced. A dense pall of acrid, greenish-brown smoke drifted east over the city as a whole area became a seething cauldron of flame. Thick smoke rolled from the Norte station.

Madrid, Nov. 12 (UP)—A heavy artillery barrage rocked Madrid and its environs today as government and nationalist batteries resumed a fierce cannonade. With rain and poor visibility preventing the powerful aviation forces of either side from operating, the leftists’ artillery began shelling the insurgent positions on almost the entire Madrid front, the nationalists quickly responding and concentrating on the government batteries. Loyalist militiamen trapped 1,000 picked nationalist storm troops in the western part of the city today and expected to annihilate them. Try Desperate Sortie Moors and foreign legionnaires, the nationalist soldiers tried a desperate sortie into the heart of the city. In the night they filtered through the upper slopes of the Casa Del Campo park on Madrid’s west side and managed to cross the Manzanares river near the Franceses. A secretly strengthened militia lin

1936-10-12.text: WORCESTER, Mass. (AP) — A childhood romance that began in England was at an end here today with Mrs. Mary Ellis Crosbie, 49, dead and her husband, Frank, 54, shell-shocked war veteran and an insane hospital patient, held for her murder. Crosbie, Police Inspector James F. Sheahan said, hacked his wife to death a few hours after, with tearful pleading, she induced a young interne to grant him a day of liberty from Worcester state hospital yesterday. “I killed her because I had disgraced her,” Sheahan quoted the husband as saying, after he had been remanded to Worcester jail pending formal hearing on a murder charge Tuesday morning. The husband declined to amplify that statement, the inspector added. Sheahan reconstructed the crime as follows: Mrs. Crosbie pleaded for several minutes yesterday to have her husband granted liberty until 8 p.m. last night. An interne, unmindful of Crosbie’s ho

LONDON, Oct. 12,—(U.P)—Germany delivered a note to Great Britain today which it was understood implies that Germany will feel ‘constrained to enlarge her navy substantially if the pending Anglo-Soviet naval pact is signed. The note was delivered to the foreign office by the German Charge d’Affairs, Prince Von Bismarck, and the naval attache, Admiral Erwin Wessner. The Anglo-Soviet naval pact permits Russia to build seven cruisers with 71-inch guns, which is above the cruiser building agreed to in the British-French-United States treaty last March. The exception is made for Russia because the other powers already possess heavy cruisers which the

London, Oct. 11.— (4) —Hundreds of police, wielding batons, repeatedly charged a crowd of several thousand persons tonight at Liverpool, where hand-to-hand fighting broke out after Sir Oswald Mosley, leader of the British Union of Fascists, delivered a speech. (Scores of persons were hurt last Sunday when Mosley's followers, planning a parade through the heart of the Jewish quarter in London's east end, clashed with anti-fascists). In London, a disorganized crowd shouting fascist yells but not wearing fascist uniforms smashed the fronts of 15 shops today and pilaged the contents of store windows. Most of their raids were on establishments owned by Jews. They burned an automobile belonging to one shop owner who protested, and stoned others. All Day The window-smashing was the climax of day-long disturbances in the east end quarters between Communists and fascists in which police vigorousl

WASHINGTON, Oct. 12 (P).— Two eminent scientists expressed the conviction today that long-range weather forecasting will eliminate the terror of droughts and floods in the future. Dr. Charles G. Abbott, secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, and Sir Gilbert Walker, British meteorologist, said in articles in the annual report of the institution that the much-disputed problem of predicting weather months in advance will be solved by intensive application of known methods of science. Reporting on weather studies, the two men arrived at their conclusions by different routes. Dr. Abbott worked out a cycle of 23 years in the general trends of weather. The cycle was based on periodic fluctuations in the output of radiation of the sun. Sir Gilbert founded his opinion on correlations between seasonal weather changes and atmospheric conditions in nearby regions of the world. The Smithsonian Ins

Madrid, Oct. 12.—(UP)—Loyalist troops retreated on Madrid today for the final defense of the city. They retreated stubbornly and counterattacked on occasion, but they were outnumbered, the rebels were better armed and the rebel officers were regular army men. All along the front west of Madrid the insurgents thrust first at one point, then at another, while the Loyalists gave ground awaiting reinforcements. It was reported that the rebels started their advance northward on the Madrid highway from Toledo, But the main shock of the terrific offensive was expected toward Navaicarnero and El Escorial, On the western front, the rebels had passed Navalperal De Pinares, El Hoyo and San Martin De Valdeiglesias in three attacking columns, Strict Censorship A most stringent censorship was clamped down last night and all dispatches dealing with the situation at the front were slashed. The city was

PARIS, Oct. 12—(/)—French communists, their propaganda tour of Alsace-Lorraine ended quietly, announced today they would re-invade the region for 122 meetings in the near future. Rightists ridiculed the communist party rallies, asserting the "mobilization of the masses" brought only 12,000 persons to propaganda meetings in a region with 2,000,000 population. "The striking thing is the enormous expense, trouble, discredit and loss of time these Moscow gentlemen imposed upon France to obtain their pitiful results," commented sarcastically the newspaper Le Matin. The eastern border region was calm as strong forces of mobile guards prevented the leftist partisan sessions from developing into political riots.

HOF, Germany, Oct. 12. ()— Rudolf Hess, Reichsfuehrer Adolf Hitler’s minister without portfolio, warned Europe tonight that Germany might have to employ “dumping” methods in international commerce if she fails to get her lost colonies back. Hess, speaking at the opening of a new meeting hall, declared the restoration of the colonies, taken from Germany as a result of the World War, would be in the interest of foreign nations because, otherwise, “Germany would be forced to export at any price, thus impairing the exports of other nations.” Der Fuehrer’s deputy asserted the only way out of present economic difficulties lay in the “world giving Germany colonies having raw materials.” Then, he said, “we could produce in our own territory the raw products which we now are forced to buy abroad.” Food imports have been cut, said Hess, because Germany must import other raw material. The Reich's s

MOSCOW, Oct. 12 UP—The captain of a Soviet steamer, carrying 2,500 tons of clothing and foodstuffs to Spain, today invited Italian representatives to board the ship and see for themselves she carries no arms. The invitation came from Captain Korenevsky of the Neva, which put out yesterday from Odessa, bound for Alicante, Spanish government Mediterranean port. Soviet spokesmen, declaring the Italian ambassador to London, Dino Grandi, charged the Neva secretly carried munitions to Spain on its previous trip, said this was obviously false.

1936-06-12.text: Washington, June 11—Finland notified the United States today it would meet its regular semi-annual war debt installment of $164,315.50 on June 15. The little Baltic republic is the only war debtor nation that has not defaulted on obligations to this country. Great Britain and Italy already have notified this government they would continue in default after June 15, as they have been for the last two years, and none of the other 13 debtor nations is generally expected to do otherwise.

Washington, June 8 (#)—A British default on its June 15 installment coincided today with a prediction on Capitol Hill that the French, British, and Italian governments soon would make new proposals for settlement of their war debts to the United States. The prediction was made to reporters by Senator Lewis of Illinois, long a bitter critic of war debt defaulting nations. State Department officials said, however, they had not heard of such moves. Lewis described a plan by which he said the three European powers would offer goods and services to this country to be credited to their existing obligations.

LONDON, June 11 (4).--James H. Thomas, the former colonial secretary who was forced from the British cabinet by the celebrated "budget leak" scandal, told the house of commons today he would resign from parliament at once. For the fifth time he denied he wilfully had disclosed any secret of the government budget.

Paris, June 2, (4?)—Great Britain and France moved forward a common "sanctions front" today which informed sources predicted would reach its culmination at Geneva late this month, The new socialist administration, harassed by strikes at home, began a study of a British proposal to lift war sanctions from Italy and revamp the covenant of the League of Nations.
By The Associated Press ETON, Eng., June 12.—Dr. Montague Rhodes James, provost of Eton College for eighteen years and noted Biblical scholar, died today. He was 73 years old.

JERUSALEM, June 12,—(U.P)— Assistant Police Superintendent Alan Sigrist was wounded from ambush late today while driving his automobile near Herod’s Gate as Arab disorders continued in Palestine. Sigrist lost control of his car, which plunged down a 30-foot embankment. British Constable Doxat, who was a passenger in Sigrist’s automobile, jumped clear. He shot and captured one of the assailants. Earlier 11 persons were reported wounded when a military escort returned the fire of Arabs who attacked the Haifa-Jerusalem train.

PARIS, June 12—Police acted today to prevent mass demonstrations from foreign elements in the French crisis. The chamber of deputies at the same time passed a bill to compel the 40-hour week, one of the strikers’ principal demands. The vote was 385 to 175. Roger Salengro, minister of the interior, declared strikers were gradually resuming work. Vincent Auriol, minister of finance, declared he considered the valuation would be a disaster and said the government intended to relieve exporters by tax reforms and reorganization of credit facilities. More Spanish Disorders. (By Associated Press) MADRID, Spain, June 12—Few disorders in one syndicalist and another seriously wounded flared up between syndicalists and socialists in Malaga today. Carlos Santiago Robles, 24, was found dead.

MOSCOW, June 12 (UP)—Russians, for 181-2 years under a ‘Steel dictatorship, were handed a new charter of government today, a constitution which marks a decisive step in the history of the world’s first communistic republic union. It provides for universal suffrage, for the secret ballot, for a Supreme Soviet elected by the people. It provides for freedom of press and speech, for secrecy of mails, for the right of all to vote regardless of past activities. The new constitution was approved by the presidium of the central executive committee that is by the presidents of the Soviet socialist republics which comprise the union. The constitution will bring no basic change in the Russian concept of government but it does mean that the leaders who have struggled since the revolution of 1917 to solidify their rule in vast Russia feel that the time has come to make a long step forward. The vote w

1936-07-20.text: Washington, D. C.—(AP)—A British warship was standing by today at Malaga, Spain, prepared to safeguard British and American citizens in that southeastern Spanish seaport. Word of this precaution against harm in Spain's fierce civil war was received by the state department from Herbert O. Williams, the American consul at Gibraltar. Williams cabled the department this morning that British officials at Gibraltar informed him that the captain of the British ship H. M. S. Shamrock was in contact with the British and American consuls at Malaga "and has assured that all possible measures will be taken for the safeguarding of British and Americans in Malaga." No Americans Menaced, Thus far the state department has received no reports that any American lives were in jeopardy in the revolution. The number of Americans in Spain was estimated by the department at 1,582, however, in-

TAMPA, Fla. July 19 17 The third day of a search by American and Cuban craft passed today without a trace of the British motorship Nunoca, unreported since leaving the West Indies for Tampa July 4 with 21 persons aboard. The United States Coast Guard had three cutters and a plane looking for the 110-foot, combined.

PARIS (UP)— Jay Allen, of Oregon, correspondent for the "Chicago Daily News," was wounded when bullets hit a motor car in which he was driving with other American and British newspaper men in southern Spain toward Gibraltar. Allen's friends here were concerned.

London, July 20.—England said special prayers of thanksgiving for King Edward's escape from a pistol attack yesterday while the monarch spent a quiet week-end at his Fort Belvedere country home. The king was able to relax after a trying week, although intermittent showers interfered with his hobby of gardening. In addition to the usual prayers for his majesty, special prayers for thanksgiving were offered in the Chapel Royal at St. James's Place where the bishop of Truro, in a sermon, mentioned the nation’s “heartfelt thankfulness” that Edward was unharmed.

By LESTER ZIFFREN (Copyright 1936 by United Press) MADRID—An official government announcement said today the revolt in Madrid had been quelled. Airplanes began to fly over the Montana barracks, where the rebels were holding out, at 6 a.m. and began a bombardment. Socialists, militia and loyal storm guards surrounded the barracks and attacked it with artillery and rifles. At 11 a.m. the barracks surrendered. (Refugees arriving at Gibraltar said more than 200 had been killed in fighting at La Linea, near Gibraltar.) The Montana barracks is near the presidential palace and was the principal rebel stronghold. (Turn to Page 8—No. 5.)

MADRID, Spain, July 20—The government today announced itself master of the situation in Spain after loyal forces using artillery and bombing planes had blasted rebellious capital garrisons into submission. However, rebel troops apparently under the leadership of the rightist general, Francisco Franco, were reported in control of Spanish Morocco where an insurrection broke out Friday. More than 1,000 army officers were announced as under arrest by their commands in Madrid by order of the government. The government declared the rebels’ columns in Segovia province had been scattered by a loyal air corps attack.

Seville, Spain, Sept. 1.—(Tuesday)—(P)—The rebel radio station here asserted in a broadcast today insurgent airplanes bombed Madrid yesterday, causing 300 casualties. The announcement declared the ministry of war, the ministry of interior and the northern railway station in the capital were hit.

ABOARD SCHOONER LIBERTY, Shelburne, N. S., July 19 (AP)—A chilling rain and fog set in today for the first time since President Roosevelt began his vacation cruise, causing abandonment of plans to sail farther up the east coast of Nova Scotia tomorrow. Instead, the skipper of the Presidential yacht Sewanna chose to turn south and beat back around the southern tip of the Canadian province of Yarmouth, about a 50-mile run from this harbor where the President anchored last night after a 45-mile cruise under canvas from Cape Sable. The President started on his trip Tuesday.

1936-02-08.text: LONDON, Feb. 7, (?) — The United States stood firm in demanding 35,000-ton battleships and 10,000-ton cruisers tonight in the face of British, French and Italian proposals before a technical subcommittee of the four-power naval conference for smaller ships. The first discussion of the qualitative limitations brought to the forefront a week-long simmering clash of viewpoints. Observers doubt the disagreement could be compromised. Should the anticipated deadlock not be broken, the committee is expected to refer the matter to the full conference for decision. The conference, in the two months it has been in session, has arrived at only one tentative agreement—the matter of yearly exchange of building programs in advance and notification of construction. The development today, while not a hopeful one, was welcomed by the Americans since it brought the conference back to tangibles after a wee

LONDON (AP)— The United States delegation to the International Naval Conference, confronted by British, French and Italian proposals to the technical committee for smaller vessels, maintained today its stand for 35,000-ton battleships and 10,000-ton cruisers. Informed sources expressed doubt that the differences in the viewpoints of the powers could be compromised, in view of past positions, and looked for the question to be turned over to the conference as a whole for a decision, if the anticipated deadlock could not be broken.

HOLLYWOOD, Feb. 8—Hollywood today was saddened by the death of Oliver Pete Heggie, veteran English character actor of the stage and screen, who died suddenly yesterday of pneumonia. He was 57. Heggie started his stage career in Australia and while still a young man went to England where he soon achieved success on the British stage. For more than a decade he had been a leading performer.
LEEDS, England, Feb. 8.—Market men are using lipsticks to paint the faded combs of old hens so they can be sold for pullets, farmers complained at a union meeting today.

- PARIS, Feb. 7 (#)--Mikhail Toukatchevsky, the youngest marshal of the Soviet army, met France's general staff today to draft the first measures of military co-operation between the two nations in the face of the “menace” of Nazi Germany. - France hopes to get Russia, her military ally, in a condition to fight effectively. - With their bilateral mutual defense pact awaiting only formal ratification by the chamber of deputies, the general staffs of the two nations began the work of co-ordinating their tasks if Reichsfuehrer Hitler's army attacks either. A loan of 800,000,000 francs (about $54,000,000) in credits to enable the Soviet to repair her western frontier railroads and highways has been (Continued on Page 8, Col. 5)

Rome.—(AP)—Luigi, Cardinal Sincero, secretary of the Rome conclave, died today. Cardinal Sincero, 66 years old, preserved consciousness until the end. He was stricken by paralysis a week ago at his home. Pope Pius sent a special benediction. Cardinal Sincero had many friends in the United States, made frequent visits to the American college in Rome and was a protector of the Knights of St. George of the United States.

SHANGHAI, Feb. 8.-- (Pp = Alarmist reports that hostilities between Japanese and Russians impended on the frontiers of Soviet-influenced outer Mongolia and Japanese-advised Manchoukuo have reappeared recently in North China’s circulation. The reports, which informed sources said should be accepted with greatest reserve, said Japanese and Manchoukuoan armies were moving toward the outer Mongolian border, while Soviet and Mongolian forces supposedly were approaching Manchoukuo. Informed sources said, however, there was nothing to indicate the situation in the affected area had changed from that existing for many months, characterized by recurring border incidents, but with no large scale hostilities immediately indicated.

MOSCOW — Three passengers and the pilot of an airplane were killed in a crash in a heavy snow storm and two men seeking their bodies froze to death, a dispatch from Sakhalin said today. The The body who sought to cross a during the storm was buried now, the dispatch said, and apparently frozen.

1936-03-15.text: (Copyright by Associated Press) LONDON — France announced tonight its willingness to consider an alternate plan whereby Germany might retain her troops in the Rhineland.

Rome, Mar. 14. UP — Marching into lush jungle country, a far western fascist column moved down the Ethiopian-Sudanese frontier lands today, driving a wedge toward Lake Tana and Great Britain’s sphere of influence. One of four full army corps in motion on the northern African front, the western column’s advance guard was nearing the important trail junction of Nogara, in the northwestern corner of Ethiopia, not more than 100 miles from the great inland sea which supplies the lifeblood of the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan’s blue Nile. South and east of it warplanes were reported to have bombed Ethiopian concentrations in the Enctab section, north of the Amhara capital of Gondar. Gondar lies but 23 miles north of Lake Tana. Moving in a southwesterly direction, other troops had crossed the Takkaze river and penetrated deep into the Tzellemti region, northeast of the lake.

BERLIN, (UP).—Germany will not attend Monday's League of Nations council session in London, it was indicated today. The United Press was informed that the major factor prompting German impulse to decline the invitation is the fact that the Reich was invited as a signatory of the Locarno treaty. “Germany considers the Locarno pact dead and buried,” an unofficial but well-informed source pointed out.

Boston, Mass., March 14--(U. P)— Forecasts of rain carried threats today of still worse floods in the northeastern states and a part of Canada. The death toll already was approaching 60 and 10,000 persons have been driven from their homes. Property damage runs into the millions, New England rivers, particularly the Merrimack, which isolated Concord, New Hampshire, and forced 3,000 families to seek higher ground, receded slightly this morning. Floods also were abating in the Hudson Valley, New York. The forecast of rain tonight and tomorrow caused apprehension, however. Officials in New England are appealing for army bombing to break the ice jam which backed up the flood waters. It was estimated that 75,000 New Englanders are left jobless by the inundation of mills.

LONDON, March 14 (P)—War is at least six months off, according to latest quotations by Lloyd's. The odds: A European war in six months — 9% to 1 against. French troops enter the Rhineland zone within the next three months — 48% to 1 against. Two days ago Lloyd's refused to quote odds on a European war.

MANCHESTER, Eng. --(4..- The hanging of Dr. Buck Ruxton, convicted Friday of the ‘devil's heef-tub’ slaying of his wife, was set by the Manchester assizes court Saturday for April 1. Presiding Justice Singleton sentenced the Indian-blooded physician to be hanged immediately after a jury found him guilty of murder in connection with the deaths of Mrs. Isabella Ruxton and her maid, Mary Jane Rogerson.

LONDON, March 14 (U.2)—Powers signatory to the Locarno treaty tonight decided to refrain from all negotiations with Germany until Fuehrer Adolf Hitler has made amends for what they regard as his illegal occupation of the Rhineland and his denunciation of the pact. The decision was taken after the League of Nations council invited Germany, as a Locarno treaty signatory, to sit with it Monday and after France demanded economic and for its treaty violations. To Punish Germany— France, supported by Belgium, is determined to punish Germany unless the gray-clad forces of the Reich army are withdrawn from the banks of the River Rhine. The report that the Locarno signatories, in a late afternoon meeting, assented to the French demand to refuse to deal with Hitler until he moves to regularize his Rhineland coup by giving adequate pledges and taking suitable action was regarded as indicating a sig

LONDON, March 14— (UP) — Italian planes have heavily bombed Harar and Jijiga on the southern front and civilians in those towns have been evacuated, the exchange telegraph correspondent with the Italian army reported today: on the basis of unofficial advices,

1936-06-03.text: London, June 0—(4@)—The British public gave Haile Selassie a great ovation today as the emperor whom Italy deposed completed a journey of exile from Addis Ababa. Thousands of spectators, carefully held back by reinforced detachments of police, cheered repeatedly as the former "King of Kings" arrived in a special railroad coach at Waterloo station. The ancient station was packed with throngs. Many of the spectators held up banners bearing messages of greeting. All traffic throughout the area was hopelessly tangled by the press of the crowds. Officially, Haile Selassie was received by O. C. Harvey, private secretary to Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden. The former ruler stood silently, with his eyes cast down, while a delegation of Ethiopians read him an address of welcome. Other delegations represented "The Friends of Ethiopia" and similar organizations. Another outburst of cheering greeted

SOUTHAMPTON, Eng. June 28 (UP)—Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia arrived today on his way to London to seek aid against Italian annexation of his country. Passengers on the ship and crowds ashore cheered the emperor as he debarked, wearing a flowing black cloak over a long white robe, fastened at the neck. Police took precautions to guard him and the customs shed was closed to the public until he had passed through. He left for London in a special coach attached to the boat train. The crown prince and the emperor's two daughters were in the retinue.

SOUTHAMPTON, Eng. (P) Haile Selassie, self-exiled emperor of Ethiopia, arrived here today aboard a passenger liner from Gibraltar. The greeting of Haile Selassie was without official ceremony, although he was guarded by British authorities as though his life were in danger. Selassie expressed a desire for privacy and even friends of other passengers were forbidden to board the S. S. Orford.

London, June 2 (#)—A high tribunal of inquiry today found James Henry Thomas, resigned Colonial Secretary, had revealed the sacred budget secrets of His Majesty's government. Climaxing Great Britain's major political scandal since the World War, the tribunal decided Thomas, who quit his post because of the budget leak furore, disclosed the secrets to Sir Alfred Butt, wealthy member of Parliament and to Alfred Bates, an advertising agency executive. It found further that Bates and Sir Alfred gambled and won as a result of the tip. Thomas, stunned by the fast-moving events of the last six weeks, went into seclusion to await the verdict of his House of Commons constituency as to whether he must resign from Parliament. First, however, he termed the verdict a “cruel one” and declared: “I repeat what I previously stated upon oath before the tribunal; that I made no disclosures of budget secret

SOUTHAMPTON, England.--Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia arrived today on his way to London to seek aid against Italian annexation of his country. Passengers on the ship and crowds ashore cheered the emperor.

VANCOUVER, 2. G0, sme ome (AP)—New electrical storms followed by heavy rainfall brought further flood threats to British Columbia today. While no flood deaths have been reported, lightning killed 13-year-old Keith Berkeley and his dog near Merritt. The electrical storms moved northeastward across the province and the accompanying downpours swelled already flooded rivers. The situation east of Prince Rupert continued acute as the Skeena River swept away bridges, houses, railway tracks and spread over lowlands. Hazelton, Kisplay and Glenvowell were flood-hit. The flood tore away many buildings and scores of families were homeless.

- MADISON, Wis., June 2 (#)—Mrs. William Ellery Leonard, 28-year-old wife of the eccentric, white-haired poet and English professor at the University of Wisconsin, became Miss Grace Golden today through a divorce decree that sealed the fate of an unsuccessful romance of less than a year. Without any protest, Prof. Leonard, who had been married twice before, the divorce was granted in circuit court here late yesterday by Judge A. C. Hoppmann. Mrs. Leonard was permitted to resume her maiden name and she accepted a property settlement of $4,400 in lieu of alimony. The 60-year-old poet, victim of a him confined to a small area around the university campus, was not there to witness the official end of the romance. He was represented only by his attorney, Robert B. L. Murphy. The property settlement was arranged in advance. Divorce Counsel Herman Sachtjen had given up hope of a reconciliation

Geneva, June 3 (UP) — The full assembly of the League of Nations, comprising 56 nations, most probably will meet here June 23 for a finish fight on the Italian-Ethiopian problem which entails the League’s whole future, it was learned authoritatively today. It was expected that the league council would meet June 22 to prepare for the assembly. It seemed certain that the meeting must be one of the most important in the 17 years since Woodrow Wilson’s dream of a world parliament of nations to enforce peace was incorporated into the Versailles treaty. As a result of the meeting, Italy may be forced by its national pride to leave the League. A start may be made toward revision of the League covenant and its Article X. It may start continental European nations on the way at last to a new political alignment. And it may start Europe toward either a war or a more secure peace. Argentina demanded

1936-08-17.text: MANILA, Aug. 17 (Monday) (*) —Distress calls from a third ship, a British vessel carrying passengers, and report of heavy damage and two deaths reached here today in the wake of a typhoon sweeping northern Luzon Island, - The Radio Corporation of America said it had intercepted an SOS from the British vessel Sunning, which asked immediate assistance at its position off Junk Bay on the China coast. Shipping men here said the Sunning, which carries an undetermined number of passengers, probably was hit by the same typhoon which swept across northern Luzon, wrecking native dwellings and destroying crops. Native Houses Wrecked Meager reports from Aparri said practically all native houses in that region were destroyed. An aged man and a little child were reported killed in the collapse of a hut at Cabenatuan in Nueva Ecija province, Advices indicated the storm, which was north of Manila, was

Kirkland Lake, Ont.—(#)—Three miners working on the 2,700-foot level of the Lake Shore gold mine were buried today in a cave-in. They were believed to be alive. Two others escaped. Names of the entombed men were given as Jack Bottrell, the shift boss, Jack Casey and William Morgan. Mining experts hoped to reach the men today. Rescue squads began to work frantically in an endeavor to reach them. Definite word on the condition of the entombed men awaited removal of rock blocking the passage to the mine shaft, it was said.

General Headquarters, Spanish Northern Rebel Army, Burgos, Aug. 17, (W.P)—Rebel chieftains believe they have broken the back of the government's resistance and that an army-fascist government for Spain is certain. "It is a veritable crime—it is more, it is insane—for Madrid to prolong its resistance," General Emilio Mola, rebel commander in chief in the north, said today. A column of 4,000 picked Moors and veterans of the Foreign Legion is being organized at Badajoz, taken at the bayonet point, to march eastward on Madrid from the Portuguese frontier. A rebel column is driving victoriously for Malaga, the government stronghold in the far south and has reached Antequera, only 23 miles north of the city—to find that 150 right wing adherents had been assassinated, according to official statements. A rebel column, it was asserted

LOUISVILLE, Que., Aug. 15.—(#)— A thundering freight train killed 22 persons and injured 12 others, six of them seriously, at a grade crossing here today. A large truck, loaded with 43 passengers, rolled onto the open, unobstructed crossing in the path of the racing locomotive. "Don't pass! Don't pass!" cried occupants of two other cars as the truck whipped around them and approached the tracks. A split second later the train struck. Bodies Hurled Many Feet The truck splintered. Bodies were catapulted dozens of feet on the right of way, under the wheels of the freight train. As it knifed through the mass of human forms, the locomotive applied its brakes. A handful of spectators sat transfixed. Flung 90 feet and tossed into the ditch beside the right of way, the truck caught fire. Flames licked back from the engine over the wreckage. A half dozen of the seriously injured ones groaned as r

MADRID, Aug. 15. — The Spanish government, its troops flung across the countryside in bloody battle against fascist rebellion, tonight ordered new socialization of industry and sought to halt flight of capital that might reach rebel hands. Oil, tobacco and other industries were given over to operators to operate under state control. A government decree forbade buying, selling or lending of securities and banned any transfer of real estate. The decree was applied to Spaniards both within and without Spain. The objective was to prevent members of the one-time nobility and rebels from liquidating their holdings for cash that might be used to purchase arms. The new step toward socialization was another in the program of the liberal government that originally was the cause of the rebellion. Rebels Forced Back The result was rebellion, now in its 29th day of bitter conflict and with neither si

Hendaye, France, Aug. 16 (/P) — A rebel war plane tonight dropped three bombs on the frontier French village of Biriatou apparently by accident. One of the bombs hit a small cafe. Another barely missed a church. No one was hurt. Two men playing cards in the cafe escaped safely. The rebel plane, supporting a general Fascist advance in Irun and other Government towns in the North, evidently intended to drop the bombs on Government troops defending the Spanish side of the Bidasoa river near Irun. It missed its target, however, and plopped three of the bombs on the French side. Earlier, other rebel bombing planes wrecked huge gasoline tanks at Bilbao which the Government had guarded successfully against sea attack with a living wall of rebel prisoners.

(Copyright, 1936, Associated Press) | Madrid, Aug. 16 (®) — Spain’s government, stumbling into the closing days of a month of civil war beset both by armed Fascist siege and by rising Communist clamor for a “baby Russia,” announced tonight the seizure of a vast store of clerical wealth. While huge excavating machines were being put into trench digging service to bulwark Loyalist positions in the Guadarrama mountains, authorities said more than 200,000,000 pesetas (nominally about $26,200,000) worth of currency, gold, jewels, and negotiable securities belonging to the Sisters of St. Vincent de Paul had been found by government accountants registering deposits at the Bank of Credit Lyonnais. Gasoline Destroyed Radio messages exchanged by foreign warships on the northern coast indicated, meanwhile, that rebel airplanes had destroyed a huge store of gasoline at Bilbao, after the tanks had be

Hendaye, France, Aug. 17 UP)—Rebel warships bombarded Irun and San Sebastian today and Spanish loyalists were reported executing fascist hostages in retaliation. Loyalists had served an ultimatum that the first shell from a rebel warship would be the signal for massacre of the prisoners held aboard two steamers in the Bay of Biscay harbor and frontier reports said the executions had begun. The huge battleship España directed heavy fire against Guadalupe but the government stronghold had not been hit after an hour and a half of bombardment. The attacks against Irun and San Sebastian began simultaneously, indicating a major offensive along the northern seaboard. The mighty guns of Fort Guadalupe did not reply at once and were faced with the dilemma of submitting to rebel fire or shelling the rebel warships at the risk of dropping projectiles on French territory across the Bay of Biscay. Th

1936-03-22.text: LONDON— (® —With the next move in European developments up to Reichsfuehrer Hitler, officials of the League of Nations said Saturday the threat of immediate peril has been removed from Europe. They declared that the League’s possibilities as a power for peace had been increased by the recent developments which included Germany’s remilitarization of the Rhineland and the league council’s decision that Germany had violated both the Versailles and Locarno treaties. Official British quarters said that now it was up to Hitler to make counter-proposals to the virtual ultimatum given him by Great Britain, France, Belgium, and Italy. MAKE PROPOSALS Those four nations which, with Germany, are the signatories of the Locarno pact, made a series of propositions to Germany under which they believe the peace front may be realigned. Most important of these proposals is France's offer to submit her mili

Germany, given a ‘virtual ultimatum’ by co-signatories of the Locarno treaty, has been placed in the position of having to make the next move in the proposals for revising Europe's peace machinery. Great Britain, France, Belgium and Italy have informed Germany, in effect, that her violation of the Locarno and Versailles treaties will be overlooked if she will agree to two main propositions: 1—To abide by a verdict of the court of international justice at the Hague as to whether France violated the Locarno pact in concluding her military alliance with Soviet Russia; 2—To permit an international police force in the Rhineland while the court acts on the case. Germany objects to the idea of foreign troops on her soil.

By The Associated Press Rome, March 21—A reliable source disclosed tonight representatives of Italy, Austria and Hungary had agreed, after conferences here, to sign a new consultative treaty strengthening and replacing the Rome accords of 1934. Premier Mussolini had made a renewed bid for continued friendship of Austria and Hungary in consultations with Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg of Austria and Premier Julius Gömbös of Hungary. It was nations which expressed their sympathy for the Italo-Ethiopian war with sanctions, The terms of the new treaty were still under discussion, but the principal points were said to have been covered. Austria wishes her independence guaranteed, but it was learned that Hungary is not very enthusiastic on that point. Nevertheless there were indications that this matter would be touched on in the treaty which would bind the three countries closer than the old acc

The unruly rivers roared fresh threats at people and property last night. Behind them, in the 13 states through which they course, were 167 dead—a figure that was increased only by two yesterday. The energetic heroism of thousands of relief workers had much to do with that. Behind them, too, were 221,500 homeless men, women and children. Even that figure was admittedly conservative. The property damage was at least $270,000,000. There was little doubt but that it would rise much higher. If the loss to wage earners and to retailers is considered, together with the eventual cost of relief and rehabilitation, the money cost may exceed a billion dollars. The state which suffered most during the week of unprecedented flood — Pennsylvania — appeared last night to be past the worst. The waters of the Monongahela and Allegheny which converge at Pittsburgh to form the Ohio, were falling. They wer

WASHINGTON, March 21.—(P)—Tentative agreement upon a plan to tax the entire net income of corporations upon the basis of earnings withheld from dividends tonight paved the way for starting open hearings March 30 on new tax legislation. The new proposal, designed to avoid a “tax on taxes,” was regarded as a sharp departure mechanically from President Roosevelt's original proposal, but as capable of carrying out his aims to force more corporate funds into circulation as well as raising $620,000,000 annually in additional revenue. It also contemplates through a graduated rate based upon the size of corporate earnings, helping small business build up depression reserves, while at the same time enabling large corporations to maintain what were described as “adequate” surpluses for hard times.

Washington, March 21,—(4)—Announcement of some details of the new farm program brought a quick response today in telegraphed protests against rates and conditions for paying soil conservation subsidies to producers of rice, sugar cane and sugar beets. The protesting farmers were understood to be contending they would not receive sufficient reimbursement under the payment plan outlined yesterday by Secretary Wallace. As agricultural extension directors arrived from several states to confer with the AAA, two main problems were reported bringing knitted brows in conferences of officials responsible for administration of the new farm relief plan. These were: 1. Division of the — $470,000,000 subsidy fund among the states. 2. Working out exact definitions for soil “depleting,” “conserving” and “building” crops, and classification of crops under such terms. (In a general way, the soil conserva

TRENTON, N. J., March 21.—(P)— Two moves will be made next week by defense lawyers to save Bruno Richard Hauptmann from death in the electric chair the night of March 31. C. Lloyd Fisher, an authoritative source disclosed today, will ask for a new trial, and failing in that direction, will seek mercy from the court of pardons for the man convicted of kidnapping and killing the Lindbergh baby.

By The Associated Press Akron, March 21—A seven-point agreement settled the Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company strike late today and the company announced work would be resumed “as quickly as possible.” Company spokesmen said full operation will hardly be underway for more than a week. A meeting of 3,000 of the United Rubber Workers of America voted almost unanimously to accept the terms offered by the company. The settlement terminates the strike which was started five weeks ago in protest over layoff of 63 men in the tire building department. A picket blockade has prevented any activity whatever at the three plants. The union endorsed the strike after it started. Many of the employes belong to the Goodyear assembly which the unionists call a “company union” and leaders of this group had protested against the strike. Seven Points Listed The seven points of the agreement were: All employes

1936-02-21.text: GEORGETOWN, British Guiana, Feb. 21.—(#)—Art Williams, American aviator seeking Paul Redfern in the Brazilian jungle, insisted today that whatever befell Redfern in his 1927 flight from Brunswick, Ga., to Rio de Janeiro, it was still a mystery. Williams, the man who taught Redfern to fly, said of his recent aerial expedition into the interior, where Redfern is believed by some to have crashed and still to be alive: "We made a new contact with ten new Indian villages and collected a great deal of information, and the most that was established is that Redfern did not land in that area." Took Photographs. The aviator said most of the evidence he had collected consisted of photographs, which he indicated he had sent to the long-lost Redfern’s father in the United States. Alfred Harred, a reporter, asserted in the Paramaribo newspaper "Banier" yesterday that he and Williams had located Redfer

| GEORGETOWN, British Guiana, Feb. 20 (#)—Another unsupported tale of the finding of Paul Redfern, long lost aviator, in the jungle of Brazil, brought action by two governments and a denial by one of the purported rescuers today. Alfred Harred, reporter, declared through his newspaper, Baniern of Paramaribo, Dutch Guiana, that he and Art Williams, former United States Army flier, had found Redfern, crippled, in an Indian village in the Tumuc Humac Mountains. Williams, who has been making the flights into the interior, denied the story, saying: “I do not know Harred and he most certainly did not accompany me on my recent search.” U. S. and Brazil Act. The State Department at Washington cabled instructions to the American consul at Port of Spain, Trinidad, to investigate Harred’s story. The Brazilian foreign office asked its boundary commission, working in the northeastern jungles, to dete

LONDON, Feb. 20.—(4)—The shadow of sanctions fell across the entangled international naval conference today with a report Italy may “counter-sanction” by refusing to enter a naval agreement until the League of Nations lifts embargoes against her. British sources said they are confident the sanctions problem could be staved off. In some quarters the belief was expressed only extraordinary conciliatory efforts by the British could prevent the failure of the conference.
BREMERHAVEN, Germany, Feb. 21.—A Dutch tanker sank today and four of her crew were missing after a collision with the British steamer, Logosian, during a fog over the Weser River.

OSAKA, Japan, Feb. 21, (4)—An earthquake extending over 10 prefectures killed five persons and injured 16 seriously today, police survey there showed. Twelve buildings were destroyed and 17 badly damaged. Interurban railways, telephone and telegraph lines were temporarily disrupted.

OSAKA, Japan — Friday — Feb. 21. () — A strong earthquake shook the Osaka-Kobe district today and reserves of police and firemen were mobilized to fight fires, which broke out in 12 places, and to prevent a panic. Three persons were known to have been killed and several houses were reported to have collapsed in the quake which occurred at 10:07 a.m. Electric wires were broken in the city. The Osaka stock exchange suspended business temporarily, but later the session was resumed. Osaka’s three known dead were chimney sweeps, shaken from tall smokestacks. The Kobe observatory placed the quake’s epicenter at 50 miles to the east of Kobe, and said it lasted for one minute. There was no report of damage from the city of Nara, which felt the shock. The city of Kyoto also was reported to have been shaken heavily. Broken telephone and telegraph lines delayed receipt of news from the countryside.

Munich, Germany —(#)— Charles Nisselbeck, naturalized United States citizen tried for “attempted high treason”, was sentenced today to two years imprisonment, of which he has served nine months while under investigation. The prosecuting attorney had asked that Nisselbeck be sentenced to six years imprisonment, charging that the defendant “was prepared to enter into communication with Otto Strasser,” exiled leader of the anti-Hitler “black front.” The defense insisted, however, that Nisselbeck was an agent of the steel helmets, disbanded war veterans organization, and that he had no intention of overthrowing the German government.

BERLIN, Feb. 20. (?)—The possibility of an Italo-German rapprochement became the center of interest for diplomats tonight as Ulrich von Hassell, Germany’s ambassador to Italy, left for Rome after his second conference in five days with Reichsfuehrer Adolf Hitler. Belief was expressed in diplomatic circles that Hitler and Premier Mussolini were discussing, through Von Hassell, the possibility of Italy taking reprisals against France by withdrawing as a guarantor of the Locarno pact if sanctions were voted against Italy. Von Hassell had flown here after a conference with Fluvio Suvich, Italian undersecretary for foreign affairs. German officials declined to discuss the reasons for the ambassador's flying trips, and ignored reports from Italy that Hitler and Mussolini were seeking an agreement regarding independent Austria. Regarding the Locarno pact, diplomats pointed out that France and G

1936-02-02.text: ME RAI ANNOUNCING Press The “annihilation” of a northern Italian army by Ethiopian warriors was reported Saturday in a Reuters (British) news agency dispatch from Dessye. It said the Italians, under General Diamanti, were defeated in the largest battle of the war and that the famous blackshirt division “28th of October” participated in the engagement. Leaders In Conference Fascism’s highest leaders gathered in Rome under Premier Mussolini for a crucial meeting of the grand council. They came together shortly after Il Duce’s own newspaper said in an editorial that a blockade of Italy is possible and that such a step by sanctionist nations would mean a European war. Emperor Haile Selassie sought to bulwark his southern army, reportedly falling back before hard driving Italian motorized columns. He dispatched two experienced Turn to Page 9, Column 6 Plea

London.--(AP)-- Bound for the “last great adventure on earth,” the first members of the 1936 Mt. Everest expedition left here today, en route to Darjeeling, India, for a new assault on the world’s highest mountain. Three men and one woman departed, and the nine other members of the party will follow in a few days. The woman, Mrs. Noel Humphreys, will accompany her husband, Dr. Humphreys, only as far as Darjeeling. Hugh Ruttledge, veteran leader of the 1933 expedition, again will lead the drive up the perilous, snowbound heights toward the 29,000-foot pinnacle which has defied four previous attempts and has taken nine lives. “I believe we'll make it this time,” he said quietly, standing in the crowded boat-train station, “With any reasonable weather, I'm confident of success.” In the 1933 attempt, Ruttledge’s party fought its way to within 1,000 feet of the top, only to be driven back by

ROME — Premier Mussolini summoned his Fascist grand council today to a solemn session and led a simultaneous celebration of Italy’s “Militia Day,” amid grim warnings of peril of a European war arising from the Ethiopian conflict. A bluntly-phrased editorial in Il Duce’s own newspaper, Popolo D'Italia of Milan, charged that “if sanctions were extended” and a political victory was won by the pressure of “imperialists and the blood thirsty,” Europe would fall fatefully toward humanity's “most terrible, unjust war.” An informed source said this admonition was decided upon only after Mussolini learned by telephone of the results of a private London conference between Emanuele Grandi, Italian ambassador to Great Britain, and British Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden. Given Wide Publicity The editorial, occupying two newspaper columns, received extraordinary publicity. The government-controlled pr

| ROME.—Fear of a European war growing out of the East Africa situation, a fear that has been subdued for more than a month, was expressed officially today by a spokesman of the Italian foreign Office. | “Once again we say,” the spokesman said, “developments are taking place in Geneva which are leading Europe to war.” | In Geneva the League is meeting to consider an oil embargo. Rome is making it known officially that oil sanctions would be considered more than an economic measure. The move of Great Britain to ally other countries to this move has tended to create a tense situation in Europe. A spokesman in the War office ridiculed Ethiopian claim of a major victory.

ROME, Feb. 2.—(Sunday)—(AP)—Premier Mussolini talked for two hours on the Italian political military situation at a session of the Fascist grand council which closed early today. The meeting of the Fascist leaders came after Italians had read a warning in Il Duce's own newspaper that “Italy will defend herself with teeth and nails. She has long been prepared for any eventuality.”
SAINT B, Jan, 18—A steel engraving of the world’s first fog horn, erected on Partridge Island, near here, in 1855, has been found among old Winchot papers lately.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 1.—(AP)—The United Mine Workers formally endorsed President Roosevelt today for re-election and decided to contribute to the Democratic campaign fund. “It might be well for the American Federation of Labor to take cognizance of what this convention has done,” said John L. Lewis, the miners’ president, when the 1,700 delegates had unanimously adopted the Roosevelt resolution. “If the A. F. of L. would follow suit, as it should, then for all practical purposes, the result of the next election would no longer be in doubt.” The Federation traditionally takes no part in presidential elections. ——-(Concluded on page 3)———

Los Angeles, Jan. 31.—(/P)—Two bank robbery suspects were killed and another seized today after they had held up a bank one block from the sheriff’s department pistol range in suburban El Monte. Eighteen of the best pistol marksmen of the sheriff's office answered when a telephone operator relayed the bank’s call to the target range. The deputies, their pistols warm from firing, climbed into automobiles and were ready for action when they halted their cars only a block away. Dead The dead men were identified by sheriff's deputies as Clarence Smith, of Glendale, Calif., and E. C. Yates, of Beverly Hills, Calif. More than a score of the bank’s employees and customers were in the bank when the 18 sheriff's deputies surrounded the bank and opened fire with the bandits, who were armed with submachine guns. Frank F. Smith, brother of the (Continued on Page ?%)

1936-02-15.text: London--(INS)—Condition of Earl Beatty, one of the greatest naval figures of the World War, “gives cause for anxiety,” his physicians announced Saturday. The noted admiral has been in poor health recently, and yesterday a complete rest was ordered. A leading participant in the battle of Jutland, then commander-in-chief of the British Grand Fleet, and first sea lord, Earl Beatty is 65 years old. His wife, the former Ethel Field of Chicago, died in 1932.

Copyright, 1936, Associated Press London, Feb. 15. -—-(#)— British government opposition sources advanced a suggestion today that the stormy House of Commons defense debate might precipitate a government crisis, imperiling the position of Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin. The criticism turned upon Baldwin by Sir Austen Chamberlain during yesterday's Commons discussion of the government project for increased national defenses, opposition sources said, might set in motion forces leading to a crisis. Sir Austen, former foreign minister and first lord of the admiralty, called attention during the debate to what he said were “errors” by Baldwin in defense questions. The prestige of the prime minister has been a much-debated topic in the Commons lobbies since the collapse of the Anglo-French proposals for Italo-Ethiopian peace. Some opposition sources contended

LONDON, Feb. 14 (#)—The British admiralty moved quietly to man its depleted home fleet today while defense debate raged in the house of commons and the navy’s ability to withstand aerial attacks was seriously questioned. An order permitting pensioners to rejoin the navy reached fleet ports from the admiralty as the outgrowth of the massing of ships in the Mediterranean and the recommissioning of decommissioned craft for service in home waters.

Boston.-(AP)—Distress calls from far out on the storm whipped north Atlantic sent coast cutters hurrying to crippled vessels of New England's deep sea fishing fleet today. - The cutter Algonquin put a tow line aboard the disabled auxiliary schooner Mary and Julia at 4 a.m., (E. S T.) The small New Bedford fisherman had wallowed in mountainous seas off Nantucket since Thursday night, pine To the north, the cutter Cayuga, Boston bound with the crew of the schooner Gertrude M. Fauci, turned about to answer a call for immediate aid from the Boston trawler W

English-born Irene Phister, 28, herself critically wounded, scorned questioners today as they sought a motive for the fatal Valentine’s Day shooting of her 26-year-old American husband in a hotel here. She was unaware that the young husband, who blew kisses to her as they were carried to a hospital, had died, or that a coroner’s jury had accused her of firing the bullet that killed him. She admitted shooting herself. The husband, Warren Thornton Phister, member of a prominent Kansas City family and student at the University of Missouri here, died eight hours after he was shot mumbling: “She did it—we had a quarrel, but it doesn’t matter, it doesn’t matter.” Mrs. Phister would not say who fired the first shot. Police Detective Frank Fenton said the shooting “looks like a clear case of suicide pact,” but Prosecutor William H. Sapp said Phister, before his death, denied that such a pact exi

LONDON, Feb 15.—(INS)—The London Naval Conference seemed likely Saturday to dash itself into oblivion against the steel sides of Germany's new and growing war fleet. The British are insisting that they will not sign any qualitative treaty unless Germany also signs. The French are even more insistent on the same point. And the Americans, who entered the conference on conditions that they would not be drawn into any European squabbles, are so irritated at this French and British attitude that they are likely to insist that Japan signs, too. Thus, even if some agreement is arrived at over capital ships, it will likely be only a “ghost treaty”—a protocol initiated by four powers, which would become a treaty only when and if Germany, Japan and Russia added their signatures to it.

MOSCOW, Feb. 15 (Saturday) (#)—The Soviet and Japanese governments have agreed in principle to the appointment of a mixed commission to investigate clashes on the Soviet-Manchoukuoan border, an official communique said early Saturday. The offer of the Japanese Government to enter into such an arrangement was communicated to the foreign office by Japanese Ambassador Tamekichi Ota. G. S. Stomoniakoff, Russian vice-commissar for foreign affairs, pointed out that the Soviet Government frequently has made similar proposals in the past.

Moscow, Feb. 1! Indignantly rejected a Japanese answer to its protest regarding a clash on the Manchukuoan frontier, it was announced today. Tamakichi Okta, Japanese ambassador, delivered the Japanese reply yesterday. It said that Russians, not Manchukuoans, were the attackers and that the clash occurred on Manchukuoan, not Russian soil. B. S. Stomonyokay, assistant commissar of foreign affairs, rejected the reply indignantly, it was said, calling it unfactual and a gross invention and slander hiding the real actions of Japanese militarists. Okta told correspondents that Japan would agree to a frontier commission to investigate this and similar charges.

1936-11-12.text: LONDON. (UP). Uncensored, telephonic advices from a neutral source in Madrid said a heavy artillery duel was in progress and that the government forces were holding their own. JACA, Spain. (UP). A nationalist broadcast at 3:45 p. m. said "many edifices in Madrid are afire as a result of our artillery and aviation." The broadcast described heavy losses by the loyalists. MADRID. (Copyright by UP). A heavy artillery barrage rocked Madrid and its environs as government and nationalist batteries resumed a fierce cannonade. With rain and poor visibility preventing the powerful aviation forces of either side from operating, the leftist artillery began shelling the insurgent positions on almost the entire Madrid front, the nationalists quickly responding and concentrating on the government batteries. Food Supply Drops. Its food supply scant and its general supplies waning, Madrid was put under d

LONDON, Nov. 12—(AP)—Great Britain's decree nisi system of divorce, which provisionally severed the marital bonds of Mrs. Ernest ('Wallie') Simpson at Ipswich, came under fire today in the House of Commons. Led by A. P. Herbert, M. P. for Oxford University, sponsors of the reform can be seen advocating the revision of the present system of divorce laws.

LONDON, Nov. 12.—(UP)—Mrs. Wallis Simpson intends soon to leave for the continent, perhaps to remain there until her decree of divorce becomes absolute next spring, it was learned today. She will stay on the Riviera with her friends, Mr. and Mrs. Herman Rogers of New York, who were members of the party which, including Mrs. Simpson, the king entertained at Balmoral Castle, Scotland, several weeks ago. Mrs. Simpson's consideration of the possibility of a long stay coincides with an increasing crowded engagement list for the king. He was at Portland today to inspect the fleet. He must go next weekend to visit distressed areas—in which, as in housing and slum clearance, he is deeply interested. Further, from now until his coronation next May he will be increasingly busy with details of arrangements for the ceremony, which he personally must approve.

- LONDON, Nov. 12 (AP)—The Marquess of Donegall, London society columnist, lamented his journalistic curiosity today. The Marquess ordered a Milwaukee, Wis., clipping bureau to send him all newspaper stories on the divorce of Mrs. Ernest Simpson, King Edward's American friend. He and a few colleagues just wanted to see how American newspapers would handle the story, Lord Donegall declared. Now he’s inundated with information. He ruefully surveyed his littered apartment and office, piled high with batches of clippings, and hoped now “the damn things will stop coming.” His rooms are overflowing. Beside those clippings that had come before, 6,000 more arrived this week and still they come.

LONDON, Nov. 11 (UP).-- Vivian Jackson, wealthy young astronomy professor and gentleman jockey, nominated himself today fifth husband of Peggy Hopkins Joyce, the American actress. But, he pointed out, he is married to someone else and, though he is now in the midst of a divorce proceeding, it probably will be next summer before he and Miss Joyce can make their trip to the altar. Miss Joyce has been a guest at the Jackson home in suburban Cranleigh for several days.

MANCHESTER, Eng., Nov. 12—A cotton strike by Christmas threatened Lancashire Textile Mills today. Textile union officials have decided to poll the membership for authority to call the strike. The voting is expected to be completed within two or three weeks. If the workers vote to strike, officials said, they would quit their jobs during Christmas week.

Chicago, Nov. 11.—(4?)—Penniless Alfred H. Kitchener Floyd, 58 years old, formerly a captain in the British royal horse artillery, will be buried Saturday afternoon with the full rites of a military funeral. Today—Armistice Day—friends of the world war hero who had eight campaign medals and three citations for gallantry in action, were raising a subscription fund to defray the costs of the funeral. Floyd died October 30 in the county hospital after he had become ill in a Kansas WPA work camp.

PORTLAND, England, Nov, 12—King Edward, with his own memories of midshipman life in the navy, opened his inspection tour of Britain’s home fleet today by asking rapid-fire questions about the food and general comfort of lower-deck jack tars. Glad in the undress uniform of an admiral of the fleet, with heavy grey coat to withstand the buffeting of wind-lashed rain, the bachelor monarch began his two-day visit at 9:15 am. He visited five battleships, chatting informally on the quarterdeck with each commanding officer.

1936-11-04.text: London, Nov. 4 (UP)—Countries in every continent expressed joy today at the re-election of President Roosevelt. In Nazi Germany alone of the many nations was there a lack of enthusiasm. Germany's commentators would have preferred a conservative victory. Elsewhere, the president's good neighbor policy came home to him. He was hailed from London to Japan, from Rome to the little Negro Liberia, as a friend who while mindful of his own country’s interest found time, and had the capability to understand the problems of others. Even in such dictatorial countries as Italy, the victory was acclaimed. Italians remember that during the war, when other nations were penalizing Italy, President Roosevelt preserved strict neutrality—which was all Italy asked.

(By United Press.) Europe watched the outcome of the American presidential election Tuesday night with interest unequalled since 1920 when James M. Cox battled with Warren G. Harding over the League of Nations issue. Press comment from London, Paris, Berlin, Rome and Madrid showed that the majority of newspapers were predicting President Roosevelt's re-election. It also revealed that Europe is primarily interested in the part the United States will play in world affairs as the result of the elections. There was only a mild interest registered in Mr. Roosevelt's domestic social and economic policies. Press comments, briefly: LONDON—The London press, with the exception of the Daily Mail, predicted Mr. Roosevelt's re-election. The News-Chronicle called the President “America’s Lloyd George” and Governor Alfred M. Landon “America’s Baldwin.” The Washington correspondent of the Times, Sir Wil

London, Nov. 4. (UP) — An agreement for humanizing submarine warfare as envisaged by the naval treaty of 1930 is expected to be signed here Friday by delegates of the United States, Great Britain, the British dominions, India, Japan, Italy and France. Afterward Germany and other powers will be asked to sign. New York, Nov. 4. (UP)—The liner American Trader sailed today with a crew supplied by officials of the International Seamen’s Union as the waterfront awaited developments in the seamen’s sympathy strike.

MADRID, Nov. 3.—(AP)—Madrid’s terrified inhabitants watched today from their housetops the fight for possession of their city’s suburbs. The familiar warning sirens sounded every half-hour as the enemy planes flew over the capital. There was no attempt to continue the serial bombings which have taken a toll of 216 lives since last Friday. Insurgent aviators today contented themselves with showering down leaflets calling upon the populace to surrender. Flying high, the planes banked and dived far out of range of government anti-aircraft batteries. On the rooftops, the city’s residents clustered silently to watch the battles their fighting forces were waging to halt the enemy advance almost within the city's suburbs. Flames shot skyward through the evening dusk as insurgent planes loosed incendiary bombs near (Continued On Page 4, Col 7)

Spanish Nationalist artillery blasted the southern suburbs of Madrid today and Nationalist shock troops, confident of victory, awaited the order to storm the city. A rebel broadcast communique from Corunna asserted the Getafe airdrome and artillery barracks, six miles from the city proper and actually one of its suburbs, was destroyed by artillery fire along with a neighboring railroad station. Infantry, led by racing whippet tanks, moved forward irresistibly and the Nationalists joined their lines on a wide front extending from south to west of the city. Mostoles, Villaviciosa and other towns were taken and the next objective was Carabanchel, a great military barracks on the city limits. Nationalist airplanes, flying high over the sleeping city this morning, dropped new demands for peaceable surrender. Townspeople were advised, in leaflets, that they had nothing to fear; that only the g

By United Press WARSAW, Nov. 3.—General Edward Rydz-Smigly today was named marshal of Poland. The move was interpreted in political circles as making him virtual dictator, inheritor of the mantle of the late Marshal Pilsudski.

BARCELONA, Spain.— Fifteen death sentences against rebels were carried out at 9:30 a.m. today. Those executed included officers condemned aboard the warship Uruguay and persons condemned by the popular tribunals.

By United Press MADRID, Nov. 4—"The loyalists fell back before the attacking rebel armies today, evacuating the major airport at Getafe and the town of Leganes, both less than seven miles from the capital’s city limits." Prior to the evacuation of Getafe Airport, members of the cabinet after a meeting at the war ministry said loyal government war planes had downed four enemy planes during sharp engagements near the city. Two others described as Junkers (German-made) fled. The planes were challenged after flying over Carabanchel and dropping several bombs in the vicinity of a military hospital there. Six civilians were wounded in this air raid. The rebels launched a big counter-offensive against Getafe airport and Leganes. Three tri-motored rebel airplanes bombed the loyalist lines at Getafe. Incendiary bombs set fire to part of the village.

1936-09-01.text: WATERBURY, Conn., Sept. 1.— Col. Frank Knox Republican nominee for the vice presidency, carried his national campaign tour deep into New England today, leaving with a Connecticut audience a declaration that “Professions of friendship and promises of legislation” have “beguiled” the American working man. “Wages are not and cannot be set by law,” Knox told an open air rally at Hamilton park last night, “they are set by the productivity of the land, the capital and the worker himself. When government attempts to set wages, it only disturbs industry and lowers total wages.” Knox said the Roosevelt administration’s recovery program, and not the depression, was responsible for continued unemployment and predicted that historians “will be wracking their brains to explain what this administration was trying to do” for the next 25 years.
JERUSALEM, Sept. 1. (Palcor Agcy.) — British troops and a police patrol yesterday killed two members of an Arab band and wounded four others, the government announced today.

LONDON, Sept 1.—(INS)— Mrs. Beryl Markham, London society aviatrix, postponed a projected solo hop across the Atlantic today because of unfavorable weather. LONDON, Sept. 1—(INS)—Mrs. Beryl Markham, 41-year-old mother prominent in London society, planned to hop off for New York today in an attempt to be the first woman to fly alone westward across the Atlantic. Shortly after 3 p.m. Mrs. Markham ordered her plane rolled out onto the field at the Royal Air Force airport at Abingdon and tuned up for the hop-off.

(DY LHe ASHOCI“NTECU Fess) Madrid, Sept. 1—Careful estimates from Madrid today placed the dead in the first five weeks of civil war at between 75,000 and 100,000. The wounded were estimated at 800,000. Today in the middle of the seventh week of war air fleets and big guns of both the socialist government and the fascist rebels blasted new ruin and death. U. S. Takes Steps The United States government, with one of its warships already the target for air bombs, moved to get all its vessels out of the danger area. A rebel bombing fleet again bombed the streets while the government mapped a cabinet reorganization which would put a communist as well as a socialist “strong man” Indalecio Prieto in a ministry position. Women, children and old men were evacuated from the city after a rebel bomb had blown two women to pieces during the earlier bombardment of the besieged city. The Archbishop of Canterbury warned that “the world seems to be going mad.” The German embassy was moved from Madrid where defenders were preparing to repel a rebel air attack. Madrid, Sept. 1.—Prospective reorganization of the Spanish Socialist cabinet to include one Communist member was reported today as the capital was awakened shortly before dawn by a fresh rebel air attack. Fascist bombing planes dropped a number of bombs into the city streets but a preliminary survey showed only slight damage. The population was aroused by screaming sirens. Searchlights swept the sky. Anti-aircraft batteries and machine guns roared out against the aerial raiders. The bombardment lasted for almost three-quarters of an hour. Then small groups of frightened citizens began to emerge from subway stations, basements and lower floors of their homes. Revision of the membership of Premier Jose Giral Pereira’s cabinet, “to comply with demands of the present circumstances,” was outlined by a high authoritative source. The personnel changes, it was declared, would be designed to give

Moscow, Sept. 1--Nine hundred thousand recruits were ordered into the army today in a call which, while of routine nature, served to bring the army's strength to 3,600,000, a net increase of 300,000. The entire class of 1914—men born in that year—was called to the colors as a regular seasonal measure. In addition, in keeping with the decree for army increase, which was issued August 11, half of the class of 1915 was called up. The 600,000 men in the 1914 class will replace an equal number of the last class, who will be released. The 300,000 men of 1915 will provide the increase. The official newspaper Izvestia, commenting on the call, warned that recruits must be selected carefully to keep out “class enemies” who might try to carry out subversive work.

TORONTO, Ont., Sept. 1 (UP). Rudy Vallee revenged a beer bottle salute in the ballroom of the Canadian National Exhibition with a right to the jaw early today. Later he discovered he had knocked down the wrong man and apologized. Directing his orchestra, his back to the dancers, Vallee turned in time to see the beer bottle flying at his head. He ducked. “Who threw that?” he shouted, bringing the dancers and the orchestra to a stop. There was no answer except for a chorus of guffaws. A member of the orchestra pointed to a man in the group. “That's the guy, Rudy,” he said. Vallee stepped down from the stand, strode up to the man and with one blow knocked him down. A moment later the band was playing and the dancers were dancing. The victim protested he had not thrown the bottle. Several witnesses corroborated him. Vallee returned to the floor and told him he was sorry.

1936-05-08.text: Rome, May 8. (4?)—White clad and wan, Emperor Haile Selassie reached his exile goal of Palestine today while the second city of his fallen Ethiopian empire—Harar—was reported in flames. A British warship carried the fleeing “King of Kings” to a respectful military reception in Haifa and the Negus rode through streets patrolled by heavily armed troops to board a train for Jerusalem. The armed patrols were there primarily to curb any Arab-Jew outbreaks current in Palestine. Harar, long the goal of the Italian forces from the south, was reported captured by the troops of General Rodolfo Graziani after rioters had looted and burned in a fashion similar to that experienced in Addis Ababa. The capture of Harar was said to complete Italy's military objective in Ethiopia.

JERUSALEM, May 8.—Emperor Haile Selassie and the exiled Ethiopian imperial family arrived here today from Haifa where they were put ashore from the British cruiser Enterprise as political refugees seeking asylum in Palestine.

(By Associated Press) London, May 8—Great Britain was declared by responsible sources today to be putting renewed pressure on Germany for the inclusion of Soviet Russia, Latvia and Estonia in the Reich's proposed non-aggression pact. That point, said the source, was the most important contained in the Locarno questionnaire which Great Britain has handed to Germany after consultation with France and Belgium. Germany, when she precipitated the Locarno crisis by rearming the Rhineland, put a major share of the responsibility on Soviet Russia. She contended that the Franco-Russian mutual assistance pact threatened central and western Europe with the introduction of Bolshevik terrorism. Britain likewise requested a clear declaration from Hitler as to whether Germany now regards herself in a position to conclude “genuine treaties.”

London, May 8, (W.P.)——Great Britain, in a questionnaire of historic importance to Adolf Hitler, asked him whether he now considers Germany to be in a position to conclude “genuine treaties,” it was disclosed today. The question, in a note calculated to conciliate Germany rather than to antagonize her, was a direct invitation to Hitler to say frankly and formally whether he now considers his Nazi Germany to be on an equal status with other powers. Hitler's reason for violating the Versailles Treaty and for denouncing the Locarno Treaty by reoccupying the demilitarized Rhineland zone was, he said, that Germany did not negotiate those treaties as an equal.
