The questionnaire, presented to Baron Konstantin von Neurath, German foreign minister yesterday by Sir Eric Phipps, British ambassador, was published today as a foreign office “white paper.” It asked Hitler his attitude on “the remaining

By The Associated Press. LONDON, May —(Palcor agency)—Reliable sources said today that the British government had ordered transport airplanes filled with British soldiers to fly from Cairo to Palestine to prevent further rioting between Arabs and Jews.

LONDON, May 7—(AP)—The Dutch Steamer Alphard was sunk in the North Sea tonight when it collided with the Hamburg-American liner New York, but all 26 members of the Alphard’s crew were saved. In a crash in the Straits of Dover, the forecastle of the Antonietta Lauro, an Italian vessel, was smashed as it collided with the Steamer Columbus of the North German Lloyd line. The New York, a 21,000-ton vessel bound for Hamburg, rescued the Alphard’s crew after the accident and put about for Southampton. The collision occurred in a mist in the open sea north of Ostend, Belgium. The Columbus, of 32,565 gross tons, was en route to Bremen, Germany, from New York. Both the New York and the Columbus left New York City April 30. Neither the Columbus nor the Antonietta Lauro, a vessel of 5,428 tons, requested assistance. The Italian ship headed for Dover after the crash. The exact position of the collis

LONDON, May 8 (#)--A clear declaration from Adolf Hitler as to whether Germany now regards itself in a position to conclude "genuine treaties" was requested today in a British questionnaire, arising from the Locarno crisis. The questionnaire, presented to the Berlin foreign office yesterday, was made public in London today in a white paper, or government report. "It is of course clear that negotiations for a treaty would be useless if one of the parties hereafter felt free to deny its obligations on the ground that that party was not at the time in a condition to conclude a binding treaty," the questionnaire said. Great Britain called attention to the German memorandum of March 24, calling for negotiations of new treaties, and suggested it was the German government's view that by its occupation of the Rhineland, in violation of the Locarno pact, it had established a position for conclusi

LONDON, May 8 (4)—Three damaged ships proceeded to port today. One was sunk and its crew of 26 rescued after two collisions last night in fog that enveloped the English Channel. The 3,551-ton Netherlands cargo steamer Alphard went down near Ostend, Belgium, just north of the channel after colliding with the 21,000-ton Hamburg-American liner New York. The German vessel reported all members of the Alphard’s crew were saved and taken aboard the New York. The liner, bound from New York to Hamburg, suffered damage to its bow in the collision but proceeded to Cuxhaven, port of Hamburg, to land the rescued seamen there. Less than an hour after the Ostend collision, the 5,428-ton Italian cargo ship Antonietta Lauro and the 42,565-ton steamer Columbus of the North German Lloyd line crashed in the Straits of Dover, the channel between England and France. The Italian ship, badly battered and its fo

1936-07-21.text: Tampa, Fla. (#)--The United States Coast Guard concentrated a large fleet in the Yucatan Channel and Caribbean Sea today under orders to learn the fate of 22 persons aboard the missing British motor ship, Munoca. Preparations were guided by knowledge of the vessel’s stores probably were exhausted many days ago. Three ships of the Cuban Navy joined the search. Nine Coast Guard boats were told to disregard territorial boundaries and carry the hunt as far south as Grand Cayman Island. The 100-foot Munoca left Georgetown, chief port of that island, for Tampa July 4 and was due here four or five days later. Aboard the Munoca were nine Americans, four British subjects and a crew of eight under command of Capt. Moses I. Kirkconnell.

TAMPA, Fla. July 20.—()—The United States Coast Guard extended its search for the missing British motor-ship Nunoca outside the country’s territorial waters today as another day passed without word of the sturdy little banana boat and the 22 persons aboard her. The 110-foot craft left Georgetown, Grand Cayman Island, July 4 carrying nine Americans, four Britons, and a crew of eight commanded by Captain Moses J. Kirkconnell. She was due here July 9. She has no radio and was provisioned for only five days. Today was the fourth that Coast Guard craft have scanned southern waters for the missing ship. The Cuban navy joined the hunt yesterday. Coast Guard officials and port authorities theorized the Nunoca might have developed engine trouble and made a safe but isolated anchorage or that she is drifting helplessly in the open sea. Service planes from the St. Petersburg base have combed the Gu

London, July 21.—(AP)—Formal agreement on a three-power Locarno parley here, beginning Thursday, was reached today at a conference between Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden and the French and Belgian ambassadors. The consultations were followed by a cabinet meeting. Authoritative observers expected the talks would be confined to arrangements for a later five-power conference. A British foreign office communique stated the object of the meeting was ‘to consider how best to further the desires of the three powers to consolidate the peace of Europe by means of a general settlement.’

London, Tuesday, July 31.—The Reuters (British) news agency reported early today word received at Bayonne, France, said 8,000 Spanish Monarchists and 4,000 rebel troops were marching on Madrid. The insurgent force, reported to be under the command of General Mola, was said to be accompanied by an artillery regiment. Toulouse, France, July 26—Passengers on the regular Casablanca to Paris plane reported tonight Spanish government planes were continuously bombing the Barcelona arsenal and artillery barracks. Many buildings in the northeastern city, including the Church of Our Lady of Larepo, were reported in flames.

TAMPA, Fla. —(U.P)— Coast patrol cutters and amphibian planes of five nations deployed in tropical waters from Yucatan to Jamaica today in search of the missing British motor-ship Nunoca whose disappearance is another chapter in the tragic saga of the Kirkconnell family. Carrying 13 passengers, including nine Americans and women and children and a crew of nine commanded by Capt. Moses I. Kirkconnell, the 110-foot motorship cleared Grand Cayman, 13 days ago. She has not been heard from since. Along the waterfront in Honduras and Grand Cayman veteran sailors feared the ship had foundered. They recalled that the ship’s captain is a member of a famous seagoing family which has lost four of its members in unsolved mysteries of the treacherous Gulf Stream. Humphrey and MacGregor, ship brokers, said today they were advised by Capt. H. Wheeler of the Hondurian motorship Anger that he had sighted
LONDON, July 21.—(UP)—The Spanish gunboat Dato was reported to have been sunk by gunfire from government submarines off Ceuta, Morocco, an Exchange Telegraph dispatch from Tangier said today.

LONDON, July 20—(1?)—King Edward, it was learned tonight, may delay his vacation on the French Riviera for a few days. The King, who tonight completed his first six months on the throne, was understood to be contemplating returning to London to conduct state business after Sunday's dedication ceremony at the Canadian monument erected on Vimy Ridge. There was no question, authoritative sources said, of calling off the vacation entirely. The King has arranged to occupy the Villa of the American actress, Maxine Elliott, near Cannes. With the prosecution working up its case against George Andrew McMahon, now charged with “possession of a revolver with intent to endanger life” of the King, the Monarch will end his full mourning for his late father, King George, tomorrow. At the same time, he will hold his first ceremonial function since the seeming attempt at his life as he rode through the c

WIMBLEDON, Eng., July 21. (P)— Australia gained the Davis Cup challenge round against England today as Vivian McGrath defeated Heiner Henkel of Germany, 6-3, 5-7, 6-4, 6-4 for the Aussies’ third and clinching victory in their tennis series against the Teutons.

1936-02-22.text: MADRID. (Copyright by AP). Civil guards killed two extremist rioters and wounded 10 more at Bollullos del Condado, Huelva province, raising the total of election dead to 27 persons. The new leftist government of Manuel Azana was forced to declare martial law in many communities as a result of increased rioting by the celebrating leftists. Civil guards and troops were active everywhere, attempting to restore order while hundreds of political prisoners were released from jails. Red flags were raised by communists in several isolated villages. The killings at Bollullos del Condado were precipitated by a crowd of extremists who attacked conservatives of the village. The civil guards, Spain's semi-military constabulary, tried to break up the fight but, failing, shot a volley into the extremist ranks. One of the men wounded in Barcelona rioting died. One hundred guards, armed with machine guns

(Copyright, 1936, Associated Press) MADRID, Feb. 22—A general amnesty decree, offering unconditional freedom to all political prisoners, lent a calming influence to Spain today, but radicals persisted in some sections in their riotous celebration of the Leftist assumption of power. The fresh disorders, carrying on the demonstrations in which 27 persons have died since the Leftists defeated the former government Center-Rightist coalition in last Sunday’s parliamentary election: (Continued on Page Two)

SOPOTTI, 22 PR A EP ROME, Feb. 22.—()~Fresh Italian reports arose today that Emperor Haile Selassie was suing for peace, just as Fascists said their blackshirt legions were menacing their next major Ethiopian objective—Amba Alaji. Informed sources reported the Ethiopian king of kings was advancing peace proposals directly to the League of Nations, with an offer understood to contemplate a league protectorate over his empire. Whether he would cede any territory, however, or yield the broad sections of Ethiopia already occupied by the advancing Italians was not specified. Fortified by their recent victories, insisted nevertheless that they looked with little favor on Haile Selassie’s purported plans to save his empire from conquest by mandating it to Geneva. Premier Mussolini has declared openly that no Italian subject would settle in Ethiopia without the protection of the tricolor and inf

Rome, Feb. 22 (Saturday) (P) - Emperor Haile Selassie, it was said in informed circles early today, has advanced proposals to the League of Nations for termination of the Italo-Ethiopian war. The emperor's plan, it was understood in these quarters, contemplates a League of Nations protectorate over Ethiopia. In circles where Italian government information generally is distributed, it had been denied Wednesday that there was any possibility of peace negotiations as the result of an Italian victory in northern Ethiopia. Informed persons said, however, that the lack of official confirmation of the emperor's reported move was due to the fact his plan was said to have been submitted directly to the league. Acceptance Unlikely In quarters where the emperor's reported move for peace was mentioned, it was not specified whether Haile Selassie would cede any territory or yield those parts of Ethio

Madrid, Feb. 22.—(UP)—Songs and cheers rang throughout the country today, to mingle with the joyful tears of women, as prisons poured out thousands of political prisoners, freed under an amnesty that affected 30,000 men and women. The amnesty, decreed yesterday, will free all people held for political offenses committed up to last Sunday, date of the general parliamentary election which put left wing parties in power. As the prison gates swung open today, entire populations of some towns turned out to welcome bands of men who had been sentenced for fighting in the socialist revolt in 1934. Reports from all over the country showed the jubilation of people who welcomed the freed men and women. Wives, mothers, sweethearts, children hurried to (Continued on Page Three)

(Ry United Press), : Geneva, Feb. 22. ~ Augusto de Vasconcellos of Portugal, as chairman, today called the league’s committee of 18 nations to meet March 2 to consider the question of imposing an oil embargo or other new penalties against Italy for its war on Ethiopia. The committee, called the general staff, has general charge of penalties subject to approval of the big penalties committee of odd nations.

Tokyo, Feb. 22.—-(Saturday)— Possibility that a third party, opposed to the militarist domination of the government, might hold the balance of power in the new house of representatives arose today in returns from the general election. This is the proletarian shakai taishuto, or social masses party. It, however, was far behind the two major parties, the minseito, closely linked with the government of Premier Keisuke Akada, and the seiyukai, principal foe of the government.

| MOSCOW, Feb. 22 (UP) A hit-run driver of the government transport service has been sentenced to death before a firing squad, it was announced today, for killing a horse and injuring three persons in a farm wagon near Moscow. It was the second traffic accident in which the driver was concerned, and he had been reprimanded five times for reckless driving.

1936-05-28.text: JERUSALEM, May 28 (4)—British troops returned rioters’ fire at Kubatia, North Palestine, today, killing two and wounding three. The British reported no casualties. Earlier Robert Beard, British policeman, and one Arab were slain here. The outbreaks came as disorders in the Arab anti-Jewish campaign of terrorism appeared to be waning. The British continued rigorous campaigning against the terrorists,

LONDON, May 28—(UP)—Premier Benito Mussolini moved vigorously today to terminate Anzio-Italian friction and inaugurate a generation of “Roman peace” which he recognizes is necessary for constructive, profitable enjoyment of Italy’s conquest of Ethiopia. Under instructions from Il Duce, Dr. Dino Grandi, Italian ambassador, visited Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden to renew Italian efforts for reconciliation with Great Britain. Grandi’s visit to the foreign office followed immediately upon Mussolini’s own bid for friendship with Great Britain voiced yesterday in a Rome interview with the London Daily Telegraph’s correspondent. In the interview Mussolini insisted that amity with Britain is the guiding aim of his foreign policy now that an Italian administration has been established in Ethiopia and that the negus is an ‘exile without a country and without a people.

LONDON, May 28. (P)—Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin today set May 12, 1937, as the day on which King Edward VIII will be formally invested with the authority of the British throne in a centuries-old coronation ceremony. The announcement was made in a special issue of the official Gazette. The date will be officially proclaimed at colorful ceremonies in the center of London tomorrow.

ABOARD THE S. S. QUEEN MARY, May 27—(AP)—The stately liner Queen Mary steamed westward tonight on her maiden voyage to the United States. With a convoy of planes circling overhead and her path jammed with hundreds of other ships—small by comparison to the gigantic pride of Great Britain—she moved quietly from her dock at Southampton amid the cheers of thousands of spectators. Pigmy speed boats raced alongside the ponderous liner carrying 2,139 passengers and a staff of 1,200. The ship had been in clear water for little more than an hour and a half before the first lifeboat drill was called. Passengers were summoned on deck from cabins, lounges, bars and tea rooms. There, the formality of the protective organization was quickly completed. The Queen Mary forged ahead through Cowes Roads, fashionable yachting water, and received salutations from two British warships—the Royal Sovereign and

Aboard the S.S. Queen Mary, en route to New York, May 23.—Stepping up her speed gradually, Britain‘s greatest liner progressed smoothly Thursday on her maiden voyage to the United States under conditions favorable thus far for a record trip. Whether the Queen Mary would attempt definitely to win the blue riband for trans-Atlantic speed her first time out remained an open question—apparently not yet decided by officers. Second only to hope for a record, passengers' interest centered on how the Queen Mary would react as she approached her top speed of about 32 knots. On the first leg of the trip, across the English Channel from Southampton, she maintained a speed of 28 knots Wednesday night, with extremely little vibration. Thursday was the first of the four days at sea. The French liner Normandie’s record westward crossing was made in four days, three hours, 12 minutes from Bishop's Rock,

ABOARD the S. S. Queen Mary Enroute to New York, May 28 (P)— Metal furniture rattled today as the Queen Mary's powerful turbines pushed Britain’s new pride of the seas toward her maiden landing in America. The slight vibration became noticeable, especially aft, as the Queen Mary touched a speed unofficially estimated at about 32 knots. It did not, however, disturb the passengers. There were increasing indications of an attempt to beat the Normandie's record average speed of 30.35 knots, if favorable conditions continue.

JERUSALEM, (UP). — Rioting Arabs, who killed a British policeman in Jerusalem, plunged all Palestine into violence today. After a brief lull, disturbances flared anew throughout the country. Snipers hidden in the hillsides attacked the British police and military and fired into Jewish settlements. Numerous bombings were reported as the police skirmished with demonstrators protesting Jewish immigration. Two Arabs were killed and one was wounded in the village of Qubatia. Three others were wounded near the village of Silat El Dahr where British troops on patrol went into action and returned the fire of snipers. Bombings apparently gained favor as a method of emphasizing Arab unrest. Bombs were tossed by Arab demonstrators at Haifa, Jaffa, and Safed.

LONDON, May 28—(AP)—Prime Minister Baldwin today made William George Arthur Ormsby-Gore, former postmaster general, colonial secretary. The new cabinet minister, who is 51 years old and a conservative, succeeds J. H. Thomas, the laborite who resigned from the ministry last week because of the government budget leakage scandal. Ormsby-Gore served with the infantry in Egypt during the early years of the World War, was called to London in 1917 as an assistant secretary in the war cabinet, and served his last months of the war with the British military intelligence in Egypt. From 1922 to 1924 he was parliamentary undersecretary of state for the colonies. In 1931 he was postmaster general.

1936-06-14.text: Sheffield, Eng., June 13. (#)— British medical circles today heard the astounding story of Mary Devonport’s seven minute interlude of “death” in a dental chair, how she lost two frozen teeth and how she went back to work in a steel factory. “The case poses a question for those who believe the soul leaves the body on the instant of death,” remarked Dr. Alfred A. Masser of Sheffield. He described the case for the British Medical Journal, “She remembers nothing about her strange experience,” the doctor asserted today. “There were no dreams under the chloroform. Her brain registered no reaction to what death is like, because the brain cells still were under the effect of the anaesthetic during the seven minutes of lifelessness.” Dr. Masser reported the 20-year-old girl's heart stopped beating shortly after the dentist began to work on her teeth.

PASSING, Germany, June 13.—(#)— Dr. Hugo Eckener, veteran German zeppelin commander, was injured slightly today when a tire on the automobile he was driving blew out, throwing his car into a ditch in this Munich suburb. Three other passengers were shaken.

PARIS (AP)— Contented strikers evacuated the besieged factories of France Saturday. Cheered by quick parliamentary votes on laws to give them shorter hours, vacations with pay, and other advantages, thousands of workers formed impromptu parades outside their plants, crippled for more than two weeks, to honor their Leftist leaders. Premier Leon Blum announced a “return to a normal situation” within a few days. The gay and marching erstwhile strikers carried big pictures of Premier Blum and Maurice Thorez, secretary-general of the Communist party in France.

St. Charles, Ill., June 13.—(?)— Shot through the head and apparently beaten, the body of Miss Nella Penunzi, 23, manager of the Red Parrot tea room at the Club Arcada here, was found on the Dunham gravel road about two miles north of St. Charles in the exclusive Wayne residential district about dawn today. Her body was discovered slumped in a ditch by Sheriff A. J. Kantmeyer and deputies, about a mile south of the spot where her coupe had been found an hour earlier by a night patrolman. Sheriff Kantmeyer sought Rinaldi di Pietro, 50, for questioning after talking with relatives of the slain girl, at Geneva, Il. Sheriff Kantmeyer said di Pietro, a resident of Geneva and Chicago, had been ordered by the family to stop paying attention to the girl.

Cleveland, June 13, (4)—Plans for a militant and whirlwind opening of the Republican campaign to defeat President Roosevelt, possibly within the next ten days, tonight were mapped here by members of the party's high command. Among the rear guard remaining here after the Republican national convention it was tentatively decided that the spearhead in the earlier campaigning would be John D. M. Hamilton, energetic new chairman of the national committee. Alf M. Landon of Kansas, the standard bearer, will take a hand and become increasingly active in behalf of his own call for a “fighting campaign” as the election nears. Landon men said both he and Hamilton would travel extensively and turn to the radio frequently. Will Invade East Friends of the Kansas governor, disclaiming that they spoke for him, said they expected him before long to invade the east as well as the far west. They spoke of a

- HONGKONG, June 14.—(Sunday) —(P)—Japanese warships and Japanese marines came to South China today. While Cantonese, massed in the crooked streets of that city, asked anew for resistance to Nippon, Chinese reports stated a Japanese naval squadron had landed blue-jackets at Amoy, Fukien province, on the coast a few hundred miles to the north. The marines, ostensibly, were landed to protect Japanese lives and property, but the commander of the vessels said they were ready to steam toward Canton at a moment's notice, if they are needed.

Pittsburgh, Pa.—(4#)—The mayor of Pittsburgh, William M. McNair, was arrested Saturday and held for the grand jury on charges of halting the machinery of the law and preventing magistrates from sending prisoners to jail. Deputy sheriffs served a warrant upon McNair at city hall and hailed him into court where Judge Ralph E. Smith set his bond at $5,000. The warrant charged misbehavior in office. McNair went home Saturday night after his bond was furnished by Michael Grogan, a citizen, at the request of the Police Protective Association. Tumultuous Day The mayor's arrest climaxed a day of turmoil in the city, with reports of disorderly conduct and confusion stemming from orders from McNair and Safety Director Thomas Dunn. Judge Smith Saturday night appointed Sheriff Frank I. Gollmar as emergency guardian of the public—until the situation in the police department is resolved. Asked About O

DALLAS, Tex. — Burns received in the crash of a burning airplane near Ferris Friday proved fatal Saturday to Eugene Schacher of Houston, 32-year-old co-pilot. Schacher died a hero, Jesse Jones, chairman of the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, ex-Gov. and Mrs. W. P. Hobby, and Joe Toomey, passengers, all proclaimed his bravery in battling the blaze which forced the ship down from a 7,000-foot level. His death came less than three hours after his passengers, leaving Dallas for Houston, paid a farewell visit to his hospital room, wished him well and thanked him again for his supreme devotion to duty. Mrs. Hobby described her husband’s condition Saturday as stiff and sore after the shaking up, and said his eye was black from a bump he received. Jones boarded a private railway car for his trip to Houston nursing a bruised chest, but otherwise uninjured. Mrs. Hobby was uninjured and Toomey

1936-01-11.text: LONDON, Jan. 10—(AP)—Raging storms which buffeted the British Isles and northern Europe left at least 21 dead tonight, several injured, and extensive damage. Seventeen persons were killed in the British Isles. The wind which blew in from the Atlantic yesterday swept on eastward after knocking down walls, uprooting trees and damaging ships. Germany’s Rhineland was struck by a freak wind and hailstorm which killed four. Two factories and a railroad warehouse were wrecked, and the roof of the Duesseldorf Municipal Gymnasium was blown off. Five members of the crew of the steamship Bradda were drowned when the vessel went down in the Mersey River. A fire in its hold forced the Swedish steamer Sumatra to seek shelter on England’s southwestern coast. The trawler Comrade brought into port the body of a deckhand who drowned when a wave hurled him overboard. Roofs of two Dublin railway stations we

London, Jan. 10 (7) — An apparently authoritative hint from Japanese quarters that they are preparing a new proposal in order to obtain parity and save the international naval conference from foundering was given tonight. This varied from the belief held in other delegations that the Japanese would walk out of the conference next week. In British official circles it was said if the Tokyo delegation withdraws, Soviet Russia and Germany will be asked into the conference and it will proceed on a six-power basis. The United States and Great Britain, it was stated, have agreed they will reconsider Japan's insistent demand for tonnage equality — but even the Japanese themselves held no hope it would be granted. The conference is in recess until Monday. It appeared certain the other powers will give Japan the floor at the next meeting, which may be postponed until Tuesday to allow the easterner

London, Jan. 11. (Pi—Authoritative sources said today the next meeting of the international naval conference, which is expected to reconsider Japan’s demand for naval equality with all nations, probably will not be held until Tuesday. - Although the reason for the expected postponement of the session scheduled originally for Monday was not given in these quarters, it was understood the move was an attempt to give delegates more time for further contacts before the next meeting, when the conference generally is expected to break down unless some compromise is found. Despite the reported plan to resume consideration of Japan's request for parity, the other powers were not expected to be willing to grant such equality.

| SINGAPORE, Jan. 11. (UP)— Plans for fortification of Hongkong have been drafted by naval, military, and air force experts, it was understood today, in expectation of the failure of the London naval limitations conference. Fortification of Hongkong, British crown colony at the mouth of the Canton river, is forbidden under the Washington naval limitation treaty which expired December 31. Strategically it is of almost incalculable value.

London, Jan. 11 (UP) -- A meeting of the naval limitation conference set for Monday was postponed today until Tuesday at the request of the Japanese delegation. Japan must decide whether to insist on discussion of its demand for equality with the United States and Great Britain before other topics are considered. If Japan insists, it is indicated that the conference is doomed to failure insofar as an agreement embracing a treaty among navies is concerned, and that a four-power conference will follow, with America, Britain, and Japan.

RIS, Jan. 11.—A new, strong effort to settle the Italian-Ethiopian war seemed imminent today. Reports indicated that Italy was taking the initiative, through secret diplomatic channels, and that peace terms would represent major Italian concessions. As the United Press reported yesterday, Count Charles De Chambrun, ambassador to Italy, talked at great length to Premier Pierre Laval. Though it was emphasized that he brought no peace overtures from Italy, it was understood he told Laval that Premier Benito Mussolini hoped the League of Nations would consider Italy's need for raw materials and an outlet for its surplus population. Today, Mme. Genevieve Tabouis, unusually well-informed political expert of the newspaper L'Œuvre, prophesied in detail the early conclusion of the Italian-Ethiopian war. Particular interest attached to her assertions because she forecast accurately other important

Addis Ababa.—Ethiopia says several hundred Italian native troops killed in battle on southern front. Cairo,—Egypt to protest to Italy against reported bombing of Egyptian Red Cross units in Ethiopia; Italy denies charge.

Copyright, 1936, By The Associated Press STATE HOUSE, TRENTON, N. J., Jan. 11—Governor Harold G. Hoffman today sought the arrest ‘for questioning’ of the Lindbergh murder case’s famous “Jafsie”—Dr. John F. Condon—as the court of pardons went into session to hear Bruno Richard Hauptmann's plea to escape the electric chair. Condon sailed suddenly last night for South America after a magazine began publication of “Jafsie tells all”—a series of articles by Dr. Condon purporting to offer new details of the case, including his belief that Hauptmann had a confederate. The governor said he would ask Attorney General David T. Wilentz, who directed the Hauptmann prosecution at Flemington, to seek Condon’s arrest. “Condon makes the flat statement that more than one person was involved in the plan,” the governor said. “He goes so far as to write he knew two of those involved. If Dr. Condon knows the

1936-02-29.text: LONDON, March 3 — (AP) — The condition of Countess Barbara Hutton Haugwitz-Reventlow was reported greatly improved today. The Woolworth heiress, seriously ill after the birth of her first child nearly two weeks ago, has progressed so satisfactorily that her father and step-mother, Mr. and Mrs. Franklyn Hutton of New York, have gone to Paris for a brief holiday.

(Copyright, 1936, by United Press.) LONDON, Feb. 29 (UP).-—Barbara Hutton Mdivani von Haugwitz-Reventlow, whose $40,000,000 hasn't protected her from her share of unhappiness, was in serious condition today following an abdominal operation. Three doctors, one King Edward's physician, were in attendance. In its four-room nursery adjoining Barbara's rooms in the rented Von Haugwitz-Reventlow London mansion, her five-day-old son squalled lustily. Countess Barbara had spent a fairly good night. A close acquaintance told the United Press she had improved. Yet there was no doubt as to the seriousness of her condition. She gave birth to her 7 1-2 pound son Monday. (According to two London newspapers, a caesarian operation was necessary.) Thursday she was operated on for an abdominal obstruction. Yesterday her condition grew so grave that at one time three physicians were at her bedside constant

London, Feb. 29 — Lord Horder, physician in ordinary to King Edward, paid an unexpectedly early visit today to Countess Anna Reventlow, the former Barbara Hutton, hovering between life and death after the birth of her first child and an operation. The famous physician left the hushed town house, where the healthy 7-pound son was born Tuesday and where the mother was operated upon Thursday night, at 8:30 a.m. (B.H.S.T.), and a bulletin was issued, announcing: "The Countess had a fairly restful night." CONDITION GRAVE The condition of the Countess, heiress to the Woolworth millions, was understood to be grave and causing considerable anxiety. Lord Horder hurried from the house, dressed in sombre grey and wearing a black arm band in mourning for the late King George V. He shook his head doubtfully and declined to commit himself on the outlook for the future of his patient. The early visit,

LONDON — Four physicians labored Saturday night to save the life of Countess Barbara Hutton Haugwitz-Reventlow, Woolworth heiress and one of the wealthiest women in the world. She was reported to have survived two operations—a Caesarian delivery of a son last Tuesday and another for the relief of an abdominal obstruction Thursday. The doctors in attendance on the countess at her home were Lord Horder, physician-in-ordinary to King Edward, Dr. Cedric Sydney Lane-Roberts, noted gynecologist, Dr. James Slessinger, her personal physician, and an unidentified colleague of the latter. The young mother’s husband, Count Court Haugwitz-Reventlow, scion of an ancient Danish family, stayed constantly in the house. While his mother went through her ordeal, the baby was reported thriving in his germ-proof nursery on the top floor of the house. Every precaution had been taken to safeguard his health.

London, Feb. 29, (U.P)—One of the Japanese extremist rebels shot himself dead in front of the Sanno Hotel in Tokyo today when his comrades surrendered to regulars, the Exchange Telegraph Tokyo correspondent reported.

London, Feb. 29. (INS)—Weakened by long dieting, Countess Barbara von Haugwitz-Reventlow, Woolworth heiress, lay perilously close to death under the care of five doctors today as the result of an operation following the birth of her son five days ago. Her condition this morning was unchanged, Lord Horder, one of King Edward’s physicians-in-ordinary, said after an early visit. A bulletin issued at the home of the former Barbara Hutton Mdivani, No. 2 Hyde Park Gardens, said “the countess had a fairly restful night.” The bulletin, which friends interpreted as meaning that the patient had failed to rally overnight, was issued following an hour's examination by Lord Horder and a consultation with Dr. Cedric Lane-Roberts. Both the doctors then left the residence. Lord Horder, it was learned, had planned to go to the country for the weekend, but now plans to remain in town to be ready for any c

The Japanese army rebellion collapsed today under threat of machine gun fire as Premier Keisuke Okada, previously reported assassinated, reappeared on the scene, unhurt. Surrender of the troops which on Wednesday attempted a massacre of government leaders and apparently succeeded in three instances was swift and bloodless after the martial law administration issued them an ultimatum. Okada, hard-drinking liberal whose regime has been sharply at odds with the militarists refusing to bow to civil authority, survived assassins’ bullets only because his intended assailants mistook his secretary for him. Death Was Announced, The government itself had announced Okada's death. The secretary felled in the snow outside the premier's residence early Wednesday morning was Col. Denzo Matsuo, the premier's brother-in-law. Okada had an audience with Emperor Hirohito last night. Yesterday morning he su

TOKYO, Feb. 29—A man thought dead headed Japan's government today. A second man, also listed officially as dead for 3 days, held the high post of grand chamberlain in the imperial household. Coincident with the collapse of a revolt of young extremist army officers, it was disclosed officially that Premier Keisuke Okada and Grand Chamberlain Soroku Suzuki, who had been listed as among the five liberal statesmen killed by the extremists, were alive. Okada was at the Imperial Palace tonight conferring with other ministers of his government. Admiral Okada was not even wounded. In his place his brother-in-law, Col. Natsuo, walked stiffly into the garden of the Prime Minister’s residence, presented himself to the execution squad of the rebel force, and was shot down in cold blood. Suzuki was wounded. He was reported improving tonight. Hence the rebels killed only Korekiyo Takahashi, finance mi

1936-01-25.text: LONDON, Jan. 25.—(/P)--European royalty converged on London in virtual full force today to pay last respects to the late King George V of England. While the new King Edward VIII dealt with a mass of state affairs awaiting his attention and the public paid homage to the old Monarch at his lying-in-state in Westminster Hall, other kings, queens and princes came for the funeral services Tuesday at Windsor. The sounds of hammering echoed in the streets of this capital as workmen ran up stands and barriers along the route to be followed by King George's funeral procession. Tall masts, which had been swathed in blue, gold and silver for the silver jubilee celebrations of George's reign last summer, re-appeared, this time draped in purple and black. Some shop windows were converted into grandstands, with tiers of seats commanding upward of $50 apiece. Other windows were barricaded stoutly again

LONDON, Jan. 24 (#)— The British people marched through cold, fog, and darkness tonight to keep their last respects to King George. Despite a chilling wind they came in throngs to Westminster Hall where the dead monarch lies in state, to walk swiftly past the catafalque. The late king’s subjects presented a scene rare in British history. It appeared that the entire nation was moving like pilgrims towards a single spot. Sorrowing citizens came through the streets in solid phalanxes, sometimes filling the roadway from curb to curb. The only break in the continuous public pilgrimage to the catafalque was at 6 P. M. Then the hall was cleared as King Edward, the widowed Queen Mother Mary and other members of the royal family came for 15 minutes of silent tribute. Their visit, to gaze upon the face of the dead king, was unexpected. It was officially announced that a two-minute silence is to be

(By Associated Press) Rome, Jan. 25—Benito Mussolini served a sharp and direct warning on his 52 sanctionist adversaries yesterday against ringing Italy with steel. Calling the British-initiated Mediterranean security arrangements a “danger to European peace,” il Duce reaffirmed his country’s contention that sanctionist nations must take individual responsibility for their actions. He sent Italy’s “most formal reservation and protest” against the League of Nations announced British memorandum on a 5-Power Mediterranean mutual assistance accord direct to the half-hundred sanctionist nations, ignoring the League’s Sanctions Committee of 18. Great Britain, France, and the other nations, Mussolini charged, have improperly based their negotiations for Mediterranean security on an “arbitrary and nonexistent hypothesis” on Italian attack. The arrangements, Italy contended, were conducted outsid

| London, Jan. 25.— (AP) — King Edward VIII went to his country home to rest for the weekend today while thousands filed past his father's bier. A blind holder of the Victoria Cross, Captain Sir Ernest Beachcroft-Twose, took a place among the bodyguard watching over the catafalque in Westminster Hall. The new king went to his private residence at Fort Belvedere for much needed rest after a trying week. Sing at Games The memory of King George was honored at football games throughout the country. Audiences stood and sang “Abide With Me,” the late monarch’s favorite hymn and one which will be sung at his funeral Tuesday, and the national anthem was played. Among royal arrivals for the funeral were Prince Rudiger Ernst von Starhemberg, vice chancellor of Austria, and Nicolas Titulescu, foreign minister of Rumania, who will represent their countries. Most of the royalty and other delegations

Rome—Premier Benito Mussolini has warned the French government that he may revise his attitude toward the Locarno treaty because of the Mediterranean agreement by which Great Britain will receive aid in event of an attack by Italy, it was understood today in foreign quarters. The warning was said to have been conveyed in a conversation Mussolini had yesterday with Count Charles De Chambrun, French ambassador. Under the Locarno treaty Great Britain, France, Belgium, Germany and Italy pledged mutual support. It was provided that if France, Belgium or Germany unjustifiably attacked each other, the remaining signatories would go to the aid of the nation attacked. This was intended to guarantee mutually, the inviolability of the German-Belgium and German-French frontiers as fixed by the Versailles treaty.

London, Jan. 24 (#)—A furious European air armament race, disclosed by Eugene L. Vidal, air commerce bureau chief, in testimony in Washington yesterday, is an open secret in informed quarters in London. Authorities said tonight that only an early war or the admittedly dim chances of negotiating an air security pact among Great Britain, France, Germany, Italy, and Russia could halt the mad scramble to maintain armed altitude in the skies. Diplomatic and military observers said they believed Vidal was, if anything, too conservative when he told the house military affairs committee that one European power recently had ordered 1,500 airplanes.

Bellefontaine, O., Jan. 24 — John Mills, 30, bass with the Mills Brothers vocal quartet, died today at the home of his mother, Eathel Mills Jackson. He had been suffering with a lung ailment. He became ill several months ago while the Negro songsters were touring England; since that time his father, John Mills, Sr., has been singing bass with his other three sons. The Mills brothers began singing a number of years ago in their hometown of Piqua, O.

CHICAGO, Jan. 25 (#)—Attorneys for the 20 defendants in the Drake estate mail fraud trial today sought a court order for the government to restore $75,000 in impounded United States and English banknotes to the owners. They announced that at the resumption of the hearing Monday after the weekend recess, they would ask that the money be returned both to defendants still on trial and 21 others who were freed by directed acquittal verdicts last week.

1936-02-01.text: London, Jan. 31. (AP)—The four-power naval conference unanimously adopted a plan for annual confidential exchange of construction programs today in an effort to diminish the threat of a world naval race. Great Britain, the United States, France and Italy then decided to push toward a general treaty on limitation of sizes and types of ships and calibers of guns. The plan adopted today will be incorporated in that treaty. Then the powers hope to get Japan, Germany and Russia to agree later to the conference. A summary of today’s action said: “Should these proposals receive general acceptance by the naval powers, a great advance will have been made in the removal of suspicion which has had so strong an effect on competitive building, thus a contribution would be made to quantitative (total) tonnage reduction in naval armaments throughout the world.”

CALCUTTA, Jan. 31 () - Four British, one Italian and 32 Indians were killed in a fire and explosion at the Loyabad colliery in Jharkhand Bihar province, an official announcement said today. The disaster occurred last night.

Addis Ababa, Feb. 1. (UP)—An official communique asserted today that 3,000 Italians were killed in a battle on the northern front that ended Thursday. It was said that a Fascist Blackshirt militia division was “completely wiped out.” (A Fascist militia division usually numbers about 12,000 men. It was assumed the communique meant that it was routed.) 5,000 Italians Wounded About 5,000 Italians were wounded, the announcement said, and 18 tanks, 33 field guns, 175 machine guns, and 2,605 rifles were captured. The battle, in which the Fascist militia division was “wiped out,” the communique said, occurred north of Abbi Addi, which is in the Tembien region northwest of Makale, peak of the Italian front in the north. It is in this area that Marshal Pietro Badoglio, Italian commander-in-chief, has been active for many days, trying to drive Ethiopian guerrilla bands from their positions which m

Athens, Jan. 31.—Death cut short today Gen. George Kondylis’ effort to prevent formation of a new government under the banner of his political enemies. He died of a heart attack, complicated by asthma from which he had long suffered. He was 55. Unconfirmed reports that the former regent had been poisoned by his political enemies were quickly denied.

(Copyright, 1936, by United Press) Rome, Feb. 1 (UP)—Premier Benito Mussolini prepared today to take the diplomatic offensive against nations favoring an oil embargo. It was widely expected that the Fascist grand council—the supreme ruling body of the country—at a meeting at 10 o'clock tonight (5 p.m., CST) would approve decisions of great importance in connection with the possibility of embargo. The meeting will be held secretly. Act of War It was widely reported that it would result in the dissemination of information that (1) a naval blockade to enforce an oil embargo would be considered an act of war and treated accordingly; (2) that Mussolini may have to revise his idea of the British-French agreement to cooperate in the Mediterranean. Under the Locarno treaty, Italy, France, Great Britain, Belgium and Germany are pledged to protect, by force if necessary, the existing German-French

Washington, Jan. 31 (4)—A drive to enact at this session a new tax program, aimed at increasing Federal revenues by around $730,000,000 to offset farm relief and bonus costs, was declared in Administration quarters today to be under consideration. An inflation movement apparently gained momentum in the House, emphasizing the possible difficulties of pressing new levies through Congress in a campaign year. President Roosevelt put Congress on notice at least $500,000,000 in new taxes would be needed for the farm program. His notice coincided with the projection of plans by Senate leaders for action next week on the two-year soil-conservation subsidy bill to replace the AAA, and on huge appropriations to finance both that program and the $2,249,000,000 soldier debt. Another Administration authority let it be known consideration is being given to taxes to raise another $530,000,000 annually

NEW ORLEANS, LA., Feb. 1.—(4)— The 42-year-old widow of Senator Huey P. Long, whose tireless assistance aided her husband's rise to fame, made enthusiastic plans today to complete his term in the United States Senate. Although Mrs. Long said she was “very grateful” for the opportunity to complete his term, she made no reference to the “share-the-wealth” movement he started. Appointment of Mrs. Long by Governor James A. Noe, yesterday, came as a surprise. Political leaders had previously expressed belief Allen J. Ellender, speaker of the state house of representatives, would be the choice. Ellender, who has been nominated for the full six-year senate term, did not comment on the governor’s decision. Governor Noe, who became Louisiana’s chief executive last Tuesday after the death of Governor O. K. Allen, said members of the democratic state central committee had assured him they would app

Baton Rouge, La., Jan. 31.—A)—Mrs. Huey P. Long, widow of the late senator, late today was appointed to serve his unexpired senate term by Gov. James A. Noe. The appointment resulted from the death this week of Gov. O. K. Allen, an associate of the late senator, who had been nominated for the unexpired term. Mrs. Long had shown little interest in politics during the long and turbulent political career of her husband. Two Women Members, Two women will sit in the United States Senate for the first time in history when she takes her seat there. Sen. Hattie W. Caraway, who also succeeded her husband, is the lone woman member at present. Informed in New Orleans of the appointment, Mrs. Long said, "That’s fine. That’s very fine." She did not comment further. Governor Noe, who became Louisiana's chief executive upon the death of Allen, predicted the democratic state committee would also designa

1936-09-03.text: LONDON— (UP) —The airplane Lady Peace, carrying Richard Merrill and Harry Richman on the season’s first successful flight across the Atlantic, landed today in Wales. The Air Ministry announced officially the Lady Peace landed at Llandilo, Carmarthenshire, in Western Wales. Jimmy Town, Canadian pilot, a friend of the fliers, said they ran out of gas and their radio broke down. They landed safely in a field, he said, and would continue to London after refueling. Llandilo is well inland, just north of Black Mountain in Southeastern Carmarthenshire. The Lady Peace took off from Floyd Bennett Airport in New York at 3:37 p.m. EST, Wednesday. It carried 1,000 gallons of gasoline, which it was estimated would be sufficient to keep the 1,000-horsepower cyclone motor going for 22 hours. Apparently, however, the fliers encountered heavy weather and the supply was drained prematurely. The original r

LLANDILO, Wales, Sept. 3— (OP) — Successfully crossing the Atlantic, the two American fliers, Richard Merrill and Harry Richman of New York, landed safely at a country estate near here today after hours of blind groping for Croydon airport, London. Unable to locate their objective and with their radio dead, they finally ran low on gas and were forced to land in a field full of cattle and sheep. Richman told newspapermen the one-day flight across the Atlantic was "pretty tough." He was "terribly sorry" he and his companion failed to reach London." They landed within 175 miles of London. Richman, famous on Broadway for years as an actor and night club entertainer, said he and Merrill, a veteran transport pilot, expected to take off for Croydon as soon as a refueling plane brought them more gasoline. They needed, he said, about 75 or 100 gallons. The Lady Peace, their ship, was unharmed in

New York, Sept. 2—After missing disaster by inches on their takeoff, Dick Merrill and Harry Richman roared into fog and rainstorms tonight on the first leg of a projected round-trip flight between New York and London. A sudden gust of wind nearly upset the heavily loaded monoplane as it thundered down the long concrete runway at Floyd Bennett field but Merrill, a veteran airmail and transport pilot, brought it back to an even keel and lifted it gently. Flagmen stationed at the far end of the field reported that Merrill and Richman were grinning broadly as the "Lady Peace," loaded with three tons of fuel, climbed into the eastern sky. Don't Mind Dirty Weather Just before taking off on the oft-postponed flight, Richman said: "We don't care about the dirty weather ahead. We have the winds we need." Richman, singing star of the stage and screen, operated the ship's two-way radio. A half hour

| ATHENS UP)—King Edward of Great Britain, cruising in the yacht Nablin, was thrown from a skiff into the Gulf of Euboea, it was reported Thursday, by the wash of a motorboat from the yacht. British legation attaches and Greek government spokesmen denied the story of capsizing. | The report said the king was rowing when the motorboat passed at full speed and his skiff was capsized. It was the first time the king had been thrown from a bucking boat, if true.

New York, Sept. 3—(AP)— Dick Merrill and Harry Richman established an unofficially computed record of 18 hours, 38 minutes from New York to Great Britain today when they set their monoplane, “Lady Peace,” down in Wales. Aviators praised the flight as “hitting it on the button,” saying the point of landing indicated the ship was flown on a perfect great circle course for London.
CLEMENTON, N. J., Sept. 3.—Routing their British foes with decisive victories, the United States today won the Walker Cup, emblematic of international team golf supremacy.
| LONDON, Sept. 3. (')—King Ed-ward got a ducking when a skiff he was rowing overturned at a Greek watering place, but he escaped unhurt.

LONDON, Sept. 2.—Japan served notice to the world tonight that she will maintain at full force her mighty submarine armada another step in the world’s race for strong armament. Japan's decision to retain submarines originally scheduled for destruction under the London naval treaty was made known in a formal note. She would, the Pacific power signified, keep in service, with 52,700 tons allowed, an additional 15,598 tons of submarine craft—the tonnage scheduled for scrapping before expiration of the London treaty January 1, 1937. This would give Japan a strength in undersea warships—one-third greater than that of either the United States or Great Britain. The London treaty provided the three nations should limit their submarine force to 52,700 each. To accomplish this, the treaty signatories would resort to the scrap heap before the end of the treaty.

1936-07-17.text: Copyright 1936 By The Associated Press) LONDON, ENG., JULY 17. (AP).—George Andrew McMahon, whose loaded revolver menaced King Edward, said today the weapon was not knocked from his hand but that he deliberately threw it into the street toward the king as the monarch rode by. This version relayed by an authoritative source which said McMahon told police he never had the least intention of shooting the king. McMahon was taken to a hospital ward for mental observation and medical treatment,

(Copyright, 1936, by United Press) London, July 17.—(UP)—Special Constable Anthony Gordon Dick, 36, travelling salesman and former navy stoker, became a national hero today, officially affirmed as the man to whom King Edward owes his life. It was Dick who first saw George Andrew McMahon, 34, eccentric journalist, aim a pistol at King Edward as the young monarch led a parade of his foot guardsmen down Constitution Hill. Dick sprang unhesitatingly on McMahon, knocked the pistol from his hand with a backhand blow, and grappled with him, facing the gaping muzzle of the assassin's weapon. It took Scotland Yard nearly 24 hours to get the real story of the attempt to kill the most popular king in the world. But today Dick was lionized throughout the United Kingdom. He took it modestly, and sharing honors with him was King Edward, who from the moment he glanced from his charger over his left sho

London, July 16. (P)—Edward of England, a king for almost six months, rode unharmed today into range of a loaded, levelled pistol which was knocked from the hands of a London malcontent. The pistol, taken from the hand of its crippled, baldheaded owner by a middle-aged heroine in grey, clattered harmlessly to the roadway behind the king's horse on crowded Constitution Hill. Act Of Protest The malcontent, George Andrew McMahon, 34, once an editor and a native Scotsman, struggled in the strong arms of London Bobbies. Whisked to a Bow Street dock, he wailed: “I didn’t want to hurt him, I only did it as a protest!” His “protest” was not explained, for the man was incoherent. Since he assailed Sir John Simon, the home secretary, and said he had tried to reach him, some suggested he may have sought to plead against capital punishment. Placed In Jail He was charged with ‘unlawful possession of

By The Associated Press Paris, France, July 17—Three Locarno powers seeking to reconstruct the European peace framework reached an agreement today on three points for a prospective discussion. Great Britain, France, and Belgium have formed an accord, informed sources said, on these points: 1. Representatives of three powers will meet next Wednesday in a compromise session. 2. The meeting will concern itself with an “exchange of views” rather than detailed consideration of the Locarno question thrust before the signatories by Adolf Hitler’s reoccupation of the Rhineland last March. 3. The French and British will publish a statement before the meeting to assure Germany and Italy the conference is not directed against them.

LONDON, July 17 (AP)—Steel bars and strong police guards encircled an incoherent “social reformer” today as a jubilant empire celebrated the escape of King Edward from possible harm by the armed malcontent. Feverishly active, squads of Scotland Yard operatives labored to bring to light the motives which led George Andrew McMahon, 34, to level a loaded pistol at the monarch during a royal procession yesterday. Behind the bars of a London jail, the baldheaded Irishman muttered almost unintelligible denials he meant to harm the British ruler. John Bannigan, McMahon's father in Glasgow, said his son's true name was Jerome Bannigan, which had been changed three years ago to McMahon. “I didn’t want to hurt him!” the shaking McMahon was quoted. “I only did it as a protest.” His questioners were unable to determine the nature of the “protest,” although they did learn the crippled social crusader

BOSTON, July 17—-(#)—Chairman John D. M. Hamilton, of the Republican national committee, said today New England would go Republican in the national election this fall. Hamilton also said, “there isn't the slightest question in the world what we are going to do in Maine. We are going to get three congressmen, a United States senator and a governor. Throughout the country, Hamilton declared in an interview, the Republican party is gaining support from persons who never before have taken an active part in politics.

London, England. (INS)—Apparently suspecting the attempted assassination of King Edward near Buckingham Palace had been planned by a group, Scotland Yard appealed for public aid today. As the youthful monarch resumed his duties calm and unperturbed, officers were searching for information that might lead to others involved. In connection with the incident, the police requested any person who witnessed the occurrence to communicate with Scotland Yard as soon as possible. Scotland Yard also asked newspapers to supply the names and addresses of all persons who gave eyewitness accounts of the disorder. A spokesman said the appeal was made because of conflicting reports regarding the incident, but Scotland Yard officials were reticent to disclose just what they hoped to learn from witnesses of the attempted assassination. It was apparent, however, Scotland Yard may not be completely satisfied

COLUMBUS—U.P.—The Ohio Board of Parole today refused to grant parole to Grover Fleming, former publisher of The Ohio Examiner, who is serving an indeterminate sentence at the London Prison farm on a charge of publishing obscene literature. Fleming's case was continued until next January to permit a check of pending indictments, records disclosed. He was sentenced from Athens County.

1936-04-26.text: ROME, April 25. (®)—As Marshal Pietro Badoglio, commander of the Italian armies in Ethiopia, announced the complete occupation of the Lake Tana region, an authoritative fascist warned Great Britain that Italy will soon have a huge military force ready for other parts of Africa. Simultaneously, Premier Mussolini declared Italy, despite sanctions which “augment the disorder and misery of the world” would remain “always methodical, tenacious, and indomitable.” He told celebrants at the inauguration of the new town of Aprilia, in the reclaimed Pontine marshes: “A new victory will be added to the others which the Italians have firmly desired and merited.” Badoglio reported that the Italian forces now had even the mouth of the Blue Nile which, flowing from Lake Tana, supplies the source of the Nile which irrigates the Anglo-Egyptian. (See DUCE on Page Six)

Italy's army in northern Ethiopia prepared Sunday for its next push toward Addis Ababa and claimed complete occupation of the area around Lake Tana, in which Great Britain is vitally interested because it is the source of the Blue Nile, flowing through Egypt and Anglo-Egyptian Sudan. An authoritative Italian, in a newspaper article, warned Britain that "not only in the Mediterranean but in the Alps and Africa itself, within a few weeks, we shall have a huge military force which has annihilated Ethiopian resistance." The truck lines agreed to haul to Ababa within two weeks. Troops were rushing the conversion of a mule train to the rear to provide a stone road over which trucks can travel, bringing up supplies and more men. The Italian press reporters claimed a success in the southeast as invaders moved toward Sasa.

PARIS (#) — Political leaders prophesied Saturday night that national balloting Sunday would bring a slight swing to the left in the composition of a new chamber of deputies. Sunday’s balloting will be the first voting for new deputies to cope with economic worries and the danger of war. Overshadowing the election is the anxiety over Germany's rearmament and reoccupation of the Rhineland. Italy’s war on Ethiopia and the League of Nations sanctions. Unrest and discontent over the continued economic depression figure largely too in the campaign, whose main issue has been “national safety and bread,” which is another way of saying “peace and plenty.” For the 615 seats in the chamber to be filled for a 4-year term, there are 4,807 candidates. Not all the seats will be filled Sunday. In districts where there are no majorities Sunday runoff elections will be held next Sunday.

CAIRO, Egypt (AP) — King Fuad I of Egypt, desperately ill, underwent an emergency blood transfusion late Saturday in an effort by his doctors to check the ravages of a disease which made them despair of his life. The king was suffering from stomatitis of a necrotic character, meaning an inflammation of the mouth complicated by the breaking down of tissue. Severe hemorrhages added to the gravity of his condition. The king was at his Koubbeh palace, near Cairo. He was attended by a group of eminent physicians from many countries, headed by Prof. Cesare Fragoni, noted Italian specialist, who was summoned here by airplane. The king has been in poor health since an attack of pleurisy in January, 1934, which weakened his heart.

Halifax, N. S. —(‘)— A “glass boot,” developed in Cincinnati, O. was being used Saturday to save the feet of Charles Alfred Scadding ‘rescued from Moose River gold mine after 10 days entombment alive. His friend, Dr. D. E. Robertson who despite his age went through the ordeal in better physical shape was reported showing continued progress toward recovery. Physicians in attendance on Scadding said they were “greatly encouraged over the prospect of saving his feet.” Scadding contracted “trench foot,” an incipient case of gangrene, from the dampness of the underground prison. Dr. H. H. Langdon, superintendent of the Cincinnati General hospital, where the glass boot was developed, described it as a “pavaex unit.” It is so called after the “passive vascular exercise,” since it increases the circulation of damaged arteries by alternating negative and positive air pressures.

ROME—Premier Benito Mussolini ploughed the boundary marks of a new city in the reclaimed Pontine marshes Saturday, and renewed his defiance of League of Nations sanctions against Italy while at the same time his armies were making important advances in Ethiopia. Authoritative advices were that the Italians had occupied Sasa Baneh, the important fortified Ethiopian position 105 miles southeast of Jijiga. Sasa Baneh opens the way to Harar, Jijiga and Dire Dawa, the latter being a key city on the Djibouti-Addis Ababa railroad. An official communique said the Italians had completed the encirclement of Lake Tana, which is in the British sphere of influence in the north and of vital importance to irrigation in the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan. The Italians, already having occupied the northern, eastern and western shores of the lake, reached Bahr-Dar Ghiogis, at its southern extremity. War communique

WASHINGTON, April 25 — The constitutionality of one phase of the $803,000,000 tax bill was questioned in the Senate finance committee today as administration pilots sought to avoid clashes with the House that might delay adjournment of Congress until late in June. Senator Bailey (D-N.C.) injected the constitutional issue into the finance committee's tax studies in connection with provisions in the House bill for special treatment for debt-ridden corporations. Chairman Harrison (D-Miss.) immediately jumped to their defense. "My own opinion," Harrison told reporters, "is that it is merely a question of classification, and Congress certainly has the right to classify these rates of taxes and give credits to debt-burdened corporations." Different classifications and rates, he said, were worked into a graduated corporation income tax in last year's revenue bill. Provides Flat Rate The bill, n

The Associated Press Philadelphia, April 25—President Roosevelt will accept the re-nomination, which the Democratic national convention is expected to give him, in an outdoor demonstration the night of Saturday, June 27, on Franklin Field, famous athletic grounds of the University of Pennsylvania. Announcement of this plan was made today by Postmaster General James A. Farley, national chairman, who also announced that Senator Alben W. Barkley, of Kentucky, will be the temporary chairman and keynoter, and Senator Joseph T. Robinson, of Arkansas, the permanent chairman. Barkley was the keynoter at Chicago four years ago, and Robinson the permanent chairman of the national convention in San Francisco in 1920 when James M. Cox was nominated for president and Roosevelt for vice president. The committee on arrangements of the national committee met here today, adopted convention plans and made

1936-11-16.text: LONDON, Nov. 16. (AP)—Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden today rebuked Germany for repudiating the clauses of the Versailles treaty internationalizing several of Germany's important rivers. Speaking before the House of Commons, Eden expressed the British government's regret that “at a time when discussions were proceeding, and despite last year’s assurance, the German government should again abandon procedure by negotiation in favor of unilateral action.” The foreign secretary explained: “Our regrets are not due to fear that any important British trading interests are jeopardized, but because of the fact that action of this character must render more difficult the conduct of international relations.” Germany on Saturday announced renunciation of the treaty provisions which affected the Rhine, Elbe, Danube and Oder Rivers and the Kiel Canal.

Wilmington, Del, Nov. 15.—(4)— A romance between Miss Ethel duPont and Franklin D. Roosevelt Jr., son of President and Mrs. Roosevelt, which began three years ago when they were students in New England schools, will be climaxed with their marriage in June. Mr. and Mrs. Eugene duPont announced their daughter's engagement last night while young Roosevelt was a guest at their home at Greenville. Miss duPont is the eldest of their four children. DuPont is a member of the board of E. I. duPont de Nemours & Co. Unlike his cousins, Lamm T. duPont, president of the company; Pierre S. duPont, chairman of the board; and Irene duPont, a member of the board, he has never taken an active part in politics. The post-election announcement that marriage would unite two families decidedly at odds in pre-election activities created a flurry of excitement in social Washington. But the word was not a surpris

SOUTHAMPTON, Nov. 16—()—Post-master-General James A. Farley of the United States reached here today and predicted a prosperity for his country “greater than anything we ever have known.” He said the boom even would surpass that of 1929 “because the country will be built on a sound foundation.” Farley is en route to Ireland for a holiday.

New York, Nov. 15 (4)—Leland Hayward and Margaret Sullavan, stage and screen actress, who were married today at Newport, have been married before. Miss Sullavan formerly was the wife of Henry Fonda, screen actor who recently wed Mrs. George T. Brokaw, socially prominent New York widow. Hayward, business manager for several screen actresses, was twice the husband of Lola Gibbs, Park Avenue debutante. Their first marriage followed an elopement in 1924 when Hayward was a student at Princeton. After a divorce they remarried in 1930 but again parted four years later. Hayward's name was linked in a romance with the motion picture star, Katharine Hepburn, in 1934 at the time Miss Hepburn obtained a Mexican decree. He was her business manager.

EDMONTON, Alta. Nov. 16 (P)—(Canadian Press)—The violent deaths of six persons, wiping out the entire population of Tieland, tiny railway settlement 100 miles north of Edmonton, brought an inquest today. Carl Nelson, railway section foreman, his wife and son Edward, 3, were clubbed to death. John Marciniuk, section hand, and George Renel were shot through the head. The body of Carl Sheits, alleged to have been the slayer, was found near the railroad tracks at Tieland. Sheits formerly was section foreman at Tieland, his place having been filled by Nelson. Officials said they believed the slaying occurred early Saturday. That afternoon a housemaid arrived by train from Hondo to go to work for Mrs. Nelson. She found all buildings at the settlement locked, police reported, and broke into a shack where she spent the night. Early Sunday, police said, Sheits went to the shack and he and the mai

MADRID, Spain. (UP) — Rebel planes and artillery rained more bombs and shells on Madrid today, following up attacks of yesterday in which fifty, mostly women and children, were killed. Shells fell around the national palace near the center of the city today. Three insurgent bombing planes flew over the city at 9:10 a.m. and bombed the outskirts. Bombs fell near the university city, the ruins of Frenchmen's bridge which was dynamited by the defenders to prevent the insurgents from crossing. The capital passed a sleepless night, as artillery, machine guns, rifles and hand grenades kept up an incessant barrage beginning at 2 a.m. and still in progress at noon. (A sentence of this was censored here). The windows of the United States embassy, some distance from the lower part of the city, rattled continuously. The crackle of machine guns was audible all night south and west of the city. Natio

MARSEILLES, France (P)—A violent explosion occurred Monday at the National powder factory at Saint-Chamas. A preliminary estimate said it was believed 20 were dead and 100 injured. Communication was difficult because the telephone lines went down after the explosion. A shock like an earthquake tremor rocked the countryside for miles around. A few minutes later frantic telephone appeals for ambulances and doctors came from the town of Miramar, near Saint-Chamas. All workers in government plants immediately were mobilized and the highways were soon jammed with ambulances and official cars speeding toward Saint-Chamas, from which rose a thick pall of smoke. The blast destroyed electric lights and cables, and plunged the entire area around the shattered factory into darkness. Authorities rushed mobile searchlights to the scene from the nearby Istres and Marignane airdromes, to enable rescue

(United Press Staff Correspondent,) MADRID, Nov. 15.—(UP)— The government tonight blew up the great Frenchman's bridge across the Manzanere river after rebels, in a smashing attack, had attempted to enter the city. Bitter fighting at the bridge climaxed a day in which rebel “blackbirds” again spread death and destruction throughout Madrid. Sixty persons were killed and more than 100 wounded as bombs terrorized the capital. The government announced its troops had captured several rebel tanks which supported the infantry advance on the bridge. None of the insurgents succeeded in crossing before the structure was destroyed. All the bridges leading into Madrid have been mined and can be destroyed on a moment's notice if rebel troops start across them. Loyalists announced that two of the invading bombers were shot down; I saw one fall in flames. Raids Daily The air raid—already a daily featur

1936-01-01.text: LIVERPOOL, Jan. 1—(#)—Colonel Charles A. Lindbergh left the United States, his official spokesman said today, "because he wants quiet and a peaceful, restful time." The flying colonel’s representative, W. H. Gregory of Morgan, Grenfell and Co., made this statement in a meeting with the press, but declined to answer a direct question as to whether the Lindberghs quit America because their second son Jon was threatened with kidnapping or because of the Bruno Richard Hauptmann case. "You will have to read between the lines regarding that," Gregory asserted. The spokesman declared, however, that he could not present a denial from Lindbergh that the family left the United States "because they were driven out by crime." Gregory said "Lindbergh was not surprised when he read the newspapers and saw the furore he had created. He feels the reason he left does not concern the public. The London ban

LONDON, January 1—Nine passengers of the airliner, City of Khartoum, and three crew members are believed dead after the plane crashed in the Mediterranean. Searchers abandoned hope that any would survive, except the pilot, who was picked up last night, after the ship's wreckage was found submerged four miles southwest of Alexandria, Egypt. The passengers included, C. Luke, an American. The disaster apparently was due to engine failure.

LONDON, Jan. 1 (4)—Hope was abandoned tonight for 12 persons, including the American James C. Luke, lost in the Mediterranean crash last night of the Imperial Airways liner, City of Khartoum. Luke, one of the nine passengers, was a member of the staff of E. B. Badger and Sons, of Boston, the firm's London representative, I. F. B. Nisbet, said. He had been loaned temporarily to the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company and was en route to Basra, Irak. Three members of the crew also were lost, the only survivor being a pilot who was picked up last night after the wrecked airship was found submerged four miles off Alexandria, Egypt. Luke, 57 years old, was a native of Southampton, England, and adopted American citizenship after his marriage in London. Until last July he had lived in Philadelphia. Searchers abandoned virtually all hope that any occupants of the 15-passenger flying boat would survive, th

Liverpool, England, Jan. 1— Colonel Charley A. Lindbergh said today that he intended to stay in England at least six months with Mrs. Lindbergh and their son, Jon. Indirectly, he confirmed accounts of his fears of another kidnapping and spoke bitterly of the death of his firstborn. The Colonel, sharp and at times almost sarcastic to newspapermen, said he was not in England on business as had been suggested by some in explaining his departure from the United States. Asked if he were here because of the kidnapping danger in the United States, Lindbergh said: "When you think it all out, that conclusion almost follows. We are simply here for a nice quiet visit. "We have come here for peace and quiet and a restful time. We are perfectly fit and well and the three of us enjoyed a good voyage. We are greatly pleased with the courtesy extended us by the British people." Lindbergh did not see the

LONDON, Jan. 1—(4)—A wide section of the British press apparently acceded today to Col. Charles A. Lindbergh's desire for less publicity. Three great conservative London newspapers—the London Times, Telegraph and Morning Post—barely referred to the arrival of the Lindberghs yesterday at Liverpool. The Times reported the arrival in two paragraphs. Other London newspapers illustrated their accounts with pictures, taken as the family hurried down the gangplank, but there was no metropolitan editorial comment. The Western Mail of Cardiff said editorially that Lindbergh's picture might appear in English newspapers from time to time, but asserted: “He will certainly be spared the attentions of blackmailers, gangsters and other human reptiles who flourish in the American undergrowth and have made his life there intolerable. “There must be something rotten in the state of America, despite her mu

LONDON, (Wednesday), Jan. 1 (#)—The ship Brilliant reported Wednesday it had discovered the wreckage of the Imperial Airways liner City of Khartoum in the Mediterranean Sea; but had found only one member of the crew and none of the passengers. The plane was forced down between Mirabelle, Crete, and Alexandria, Egypt, Tuesday. The number of passengers was unknown, but the plane carried a crew of four. The H. M. & Brilliant wirelessed it had picked up Pilot Vernon Gerry Wilsen, who apparently had been swimming in the water from the time the plane came down, but that there was no trace of any other occupants.
