PARIS (.P)—France and Great Britain started the new year Wednesday pledged that neither would negotiate individual land or air force treaties with Germany, The agreement healed the breach caused by Great Britain’s naval treaty permitting Germany to build up to 35 percent of the British fleet, in violation of the Versailles treaty. Back of the new Franco-British accord is the anxiety over Russia's increasing air force which military sources say will reach 5,000 planes by the end of this year and will have 1,000,000 pilots, 500,000 glider fliers by the end of 1937. France and Britain also have agreed it was revealed, to consult early in January on a plan to invite Germany back into an arms limitation conference. Germany left the world disarmament conference and the League of Nations in 1938 because the powers would not recognize her right to defense weapons.

STOCKHOLM, Jan. 28 (WP) = Anti-Italian feeling mounted today among incensed citizens who abandoned New Year's celebrations after they learned of the bombing of a Swedish Red Cross unit in Southern Ethiopia. Fear of grave international consequences spread with reports of the bombing. Extra guards were placed around the Italian legation and Chief of Police Baeckman said he would do his utmost to prevent terrorism. The Italian minister, Marquis Palermo remained behind the barred legation doors while reports were awaited from Swedish representatives to Italy and Ethiopia on the incident. Strong protests were expected to be made at Rome and Geneva. Word of the bombing at Dolo where nine Swedes and 24 Ethiopians were killed electrified the entire nation. Special editions of newspapers broadcast the news.

1936-01-29.text: LONDON — (P) — Britain’s new monarch, King Edward, gave his attention to European relations today as the British cabinet met to debate expansion of home defenses after more than a week devoted to obsequies for his late father, King George V. The new king conferred separately with Prince Erast von Starhemberg, anti-Nazi and pro-Italian vice-chancellor of Austria, and Baron Konstantin von Neurath, foreign minister of Nazi Germany. Official information from the Buckingham Palace conferences was lacking, but observers, viewing the European peace situation, were aware of Edward's apparent determination to follow his late father’s policy of strengthening international relations.

WINDSOR, England, Jan. 28. (?)—George V was buried beside the bodies of his father and mother today in the vaults under the chapel of his 1,000-year-old castle. He was laid to rest after a simple service—in contrast to the pageantry of a great funeral procession which brought his body here from Westminster Hall, London. The mighty of Europe walked behind his coffin, borne through massed hundreds of thousands. Two minutes of silence was observed and millions followed the broadcasts of the services. Before they lowered him into the vault they removed the symbols of his kingship—the crown, scepter and orb. The archbishop of Canterbury recommitted George’s soul to God, his body to eternal peace. Then Edward VIII, his son and successor, sprinkled earth from a silver urn on the coffin as it was lowered into the crypt. As the plain oak coffin disappeared Edward stepped back and turned to the qu

London, Jan. 29.—(UP)—King Edward VIII, on his first morning of work after King George's burial, received at Buckingham Palace today the special envoys of Germany and Austria, sent to attend the funeral. With envoys and heads of foreign States present in London, among them those of countries allied with Britain in the world war, the new king received the special ambassadors of Britain's two chief world war enemies. King Edward also granted an audience to Maxim Litvinov, Soviet foreign commissar. He rose early, breakfasted at his quarters at York House, St. James's Palace, and motored across to (Continued on Page Three)

CAIRO, Egypt, Jan. 29 (P)-- Nearly 100 students and 20 police were injured today in a three-hour battle in which police for the first time used ink-sprinklers to disperse the anti-British demonstrators. Police finally had to use firearms against the crowd, which sacked and set fire to the theological college.

GEORGETOWN, British Guiana, Jan. 28 (JP)—Art Williams and his copilot, unreported on a search for the long missing Paul Redfern, are safe on the Dutch Guiana frontier, authorities here were advised late today. A message said Williams and Harry Wendt were at Springlands, a border town on the Corentyne river. They had left Georgetown Sunday to renew their search for Redfern, who disappeared in 1927 on a projected flight from Brunswick, Ga., to Rio de Janeiro.

N— WP) —Police Commissioner Philip Game called a meeting of the chiefs of Scotland Yard. The arrangements broke down for the handling of the vast crowds at today's funeral for the late George Y. There had never been so many casualties recorded during a procession in this capital of an empire, having received ample appointment.

London (2P)—Great Britain’s ministers turned today to questions of State and defense reinforcements after more than a week devoted for their late king, George V: Budget estimates for expansion of the nation’s armed forces were sent to No. 1 Downing Street for consideration by the cabinet in its regular Wednesday meeting.

‘Paris, Jan. 29.—(U. P.)—French dele- gates, returning today from the funeral of King George V, informed the foreign office that Germany had promised Britain she would not violate the demilitarization provision governing the Rhineland, The British government informed Foreign Minister Pierre-Etienne Flandin, in London, of a German pledge not to send any military formations into the demilitarized zone.

1936-03-14.text: LONDON, March 14,—France invoked the crushing power of the 50 odd countries in the League of Nations today to force Germany to evacuate the Rhineland. Pierre Etienne Flandin, foreign minister of France, at an emergency meeting of the League of Nations Council, called by France and Belgium to force evacuation or punish Germany, demanded: 1. Full immediate support of France’s fellow signatories of the Locarno treaty. 2. Punishment of Germany by economic and financial penalties if she refuses to withdraw her troops. The council, meeting in historic St. James Palace, heard Flandin, Paul Van Zeeland, foreign minister of Belgium, and Anthony Eden of Great Britain. It went immediately into secret session and agreed to invite Germany to attend the next meeting Monday afternoon and defend her course in occupying the Rhineland in violation of the Versailles and Locarno treaties. (Copyright 1936 By The Associated Press) LONDON, MAR. 14. (AP).—The League of Nations council, formally requested by France and Belgium to condemn Germany as a treaty violator, invited the Reich today to send a representative to London as a last chance to make peace with the Locarno powers. The council, meeting in secret session, extended its offer to Reichsführer Adolf Hitler to lay his cards on the council table after being assured by Britain, in a public meeting, of fullest co-operation for the building of a new peace structure. France and Belgium joined in a demand at the public meeting of the council that the League condemn the Reich as a breaker of treaties for its occupation of the demilitarized Rhineland just a week ago in violation of the Locarno pact and the Versailles treaty. Anthony Eden, Britain's foreign secretary, supporting the charge that an “incontestable breach of trea

While some rivers were receding, heavy thaws of snow and ice floes in other rivers brought new danger zones today to eastern and northeastern states, and the maritime provinces of Canada. At least 28 persons were dead as a result of the flood, 18 in Canada, ten in New England and four in Kingston, Pa., and one in New York.

LONDON, Mar. 14—The League of Nations Council put the question of peace up to Chancellor Adolph Hitler today, by inviting Germany to attend its meetings. By asking the Reich to participate, the Council reopened the door for Germany to return to the League, and revealed wide chances for establishment of security on a continent which has almost despaired of avoiding war. The Council's invitation to Germany constitutes an amazing victory for Foreign Minister Anthony Eden, of Great Britain, who apparently succeeded in persuading France to abandon her demand that Hitler withdraw his troops from the Rhineland before France would negotiate peace. The sudden change of plans shows advancement, because up until this morning France resolutely refused to talk with Germany as long as the Reich troops were in the Rhineland. The question now asked is what did England promise France to induce her to cha

Pierre Lrienne Flandin, foreign minister of France, at an emergency meeting of the League of Nations Council, called by France and Belgium to force evacuation or punish Germany, demanded: 1. Full immediate support of France’s fellow signatories of the Locarno treaty. 2. Punishment of Germany by economic and financial penalties if she refused to withdraw her troops. London—(#)—The explosion of a fire extinguisher outside the meeting room of the League of Nations council startled delegates attending today’s session. Several persons were drenched by the spurting liquid and officials rushed to the corridor to determine the cause of the blast. After delegates entered the room Stanley M. Bruce, council president, requested the diplomatic representatives to refrain from smoking. He said the British government did not want to hang “No Smoking” signs in the building but that it wanted to protect valuable carpets and tapestries.

PARIS, March 13—A German financial official, a usually reliable source said tonight, is in Paris seeking to persuade France to drop her demand for sanctions against Germany because of the remilitarization of the Rhineland. Emil Georg von Strauss, third vice-president of the Reichstag and director of the Deutsche Bank, was said to be here as the confidential emissary of Dr. Hjalmar Schacht, German minister of economics and Reichsbank president. This source said the emissary warned Georges Bonnet, French minister of commerce, and leading Paris bankers that huge amounts of French capital invested in Germany would disappear if there were a financial collapse in the Reich. Bee, Strauss was quoted as saying Schacht submitted a memorandum to Adolf Hiller 15 days ago warning him against violating the Locarno treaty and pointing out that “ruinous sanctions” were likely to follow. Schacht, von Str

BERLIN, Mar. 14—(Saturday)—(V/P)—The Deutsche Diplomatische Korrespondenz, mouthpiece of the German foreign office, disclosed today that Germany will build fortifications at strategic points in the Rhineland, demilitarized until its reoccupation by German troops last Saturday. “Pillbox” fortifications will be placed along the western frontier, the publication stated in giving the first official confirmation of action which had been generally expected in Germany. Unlike the French system of fortifications, the Deutsche Diplomatische Korrespondenz said, the German frontline facing France will be small and disconnected. “Germany cannot afford to spend 8,000,000,000 francs, as France has,” the foreign office organ stated.

1936-12-19.text: ENZESFELD, Austria, Dec. 18.—(AP)— Edward of Windsor, grave-faced and wan, emerged briefly from retirement today to pose for photographers and then slipped back quickly into the seclusion of the chateau of Baron Eugene de Rothschild. There were dark circles beneath the former ruler of Britain’s eyes and his forehead was deeply wrinkled with lines not there a month ago, said those who had seen him then. “Gentlemen, how do you want me?” he greeted the photographers in the chateau courtyard for his three-minute picture interview. He replied to only one statement from among a flurry of queries. “We wish your highness every happiness,” a British photographer said. “I wish you luck also,” the duke replied. Then he turned and departed quickly. Hiring a valet was his main concern later in the day. Several candidates for the post appeared and Windsor interviewed two of them. He questioned both as

Parliament Startled While foreign secretary Anthony Eden startled Commons with the disclosure of sale of 5,000 gas masks to the Spanish Socialist government from British government stocks. Home secretary Sir John Simon exhorted financial leaders to take precautions against air raids, and city police were fitted with new masks. Eden told Commons a “small consignment of gas masks” had been sent to Spain. Government spokesmen emphasized quickly that fascist Gen. Francisco Franco's forces were equally entitled to them at the same prices because the masks are under a non-intervention classification of “medical supplies” — not munitions. The foreign secretary assured Commons the present war-like situation in Europe was not satisfactory and continued that “neither we nor the French government have any intention of desisting in our

Washington, Dec. 19—The navy, seeking to build up its floating fighting strength, faced double delays today in a threatened lack of steel and uncertainty over what will happen when the London naval treaty expires. Secretary Swanson said President Roosevelt, weighing the building of two new battleships, has decided to put off a decision until after the London pact dies on December 31. The President is free to order the laying down of keels, under an act of Congress, if the new floating fortresses are warranted by the building activities of any other power. The navy was snagged again in its quest for materials to build ships already approved. Steel firms bid in only one-quarter of the 8,784 tons of the shell-resisting metal sought for ship construction. Copper contracts had gone begging two weeks ago. In a lengthy meeting with his cabinet yesterday, President Roosevelt considered both prob

BERLIN, Dec. 19.— (#) —The third reich strove today to find the bread it must have by spring. An iron clamp, by nazi decree, pinched the already slim trickle of butter and fat products to the German consumer. Now, experts affirmed, the reich must face the prospect of empty domestic bread bins by April. To get the wheat to make the bread that Germany eats means going abroad—and there lie grave difficulties. The stringencies imposed on German households in preserving dwindling food supplies were disclosed yesterday by the issuance of ration cards for butter and lard. Will Prorate Fats. Under new orders allowances of fats will be prorated according to the size of families. Purchases will be limited to 80 per cent of October consumption each month, starting Jan. 1... Agricultural estimates agreed Germany must increase wheat importations after having reduced them in 1935 to 160,000 tons as co

Madrid, Dec. 19.—Spanish government officials heard yesterday that Fascist naval shells narrowly had missed the United States gunboat Erie while insurgent land forces pushed on toward encirclement of this sombre, half-dead capital. The Febus News Agency reported the insurgent cruiser Espana fired seven 12-inch shells at the Erie as the latter swung at anchor Thursday in the port of Musel, on the northern coast. (A report to Washington from the Erie’s commander said, however, there was nothing to indicate the Espana was firing at the gunboat, although one of two shells fired into the port fell within 500 yards of the Erie. No action was contemplated by the State Department.) The Febus report said the Espana fled hurriedly when the Erie’s crew uncovered its guns for action after running up the United States flag. Only one shell struck near the Erie, the others falling on a hillside behind

SHANGHAI, Dec. 19.—Apparently reliable advice was received at Nanking, the capital, today that "young marshal" Chang Hsueh-Liang had telegraphed the government resigning all his posts, consigning temporary control of his army to Gen. Yeh Hsi-Shan and announcing his intention to go abroad. The news lacked confirmation, but it was believed that the release of Generalissimo Chiang Kai-Shek, whom the young marshal seized at Sian-Fu in a daring attempt to force a war against Japan, was imminent. It was announced officially at Nanking that the government had ordered its airplanes to bomb Sian-Fu tomorrow unless the generalissimo was released. Two transport planes left Nanking for Sian-Fu and it was believed that the generalissimo and the distinguished group seized with him would return in them to safety. T. V. Soong, former finance minister, a brother-in-law of the generalissimo, left soon aft

Cannes, France, Dec. 18 (AP) Gendarmes were called back to duty tonight to keep the curious away from Wallis Simpson's Riviera refuge. The local police said they expected to be posted at the fork of the road about 150 yards from the entrance to the villa of Mr. and Mrs. Herman Rogers, Mrs. Simpson's hosts. Despite the renewed guard order, it was indicated the beloved of former King Edward hoped to get about more in the near future. She took a short drive through the countryside last night and later played bridge with friends in Cannes. Her "fan mail" continues, police said, but all of it is consigned to the wastebasket.

MADRID, Dec. 19. (U.P) — The Loyalists defending besieged Madrid, fearing a Rebel air raid as dense fog lifted, began a terrific artillery attack on the Insurgents’ positions today. Heavy guns roared from the capital defenses after a night of terror awaiting the Rebel raid. The Rebels had flown over Madrid dropping leaflets announcing that when the thick mists dispersed they again would bomb the capital.

1936-11-09.text: PARIS, Nov. 8 (©) — Premier Leon Blum told a Socialist meeting today he was ready to scrap the non-intervention agreement and supply arms and munitions to the Spanish Madrid government if Britain would agree to aid France. The premier said assurance by England that she would stand by France would make French aid to the cabinet of Socialist Premier Francisco Largo Caballero’s government possible. Would Aid Russia Lack of such assurance of English aid, he intimated, had been one reason that France proposed signing the European non-intervention agreement. “We could not allow the working class to walk into a blind adventure,” he said. “If a general war had come along we would have found ourselves along with Russia.” The premier did not say whether there had been negotiations with Britain or whether any were planned, Stand Indicated Indications Blum’s remarks pointed to a more firm stand by t

LONDON—U.P.—From mountainous seas 200 miles off Land's End, England, early today the S. S. Westernland picked up a life boat containing one man, a cabin boy. He was the lone survivor of the 40-man crew of the motorship Isis. Three times through the raving winds and gigantic seas of the season's worst storm, crackled an SOS from the little German freighter. The German Red Star liner Westernland arrived at dusk Sunday and all night, while she plunged and rolled, all but helpless, her searchlights fingered through the wind driven rain and spray. She picked up the one man in the one boat, and, at 9:30 a.m. (4:30 a.m. EST) her commander abandoned hope of finding the others and ordered her put about for Southampton, her destination. The British freighter Seminole had assisted in the search, and even the great Queen Mary, the largest ship afloat, turned off her course, though she was rolling so

New York Nov. 9 (#)—Fred Perry of England, world amateur tennis champion, has turned professional. Francis T. Hunter and S. Howard Voshell jointly announced today. Perry, three times winner of the American and All-England singles championships and backbone of the British Davis Cup team for the past four years, signed a contract with Hunter and Voshell to make a barnstorming tour of the country this winter, with Ellsworth Vines, and probably Bill Tilden and either George Lott or Lester Stoefen. The tour will open in Madison Square Garden, January 6, undoubtedly against Vines.

Comment was withheld until spokesmen have time to study the text of Blum’s speech carefully. London, Nov. 9.—King Edward will marry Mrs. Wallis Simpson in the private chapel of Buckingham Palace, and the ceremony, which will take place several weeks after the monarch’s coronation next May, will be performed by one of the chaplains to the king, it was disclosed today. Before the marriage takes place, a high authority declared, Mrs. Simpson will be made a peeress in her own right and after the marriage she will take one of the king’s ducal titles, becoming the Duchess of Lancaster or the Duchess of Cornwall, probably the former, according to the plan contemplated by the king at present. The plan and its details are subject to possible modification which may arise from the numerous problems involved in the romance, it was stated, however. London, Nov. 9—Great Britain plans to hold firm to her Spanish non-intervention policy, despite Premier Leon Blum's reported desire to give French aid to Madrid, informed sources said today. The French suggestions to send help to beleaguered Spanish Socialists were discounted in some quarters today as “mere internal politics” of Premier Leon Blum. The proposal advanced in Paris was discussed informally as members of the international non-intervention committee assembled for fresh discussion of neutrality problems. Agenda for the meeting included debate on measures to make the “hands-off” agreement more effective. Lord Plymouth, committee chairman, was expected to attempt to prevent filing of fresh charges of assisting Spanish insurgents against Germany, Italy and Portugal by Russian delegates.

London, Nov. 9. (AP)—Abandoning hope for 39 members of the crew of the lost German motorship Isis, the rescue steamer Westernland plowed through mountainous seas toward Southampton today with the lone survivor, Cabin Boy Fritz Roetheke. The Isis was believed to have foundered soon after she flashed her last SOS last night from a point some 200 miles east of Land's End. Roetheke, exhausted from all-night exposure to the howling gale in an open boat, was picked up by the Westernland this morning. His condition was such that he was unable to say more than that he thought all his 39 comrades had been lost when an east Atlantic storm crushed the 4,454-ton cargo boat. | BERLIN (UP) — Thirty-nine men drowned when the motor-ship Isis foundered 200 miles off Land’s End, Eng., the commander of the S. S. Westernland, one of the rescue ships, wirelessed Monday. The Westernland’s master reported that he had rescued Fritz Roethke, 17, the Isis’ cabin boy, and that the youth was the only survivor. The Queen Mary and the S. S. Mirror and the Westernland gave up the search and proceeded on their courses Monday morning, he reported.

Morgan sitting down with the British war council, was revealed Wednesday by the Senate munitions committee. The arms companies concerned, it was testified, were Winchester and Remington. In addition, committee investigators disclosed that the State Department, with the 1916 election approaching, withheld from publication for three weeks a British note received in the course of the controversy over British interference with American commerce. Evidence to this effect was brought out during the protracted sessions Wednesday, with Morgan, head of the powerful financial house, and several of the partners on the witness stand for the second consecutive day. LONDON, Jan. 8 (®)—Great Britain and France moved suddenly today to increase their naval strengths in and around the Mediterranean. They will do so at the time the council of the League of Nations meets in Geneva January 20, when a proposed oil sanction against Italy is to come up for consideration. France will send two squadrons, a total of 92 warships, to the Mediterranean. The British 21st destroyer flotilla, accompanied by four men-of-war of the home fleet, will hold a “spring cruise” near Gibraltar and replacements will be made which will strengthen the Mediterranean fleet. Lindbergh, arrived aboard the liner Bremen with her daughter, Constance, today and left hurriedly for London by automobile. It was believed Mrs. Morrow and her daughter will go tonight to Llandaff, Wales, where Colonel and Mrs. Lindbergh and their small son are staying.

By what may be a coincidence, the fleets will be in excellent position for quick action when the League of Nations resumes its study of the Italian-Ethiopian crisis probably January 20. Not only will two gigantic battleships, an aircraft carrier, a cruiser and a destroyer flotilla of the British home fleet be cruising near Gibraltar, but one powerful French fleet will be conducting maneuvers in the waters adjacent to Toulon and Corsica, off the Italian coast, and another will be cruising near Casablanca, Morocco, 160 miles from the straits of Gibraltar. Italy has been reported unofficially to feel that such a sanction would mean war in Europe. The French fleet will hold maneuvers in the Mediterranean. London, Jan. 8 (4).—Charges that foreign agents of the Vickers armaments interests tried to “promote war” by urging countries to buy munitions climaxed crossfire today between the royal commission on private manufacture of arms and British manufacturers. Dame Rachel Crowdy, British social worker, who is a member of the royal commission, made the accusations after Commander Sir Charles Craven, managing director of Vickers-Armstrong, Ltd. and director of Vickers, Ltd., denied his agents had tried to boom foreign sales. Dame Crowdy read a letter signed by Craven which said: “IT am trying to ginger up the Chileans to buy three more boats.”

LONDON, Jan. 8—(4)—A breakup of the Five Power international naval conference Friday unless the Japanese make a last-minute about face in their demands for equality was seen as a possibility tonight in informed circles. Great Britain’s delegation in an eleventh-hour move to prevent a crash of the conference, asked the Japanese to meet it privately tomorrow to discuss the serious turn of events. The conference itself is in recess until Friday. Admiral Osami Nagano of the Japanese delegation insisted at today’s session that his demands for equality with the United States and Great Britain must be disposed of before anything else. P.)—Italy is ready to cease hostilities against Ethiopia, if sanctions against her are lifted, League of Nations officials announced today. Officials said Italy had informed the members of the League committee of thirteen on Ethiopia to that effect. The committee members said they expect Italy to make the announcement formally after the committee meets tomorrow. They believe, however, that Italy should first require a pledge that sanctions would be lifted.

LONDON, England, (UP) — The council of the League of Nations today formally declared Germany’s occupation of the Rhineland a violation of the Locarno and Versailles treaties, as a prelude to discussion among the powers of a general European peace. The council passed a Franco-Belgian resolution declaring the treaty violation by unanimous vote. The German representative voted no, but his vote was not counted. Neither were those of France and Belgium, as parties to the dispute. There was no bitterness apparent. The resolution was passed mainly as a formality and a matter of record. After the vote on the resolution, the council adjourned. It called a meeting of the committee of thirteen on the Ethiopian war for tomorrow, and decided to hold another session after the meeting of thirteen, to decide on further procedure in the Rhineland dispute.

Officers and men of all insular defense units were instructed to take their posts Tuesday and Wednesday at the same time the League of Nations council debates war sanctions at Geneva. The demonstration was designed to show the reinforced strength of the island base, virtually evacuated by the grand fleet last August when Italy’s east African campaign threatened British interests in the Mediterranean. All shore and foreign leaves of British defense forces were cancelled for the period of the mobilization. Scouting planes will be sent to sea to make aerial observations. Some nations, this official added, regarded Italy’s move to annex outright as ‘pretty raw.’ He conceded, however, that the business interests of many nations demanded a prompt lifting of the penalties of ‘aggression.’ (In Paris, the Ethiopian envoy Wolde Mariam announced he would go to Geneva Monday to plead for “justice again.” He said he was acting on orders from Ethiopia’s “new secret capital” and claimed the Ethiopian government still was functioning from this undisclosed seat.) ATHENS, Greece, May 9 (®)— Fierce fighting between tobacco strikers and troops in Salonika ended tonight after 30 persons had been killed and more than 100 wounded and after striking transportation workers had been “mobilized” to keep them at their posts. Army commanders took control of the situation and order was restored by nightfall. Workers and owners conferred at the residence of General John Metaxas, minister of war, in search of an agreement. The major fighting began when strikers fired on an armored car which was patrolling the streets. After that, firing became general, but calm was restored after a stiff battle during which police stormed barricades in the streets. Infantry forces, armed with machine guns, deployed in danger zones.

United Press Staff Correspondent ROME, May 9.—Rome's new Caesar, Benito Mussolini, tonight proclaimed to the world that “Italy finally has its empire.” Achieving his ambition to create a new Roman empire, Il Duce proclaimed the formal annexation of Ethiopia and announced that King Victor Emmanuel is its Emperor. Il Duce, the man of destiny, achieved the zenith of his power with a thundering speech from the balcony of the Palazzo Venezia. In the square below 350,000 people cheered “Il Duce, Il Duce,” and “A noi, a noi.” His proclamation that Italy had annexed Ethiopia and elevated little Victor Emmanuel to the status of a king-emperor was heard by 30,000,000 people rejoicing throughout Italy. LONDON, May 23 (UP).—Haile Selassie, the emperor without a country, headed for London and an uncertain British reception tonight. Bringing ticklish diplomatic problems for Whitehall, the sad-eyed Negus left Jerusalem en route to Haifa for embarkation aboard a British cruiser, H. M. S. Cape Town.

Uniformed defenders of the ousted vice chancellor’s Waxenburg castle crushed what was officially called a Nazi attack, killing two men. Seven others were seized. The brisk counter-thrust indicated to some that the Heimwehr’s young officers were clamoring for more. Radical leaders of the private army, chafing at Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg’s removal of Von Starhemberg from the cabinet and the chancellor’s move to make the Heimwehr part of the national militia, were urging a sudden stroke to impose the Heimwehr’s particular brand of fascism on the country. | PARIS, May 23—(AP)—The play, “Hitler,” dramatized largely from a suppressed newspaper account of the German chancellor’s “love life,” was banned tonight by the minister of the interior, acting “in accord with the minister of education.” Officials of both ministries declined to comment, but informed sources said the action was a question of “politics and morals” and taken in order to avoid diplomatic incidents. The management of the theatre, where the play was to have opened tonight, bewailed the closing because it was their first “sell-out” in months. A squadron of police watched the box office to refund money to files of disappointed play-goers. The actor, Georges Norel, a wounded war veteran who was to take the part of Hitler in the play, insisted the ban showed “a disgusting fear of Germany.”

VIENNA, Austria. (UP) — Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg last night ordered the arrest of Nazi leaders throughout the country, after a pitched battle at Prinz Ernest Von Starhemberg’s Wachsenberg castle. Two were killed, and several injured in fighting when Nazis attacked the castle in an effort to seize arms believed stored there for the Heimwehr, Starhemberg’s private army. With a nation-wide round-up of Nazi leaders ordered, Starhemberg, ousted from the government a week ago by Schuschnigg, self-proclaimed dictator of Austria, rushed back to Vienna by plane from his country estate. Last night 28 prominent Nazi leaders were under arrest and police were continuing search for others. All persons suspected of complicity in the Wachsenberg attack were ordered arrested. Enzesfeld, Austria, Dec, 22.— Edward of Windsor parted reluctantly tonight with his chauffeur for the past 18 years, breaking another "last tie" with the England he left for love of Wallis Simpson. The chauffeur, George Stanley Ladbrook, who drove Mrs. Simpson from England to Cannes, brought Edward's personal automobile here along with ski equipment and other baggage. The duke busied himself with plans for Christmas tonight, and his first present, presumably from Mrs. Simpson, arrived from Cannes. It was a small package, heavily insured, apparently a ring or other jewelry.

Boston, Dec. 23.—(AP)—The Boston Weather Bureau forecast a “Green Christmas” for most of New England today. The southern limit of the snow blanket now runs through central Vermont, the southern slopes of the Presidential Range in New Hampshire and north central Maine, and those were the only areas for which the Weather Bureau foresaw even snow flurries before Friday night. The mercury, which dropped to 12 degrees above zero in Boston early today, was expected to climb to about 30 degrees during the day, with warmer, cloudy weather forecast for most of New England the next two days.

She was known locally as ‘“Mam Kit”’ and is married to a match seller known as “Blind Dan.” After talking to her for five hours, Ford said he was convinced she was the mother he had sought for years. Ford, whose real name is Samuel Jones, was placed in Dr. Barnardo’s Home as a foundling when he was three years old—85 years ago. With 300 others, he was sent to Toronto at the age of seven. He went on the American stage in 1915 and then began his long search to locate his mother. The only clue he had was her name—Catherine Jones. Geneva, May 13. — League council members feared today that the situation threatening the league’s effectiveness if not its life, depended for solution upon restoration of friendship between Italy and Great Britain. Preparing to adjourn until mid-June, leaving in force penalties exacted against Italy for its war on Ethiopia, delegates felt that the league can do nothing to extricate itself from a threatening position while Italy and Britain are estranged. Hence they felt the anger of Italy at Britain overshadowed for the present the situation precipitated by Italy’s withdrawal from the council meeting. Italy has left the council table before during the Italian-Ethiopian war. This time Premier Benito Mussolini not only withdrew his delegation but ordered all Italian cooperation with the league suspended until the 50-odd nations in the league repudiate their pledge to aid E

Manchester, Eng., May 12 (4)—An Indian physician was hanged today for the dismemberment murders of his wife and a nursemaid and a coroner's jury returned a verdict condemning a wealthy woman campaigner against capital punishment for “self advertising propaganda.” Nothing daunted, the woman, Mrs. Violet Van Der Elst, said tonight she planned to carry her anti-capital punishment crusade to the United States, Dr. Buck Ruxton, 36, was placed on the gallows for the “Devil's Beetub” slayings of the two women, one of England's most gruesome crimes of this century. Mrs. Van Der Elst, who makes it a practice to publicly protest all hangings, met a hostile reception from a jeering crowd. After the hanging she was arrested on charges involving breach of peace, obstructing traffic and dangerous driving and was released under bail for a week, The Coroner’s jury returned a verdict that Ruxton died in

WASHINGTON, May 12—(AP)—The naval treaty signed at London by the United States, Great Britain and France was sent to the Senate today by President Roosevelt, and promptly was met by a prediction that it would be ratified at the present session of Congress. Chairman Pultman, Democrat, Nevada, of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, immediately set hearings on the pact for tomorrow and forecast early approval. The pact would limit the size of certain types of ships without restricting their numbers, and provide for exchange of building program information between the signatories.

Steeplejack Unhurt After 140-Foot Drop But Statue Breaks Leg. LOS ANGELES—Charles England, steeplejack, fell 140 feet and caught a rope in time to save himself. An eight-foot statue of Diana, made of copper, fell with him and received a broken leg. England brushed himself off and began taking stock, “I bet I smashed my canteen,” he said.

Rome, May 13—Premier Mussolini's Popolo D’Italia defied challengers of the new Roman empire today with a warning that “the Italian people created it with their blood, they will cultivate it with their labor and defend it against anyone with their arms.” The editorial in Il Duce’s newspaper coincided with the return from Geneva of Baron Pompeo Aloisi, who was recalled yesterday as Italy laid before the League of Nations implicitly the choice of accepting the fascist empire or losing Italian membership. Informed sources read in the editorial a slightly veiled reference to Great Britain in the words: “The Italian people ask themselves why the occupation by some powers of civilized and even independent countries should be considered legitimate while Italy's occupation of territories horribly depopulated by barbaric organization and slave trade should be illegitimate.” The editorial asked, “I

ROME, May 12. (?)— The walkout of the Italian delegation at Geneva, an authoritative source indicated tonight means that Italy will refuse to cooperate with the League of Nations until her annexation of Ethiopia is recognized. This source, a high fascist official, would not state explicitly the implied significance of the action except to say it was ‘very important.’ Premier Mussolini plans to refuse any collaboration in European affairs, it was indicated, although he may not openly declare such a policy, until the “Italian empire” is recognized. The Geneva withdrawal was likened by a well-informed source to the step of severance of diplomatic relations before a declaration of war, It was not regarded by this source as a definite withdrawal from the league. He pointed out ‘a withdrawal of diplomatic representatives does not necessarily mean war. It is only a step. “However, it is entirel

MADRID, (UP).—Storm guards dispersed rioting mobs of right-wing political partisans today and saved the American-owned telephone exchange at Valencia and the Spanish Credit Bank building from burning. The rioters burned two right-wing political clubs and two churches.

1936-04-08.text: | Anthony Eden, British foreign secretary, protested to the league conciliation committee of 13 today against the alleged use of poison gas by the Italian armies in Ethiopia, while Premier Mussolini, in an extraordinary session of his cabinet, said Italy would fight for the “total annihilation of the Ethiopian military formation.” The French came forward, at the same time, with the publication of their plan to maintain peace in Europe with the establishment of permanent military forces to guard against violation of frontiers. At the first meeting of the conciliation committee, Eden called Italy to task on the charge of using asphyxiating gases on the Ethiopian war front, in violation of the convention signed at Geneva in 1925, by both warring nations. The foreign secretary asked the international Red Cross to disclose any information it possessed regarding these charges. | Mexican Protes

London, April 8—()—The British government published a white paper today disclosing Reichsfuehrer Hitler’s fear that Berlin “might easily be reduced to a heap of ashes” from a Russian air attack. The white paper, outlining Anglo-German-French diplomatic discussions for securing European peace from June 1934 to March 1936, showed that der Fuehrer expressed that view to Sir Eric Phipps in Berlin Dec. 16, when the British ambassador pressed him to start conversations for an air pact. Previously the Reichsfuehrer had stated a pact for air force limitations must be held in abeyance because of the Italo-Ethiopian uncertainties. Phipps, reporting to Sir Samuel Hoare, then foreign secretary, said Hitler referred to “Russia’s enormous military strength on land and in the air.” Der Fuehrer said, “Berlin might easily in a few hours be reduced to a heap of ashes by a Russian air attack before the lea

LONDON.—Evidence which convinced the British that Italy was using poison gas in her war with Ethiopia has been turned over to the League of Nations for consideration by the "committee of 13." This was learned Tuesday night from a high source shortly after Anthony Eden, foreign secretary, departed for Geneva to attend the committee session. The evidence, which Sir Sidney Barton, British minister to Ethiopia, cabled to his government last week came from various international sources whose neutral observations the British claimed to be unimpeachable. Recent Development According to these reports, the Italian planes began using gas bombs about March 1 and have continued their use since then during their aerial attacks. Although the poison gas may be essentially meant to disperse the Ethiopian troops, it was claimed that thousands of civilians, including women and children have also suffered

ROME, April 8.—In a statement timed to catch the ears of League of Nations statesmen debating the Italo-Ethiopian war in Geneva, Premier Benito Mussolini called today for "total annihilation of Ethiopian military formations" without delay. Acting dramatically as Britain prepared to call for consideration of Ethiopia’s case at Geneva, Il Duce summoned a special meeting of his cabinet and told them the Ethiopian army must be wiped out completely, adding such action cannot be avoided. "The superb victories of our troops, and in particular the victory at Lake Ashangi over troops of the Negus who were trained and equipped and armed by Europeans, bring Italy nearer the realization of our first objective—the security of our colonies," Il Duce said. "It was with this objective that Italy was obliged to take recourse to arms after mobilization of the Ethiopian forces. This security will be attain

| ROME, April 8—Premier Mussolini proclaimed to his ministers today that security for Italy in its East African colonies would be realized only with “total annihilation of the Ethiopian military formation.” Il Duce met his council of ministers in a sudden, extraordinary session which had not been announced in advance. It was held just as the League of Nations conciliation committee of 13 was meeting in Geneva.

(Copyright 1936, by Associated Press.) - GENEVA, April 8.--The League of Nations’ “committee of 13” today appointed a sub-committee of jurists to investigate charges that Italy was using poison gas in Ethiopia. At the same time, the committee of 18--which is made up of every member of the league council except Italy—empowered its president, Salvador de Madariaga of Spain, to try to learn Premier Mussolini’s terms for making peace. He was instructed to talk to Baron Pompeo Aloisi, the Italian delegate to the league, when the latter comes to Geneva tomorrow. (In Rome, Premier Mussolini declared to his cabinet that security for Italy would be reached only with the “total annihilation of the Ethiopian military formation.”) Anthony Eden, foreign secretary of Great Britain, gave the committee of 13 a specific list of alleged occasions on which Italian troops used poison gas.

1936-02-16.text: (By the Associated Press) LONDON, Feb. 15. -- European nations, taking as their slogan "only in strength lies peace," were generally strengthening their defense forces today. No less than seven nations was the question of national defense the chief problem before the government. Those nations are Great Britain, France, Russia, Germany, Belgium, Spain, and Italy. One Vast Arsenal In the wake of a statement made in the House of Commons yesterday by George Lambert, former civil lord of the admiralty, that "Europe today was one vast arsenal," a survey by the Associated Press showed the following: Great Britain — A program for "repairing the gaps" in defenses will be made public in March. It will call for an expenditure generally expected to total about £200,000,000 ($1,500,000,000), roughly double the annual expenditure since 1925. LONDON, Feb. 15.—%—Under a page-wide headline, “Woolworth Baby to Live in England,” the Sunday Pictorial will say tomorrow that the baby expected by Countess Barbara Hutton Haugwitz Reventlow “will never go to America.” The newspaper will say: “The countess is terrified that in the land of racketeers her baby may be kidnapped.” The Pictorial will add that the countess, who is heiress to the Woolworth millions, will make her permanent home in Great Britain. Recent dispatches from America printed here said Mr. and Mrs. Franklyn Hutton, the countess’ parents, would return to America with their grandchild.

Mongolian Frontier. MOSCOW, Feb. 15 () — A government spokesman reaffirmed tonight the Soviet Union's intention to stand pat on the present border lines in the far east. His statement, made on the anniversary of the formation of the Soviet frontier troops, came as a new clash along the Mongolian border was reported in Tokyo. This report was denied, however, in Soviet dispatches from Ulan Bator, Outer Mongolia. Official Mongolian quarters were quoted as saying there had been no further border trouble since a clash on Feb. 12, which Soviet accounts said resulted "from invasion" of Mongolian territory by Japanese-Manchoukuoan troops. MADRID, Feb. 15 (7P)—Disorders broke out in some sections of Spain today on the eve of the general election. Premier Manuel Portela Valladares announced that 34,000 civil guards and 17,000 assault guards would be ready to maintain tranquillity during the voting tomorrow. A bystander was shot and seriously wounded at Madrid's Puerto del Sol when a youth on a truck, reported to be carrying fascists, fired into a crowd. In the town of El Padul, unidentified persons fired three shots at an automobile occupied by Fernando de Los Rios, former socialist minister, but none of the shots took effect. Police dispersed fascists and leftists who engaged in a verbal demonstration in Madrid. Premier Portela, in a nationwide radio address, appealed to the people for quiet tomorrow, announcing at the same time that every precaution had been taken to guarantee all citizens the right to vote. The reports, brought to Tokyo by the Domei (Japanese) news agency, said 1,000 Mongolians had attacked a military post at Asailsumu, within Manchoukuo. Washington, Feb. 15, —(#)— Plowing under bipartisan opposition by an almost three to one margin, administration forces today won senate passage of the $500,000,000 soil conservation subsidy brand of crop control. The bill now goes to the house. The senate vote, climaxing eleven days of debate during which the measure’s constitutionality was challenged and defended, was 56 to 20. Split Forty-nine democrats, five republicans, the farm-laborite, Benson, and the progressive, LaFollette, voted for the bill. Nine democrats and 11 republicans opposed it. Just before the last roll call, a motion by Senator McNary, the republican leader, to send the bill back to committee with instructions to report out a new proposal in three weeks, was rejected 54 to 21. McNary contended the bill was “unworkable and unconstitutional.” He predicted after the senate quit for the day that some state would challeng

The cause of peace in the new world, he said, is a matter of ‘vital concern.’ “These steps, furthermore,” he said, “would advance the cause of world peace, inasmuch as the agreements which might be reached would supplement and reinforce the efforts of the League of Nations and of all other existing or future peace agencies in seeking to prevent war.” Sure to Meet A favorable response to Mr. Roosevelt’s suggestion was generally conceded. By The Associated Press Chicago, Feb. 15—Airplanes and dynamite sped food and fuel to starving prisoners of the snow in the northwest tonight as zero sank deeper into the east. Pleas for “pretty quick” aid from a dozen towns hurried ski-equipped planes into the air and over huge drifts that blocked land rescue crews. The ships could carry only light supplies and snowplows, sleds and trucks floundered on. Dynamite blasts shot snow and ice high in the air after winter’s barriers repulsed the plows. Four South Dakota communities—Red Owl, Twilight, Stoneville and Fairpoint—were in a critical plight when the first ski-ship visited them. Another plane was loaded with 800 pounds of food for a second trip. Snow plows, trucks and tractors turned back once for repairs, bored on with greater supplies for them and for the residents of Marcus, Opal, Murine, Mud Butte and Sulphur. A snowplow burrowed

1936-12-28.text: LONDON, Dec. 28.—(AP)—Hope grew today in the foreign offices of Europe's great powers for a diplomatic solution to the threatened spread of the Spanish civil war through German intervention. The continent focused its attention on snow-covered Berchtesgaden in Bavaria, where Adolf Hitler pondered problems which may decide the question of peace or war for Europe. London circles pointed out the decision der Führer must make in his Christmas retreat might go far beyond any question of going to the aid of the Spanish Fascists. In effect, these sources said, Hitler faced the alternative of leading Germany back to western cooperation for peace or plunging his country into deep isolation. Firm refusal of the Spanish Socialist government to heed a German ultimatum to free the captured steamer Palos in the face of Nazi threats.

LONDON, Dec. 28 (UP)—Great Britain has hope that Italy, as a contribution to Europe's peace, may offer to cease its intervention in behalf of the Nationalists in the Spanish civil war, it was understood today. Intense interest was evident in the reply which Italy is to make to joint French-British pleas for cessation of intervention. It was hoped that the reply might give the first factual indication of a change in Italian policy. A favorable Italian answer would be regarded by many as foreshadowing Premier Benito Mussolini's willingness to curtail his assistance to Gen. Francisco Franco, the ‘Nationalist dictator. (Copyright 1936-by U. P.) ROME, Dec. 28 (UP)—Italy has suspended shipment of “volunteers” to Spain pending negotiations for a general agreement to forbid the dispatch of men to either faction in the civil war, persons close to the government said today. Soviet Russia supports the sensational French scheme, and it will be brought up before a sub-committee of the 27-power non-intervention committee, composed of naval attaches to major embassies, on Thursday. Vienna—()—Edward, Duke of Windsor, came to Vienna today and: on Took a Turkish bath. Visited the British legation. Ate a big slice of chocolate cake at a cafe. Returned to Chateau Enzesfeld, where he is staying.

Berlin, Dec. 28—Chancellor Adolf Hitler is willing to cooperate with Great Britain and France in attempting to obtain an armistice in Spain and solution of the "volunteers" problem provided London and Paris guarantee complete cessation of "soviet intervention" in the Spanish war, International News Service learned in high quarters today. Russia, and not Germany, is the real culprit in the Spanish crisis according to the German view, and definite annoyance was shown by high officials that Britain and France should have warned Germany so strongly on the "volunteers" issue. Separate Affair Germany, it was disclosed, considers seizure of the German merchant vessel Palos by Spanish loyalists an important matter but one apart from the "general Spanish situation," and as a result will not allow it to interfere with "the regular negotiations" for settlement of the

(International News Service) MADRID, Dec. 28—Great Britain today ordered its Madrid embassy closed as soon as possible, following the move the United States made several weeks ago. As new fighting broke out around the capital and the shell-wrecked, widely-ruined city faced further destruction, Britain ordered that all persons living as refugees in the embassy evacuate it by Wednesday. G. A. D. Ogilvie-Forbes, counsellor of the embassy, will establish a new embassy at Valencia, on the eastern seaboard where the Loyalist parliament now has its headquarters.

LONDON, Dec. 27.-(U.P)—The Archbishop of Canterbury, in a broadcast tonight, told dignitaries of the Church of England to cease their attacks on former King Edward. The primate—one of the first to criticize Edward for his romance with Mrs. Wallis Warfield Simpson—said it was time England and the empire stopped referring to the crisis on the monarch's abdication. “In our national history the year that is going never can be forgotten, but its most recent vivid memories had better now be kept in silence,” the archbishop said. His appeal to churchmen and the people to forget Edward and Mrs. Simpson, whose contemplated marriage he once called “un-Christian,” was regarded as a polite rebuff to the archbishop of York. The latter, Dr. William Temple, recently reopened the controversy over the “moral status” of Edward's romance by inferring that the former king was a man of honor because he took

EUROPE emerged from holiday celebrations to find a new crisis facing it over the Spanish civil war. Highlights in the situation last night were: BERLIN—Germany gives Spanish Socialist government "another day" to release freighter Palos. British and French ambassadors deliver notes demanding a halt of foreign volunteer enlistments in the Spanish conflict. PARIS—Basque nationalists authorities in a statement issued through the Spanish embassy announced refusal to release the Palos. LONDON—Observers see Europe's stage setting calling for one of Hitler’s spectacular coups, but authoritative sources said they expected something less despite reports German warships already were at Bilbao. Peace seen continuing well into 1937 with the issue depending on Hitler’s decision whether to back Spanish Fascists to the limit.

1936-03-01.text: | LONDON, Feb. 29 —(UM)— A high source disclosed tonight Hitler made a gesture of friendliness to Great Britain by consenting to negotiations in London for a proposed new Anglo-German naval treaty. The report said instructions from Hitler had been received by the German embassy but will not be communicated to the British until next week. The proposed pact is said to contain: Limitation on the size of armaments; aircraft carriers; halt in construction of heavy cruisers; restriction in size of cruisers to 8,000 tons with moderate caliber guns; limitation on the size of armaments for submarines. Both British and Americans impatiently awaited a statement from the French as to whether they would sign the new general naval treaty—the pact Italy indicated she was “not ready” to agree to.

London, March 1.—(Sunday)—(P)——Dr. Cedric Sydney Lane-Roberts, one of the physicians attending Countess Haugwitz-Reventlow, said at 5:25 a. m., today, “everything is satisfactory.” He intimated, as he left the house where the former Barbara Hutton was seriously ill, that a bulletin to that effect would be issued at about 10 a. m. She was reported to have survived two operations——a caesarian delivery of a son last Tuesday and another for the relief of an abdominal obstruction Thursday. It is known that previous to the countess’ confinement she suffered from anemia and was under treatment for this condition.

LONDON, Feb. 29 (UP)—Countess Von Haugwitz-Reventlow, the former Barbara Hutton, Woolworth heiress, was conceded a good chance to live tonight, although previously her life had been despaired of. The countess was gravely ill from an abdominal operation which was performed three days after the birth of her son. She was not yet out of danger, but she was said to be very much better and to have shown great improvement. The baby was in excellent condition. Lord Horder, the king’s physician, visited her this evening, interrupting a weekend in the country, as previously planned. He found her condition very satisfactory, although the crisis has not yet been passed. The worst period of her illness was Friday night, when for a time her life was despaired of and she was not expected to live until morning. Mrs. Franklyn L. Hutton, her stepmother, arranged to spend tonight with her, as did Dr. Cedri

Landon, Feb. 20.-2—A report that Russia was shipping "knocked down" submarines from Europe to her naval bases on the Pacific Ocean circulated among members of the naval conference tonight. The report stated that the submarines, of various sizes, were being hastily reassembled in the East "to meet any emergency." The exact sizes and tonnages of the undersea boats was not disclosed. According to other sources in Landon, the government at Moscow now is thoroughly alarmed as to the situation in the Pacific and considers that much larger naval defenses are needed on the east coast than previously. It was declared that the Soviet was determined to prevent encroachments by Japan in the Russian sphere of territorial influence and was, therefore, taking large scale steps to strengthen her defenses. TOKYO, March 1.—(Sunday)—(by telephone to Shanghai)—Capt. Teruzo Ando, alleged leader of the Tokyo rebellion, shot himself in the head and died late last night. Capt. Shiro Nonaka, chief lieutenant to Capt. Ando, was understood reliably also to have attempted suicide by shooting. The remainder of the 20 leaders of the mutiny which ended Saturday with the rebel’s surrender were reported reliably to be still alive at a military prison on the outskirts of Tokyo where they were being held.

(Copyright, 1936, by Associated Press) TOKYO, March 1—(Sunday)— (AP)—Premier Keisuke Okada, back from official “death,” directed the Japanese government again today as soldiers maintained peace in the governmental office district from which rebels had departed. The citizenry stayed indoors, thankful for peace and for the fact their beloved Okada lived. They and the world were told officially last week the states— Although he is still nominally head of the government, political observers were of the opinion Okada will not be in power much longer. Authoritative sources stated his premiership must be terminated and replaced by a government headed by “a man of great prestige and influence, capable of restoring the shaken national morale.” Government Reveals Secret The government itself disclosed Okada still was living as loyal troops moved into the area of government buildings which 1,000 re

ROME, March 1. (Sunday)—(.) Virtual annihilation of all Ethiopian armies on the northern front was claimed early today in semi-official messages from Asmara. The rout was said to have been completed by sundown Saturday. Earlier advices had contended that the combined armies of Ras Kassa and Ras Seyoum, a concentration of 45,000 warriors in the Tembien sector, were in the process of disintegration under the pressure of Marshal Pietro Badoglio’s fighting machine. The spectacular battle of the Tembien has been in progress since Friday morning and latest reports claimed the Ethiopians had been bottled up for several days in the regions of Abbi Abbi and Andino. Observers here believed the Ethiopian forces apparently were materially weakened by their inability to obtain supplies from the south. It was learned from an authoritative source that Gen. Melbourne, Australia, Feb. 29 | (P)-- Lincoln Ellsworth, explorer who was rescued after being lost in Antarctica, sailed for the United States today aboard the Steamship Mariposa.

1936-06-07.text: PARIS, June 6 (—Newspaper) pickets fought with republican guards, students clashed with police and Leon Blum, leftist premier for two days, walked out on a tumultuous chamber of deputies attack in strike-locked France tonight. It was an uproarious climax to a dramatic day in which Blum sought to meet the demands of nearly a million strikers with an elaborate program for social reform. Late tonight, after the tumult had died down, the deputies gave Blum a vote of confidence, 384 to 210. The vote was on a motion of confidence that the government would carry out a program of the peoples’ front “as rapidly as possible,” and particularly approving its efforts to settle the strikes. A few hours earlier, husky sergeants-at-arms kept rightist and leftist deputies from fighting while the premier’s foes shouted “Jew!” and “back to Moscow!” Blum strode out and the chamber was suspended, but he came

PARIS — The Socialist coalition government headed by Leon Blum, confronted with labor protest strikes involving 1,000,000 workers and a brief outbreak of violence in Paris, was given a strong vote of confidence by the chamber of deputies last night. The government won overwhelmingly by 388 votes to 210. The vote was on Blum's popular front “new deal” program, involving speedy social and economic reforms. Blum assured the chamber that a full socialist revolution is a matter for the future, and that the new regime would content itself with carrying out the popular front program. The latter includes the labor reforms demanded by the strikers, such as the 40-hour week, collective bargaining contracts, reform of the Bank of France and nationalization of arms industries. OKLAHOMA CITY, June 6 (7). Nine persons were killed, dozens of homes and business buildings wrecked and widespread suffering caused by a 48-hour series of Oklahoma and Kansas tornadoes, rainstorms and floods that apparently were ending tonight. Freak twisters whipped into isolated Oklahoma communities, taking five lives. Two Kansas and one Oklahoma farmer were killed by lightning. OGDEN, Utah, June 6. (P— A vigorous declaration that the states should be given authority --by constitutional amendment if necessary—to regulate both the hours and wages of women workers was voiced by former President Herbert Hoover as he paused here between trains tonight en route to the Republican national convention at Cleveland. “Something should be done to give back to the states the powers they thought they already had,

By The Associated Press Washington, June 6—With the bitter scrap over the key tax bill transferred to a Senate-House conference, Congress set out today to sweep legislative odds and ends from the path of adjournment. Leaders viewed as extremely unlikely passage of any additional major legislation. They planned to wind up the session shortly after mid-June. Both chambers will recess Monday for a week. One of the first Senate actions today was appointment of two Republicans to the tax bill conference committee. Hastings of Delaware and Metcalf of Rhode Island accepted appointment. Little chance for enactment of the ship subsidy, Wagner housing and substitute coal regulation bills was seen by most congressional chieftains.

Nashville, Tenn., June 6.—(#)— Joseph W. Byrns took his place among Tennessee's great today while President Roosevelt joined sorrowing Tennesseans in solemn tribute at funeral services for the late speaker of the national house of representatives. From all walks of life 40,000 persons came to pay their last respects to the man who served his state with distinction during 40 years of public life. Byrns, a representative in congress for 27 years, died suddenly Thursday night. Over his flag-swathed casket such eulogies as have rarely been accorded a Tennesseean were spoken, while President Roosevelt, Secretary of State Hull and Mrs. Hull, Postmaster General Farley and a number of other dignitaries listened in silence. With the president's party was a congressional delegation of 60 representatives and 14 senators. They heard the Rev. James Shera Montgomery, house chaplain, quote from the gos

HONGKONG, June 6.—-(/)—South China’s patriots, apparently feeling they had dared Japan far enough, tonight disclaimed desires to wage a lone war upon Nippon. Amid indications of concern for both Japanese and world-wide reaction, the Canton leaders issued statements denying they wanted to fight Japan independently or that they intended to force a crisis with the central (Nanking) government. They explained their decision to send Kwangtung and Kwangsi provincial armies northward as an anti-Japanese expedition amounted merely to a patriotic offer of southern services against Japanese aggression and a request for permission to reinforce Nanking’s troops in the north. (The southern troops, estimated as high as 100,000 have been reported occupying towns in Hunan province and heading northward.) Doubt Stories.
