LONDON, Dec, 5.—U1—Britain’s “John Bull” and “Joan Bull” speak their minds tonight over the conflict between King Edward VIII and the cabinet over Mrs. Wallis Warfield Simpson. The man-in-the-street (and woman) rallied on the one hand to King Edward's side, on the other to Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin, while a number suggested compromises. Typical comments of those favoring King Edward were: Richmond Hill housewife: Hands off King Edward, We should be thrilled by his courage. A man in Surrey: We can do without Mr. Baldwin; we won't do without our king. Likes Wally’s Looks A shopgirl: I like the looks of Mrs. Simpson. He (the king) should go the way his heart tells him. Among the comments of those rallying to the support of Prime Minister Baldwin were: A dining room steward: The king has let us down. A filing clerk: Well done, Mr. Baldwin. You have the support of those believing hearts

MADRID, Dec, 3.—(AP)—A fascist aerial bomb wrecked an occupied house near the American embassy today in a raid apparently aimed at razing an entire section of Madrid not half a mile from the United States official building. At least a score of Madrilenos were killed in the second raid in as many days.

Cannes, France, Dec. 5.—(A)—Wallis Warfield Simpson tonight ended her two-day flight across southern France and was driven at great speed through the gates of the villa belonging to her intimate friends, Mr. and Mrs. Herman Rogers, of New York. The car bearing Mrs. Simpson, her secretary and a bodyguard, roared through the opened gates of the villa at 11:45 p.m., while a crowd of the curious scattered for safety. Under Guard After the car entered, the gates were slammed shut while British and French detectives joined a guard of local police. They warned hundreds of craning bystanders gathered outside the villa that they “might as well go home because she’s tired and wants to sleep.” Old and tried friends tonight had a yacht and a secluded villa ready for Wallis in her flight from the storm raging over her influence on Britain's throne. Steam was got up in the 70-ton yacht Sister Anne, ri

PARIS, Dec. 5—(UP)—The “Popular Front” government of Socialist Premier Leon Blum tonight successfully weathered the gravest political crisis in its history. The premier and his supporters emerged victorious in a test vote of confidence on Spanish neutrality on which the premier had pinned the fate of his regime. Despite Communist abstention, the vote was 350 to 171 in favor of the premier, who announced he was determined to over-ride Communist and other opposition to his neutrality stand.

1936-01-06.text: (Copyright, 1946, Associated Press) LONDON, Jan. 5—Great Britain moved suddenly tonight to strengthen her military position in Africa while the Ethiopian government, harassed by the most vigorous Fascist aerial offensive of the 8-month-old war, announced the town of Daggah Bur and an Egyptian Red Cross unit have been wiped out by Italian bombs. Britain has converted the Cunard White Star liner Scythia into an army transport, it was disclosed. The 17,961-ton craft has been taken off her Atlantic run and will sail January 8 with troops and guns, probably for Alexandria. Prepare Other Ships It was reported two other Cunarders, the Laconia (19,695 tons) and the Samaria (19,597 tons) would be requisitioned next. In some French quarters, observers discussed the possibility a new Italo-Ethiopian peace plan might be devised in a week or so. There was no related development at Geneva, but Parisia

Italian war planes, engaged in an intense bombing campaign over many sectors of Ethiopia, claimed a second Swedish life today. The British legation in Addis Ababa reported to London and Stockholm that a second Swedish Red Cross worker had died as the result of last Monday's bombardment of a Swedish Red Cross unit in the south. Belated reports of hard fighting in the southern sector as Great Britain began reinforcing its African military positions. Air bombing, in which several hospitals and Red Cross units have been struck or destroyed, is being resorted to on both the northern and southern fronts of the Italo-Ethiopian war in an attempt to halt advances by the defenders, Ethiopian authorities said. In the Mediterranean, where international tension was relaxed for weeks incident to the advancement of peace proposals, Britain used commercial liners to carry troops to British posts near th

LORDGONR——VT/—iI Ne Gelesgates to the international naval conference returned to their tasks today, facing a critical turn toward the security of fleet limitations or the danger of a naval building race. In an atmosphere of undeniable gloom, the representatives of five powers reconvened after their Christmas holidays with authoritative opinions prevailing that the discussions were entering their most important phase. Any agreement to replace the expiring Washington and London naval limitations treaties was expected to be determined in the next three weeks. The immediate business before the delegates of the United States, Great Britain, Japan, France and Italy was the British compromise plan under which it was understood each power would announce in advance its naval program for ensuing years, based on defense noacde.

New York—(INS)—Moving with well-drilled precision, four bandits today invaded the offices of an exclusive jewelry firm in the British Empire building in Radio City today, menaced the manager, clerks and customers with guns, scooped up diamonds and emeralds valued at $100,000 to $150,000 and escaped. “Keep quiet five minutes or we'll take care of you—and you won't like it,” they warned their victims. The warning was emphasized by poking pistols. The bandits, leaving the office of the gem firm by three entrances, lost themselves in the noon-hour crowds on Fifth Avenue a few minutes later.

BY SPURL ARNT SPEIER (Copyright, 1936, by the Associated Press.) LONDON, Jan. 6—Great Britain turned abruptly to reinforcement of its African military position, pressing several liners into Mediterranean troop transport service, it became known today, amid renewed discussion of the possibility of oil sanctions against Italy. Three liners, including the popular Scythia, it was learned already have been converted suddenly into army transports. Two more may be requisitioned soon to carry troops to British posts near scenes of European tension and the Italo-Ethiopian conflict. Captain David W. Bone, former commodore of the Anchor Line and one of the British seamen best known to Americans, has entered the transport service. He was aboard the liner Cameronia, arriving at Southampton today from a voyage with troops to Gibraltar. SAILS WEDNESDAY WITH TROOPS AND GUNS The Scythia, 17,961-ton vesse

By STEWART BROWN | (Copyright, 1935, by United Press.) ROME — Two fresh divisions of Italian troops, 27,000 men in all, have arrived in Italian Somaliland and a third division may be sent, it was understood today. This news came coincident with reports from Addis Ababa that the Italians seem preparing for a big offensive in the south. The divisions understood to have gone to Somaliland are the Assietta division of regulars, numbering 15,000 men, and the fascist black shirt militia Tevere division, numbering 12,000. It is reported without confirmation that the crack Trenton division, the entirely mechanized force which is the army’s pride, may be sent soon. The Tevere division has been stationed in Cyrenaica, on the Egyptian frontier. The Trenton division, normally stationed on the Austrian frontier, also has been in Cyrenaica for about a month. All the troops would reinforce the mixed It

Ethiopian communiques today stated the "whole town" of Daggah Bur and its Egyptian Red Cross hospital had been destroyed by Italian bombs. The communiques stated: "The number of victims is unknown." The announcements disclosed the most intensive campaign of aerial warfare by the Fascist invaders on all fronts since the war began more than three months ago. (Dispatches from Addis Ababa Saturday stated that Dr. Fried Hylander, American head of the Swedish Red Cross, had announced a message reporting the bombing of the American field hospital at Daggah Bur.) (Sunday’s communique mentioned only the Egyptian hospital and a Havas-French agency dispatch from the Ethiopian capital said the Red Cross hospital bombed was Egyptian and not American.) Il Duce’s name nowhere was mentioned, but many said Gayda never would have dared to have published such statements without governmental approval. Answering the American President's expressed preference for democracy as compared with autocracy, Gayda declared: 1. United States wealth was “attained with cards of expansion and conquest during which they exterminated all colored and native races.” 2. Roosevelt democracy “nevertheless has not known how to stamp out crimes of gangsters, and finally Lindbergh, America’s national hero, has been obliged to seek safety for his child in voluntary exile across the ocean.” 3. 1936-03-26.text: LONDON, March 26—(AP)—Anthony Eden, foreign secretary, told the House of Commons today that the British government would back up the Locarno pact. Many of the legislators he addressed, in a parliamentary debate on the European crisis, sought assurances that Great Britain contemplated no further commitments on the continent. Eden pointed out to them that Great Britain was obligated under the Locarno treaty to guarantee that there be no aggression between Germany, France, and Belgium. "I'm not prepared," he said, "to be the first British foreign secretary to go back on a British signature. "I believe it to be the judgment of this country, even if we think Germany has a strong case, that we deprecate the fact that she has chosen to present it by force and not reason. "We must distinguish between what might be national sentiment and what are our national obligations."

LONDON, March 26.—P)_The Locarno powers’ proposal to settle the Rhineland crisis allayed the immediate prospect of war moves, Anthony Eden, foreign secretary, told the House of Commons today in reaffirming Great Britain's obligations under the Locarno treaty. Declaring Germany must make a contribution toward easing the situation, the Foreign Secretary emphasized its critical nature, saying: “I believe we are beginning a period which must, at best, be one of the most critical in international negotiations.” “We must have a contribution from Germany toward easing the situation,” he declared. “So far none has been forthcoming save the Chancellor's undertaking not to increase the number of troops which originally entered the zone.” “The proposals from Germany which are to come next week will be received with an open mind and with a keen desire to make the best use of them that we can in orde

London, March 26, (U.P)—Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin has asked Joachim Von Ribbentrop, chief German delegate, to take a personal message to Adolf Hitler urging him to submit practical proposals to end the Rhineland crisis, it was understood today. Baldwin invited Ribbentrop, Hitler’s chief adviser on European affairs, to No. 10 Downing Street, his official residence, for breakfast. They talked for an hour and a half. The prime minister’s intervention came when hope for an early settlement of differences between Germany and France, which Britain alone is in position to mediate, were receding rapidly. Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden, at the cabinet’s order, was reported to have told Ribbentrop yesterday that Hitler’s broad plans for European appeasement could be discussed usefully only if he previously submitted a practical scheme for the transitional period before broad negotiations. (Copyright 1936 by United Press) LONDON, March 26.—Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden assured the House of Commons today that Britain would be strictly loyal to her solemn pledge to help maintain the security of France and Belgium. At the same time, he insisted there is no military alliance of Britain with those two countries. Eden's address opened general debate on foreign policy. He appealed to Fuehrer Adolf Hitler to make constructive proposals to the Locarno powers so that the Rhineland dispute could be adjusted amicably. Shortly after his speech, Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin was understood to have asked Joachim Von Ribbentrop, German diplomat, to take a personal message to Hitler, urging him to submit practical proposals for ending the crisis.

(By The Associated Press) More villages along the mighty Ohio River suffered today from the force of its high waters, but swollen streams throughout New England began to recede. The death toll from storms and floods in 13 states stood at 181. OHIO VALLEY—Two more Ohio villages inundated; crest passes Huntington, W. Va., and nears Portsmouth, Ohio, with Cincinnati set for peak tomorrow; more families flee; flood below 1933 level. NEW ENGLAND—All rivers but Saco in Maine fall; militia enforces stringent safety measures in crippled Hartford; Connecticut and Maine seek funds in Washington; several Massachusetts cities still partly inundated. PENNSYLVANIA — Red Cross cares for 110,000 in western part of state; Pittsburgh water shortage over; communities bury flood dead; little danger of epidemics seen. PARIS, March 26 (#)—France feared that Great Britain would “torpedo” the mutual assistance agreement of the Locarno powers in the Rhineland crisis today by refusing to abolish sanctions against Italy. Premier Mussolini, French officials said, refused firmly to accept the accord by which Britain and Italy would assure military aid to France and Belgium, unless the League of Nations lifted the Ethiopian war penalties. British Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden told French Minister of State Joseph Paul-Boncour equally firmly at London yesterday, the officials said, that Britain was unwilling to “pardon” Italy for its East African campaign of conquest. The officials said Eden declared further that Britain would not consider the virtual military alliance of the Locarno powers, proposed after Germany occupied the Rhineland and binding until Italy gave formal ratification. PARIS, March 26 — French officials said tonight Italy has flatly refused to accept the Locarno proposal to negotiate a new European peace. Simultaneously, these official sources declared, British Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden has indicated Great Britain will not consider a virtual military alliance between the four remaining Locarno nations as binding until the fascist acceptance is delivered in London. The Locarno agreement, approved by representatives of Great Britain, France, Italy and Belgium, would draw the four powers together for mutual assistance in the event of an “unprovoked” attack. It was formulated after Germany rearmed the Rhineland and was rejected yesterday by Reichsführer Hitler because it included a “buffer zone” along the Rhine to be policed by an international force.

Bedford, March 26. () — Floyd Horton's attorneys gained from Ruth Slagle, young school teacher, who lived with his paramour, an admission today that she was not certain that the powder which Mrs. Johnston put in capsules she prepared for Horton's wife, was cold medicine. Horton, 38-year-old farmer, is on trial here for the poison capsule murder on Feb. 15 of his wife, Etta, 37. Mrs. Johnston, widow neighbor, confessed that she purchased the poison which the state contends killed Mrs. Horton, but claims that Horton gave it to his wife. Both admit illicit relations. Dramatize Preparation. The buxom woman is awaiting sentence, pending the outcome of the trial, the evidence taken now being evidence against her. Defense Attorney Homer F. Stephens dramatized for the jury, the preparation of the capsules with Miss Slagle playing her own part and Stephens playing the role of Mrs. Johnston. The s

1936-07-23.text: LONDON, July 23 (4%.—King Edward was called a “despicable individual” and Home Secretary Sir John Simon was referred to as a “liar” by laborite speakers in a tumultuous session of the House of Commons today. Three laborites who participated in the name-calling were ousted from the chamber and a recess of 15 minutes was called to get the members’ tempers under control.

Casablanca, French Morocco, July 23.—(?)—The British destroyer Whitehall routed a rebel Spanish plane with gunfire today after the aviator had bombarded a British steamer bringing fuel oil to loyal Spanish cruisers in Tangier harbor. The steamer was identified in first reports as the Gibel Dris of the Bland line, but was believed to be that line’s steamer Gibel Dern: It had arrived from Gibraltar and anchored in the harbor, where it was bombarded at noon. Ship Fires Warning. Gibraltar, July 23.—(#)—British destroyer sent out a “warning” volley off Tarifa, Spain, in answer to air bombs which splashed close to the warship’s bows, Simultaneously, British naval authorities warned the rebel chieftains they must cease their “deliberate and irresponsible bombing of the shipping straits” near the rock, Britain and France joined, too, in telling the liberalist Spanish government to keep its fleet

Gibraltar —(7)— British naval guns boomed off this famous rock Thursday in grim warning to reckless Spanish fascist air rebels. H. M. S. Wild Swan, a British destroyer, sent out a “warning” volley off Tarifa, Spain, in answer to sir bombs which splashed close to the warship’s bows. Simultaneously, British naval authorities warned the rebel chieftains they must cease their “deliberate and irresponsible bombing of the shipping straits” near the rock. Britain and France joined, too, in telling the liberalist Spanish government to keep its fleet out of the international harbor at Tangier, on the Moroccan passage. The aviators, presumably rebels, were stated to have dropped a number of bombs which exploded close to the Wild Swan’s bows. After delivering an answering fire, the British warship returned to Gibraltar. Casablanca, French Morocco—(?)—The British destroyer Whitehall routed a rebel S

WORTHING, England, July 23 — Haile Selassie, toying with the idea of going to the United States to enlist popular sympathy for Ethiopia, celebrated his forty-fifth birthday today. Disillusioned and sad, he spent a quiet day in contrast to the last formal observance of his anniversary at Addis Ababa with a great raw meat feast for his chiefs and warriors. Future plans, this intimates said, were solely concerned with the furtherance of efforts to regain his African empire.

BERLIN, (AP).—Germany pointed out to Col. Charles A. Lindbergh today its accomplishments in military and civil aviation. The famous aviator, who arrived from England yesterday with Mrs. Lindbergh, was acclaimed by high Nazi officials, the press and the Berlin populace. The air ministry honored him at a luncheon which brought together the finest of the nation’s flyers. Colonel Lindbergh shared the spotlight with the Olympics as the Führer Adolf Hitler is seeking to impress upon German youth. The simple attire of both Colonel Lindbergh and his wife, sharply contrasting with the brilliant uniforms of their hosts, was noted by the newspapers. One reporter, admiring their unpretentious appearance, said “they might have just stepped off a streetcar.”

TAMPA, Fla., July 23 ()—A coast guard vessel hurried to investigate reported distress flares in the Gulf of Mexico today while other cutters and planes far to the south continued their hunt for the British motorship Nunoca, missing with 22 aboard. There was no means of communicating with the picket boat this morning after it was sent to the vicinity of Panama City, Fla, where M. E. McCorquadale said he saw rockets last night. Capt. W. J. Wheeler, coast guard commander at Mobile, said that he doubted the flares could have been sent up from the Nunoca. To have reached the vicinity, the Nunoca, bound from Grand Cayman Island to Tampa with 22 persons aboard, would have had to drift nearly 175 miles beyond its call.

LONDON, (PP) — The British destroyer Wild Swan yesterday fired warning shots to drive off Spanish rebel airplanes which dropped four bombs near the British steamer Chitral in Gibraltar Straits, it was disclosed today. The British destroyer Shamrock, it was revealed, was bombed from a high altitude by a rebel plane last night as it lay in the straits. Four bombs fell close and splinters struck the ship's deck. The foreign office said the British embassy in Madrid had been instructed to act in concert with the French embassy to draw attention of the Spanish government to the difficulties which might arise if the international port of Tangier is used as a base of operations by the Spanish fleet. There has been no word from the Ambassador for two days. It was believed he might be trying to reach Madrid from San Sebastian. The Shamrock was patrolling the straits when it was bombed. Two bombs

BERLIN, July 22—(AP)—The Charles A. Lindberghs, in informal mood, sped over Europe today to a heel-clicking Nazi welcome at Staaken airport and prospects of an early meeting with Reichsführer Adolf Hitler. Neither Der Führer nor his air minister, General Hermann Wilhelm Göring, was at the airport when the famous flier and his wife stepped from the monoplane. Both were otherwise occupied in southern Germany, but it was learned from authoritative sources they would see Col. Lindbergh before he leaves Germany.

1936-05-21.text: - London, May 21.—The House of Commons broke into cheers today as Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin warned Italy that any interference in the affairs of Egypt would be regarded as an “unfriendly act” and he hinted that British defenses in the Suez Canal area would be strengthened. Other attacks on Italy by members of the House followed Baldwin’s sensational declaration, while Anglo-Italian tension was further increased with fears that Italian military authorities in Ethiopia have executed L. J. Bonner, nursing orderly with the British ambulance unit, who has been missing since Monday.

DUBLIN, May 21. — President Eamon de Valera’s government today launched its biggest offensive against opposition factions with the arrest of Maurice Twomey, commander of the Irish Republican Army, and his chief of staff, Ira Conlehane, prominent lawyer. Twomey and Conlehane were arrested by officers of the political branch of the civic guards while they were leaving a church, where they attended mass, at Drumcondra, a suburb of Dublin. Both were hustled off to Bridewell Prison where it was explained they had been arrested under the public safety act. The government long has been active against the Irish Republican Army because of its opposition to De Valera's policies but the arrest of Twomey and Conlehane represented its biggest move to date.

Jerusalem, May 21. (UP) — Two Jews and three British soldiers were wounded this afternoon during a battle 13 miles from Jerusalem after an Arab gang had ambushed a Jewish bus and three cars in which a number of prominent Jews were riding. The soldiers and one of the Jews, Isaiah Fishman, were wounded seriously.

London, May 20. (4) — Great Britain will leave three class A cruisers from being scrapped under limitations of the London naval treaty, it was disclosed today as the government began negotiations with Soviet Russia for a sea treaty. The Anglo-Russian conversations are aimed at securing Russian adherence to provisions of the recent London treaty, signed by Britain, the United States and France. While these talks opened at the foreign office, Lord Stanley, financial secretary of the admiralty, told the house of commons the government would rebuild and reduce armaments on three class A cruisers to prevent them from being scrapped under the 1930 London treaty. Britain has already asked the United States and Japan to lift limitations in the treaty on destroyers so she may save some 30 destroyers from being junked. The 7.5-inch guns on three cruisers of the Hawkins class will be replaced by sm

Westport, Conn, May 21—Funeral services were being arranged today for John Chapman Holder, 43, author and retired editor of nationally known magazines, who died yesterday after a long illness. He was a native of London and came to this country in 1905. Abandoning an architectural career, he applied himself to writing and in 1913 was named literary editor of the Delineator. Later he became editor of Vanity Fair, Harper's Bazaar, Motor Life and the Elk’s magazines. His widow and a son survive.

Southport, England, May 21 (AP)—Nineteen-year-old Pamela (Pam) Barton, of London, today won the British women’s golf championship, defeating the qualifying medalist, Bridget Newell, seven and five, in the 36 hole final. Miss Barton, who was a member of the 1934 and 1935 British Curtis Cup teams, reached the finals of the 1934 and 1935 championships, first bowing to Mrs. A. Holm, six and five, and then to Wanda Morgan three and one. The husky young star ended her match against Miss Newell on the 31st green after Miss Newell, a barrister, experienced trouble on the third nine with her approach shots and putts and trailed her younger rival six up at the three-quarter mark.

itv The Associated Press Paris, May 21—France refused today to withdraw her troops from Diredawa, key point on the Italian occupied Franco-Ethiopian railroad. Official sources said the 150 troops would continue to guard the Diredawa shops on the French owned railroad despite a request from Italy that they withdraw. Such a withdrawal, these sources believe, would be tantamount to recognition of the Italian regime in Ethiopia. In asking that the troops be moved, Italy insisted her army of occupation was capable of maintaining order.

WASHINGTON, May 21 (UP).-— The U.S. Treasury will float a bond issue of $1,000,000,000 or more on June 1, Secretary of the Treasury Henry Morgenthau Jr. revealed today. Formal announcement of the issue will be made on June 1, and the bonds will be dated June 15. Morgenthau declined to reveal the exact amount of the new financing, but it is known that $686,616,416 of 1% treasury notes mature on that date and the amount of new money required to meet payments of soldiers' bonus bonds soon after June 15 is expected to bring the new bond issue well above $1,000,000,000. An additional $364,138,000 of short-term treasury notes mature Aug. 15. Morgenthau said there has been no change in the treasury’s plans to float $100,000,000 of treasury bills each week.

1936-02-17.text: By United Press LONDON, Feb. 17.—Great Britain curtly put an end today to correspondence resulting from an Italian protest against its defensive arrangement with Mediterranean powers which would become operative in event that Italy attacked Britain. In a note delivered to the Italians February 14, it was revealed, the government said: “The British government does not feel that any useful purpose could be served by prolonging the correspondence.” The correspondence began when Dino Grandi, Italian ambassador, in a communication to Anthony Eden, foreign secretary, on January 24 protested against the new mutual assistance arrangement. It was understood France, Greece, Yugoslavia, Turkey, Roumania, Spain and Czechoslovakia, whom Britain consulted before replying to Italy, would deliver similar notes to Rome. The foreign office sent a copy of its note to Geneva with the request it be circulate

LONDON. (4). — Great Britain’s fighting forces asked the House of Commons today for an additional appropriation for this year of £7,811,000 (about $39,055,000), most of which would be expended upon special measures taken in connection with the Italo-Ethiopian dispute. Four supplementary estimates were issued, asking £4,850,000 (about $24,250,000) for the navy, £1,350,000 (about $6,750,000) for the army, £1,611,000 (about $8,055,000) for the air service and £100 (about $500) for the Royal Ordnance factories. To Bolster Mediterranean The sums requested, which must be approved by the House of Commons, would be in addition to the appropriations for the fighting services provided by last Spring's budget. The navy estimate was explained as “due to the 3,500 additional personnel required” in addition to “special measures” in the Italo-Ethiopian conflict. The issuance of the supplementary estima

LONDON, Feb 16.—(U.P.)—A case of sabotage aboard the British cruiser Cumberland at Chatham was announced tonight by the admiralty. The matter is under investigation, but further announcement 'would not be in the public interest,' the admiralty stated. It was understood electrical equipment of the warship was damaged. This is the third warship sabotage incident in the last three months.

Weymouth, England, Feb. 17.—CUP—Three hundred and thirty-eight passengers were removed early today from the 20,000-ton Union Castle liner Winchester Castle, which went aground in fog off Portland last night.

COPENHAGEN, DENMARK, (P).—The newspaper Aftenbladet quoted Count Haugwitz Reventlow today as saying in an interview with its London correspondent that he and his wife, the former Barbara Hutton, Woolworth heiress, had decided not to return to the United States. The reason for the decision was given that they feared the baby, shortly to be born to them, might be kidnapped. “We have decided,” the count was quoted as saying, “to stay in England where there is still safety for the life of child and property. “We intend to buy an estate in Surrey near the Lindbergh family.

LONDON, Feb. 17. (U.)—The Cabinet met today to shape its 300,000,000 pound ($1,500,000,000) rearmament program which it believes vital to the country’s defense. The meeting was the climax to a dozen meetings of the cabinet's sub-committee on defense within a month. As the ministers gathered at No. 10 Downing Street, supplementary estimates were published totaling 7,811,000 pounds ($39,055,000) for defense. It was reported that the cabinet discussed the following topics: 1—Allocation of the $1,500,000,000 fund among the defense services over a three year period. 2—The method of financing the projects, presumably by treasury bills and possibly in part later by a public loan. 3—A scheme for coordination of the defense services, which was expected to entail appointment of Eustace Percy, minister without portfolio and one of the “young planners” group, as head of a committee of the combined n

ARMISTICE SOUGHT BY ABYSSINIA, REPORT London, Feb. 17.—(INS)—The Abyssinian government is seeking an armistice as a result of the defeat of its northern army, according to Rome reports, telephoned by International News Service.

HAGLEY, England, Feb. 17. — Mrs. J. L. Garnsley, sister of the late Violet Sharpe, maid at the home of Mrs. Dwight W. Morrow when the Lindbergh baby was kidnapped, has received a letter from New York alleging Miss Sharpe was killed because she knew too much, it was learned today. The letter was postmarked at the Madison Square post office in New York City. It was signed "Madge Bush." Miss Sharpe did not commit suicide during the kidnapping investigation, the letter said, but was shot and killed because she knew, or suspected, the kidnapper, Mrs. Garnsley said she did not intend to check the letter because she has heard too much of the case.

1936-07-19.text: TAMPA, Fla., July 18—(#)—Coast Guard craft searched in vain by air and sea today for a trace of the British motorship Nunoca, 10 days overdue here with 21 persons aboard from British West Indies. Reports from Havana said the Cuban government was without word of the 110-foot combination passenger and freight boat which left Georgetown, Grand Cayman island, July 4, with nine Americans, four Britons and a crew of eight. Two Coast Guard planes from St. Petersburg covered the Florida west coastal waters from Tampa to Cape Sable. The patrol boat Nemesis cruised the southeastern Gulf of Mexico and the Florida straits. Marine reports from Cape San Antonio, on the western tip of Cuba, said the motorship had not been sighted there. Cape San Antonio is on the normal route of the vessel. Working on the theory the Nunoca ran into trouble before it reached the gulf, owners of the Nunoca asked official

By The Associated Press Venice, Italy, Oct. 18.—At least 25 persons died today in a roaring earthquake which shook northeastern Italy and touched the northwestern section of Yugoslavia and a small section of Austria. Property damage in the Italian area was extensive and all the dead reported were from that sector. Panic Venice itself felt the temblor but damage there was slight. Dispatches from Trieste said the Croatian capital of Zagreb and the important city of Lubiano were thrown into panic by the quake which caused moderate damage there. Fifteen died in the Italian province of Caneva de Sacile, among the mountains in the province of Friuli. The earthquake, preceded by a long roar, killed one and injured six at Corneliano. Several hundred houses, churches and even castles were knocked down by the temblor. There was panic throughout the province of Carnia Treviso. Flee Tens of thousand

| Madrid, early 1936.— (Sunday)— (P)—The Spanish cabinet of Premier Santiago Casares Quiroga, harassed by a military revolt in Spanish Morocco and the Canary Islands and outbreaks in Spain itself, resigned early today. Diego Martinez Barrio, chief of the republican union and for a brief time president of Spain, immediately organized a new cabinet, containing five members of the previous group. The resignation of the Casares Quiroga government came only a few hours after it had sent air and naval forces against the rebellious soldiers in the two Spanish possessions and had claimed complete control of the internal uprising, which it is said centered at Seville. Set Up on May 18 - The leftist Casares Quiroga cabinet—installed May 13 when former Premier Manuel Azana was raised to the presidency of the republic—had won the support of a solid labor front against the revolt, Socialist, communis

July 14 President Franklin D Roosevelt and his three sons brought the sturdy little schooner Sewanna in to the sheltered waters of Shelburne Harbor late today after a 45-mile trip, partly through fog, around the southern tip of Nova Scotia from Cape Sable. Twice the president's vacation craft pierced fog banks; once as it sailed east into the Atlantic and the second time about ten miles up the east coast of the Canadian province. Fox horns droned out their monotone warnings from Cape Sable light, but the Sewanna, with the escorting destroyer Hopkins and

FREE CITY OF DANZIG, July 18 —(AP)— Nazi power sought tonight to crush opposition to its control of this free city. By administrative decree, Dr. Karl Greiser, president of the Nazi-controlled senate, limited activities of independent groups seeking to halt the growing influence of German National Socialism. He ordered: ENDANGERS INTEREST 1. Dissolution of any organization whose members, with knowledge of its executive board, spreads news “endangering the state interest.” 2. Prohibition of review by the courts of police measures of a political nature, including those aimed at the right of assembly, the press and free speech. 3. Prohibition of Jewish ritual slaughtering for food purposes. 4. | MONTREUX, Switzerland, July 18. (4)—Immediate right to re-militarize the Dardanelles was granted to Turkey tonight by nine signatories to the Lausanne post-war treaty. Delegates to the international conference resulting from the Turkish request to rearm the Straits agreed to sign a convention Monday. The decision was unanimous, with only the Japanese making slight reservations because of what a spokesman described as Japan's “unfortunate departure from the League of Nations.” The countries agreeing to the convention included Great Britain, France, Russia, Japan, Turkey, Greece, Romania, and Bulgaria. The convention would grant complete liberty to merchant marine passage through the Straits in peacetime and wartime even if Turkey was at war, provided the commercial vessels do not assist the fighting powers. The Russian navy would be granted complete freedom in peacetime to leave and ent

Aboard Schooner Liberty off the Maine Coast, July 14. — President Roosevelt cast aside his business clothes today for a battered fishing outfit and pushed off from Pulpit Harbor in the schooner Sewanna for a good long “loaf.” The president, who will navigate the 56-foot auxiliary-motored sailing craft, reached Pulpit Harbor on North Haven island on the government yacht Potomac from Rockland, Me., where he arrived by special train this morning from Hyde Park, N.Y. His three sons, James, Franklin, Jr. and John, greeted him on the Sewanna. They will be his sailing companions for two weeks in North Atlantic waters. He is expected to sail up the Maine coast, bearing northeast, and around New Brunswick and Nova Scotia before winding up at Campobello Island, N.B., at the Roosevelt summer home, July 22.

CLEVELAND, Oct. 18.—(#)—Eighteen crew members and a woman passenger of the Canadian ship, Sand Merchant, drowned last night when the 252-foot sand-sucker rolled over in a 50-mile gale which swept across treacherous Lake Erie 14 miles northwest of Cleveland. Many of the sailors desperately clung to two capsized lifeboats for hours before sliding off to their death. Seven men were rescued about 8 a. m., today by two freighters en route to Lake Erie ports. Those saved were: Jack Meuse, deck engineer, Yarmouth, Nova Scotia. William Gifford, crane operator, New Castle, New Brunswick. Fred Morse, crane operator, address unknown. Martin White, second engineer, Cape Breton, N. S. Capt. Graham Maclelland, Cape Tormentine, N. B. Herman Dault, dragline operator, Victoria Harbor, Ont. John L. Ideson, deck hand, Fort William, Ont. 1936-05-31.text: | HOLLYWOOD, May 30 (GP)—Members of the Bartholomew family met today in a private conference aimed at settlement of the guardianship of 12-year-old Freddie, $1,000-a-week film actor. Conferees were Freddie's father, Cecil Lewellyn Bartholomew, who arrived Friday from England; his mother, Mrs. Lilian May Bartholomew, who has been here six weeks seeking to wrest custody of the boy from his aunt, Miss Millicent Mary Bartholomew; the aunt, and Freddie's grandparents, Mr. and Mrs. Frederick Robert Bartholomew.

Washington, May 30. (4)—Clashing opinions sounded today over the Senate finance committee’s revised bill to boost income surtaxes and levy heavily on corporations with battle lines forming on three fronts. Senate Republicans were called to confer before the opening of floor debate next week to determine their attitude toward the bill. Senators who forced committee approval of the compromise bill which ignored President Roosevelt's call for higher taxes on undistributed corporation income predicted it would be passed by the Senate. On a third front, administration forces served notice that they would fight on the floor to shove the bill back into line with White House wishes. Senator Black (D-Ala.) spent the morning writing a minority report and he would attempt to insert more drastic taxes on undistributed corporation profits when the bill comes before the Senate for consideration. Salt Lake City, May 30.—(#)— The plane in which Howard Stark, Department of Commerce aviator, disappeared last January, was found in Lost Creek canyon, 12 miles northeast of Morgan, Utah, late today. Fred Weyland of Salt Lake City, hiking through the mountains, found the ship in rugged terrain. No trace of Stark's body was found. Preliminary examination of the craft revealed a broken wheel and Department of Commerce officials said they believed Stark escaped serious injury in a forced landing only to die in a mid-winter blizzard.

(By The Associated Press) WASHINGTON, May 30, — Another week of teeming politics has illustrated the explosive possibilities of the Republican convention but left the prospects for the presidential ticket and platform still beclouded. On the surface, the developments did not appear highly significant. But the presence of strong undercurrents was indicated. A final formal protest against the regular leadership in the party by Senator Borah of Idaho led to new queries about what he would do, if frustrated at Cleveland. He would not say. Hoover May Speak The decision by former President Hoover to attend the convention, and possibly make an address as titular leader of the party, was accepted as of great potential importance. The presence of Hoover and Borah on the scene at the same time presents the possibility of a clash over their opposing convictions. Appearance Welcomed The quickness wi

The nation’s holiday last night, with major train and plane accidents claiming at least 60 lives. Drowning added its grim quota of Memorial Day victims. Automobile accidents on highways in more than 16 states brought death to 45 persons. Airplane crashes in Illinois and Massachusetts added three dead to the list, and there were six drowned and two more missing in rivers. Motor accidents cost at least two lives in West Virginia. Lucian Wiley, 50, of Cove Gap, W. Va., salesman for a Huntington concern, was killed early in the morning. His automobile struck a pole. Miss Edna Booth was injured. James H. Acasley, 21, of Superior, died in a Princeton hospital shortly after his motorcycle struck an automobile. Another accident in Huntington caused injuries to three persons. An automobile driven by Kenneth Chenoweth of Dunbar struck Edward Lovejoy, 4, and Mrs. Helen.

GUTHRIE, Okl. (?). Two men were killed as the result of a 35 foot plunge of a passenger train’s baggage car into rain swollen Cimarron River. Four passenger cars, carrying approximately 150 persons, were jerked off the rails to the edge of the swift, deep stream. None of the passengers was injured seriously. The body of Leonard F. Guiff, Kansas City, was removed from the baggage car after rescuers battled the current and used blow torches to reach the interior. He was a railway clerk. Rescue workers later located the body of Raymond McNulty, Guthrie, Okl., another railway clerk, but were unable immediately to extricate it from the wreckage of the car compartment, submerged under 12 to 13 feet of water.

Washington, May 30.—Representative Marion A. Zioncheck (D-Wash), arrested tonight on a charge of disorderly conduct, was released by police after almost two hours in jail when his secretary posted $921 collateral. Police said the congressman elected to forfeit bail and would not appear in police court. Zioncheck slipped out through the back door of the station house when released. His attorney, L. C. C. Lamar, said, "He's going to Atlantic City," and hurried away. He added that Zioncheck, who had been brought into the station barefooted and coatless, wore clothes brought to him by his secretary. Washington, May 30—()—Representative Marion A. Zioncheck of Washington state renewed his frequent contact with the police tonight when he capped a tumultuous 24-hour round by ending up in a local police station charged with disorderly conduct. By The Associated Press Powder smell and the roll of drums wafted across three continents yesterday as the world honored its soldier and sailor dead. Flowers were dropped between rows of crosses and rifles cracked over graveyard stones in memory of war’s victims. Peoples from the Rhine to China to Arlington joined in a common tribute. The blue and the grey of '64 were faded and almost gone, but the Memorial Day custom they inspired had spread through the nation and around the globe. President Roosevelt, silent before the tomb of the Unknown Soldier, led the United States in homage to its war dead. At Arlington cemetery in Washington, he heard the World War commander of America’s warriors, Gen. John J. Pershing, plead for preservation of the national ideal of liberty. In France Across the Atlantic in France, 31,000 United States veterans’ graves were wreathed. In England, Belgium, and Den

1936-09-20.text: Copyright, 1936, by The Associated Press Toledo, Spain, Sept. 19.—(AP)—With shot, shell, and crude smoke bombs, government militiamen tonight fought to route surviving fascists from the dungeons of their dynamited citadel, the Alcazar. Fighting their way inch by inch behind a rolling smoke barrage, the government militiamen rushed one after another of the fascist “pill-boxes” hastily fashioned from piles of the jagged debris. How many were still alive within the blood-spattered fortress no one on the outside knew, although militiamen said they thought at least 1,200 of the besieged men, women and children had been blown to bits when two T.N.T. mines were touched off Friday. Hang On Those still alive kept up a bitter resistance, their hail of bullets cutting through the stifling pall of smoke laid down by tins of ignited gasoline hurled at them by the government attackers. From a distance

By The Associated Press The fascist junta asserted last night that its armies had encircled Madrid and were ready for a “final attack” on the Spanish capital. The fascist forces in the northeastern coastal sector under Gen. Emilio Mola drove at Bilbao and Santander, the only remaining government strongholds in that sector. Weta reported converging on the capital. The northern wing of the army, the Junta announced, had penetrated the Lozoya valley, south of the Guadarrama mountains rimming Madrid. The position of these forces, it was announced, laid the government troops open to an attack from the rear. The southern fascist army was reported split into two columns—one advancing toward Madrid through San Martin Valdeiglesias, 26 miles west of Madrid; and the other marching along the main highway to Toledo to restore their comrades in the Alcazar.

| BERLIN, Sept. 19—(2—The Berlin Tageblatt asserts Dictator Joseph Stalin of Russia is critically ill and will be succeeded by Klementi E. Voroshiloff, commissar of war and marine. The story, under a Berlin date and giving no indication of its source, says Stalin is suffering from hardening of the cardiac artery. Stalin's assertedly serious illness, the paper states, has resulted in a struggle for his succession going on in inner Kremlin circles. “Although the present War Commissar Voroshiloff often found himself in opposition to Stalin, especially over the influence of Stalin's present policy on the army, it can be assumed Voroshiloff will step into Stalin’s place.” The predicted succession, the paper says, will result in radical changes of the present government.

GENEVA, Sept. 19.—(P)—Little nations and big powers were aligned against each other Saturday night over the delicate question of whether the Ethiopian delegation to the League of Nations should be barred to placate Italy's premier, Mussolini. At the League council meeting Saturday, preparatory to convocation of the annual assembly Monday, it was tentatively decided that the lesser of two evils would be to ban Ethiopia, authoritative informants said. Thus, diplomats of the larger powers said, powerful Italian cooperation in peace efforts could be obtained, while if the League flaunted an Ethiopian delegation before Italy, it was felt that the breach with Mussolini might be widened. Against this view, the representatives of the smaller powers were reported alarmed lest a precedent be established which they felt might presage League domination of smaller nations to please the major powers.

Gen. Jose Asensio, commander of all government forces in central Spain, who is supervising the efforts to “mop up” the Fascists remaining in the dynamited citadel, instructed his men to prepare to spray the ruins with gasoline at 5 a. m. Then, when an attack is made, he said, “the whole place will blaze up.” His orders for the dawn attack came after shot, shell and even smoke bombs had failed to dislodge the Fascists from the besieged fortress. MADRID, (?). Fernando de los Rios, one time foreign minister and now dean of Madrid university, was named ambassador to Washington. He will succeed Luis Calderon, who resigned Sept. 5. The Spanish embassy in Washington in announcing the resignation of Calderon, who had been there since June, 1934, said “he feels unable to co-operate with certain tendencies within the new republican government.” Five other members of the staff resigned before Calderon. De Los Rios, who is 60, has been a member of the Spanish socialist party, one of the principal units in the present government, for most of his life.

TOLEDO, Sept. 19. — (U.P) — Loyalist troops poured gasoline from fire hoses tonight on a rebel sortie position in the military governor’s building under the walls of the Alcazar as they fought with flame, dynamite and every destructive instrument of warfare to dislodge more than 1,200 rebel men, women and children besieged in the ancient fortress. The flame attack proved a boomerang when the resultant clouds of choking, thick black smoke repulsed the attackers as they tried to follow up their gasoline barrage. The rebels retreated to the Alcazar. Although their stronghold had been dynamited and blasted into ruins, the rebels proved their indomitable will to die gloriously by stealing forth from the rock-hewn cellars of the Alcazar and seizing the Governor’s building in the shadow of the Alcazar's southeast tower, the only one left standing.

BRUSSELS, Belgium, Sept. 19. (U.P.)——Police were reported today to have discovered an extensive revolutionary movement by left extremists against the enemies of the leftist popular front. Arms and plans for the uprising were said to have been discovered at Communist and Socialist headquarters, allegedly proving that the revolt had been arranged, not only against the conservative rightists but against gendarmerie barracks and public buildings. Police also were said to have uncovered in the Antwerp apartment of a foreign diplomatic agent documents outlining plans to assemble arms in Belgium for use in Spain. Authorities declined to give out any information.

1936-03-28.text: Washington, March 27.—(A?) A bipartisan attack in the Senate against what was termed repudiation of British and French war debts ended today with a Democratic request to ascertain if the administration has made any fresh efforts to collect. Senator Borah of Idaho, ranking Republican of the Foreign Relations Committee, and Senator Lewis of Illinois, a Democratic member of the same committee, took Britain and France to task for failing to make remittances on their war obligations. The two speeches were followed quickly by a question from Senator Walsh (D.; Mass.) as to whether the Foreign Relations Committee had any information that the administration had notified the debtors recently that millions were overdue which the American taxpayers had furnished to assist the Allies at the height of the World War. By the Associated Press LONDON, March 27—Week-long Anglo-German conversations over the Rhineland crisis ended today in a deadlock—with no solution sighted. Joachim von Ribbentrop, Germany's special ambassador, flew home bearing Great Britain's last word to Adolf Hitler after another conference with Anthony Eden, British foreign secretary. Eden reiterated to von Ribbentrop that progress is impossible without some concrete guarantee of Germany's good faith—for example, a promise not to build fortifications in the Rhineland pending new security negotiations. Eden disclosed yesterday the dictator has been unwilling to make such a guarantee. Hitler’s viewpoints may be disclosed Tuesday, when he has promised to make definite proposals, following Sunday’s Reichstag elections. Informed sources said von Ribbentrop pressed Eden for information as to how soon Franco-British general staff talks woul

Addis Ababa, March 28....(/AP) - The Ethiopian government reported today that two Italian planes had been brought down yesterday at Quoram, The government protested to the League of Nations against the bombing March 20 of a British Red Cross unit at Tchilga and also against the bombing of a French Lazarist mission in the Gondar region March 19.

London (P) -- Authoritative British sources expressed the hope today for constructive proposals from Adolph Hitler to start off new European peace negotiations. These sources said that discussion at a British cabinet meeting Monday, on the heels of the Germany election tomorrow, depends entirely on any communications received from the dictator.

ESSEX, Germany, March 27.—Adolf Hitler, speaking from the heart of Germany's steel producing center, reforged old phrases of defiance today and warned foreign statesmen he will not relinquish so much as one room in a German house nor permit any outsider to say what shall happen here. He stood in the historic Krupp munitions plant—where the World War 'Big Berthas' were made—to bring to a militant climax his comprehensive speaking tour preliminary to the election Sunday of a new Reichstag. A vast audience of 870,000 heard Der Fuehrer. His platform was the chassis of a locomotive. Towering all around him, the vast equipment of the Krupp works was a symbol of tremendous capacity to produce for peace or war. The newspaper of Dr. Paul Joseph Goebbels, minister of propaganda, in describing the scene used the headline: "War and Krupp steel." Germany's two giant Zeppelins, the Graf Zeppelin and t

MOSCOW, March 28—Russia and Japan have exchanged protests regarding two military clashes which occurred this week on the Manchukuoan frontier, it was announced today. Russia, insisting firmly that both clashes occurred within well marked Soviet territory, reserved the right to demand compensation and demanded prompt punishment of the Japanese-Manchukuoan soldiers who participated. Tamekichi Ohta, Japanese ambassador, called on Boris S. Stomoniakov, vice commissar of foreign affairs, to protest a clash which occurred Wednesday. At the same time, Constantin Yurenev, Russian ambassador, protested to Koki Hirota, Japanese premier. Stomoniakov took occasion to protest in turn to Ohta a new clash, not previously made public, which occurred at 1 a.m. yesterday and in which, he said, three Japanese-Manchukuoan cavalrymen were killed. MOSCOW, March 28. (Saturday) (/P) Soviet advices early today reported that Japanese cavalrymen had made a new incursion on Soviet far eastern territory and that three of the alleged invaders were killed in a clash with Russian border guards. M. Stomanyakoff, Soviet vice commissar for foreign affairs, immediately protested against the alleged aggression on Soviet territory to Japanese Ambassador Tamekichiota. The reports of the encounter, which occurred Friday, came just after the Japanese government had rejected a Soviet suggestion for the appointment of a mixed commission to probe the causes of disputes on the entire Soviet-Manchukuoan border. The latest reported engagement took place along the Arguni river, near the settlement of Borzingky, Soviet accounts related. Five Japanese cavalrymen were said to have penetrated Russian territory, where they encountered a Soviet border patrol. Th
NUORO, Sardinia, March 28.—Antonio Pintore, convicted of the murders of eight persons, mutilation of their bodies and four attempted slayings, was executed today by a firing squad.

1936-11-22.text: Moscow, Nov. 21--A blunt warning to Japan that Soviet Russia will not co-operate further in granting “vital” Japanese fishing concessions until the reported Japanese-German military pact is cancelled, was sent to the Japanese embassy here tonight. The 11-hour development came just as Japanese diplomats were preparing to go to the Soviet foreign office to sign the fishing agreement. The new pact, fruit of a year's patient negotiations, would have extended for eight years the Japanese right to fish in Soviet waters off eastern Siberia. The great bulk of Japan's seafood is obtained from these waters, and Japanese officials repeatedly have said the concessions were vital to Japanese interests. In notifying the Japanese embassy of Russia's refusal to renew the agreement, which expires Dec. 31, the Soviet foreign office emphasized the

Owen Sound, Ont., Nov. 21.—(Canadian Press)—The 100-foot motorship Hibou heeled suddenly and sank in Georgian Bay today, drowning the captain, the stewardess and five seamen. Ten survivors reached shore on rafts which they paddled with their hands for half a mile. None of the survivors could explain the foundering.

BERLIN, Nov. 21 (UP)—Germany acknowledged today her readiness to act with Japan, partner in a common antagonism to bolshevism, “in given situations,” but continued to disclaim knowledge of any pact between the two nations aimed against Russia. Japan and Germany, a high government spokesman said, “have much in common in their authoritarian conception of government,” but there is no “hard and fast alliance between the two.” “It is quite conceivable Germany and Japan—opposed as both are to bolshevism—may in given situations decide to proceed jointly,” he added. “It is also possible, if either should become involved in a war with Soviet Russia, the other would exercise at least a benevolent neutrality.” (The Japanese-German alliance “has been reported repeatedly by Moscow which asserted today the past was “a progressive but not final action directed in preparation for a world war.” The Mosco

BORDEAUX, France. (7 Spanish government forces on the Bilbao front, where comparative quiet has existed for weeks, smashed forward in a general offensive, said border advices. The attack along the northern front apparently was aimed at diverting the fascists’ attention from the capital and retaking territory from which insurgent soldiers have been removed for the assault on Madrid. Dispatches said the government forces received fresh supplies and attacked vigorously in the Basque country, hoping to recapture San Sebastian and eventually drive toward Irun, much of which was burned by retreating anarchists when the government quit the city early in the civil war.

Addis Ababa, Nov. 21.—(%)—Italian troops pushed to within 60 miles of Gore, which Ethiopians now claim as their capital, officials announced today. The troops captured Qlren, capital of Jimma province, and occupied Judbo, platinum center. An Italian (Stefani) News Agency dispatch from Diredawa reported a company of French Senegalese troops had been stationed there to guard the Djibouti railroad.

Budapest, Nov 21—(AP)—The absence of goulash from the family dinner table—not the nine duels he intends to fight Monday and Tuesday mornings—but rather Dr. Franz Sargas tonight. Sitting down to his evening meal after a day of brisk practice with a cavalry saber, interspersed by announcements he was ‘very confident,’ Dr. Sargas said he could not understand why a physician had forbidden Magda, his pretty blonde wife, to eat the national dish. Magda, who is expecting a baby, has been placed on a strict diet. While Dr. Sargas fretted about the missing goulash, his opponents, all young men like their challenger, rehearsed diligently at fashionable clubs where fencing is popular. The origin of the nine challenges dates from the time last February that Magda disappeared from the home of her father, Eugen Darko, a university professor. That was prior to the wedding. TAMPA, Fla., Nov. 21 —(>»— The American Federation of Labor convention's legislative committee asserted tonight that ‘millions of dollars’’ would be available this winter to a lobby seeking to kill the senate investigation of strike-breaking and labor espionage. The committee urged the convention, in its report, to demand an ample appropriation to continue the inquiry directed by Senator LaFollette (Prog.-Wis.) "All the lobbies of the great anti-union financial forces and all their secret pressures are being mobilized to prevent the senate granting an appropriation to carry on the investigation," the report said. Greatest Lobby Opposes "If our reports are as accurate as we believe them to be, the greatest and most adroit lobby that has ever operated in Washington is being organized to kill this astounding expose. "The LaFollette committee has made only a beginning, but what a beginning.

New York, Nov. 21 (4)—Merchants prepared today for an expected nationwide Christmas shopping surge, partly supported by industry's year-end outpouring of extra dividends, wage increases and bonuses. The National Retail Dry Goods Association estimated nearly 600,000 additional workers would be needed to handle the prospective increased holiday trade, the largest extra force since pre-depression years. The nation’s stores, the association said, have made “lavish plans,” laid in large stocks of merchandise and emphasized a “festive tone” more strongly than in any year since 1929. Retail men are looking to the distribution of many millions of dollars next month to shareholders and workers for stimulus to trade gains already achieved on the rise in national income, the association added. Disbursement of about $300,000,000 in extra and increased dividends is in sight for the year-end following

1936-06-21.text: London, June 18 (#) — The British government, as Laborites jeered, announced to a tense House of Commons today it would take the lead to remove sanctions from Italy in an attempt to stave off a European war. Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin, asserting collective security has failed, ended bitter debate by calling for a peace understanding between Britain, Germany and France. He made no specific proposals. Earlier, Anthony Eden, young Foreign Secretary, blushed when opposition members shouted: “Shame: Resign.” as he explained Britain's about face on the question of sanctions. Laborites, attacking the government, charged it has destroyed the League of Nations. David Lloyd George, World War premier, said Eden was going to Geneva to smash the League. He thundered: “There is nothing but anarchy as an alternative; there will be international anarchy the moment this is known.” Eden, visibly anger

DUBLIN, June 20.—(—The Free State called out soldiers in full kit tonight to reimpose a ban on the irrepressible Irish Republican Army. The defense ministry, moving to stop an intended I.R.A. assembly at Bodenstown, twenty miles south of Dublin, ordered troops thrown around the entire town. Other regiments were mobilized in reserve, nearby at Curragh, Belfast police were reinforced. With Dublin municipal elections but ten days away, some thought the militant rampart of Republicanism might check an anticipated landslide for President Eamon De Valera's Fianna Fail Party.

PARIS, June 20, (AP)—France hastened tonight to counter Great Britain's plan to change the League of Nations, parts it might reduce her to a “state of dependency” in Europe. A series of “suggestions” were rushed to foreign governments as a prelude to a scheme to strengthen the league—a scheme which the cabinet hoped would protect the French position. Leon Blum's proposal, it was stated, would retain the present league machinery which links her to her little entente and Russian allies. The government feared the British plan, reported as envisaging regional security pacts for western, central and eastern Europe, would force her into isolation. The French plan would require signatories to the proposed regional alliances to take immediate military action in the event of aggression within their own district. Nations outside the affected region would be obliged to apply economic sanctions agai

(B- Associated Press) PARIS, June 20. — A general strike of hotel and restaurant workers closed the doors of fashionable Riviera resorts at Cannes today and forced a prince to hunt for his lunch. The Riviera strike coincided with the first move by Paris rightists to eject idle workers occupying their place of employment. The rightists, numbering 200 under the leadership of Deputy Raoul Sabatier, smashed into a restaurant, threw seven strikers into the street and occupied the place themselves. Sabatier said it was the start of a “counter-revolution.” Since the labor occupation movement hit the Cote D'Azur early in the season, there were few guests, but the strike came just as Cannes heard King Edward VIII of England would arrive late in July for his summer vacation. It also provided a bad day for Prince Andrew of Greece, uncle of King George, who was living at one of the affected hotels.

SEVILLE, June 20.—Twelve persons were killed and many injured tonight, when an explosion occurred at the Reunion coal mine near Villanueva. Families of the dead and injured gathered at the pitheads hysterically waiting news.

By The Associated Press - New York, June 20—The body of the 16th victim of an apartment building collapse was dug out of the debris tonight with six feet of wreckage holding the possibility still more bodies may be found in the mass of twisted girders and crumbled stone. A dozen others were in hospitals, two seriously injured. City and county officials had launched a many-sided investigation into the cave-in of the apartment building in Mosholu Parkway in the Bronx, which still was under construction when the roof and seven floors of the building fell through Friday. Attached to the standing walls were banners which proclaimed the structure, ironically, “the house of tomorrow.” The victims were workmen.

Washington, June 20 (AP) — Declaring the Italo-Ethiopian war has "ceased to exist," President Roosevelt today lifted the embargoes and restrictions clamped on those nations as a means of safeguarding American neutrality. His proclamation, revoking the application of arms and financial embargoes and warnings against trading with the belligerents or travelling on their ships, closed the first test of planned United States neutrality since the world war. Mr. Roosevelt’s action preceded league of nations consideration of British proposals to abandon collective sanctions against Italy as an aggressor nation. Proclamation Mandatory Coupled with the specific restrictions and likewise rescinded was government pressure to prevent ‘abnormal’ shipments of materials essential for war purposes such as iron, steel, oil and copper, to both countries. WASHINGTON, June 20.—(C4P)— Foregoing his customary week-end yachting, President Roosevelt stuck close to the White House tonight to help wind up a half year's session of Congress. We signed several score bills, including the Robinson-Patman proposal which proponents said was intended to give independent merchants an equal price advantage with chain stores and other big buyers in purchases from manufacturers; shook hands with bright-badged members of the California and Arizona delegations to the Democratic national convention, and held a long conference with Frank Murphy, American high commissioner to the Philippines. 1936-10-25.text: DUBLIN, (GP) — Crippled and buffeted by heavy weather in the Irish sea, the American merchant liner American Shipper today appealed for more help after two tugs failed to take the disabled ship in tow. The office of Lloyds, Ltd. in Liverpool relayed a message from the distressed vessel saying, “Two Dublin tugs made fast at 6 a.m., but have not power to handle the vessel. We need large tugs with hawsers. Barometer falling.) The American Shipper radioed she had lost her rudder and was wallowing helplessly in high seas near Wicklow Head, off the Irish Coast. The American Shipper, 7,436-ton vessel, carried 22 passengers and a cargo which included 5,000 cases of scotch whiskey. The United States line denied the ship sent out an SOS last night. Officials said the liner wired its own company asking for assistance after it had lost its rudder.

LONDON, Oct. 24—(AP)—Socialist Spain and Fascist Portugal struck at each other today. Portugal broke off diplomatic relations with the war-torn Spanish government and in reply, the Spanish embassy in London charged Portugal with killing 40 Spanish sailors in a naval battle off the African coast. Russia at the same time renewed her demands that the Spanish non-intervention policy be enforced to halt any Fascist aid to the Spanish insurgents. Specifically, the Spanish embassy charged Portugal with sending the motorship Ciudad De Macao into African waters. The vessel, the Spanish allegations asserted, fired on and sank the Spanish motorship Fernando Po with all hands lost. The ship was sunk Oct. 14, the Spanish charged. | Ipswich, Eng., Oct. 24.—(AP)— Bewigged Justice Sir John Anthony Hawke today opened the session of courts which will hear the divorce suit of Mrs. Ernest (Wallie) Simpson, the admired friend of King Edward. All indications were, however, the suit would not come up until Tuesday, as there were a few criminal cases to be cleared up first. Preview The townspeople were treated today to a preview of what they might expect to see when Mrs. Simpson, the former Baltimore debutante, comes to court to press charges of her husband's misconduct, the only grounds for divorce under British law. The folk of Ipswich gaped today as a strange demonstration of constables escorting an imaginary person through the crowds of the curious and into the courtroom. LONDON, Oct. 24. — (U.P) — The British government, seeking to avert a serious clash between Soviet Russia and the Fascist nations of Europe over intervention in Spain, accused both Russia and Italy today of having delivered large quantities of war materials to Spain. The British charge apparently was designed to offset Russia's virtual withdrawal from the general non-intervention agreement on the ground that Germany, Italy and Portugal, Fascist nations, had aided the Rightist Spanish rebels. Russia has demanded that the French and British navies patrol Portuguese ports to prevent shipment of arms through Portugal to Spain. There have been veiled intimations that German and Italian vessels might patrol the Mediterranean coast of Spain to prevent the landing of Russian munitions from the Black Sea if ships disguised as carriers of food relief supplies. MADRID, Oct. 26. (4°)—Fascists, overwhelming fierce government resistance, captured a vital highway railroad intersection about 25 miles south of Madrid today. Forced back closer to the capital by the successful insurgent thrusts, government commanders rushed truckloads of newly recruited militia to bolster the sagging but intact Madrid line. Battering the capital's defense after a day-long battle, the insurgents took the junction between the Aranjuez highway and the Levante railroad below Sesena as the devastating civil war entered its fifteenth week. The intersection also is at a point where a bridge spans the Jarama river, which the fascists must cross to reach Madrid from the south. Fascist artillery supported by bombing planes hammered away at government positions north of the Tagus river in an effort to cut off Aranjuez to the south of the capital. MUNICH, Oct. 24 (UP)---Dictator Adolf Hitler announced tonight definite agreement toward formation of an Italo-German fascist front to stand against the rest of Europe. Chancellor Hitler gave his final approval at Berchtesgaden to a joint Italo-German statement after conferring with Count Galeazzo Ciano, Italian foreign minister and Mussolini's son-in-law. The statement was a declaration of nazi-fascist friendship and determination of the two nations to consider each other's wishes before moving any pawns on the European chessboard.

Seven out of every 10 men between the ages of 18 and 40 were in uniform. Insurgent planes dropped leaflets giving the Capital 48 hours to surrender. Most of the population was inclined to regard the statement as an idle threat. Meanwhile, the Fascist cavalry and tanks pushed to the right end of the insurgent lines at the Madrid front, 11 miles eastward to end the week with an almost unbroken semicircle closing in on the Capital from the west and southward.

1936-06-28.text: GENEVA, June 27.—UP—The decision of the League of Nations council to abandon Ethiopia to her fate was protested vigorously by the vanquished African kingdom today. Dedjazmatch Nassibu, one of Emperor Haile Selassie’s right hand military leaders, who is in Geneva with the negus, sent a letter to the league calling on the signatories of the covenant to fulfill their obligations. The letter, denouncing anew the Italian occupation of Ethiopia, said half the country is still occupied by Ethiopians, and in that half the Ethiopian government is functioning regularly and is in contact with the emperor. The league's loss of prestige because of its failure to save Ethiopia was further emphasized today when Nicaragua, following the recent example of Guatemala and Honduras, telegraphed its resignation. ESTES PARK, Colo., June 27— A week-end of “no visitors and more fishing” was the program outlined today by Gov. Alf M. Landon of Kansas in his Colorado mountain vacation retreat. The Republican presidential nominee came to Estes Park from the vacation ranch for his daily press conference today, but continued his silence on all matters political. He declined comment on the renomination of President Roosevelt and Vice President Garner and other matters relative to the Democratic National convention. Today’s program, he said, included a session of wood chopping, giving his two young children, Nancy Jo and Jack Cobb a horseback ride and just resting. He admitted his shoulder was somewhat stiff from casting for trout yesterday, but added he was “pretty well rested.” Landon said he had virtually completed his message to the special session of the Kansas Legislature, which meets July 7. HOLLYWOOD, Calif. (®) — The titian-haired Myrna Loy, who the late Rudolph Valentino converted from a sculptress to a movie vamp, became Mrs. Arthur Hornblow Jr. Saturday. The wedding ceremony was performed in the sleepy little seashore Mexican town of Ensenada, Lower California. It was her first off-stage romance, and Hornblow’s second, he recently having been divorced at Reno, Nevada, from Juliette Crosby, of the stage.

From Montana The British government earlier had made tentative plans to send British sailors to the mine, threatened by the approach of rebel troops. J. O. Ambler of Montana and San Antonio, Texas, consultant in the smelting department of the mine, was the American held.

GLASGOW, Aug. 19.—Ambrose “Sam” Ramsbacher, 30, employee at the Fort Peck dam project, and Mike Gunderman, 47, Valley county rancher, were killed instantly in an airplane crash at the airport at Wheeler, 16 miles southeast of here. Witnesses said the plane, owned and piloted by Ramsbacher, went out of control in a vertical bank and plunged to the center of the airport from an altitude of about 400 feet. The plane burst into flames as it hit the ground and bystanders worked frantically to get the men out. They finally pulled the craft apart with the use of hooks and ropes and recovered the bodies. Mrs. Gunderman, who had been a passenger in the plane a short time previously, was standing on the field and saw the crash fatal to her husband. She ran toward the wreckage and collapsed. LOUISEVILLE, Que., Aug. 15. UP—A truck carrying 40 singing and cheering men and boys returning from a political rally sped up the incline of an obscured grade crossing early today and was struck squarely in the center by a fast freight train. The truck burst into flames and bodies of many of the occupants hurtled like comets into a field and along the roadway. Tonight 25 of the truck's passengers had died. The 15 others were in a hospital here. None escaped injury. Several of the injured may die, physicians said. The victims were residents of this community. Seventeen probably were killed instantly. Crushed and burned, they were dead when rescuers reached them. Four died in ambulances. Four others died in a hospital within a few hours. WERLIN, Aug. 18th - The "Olympic kiss," which a woman spectator planted on Adolf Hitler's cheek during the swimming finals after obtaining the Fuehrer's autograph, was the talk of the boulevards tonight. The woman disappeared into the crowd shortly after the episode, which delighted the multitude in the stadium as much as it startled Germany's bachelor chancellor, but later she was reliably identified as a woman who lived in Los Angeles. Unconfirmed reports gave her name as Carola De Vries. She achieved distinction despite the vigilance of at least two score blackshirts, as Hitler’s bodyguard is known. Hitler readily gave his autograph, then was startled she leaned over the low railing and kissed him. The chancellor took the incident good-naturedly while his aides looked on dumbfounded.
